units.la: NUllus argento color est avaris Abdito terris &c. nisi temperato Splendeat usu. ut Lyricus canit. Idem perè de re longè prestantissima, quae neque argento, neque auro, neque gemmis veneat contra: excellentissimarum ingeniorum dico monumenta, pronuntiare nobis liceat, quamdiu illa situ & squalore obsita, privatis in Bibliothecis latent, aeternis, ut ita dicam, quasi tenebris: nullam eorum esse utilitatem, nisi ut blattas, tineasque, infectorum ia jactissima pascant: Eadem vero in lucem producta, cum studiosorum hominum manibus teruntur: Deum immortalem, quos non sic ex thesauros ubertim affatim que profundunt? Quae consideratio utilitatis publicae, Lector carde, me permovit, ut Nobilissimi illius Germaniae Jurisconsulti Dn. HUBERTI GIPHANII Antecessoris quondam celeberrimi, & Consiliarii S. Caes. Majest. prudentissimi, Commentariis luce publica donandis, curam manumque admorerem. Sciel am ea anxie nimis & solicite a bis expedere vera ac genuina Jurisprudentia, vere ac sincere vijud carenorunt: Studiosos vero Juris adolescentes, cum suspiriis pene & indigratione quiritari, quod amdiu illa, ingenti cum dispendio suo quasi vinculis iniectis detenta, supprimerentur. Et usus est quidam
units.tr: "No colour is there in silver hidden in the greedy earth, unless it shines with temperate use," as the lyric poet sings. The same may fairly be said of something far more excellent, which is sold neither for silver, nor for gold, nor for gems. I mean the monuments of the most outstanding minds. As long as they lie in private libraries, covered with dust and grime, they are buried, so to speak, in eternal darkness. They then serve no purpose except to feed book-lice, moths and other destructive insects. Once they are brought into the light and handled by the hands of studious men, what gods could pour forth their treasures so generously and abundantly? It was this consideration of public benefit, kind reader, that moved me to give my care and labour to the publication of the Commentaries of that most noble German jurist, Dr. Hubertus Giphanius, once a most celebrated teacher and a most prudent councillor of His Sacred Imperial Majesty. I know that others, too anxiously and too laboriously, have tried to set forth the true and genuine jurisprudence, and have not done so truly or sincerely. I know too that young students of law have complained, almost with sighs and indignation, that these works were kept back for so long, held as if in chains to their great loss. And the author himself, as a man most knowledgeable in affairs, followed a certain settled plan of his own.

units.la: { } ~ auctor ipse, ut vir rerum intelligentissimus, certo quodam consilio suo: ut qua in Iure civili elaborata haberet: non praecipiti quadam ambitione, in vulgus ed referre festinaret: sed premeret etiam ultra eum annum, quem prudentissimus Poëta, ingenii foetibus in lucem producendis, terminum posuerat. Nunquam ca sunt ingenii ipsius monumenta, ut in ipsis etiam cunabulis adolevisse, & maturitatem cum ortu suo accepisse judicarentur. Sed est is doctorum virorum mos, a vulgo admodum diversus ingenii sui foetus nunquam pro dignitate sua satis sibi elimasse videantur. Est tamen religiosa illa cura aequi boniqueconsulenda, quod operis praestantia, nascendi moram recompensat: qua in re naturam ducem ut decet sequuntur: est enim ab illa ita comparatum, ut durabile non sit, quod subito nascitur: e contrario, qua tractum temporis longiorem desiderant ut producantur, ea ad longam posteritatem vivere consueverunt. Nunc vero post quam ea sunt tempora, ut nullius quamvis doctissimi hominis lima accuratissimis auctoris nostri monumentis, ipso ex hominum consortio nobis erepto, decoris aut dignitatis quicquam addere possit: quid causa est, cur diutius ista patiamur, in privatis paucorum delitescere loculis? cur publico omnium desiderio & votis negentur? cur communibus totius Europa commodis invideantur. Certum persuasum habemus, ea qua auctor ipse adunguem, quod ajunt, perfecerat, ejusmodi esse, ut ne abivive pso vivo ad li quid ultra potuerit, nedum ut ab aliis quicquam ipsis accedere praestantia queat. Si qua vero adfecta reliquit & nondum omnibus numeris absoluta ea talia sunt, tam extra vulgarium ingeniorum acam posita: ut qui in seculari sunt, aq; sint illa relicturi imperfecta atq; ab Apelle inchoatam Venerem, nemo aggressus est absolvere. Curigitur absolutis consummatis q; praestantissimi ingenii laboribus non fruantur qui juri vel dicundo, vel docendo, vel discendo opera navant? Cur non iis utantur, qua idem mille auctor noster, ita affecta habet ut a perfectione quam proxime absint. Neq; enim viro tanta doctrina, tanto ingenio, tanta industria, atq; fuit hic noster Giphanius, quicquam excidere posset, quod non bonorum atq; doctorum approbandum sit calculo. De doctrina & eruditione illius quid attinet pauca dicere, cum paucis ut debet satis exprimi nequeat: multa dicere pro ipsius dignitate, mea mihi non permittat facultas. Norunt omnes, qua ipsius fuerit perfectio in omni humaniori disciplina qua quidem ingenuis ortos parentib. addeceat? qua fuerit praditus facultate praecipuarum illarum linguarum, qua vel ad animi cultum faciunt, vel ad humana, tum privata, tum publica dextre obeunda negotia, his temporibus maxime frequentantur. Nihil in omni Philosophia, quod intactum ille inexcusum reliquerit. In ea doctrina parte qua vitam mores q; hominum gubernat, quaq; prima elementa Juris prudentia sub-
units.tr: Being in no hurry out of a headlong ambition, he did not rush to offer to the public what he had worked out in civil law. Instead he held it back even beyond the year which the wisest of poets set as the limit for bringing forth the offspring of genius. His writings are never of such a kind that they could be judged to have grown up in their very cradle and received their maturity at birth. This is the custom of learned men, quite different from the common run: they never seem to have polished their offspring enough to match their own worth. Yet that scrupulous care must be accepted with fairness and goodwill, since the excellence of the work repays the delay in its birth. In this matter they follow nature as their guide, as they should. For nature has so ordained that what is born suddenly does not last, whereas those things which need a longer span of time to be brought to completion usually live on into long posterity. Now, however, the times are such that the file of no learned man, however accomplished, could add anything of grace or dignity to the most careful monuments of our author, since he has been snatched from the company of men. Why then should we suffer these works to lie hidden in the private chests of a few? Why should they be withheld from the public desire and prayers of all? Why should the common advantages of all Europe be grudged to us? We are firmly and assuredly persuaded that what the author himself finished to the last detail, as they say, is of such a kind that, while he lived, nothing could be added to it, still less could anyone else add anything of greater excellence. If he left some parts unfinished and not yet complete in every respect, those parts are so far beyond the reach of ordinary minds that those who are among the common herd would leave them unfinished, just as no one has undertaken to complete the Venus that Apelles began. Why then should those who labour at law, whether in judging, teaching or learning, not enjoy the finished and perfected labours of so outstanding a mind? Why should they not use what our author left in such a state that it comes very near to perfection? For no mind so learned, so gifted and so industrious as that of our Giphanius could produce anything that would not deserve the approval of good and learned judges.

units.la: AD LECTOREM.
units.tr: To the Reader.

units.la: ministr a t, quantum praestiterit, norunt illi, qui ipsum Aristotelica Ethica, & Politica explicantem audierunt, qui ab auditoribus praelectiones ipsius m a gnis sumptibus sibi comparaverunt in optimis aliis auctoribus. Quid operae quaesiliciter posuerit, loquuntur Agellius, Symmachus, Lucretius, Homerus alii, testatum secerunt, qui super ori vixerunt seculo viridi docti, Muretus, Manutius, Turnebus, Fornerius, alii. Quam in arte illa praestiterit, quae docet rem universam tribuere in partes, latentem explicare, definiendo obscuram explanare interpretando, ambigua primo videre, deinde distinguere, postremo haberet quid vera & falsa judicarentur, & quae quibus positis esset, quaeq; non essent consequentia, id viva voce in docendo tum disputando ad dientib. semper quaplurimis, secundo auditorio probavit abunde demonstrantem idem universa ipsius, quae publice ppedium videbuntur pulcherrima pulcherrimi ingenii monumenta, ad eo ut amussim videatur secutus illud consilium, quod [illegible, ~6 letters] I Cujacius filio suo unico praescripsit aliquando in praefatione Pofter. tract. ad Afric. ut cognosceret ea quae Philosophi scripserunt, non ea tantum parte, quae ad jus pertinet, verum etiam reliquis, ut iis artib. probe instructus comparatus, ut iis etiam rebus tractandis animum applicaret, quae in regnis & civitatibus quibusque versantur, codem tenere ad Juris capessenda studia se accingeret.
units.tr: How greatly he excelled, those know who heard him expounding Aristotle's Ethics and Politics, and who at great expense acquired for themselves his lectures as taken down by his hearers, alongside the best other authors. What pains he took, Agellius, Symmachus, Lucretius, Homer and others bear witness, as do the scholars who lived shortly before our own age: Muretus, Manutius, Turnebus, Fornerius and others. In that art which teaches how to divide a whole into its parts, to unfold what lies hidden, to explain the obscure by definition, to see ambiguities first and then distinguish them, and finally to judge what is true and false, and what follows or does not follow from given premises, he showed his excellence in teaching by voice, both in lectures and in disputations, before audiences that were always very large, and he demonstrated the same abundantly to a second audience in all his works, which are published and will seem the most beautiful monuments of a most beautiful genius. So closely did he seem to follow the counsel which I. Cujacius once gave to his only son in the preface to the Posterior tract. ad Afric.: that he should learn what the philosophers wrote, not only the part that pertains to law but the rest as well, so that, being thoroughly instructed and equipped in those arts, he might apply his mind also to the matters that concern kingdoms and states of every kind, and so prepare himself for the study of law with the same mind.

units.la: Et huic quidem in finem adolescens adhuc G. Ophanius noster. noster peregrinationes suscepit in Galliam, Italiam, aliasq; praecipuas orbis regiones, non modo ut uberiorem ingenii culturam caperet, atq; in eorum se insinuaret notitiam ac familiaritatem, qui per universam Europam ob excellentiam doctrinae tum celebrabantur, verum etiam eorum sibi thesaurum quendam colligeret, qua in Rerumpublicis regnorum atq; diarrhiarum diversarum administratione, observatu notatuq; digna occurrerent. Quo impetravit, ut pauci essent, qui ipsi contend reauderent, qui se ipsi praeferret vix quisquam. Is igitur cum fuerit Giphanius noster, non est dubitandum, quin cuncta ipsius opera, quae in lucem publicam proferentur omnibusq; legum & aequitatis Studiosis communicabuntur, eorundem sint studiis futura longe utilissima. Quam vero sit necessarium istud, quod nunc publico consecramus opusculum, de librorum titulorum atq; Juris Justinianei perpetuo ordine ejusq; ratione, ex eo facile apparet, quod omnes ii, qui hactenus vel Paratitla ediderunt, vel titulos Juris ordine suo explicarunt, in eo sibi laborandum esse duxerint, ut ostenderet, quo vinculo sequentes titulus quisq; praecedentib. cohaereret: quod ad memoriam juvandam in tam magni operis difficillimo itinere faciat plurimum ratio illa, qua plane facit quemadmodum singulae partes apte sibi invicem succedant, id vero in compendio & uno quasi intuitu atq; momento, stylo tam facili atq; perspicuo, rationibus tam apertis atq; convenientib. qui ita praestiterit, fortassis hactenus extitit nemo. sint sane qui ordinem tabulis amplis atq; commentariis comonstrarint: rationem tamen ejus quam ita plane in luce quasi meridiana proposuerit, nō est quisquam, sint qui in singulis tractatib minutiores partes satis appositè inter se conjugatas esse planum fecerint, sed augustissimi illius [illegible, ~4 letters] concinnam structuram in universum Studiosis spectandam qui exhibuerit, cōspectus nondum est. Quid quod singularis illud etiāmest industria nō minus q; ingenii monumentum, structura edicti perpetui observata: cujus serie & in C. The. & à Justiniano in C. suo offtorum q; opere observatā ut plurimum videmus, non minus q; à veteribus ICtis ad edictum qui scripserunt: nisi ubi justissima causa ab Edicti ordine sibi Justinianus discedendum putarit. id vero cum sit opus hactenus ab aliis ne tentatum quidem, quin juris Studiosis id sit futurum quam gratissimum: cumq; auctor noster id in caeteris ferè suis lectionib. ubi de ordine disserit, sequatur: quin idem vobis longè sit futurum utilissimum, dubitare mihi fuerit religio. id solum si obtinuero, ut intelligant omnes me maximè juvetutis studiosa atq; in spem Reip. succrescentis, commodis gratisicari velle, voti mei mihi compos factus videbor: atq; ad majora in publicam utilitatem promovendam suscipienda incitabor. Vale Lector amice atq; candide.
units.tr: And to this end, while still a young man, our G. Giphanius noster undertook journeys to France, Italy and other notable regions of the world, not only to gain a richer cultivation of mind and to insinuate himself into the acquaintance and friendship of those who were celebrated throughout Europe for the excellence of their learning, but also to gather for himself a kind of treasury of what was worthy of observation and note in the government of various commonwealths, kingdoms and principalities. By this he achieved that few could rival him and hardly anyone surpassed him. Since he is our Giphanius, there is no doubt that all his works which are brought before the public and communicated to all students of law and equity will be far most useful to their studies. How necessary is this little work which we now dedicate to the public, on the titles of the books and the perpetual order of Justinian's law and its rationale, is clear from the fact that all those who have hitherto either published Paratitla or explained the titles of the law in their order have thought it their task to show by what bond each title coheres with those that precede it. That reasoning, which shows plainly how the individual parts fit one another in succession, greatly helps the memory on the most difficult road of so great a work. But who has so excelled in presenting this in brief and, as it were, at one glance and in one moment, in a style so easy and clear, with reasons so open and fitting, perhaps no one has existed until now. There are indeed some who have displayed the order in large tables and commentaries, but there is no one who has set out its rationale so plainly, as in a noonday light; there are some who have made clear that the smaller parts within the individual treatises are fitted together aptly, but no one has yet presented for students to behold the neat structure of that most august [illegible] as a whole. And what of the fact that the structure of the perpetual edict, observed by that singular diligence no less than a monument of genius, is found to be followed, in its sequence, in the Theodosian Code and in Justinian's Code and in his work on the offices, as we mostly see, and no less by the ancient jurists who wrote on the edict? Unless in some very just case Justinian thought he should depart from the order of the edict. Since this is a work that has hitherto not been attempted by anyone, it will surely be most welcome to students of law; and since our author follows it in most of his other lectures wherever he discusses order, I would hesitate to doubt that the same will be most useful to you. If I obtain only this, that all may understand that I wish, above all, to oblige with conveniences the studious youth who are growing into the hope of the commonwealth, I shall feel I have gained my wish, and I shall be spurred to undertake greater things to advance the public good. Farewell, friendly and kindly reader.

units.la: SOCRATES apud Xenophontem libr. 3. de dictis Socratis, qui vulgo Oeconomicôn inscribitur: Ordine, inquit, ac dispositione, nihil vel pulcrius est, vel ad usum accommodatius: idque exemplis suo more in Choris scenicis, in exercitu, in triremi, in navi oneraria, in domo, in ipsa denique Rep. demonstrat. Et pulcritudo ex ordine quidem ita perspicua est, ut pluribus eam verbis non sit opus docere. Nam & apud Græcos κόσμος & τάξις idem valent: Et Plato in Timæo hanc ordinis pulcritudinem in ipso mundo elucere ostendit. Utilis est autem ordo primum ob memoriam, quia, ut Aristoteles ait, in libr. de memoria, ea quæ sunt ordine disposita, facilius memoriæ mandantur: partim quia, ut Socrates eo loco disserit, eadem facilius reperiri, & si opus sit, depromi possunt. Denique facit ordo ad intelligentiam rei, de qua agitur, eò quod rem planiorem reddat: ut ordinis perturbatio obscuriorem. Præterea ad hoc quoque prodest ordo, ut suum quisque officium commodius faciat altero non impediente: Ad brevitatem quoque mirifice utilis est ordo, ut eadem res bis, terve non reiteretur, teste Gal. lib. 6. de tuend. val.
units.tr: Socrates, in Xenophon's third book of the Memorabilia of Socrates, which is commonly entitled the Oeconomicus, says: Nothing is either more beautiful or more useful than order and arrangement. He demonstrates this in his usual way by examples drawn from choruses in the theatre, from an army, from a trireme, from a merchant ship, from a household, and finally from the commonwealth itself. Indeed the beauty of order is so evident that it needs little explanation in many words. For among the Greeks κόσμος [kosmos] and τάξις [taxis] have the same meaning, and Plato in the Timaeus shows that this beauty of order shines forth in the world itself. Order is useful first for the memory, because, as Aristotle says in his book On Memory, things arranged in order are more easily committed to memory; and partly because, as Socrates argues in that passage, the same things can be found more easily and, when need arises, brought forth. Finally, order helps us understand the matter under discussion, since it makes the subject plainer, just as disorder makes it obscurer. Moreover, order also helps each person to perform his own task more conveniently, without hindrance from another. Order is also wonderfully useful for brevity, so that the same thing need not be repeated twice or three times, as Galen testifies in book 6 of On the Preservation of Health.

units.la: Cum autem aliarum artium, tum in primis & legum periti ordinis studiosi esse debent, primum propter negotiorum civilium, & præceptorum juris infinitam fere multitudinem & varietatem, quasi & ipsa justitia, jam olim ut memoria quoque Jurisconsultorum velut proverbio celebretur, cui memoriæ, ut jam dictum, ordo & methodus plurimum inservit. Denique quia ordo suum cuique tribuit: quod juris & justitiæ est proprium. Unde & eleganter Plato τάξιν vocat τὸ ξιν sive ordinem. Recte igitur veteres Jurisconsulti, qui ordinem tam in legibus & edictis interpretandis, quam in libris scribendis diligenter adhibuerunt, ut videre est in sententiis Pauli in libris ad Edictum. Nō ignoro quod M. Cic. lib. 1. de orat. & in Bruto antiquioribus Jurisconsultis usum Juris quidē concedat, attamen ordinem in iis requirat. Nam idem Cicero artem Servio Sulpitio magna cum laude tribuit, cumq; secuti recentiores, Athenus, Labeo, Sabinus, aliiq; Jurisconsulti arte & ordine omnia tractare coeperunt. Juliani certè, qui est auctor Edict. perpet. diligentiam in eo Edicto ordine describendo, & cōponendo laudat ipse Justin. Imp. quin etiam in antiquo XII. Tabul. libello ordine quodam omnia fuisse collocata: Cicero cūimitatus in libro de legib. & Cajus ad LL. XII. Tab. ul. declarat. Quare de libris Juris Justiniani Digestis, inque Codice & Instit. à Tribon. Justiniani mandato compositis, dubitari non debet, quin & hi bono ordine sint scripti. Neq; enim assentiendum est iis, qui Pandectarum hos libros, quovis alio potius, quam Digestorum titulo dignos exi﻿stimant.
units.tr: Not only of other arts but especially of lawyers, there should be a careful regard for order. This is first because of the almost infinite number and variety of civil affairs and of the precepts of law, and because justice itself has long been celebrated, as the saying of the jurists goes, as something like memory; and, as already said, order and method contribute greatly to memory. Finally, order gives each person his due, which is the very nature of law and justice. Hence Plato elegantly calls order τάξις [taxis]. Rightly, therefore, the ancient jurists, who applied order carefully both in interpreting laws and edicts and in writing books, as may be seen in the opinions of Paul in his books on the Edict. I am not unaware that M. Cicero, in book 1 of On the Orator and in the Brutus, grants the older jurists a knowledge of law, yet requires order in them as well. For the same Cicero attributes the art to Servius Sulpicius with great praise, and the later jurists who followed, Athenaeus, Labeo, Sabinus and other jurists, began to treat everything with art and order. Indeed Justinian himself praises the diligence of Julian, the author of the Perpetual Edict, in describing and arranging that Edict in order. Moreover, Cicero in his book On the Laws and Gaius, in commenting on the Twelve Tables, declare that everything in the ancient little book of the Twelve Tables was arranged in a certain order. Therefore there ought to be no doubt that the books of Justinian's law, the Digest, the Code and the Institutes, composed by Tribonian at Justinian's command, are also written in good order. For we ought not to agree with those who think these books of the Pandects are worthy of any title rather than that of the Digest.

units.la: Neq; iis assentiendum interpp. qui eos ita perturbare, nulla adhibita via aut ratione explanant, qui tenebras potius & caliginē, quam lucem afferre videntur. Sunt enim hac ætate eruditi nō pauci, qui confusè Jus nostrum interpretantur, & tractant, omniaq; in unum acervum congerunt. Ut cum verbi gratia tit. de nupt. explicare suscipiunt, & suo ipso interdum leviter mentio fiat testamenti, aut tutelæ, statim omnia, quæ de tutelis, quæ de testamentis adferri possunt, eo congerunt. Quos eleganter Socrates non absimiles agricolis esse dicit, qui in eandem aream sive cumeram, conjiciunt hordeum, triticū, & legumina. Cui postea cum juxculo, cum pane, cū obsonio sit opus, cogatur prius singula seligere, quę ordine prius distincta, statim ad usum sumere possint. Nō absimiles quoq; patribus fam. qui panem n dolio sive cella vinaria, & vinum in pecuaria recondunt. Sed de his alias.
units.tr: Nor should we agree with those expositors who explain them in such confusion, with no method or reason applied, so that they seem to bring darkness and gloom rather than light. For in this age there are not a few learned men who interpret and treat our law in a confused way and heap everything into one pile. For example, when they undertake to explain the title On Marriages, and some mention of wills or guardianship is made in passing, at once they heap together everything that can be said about guardianships and wills. Socrates aptly compares such men to farmers who throw barley, wheat and pulses into the same threshing floor or heap. Afterwards, when they need broth, bread and relishes, they are forced first to pick out each item, which could have been kept separately in order and taken straight to use. They are also like the heads of households who store bread in a cask or storeroom and wine in the cellar. But of these things elsewhere.

units.la: Nunc illis ordinem in libris nostris desiderantibus est accurrendum atq; demonstrandum, omnia in his libris optimo ordine & divina quadā methodo esse pertractata. Cujus mei instituti & consilii h& lii hæ ferè sunt rationes. I. Ut auctoritas Juris nostri confirmetur, quæ certè ab iis minuitur, qui confusionem vocant. Deinde, ut sapientia auctorum Juris (est enim ordo, velut anima, & ut Plato in Gorgia, velut substantia rerum tractandarum) demonstrata, hos libros magis admiremur, eosque majore diligentia cognoscere studeamus. III. Ut faciliores quoque, cum ad intellectum, tum ad memoriam retinendam adjumento ordinis efficiamur. IV. Ut ex ipsis titulis eorumq; ordine breviter præmisso, & indicata summa quadam Juris, ἀτιτόπω cognita, atq; universo Jure leviter hac ratione degustato, facilior sit progressus ad accuratam singularum legum & quæstionum difficiliorum tractationem. V. Postremo, ut in hoc muneris mei exordio Jus hic explicaturus aliquid adferam, quod cum ad universi Juris dignitatem & faciliorem cognitionem pertineat, tum, ut initio id semel explicatū, à nobis de ordine postea singulatim reiterare nonsit opus, atq; idem sæpius inculcare. Solent enim Doctores nostri ad singulos titulos magnopere laborare, de continuatione, ut vocant, titulorum: Deinde, quis sit ille ordo, demonstrabimus.
units.tr: Now we must run to and show those who miss order in our books, that everything in these books has been treated in the best order and by a certain divine method. The main reasons for this plan and purpose of mine are roughly these. I. That the authority of our law may be confirmed, which is surely diminished by those who call it confused. Next, that by displaying the wisdom of the authors of the law (for order is like the soul, and, as Plato says in the Gorgias, like the substance of the things to be handled), we may admire these books more and be more eager to know them with greater diligence. III. That we may become easier, both in understanding and in retaining the matter in memory, with the help of order. IV. That from the titles themselves and their order, briefly set out and with a certain summary of the law indicated, known at a glance [ἀτιτόπω], and with the whole law lightly tasted in this way, progress may be easier toward a careful treatment of the individual laws and the more difficult questions. V. Lastly, that in this opening of my office, in explaining the law here, I may contribute something which pertains both to the dignity of the whole law and to easier knowledge of it, and so that, once explained at the start, it need not be repeated by me afterwards for each part of the order, nor the same thing often pressed. For our teachers are accustomed to labour greatly at each title over what they call the continuation of the titles. Next, we shall show what that order is.

units.la: Quod ad prius attinet, in Institutionibus esse ordinem adhibitum, si quis negare audebit, eadem ille opera negare posset, solè meridie lucere, ut dici solet. De Digestis & Codice est controversia. Sed in Digestis, ea inquam ordine esse digesta, his argumentis doceri potest. 1. Digesta sunt composita ad exemplum Edicti perpetui, quod pulcherrimo ordine à summo Jurisconsulto Juliano fuit digestum, ut infra demonstrabitur. II. Quia idipsum disertis verbis, multisq; in locis testatum reperiatur, ut in dict. leg. 2. de statu homin. l. 1. ff. de possess. hered. pet. l. 1. de fideicommiss. hered. pet. l. 1. de R. V. l. 1. de pecul. l. 1. ad Trebellianum, l. 2. de bonorum possess. secundum tabulas, l. 1. sit tabula testamenti, &c. III. Quia non verisimile est, tam præclarum opus à sapientissimis viris conditum, idemq; per rerum subtilitatem difficile & obscurum, sine luce ordinis congestum temere fuisse. IV. Id & ipsum nomen Digesti convincit. Postremo ipsa id luculenter ostendam. In Codice quoq; ordinem esse doceri potest his argumentis. I. Quia Pandectæ ad ordinem Codicis sunt accommodatæ, & ex ordine Codicis digestæ, l. 1. §. cumq; hac lex, C. de vet. jur. annul. II. Quia Codex Justinianus factus est ad exemplum Theodosiani, ut in prima præfatione Codicis. In eo autem Codice Theodosiano luculentius est ordo, ut videre est in ipso Cod. Theodof. quem tamen nonnihil mutavit Tribunianus, ut infra dicetur. III. Quia absurdum est, Constitutiones Imperiales temere & sine ordine in Codicem tanquam in unum acervum congestas esse. IV. Tum quia infra in re præsente ordinem in Cod. demonstrabimus.
units.tr: As for the first point, if anyone should dare to deny that order has been applied in the Institutes, he could with the same effort deny that the sun shines at midday, as the saying goes. There is controversy about the Digest and the Code. But that the Digest is arranged in order can, I say, be shown by these arguments. 1. The Digest was composed on the model of the Perpetual Edict, which was arranged in most beautiful order by the great jurist Julian, as will be shown below. II. Because this is attested in plain words and in many places, as in the said law 2 de statu hominum, law 1 ff. de possessione hereditatis petitione, law 1 de fideicommissariis hereditatibus, law 1 de regulis iuris, law 1 de peculio, law 1 ad Trebellianum, law 2 de bonorum possessione secundum tabulas, law 1 si tabula testamenti, and so on. III. Because it is not likely that so splendid a work, composed by the wisest men, and difficult and obscure through the subtlety of its matter, was gathered together carelessly and without the light of order. IV. The very name of Digest proves it. Finally, the work itself will show this clearly. In the Code too it can be shown that there is order, by these arguments. I. Because the Pandects were adapted to the order of the Code and were digested according to the order of the Code, law 1, §. and since this law, C. de veteri iure enucleando. II. Because the Justinianic Code was made on the model of the Theodosian, as in the first preface of the Code. Now in that Theodosian Code order is more clearly seen, as may be observed in the Theodosian Code itself, which nevertheless Tribonian somewhat changed, as will be said below. III. Because it is absurd that the imperial constitutions were gathered into the Code carelessly and without order, as into one heap. IV. Also because below, in its proper place, we shall show the order in the Code.

units.la: Verum plerique; Dd. de libris quidem & titulis librorum singulis facile consentiunt, & assentiuntur eos ordine quodam descriptos esse, & serie quadam connexos: de LL. verò, quæ sub titulis singulis continentur, plerique; omnes etiam recentiores dissentiunt, nulloq; eas ordine sub titulis contineri existimant. Nos tamen contra demonstrabimus Tribunianum in his quoq; disponendis tàm in Cod. quàm in Digest. ordine quodam esse usum, quemadmodum & in jure non tantum est ordo librorum & titulorum inter se, sed etiam singulorum §§. qui sub titulis continentur. Cujus rei demonstratio erit illa quidem nova, sed ad ipsorum sententiam assequendam non infructuosa. Hæc de priore parte sive capite sint satis.. -
units.tr: Indeed, most of the learned writers readily agree about the books and the titles of each book, and they assent that these were arranged in a certain order and linked by a certain sequence. But about the laws contained under the individual titles, most, indeed nearly all, even more recent writers disagree, and they think the laws are not contained under the titles in any order. We, however, will show on the contrary that Tribonian used a certain order in arranging these also, both in the Code and in the Digest, just as in the law there is an order not only of the books and titles among themselves but also of the individual paragraphs that are contained under the titles. The demonstration of this matter will be indeed new, but not unfruitful for grasping their opinion. So much may suffice concerning the first part, or chapter.

units.la: Nunc de altera, in qua videndum, quis ordo, & quam ob causam à Tribuniano in his tribus libris Juris Digest. & Cod. & Inst. sit adhibitus. Nam quartus liber, qui Novellarum, à (Glph. Authenticarum) à 175. Novellis Justin. constitutis dicitur non Justiniani mandato, sed eo demum mortuo in ordinem à privato quodam homine redactus est, qui tamen & ordinem temporis in iis est secutus plerumque; sæpè enim aberrat. Et primùm quidem de Instit. ordine explicabimus, tum quia id recta ratio ordinis postulat, ut à facilioribus ad difficiliora fiat progressus: tum quia tempore sunt priores Digest. uno scilicet mense, prius editæ, ut in sin. præfationis Inst. l.1.2. C. de vet. jur. enucl. tum deniq;, quia Digest. non tantum ad Edict. perpet. ordinem, sed ad Institut. partim sunt accommodatæ.
units.tr: Now we must consider the second part, in which it must be seen what order was adopted by Tribonian in these three books of the Digest, the Code and the Institutes, and for what reason. For the fourth book, which is called the Novels, or the Authentics, consisting of the 175 Novels issued by Justinian, was not put into order at Justinian's command but only after his death, by a certain private person; yet he too followed the order of time in them for the most part, though he often departs from it. And first we shall explain the order of the Institutes, then because right reason requires that progress be made from the easier to the more difficult; then because the Digest, which was published earlier, namely within a single month, as at the end of the preface of the Institutes (Inst. l. 1, 2, C. de vet. jur. enucl.) ; and finally because the Digest was in part adapted not only to the order of the perpetual Edict but also to that of the Institutes.

units.la: OECONOMIA, INSTITVTIONVM
units.tr: THE ORDER OF THE INSTITUTES

units.la: Liber I.
units.tr: Book I.

units.la: INSTITUTIONES in duas partes rectè diuidi possunt: Communem, ut ita dicam, & propriam. Communem voco eam, quæ ad communem Juris scientiam pertinet, ut sunt Juris Etymon, Definitio, diuisio, finis & materia. Proprium voco qua singuli juris articuli suo quisque loco separatim explicantur, ut de seruitutibus, manumissionibus, matrimoniis, tutelis, &c. Et prior quidem pars duobus titulis continetur. In reliqua parte, reliqui Inst. libri consumuntur. Ratio est, quia plerumque communia propriis & singularibus prióra esse debent.
units.tr: INSTITUTES may rightly be divided into two parts: the common, as I may call it, and the particular. I call common that part which belongs to the general science of law, such as the etymology of law (ius), its definition, division, end and matter. I call particular that part in which each legal topic is explained separately in its own place, such as servitudes, manumissions, marriages, guardianships, and so on. The first part is contained in two titles. The rest of the book is taken up with the remaining books of the Institutes. The reason is that, as a rule, general matters ought to come before particular and specific ones.

units.la: Jam verò pars posterior rursus ad tria membra reuocatur. Ratio est, quia jus omne ad tria potissimum capita pertinet, personas, res, & actiones, quæ de re paulo subtilius est explicandum, eo quod in hac tripartita partitione, non tantum ratio ordinis, de quo potissimum agimus, sed fundamentum universi juris sit collocatum. Hujus igitur partitionis auctor est Cajus Jurisconsult. quem Tribunianus maximè secutus est in Institut. componendis.
units.tr: Now the second part is in turn reduced to three members. The reason is that all law relates chiefly to three heads: persons, things, and actions. Action must be explained a little more carefully, because in this threefold division is laid the foundation of the whole law, not merely the order of which we are chiefly speaking. The author of this division is Gaius the jurist, whom Tribonian followed most closely in composing the Institutes.

units.la: Ratio autem, cur Caium maximè sit secutus, hæc mihi videtur, tum quia aliorum veterum Instit. aliæ essent nimis prolixæ, ut Florentini, & Martiani, aliæ nimis breves, ut Ulpiani, aliæ nimis difficiles, Caij vero essent & modicæ, (erant enim 4. tantum libri, ut in indice Digest.) & faciles, ut videre est, in reliquiis Inst Caij. Brevitas autem cum facilitate conjuncta utilis est Juvenibus & Tyronibus, tum quia Inst. Caij ætate Justiniani & superiore, multos jam annos in scholis essent receptæ, §. & antea, in præfat. Digest. Nihil autem temerè mutandum & nouandum; præsertim in Institutione adolescentum. Hæc igitur causa est & ratio, cur Caium potissimum Tribunianus sit secutus, tàm in ordine, quàm in rebus ipsis, quàm denique in librorum numero.
units.tr: The reason why Tribonian followed Gaius most of all seems to me to be this: the Institutes of other ancient writers were either too long, like those of Florentinus and Marcian, or too short, like those of Ulpian, or too difficult, whereas those of Gaius were both moderate (for there were only four books, as the index of the Digest shows) and easy, as may be seen from the surviving fragments of Gaius's Institutes. Brevity joined with ease is useful for young people and beginners. Moreover, the Institutes of Gaius had been received for many years into the schools, in the age of Justinian and before, §. and before, in the preface to the Digest. Nothing should be changed or renewed rashly, especially in the instruction of young people. This, then, is the cause and reason why Tribonian chiefly followed Gaius, both in order, in the matters themselves, and finally in the number of books.

units.la: Planè interdum in ordine, & sæpe in rebus ipsis à Cajo discedit. De numero jam dictum. De ordine, verbi gratia, in Cajo pars illa prior, de qua supra dictum, de juris origine, definitione, &c. non erat in Cajo, ut in fragmét. Instit. De rebus autem ipsis passim id liquet, & ratio est, quod in Cajo essent multa jam inutilia constitutionibus Imperialibus, & maximè à Justiniano jam abrogata, quorum in locum Tribunianus meliora, & usu jam receptæ reposuit, d.§. & autem, & in § res vero, in præfat. pand. &c. quæ fere & sola caufuit, cur Justinianus novas Institutiones componi mandavit, utscilicet Institut. Digest. & Cod. omnia tanquam unius corporis membra, inter se consonarent, & ut nihil nisi quod utile usuque receptum Iuris studiosi addiscerent, d. §. nec vero, §. cumque hoc, cum §. seq. in prefat. Institut. Et haec de Cajo hujus trimembris partitionis auctore.
units.tr: Indeed, he departs from Gaius sometimes in order, and often in the matters themselves. The number has already been mentioned. As to order, for example, in Gaius that first part of which we spoke above, on the origin, definition and so on of law, was not present, as is clear from the fragments of the Institutes. Concerning the matters themselves, the departure is evident everywhere, and the reason is that many things in Gaius were already useless because of imperial constitutions, and especially had already been abrogated by Justinian; in their place Tribonian put better things that were already in use. d.§. and indeed, and in § but the things, in the preface to the Pandects, etc. This was almost the only and sole reason why Justinian ordered new Institutes to be composed, so that the Institutes, the Digest and the Code, as members of one body, should agree with one another, and so that students of law should learn nothing but what is useful and in actual use. d. §. nor indeed, §. and this, with the following §. in the preface to the Institutes. And so much concerning Gaius, the author of this threefold division.

units.la: Ratio hujus divisionis paulo altius ex Politia peti debet. Ergo id intelligendum est, Jus omne, etiam Justitiam in actionib. & negotiis humanis, iisque non omnibus, sed iis tantum, quae cum alio contrahuntur, versari tanquam in proprio quodam subjecto, quod in Ethicis tractatur. Negocia autem humana partim sunt publica, partim privata, unde divisio juris nascitur in publicum & privatum, l. 1. §. huius studii. de iustit. & iur. (Nam de privato jure tantum agitur in inst. §. ult. de inst. & iur.) Omnia aguntur vel privatim inter homines, vel publice coram magistratu, & judice. Quae autem privatim fiunt, aut contrahuntur, ea omnia vel ad personas, eorum quae contrahunt, vel ad res & patrimonia eorum pertinent. Hujus autem rei haec est ratio, quia duo tantum in cive & homine privato considerantur, de quibus ipsi inter se homines agere & contrahere possint, quaeque sunt in commercio hominum, status scilicet personae & res. Animus enim ad Deum pertinet, in quo neq; Reip. neq; singulis privatim jus est. Quare cum duo tantum sint persona & res, quae in commerciis hominum versantur, recte quoq; inde duplex juris materia oritur, ut vel ad personas jus pertineat, vel ad res. Verum cum negocia humana propter naturalem ad dissentiendum facilitate, saepe exitum per ipsos reperire non possunt, velut medium judex & arbiter intervenire solet, qui sua jurisdictione cum eos compescere possit, pati non debet, ut res ad rixas & arma veniat: Tertium de actionibus tanquam ad executionem priorum maxime necessarium fuit.
units.tr: The reason for this division must be sought a little higher, from Politics. We must understand, therefore, that all law, and justice too, is concerned with human actions and dealings, and not with all of them, but only with those which are carried on with another, as with a certain subject, which is treated in Ethics. Human dealings are partly public and partly private, whence the division of law into public and private arises, l. 1. §. of this study. de iustit. & iur. (for private law alone is treated in the Institutes, §. last, de inst. & iur.). Everything is done either privately between people, or publicly before a magistrate and judge. Whatever is done or contracted privately pertains either to the persons who contract, or to things and estates. The reason for this is that only two things are considered in a citizen and a private person, concerning which men themselves can act and contract with one another, and which are in the commerce of men: namely, the status of the person and things. For the mind pertains to God, over which neither the commonwealth nor individuals privately have any right. Therefore, since there are only two things, persons and things, which are involved in the commerce of men, it is rightly that a twofold matter of law arises from this, so that law pertains either to persons or to things. But since human dealings, because of man's natural readiness to disagree, often cannot find an outcome by themselves, a judge and arbiter usually intervenes as a go-between, who, since he can restrain them by his jurisdiction, ought not allow matters to come to quarrels and arms. Thus the third head, concerning actions, was most necessary as the means of carrying out the first two.

units.la: Duaremus l. b. 1. d. §. c. 55. de compositione, ordine, methodo ff. tria haec capita personas, res & actiones longe aliter interpretatur. Putat ille, Cajum hoc velle, nullam partem juris esse, nullum contractum, nullum negocium nullum judicium, in quo tractando hi tres titulinon concurrant. Ut ex Institut. primum in stipulatione de personis quaeritur, quae stipulationem non contrahere possint, sitne servus an liber, filius f. minor, pupillus, furiosus, prodigus &c, deinde quaeritur de rebus, quae in stipulationem veniunt, sit ne sacra, publica, religiosa, corporalis, propria an aliena: & tandem de actionibus, sit ne in personam, an in rem, bonae fidei, an stricta, temporalis, an perpetua: civilis, an praetoria. Idemque in caeteris juris articulis & disputationibus, ut in mutuo, commodato, observare licet, quae & Balduini est sententia in Institut.
units.tr: Duaren, in his De compositione, ordine, methodo, on the Digest, [and] in the commentary on the Institutes, interprets these three heads, persons, things and actions, quite differently. He thinks Gaius meant that there is no part of law, no contract, no transaction, no judicial proceeding, in the treatment of which these three titles do not concur. Thus, in the Institutes, first in the stipulation, one asks about persons who cannot contract a stipulation: whether one is a slave or free, a son under power, a minor, a ward, a madman, a spendthrift, and so on; then one asks about things which come into the stipulation: whether they are sacred, public, religious, corporeal, one's own or another's; and finally about actions: whether they are personal or real, of good faith or of strict law, temporal or perpetual, civil or praetorian. The same may be observed in the other legal topics and disputations, as in loan for consumption and loan for use, and this is also the opinion of Baldwin in the Institutes.

units.la: Sed cum ea Just. & Caii mente plane est aliena, tum recte ita refellitur, Primo enim ordo Inst. eam non fert, quo perspicue jura personarum a rebus & actionibus distinguuntur, & separantur. At persona, res & actio, fiaccipiantur ut attributa, ut ea accipit Duaren. non tantum non separantur, sed plerumque in unum juris articulum concurrunt: ut modo de ipsa stipulatione ex Duar. indicatum est. Verum tit. de statu hom. in ff. & ille in Inst. de jur pers. satis indicant, hic non agi de attributo personæ (ut vocant Rhetores) sed de jure, quod ad statum hominum, ac personæ pertinet ut servitus, libertas, jus sui, adoptio, tutela, &c. Præterea attributa, ut Duar. fatetur, concurrunt omnia, in articulos, sive tractatus jurisdictionales: at hæc tria capita plerumq; non concurrunt, ut in testamentis nunquam quæri solet, an tutor fecerit testamentum, an magistratus, maritus vel uxor &c. Tertiò multa de persona ut attributo dici solent, quæ ad personam (ut hic accipitur) sive jus personarum non pertineant. Verbi gratia, ad personam, ut attributum, quæritur interdum ex qua fit natione, qua fit statura, quo colore, sit ne hæreticus, mas an fœmina? At hæc omnia ad jus personarum, de quo hic agitur, non pertinent. Quartò persona, ut attributum, est accidens, sed ut hic est substantia civilis, cui accidunt varia, maximè libertas ac servitus. Postremo, si Cajus hic attributa intelligeret, peccasset in divisione: sunt enim longe plura attributa, locus, tempus &c. quorum in jure non est minor usus quam personæ.
units.tr: But since this is entirely foreign to the mind of Justinian and Gaius, it is also rightly refuted in this way. First, the order of the Institutes does not bear it out, in which the law of persons is clearly distinguished and separated from things and actions. But if person, thing and action were taken as attributes, as Duaren takes them, they would not only not be separated, but would for the most part concur in one legal topic, as has just been shown from Duaren's own example of the stipulation. Yet the title de statu hominum in the Digest, and that de iure personarum in the Institutes, sufficiently indicate that here is not treated the attribute of the person (as the rhetoricians call it) but the law which pertains to the status of men and of persons, such as servitude, liberty, sui iuris, adoption, guardianship, and so on. Besides, as Duaren admits, attributes all concur in the topics or treatises of jurisdiction; but these three heads do not generally concur, as in testaments one never asks whether a guardian made the will, or a magistrate, a husband or a wife, and so on. Thirdly, many things are commonly said of the person as an attribute which do not pertain to the person (as it is taken here), or to the law of persons. For example, as an attribute of the person one sometimes asks of what nation he is, what his stature is, what his colour, whether he is a heretic, male or female. But all these things do not pertain to the law of persons, which is what is treated here. Fourthly, the person as an attribute is an accident, but here it is a civil substance, to which various things accrue, chiefly liberty and servitude. Lastly, if Gaius meant attributes here, he would have erred in his division, for there are far more attributes, place, time and so on, of which the use in law is no less than that of the person.

units.la: Ut autem aliud ex alio, ita Duarenus putat, quod Tribunianum in ff. notria illa Caii, sed duo tantum personas & res posuisse, omisso tertio, quod est de actionibus. Quod valde absurdum est. Nam contra demonstrabitur Pandectarum magnam partem constare ex actionibus & judiciis, priora autem duo leviter attingi tantum lib. 1. titul. 5. 6. 7. & 8.
units.tr: So Duarenus thinks, as the other has done, that Tribonian in the Digest took over Gaius's division, but that he set out only two things, persons and things, leaving out the third, which concerns actions. This is quite absurd. For I shall show against him that a large part of the Pandects consists of actions and judgments, while the first two topics are touched on only lightly in lib. 1. titul. 5. 6. 7. & 8.

units.la: Etiam Joh. Apellus, in Dialog. ad Inst. in eadem fuit fere opinione, ut putaret res & personas esse attributa, ideoque non illa, sed potius, hæc duo, dominium & obligationem juris capita, sive strata & fundamenta esse statuenda. Sed cum dominium & obligationes sint tantum affectiones rerum (ut videre est sub tit. de rer. divis. & tit. de adquir. rer. domin. & adquir. poss. quo referemus, quæ so, disputationem de personis, ut sunt de servitute, manumissione, nuptiis, adoptione, patria potestate, tutela &c?
units.tr: John Apellus, in Dialog. ad Inst., held much the same view. He thought that things and persons are attributes, and that therefore not these but rather the two, ownership and obligation, should be set up as the heads and foundations of law. But since ownership and obligations are only affections of things (as can be seen under de rer. divis. and de adquir. rer. domin. and adquir. poss.), I ask, where would we put the discussion of persons, as of slavery, manumission, marriage, adoption, paternal power, guardianship, and so on?

units.la: Restat Connan. lib. 2. Comment. jur. civ. c. 1. & lib. 5. c. 1. qui de duobus, puta de personis & rebus satis recte; sed de tertio, de actionibus, existimat actionum verbo contineri non actiones; quibus in judiciis utimur, sed omnia facta hominum, & contractus, & delicta, testamenta, donationes, &c. ut actionis verbum tam late hic pateat, atque apud Aristotelem verbum πυαχ- ρα. Sed fieri id non potest. 1. quia sequeretur, ut jam etiam ad actiones non jus personarum pertinerent matrimonium & tutela & adoptio, sunt enim actiones, usucapiones quoque & adquisitiones dominii, quæ ad tractatum rerum pertinent, referri quoque deberent ad actiones. II. Jurisconsulti Actionis verbo proprie de forensi, & interdum latius de legitimis actionibus uti solent. III. ipso quoque Institut. ordine refellitur, quod Connanus non diffitetur. Atque hæc de prima illius partitione, sive de trimembri juris materia, personis, rebus & actionibus dicta sint.
units.tr: There remains Connanus, lib. 2. Comment. jur. civ. c. 1. and lib. 5. c. 1., who is fairly right about the first two, persons and things, but about the third, actions, he thinks that under the word actions are contained not the actions we use in courts, but all the deeds of men, contracts, delicts, wills, gifts, and so on, so that the word action extends as widely here as the Greek word for deed in Aristotle [πρᾶξις]. But this cannot be. First, because it would follow that marriage, guardianship and adoption, which are also actions, would not belong to the law of persons; and acquisitive prescription and the acquisition of ownership, which are also actions, would have to be referred to actions rather than to the treatment of things. Second, the jurists are accustomed to use the word action properly of a lawsuit, and sometimes more broadly of the legal actions. Third, the order of the Institutes itself refutes him, which Connanus does not deny. Let these things be said about that first division of his, or about the three-part matter of law: persons, things and actions.

units.la: Nunc ad ordinem & Oeconomiam Inst. redeamus. Et quod ad duas summas Instit. partes attinet, quas supra indicavimus, communem, quæque proœmium, & principia juris continet, & propriam, in quo juris tota tractatio & scientia continetur.
units.tr: Now let us return to the order and arrangement of the Institutes. As regards the two main parts of the Institutes which we indicated above, one is the common part, which contains the preface and the principles of law; the other is the proper part, in which the whole treatment and science of law is contained.

units.la: Prioris quidé hic est ordo, ut prius definitiones deinde divisiones juris & justitiæ collocétur. Et primū quidem definitio justitiæ, deinde juris, tū etiam dignitas hujus scientiæ (est enim hæc virtus ut lucifer inter sydera apud Arist. V. Ethic.) statim initio appareat, tū etiam ut studiosos & Jurisconsultos officii admoneant, scopo statim propositó, ad quem omnia Juris præcepta dirigantur: tum deniq; quia civilem scientiam etiam Philosophi à fine (est autem Juris finis justitia sive æquitas. Cic. in Topic.) exordiuntur, ut videre est in Ethicis Aristotelis. Postea juris definitio, & tres divisiones adjunguntur, & ordine explicantur. Postulat enim ratio ordinis ut omnis quæ suscipitur disputatio, à definitione proficiscatur, ut, inquit Cic. Cui ex arte statim adjungi solent divisiones.
units.tr: The order of the first part is this: first the definitions are laid down, then the divisions of law and of justice. And first the definition of justice, then of law, and then the dignity of this science (for it is, as Aristotle says in the fifth book of the Ethics, a virtue like the morning star among the stars) appears at once at the outset; and also so that the students and jurists may be reminded of their duty, with the aim set out at once, to which all the precepts of law are directed; and finally because philosophers too begin the civil science from its end (and the end of law is justice or equity, Cic. in Topic.), as can be seen in Aristotle's Ethics. Afterwards the definition of law and its three divisions are added and explained in order. For the reason of order requires that every discussion undertaken should proceed from a definition, as Cicero says; and divisions are customarily added to it by the rules of the art.

units.la: Quarum prima hæc est in publicum & privatum. Altera est subdivisio, qua Jus privatum (de eo enim tantum agitur in Instit.) in naturale, gentium & civile dividitur; & hæ partes ordine explicantur. tit.2.
units.tr: The first of these is the division into public and private law. The second is a subdivision by which private law (for only this is treated in the Institutes) is divided into natural law, the law of nations and civil law; and these parts are explained in order. tit. 2.

units.la: Tertia divisione juris jus civile in scriptum & non scriptum distinguitur. His adjungi potest & quarta divisio (vel potius subdivisio) Juris scripti in 6. partes. ff. de iur. scripta d. tit. & quinta qua Jus vel ad personas pertinet, vel ad res, vel ad actiones. Et hæc depriore parte Instit.
units.tr: By a third division, civil law is distinguished into written and unwritten law. To these may be added a fourth division (or rather subdivision) of written law into six parts, ff. de iur. scripta, d. tit.; and a fifth, by which law concerns either persons, or things, or actions. And this is taken from the first part of the Institutes.

units.la: Nunc de altera, de qua diligentius explicandum, primum summatim, deinde singulatim. Et summatim ejus partis hic est ordo, ut de personis lib. 1. lib. 2. & 3. de rebus, ut & 4. lib. 5. tit. Postremo de actionibus à tit. 6. usque ad finem operis explicetur. Ratio ordinis de personis quidem, cur de iis primum agatur, indicatur in d. f. ult. propter dignitatem personarum, sive hominum, quorum nomine jus est constitutum, ff. in pecudum. de rer. divis. De rebus autem cur prius agatur, quàm de Actionibus, hæc est ratio, tum quia res personis sint similiores, in eo, quod utrumq; Jus personarum & rerum fit privatum, cum actiones publicè exerceantur, ut supra dictum; tum quia actiones sint priorum duorum capitum; velut executio & finis, quibus licet priora illa duo ad exitum perducuntur, ut supra dictum.
units.tr: Now we must explain the second part, of which we shall speak more carefully, first in summary and then in detail. The order of this part in summary is this: first on persons, in book 1; then books 2 and 3 on things, and 4 as well; book 5, title 6 onwards; finally actions are explained from title 6 to the end of the work. The reason for the order, why persons are treated first, is indicated in the last law cited, on account of the dignity of persons, or of men, in whose name the law was established, ff. in pecudum, de rer. divis. As for why things are treated before actions, the reason is this: partly because things are more like persons, in that both the law of persons and the law of things are private, whereas actions are exercised publicly, as said above; and partly because actions are the execution and end of the first two heads, as the first two are brought to their conclusion through them, as said above.

units.la: Id quoque summatim hic indicandum, hæc 3. Juris capita, hoc est, totū opus Instit. ordine & via diæretica (partitiones Cicero vocat) dispositum & explicatum esse. Nam primum caput de personis duabus divisionibus principalibus, & tribus accessoriis & subdivisionibus continetur. II. De reb. quatuor ferè divisionibus: Tertium quatuor item divisionibus principalibus continetur. Atque hæc de altera Instit. parte, summatim atque universe, quò ad ordinem dicta sint.
units.tr: This too must be indicated in summary: these three heads of law, that is, the whole work of the Institutes, are arranged and explained in order and by the method of division (which Cicero calls partitions). For the first head, on persons, is contained in two principal divisions and three subsidiary ones and subdivisions. The second, on things, in roughly four divisions. The third likewise is contained in four principal divisions. And let these things be said about the second part of the Institutes, in summary and in general, as regards order.

units.la: Nunc & singulatim omnia recte & ordine disposita esse demonstremus. Videamus primum caput sive personarum divisiones, quarum duæ, ut dictum est sunt principales, una: Omnes homines liberi sunt, aut servi, quæ summa dicitur, & priore loco explicatur. Ratio est, tum quia libertatis status est primus, & cum ipso homine natus; tum quia hæc divisio continet Jus naturale. Est enim libertas Juris naturalis. Altera autem divisio principalis continet Jus civile, ut patriam potestatem, quæ est civilis, §. 1. de patria potest. Jus autem naturale prius est civili. Et de hac igitur divisione, ejusque una subdivisione. tit. 3. & 5. consequentibus tit. agitur.
units.tr: Now let us show, one by one, that all things are rightly and orderly arranged. Let us look first at the first head, or the divisions of persons, of which two, as has been said, are principal. The first is this: all men are either free or slaves, which is called the principal division, and is explained first. The reason is that, first, the state of liberty is the first and born together with man himself; and second, this division contains natural law, for liberty is of natural law. The second principal division, however, contains civil law, as paternal power, which is civil, § 1. de patria potest. Now natural law is prior to civil law. And so this division, and one of its subdivisions, is treated in title 3 and 5, and the following titles.

units.la: Ejus autem divisionis trimembris alterum duntaxat membrum de liberis hominibus subdividitur, deinde in ingenuos & libertinos, & de ingenuis prius agitur tit. 4. posterius de libertinis tit. 5. Ratio est perspicua, tum quia ingenuorum status est prior, ut ex jure naturali, & dignior, cum libertinorum sit posterior ut ex jure gentium & vilior.
units.tr: Of this three-membered division, only one member, that concerning free men, is subdivided, into freeborn and freedmen; and the freeborn are dealt with first, in title 4, and freedmen afterwards, in title 5. The reason is clear: the status of the freeborn is prior, as it derives from natural law, and more worthy, whereas the status of freedmen is later, as it derives from the law of nations, and lower.

units.la: Quia autem libertini definiuntur, qui ex justa servitute manumissi sunt, justo ordine deinde explicat de manumissionibus, §. multis, & seqq. tit. 5. §. toto t. 6. & 7. Et hæc de prioreme personarum divisione.
units.tr: Since freedmen are defined as those who have been manumitted from lawful slavery, the order then explains manumissions in due sequence, § multis and following, title 5; § toto, title 6 and 7. And this is what is said about the first division of persons.

units.la: Huic divisioni statim conjungitur altera tit. 1. qua persona quædam sunt sui juris, quædam alieno juri subjectæ, d. tit. 8.
units.tr: To this division is immediately joined another, title 1, by which some persons are sui iuris and some are subject to another's power, d. tit. 8.

units.la: Hujus autem divisionis duæ sunt subdivisiones, prius enim membrum, quod est de personis, quæ sui juris, subdividuntur in eas, quæ vel in tutela sunt vel curatione, vel neutro jure tenentur, tit. 13. de tutelis. Alterum membrum, quod agit de personis alieno juri subjectis, subdividitur in eas, quæ sunt in potestate vel parentum, vel dominorum.
units.tr: Now this division has two subdivisions. For the first member, which concerns persons who are sui iuris, is subdivided into those who are either under guardianship or curatorship, or are held under neither, title 13, de tutelis. The second member, which deals with persons subject to another's power, is subdivided into those who are in the power either of parents or of masters.

units.la: Harum subdivisionum ordo hic est, ut illa quidem subdivisio de tutela, &c. posterius, d. tit. 13. & seqq. hæc vero de potestate prius explicetur, tit. 10, & 4. seqq. Ratio est quia hæc subdivisio de patria potestate similitudinem & cognationem habet cum priore divisione de liberis & servis.
units.tr: The order of these subdivisions is this: the subdivision on guardianship, etc., is explained later, d. tit. 13 and following; but this one on power is explained first, title 10, and 4 and following. The reason is that this subdivision on paternal power has a resemblance and kinship with the earlier division on free men and slaves.

units.la: Cur autem hujus subdivisionis de potestate membrum, quod est de potestate Dominorum, prius sit membro de potestate parentum, ratio hæc est, quia potestas dominorum est antiquior, ut ex jure gentium, cum patria sit ex jure civili.
units.tr: Why the member of this subdivision concerning the power of masters comes before the member concerning the power of parents: the reason is that the power of masters is older, since it arises from the law of nations, whereas paternal power arises from civil law.

units.la: Hinc sequitur titul. 10. de nupt. eumq; titul. 11. de adopt. Ratio est, quia patria potestas duobus præcipue modis comparatur, nuptiis & adoptione, §. alt. de nupt. & §. ult. de patria potest. & initio, tit. de adopt.
units.tr: Hence follows title 10, concerning marriage, and then title 11, concerning adoption. The reason is that paternal power is acquired chiefly in two ways, by marriage and by adoption: see the penultimate paragraph of the title on marriage, and the final paragraph of the title on paternal power, and the beginning of the title on adoption.

units.la: Tandem eos sequitur, tit. 12. quib. modis potestas solvatur. Postulat enim ratio, ut prius de modis inducendæ potestatis, tam dominorum quam parentum, post remode modis tollendæ agatur. Nam hic titulus est communis, tam dominorum quam parentum potestatis: quare rectius sic scriptum est in libris veteribus, quib. mod. imp. potestatis solvit. Hactenus de priore subdivisione.
units.tr: Lastly, title 12 follows, on the ways in which power is dissolved. For reason requires that, first, the ways of introducing power, both of masters and of parents, be treated, and afterwards the ways of ending it. For this title is common to both the power of masters and the power of parents; so the older books rightly read, "by what ways power is dissolved" (quibus modis imperii potestatis solvitur). So much concerning the former subdivision.

units.la: ¶ Eam justo ordine sequitur posterior tit. 13. quadixi ex illis personis, quæ sunt sui juris quasdam esse in tutela velcura, quasdam neutro jure teneri. Hujus autem subdivisionis tantum prior pars explicatur: ea enim cognita etiam altera intelligitur; contrariorum enim eadem est disciplina.
units.tr: Following this in proper order comes the latter subdivision, title 13, which divides those persons who are sui juris into those who are under guardianship or curatorship and those who are under neither. Of this subdivision only the first part is explained, for once that is known the other is understood as well; the discipline of opposites is the same.

units.la: Pars aurem ea prior duo cōtinet, tutelam & curationem, & prius quidem de tutela posterius de curatione: tit.23. Ratio est facilis, quia tutela est in pupillum curatio est adolescentis attamen prior est pupillus adolescente.
units.tr: The first part contains two matters, guardianship and curatorship, and the former is treated first, the latter afterwards: title 23. The reason is easy: guardianship is over a ward (pupillus), curatorship over a young man (adolescens); but the ward comes before the young man.

units.la: Jam vero de tutela, cum ea sit triplex: testamentaria, legitima & dativa, primum de testamentaria, tit.13. & seq. deinde de legitima tit.15. & seq. Postremo de dativa sive Attiliana tit.20. Ratio cur primum de testamentaria, quia quamdiu speratur testamentaria, cessat legitima. Ratio responsionis sive hujus rei est, tum favor ultimæ voluntatis, tum quia lex præsumit parentem filio optime de tutore prospecturum.
units.tr: Now, guardianship is threefold: testamentary, legitimate and dative. The testamentary comes first, titles 13 and following; then the legitimate, title 15 and following; lastly the dative, or Atilian, title 20. The reason the testamentary comes first is that, so long as a testamentary guardian is hoped for, the legitimate one does not arise. The reason for this order lies both in the favour shown to the last will and in the presumption of the law that a parent will provide the best possible guardian for his son.

units.la: Ratio autem cur legitima præcedat datiuam, est, quia legitimi tutores sunt cognati, qui certe extraneis ut sunt datiui merito præferuntur, partim quia melius sint affecti erga pupillum; partim quia ut ad eos hereditatis commodum, ita & onus tutelæ pertineat.
units.tr: The reason the legitimate guardianship precedes the dative is that legitimate guardians are kinsmen, who are rightly preferred to strangers such as dative guardians: partly because they are better disposed towards the ward, partly because the burden of guardianship falls on them just as the advantage of the inheritance does.

units.la: Legitima autem tutela cum sit quadruplex, agnatorum, patronorum, parentum & fratrum, sive fiduciaria, ordine hæ species explicantur, tit.15.17.18. & 19.
units.tr: Since legitimate guardianship is fourfold, of agnates, of patrons, of parents and of brothers (the fiduciary), these kinds are explained in order in titles 15, 17, 18 and 19.

units.la: Interjicitur tit.16. de cap.dimin. (quæ ad legitimas tutelas pertinet, & non ad alias hoc est legitimæ capitis diminutione pereunt, aliæ non item) interjicitur, inquantum hic tit. inter legitimam agnatorum & legitimam patronorum tutelam quia capitis diminutione tollitur legitima duntaxat, alique non item. Vlp t.t u §. exceptam lib.reg.
units.tr: Title 16, on capitis deminutio, is inserted (which pertains to legitimate guardianships and not to others: by loss of civic status (capitis deminutio) the legitimate guardianship alone perishes, and not the others). It is inserted between the legitimate guardianship of agnates and that of patrons, inasmuch as by capitis deminutio the legitimate guardianship alone is removed, and not the others. See Ulpian, title on the rules, the paragraph "exceptam".

units.la: Cur autem priore loco collocetur legitima agnatorum quam patronorum, hæc est ratio, tum quia agnatorum est ex verbis & sententia legis duodecim tab. patronorum tantum est sententia, infra initio tit. tum quia agnatorum, quæ ingenuorum, est dignior, libertinorum vilior.
units.tr: The reason the legitimate guardianship of agnates is placed before that of patrons is twofold: first, because the agnatic guardianship rests on the words and the sense of the Law of the Twelve Tables, whereas that of patrons rests on the sense alone (see the beginning of the title below); second, because the agnatic guardianship, which belongs to freeborn persons, is more worthy, while that of freedmen is of lower standing.

units.la: Cur autem deinde patronorum tutela præcedat parentum tutelam ratio est quia patronorum est ex duodecim tabul. saltem ex sententia, ut modo dictum, parentum non est neq; ex verbis neque sententia, sed exemplo tutelæ patronorum inducta, ut initio tit. de leg.par.tut.
units.tr: Next, the guardianship of patrons precedes the guardianship of parents, for the reason that the patrons' guardianship derives from the Twelve Tables, at least in sense, as just said, while that of parents derives neither from the words nor from the sense, but was introduced by analogy with the guardianship of patrons: see the beginning of the title on the legitimate guardianship of parents.

units.la: Cur denique parentum tutela præcedat fiduciariam, ratio est perspicua, quia pater fratri præfertur in hereditate. §. ult. de leg.agn.succeff. Has tutelæ species, testamentariam & legitimam ita expositas ordine, sequitur tertia datiua. tit.20. Ratio jam expolita.
units.tr: Lastly, the guardianship of parents precedes the fiduciary one; the reason is clear: a father is preferred to a brother in the inheritance (last paragraph of the title on the succession of agnates). Having set out these kinds of guardianship, testamentary and legitimate, in this order, the third, the dative, follows: title 20. The reason has already been given.

units.la: Huic subjungitur tit.21. de auctor.tut. Ratio, quia primum de tutela auctum est, quemadmodum constituatur tutor proximum est, ut de ejus effectu agatur. Cujus officii duæ sunt præcipuæ partes, gerere negocia pupilli & auctoritatem adhibere. De administratione, quia res est difficilior, in Digest. & C tam. C tantum explicatur. De altera officii Parte hic quoque agitur.
units.tr: Added to this is title 21, on the authorisation of guardians. The reason: since the first matter treated was how a guardian is appointed, the next thing is to treat of his function. Two principal parts of this office are to manage the affairs of the ward and to give authorisation. Administration, because it is the more difficult matter, is explained only in the Digest and the Code. The other part of the office is treated here also.

units.la: Huic proximus est tit. 22. quib. mod. tut.sin. naturali ratione & ordine ut prius de constituenda & gerenda, postea definienda explicetur.
units.tr: Next to this is title 22, on the ways in which guardianship ends. By natural reason and order, the appointing and carrying out of the office is explained first, and afterwards its termination.

units.la: Explicata jam separatim tutela, accedit Imp. ad curationem, quae erat pars altera prioris membri subdivisionis personarum, de qua supra. Et haec est ratio ordinis tit. 23. de curat. quem sequuntur tituli communes tam tutelae, quam curationis, tit. 24. & pen. & ult.
units.tr: Guardianship having now been explained separately, the Emperor passes to curatorship, which was the other part of the former member of the subdivision of persons, mentioned above. This is the reason for the order of title 23, on curatorship, which is followed by the titles common to both guardianship and curatorship, title 24 and the last ones.

units.la: Cur autem proprii, & peculiares sint priores, & his communes sint posteriores ratio haec est, quia natura rei initio semper explicanda est, quae natura ex definitione & divisione intelligitur. Natura autem rei, ut hic tutelae & curationis, ut melius explicetur, non debent res confundi tractado, quae natura sunt distinctae ut sunt tutela & curatio.
units.tr: The reason the former titles are proper and peculiar, and the latter common to both, is this: the nature of a matter must always be explained first, and the nature of a thing is understood through its definition and division. But so that the nature of things, such as guardianship and curatorship, may be better explained, matters which are by nature distinct, as guardianship and curatorship are, should not be confused in treatment.

units.la: Ex his autem communibus tribus titulis, cur hic de satisdationibus prior sit reliquis, ratio est, quia satisdatio pertinet ad tutorem semel constitutum, excusatio pertinet ad eum saepe qui nunquam tutor fuit. De suspectis autem tutoribus titulus est ultimus & posterior titulo de excusationibus, tum quia excusatio plerumque fit ante susceptam tutelam, tum quia excusatio est favorabilior, remotio & accusatio odiosior. Cur tamen in ff contrarius sit ordo, hoc est, tit. de suspectis &c. prior sit tit. de excusationibus. (est ratio quaedam ibi ex praecedente tit. sumenda) infra in ff explicabitur.
units.tr: As for why, among these three common titles, the one on securities (satisdatio) comes before the others: the reason is that the giving of security pertains to a guardian once appointed, whereas excuse pertains often to one who never was a guardian. The title on suspect guardians is the last and comes after the title on excuses, both because excuse is usually made before a guardianship is undertaken, and because excuse is the more favourable matter, while removal and accusation are more odious. Why in the Digest the order is the reverse, that is, the title on suspect guardians and so on comes before the title on excuses (a certain reason is to be drawn there from the preceding title), will be explained later in the Digest.

units.la: Liber II. Institut.
units.tr: Book II of the Institutes

units.la: ATque hoc est ratio ordinis lib. adhibitus in quo postquam primum caput juris de personis explicatum est, recte & ordine adjungitur lib. 2. caput proximum de rebus explicandum, quod, quia in jure pater latissime, in explicando e lib. 2. & 3. & initium quarti usque ad titulum 6. consumuntur. Ad hoc enim caput pertinent ad quisitiones dominii, hereditas, contractus & delicta.
units.tr: This is the reason for the order of the book. After the first chapter of law, on persons, has been explained, the next chapter, on things, is rightly and in order added in Book 2. Because this chapter is very broad in law, its explanation takes up Books 2 and 3, the beginning of Book 4 and the titles up to title 6. For this chapter covers the inquiries into ownership, inheritance, contracts and delicts.

units.la: Admonuimus jam supra hoc caput contineri quatuor fere divisionibus, quarum prima: Res sunt aut in patrimonio aut extra patrimonium. II. Res vel sunt communes omnium, vel publicae, vel universitatis vel nullius, vel singulorum. III. (quae tamen proximae ultimi membri divisionis potius subdivisio est) qua rerum dominium adquiritur aut jure naturali, id est gentium, aut civili. IV. qua res sunt vel corporales vel incorporales. tit. 2.
units.tr: We have already noted above that this chapter contains roughly four divisions. The first is: things are either within the patrimony or outside it. II. Things are either common to all, public, belonging to a corporation, belonging to no one, or belonging to individuals. III. (which, however, is rather a subdivision of the last member of the division) ownership of things is acquired either by natural law, that is, the law of nations, or by civil law. IV. Things are either corporeal or incorporeal. Title 2.

units.la: Si quis tamen subtilius consideret, poterit has quatuor divisiones ad duas revocare. Nam secunda est primae explicatio, & tertia potius modos adquirendi dominii dividit, quam rei divisionem continet. Pertinent tamen priores tres, ad unum argumentum, puta de rer divisione. Nam in hoc cap. & obligatio continetur. Sed de obligatione inferius, ubi de quarta divisione rerum corporalium & incorporalium.
units.tr: If anyone considers the matter more carefully, he will be able to reduce these four divisions to two. For the second is an explanation of the first, and the third divides the modes of acquiring ownership rather than containing a division of things. Yet the first three pertain to one subject, namely the division of things. For obligation is also contained in this chapter. But concerning obligation, more below, where we come to the fourth division, of corporeal and incorporeal things.

units.la: Ordo autem harum divisionum quatuor interest hic est, ut prius de illis agatur, quae ad dominium pertinent; posterius de obligatione.
units.tr: The order of these four divisions is this: first those matters are treated which pertain to ownership, and afterwards those which concern obligation.

units.la: Ratio, tum quia dominium continet tei substantiam civiliter loquendo, ut eleganter Joh. Ramus in Enchir. de reg. iur. lib. 2 tum quia posterior divisio de servitutib. & obligationibus ad accidentia pertinent tū quia dominium est antiquius obligatione. Nā dominium statim cum ipso genere humano per occupationem scilicet ortum est: sed cōmercia, & obligationes ex jure gentiū, ex necessitate §. jus autem gentium, sup. de jure nat. gent. & civ. l. 1. de adquir. rer. dom. l. 1. de adquir. poss. Hæc igitur est ratio, cur prius de dominio tit. 1. & seqq. usq; ad tit. de oblig. posterius de obligatione tractetur. Et primæ tres divisiones quæ ad dominium pertinent, præcedant divisionem quartam, quæ ad servitutes & obligationes pertinet.
units.tr: The reason is twofold. First, because ownership, speaking in civil terms, constitutes the substance of a thing, as the elegant Joh. Ramus says in Enchir. de reg. iur. lib. 2. Second, because servitudes and obligations pertain to accidents, and because ownership is older than obligation. For ownership arose at once with the human race itself, namely by occupation; but commerce and obligations arose from the law of nations, out of necessity, §. jus autem gentium, sup. de jure nat. gent. & civ.; l. 1. de adquir. rer. dom.; l. 1. de adquir. poss. This, then, is the reason why ownership is treated first, tit. 1. and following, up to tit. de oblig., and obligation afterwards. And the first three divisions, which pertain to ownership, precede the fourth division, which pertains to servitudes and obligations.

units.la: Priorum autem trium ratio est facilis. Nam secunda est prioris explicatio potius, ad utrumq; ejus membrū. tertia est secundæ ejus mēbri singulorū subdivisio. Nā tertia hoc tantū agitur, duos esse modos sive genera adquisitionū quibus res singulorū dominio nostro adjiciuntur: alios naturales, alios civiles, & primo quidem de naturalibus, postea de civilibus explicabitur.
units.tr: The reason for the first three is easy. For the second is rather an explanation of the first, covering both of its members; the third is a subdivision of the second member, into its individual parts.
