For the third only establishes that there are two modes or kinds of acquisition by which things of individuals are added to our ownership: some natural, others civil. The natural ones will be explained first, and the civil ones afterwards.

units.la: Illud diligenter observandum, cum hoc caput de rebus, maximè duabus, ut dictum), divisionibus, tertia scilicet de adquisitione partim naturali, partim civili, & quarta de reb. corporalib. & incorporalib. cōtineatur. In his duab eū ordinem teneri ab initio l. 2. usq; ad tit. de Action. ut initio quidē tertia prius puta tit. 1. separatim quarta tit. 23. 4. & 5 deinde utraq; permixtim & cōfuse à tit. 6. usq; ad tit. de oblig. & tandē quarta rursus separatim à d. tit. de oblig. usq; ad tit. de Actio. explicētur. Cuj' varietatis ratio in ordine modo explicabitur. Et hæc summatim sive universim de analysi hujus cap. de reb. dicta sint.
units.tr: This must be carefully observed: since this chapter on things contains, as has been said, chiefly two divisions, namely the third on acquisition, partly natural and partly civil, and the fourth on corporeal and incorporeal things, the order to be kept in these two is as follows. At the beginning, the third is taken first separately, tit. 1.; the fourth separately, tit. 2. 3. 4. and 5.; then both are treated mixed together and confusedly, from tit. 6 to tit. de oblig.; and finally the fourth is again treated separately, from the said tit. de oblig. to tit. de Action. The reason for this variation will be explained presently in the order itself. And let these things be said in summary, or in general, about the analysis of this chapter on things.

units.la: Nunc de singulis videamus. Et primum quod attinet ad primæ divisionis membra. Eorū ordo est facilis, & à tēpore petendus. Communes autē & publicæ, ut ex jure naturali & gentium sunt priores ordine, cum reliquæ (ut universitatis & nullius) sint ex jure civili, quod posterius, & quæ sunt singulorū partim sūt mixtæ. Quod ad tertiā attinet, ratio ordinis mēbri ejus est in §. singulorū mēbra sunt duo, vel ad adquisitiones naturales vel civiles pertinentia. Priusautem de naturalibus tit. 1. posterius de civilibus tit. 2. & seqq. agitur, quia inquit Imp. commodius est àvetustiori iure incipere.
units.tr: Now let us look at each part. And first, as regards the members of the first division. Their order is easy and should be taken from time. Common and public things, as they arise from natural law and the law of nations, are prior in order, while the rest (those of a corporation and of no one) are from civil law, which is later, and those belonging to individuals are partly mixed. As for the third division, the reason for the order of its members is in §. singulorum: there are two members, pertaining either to natural or to civil acquisitions. The natural ones are treated first, tit. 1., and the civil ones afterwards, tit. 2. and following, because, as the Emperor says, it is more fitting to begin with the older law.

units.la: Naturales autem adquisitionum modi, cum sint XI. §. fera & seqq. tit. 1. ad duo summa genera sunt revocandi: occupationem & traditionē, sumpto scilicet latius occupationis vocabulo, ut & Cōtius admonuit l. dig. p. 7. Ad occupationē enim pertinēt duo modi, puta ferarū captura, præda hostilis &c.
units.tr: The natural modes of acquisition, since they are eleven §. fera and following, tit. 1., are to be reduced to two chief kinds: occupation and tradition, the word occupation being taken in the broader sense, as Cujas also observed l. dig. p. 7. For under occupation fall two modes, namely the capture of wild animals, booty from enemies, and so on.

units.la: Cur autem prius de occupatione, d. §. fera posterius de traditione. § per traditionem. agatur: ratio hæc est: quia occupationis (inquit Cic. 1. offic.) est antiquissimus modus.
units.tr: Why occupation is treated first, d. §. fera, and tradition afterwards, § per traditionem., the reason is this: because occupation, as Cicero says (1. Offic.), is the most ancient mode.

units.la: Sed occupationis, quia sunt species, ut jam dictum, inter eos quæ sit ratio ordinis ita intelligitur, si rursus hęad duo summa capita revocentur, quædam enim plane natura obveniunt quædam inducti hominum requirunt. Naturales igitur adquisitiones priore loco, attificiosæ posteriore collocantur. Ratio est perspicua. Naturale voco captūra ferarū, cui similis est præda inventione lapillorū, fœtum animalium, alluvione, & Insulam. Artificiosas, & in quibus operā hominū versatur, istas quinq; voco, speciē sive speciei consectionem, corporū commixtione, superficie, fructus, & thesaurum. Et hęc de tertię divisionis priore mēbro, quæ st de naturali adquisitione tit. 1 de rer. divif.
units.tr: But since occupation has species, as already said, the reason for their order is understood thus: if these are again reduced to two chief heads, some things come to us plainly by nature, while others require the contrivance of men. Natural acquisitions are therefore placed first, artificial ones afterwards. The reason is clear. I call natural the capture of wild animals, to which is similar the finding of pebbles, the offspring of animals, alluvion, and an island. I call artificial, and those in which human labour is involved, these five: the making of a thing into a new species, the mixing of bodies, accession to the surface, fruits, and treasure. And these things are said about the first member of the third division, which is concerning natural acquisition, tit. 1 de rer. divis.

units.la: Proximum jam erat alterum de civilibus modis, quitamen ante quā tractentur, interjicitur quarta divisio. tit. 2. quā res aliæ sunt corporales, aliæ incorporales. Ratio hujus ordinis, tū ut hac quarta divisione lögīs absit à prioribus rerū divisionibus, quæ propterea in ff. uno titulo cōtinentur. tū etiam quia quæ in hac quarta divisione adferuntur servitutes & usufsr in ff. rerum tractatu continentur. & quia non tantum ex tertia, sed & hac quarta pendet totum corpus juris de rebus; merito statim initio tractanda fuit.
units.tr: Next in turn is the second, concerning civil modes; but before these are treated, the fourth division is interposed, tit. 2., in which some things are corporeal and others incorporeal. The reason for this order is twofold: first, so that this fourth division, being different from the earlier divisions of things, may be kept apart from them, which for that reason are contained in one title in the Digest; and second, because the servitudes and usufruct which are mentioned in this fourth division are treated in the Digest in the title on things. And since the whole body of law on things depends not only on the third but also on this fourth division, it was rightly to be treated at the very beginning.

units.la: Cum igitur in hac divisione tantū sit positum moneti, duo hic initio sūt quærenda. Primo, Cur tantum res incorporales hic exponantur; servitutes, usufsr. Vsus (habitatio) hereditas, & obligatio. Secundo, cur rerum divisio nes tantum quatuor sive duæ potius summæ hic adferuntur.
units.tr: Since, then, only a little is laid down in this division, two questions are to be asked here at the outset. First, why only incorporeal things are explained here: servitudes, usufruct, use (habitation), inheritance and obligation. Second, why only four, or rather two chief divisions of things, are offered here.

units.la: Nam ut de posteriore quæstione prius respondeamus, sunt multæ aliæ divisiones in jure, ut dū res dividuntur in mobiles, soli sive immobiles, & sese movētes. l. ultim. C. de quadrié. præscript. §. 1. infra de inutil. stipul. Ut cū res aliæ sunt dividuæ, aliæ individuæ. l. 23. & 4. ff. de oblig. & action. Ratio autē cur has tantum duas explicet Tribunianus est, quod ut jam supra dictum, rerū usus maxime in duobus, dominio, & commercio sive obligatione sit positus. Ad dominium autem pertinent tres primæ divisiones ad commercia & obligationes pertinet quarta, partim tamē etiā ad dominiū. Nā usufsr. est dominio similis. l. 4. ff. de usufr. ut & servitutes in eo sūt similes dominio, quæ sint jura in re.
units.tr: To answer the latter question first: there are many other divisions in law, as when things are divided into movable, immovable (of the soil) and self-moving. l. ultim. C. de quadrien. praescript.; §. 1. infra de inutil. stipul. Also when some things are divisible and others indivisible. l. 2. and 3. ff. de oblig. et action. The reason why Tribonian explains only these two is that, as said above, the use of things rests chiefly on two things: ownership, and commerce or obligation. The first three divisions pertain to ownership, while the fourth pertains to commerce and obligations, but partly also to ownership. For usufruct is similar to ownership, l. 4. ff. de usufr., and servitudes are similar to ownership in this, that they are rights in a thing.

units.la: Quod ad priore quæstionē attinet, cur s. tantū hic res incorporales ad feferantur, cum sint & aliæ, ut tutela, & libertas, teste Ulp. tit. 19. s. injure. lib. reg. 2. ut usucapio, agnatio, genus &c. teste Cic. in Top. ut possessio, teste Gallo, apud Festum, in verb. possessio. Sic & dominiū, adoptio, matrimonium, dos, peculium, &c. res incorporales dici possūt. Respondeo tantū eas res incorporales hic explicari, quæ ad tractatūrerū pertineat, nō quæ ad jura personarū Usucapio n etsi dicitur Ciceronis res in corpore cōsistēs, ànostris tamē rectius ad priore divisionē; de modis adquirēdi & dominio refertur. Præterea hicē tātū res explicātur, quæ in meo jure consistunt, ut tutela, matrimonium, usucapio, dominium & possessio, etiam in facto consistunt. Factaautem à rebus diligenter distinguenda docet Con. lib. 2. cap. 1. & lib. 5. cap. 1.
units.tr: As for the first question, why only incorporeal things are mentioned here, although there are others, such as guardianship and liberty, as Ulpian witnesses (tit. 19 §. in iure, lib. reg. 2.); usucapion, agnation, the gens, and so on, as Cicero witnesses in the Topica; possession, as Gallus witnesses, quoted by Festus, under the word possessio. So also ownership, adoption, marriage, dowry, peculium, and so on, may be called incorporeal things. I answer that only those incorporeal things are explained here which pertain to the treatment of things, not those which pertain to the rights of persons. Usucapion, though it is called by Cicero a thing consisting in body, is nevertheless more properly referred by us to the earlier division, concerning the modes of acquiring and ownership. Moreover, only those things are explained here which consist in law; guardianship, marriage, usucapion, ownership and possession, which also consist in fact. But Conradus teaches that facts must be carefully distinguished from things, lib. 2 cap. 1. and lib. 5 cap. 1.

units.la: Dices dominiū plane in Jure consistere, & tamen hic esse omissum. Ratio, dominium proprie esse rerum corporalium, ut & possessionem; ideoq; rectius
units.tr: You may say that ownership plainly consists in law, and yet it has been omitted here. The reason is that ownership properly belongs to corporeal things, as does possession; therefore more properly

units.la: OECONOMIA INSTITUTIONUM
units.tr: THE ORDER OF THE INSTITUTES

units.la: de dominio explicari eo loco, ubi de rebus corporalibus, puta in prioribus divisionibus.
units.tr: that ownership is explained in that place where corporeal things are treated, namely in the earlier divisions.

units.la: Quod autem Imp. in l. ult. C. de prescrip. long. temp. actionem rebus incorporalibus adnumerat, id quoq; non obstat. Nam actionum proprius est tractatus, distinctus à tractatu rerum propter duas causas; tum quia earum natura altissime patet; tum quia totius juris velut executio & finis in actionibus & judiciis continetur, ut & supra dictum.
units.tr: Nor does it stand in the way that the Emperor, in l. ult. C. de prescript. long. temp., counts actions among incorporeal things. For actions have their own treatment, separate from the treatment of things, for two reasons: first, because their nature is very far-reaching; second, because the whole of law is, as it were, carried out and completed in actions and judgments, as was said above.

units.la: His autem duabus quaestionibus & hoc tertio adjiciatur, ut de ordine scilicet harum rerum incorporalium breviter videamus, hoc est, cur primum de servitutibus, deinde de usufructu, & usu, postea de hereditate, postremo de obligationibus tractetur.
units.tr: To these two questions a third should be added, so that we may briefly consider the order of these incorporeal things: that is, why first servitudes, then usufruct and use, afterwards inheritance, and last obligations are treated.

units.la: Etcur ptimum de servitutibus & usufructu agatur, haec est ratio, quia aut modo dictum haec jura dominio sunt similima; ideoq; statim tractanda post tractatum de dominio.
units.tr: As for why servitudes and usufruct are treated first, the reason is this: as has been said, these rights are very similar to ownership, and so they are to be treated straight after the treatment of ownership.

units.la: Cur autem prius de servitutibus quàm de usufructu, cùm tamen usufructus dominio sit similior, d. l. 4. ratio sumenda est ex verbis tit. 2. hoc est, eodem modo sunt jura praediorum &c. His enim verbis et a servitutes &c. recte statim adjungitur ipse tit. de servitutibus. Est & altera ratio, quia tractatus de usu & usufructu, sit longior, longioraq; in posteriorem titulum rejici soleant. In ff. tamen contrarius est ordo, ubi prius de usufructu, posterius de servitutibus explicabitur. Ratio differentiae infra explicabitur. Et haec est ratio ordinis de usu & usufructu & servitutibus.
units.tr: Why servitudes are treated before usufruct, although usufruct is more similar to ownership, is to be taken from the words of title 2, namely in the same way the rights of estates etc. For with these words and the servitudes etc. the title itself, concerning servitudes, is rightly joined on at once. There is also a second reason: the treatment of use and usufruct is longer, and longer matters are usually put off to a later title. In the Digest, however, the order is reversed: there usufruct is explained first and servitudes afterwards. The reason for this difference will be explained below. This is the reason for the order of use, usufruct and servitudes.

units.la: Sequitur deinde hereditas, & posterius obligatio. Ratio ordinis est, quia hereditas est modus adquirendi dominii, sive ad dominium pertinet. Nam hereditate & legato adquiritur dominium. l. à Titio. ff. de furt. ideoq; recte de hereditate ibi explicatur, ubi de modis adquirendi dominii. Obligatio autem longe distat à dominio l. 5. de oblig. & act. Deinde quia totus de dominio tractatus prior est tractatu de obligatione, ut supra demonstravimus, merito inter res incorporales obligatio ultimum tenet locum & titulum. Praeterea cum duo sint summa rerum capita, dominii & obligatio, recte fecit Tribunianus, ut de obligatione tum demum tractet, cum dominium quod est caput naturae prius, plene fuerit pertractatum. Est & alia ratio cur obligatio ultimo loco explicetur, quia scilicet per obligationem optima fiat, & proxima digressio ad tractatum de actio. Sut enim actionum duo genera, in rem & personas: in rem actio oritur ex dominio, in personas ex obligatione. (Haec tamen ratio non satis est idonea, nam & a dominio ad actiones nō incommoda trāsitio fieri poterat, nisi quod pauca sut actiones ex dominio, plerēq; omnes ex obligatione.)
units.tr: Next follows inheritance, and after it obligation. The reason for this order is that inheritance is a mode of acquiring ownership, or belongs to ownership, for ownership is acquired by inheritance and by legacy (l. a Titio, ff. de furt.). So it is rightly explained there, where the modes of acquiring ownership are treated. Obligation, on the other hand, is far removed from ownership (l. 5, de oblig. et act.). Further, since the whole treatment of ownership comes before the treatment of obligation, as we have shown above, obligation rightly holds the last place and title among incorporeal things. Moreover, since there are two chief heads of things, ownership and obligation, Tribonian rightly arranged that obligation should be treated only once ownership, which is the head of natural things, had first been fully treated. There is also another reason why obligation is explained in the last place: namely, that through obligation the transition to the treatment of actions is made best and closest. For there are two kinds of actions, in rem and personal: an action in rem arises from ownership, a personal action from obligation. (This reason, however, is not altogether sound, for a transition from ownership to actions could have been made without difficulty, except that few actions arise from ownership, while almost all arise from obligation.)

units.la: His ita praemunitis de hac secunda rerum divisione, in res corporales & incorporales, facilior erit ot dinis ratio eorum quae sequuntur. Nā primū ex iis jā nota est ratio ordinis ad rem 3. de servitutes & tit. 4. Cur rursus de usu & habitatione. Statim subjungitur, quia usus sit similimus usufructui, initio tit. de usu & habit. partim cū usufructu, partim cū usu similitudinem habeat. l. 10. de usu & habit.
units.tr: With these matters thus introduced concerning this second division of things, into corporeal and incorporeal, the order of what follows will be easier to grasp. For first, among these, the reason for the order is already known as regards the thing (3. de servitutibus, tit. 4.): why use and habitation are treated again. Immediately it is added that use is very similar to usufruct, at the beginning of the title de usu et habitatione, partly because it has a likeness to usufruct and partly to use (l. 10. de usu et habit.).

units.la: Sequitur. ff. de usuf. c. 1 ng. temp. possessione. sed videri possit ordo hic perturbatus, Nam tribus rebus incorporalibus servitute, usufructu & usu ordine jam expositis proximum erat de hereditate, quę est quarta res incorporalis explicare, & non de usucapione qui est modus adquirēdi dominii. sed dictum est supra, duas esse præcipuas divisiones, quibus Imp in hoc capite de rebus explicando vtitur: unam de adquisitione partim naturali, partim civili; alteram de rebus corporalib. & incorporalibus, ealsq; interdū separatim, interdū conjūctim hic tractari. Nā primo titulo prior divisio de dominio, alteradivisio tit. 2. 3. 4. & 5. tractatur, idq; separatim. Hic redit ad priorēaliquot titulis intermissis idq; hac rōe, quia hereditas & usucapio sunt simul & res incorporales. & modum dominij adquirendi continent, ideoque de hereditate & usucapione ita tractatur, ut simul quoque dominii adquirendi modi explicentur. Et hunc ordinem indicat Imp. in §. ult. tit. de usu. & habit. Cum ig tur partim sint naturales, partim civiles illis jam expositis subtitulo primo postulat jam ratio, ut de his proximè explicetur.
units.tr: It follows: ff. de usufr. ... long. temp. possessione. But this order may seem disturbed. For after the three incorporeal things, servitude, usufruct and use, have been set out in order, the next thing was to explain inheritance, which is the fourth incorporeal thing, and not usucapion, which is a mode of acquiring ownership. But it was said above that there are two principal divisions which the Emperor uses in this book for explaining things: one concerning acquisition, partly natural and partly civil; the other concerning corporeal and incorporeal things, which are sometimes treated separately and sometimes jointly here. For in the first title the first division, concerning ownership, is treated, and the second division is treated in titles 2, 3, 4 and 5, and this separately. Here he returns to the first division after several titles have been left aside, and this for the following reason: inheritance and usucapion are both incorporeal things and contain the mode of acquiring ownership. So inheritance and usucapion are treated in such a way that the modes of acquiring ownership are explained at the same time. The Emperor also indicates this order in the last paragraph of the title de usu et habitatione. Since, then, some modes are natural and others civil, the arrangement now requires that, after what has been set out in the first title, these should be explained next.

units.la: Civiles autem modi cum sint universales, vel particulares d. §. ult. de singularibus prius agitur, tit. 6. & 7. de universalibus posterius, tit. 10. usq. ad tit. de obl. tū quia singulares civiles, sunt naturalib. similiores. quia & naturales sunt singulares: tum quia singularium tractatio est brevior, universalis maxime hereditatis est longior, & proinde in posteriorem titulum rejecta.
units.tr: Civil modes, however, since they are either universal or particular: the last paragraph, de singularibus, is treated first, in titles 6 and 7; de universalibus afterwards, in title 10 up to the title de obligationibus. This is because the singular civil modes are more similar to the natural ones, since the natural modes are also singular; and because the treatment of singular matters is shorter, while the universal, especially inheritance, is longer, and so it is put off to a later title.

units.la: Civiles autem modi hodie sunt quinq; si nomina spectes, & alias exiguas differētias puta usucapio longi temporis possessio, donatio, legatum, & fideicōmissum. Nam si rem spectes & jus ipsum videntur tantū esse tria. Usucapio) à qua non differt jure, sed tantum nomine & origine longi temporis possessio) donatio & legatū ( à quo ité non differt hodie fideicōmissum, quo ad jus, tantum differt nomine & origine & forma verborum. § 2. infra de legat.)
units.tr: Civil modes today, if you look at the names and some slight differences, are five: usucapion, long-term possession, donation, legacy and fideicommissum. But if you look at the thing itself and the law, there are really only three. Usucapion, from which long-term possession does not differ in law but only in name and origin; donation and legacy, from which fideicommissum today does not differ as to law, but only in name, origin and form of words (§ 2, infra de legatis).

units.la: Ex his autem tribus modis primum de usucapione agitur, titul. 6. deinde de donatione, t. 7. & tandem de legatis, tit. 20. Ratio ordinis, cur prius de usucapione quā de donatione, quia usucapio est antiquior, utpote ex XII. Tab. cū donationis quædam species fit valde recēs puta propter nuptias, ab Impp. inducta, & proinde posterior ff. 3. & est aliud infra de donat.
units.tr: Of these three modes, usucapion is treated first, in title 6; then donation, in title 7; and finally legacies, in title 20. The reason for this order, why usucapion is treated before donation, is that usucapion is older, since it comes from the Twelve Tables, whereas a certain kind of donation, namely that made on account of marriage, was introduced quite recently by the Emperors, and so it is later (ff. 3, and there is another, infra de donationibus).

units.la: Cur autem de legatis posterius agatur, ratio est tū quia legatum est species donationis, f. 1. de legat. tum quia legata pertinent ad testamēta. & proinde de testamentis prius explicandū, post usucapionem & donationē. Proximū quidem erat statim agere de legato, sed eat tractatio rejicitur post tractatum de testamentis, propter causam jam indicatam, de qua & infra latius.
units.tr: As for why legacies are treated later, the reason is, first, that legacy is a kind of donation (f. 1. de legatis), and second, that legacies belong to wills; so wills must be explained first, after usucapion and donation. It would have been most natural to treat legacy straight away, but that treatment is put off until after the treatment of wills, for the reason already given, which will be discussed more fully below.

units.la: Expositis jam modis adquirendi singularibus proximum erat de universalib. explicare ante eos tamen duo titulihic subjiciuntur, de personis dominium vel alienantib. vel adquirentibus, tit. 8. & 9. Ratio est quia cū utile est scire hæc de personis in dominio, tum id maxime pertinet ad modos civiles, & proinde hic de personis agitur, & nō illis, ubi de modis naturalib. tit. 1.
units.tr: Having now set out the singular modes of acquisition, the next thing was to explain the universal ones. But before them two titles are inserted here, concerning the persons who either alienate or acquire ownership, titles 8 and 9. The reason is that, since it is useful to know these things about persons in relation to ownership, this pertains above all to the civil modes; and so persons are treated here, and not in that place where the natural modes are treated, title 1.

units.la: Cur autem de personis alienātibus prius: & posterius de adquirētib. agatur, hæc est ratio: tum quia alienans est velut causa & origo ut adquirens sibi adquirat, hoc est alienatio prior est adquisitione, tum quia titulus de persona adquirentibus convenit non tantum modis singularibus, sed & universalibus, & proinde à tit. 9. de adquirentib. commode fit transitio ad tit. 10. de universalibus, quorum tractatus ad seqq. tit. pertinet, usq; ad tit. de oblig.
units.tr: As for why persons who alienate are treated first, and afterwards those who acquire, the reason is this: first, because the alienator is as it were the cause and origin of the acquirer's acquiring for himself, that is, alienation comes before acquisition; second, because the title concerning persons who acquire applies not only to singular modes but also to universal ones, and so a convenient transition is made from title 9, de adquirentibus, to title 10, de universalibus, whose treatment belongs to the following titles, up to the title de obligationibus.

units.la: Suntautem quatuor hodie modi adquirendi per universitatem: hereditas, bonorum possessio, successio per adrogationem, & bonorum addictio libertatis servandæ causa, §. ult. per quas pers. qui eodem ordine deinceps explicatur.
units.tr: There are four modes of acquiring by universal succession today: inheritance, possession of goods (bonorum possessio), succession by adrogation, and the adjudication of goods for the sake of preserving freedom, §. ult. per quas pers. These are explained in this same order.

units.la: Ratio autem inter eos à tempore sive ordine sumitur. Hereditas .n. quia est antiquissima, utpote ex XII. Tab. amissio tit. de leg. Falc. primo loco explicatur, puta tit. 10. & seqq.
units.tr: The order among them is taken from time or sequence. Inheritance, because it is the most ancient, being derived from the Twelve Tables, is explained first, namely tit. 10. & seqq.

units.la: Huic proximum titulum obtinet bonorum possessi, de qua lib. 3. tit. 10. Ratio, quia hereditati est simillima, & bonorum possessor est velut heres prætorius, l. prætor, 17. de reg. jur. Est enim bonorum possessio ex jure prætorio, missio tit. de bon. poss. quod est posterius l. 1. 2. 5. cum Coff. ff. de orig. jur.
units.tr: Next in place comes possession of goods, treated in lib. 3. tit. 10. The reason is that it most closely resembles inheritance, and the possessor of goods is, as it were, a praetorian heir, l. praetor, 17. de reg. jur. For possession of goods arises from praetorian law, missio tit. de bon. poss., which is later, l. 1. 2. 5. cum Coff. ff. de orig. jur.

units.la: Tertio loco tractatur adrogatio, tit. de successf. per adrog. quæ est ex jure non scripto. Inst. d. tit. Dices, jus non scriptum esse antiquius jure prætorio idcoq; prius adrogationem explicandam quam bonorum possessionem R-spōdeo, id factum propter similitudinem hereditatis & bonorum possessionis. Solet .n. Imp. Sapius in ordine habere rēm similitudinis, l. 2. de vet. ur. unc.
units.tr: Third, adrogation is treated, tit. de successf. per adrog., which arises from unwritten law. Inst. d. tit. You may object that unwritten law is older than praetorian law, and so adrogation should be explained before possession of goods. I answer that this was done on account of the resemblance between inheritance and possession of goods. For the emperors often prefer to observe the order of resemblance, l. 2. de vet. jur. unc.

units.la: Ultimo loco ponitur bonorum addictio, & recte ut puta, quia ut tempore hic modus est ultimus, sic etiam ordine & loco. Est enim inductus constitutione Imp. Marci, nst. tit. de addict. bonor.
units.tr: Last in place comes the adjudication of goods, and rightly so, since this mode is last in time, and so also in order and place. It was introduced by a constitution of the Emperor Marcus, Inst. tit. de addict. bonor.

units.la: Nunc de singulis videamus: & primum quidem de hereditate, quia est duplex ex testamento & ab intestato, prius de testamento, posterius de legitima hereditate explicatur.
units.tr: Let us now look at each in turn, and first at inheritance. Since it is twofold, by testament and ab intestato, the testamentary inheritance is explained first and the inheritance by legitimate succession afterwards.

units.la: Ratio est quia quamdiu spectatur hereditas ex testamento, cessat hereditas ex lege, l. quamdiu, de reg. jur. Idem & de tutela dictum est supra.
units.tr: The reason is that as long as an inheritance by testament is in view, the inheritance by law lapses, l. quamdiu, de reg. jur. The same was said of guardianship above.

units.la: De testamentis igitur, quia tractatio longior est primum ea exponuntur, quæ ad formam & ordinem testamenti pertinent, tit. 10. & sex seqq. deinde ea, quæ ad testamentum tollendum, tit. 17. & 18. tandem ea quæ ad testamenti finem & effectum pertinent, tit. 19. Cujus ordinis perspicua est ratio, quæ dictat, ut rei, de qua agitur, prius explicetur natura quæ est ipsa forma, l. Julianum, adexhib. & ut prius explicetur, quemadmodū quicquam fiat, posterius, quomodo jam factum desinat & tollatur.
units.tr: Concerning testaments, then, since the treatment is longer, first those matters are set out which pertain to the form and order of a testament, tit. 10. & sex seqq. Then those which pertain to the overturning of a testament, tit. 17. & 18. Finally those which pertain to the end and effect of a testament, tit. 19. The reason for this order is plain: it dictates that the nature of the matter under discussion, which is its very form, be explained first, l. Julianum, adexhib.; and that we first explain how a thing comes to be made, and afterwards how what has been made comes to an end and is annulled.

units.la: Itaq; tit. 10. ilatim de forma & sollemnibus testamenti agitur.
units.tr: Thus tit. 10. at once treats of the form and solemnities of a testament.

units.la: Sed quia testamentum aliud est sollemne sive paganicum, aliud non sollemne sive militare, expositio prius sollemni, statim adjicitur nō sollemne, tit. 11. de milit. testam.
units.tr: But since one kind of testament is solemn, or civil, and another is not solemn, or military, the exposition of the solemn comes first, and the non-solemn is added straight after, tit. 11. de milit. testam.

units.la: Jam veroad formam testamenti in primis spectantur personæ, l. 3. qui test. fac. poss. personæ autem in testamento perspicuè sunt duæ, testator & heres, de his duobus ordine explicatur.
units.tr: Now, as to the form of a testament, the persons are considered first, l. 3. qui test. fac. poss. The persons in a testament are clearly two, the testator and the heir, and these two are explained in order.

units.la: Et primum quidem de testatore, quia hic est auctor & origo testamenti,tit.12.quibus non est permiss.&c. deinde de hereditate,tit.13.& 3.seqq.
units.tr: First the testator is treated, since he is the author and origin of the testament, tit. 12. quibus non est permiss. &c. Then the heir, tit. 13. & 3. seqq.

units.la: Heredes autem sunt vel sui, hoc est, liberi in potestate existentes, velnecessarii, vel extranei,innit.tit.de hered.qual.& diff. & de liberis quidé prius, tit.13. postea de quibuslibet heredibus explicatur.
units.tr: Heirs are either sui, that is, children existing under power, or necessary, or extraneous, inn. tit. de hered. qual. & diff. Of children the treatment comes first, tit. 13., and afterwards of heirs in general.

units.la: Ratio, cur prius de liberis est: quia liberi necessario sunt vel instituendi vel exheredandi, antequam alii heredes instituantur. Et hoc est, quod ait Cajus, inter caetera, quae ad ordinanda testamenta necessario desiderantur, principale jus est in liberis instituendis heredibus, vel exheredandis, l. inter caetera 30. de lib.& posth. Et haec igitur est ratio, cur de exheredatione prius, tit.13. deinde de hered. Inst. tit.14. agatur. Dictum est de heredibus, partim suis, partim extraneis.
units.tr: The reason why children come first is that children must either be instituted or disinherited before other heirs are instituted. This is what Gaius means when he says that, among the other things necessarily required for drawing up testaments, the principal right lies in instituting or disinheriting children as heirs, l. inter caetera 30. de lib. & posth. This is therefore the reason why disinheritance is treated first, tit. 13., and then heirs, Inst. tit. 14. It has been said of heirs, partly sui, partly extranei.

units.la: Est & altera divisio in primos & secundos. Primi proprie instituti, secundi proprie substituti dicuntur,l.1. de vulg.& pup.subst. De primis jam dictum est,tit.13.& 14. Proximum est igitur nunc, ut de secundis agatur, hoc est, de subst. tutis. Sed substitutiones sunt rursus duae, pupillaris & vulgaris. De vulgari agitur prius,tit.15. De pupillari posterius,tit.16.
units.tr: There is also another division, into first and second heirs. Those properly instituted are called first, and those properly substituted are called second, l. 1. de vulg. & pup. subst. Of the first we have already spoken, tit. 13. & 14. The next task, therefore, is to treat of the second, that is, of substitutes. But substitutions are again of two kinds, pupillary and vulgar. The vulgar is treated first, tit. 15.; the pupillary afterwards, tit. 16.

units.la: Hos titulos sequitur jam tit.17. quib. mod. testa. infir. optimo jure. Ratioest expositae quae scilicet postulat, ut prius de ordinandis, postea de tollendis testamentis agatur.
units.tr: These titles are rightly followed by tit. 17. quib. mod. testa. infir. The reason is the one already set out: the order requires that testaments be treated first as things to be drawn up, and afterwards as things to be annulled.

units.la: Huic subjungitur titul.18. de inoff. test. quia inter modos tollendi testamenti est & ipsa querela inofficiosi, de qua separatim hic agitur, tum quia late pateat, tum quia multa singularia habeat jura.
units.tr: To this is attached titul. 18. de inoff. test., because among the modes of annulling a testament is the complaint of inofficiousness itself, which is treated here separately, both because it has wide application and because it has many special rules.

units.la: Tandé sequitur tit.19. de here. qual. qui in hoc tractatu de testamentis merito ultimum locum tenet, quia hic tit. tradit jus de aditione hereditatis, qui est finis & effectus ultimus testamenti.
units.tr: Finally comes tit. 19. de here. qual., which in this treatise on testaments rightly holds the last place, because this title sets out the law of entering upon an inheritance, which is the final end and effect of a testament.

units.la: Dices, si tit.19. agit de adit. hær. cur non inscriptus est de adeunda hered. sed de here. qual.& diff. Ratio est quia divisio illa heredum (quam Imp. differentiam vocat) in suos & extraneos initio h.tit. adfertur, & ab eodem initio, coeptus est titulus quamvis ipsa divisio propter aditionem adferatur, quae aditio sine illa divisione intelligi non potest. Nam proprie extranei tantum adire hereditatem dicuntur, sui vero se immiscere. Ad eundem modum & tit.de rer. divis. dicitur tantum ab initio eorum, quae sub isto titulo continentur, h.e. à divisionibus rerum duabus, quae tamen alio pertinet ad modos acquirendi, quare in illo titulo nihil mutandum, quamvis quidam libris manuscriptis repugnantes eum ita inscribant, de rer. divis.& adquir. car. dom.
units.tr: You may ask: if title 19 treats of entering upon an inheritance, why is it not headed de adeunda hered. but de here. qual. & diff.? The reason is that the division of heirs (which the emperor calls the difference) into sui and extranei is introduced at the start of this title, and the title takes its beginning from that same point, although the division itself is brought in for the sake of entering upon an inheritance, which cannot be understood without the division. For strictly only extranei are said to enter upon an inheritance, whereas the sui are said to involve themselves in it. In the same way the title tit. de rer. divis. is named only from the beginning of the matters contained under it, that is, from the two divisions of things; yet this pertains elsewhere to the modes of acquiring. Therefore nothing should be changed in that title, although some manuscript books, disagreeing with this, inscribe it thus, de rer. divis. & adquir. car. dom.

units.la: Adhuc de testamentis sive hereditatibus ex testamento dictum: proximum erat explicare de successionibus ab intestato, sed interiicitur tractatus de legatis & fideicom.& Codicillis. Rationem jam indicavimus, quod haec omnia ex testamento pendeant, & vires plerunque inde capiant, tanquam testamenti partes.
units.tr: So far we have spoken of testaments, or inheritances by testament. The next step would be to explain successions ab intestato, but the treatise de legatis & fideicommissis & Codicillis is inserted. We have already indicated the reason: all these things depend on the testament, and for the most part draw their force from it, as parts of the testament.

units.la: Et hanc causam five rationem ordinis intellexit Imp.initio tit.de legat. Quem proxime sequitur l. 1. 21. de ademp.legat. quia ratio ordinis postulat, ut prius dentur, deinde adimantur legata. Cui titulo adjungitur statim tit. 22. de leg. Falcid. quia & hæc L. ad legata, si non plane adimenda, saltem diminuenda pertinet.
units.tr: The Emperor indicated this same cause, or reason of order, at the beginning of tit. de legat. He immediately follows it with l. 1. 21. de ademp. legat., because the order of things requires that legacies be given first and then revoked. To this title is added straight away tit. 22. de leg. Falcid., because this law, concerning legacies, if they are not wholly to be revoked, at least pertains to their diminution.

units.la: Titulos 7. de legat. sequuntur duo de fideicommissis, propter eorum inter se similitudinem.
units.tr: Titles 7. de legat. are followed by two on fideicommissa, on account of their mutual resemblance.

units.la: Cur autem prius de legatis & fidei commissis agatur, hæc est ratio, quod legata sint & antiquiora & firmiora utpote ex XII. Tab. fideicommissa posterius inventa & demum ab Impp confirmata, initio tit. de leg. Falcid. & §. t. de fideicommiss. hered.
units.tr: The reason why legacies and fideicommissa are treated first is this: legacies are both older and firmer, being derived from the Twelve Tables, whereas fideicommissa were devised later and were finally confirmed by the emperors, at the beginning of tit. de leg. Falcid. and §. 1. de fideicommiss. hered.

units.la: Fideicommissa autem, cum sint vel universalia, vel particularia prius agitur de universalibus tit. 23. posterius de singularibus tit. 24. Ratio est, tum propter dignitatem, plus est enim universale quam singulare: tum exemplo hereditatis & legati quibus hæc fideicommissa comparantur. Universalia quidem hereditati tit. de fidei. commiss. hered. singularia vero legato, §. non vero de legatis.
units.tr: Since fideicommissa are either universal or particular, the universal are treated first, tit. 23., and the particular afterwards, tit. 24. The reason is partly dignity, for the universal is greater than the particular; and partly the analogy with inheritance and legacy, to which these fideicommissa are compared. Universal fideicommissa correspond to inheritance, tit. de fidei. commiss. hered., and particular ones to legacy, §. non vero de legatis.

units.la: Tandem his adjungitur tit. 25. de Codicillis. Ratio autem, cur prius de legatis & fideicommissis, quam de Codicillis agitur, est hæc: tum quia legatorum prior & antiquior est origo, tit. de Codicill. 3. tum quia legatatantum in testamento relinquuntur, l. praeterea de fideicommiss. hered. Codicilli non tantum testamento sed etiam ab intestato fiunt: quare cum Codicilli cum utraque hereditate, tam ex testamento quam ab intestato habeant aliquid commune, recte tit. de Codicillis, quasi in medio ponitur statim post tractatum totum de testamentis, & statim ante tit. ab intestato, qui est tit. 1. l. 3. Cur tamen in ff. contra fiat, hoc est, cur prius de Codicillis, posterius de legatis & fideicommissis agitur, ratio infra suo loco exponetur.
units.tr: Finally, tit. 25. de Codicillis is added to these. The reason why legacies and fideicommissa are treated before Codicils is this: partly because the origin of legacies is earlier and older, tit. de Codicill. 3.; partly because legacies are left only in a testament, l. praeterea de fideicommiss. hered., whereas Codicils are made both in a testament and ab intestato. Therefore, since Codicils share something in common with both kinds of inheritance, both by testament and ab intestato, it is rightly placed, as it were, in the middle: immediately after the whole treatise de testamentis, and immediately before the title ab intestato, which is tit. 1. l. 3. Why the Digest does the reverse, treating de Codicillis first and de legatis & fideicommissis afterwards, will be explained in its place below.

units.la: Liber III. Institut.
units.tr: Book III. Institutes

units.la: SEquitur jam proxime tractatus de hereditate ab intestato. Ratio jam est expolita. Nam cum hereditas sit duplex, testamentaria & legitima, priore jam explicata, proximum est, ut de legitima agatur, Cujus tractatus initium est in princ. lib. 3.
units.tr: Next comes the treatise on inheritance by intestacy. The reason for this order has already been set out. Since inheritance is of two kinds, testamentary and legitimate, and the former has now been explained, the natural next step is to treat the legitimate kind. The beginning of this treatise is in princ. lib. 3.

units.la: Sunt qui lib. 2. perducunt usque ad titulum de obligat. ut sit ibi exordium lib. 3. Sed iis non est assentiendum. I. Quia id repugnat omnibus libris manuscriptis. II. Ipsi Theophilo & aliis Græcis. III. Ipsi Cajo, quem tamen Imp. imitatur: Cajinenim liber tertius agebat de hereditate legitima (ut videre est in lib. Lex Dei, eferc. tit. 16. est collatio legum Mosaic. & civilium antiqui auctoris, edita à P. Pythaeo) IV. Quia sequeretur ut liber secundus justo longior, & liber quartus æquo brevior fieret.
units.tr: Some extend lib. 2. as far as the title de obligat., so that the opening of lib. 3. falls there. But these views should not be accepted. (1) They contradict all the manuscript books. (2) They contradict Theophilus himself and the other Greeks. (3) They contradict Gaius, whom the Emperor nevertheless imitates: the third book of Gaius dealt with legitimate inheritance (as can be seen in the work Lex Dei, eferc. tit. 16., a collation of the Mosaic and civil laws by an ancient author, published by P. Pithou). (4) If this view were right, the second book would be too long and the fourth book too short.

units.la: Hæc autem disputatio de hereditate ab intestato, diligenter hic & latè exponitur, à primo scilicet titulo usque ad titulum 10. de bon.pos. Ordinis generalis hæc est ratio: ut de hereditate ingenuorum legitima prius agatur, posterius de libertorum,tit.7.8.
units.tr: This discussion of inheritance by intestacy is set out here carefully and at length, from the first title through to the tenth title de bon. pos. The reason for this general order is that the legitimate inheritance of freeborn persons is treated first, and the inheritance of freedmen afterwards, tit. 7. 8.

units.la: Quod ad ingenuorum hereditatem attinet, quia hodie sunt quatuor ordines, ad quos eadefertur jure prætorio puta liberorum, agnatorum, cognatorum viri & uxoris: Jure autem civili sunt hodie duo. suorum & agnatorum sive potius legitimorum (etenim & alij non agnati sunt legitimi heredes ab intestato succedentes) primo quidem de suis,tit.1. deinde de legitimis, tit.2.3. & 4. agitur, & postremo de cognatis tit.6. ex jure prætorio. Et hunc ordinem tenuit quoq; prætor, imo ipsa etiam lex XII.Tab.
units.tr: As for the inheritance of freeborn persons: today there are four orders to which it passes by praetorian law, namely children, agnates, cognates, and husband and wife. Under civil law today there are two, the heirs of the household (suorum) and the agnates, or rather the legitimate heirs (for there are other non-agnate legitimate heirs who succeed by intestacy). First the heirs of the household are treated, tit. 1.; then the legitimate heirs, tit. 2. 3. and 4.; and finally the cognates, tit. 6., under praetorian law. The praetor also kept this order, and indeed the Law of the Twelve Tables itself did.

units.la: Quamvis inter legem XII. Tab. & prætorem, ea fuerit differentia, quod jure civili, hoc est, ex L.XII.Tab tantum duo successionis gradus sive ordines scilicet suorum & agnatorum jure prætorio olim essent 8. hodie 4. tantum sunt. Octo sunt autem infrade bon. pos.
units.tr: Between the Law of the Twelve Tables and the praetor there was this difference: under civil law, that is, by the Twelve Tables alone, there were only two degrees or orders of succession, namely the heirs of the household and the agnates; under praetorian law there were formerly eight, and today there are only four. Eight, however, are listed below, de bon. pos.

units.la: Ratio autem hujus ordinis hoc est: cur prius de ordine suorum, quam de ordine agnatorum, est plane naturalis, quæ dicat, ut hereditas primum ad liberos deferatur, quibus ea debetur natura. De his igitur, de suis inquam, sive primo ordine agitur,tit.1. de hered. quæ ab intestato.
units.tr: The reason for this order, that the order of the heirs of the household is treated before the order of the agnates, is plainly natural, since nature requires that the inheritance first pass to children, to whom it is owed by nature. So it is the heirs of the household, I mean the first order, that is treated, tit. 1. de hered. quae ab intestato.

units.la: Hunc sequitur tit. de legit. agnat. success. Ratio est perspicua, quia hic sit secundus ordo sive gradus successionis ab intestato, qui est agnatorum. Ratio autem cur agnatorum gradus sit secundus, est partim civilis, partim naturalis Civilis qui dem quia per agnatos familiæ propagantur, quod est civile Lex enim XII. Tab. ut aliis insebas, ita & in successione, maxime speciabat civilem rationem, ut in primo ordine patriam potestatem, quæ est civilis, in secundo gentem & familiam, unde gentiles & agnati. S d gentilium successio est, jam pridem publicata, teste Cajo d. tit. ult. in lege D.
units.tr: This is followed by the tit. de legit. agnat. success. The reason is clear: this is the second order or degree of succession by intestacy, that of the agnates. The reason why the degree of agnates is second is partly civil and partly natural. It is civil because families are continued through the agnates, which is a civil matter. For the Law of the Twelve Tables, in its succession as in other things, looked chiefly to civil reasons: in the first order to paternal power, which is civil, and in the second to the clan and the family, whence the gentiles and the agnates. But succession of the gentiles was long ago abolished, as Gaius attests, d. tit. ult. in lege D.

units.la: Hunc titulum seq itur tit.3. ad S.C. Tertul. & tit.4. de SC.O. Ratio est, quia secundus ordo olim quidem tantum continebat agnatos & proinde agnatorum dicebatur: sed ex novis II. sive Senatusconsult hodie continet non tantum agnatos, sed etiam matrem & liberos, ut mater liberis, & liberi matri succedant; & proinde hic ordo dicitur legitimorum.
units.tr: This title is followed by tit. 3. ad S.C. Tertul. & tit. 4. de SC.O. The reason is that the second order formerly contained only agnates and was therefore called the order of agnates. But by the new laws, the senatus-consulta, it now contains not only agnates but also the mother and children, so that the mother succeeds her children and the children succeed the mother; and so this order is called that of the legitimate heirs.

units.la: Et primum quidem, ut dictum est, agitur de agnatis, quia sunt antiquiores legitimi, ex L. XII. Tab. deinde agitur de aliis legitimis; & prius quidem de matre ut succedat liberis, posterius de liberis, ut succedant matri Ratio est, quia de matre prius fuit introductum SC. Tertul. de liberis posterius Orficianum.
units.tr: First, as has been said, the agnates are treated, because they are the older legitimate heirs under the Law of the Twelve Tables. Then the other legitimate heirs are treated: first the mother, so that she succeeds her children, and afterwards the children, so that they succeed the mother. The reason is that the Senatus-consultum Tertullianum was introduced earlier for the mother, and the Orfitian for the children later.

units.la: Hunc secundum ordinem legitimorum, sequitur tertius cognatorum ordo: Sed hic est prætorius illi civiles sunt, ideoque posteriore loco explicantur: Prætoria enim civilibus sunt posteriora.
units.tr: After this second order of legitimate heirs follows the third order, that of cognates. But this order is praetorian, whereas the others are civil, and so it is explained in the last place, since praetorian matters come after civil ones.

units.la: Huic titulo adjungitur tit.6. de grad. cognat. propterea quod in successione ab intestato graduum cognitio sit perutilis, multo magis quam in nuptiis, quia prohibitæ nuptiæ ipsa natura jure & paucis regulis sunt notæ. Quare rectius in jure civili de gradibus in materia de successionib. agitur quam in jure Canonico in materia nuptiarum.
units.tr: To this title is joined tit. 6. de grad. cognat., because knowledge of degrees is very useful in succession by intestacy, much more so than in marriage, since forbidden marriages are known by nature itself, by law, and by a few rules. Hence it is more proper for the civil law to treat degrees of kinship in the matter of successions than for the canon law to treat them in the matter of marriages.

units.la: Recte autem hic titulus in fine successionum ponitur, quia servit omnibus successionum ordinibus, primo secundo & tertio. Hunc titulum sequitur in vulgaribus libris tit. de servili cognatio. Non recte. I. Quia in manuscriptis veteribus non exstat. II. Quia Græci eum nō agnoscunt. III. s. repetitis, d. tit. satis indicat ea quæ ind. tit. de servili cognat. habentur, pertinere omnia ad tit. de gradib. cognatorum.
units.tr: This title is rightly placed at the end of the successions, because it serves all the orders of succession, the first, second and third. The common books follow this title with de servili cognatio. This is wrong: (1) it does not occur in the old manuscripts; (2) the Greeks do not recognise it; (3) the passage s. repetitis, d. tit. sufficiently shows that what is found under ind. tit. de servili cognat. all belongs to the title de gradib. cognatorum.

units.la: Hactenus de successione ingenuorum nunc de successione libertorū. Nam inter has duas successionum species, aliquæ sunt differentiæ, & olim erant multæ, s. sed nostra. de success. libert. qui est aut certe esse debet, tit.7.
units.tr: So much for the succession of freeborn persons; now for that of freedmen. For between these two kinds of succession there are some differences, and formerly there were many, s. sed nostra. de success. libert., as there are or at least ought to be, tit. 7.

units.la: Adjungitur illi tit. 8. de adsignatione libertorum, quia adsignatio facere solet, ut cum patronus plures habeat liberos, successio liberti non ad omnes liberos, sed ad eum tantum de liberis pertineat, cui à patre in testamento fuerit adsignatus libertus. Recte igitur de adsignatione hic agitur, ubi de successione.
units.tr: To this is added tit. 8. de adsignatione libertorum, because assignment usually has the effect that, when a patron has several children, the succession of a freedman does not pass to all the children but only to the child to whom the freedman was assigned by the father in his will. Rightly, then, assignment is treated here, where succession is treated.

units.la: Et hactenus de primo modo adquirendi per universitatem, puta per hereditatem, tam ex testamento, quam ab intestato dicta hæc sint.
units.tr: So far, the first mode of acquiring through a universal title, that is, through inheritance both under a will and by intestacy, has been discussed.

units.la: Huic jam proximè adjunguntur duæ species adquisitionis universalis, puta bonorum possessio, tit.9. Et huic tertia species adrogatio, t.t.10. tandem ultima addictio bonorum libertatis servandæ causa. Ratio ordinis inter has species, cur una alteram præcedat, supra jam est explicata.
units.tr: Immediately after this come two further kinds of universal acquisition, namely possession of goods, tit. 9.; and, as a third kind, adrogation, t.t. 10.; and finally the last, the adjudication of goods for the sake of preserving freedom. The reason for the order among these kinds, why one precedes another, has already been explained above.

units.la: Erant olim & aliæ species adquisitionum universalium, ut bonorum emptio, & altera ex Senatusconsulto Claudiano. Sed utraque est sublata. Prior quidem desuetudine jam pridem, altera à Justin. & de his est tit.12. quo velut concluditur totus tractatus de modis adquirendi dominii, quia ad hunc usq; titulum omnes ea sunt explicatæ tam naturales, quam civiles, & ex his civilibus tam generales, quam particulares.
units.tr: There were formerly also other kinds of universal acquisition, such as purchase of goods, and another under the Claudian senatus-consultum. But both have been abolished: the former long ago by disuse, the other by Justinian, and about these there is tit. 12., by which the whole treatise on the modes of acquiring ownership is, as it were, concluded, since up to this title all of them, natural as well as civil, and of the civil ones both general and particular, have been explained.

units.la: Ex quinq; rebus incorporalib. supra propositis expositæ sunt quatuor. Restat jam quinta, nempe Obligatio, ideoq; bono ordine jam transit ad obligationes Imp. tit.13. Nunc, inquit transeamus ad obligationes, quia hæ solæ restant ex secundo capit. de rebus, ut intelligitur ex superioribus. Diximus autem supra, cur in hoc capite ultimo locum obtineat obligatio; diximus quoq; cur non recte quidam hic novi libri puta tertij initium faciant.
units.tr: Of the five incorporeal things set out above, four have been explained. There remains now the fifth, namely obligation, and so in good order the Emperor now passes to obligations, Imp. tit. 13. "Now," he says, "let us pass to obligations, since these alone remain of the second head concerning things, as is clear from what came before." We have said above why obligation holds the last place in this head, and we have also said why certain recent books are wrong to begin the third book here.

units.la: Nunc igitur de obligationum collocatione seu ordine videamus, primùm summatim, deinde singulatim. Latè enim hic tractatus patet à tit.15. de oblig. usque ad tit.6. lib.4. de action. Ergo hujus tractatus de obligationibus duæ summæ sunt partes, una communis, altera specialis.
units.tr: Now, then, let us look at the arrangement or order of the obligations, first in summary and then in detail. For this treatise on obligations extends widely, from tit. 15. de oblig. to tit. 6. lib. 4. de action. Therefore this treatise on obligations has two main parts, one general and one special.

units.la: Communis, in qua definitiones & divisiones adferûtur, uno titulo eoq; primo continetur. Communia enim sunt particularibus priora. Arist. de part.animal. & iam sæpe dict.
units.tr: The general part, in which definitions and divisions are given, is contained in one title, and that the first. For general matters come before particular ones, Arist. de part. animal., and as I have often said already.

units.la: Specialis pars, quæ est perspicua, divisiones duas continet. §.2.ejusdem tit. Primum enim obligationes sunt aut ex contractu, aut quasi, aut ex maleficio, aut quasi. Deinde (quæ est subdivisio) obligationes ex contractu aut re, aut verbis, aut literis, aut nudo consensu fiunt.
units.tr: The special part, which is plain, contains two divisions, §. 2. ejusdem tit. For first, obligations arise either from contract, or quasi-contract, or from wrongdoing, or quasi-wrongdoing. Then (this is a subdivision) obligations from contract arise either from a thing, from words, from writing, or from bare consent.

units.la: Quod ad primam divisionem attinet, quæ est potissimum bimembris, prius agitur de contractu, quam de delicto, hac ratione: tum quia contractus delictis videantur antiquiores (homines enim initio, ut valde probi, delicta non committebant) tum quia delicta sunt odiosa, contractus favorabiliores, ut quia ex iis vitæ humanæ societas conservatur.
units.tr: As to the first division, which has mainly two parts, contract is treated before delict, for two reasons: first, because contracts seem older than delicts (at the beginning, men being very upright, did not commit delicts); second, because delicts are odious while contracts are more favourable, since human society is preserved by them.

units.la: Quod ad alteram divisionem attinet, primo loco collocant obligationes quæ re contrahuntur, tit.14.quib.mod.re contr.oblig. Sunt autem quinque contractus qui re fiunt, & primus est mutuum.
units.tr: As to the second division, they place first the obligations contracted by the thing itself, tit.14.quib.mod.re contr.oblig. There are five contracts made by the thing, and the first is the loan (mutuum).

units.la: Ratio autem, cur primus locus detur contractibus qui re fiunt, est, tum quia hi contractus, cum adquisitionibus dominii (de quibus proximè est actum) majorem habeant similitudinem, quàm reliqui, in eo scilicet, quod ut in adquisitionibus dominii, ita & in his contractibus naturalis quædam traditio ab uno in alium requiratur: tum quia & re fieri dicuntur, unde & nomen habent. hoc est, natura & facto quodam tradendi.
units.tr: The reason the first place is given to contracts made by the thing is that these contracts bear a greater resemblance than the rest to acquisitions of ownership (which we have just treated). Namely, as in acquisitions of ownership, so in these contracts a certain natural handing over from one party to another is required. They are also said to be made by the thing (re), which is where they get their name, that is, by nature and by some act of handing over.

units.la: Ex his autem contractibus cur mutuum primo loco ponatur: hæc est ratio: tum quia hic contractus est omnium celeberrimus & frequentissimus, tum quia ad dominii adquisitionem proximus: in mutuo enim transfertur dominium in reliquis non item, excepto debito.
units.tr: The reason the loan is placed first among these contracts is this: it is the most celebrated and most frequent of all of them, and it is closest to the acquisition of ownership, for in a loan ownership passes, which does not happen in the others, except for the debt.

units.la: Mutuo proprie adjungitur indebitum propter similitudinem, de quo in §. item quoq; ver. nam proinde, de obl. quæ re contrah. de quibus modis Cujac. late 3.obs.1.& 8.obs.34.
units.tr: Undue payment (indebitum) is properly joined to the loan because of their similarity. On these modes Cujacius writes at length, 3.obs.1.& 8.obs.34.

units.la: Tertius locus tribuitur commodato, quod præcedit depositum & pignus, hac ratione: quia in commodato usus etiam transfertur: in deposito & pignore, custodia excepta antichresi, quæ usum quoque continet & fructum.
units.tr: The third place is given to commodatum, which precedes deposit and pledge, for this reason: in commodatum the use also is transferred; in deposit and pledge only custody is transferred, except in antichresis, which includes the use and the fruit as well.

units.la: Cur autem sit depositum prius pignore, ratio videtur, quia commodato fit simile. Utrumque enim est gratuitum, & fit inter amicos, §.item it,z.h. tit.l sint certo, §.videndum. ff. commod. Sed in ff. contrarius est ordo, ibi pignus prius est depositò. Ratio dicetur inf. ad ff. Et hæc de prima specie contractuum, hoc est, obligationum ex contractu, quæ fieri dicuntur, hic uno titulo 14. in ff. aliquot libris explicantur.
units.tr: Why deposit comes before pledge seems to be that it resembles commodatum. For both are gratuitous and are made between friends, §.item it,z.h. tit.l sint certo, §.videndum. ff. commod. But in the Digest the order is reversed, and there pledge comes before deposit. The reason will be given below at the Digest. And these matters concerning the first kind of contracts, that is, obligations from contract, which are said to be made by the thing, are explained here under one title, 14, and in several books of the Digest.

units.la: Nunc de altera, quæ fit verbis. tit.15.de ver.obl. Ratio autem cur obligatio, quæ fit verbis, præcedat obligationem quæ fit literis, & obligationem quæ fit nudo consensu, hæc est, tum quia hæc quæ fit verbis, etiam de dominio agat, & proinde proxima debet esse mutuo, cum emptio & locatio non agant de dominio, tum quia haec duo re & verbis injure proximè opposita sint, & proinde obligationem re, commodè sequitur obligatio verbis: tum denique, quia hæ duæ species obligationum re & verbis, sunt non nudæ conventiones: cum emptio & locatio nudo consensu fiat. At non nuda sunt nudis firmiora, & proinde priora.
units.tr: Now to the second kind, which is made by words, tit.15.de ver.obl. The reason why the obligation made by words precedes the obligation made by writing and the obligation made by bare consent is this: first, because this one, made by words, also treats of ownership, and so should be next to the loan, since sale and lease do not treat of ownership; second, because these two, by thing and by words, are most closely opposed in law, and so the obligation by thing is fittingly followed by the obligation by words; and finally, because these two kinds of obligation, by thing and by words, are not bare agreements, whereas sale and lease are made by bare consent. But what is not bare is firmer than what is bare, and so comes earlier.

units.la: Inter hos autem 6.tit. de verb.obl. ratio ordinis est perspicua & optima. Primo enim ut de principali verb.obl.agitur, tit.15. & 4.seqq. deinde de acceptoria, de fidejussione. Principalis deinde verb. obl. quia alia est utilis, alia inutilis, justa ratione prius utilis explicatur, tit.15.&3.seqq. & post de inutilibus tit.19. Sic & de legatis prius de utilibus, posterius de inutilibus agitur sub tit.de legatis, §.legari autem.
units.tr: Among these titles on verbal obligations, the order is clear and the best. First the principal verbal obligation is treated, tit.15 and the four following titles; then the accessory obligation, suretyship (de fidejussione). Then, since the principal verbal obligation is of two kinds, one useful and the other useless, the useful is explained first for good reason, tit.15 and the three following, and afterwards the useless ones, tit.19. So too with legacies: the useful are treated first and the useless later, under the title on legacies, §.legari autem.

units.la: Quod ad utilem attinet, quia substantia ejus est ipsa forma: forma autem maxime in verbis sive interrogationibus & responsionibus est posita, quæ variant, puta, modo materia, persona origine, &c. primo de formalib. hoc est, formulis stipulationum agitur, & ordine quidem, primum inquam de forma, modo & materia, tit. 15. deinde de personis. tit.16.&17. de origine sive auctoritate tit.18 præcipuus autem est tit.15. qui ad modum & materiam obligationum pertinet.
units.tr: As to the useful kind: its substance is its form, and form lies chiefly in the words, that is, the questions and answers, which vary according to mode, matter, persons, origin, and so on. So first it treats of the formal matters, that is, the formulas of stipulations, and in order: first of form, mode and matter, tit.15; then of persons, tit.16 and 17; of origin or authority, tit.18. But the principal title is tit.15, which concerns the mode and matter of obligations.

units.la: Quod ad personas attinet, in aliis contractibus, cum sint tantum duæ, una obligans, altera obligata in hac obligatione id est perspicuum, ut non tantum sint duæ, sed interdum etiam binæ obligantes, binæ obligatæ.
units.tr: As to persons, in other contracts, since there are only two parties, one obliging and the other obliged, this is plain. In this obligation, however, there are sometimes not only two parties but also two obliging and two obliged.

units.la: Hinc est, quod singularis tit. de binis personis hic ponatur, qui est tit. 16. de duob. reis, &c. Fit quidem id etiam in aliis, sed in hac, verb. obl. sit sæpius.
units.tr: Hence the special title on two persons is placed here, tit.16, on two debtors, and so on. This happens also in others, but in this verbal obligation it happens more often.

units.la: Ad personas quoq; pertinet tit 17. de stip. serv. quamvis servorum non sit propriè persona ut initio d.tit. Cur autem in hac ver. obl. tit sit proprius de servis cum & in aliis obligationibus servi interveniant, ut est tit generalis, infra per quam perf. ratio hæc est: quia magna est varietas stipulationum, quod ad formam attinet & rem, de qua agitur, ita ut ad jus ipsum magnopere interfit quid, qua forma stipuletur servus.
units.tr: To persons also pertains tit.17, on the stipulation of slaves, although a slave is not properly a person, as at the beginning of that title. Why in this verbal obligation there is a title of its own on slaves, when slaves also take part in other obligations (as in the general title below, through which...), the reason is that there is great variety in stipulations as regards form and the matter in question, so that for the law itself it matters greatly what form a slave uses in stipulating.

units.la: Ad eandem formulæ doctrinam pertinet tit. 18. de divis. stipul. alia est enim forma stipulationum prætoriarum, alia conventionalium. Hunc titul sequitur tit.19. de inutil. stipul. Ratio supra expolita est, ut in titul seq. de fidejuss.
units.tr: To the same doctrine of formulas pertains tit.18, on the division of stipulations, for one form of stipulation is praetorian and another conventional. This title is followed by tit.19, on useless stipulations. The reason has been set out above, as it is for the following title on suretyship.

units.la: Cur autem, cum fidejussor omni obligationi accedat, non tantum verbis sed etiam re hic tamen ubi de verb obl agitur, ponatur iste tit. Ratio est, tum quia fidejussor in ventus potissimum videatur propter verborum obligationem. Verbis enim non statim fides habetur: tum quia fidejussor tantum verbis constituatur.
units.tr: Why, although a surety attaches to every obligation, not only verbal but also real, this title is nevertheless placed here, where verbal obligation is treated: the reason is, first, that the surety seems chiefly to be introduced on account of the verbal obligation, since trust is not at once placed in words; second, because a surety is constituted by words alone.

units.la: Et hæc de secunda specie obligationum, quæ fit verbis, quam proximè sequitur ea obligatio, quæ litteris fieri dicitur, tit.21. de litterar. obl. Ratio est propter similitudinem quae ei est cum priore ver. obl. I enim utraq; est civilis. II Litterae nihil videnturaliud, quam natura absentium. III. Quia ut modo dictum obligatio & verbis & litteris, utraque est non nuda.
units.tr: And this is what I have to say about the second kind of obligation, the one made by words. Closely following it is the obligation said to be made by writing (litteris), tit.21, de litterarum obligationibus. The reason is the similarity it has with the former verbal obligation: first, both are civil; second, letters are nothing other than the presence of absent persons; third, because, as just said, the obligation by both words and letters is not bare.

units.la: Restat 4. species, & praecipuè Emptio, locatio, cui similis est Emphyteusis de qua in §. adeò, de locat. societas & mandatum: quae species ita deinceps ord. nec exponuntur, propositò tamen brevi titulo generali, tit. 22. de obliga. quae conf. inf. Communia enim seu generalia, ut dictum sunt priora. ¶ Inter speciaila autem primo loco ponitur emptio, tum quia est frequentissima, tum quia ad vitam maximè necessaria, de qua tit. 23. ¶ Huic proximè adjungitur, l. t. 24. de locatione. ¶ Tertium locum obtinet societas, tit. 25. & praeponitur mandato ratio est quia societas prioribus emptioni & locationi magis est similis quàm mandatū in eo scilicet, quod in duobus illis prioribus uterq; contrahentium sentit lucrum quod idem fit in societate. ¶ At in mandato plerunq; alter tantum puta mandans, cujus causa fere fit mandatum lucrum capit alter mandatarius non capit nisi interdum honorariū, sed hoc ad substantiam non pertinet. l. 1. §. mandatum. l. 6. ff. mand. Quaero, cur in ff. contrariūs sit ordo? Ratio dicitur infra ad ff.
units.tr: There remains the fourth kind, and chiefly sale and lease, to which emphyteusis is similar, on which see §.adeo, de locat.; then partnership and mandate. These kinds are then explained in order, after a brief general title has been set out, tit.22, de obligationibus, which is explained below; for the general matters, as said, come first. Among the special kinds, sale is placed first, both because it is most frequent and because it is most necessary to life, tit.23. Next to it is joined lease, tit.24, de locatione. Partnership holds the third place, tit.25, and is placed before mandate. The reason is that partnership is more similar to the former sale and lease than mandate is, namely in that in those two former both contracting parties feel the gain, which is the same in partnership. But in mandate usually only one party gains, namely the mandator, for whose sake the mandate is mostly made; the mandatary gains nothing except sometimes an honorarium, and this does not pertain to the substance, l.1 §.mandatum; l.6 ff. mand. It is asked why in the Digest the order is reversed. The reason is given below at the Digest.

units.la: Exposito adhuc quadrimembris divisionis obligationum membro primo, quod est de obligationibus ex contractu, recte & ordine eiadjungitur alterum membrum de quasi contractu propter similitudinem. Adferuntur autem f. species quasi contractus, & sub uno t. t. 27. continentur, puta negotia gesta, tutela, communio hereditatis aditio & indebitum.
units.tr: Having set out the first member of the four-part division, which concerns obligations from contract, the second member, on quasi-contract, is rightly and in order added, because of their similarity. Five species of quasi-contract are brought forward, and they are contained under one title, 27: agency without mandate (negotia gesta), guardianship, co-ownership of an inheritance, acceptance of an inheritance, and undue payment.

units.la: Cur autem primus locus detur negotiis gestis, haec est ratio: quia hic quasi contractus est proximo priori mandati contra cui similLimus tantum in eo differunt, quod contractus fit mandato Domini, quasi contractus sine mandato.
units.tr: As to why the negotia gesta are given the first place, the reason is this: this quasi-contract is closest to the preceding contract of mandate, from which it differs only in this, that the contract arises from the mandate of the owner, whereas the quasi-contract arises without a mandate.

units.la: Eadem similitudo facit, ut secundus locus detur tutelae, f. tutores. d. tit. Nam in his tribus, ut mandato negotiis, tutela, gerantur negotia; in illis majorum, in hac tantum pupilli.
units.tr: The same similarity causes tutela to be given the second place, namely the tutors, as in the same title. For in these three, as in mandate, business is conducted: in negotia gesta, the affairs of others; in tutela, the affairs of the pupil alone; in the former, those of adults.

units.la: III. Exponitur communio, f. finter, d. tit. 27. Et hic quoq; ratio est à similitudine, quae est communioni cum societate, de qua dictus tit. de mand.
units.tr: III. Communio is explained, namely the joint ownership, in the same title 27. And here too the reason lies in the similarity, since communio is akin to societas, of which the title on mandate speaks.

units.la: IV. Species est aditio hereditatis quia haec est similis tertiae communioni Nam ut tertia de collegatariis & heredibus inter se, itahaec quarta est de heredib. & legatariis, qua scilicet haeres obligatus est legatariis, ut in prioriheres heredi, legatarius legatario.
units.tr: IV. Aditio hereditatis is the next species, because it is similar to the third, communio. For as the third concerns co-legatees and heirs among themselves, so this fourth concerns heirs and legatees, namely that the heir is bound to the legatees as, in the former case, one heir is bound to another and one legatee to another.

units.la: V. Locum obtinet indebitum, f. item is cui tit. 27. Ratio est, tum quia indebitum, ut neque verè est contractus licet numeretur inter contractus, f. isquoque, tit. 14. ita nec est proprie quasi contractus. Est enim verius quidam distractus, ut hic ait Imp tum quia ab hac specie commodè fiat transitio ad tit. seq. non proximum sed alterum 29. hoc est, fit transitio ab hoc distractu ad modos tollendae obligationis.
units.tr: V. Indebitum holds the fifth place, namely the title on the one to whom something is paid that was not owed, in the same title 27. The reason is twofold: first, because indebitum, although it is numbered among the contracts, is in truth not a contract (as the title 14 also says), and so it is not properly a quasi-contract either. It is rather a certain distraction, as the Emperor here says. Second, because from this species the transition is conveniently made to the following title, not the next but the one after, namely the 29th; that is, the transition is made from this distraction to the ways of dissolving an obligation.

units.la: Prius enim interijcitur tit.28.de personis,per quas obligatio adquiritur,exemplo dominii: de cujus modis adquirendi prius agitur, postea de personis, per quas dominium adquiritur, tit.9. lib.2. Notum est autem in tractatu rerum, haec duo capita, dominium & obligationem esse summa, ideoque non male eodem fere ordine explicantur.
units.tr: For first the title 28 on the persons through whom an obligation is acquired is inserted, on the model of ownership: concerning the modes of acquiring ownership is treated first, afterwards concerning the persons through whom ownership is acquired, title 9 of book 2. It is known, moreover, from the treatment of things that these two heads, ownership and obligation, are the chief ones, and therefore it is not wrongly explained in nearly the same order.

units.la: Huc igitur titulum 28.per quas personas sequitur tit.29. quib.mod.toll.oblig. Ratio ordinis est perspicua quae postulat, ut prius de re constituenda, ut hic de obligationibus & posteriùs de tollenda & finienda agatur, ut & supra de potestate dominica & patria, de tutela & testamento factum.
units.tr: Therefore the title 28, on the persons through whom, is followed here by title 29, on the ways by which obligations are dissolved. The reason for this order is plain: it requires that one first treats of establishing a thing, as here of obligations, and afterwards of dissolving and ending it, as was also done above with dominical and paternal power, and with tutela and testament.

units.la: Quaero, curde oblig.est tit,de ea tollenda & nullus est de dominio tollendo? Ratio est, quia dominium adquiri non potest, nisi admittatur prius ab altero, & proinde ex adquisitione satis intelligitur, de amissione, ut contrariorum eadem est ratio.
units.tr: You may ask why there is a title on dissolving an obligation, and none on dissolving ownership? The reason is that ownership cannot be acquired unless it is first transferred by another, and so from the acquisition one sufficiently understands the loss too, since the reason for contraries is the same.

units.la: Quod ad modos tollendae obligationis attinet, qui sunt quatuor praecipuè, de quibus hoc tit.agitur, solutio, acceptilatio, novatio & consensus sive nuda voluntas.
units.tr: As to the modes of dissolving an obligation, which are chiefly four and with which this title deals: payment, acceptilation, novation, and consent or bare will.

units.la: Ordo inter modos istos tollendae obligationis idem servatur, qui inter modos contrahendae sive constituendae. Nam I. explicatur solutio, qui modus re tollit obligationem, initi. tit secundo & tertio ponuntur acceptilatio & novatio, quae verbis, §.item per acceptilationem,& §.seq.l.1.de acceptil. 2. de novat. IV. & ultimus consensus exponitur, sive potius dissensus, §. ult.d.tit.
units.tr: The order among these modes of dissolving an obligation is the same as that among the modes of contracting or establishing one. For first payment is explained, which mode by the thing itself dissolves the obligation, at the beginning of the title. In the second and third places are put acceptilation and novation, which are effected by words: §. item per acceptilationem and the following §., l. 1 de acceptilatione, l. 2 de novatione. Fourth and last, consent is set out, or rather dissent, §. ult. of the same title.

units.la: Litterarum obligatio non habet specialem modum tollendi, tum quia hodie vox est propria species obligationum (ut videtur ex tit.) sed pertinet ad mutuum, l.1.de novat.l.1.de oblig. tum quia modus tollendi per litteras ad consensum referri potest. Sive enim quis praesens consentiat, sive absens per litteras vel nuntium, idem est Juris, l.1. de contrah. empt. Haec igitur est ratio ordinis inter hos modos tollendae obligationis, quae videtur dictare, ut idem ordo servetur in tollendis obligationibus, quae in constituendis.
units.tr: The obligation by writing does not have a special mode of dissolving, partly because today the writing is itself a proper species of obligation (as appears from the title), but it belongs to mutuum, l. 1 de novationibus, l. 1 de obligationibus; partly because the mode of dissolving by writing can be referred to consent. For whether someone consents in person or absent by letter or messenger, the law is the same, l. 1 de contrahenda emptione. This, then, is the reason for the order among these modes of dissolving an obligation, which seems to dictate that the same order be observed in dissolving obligations as in establishing them.

units.la: Est & altera ratio singularis, primo quidem de solutionibus tum denique, quia ad omnes obligationes tollendas valeat. Secundo ponitur acceptilatio. Est enim imaginaria solutio. §.item per acceptilat. Huic adjungitur novatio, §.praeterea. Eadem scilicet similitudinis ratione. Nam ut acceptilatio fit verbis, ita & novatio l.1.l.8.§.1.de novat. Ultimo ponitur voluntas nuda sive consensus: hac ratione, quia hic modus est specialis, eoque tantum illae obligationes tolluntur, quae fiunt consensu, §.sin.
