At tres priores modi sunt generales, iisque omnes obligationes sive contractus tolluntur, ut initio tit. §. 1. l. 1, de novat.
units.tr: There is also another, peculiar reason: payment is put first, because it is the most general and applies to dissolving all obligations. Acceptilation is placed second; for it is an imaginary payment, §. item per acceptilationem. Novation is joined to it, §. praeterea, by the same reason of similarity: for as acceptilation is effected by words, so is novation, l. 1, l. 8 §. 1 de novationibus. Last is placed bare will or consent, for this reason: because this mode is special, and only those obligations are dissolved by it which arise by consent, §. sin. But the three former modes are general, and by them all obligations or contracts are dissolved, as at the beginning of the title, §. 1, l. 1 de novationibus.

units.la: Institut. Lib. IV.
units.tr: Institutes, Book IV.

units.la: EXposita sunt duo membra divisionis obligationum quadrimembris, una ex contractu, altera ex quasi, cui jam proximè adjungitur tertium ex delicto, idque initio lib.4. ne vel secundus liber vel tertius æquo fit longior, vel quartus brevior, quod & sup. dictum. Ratio quoque supra exposita est, cur obligationes ex delicto in tertium sint locum rejectæ. Delictorum igitur cum quatuor sint species, furtum; rapina, damnum, injuria, ut initio tit.1. inter eas hic ordo servatur, ut prius de furto, posterius de rapinis, & reliqua deinceps explicentur.
units.tr: The two members of the fourfold division of obligations have been set out: one arising from contract, the other from quasi-contract. Next to these is immediately added a third, arising from delict, and this is treated at the start of Book 4, so that the second book does not become too long or the fourth too short, as was also said above. The reason why obligations from delict were placed third has also been explained above. Since there are four kinds of delict (theft, robbery, damage, and injury, as stated at the start of the first title), the order followed here is that theft is treated first, robbery second, and the rest in turn.

units.la: Cur prius de furto hæc est ratio, tum quia furtum est antiquissimum, utpote ex II. XII Tab. cum reliqua vel sint prætoria ut rapina & injuria, vel saltem minus antiqua, ut est damnum quod est ex L. Aquil. XII. Tab. recentiore, 6. sunt autem, de noxal. actl. De furto igitur agit primo titulo.
units.tr: The reason for taking theft first is that it is the most ancient, since it comes from the Twelve Tables, whereas the others are either praetorian, like robbery and injury, or at least more recent, like damage, which comes from the Lex Aquilia, a later law than the Twelve Tables (6, and also the title on noxal actions). So the first title deals with theft.

units.la: Cur accipiatur materia de furto specialiter, & tit. concipiatur generaliter de obligat. quæ ex del. nasc. Ratio est, quia initium tituli est generale. Solent autem initia sæpe titulo nomen dare, ut tit. de stat. hom. de tutel. de rer. divif.
units.tr: Why the subject matter of theft is named specifically, while the title is framed in general terms on obligations arising from delict, is explained as follows: the opening of a title is general. Moreover, the opening words often give the title its name, as in the titles on the status of persons, on guardianship, on the division of things.

units.la: Hunc tit. sequitur tit. vi bon. rapt. hoc est, rapina secundum tit. obtinet, quia furto est persimilis, saltem manifesto, & inde vulgo rapina dici solet improbum furtum initio d.tit.
units.tr: This title is followed by the title on goods taken by force, that is, robbery, which is treated in accordance with the title, since it is very similar to theft, at least to manifest theft; and for this reason robbery is commonly called an improper theft, at the start of the same title.

units.la: Tertio titulo explicatur damnum. l.3. ad l. Aquil. ratio, cur damnum priore loco quam injuria, de qua titulo quarto exponatur, est hæc: tum quia damnum est civile injuria est prætoria; tum quia damnum simile est duobus prioribus, injuria non est, in eo scilicet, quia tria illa sunt de re familiari sola injuria vindictam tantum persequitur. l.6. de sepulch. viol.l. 2.§. emancipatu. de collat. bon.
units.tr: In the third title damage is explained (the Lex Aquilia, title 3). The reason why damage comes before injury, which is treated in the fourth title, is this: first, because damage is a civil matter whereas injury is praetorian; second, because damage resembles the two previous delicts while injury does not, namely in that the first three concern property alone, whereas injury pursues only vengeance (the title on violation of burial, and the law on the emancipated, on collation of goods).

units.la: Restat jam quartum membrum ex quasi delicto, de quo agitur proximo tit 5. Hujus autem tres sunt species, & sub eo titulo adferuntur: judicis peccatum male judicantis dejectio vel effusio è cænaculo, & recepti in hauta, caupone, stabulario, amisso.
units.tr: There remains now the fourth member, arising from quasi-delict, which is treated in the next title, the fifth. Under this title three kinds are listed: the judge's fault in judging badly; the throwing down or pouring out from a room; and the case of the innkeeper, the stable-keeper, and the one who receives goods on board, in respect of what is lost.

units.la: De judicis peccato prius agitur, tum ni fallor propter dignitatem, tum etiam quod judex male judicando dicitur facere injuriam, ideoq; rectè hæc injuria adjungitur statim tit. de injuriis, quæ eadem quoque ratio videtur, cur dejectio secundum locum obtineat, quia hæc quoq; non tantum rei familiari noceat, sed sæpe contumelia sive injuria personam ipsam afficiat. Postremum locum obtinet quasi delictum nautæ &c. tum quia in eo tantum de damno rei familiaris agitur: tum quia hi tres, nautæ, &c. plerumque sint homines postremi.
units.tr: The judge's fault is treated first, partly, if I am not mistaken, on account of the dignity of the office, and partly because a judge who judges badly is said to commit an injury; and so this injury is rightly placed immediately after the title on injuries. The same reason seems to explain why throwing down takes the second place: this too harms not only property but often affects the person himself by insult or injury. The last place is taken by the quasi-delict of the sailor, and so on, both because this concerns only damage to property and because these three, the sailor and the others, are for the most part men of the lowest rank.

units.la: Superest inquit Imp. ut jam de actionibus loquamur initio tit. 6. de Action. Erectè superest reliquum tertium caput, totius juris, duobus aliis
units.tr: The Emperor says: "It remains now that we speak of actions," at the beginning of title 6, on actions. Indeed, what remains is the third head of the whole law, the other two having been set out already:

units.la: D de persona, & de rebus supra jam explicatis. Cur autem hoc de actionibus sit tertium ratio jam supra expositaest: & ad hoc cap. pertinet tit 6. & reliqui usque ad tit. qui proprie ad actiones non pertinent, ut infra dicetur.
units.tr: the law of persons and the law of things. Why this, on actions, is the third head has already been explained above; and title 6 belongs to this head, as do the following titles, up to those which do not properly concern actions, as will be said below.

units.la: Ordinis autem ratio in toto hoc capite disponendo, pendet ex ordine judiciorum, & recte. Nam actionis tantum est usus in judiciis, ut habet definitio actionis. In judiciis autem cum tres sint actor, reus & judex, horum tria officia maxime considerantur. Primum quidem de actoris officio quod in actione ipsa sive in agendo, deinde de rei officio, quod in exceptione: ultimo de judicis officio, quod maxime in sententia ponitur. (Ordo actionum deinceps explicatur.)
units.tr: The reason for the order in arranging this whole head depends on the order of judicial proceedings, and rightly so. For an action is used only in judicial proceedings, as the definition of action states. In judicial proceedings there are three parties, the plaintiff, the defendant and the judge, and the three offices of these are principally considered. First, the office of the plaintiff, which lies in the action itself or in the bringing of the action; then the office of the defendant, which lies in the exception; and last the office of the judge, which is chiefly expressed in the sentence. (The order of actions is explained next.)

units.la: Hujus ordinis ratio naturalis est, & per se clara ut scilicet judex ossicium illud sunm in sententia positum non ante faciat, quam duobus litigantibus auditis, hoc est, actore & Reo. At cause coguntio ex partium (ut vulgo vocant) allegatione hoc est, actione & exceptione sumitur. Hac igitur est ratio, cur de officio judicis, in hoc tertio capite de actionibus ultimo loco agatur puta tit.pen.
units.tr: The natural reason for this order is clear in itself: the judge does not perform his office, which consists in the sentence, until both litigants have been heard, that is, the plaintiff and the defendant. But the examination of a case is taken from the pleading of the parties (as it is commonly called), that is, from the action and the exception. This, then, is the reason why the office of the judge is treated last in this third head, on actions, namely in the penultimate title.

units.la: Cur autem primo de actione seu officio actoris, & secundo de officio rei, sive exceptione agatur, haec est ratio: quia exceptio nihil est aliud quam actionum exclusio. l.2.f. de except. Privatio autem ut vulgo loquuntur, praesupponit habitum. l.10. de V.O.
units.tr: As for why the action, or the office of the plaintiff, is treated first, and the office of the defendant, or the exception, second, the reason is this: an exception is nothing other than the exclusion of actions. Privation, as they commonly say, presupposes a habit.

units.la: Quod igitur ad officium actoris attinet, de eo sive de actione ipsa agitur tit.6.& 6.seq. De exceptione sive de officio Rei tit.3.& seq. Illud quoq; hic admonendum, haec duo actoris & rei officia prius explicari separatim, & tandem adjungi l.1.16. qui utrique & actori & reo sit communis, puta de paena tem. litig. quemadmodum & supra dictum de tut. & curat.
units.tr: So, as far as the office of the plaintiff is concerned, that is, the action itself, it is treated in title 6 and the following titles. The exception, or the office of the defendant, is treated in title 3 and those that follow. It must also be noted here that these two offices, of plaintiff and defendant, are first explained separately and then joined together in the law on penalties for litigation, which is common to both plaintiff and defendant, just as was said above concerning guardianship and curatorship.

units.la: Quod igitur ad ipsam actionem, sive actoris officium attinet, tractatio ea sic posita, videtur. I. est de ipsa actione sive de ejus substantia, & forma, de quo est tit.6.&3.seq. II. est, de personis agentium, de quo est tit.10.& 11. III. est de actionum fine, de quo tit.12.de perpet.& temp.act. quae tria eo ipso, quem expositi, ordine hic disponuntur: optima sane ratione, ut ea quae ad substantiam rei pertinent primum obtineant locum, quae duo ad rei interitum teneant ultimum titulum, & inter haec medium personae, cum alius titulus nullus superfit.
units.tr: As for the action itself, or the office of the plaintiff, the treatment appears to be arranged thus. First, there is the action itself, its substance and form, which is treated in title 6 and the next three titles. Second, the persons who bring actions, treated in titles 10 and 11. Third, the end of actions, treated in title 12, on perpetual and temporal actions. These three are arranged in this order for the very reason just stated, and quite rightly: those matters that pertain to the substance of a right hold the first place, while these two, which concern the extinction of a right, hold the last title, and between them lies the middle matter, the persons, since no other title remains.

units.la: Ad primum de substantia & forma pertinent haec definitio actionis, & divisiones, quae f. principales tit.6. adferuntur. Nam & sexta velut accessoria & incidenter adfertur in 5. sed ista hoc fit. Ad formam quoque pertinet dispatatio de plus petitionibus, item contra de minus, & de solido, hoc est, neque plus, neque minus, quia divisioni conjunctae optime convenit, recte quoque statim adjungitur.
units.tr: To the first, the substance and form, belong the definition of action and the divisions which are set out principally in title 6. For the sixth division is also set out, as it were as an accessory and incidentally, in title 5; but this is done for that reason. To the form also belongs the discussion of claims for more than is due, and likewise of claims for less, and of the whole sum, that is, neither more nor less; since this fits well with the division and rightly follows immediately.

units.la: Ceterum eum actiones vel ex nostro vel eorum, qui in nostra sunt potestate, contractu, sive delicto oriantur, multa quoque in his sunt singularia: ratio postulat ut singulatim & separatim, quamvis jam antea earum fuerit facta mentio, tit. 6. §. actiones. ex quo intelligitur haec quoque ad primum membrum substantiae pertinere, de quib. tit. 7. quod cum eo, &c.
units.tr: Moreover, since actions arise either from our own contract or from the contract of those who are in our power, or from delict, there are also many special points in these matters. Reason demands that they be treated individually and separately, although their mention was made earlier, in title 6, section on actions. From this it is understood that these too belong to the first part of substance, of which the seventh title treats, with that, etc.

units.la: Et primum quidem de alieno contractu. d. tit. deinde de alieno delicto. tit. 8. de nox. action. Contractus enim sunt delictis priores, ut supra dictum.
units.tr: And first, indeed, concerning contract made by another (same title); then concerning delict committed by another (title 8, on noxal actions). For contracts come before delicts, as was said above.

units.la: Huic titulo statim adjungitur tit. 9. si quadrupes pauper. &c. Ratio, ut servorum de quib. tit. 8. ita animalium. 9. quibus servi sunt similes, l. 2. de nox. act. nomine noxalis actio datur, de qua in tit. 9. Haec deprimo, sive de iis, quae ad substantiam actionis pertinent.
units.tr: Immediately after this title comes title 9, if a quadruped has done damage, etc. The reason is that as slaves, which are treated in title 8, so animals, which are similar to slaves, (law 2, on noxal actions), give rise to the noxal action, which is treated in title 9. These points belong to the first part, that is, to matters that pertain to the substance of the action.

units.la: Alterum est de personis agentium tit. 10. de iis per quos agere, &c. Vel enim ipsi agimus, vel per procuratores, de quib. d. tit. 10. Procurator autem, quia nemo intelligitur idoneus sine satisdatione, l. 10. ff. de reg. jur. titulum 10. de procurator. b. statim sequitur tit. 11. de satisdat.
units.tr: The second is on the persons who bring actions, title 10, on those through whom one may sue, etc. For we either act ourselves or through agents, which are treated in the same title 10. Since an agent is not regarded as fit without security, (law 10, Digest, on rules of law), title 10, on agents, is immediately followed by title 11, on security.

units.la: Hunc recte sequitur, tit. 12. de perpet. & temp. act. quod est tertium & ultimum membrum de actionum interitu. Ratio scilicet est expositia, quia hoc titul. de vita & morte actionum agitur, ut ita dicam.
units.tr: This is rightly followed by title 12, "On perpetual and temporal actions," which is the third and last part on the extinction of actions. The reason, so to speak, is evident: this title treats of the life and death of actions.

units.la: Et haec de actione sive de actoris officio separatim. Proximum est de Reo, cujus officium est de exceptione, ut supra dictum ideo proximus est titulus 13. de except.
units.tr: So much for action, or the office of the plaintiff, taken separately. Next comes the defendant, whose office concerns exception; hence, as said above, the next title is 13, "On exceptions."

units.la: Quem sequitur tit. 14. de replicat. hac ratione, ut actionem sequitur exceptio, ita exceptionum replicatio, & hanc duplicatio. Et haec de secundo capite sive de Reo separatim breviter dicta sunt.
units.tr: This is followed by title 14, "On replication," for the following reason: as exception follows action, so replication follows exception, and duplication follows replication. And so much has been briefly said about the second head, or the defendant, taken separately.

units.la: Proximum erat jam exponere quae utriusque esse ent communia sed interieiicitur unus titulus de interdictis, eo quod horum quoque ratio non est communis sed propria tantum actoris. Sunt enim quaedam actiones. Nam si verae essent actiones, ad titul. de actionibus, pertineret earum tractatio. Nunc potius sunt decreta quaedam praetoris, si primam eorum originem & usum spectes. Nam hodie actionum loco habentur. in pri. & §. ultim. tit. 15.
units.tr: It was next necessary to set out matters common to both parties, but a single title, "On interdicts," is inserted, because the nature of these too is not common but belongs to the plaintiff alone. For some are, as it were, actions. If they were true actions, their treatment would belong under the title "On actions." They are rather certain decrees of the praetor, if you look at their first origin and use. Today, however, they are held in the place of actions (see the beginning and the last §. of title 15).

units.la: Hunc sequitur tit. 16. de pan temp. lit. qui, quia est communis licentibus, hoc est, tam actori quam reo, recte ultimo loco ponitur. Et haec hactenus de actoris & rei officio sequitur nunc de officio judicis.
units.tr: This is followed by title 16, "On temporary pleas," which, because it is common to all litigants, that is, to plaintiff and defendant alike, is rightly placed in the last position. And so far, the office of plaintiff and defendant; now follows the office of the judge.

units.la: Ordinis ratio jam supra est expositia, cui & haec caccedat quod hic. tit. 17. priori 16. optime connectatur, quia ipsi sit communis. Judex namque operam dat tam actori quam Reo. Atque ita tertium jam totius juris caput recte & ordine est explicatum.
units.tr: The reason for the order has already been set out above; to it may be added that this title 17 is best connected with the preceding 16, because it is common to both. For the judge takes pains on behalf of plaintiff and defendant alike. And thus the third head of the whole law has been rightly and orderly explained.

units.la: Cur ergo inquies adjungitur tit. de pub. iud. quae tamen ab actione differunt? initio d. tit. 18. Nempe ut judiciorum in quibus actionis est usus utraque species (sunt enim judicia omnia vel privata, ad quas actiones, vel publica ad quæ crimina pertinent, vel accusationes) quadantenus tyronibus degustanda proponatur.
units.tr: Why, you will ask, is the title "On public judgments" added, though these differ from action? It is placed at the beginning of that title 18, namely so that both kinds of judgments in which action is used (for all judgments are either private, to which actions pertain, or public, to which crimes or accusations pertain) may be offered to beginners to taste in some measure.

units.la: Commemorantur autem sub hoc titul.13. Crimina. Et I. crimen majestatis, tum propter Imp.dignitatem, tum propter pœnæ magnitudinem. II. Locum obtinet crimen adulterii, quod cum priore simile est in duobus in auctore, aut certè in nomine, utrumque enim est ex L Julia, & in pœnæ magnitudine. III. Est homicidii etiam propter pœnæ magnitudinem, capitalem scilicet. Nam capitalia uti graviora prioremtitul.obtinent. Cur autem crimen adulterii præponatur homicidio, cum utrumque sit capitale? rationem indicavimus: quia adulterium ex L.Julia punitur, cum homicidii pœna sit ex L.Cornelia, à Cornelio, non à Cæsare lata. IV. Locum obtinet parricidium, quod item est capitale, sed gravius videri poterat homicidio, & propterea præponendum. sed homicidium est antiquius ex L.Cornelia, quę est prior L.Pompeja, ex qua punitur crimen parricidii. Sequuntur crimina non capitalia, inter quæ primum est crimen falsi. Ratio ordinis est quia est antiquissimum inter capitalia. II. Est crimen vis publicæ, & III. Vis privatæ quorum prius, quia interdum est capitale, ut crimen falsi, secundum titulum obtinet, & tertium crimen vis privatæ propter similitudinem. IV. Est peculatus, quia scilicet est furtum publicum. V. Est plagium, quia est furtum quodammodo privatum, & proinde peculatui propter similitudinem statim adjungitur. Hoc sequitur VI. Ambitus, & alia tria. VII. Repetundarum. VIII. Annonæ. IX. Et residuorum, quæ tantum hic commemorantur & non explicantur. Summo tamen digito, inquit Imp. quasi per indicem demonstrantur, quorum diligentior scientia ex latioribus ff. libris Deo propitio adventuræ est, ubi & nos de iis ordinis rationem diligentius adferemus. Et hæc de Institut. ordin. breviter sint explicata.
units.tr: Under this title 13 the crimes are mentioned. I. The crime of treason (crimen maiestatis), both on account of the dignity of the Emperor and the magnitude of the penalty. II. The crime of adultery holds the place, which is similar to the former in two respects: in its author, or at least in its name, for both come from the Lex Julia, and in the magnitude of the penalty. III. Then comes homicide, also on account of the magnitude of the penalty, namely capital punishment. For capital crimes, being graver, hold the earlier place in the title. Why, however, is the crime of adultery placed before homicide, when both are capital? We have indicated the reason: because adultery is punished under the Lex Julia, whereas the penalty for homicide comes from the Lex Cornelia, proposed by Cornelius, not by Caesar. IV. Parricide holds its place, which likewise is capital, but it might seem graver than homicide and therefore to be placed before it. But homicide is older, under the Lex Cornelia, which is earlier than the Lex Pompeia, under which the crime of parricide is punished. There follow the non-capital crimes, among which the first is the crime of falsification. The reason for this order is that it is the most ancient among the capital crimes. II. Is the crime of public violence, and III. of private violence, of which the former, because at times it is capital, as the crime of falsification, holds the second place, and the third, the crime of private violence, is placed on account of its similarity. IV. Is embezzlement (peculatus), because it is, namely, public theft. V. Is kidnapping (plagium), because it is theft in some sense private, and therefore it is immediately joined to embezzlement on account of similarity. To this follow VI. bribery (ambitus), and three others. VII. Extortion (repetundae). VIII. Profiteering in the grain supply (annona). IX. And arrears (residua), which are only mentioned here and not explained. Yet, the Emperor says, they are indicated with the tip of a finger, as it were by an index; a more careful knowledge of them will come, God willing, from the wider books of the Digest, where we shall also set out more carefully the reason for their order. And let these things be briefly explained concerning the order of the Institutes.

units.la: Finis Oeconomiæ Institutionum.
units.tr: End of the Economy of the Institutes.

units.la: OECONO.
units.tr: ECONOMY

units.la: OECONOMIA CODI- CIS IVSTINIANI.
units.tr: THE ECONOMY OF THE CODE OF JUSTINIAN.

units.la: TSi ex instituto Justiniani Codex in Scholis non docetur, sed tantum privatim legendus est, idque post Digesta. Etsi quoque hic noster Codex, qui dicitur repetitæ prælectionis, post Digesta toto anno est editus: Idcoque videri poterat de ordine ac Methodo Codicis ultimo agendum: Nos tamen de Pandectis ultimo loco tractabimus: tum quia Codex ipse, quo ad primam editionem prior est Digestis, tum quia Digesta ad ordinē Codicis sunt composita, ut ait l.1.C.de vet.jur.enucl. Ut igitur prius de Codice: tres in eo ordines considerari videntur. Librorum: qui est summus, maximeque generalis: titulorum, qui est angustior & interior: Legum denique sive capitum, quæ sub titulis continentur, angustissimus, & maximè singularis. Nam in Institutionibus duos tantum ordines, nempe librorum & titulorum exposuimus, omisso tertio paragraphorum, quod eorum tractatio & longior sit, & sine rerum explanatione vix intelligi possit. Legum autem singularum sub his titulis ordinem, semel tantum indicasse erit satis. Idem enim est eorum ordo, qui est sub uno, paucisque verbis in Codice, sed in Digestis longè pluribus explicari potest. Quod igitur attinet ad rationem primi ordinis librorum videtur illud initio admonendum, libros Codicis esse XII. Cujus numeri ratio non facile reddi potest. Solent enim sæpe sumi librorum numeri pro materiæ vel magnitudine vel commoditate. Forrassis tamen Imp. Justinian. in suo Codice vel imitari voluit 12. Tabb. quod est primum corpus juris, vel adamavit hunc numerum, quod Romanis etiam in jure valde fuerit usitatus, ut videre licet in 12. mensibus, in asse hereditatis, in 12 partes sive uncias tributo, quod ex Galeno notavit Duar. lib.2.Disput.cap.36. Theodosiani Codicis libri sunt 16. Gregoriani & Hermogeniani Codicum (hos enim tres in suo Justinianus est imitatus, initio C. praef. at. 1.) quot fuerint libri, incertum est: quia tatum eorum parva fragmenta extant. Theodosianum integrum protulit Cujacius. Id quoque admonendum, in Codice tres praefationes contineri. Nam cum duae Codicis fuerint editiones prior, & altera, quae dicitur repetitae praelectionis, quam hodie solam habemus, ad priorem quidem editionem duae pertinent praefationes, una de ipso Codice primum faciendo, deinde altera de eo confirmando: ad secundam editionem pertinet tertia de Codice emendando. Quare potest Codex totus in duas partes summatim dividi, in praefationes, & in rerum ipsarum, sive juris tractationem, quae XII. libris continetur. Ut jam ad liberos ordine accedamus, ad tria membra sive capita revocari potest eorum tractatio: quorum unum est de jure publico, de quo explicatur lib. 1. Alterum de jure privato, de quo lib. 2. & seqq. III. Est de jure quasi publico, ut ita dicam, de quo lib. 10. & 2. seqq. Ratio hujus trimembris tractationis est, quia jus omne vel est publicum vel privatum. L. 1. ff. hujus. ff. de just. & jur. Cur ergo, inquies, tertium adjungitur de jure quasi publico? Rationem hanc esse puto, quod vocabulum publici bifariam accipiatur: latius & angustius, sive proprie. Et latius quidem accepto continentur omnes juris publici species: proprie accepto, non continentur jura fiscalia, militaria, & municipalia. l. bona. 13. & l. eum qui. 16. ff. de verb. signific. Continentur autem proprie sumpto, jura de sacris, sacerdotibus & magistratibus. d. l. 1. §. hujus. Et hanc igitur est ratio, cur jus publicum dividamus in vere publicum, & quasi publicum, secuti Imp. qui hunc ordinem in C. & ff. servavit. Ratio autem ordinis, cur caput de jure publico sit primum, sive primo loco ponatur, est dignitas: publica namque privatis sunt potiora. l. sunt personae. ff. de relig. & sumpt. jun. l. ex plagis, §. in cluso. ff. ad l. Aquil. Deinde cur caput de jure privato sit secundum praeponaturque quasi publico, quod tamen privato est praestantius, ratio est: quia privatum inri vere publico est conjunctius. Nam ius vere publicum est de Magistratibus: Magistratus autem praeest & operam praestat iuri privato, puta leges ferendo, & ius dicendo: sed ius quasi publicum, ut fiscale, &c. cum iure privato nihil habet commune, aut saltem ei non servit. Dicet aliquis ius publicum non omne pertinere ad jus privatum, aut ei praeesse, ut est ius de sacris, & sacerdotibus ; Ideoque & hoc videri in ultimum locum reservari debuisse, ius, inquam, sacrum cum iure fiscali : cum tamen in C.nostro primo loco ponatur. Et certe Theodosius Junior, videtur hac ratione adductus, cur in suo Codice de sacris & sacerdotibus, ultimo loco tractarit, puta lib. 16. Sed Justinianus propter dignitatem & reverentiam religionis, primum ei locum attribuit, quam rationem ordinis & Cicero in suis libris de legibus tenuit. Nam in secundo (in primo enim generalis de origine iuris disputatio continetur) ius sacrum, in tertio ius publicum, in quarto & quinto, (qui tamen hodie desiderantur) ius privatum tractavit, ut ipse ait initio & in fine lib.3. Plato in suis libris 12. de legibus (quos item Imp.imitari potuit) duas iuris species maxime persequitur : publicum prius, posterius privatum. Sed in privato explicando, ubi de criminalibus & sacrilegiis agit, etiam de religione multa admiscet. Et haec breviter summatim, & universe de tribus his membris, eorumque ordine dicta sint satis. Nunc de iis paulo subtilius & singulatim explicemus. Quod ad primum caput de publico iure attinet, notae sunt tres iuris publici partes, sacra, sacerdotes, & magistratus. d.l.1 §.hujus studii. de just. & jur. in quibus tribus partibus hoc primum caput totum continetur. Et primo quidem de sacris agitur initio lib.1. propter dignitatem rerum sacrarum sive divinarum. Deinde agitur de sacerdotibus. Ratio est, non (ut fortasse quidam statim putaret) dignitas. Nam ut Tertullianus ait, Caesar secundum Deum est in terra Primus : sed similitudo, quod scilicet sacra, de quibus prius, tractant sacerdotes ; quemadmodum & infra in altero iuris publici membro de legibus & magistratibus (vere enim duae duntaxat iuris publici partes, divinum & humanum, constitui possunt) prius de iure ipso, deinde de personis, hoc est, magistratibus agitur. Alterum caput C. de iure privato, quia maxime in iudiciis versatur (ratio exponetur infra ad ff.) in tres partes hic distributum videtur. Una est de iudiciis privatis, altera de publicis. Tertia de quibusdam vel quasi iudiciis, vel quibusdam iudiciorum accessionibus aliisque articulis extraordinariis. Quarum trium partium ea quae est de iudiciis privatis, primo loco explicatur. lib. 2. & s.sin. Secundum locum obtinet ea, quæ est de judiciis, hoc est, interdictis & judiciorum accessionibus, hoc est, pignoribus, stipulationibus, quæ omnia in unum lib.2. sunt conjecta. Ultimo loco exponitur pars ea, quæ est de publicis judiciis toto lib.9. Ratio hujus rei est facilis: Privata enim judicia publicis anteponuntur, tum quia sunt frequentiora, tum quia magis necessaria, tum etiam quia antiquiora, cum publica sint & minus frequentia, & valde ⁊ istia; & odiosa, & proinde recte in ultimum locum rejecta. Cur autem interdicta & pignora statim post judicia privata explicentur, ratio est, quia partim privatis sunt similia, partim quia privatorum sunt accessoria. Illud de prima parte, quam de judiciis privatis constituimus, quod latissime ea patet, sex scilicet libris comprehensa, diligenter notandum, illam partem esse trimembrem. Primo enim membro judiciorum privatorum πρ. πξ. ᾱ. sive priora, ut sunt pacta, in jus vocatio, Editio continentur, de quo tractatu est totus liber 2. Altero membro ipsa judicia, & singulæ eorum species ordine exponuntur. Primo quidem judicia, sive actiones in rem, toto lib.3. Deinde actiones in personam. lib. 4. 5. & 6. Tandem vero actiones mixtæ, partim in rem, partim in personam, ut sunt præjudiciales, puta judiciorum & actionum de liberali causa. lib.7. tit.1. & 4.tit.seqq. Tertium primæ partis membrum est de posterioribus judiciorum, ut est sententia, appellatio, executio. Quod eodem lib.7. titul.42. usque ad finem libri continetur. Horum autem trium membrorum ordinis ratio est facilis, ut scilicet priora primum, posteriora ultimum locum obtineant. Restat tertium & ultimum caput Codicis, quod de jure quasi publico appellavimus, brevitatis causa; Cujus capitis duæ summæ partes mihi videntur: Una est de oneribus & muneribus, ut sunt tributa, vectigalia, curiæ munera: altera est de honoribus & dignitatibus, vel brevius (quod tamen idem valet) unum est de rebus, alterum de personis. Et de rebus quidem sive oneribus primo, puta lib.10. & 11. De honoribus sive dignitatibus posterius, lib.12. seu ultimo agitur. Qui ordo videri posset perversus, quod de personis pōtius & honoribus propter dignitatem, prius quam de rebus & oneribus agendum videatur: quemadmodum in Institut. prius de personis, posterius de rebus explicatur. Sed hæc quoque justa ordinis est ratio, cur prius de oneribus, quam de honoribus explicetur, puta quia tractatio de oneribus & judiciis (de quibus proxime actum fuerat) similis, & maxime publicis, ubi de calumniatoribus & poenis agitur. Onera autem sunt quasi poenae, ac in tributis ac jure fiscali, delatores intervenire solent, qui calumniatoribus non sunt absimiles. Deinde, quia honores gerentibus & officia, quae Caesari praestant, tam in pace, quam in bello honoraria & stipendia, nisi prius adsint vectigalia tanquam nervi, suppeditari nequeunt. Est & tertia ratio, quia de oneribus nihil adhuc dictum fuerit, de honoribus lib.1. Sed ratione jurisdictionis, non fisci aut Caesaris. Ideoq; de honoribus sive magistratu non male in ultimum locum rejicitur.
units.tr: TIf, by Justinian's arrangement, the Code is not taught in the schools but is only to be read privately, and that after the Digest. And although this our Code, which is called the Code of the repeated lecture, was published the whole year after the Digest, it might seem that the order and method of the Code should be treated last. We shall nevertheless treat the Pandects last: both because the Code itself, in its first edition, is earlier than the Digest, and because the Digest was composed to follow the order of the Code, as he says in l.1.C.de vet.jur.enucl. So, first, concerning the Code: three orders seem to be found in it. The order of books, which is the highest and most general; the order of titles, which is narrower and more inward; and finally the order of the laws or chapters, which are contained under the titles, the narrowest and most particular. For in the Institutes we set out only two orders, namely of books and of titles, omitting the third, that of paragraphs, because its treatment is rather long and can scarcely be understood without an explanation of the matters. As for the order of the individual laws under these titles, it will be enough to have indicated it once. For their order, which is under one title, can be explained in a few words in the Code, but in the Digest it can be explained at much greater length. As to the reason for the first order, the books, it seems right to remark at the outset that the Code has twelve books. The reason for this number cannot easily be given. Numbers of books are often chosen according to the size or convenience of the material. Perhaps, however, the Emperor Justinian wished in his Code to imitate the Twelve Tables, which was the first body of law, or he was fond of this number, which was much used by the Romans in law, as one may see in the twelve months, in the as of an inheritance, and in the tribute divided into twelve parts or unciae, which Duarenus noted from Galen lib.2.Disput.cap.36. The books of the Theodosian Code are sixteen. How many books the Gregorian and Hermogenian Codes had (for Justinian imitated these three in his own) is uncertain, because only small fragments of them survive. Cujacius brought forth the Theodosian Code entire. It should also be noted that three prefaces are contained in the Code. For although there were two editions of the Code, the earlier, and the other, which is called the edition of the repeated lecture, which alone we have today, two prefaces belong to the earlier edition: one concerning the making of the Code itself, and then another concerning its confirmation; the third, concerning the emendation of the Code, belongs to the second edition. Hence the whole Code may be summarily divided into two parts: the prefaces, and the treatment of the matters of law themselves, which is contained in twelve books. Now, to come to the books in order, their treatment can be reduced to three members or heads. The first is concerning public law, which is explained in lib. 1. The second is concerning private law, which is in lib. 2. & seqq. The third is concerning what is, as it were, public law, as I may say, which is in lib. 10. & 2. seqq. The reason for this threefold treatment is that all law is either public or private L. 1. ff. hujus. ff. de just. & jur. Why then, you will ask, is a third added, concerning what is quasi-public law? I think the reason is that the word public is taken in two ways: more broadly and more narrowly, or properly. Taken broadly, all species of public law are contained; taken properly, fiscal, military and municipal laws are not contained l. bona. 13. & l. eum qui. 16. ff. de verb. signific. Taken properly, however, the laws concerning sacred things, priests and magistrates are contained d. l. 1. §. hujus. This, then, is the reason why we divide public law into what is truly public and what is quasi-public, following the Emperor, who observed this order in the Code and the Digest. The reason for the order, why the head concerning public law stands first, or is placed in the first place, is dignity: for public matters take precedence over private ones l. sunt personae. ff. de relig. & sumpt. fun. l. ex plagis, §. in cluso. ff. ad l. Aquil. Next, why the head concerning private law comes second and is placed before what is quasi-public, although this is in fact more excellent than private law, the reason is that private law is more closely connected with what is truly public. For truly public law concerns magistrates; and magistrates preside over and take care of private law, for instance by enacting laws and pronouncing judgment. But quasi-public law, such as fiscal law, has nothing in common with private law, or at least does not serve it. Someone may say that not all public law pertains to private law, or presides over it, as is the case with the law concerning sacred things and priests. Therefore, it might seem, this should also have been reserved for the last place: sacred law, I mean, along with fiscal law; yet in our Code it is placed first. And certainly Theodosius the Younger seems to have been moved by this reason to treat of sacred things and priests last in his Code, namely in lib. 16. But Justinian, on account of the dignity and reverence of religion, gave it the first place. Cicero, in his books de legibus, also kept this order of reasoning. For in the second book (for the first contains a general discussion on the origin of law), he treated sacred law; in the third, public law; in the fourth and fifth (which, however, are now lost), private law, as he himself says at the beginning and end of lib.3. Plato, in his twelve books de legibus (which the Emperor could likewise have imitated), pursues chiefly two species of law: public first, private afterwards. But in explaining private law, where he treats of crimes and sacrileges, he mixes in much about religion as well. These matters have been said briefly, in summary and in general, about the three members and their order, and that is enough. Now let us explain them somewhat more finely and one by one. As for the first head, concerning public law, there are three known parts of public law: sacred things, priests, and magistrates d.l.1 §.hujus studii. de just. & jur. In these three parts the whole of this first head is contained. And first, indeed, sacred things are treated initio lib.1. on account of the dignity of sacred or divine things. Next, priests are treated. The reason is not, as some might at once suppose, dignity. For as Tertullian says, Caesar is first on earth, next to God: rather, it is similarity, namely that the priests deal with the sacred things treated before; just as also, below, in the other member of public law, concerning laws and magistrates (for truly only two parts of public law, divine and human, can be established), the law itself is treated first, and then the persons, that is, the magistrates. The second head of the Code, concerning private law, since it is chiefly concerned with judicial proceedings (the reason will be set out below under the Digest), seems to be divided here into three parts. One is concerning private judgments, another concerning public ones. The third concerns certain things that are either quasi-judicial, or certain accessories of judgments and other extraordinary matters. Of these three parts, that concerning private judgments is explained first lib. 2. & s.sin. The second place is held by that which concerns judgments, that is, interdicts and the accessories of judgments, that is, pledges and stipulations, all of which are gathered together into one lib.2. Last, that part is set out which concerns public judgments toto lib.9. The reason for this is easy: private judgments are placed before public ones, both because they are more frequent, and because they are more necessary, and also because they are older; public judgments are less frequent, and are very severe and odious, and therefore are rightly thrown to the last place. But why interdicts and pledges are explained immediately after private judgments, the reason is that they are partly similar to private matters, and partly are accessories of them. It must be carefully noted about the first part, which we have set up concerning private judgments, that it extends very widely, being comprised in six books, and that this part has three members. For under the first member of private judgments, the preliminaries [πρ. πξ. ᾱ.], or prior matters, such as agreements, summons to court, and the edict, are contained; and the whole of book 2 is devoted to this treatment. In the second member, the judgments themselves and their individual species are set out in order. First, indeed, judgments or actions in rem, toto lib.3. Then actions in personam, lib. 4. 5. & 6. Finally, mixed actions, partly in rem and partly in personam, such as preliminary ones, for instance of judgments and actions concerning a freeborn status, lib.7. tit.1. & 4.tit.seqq. The third member of the first part concerns the later stages of judgments, such as sentence, appeal and execution. This is contained in the same lib.7. titul.42. down to the end of the book. The reason for the order of these three members is easy: that the earlier should hold the first place and the later the last. There remains the third and last head of the Code, which for brevity we have called concerning what is quasi-public law. Two main parts of this head seem to me to be: one concerns burdens and offices, such as taxes, customs duties, and the duties of the town councils; the other concerns honours and dignities. Or, more briefly (which nevertheless amounts to the same), one concerns things, the other persons. Concerning things or burdens, indeed, is treated first, namely in lib.10. & 11. Concerning honours or dignities, which is later, is treated last, in lib.12. This order might seem perverse, since concerning persons and honours, on account of their dignity, it seems that one should treat before things and burdens: just as in the Institutes the persons are explained first and the things afterwards. But there is also a just reason for this order, why burdens are explained before honours: namely, because the treatment of burdens is similar to that of judgments (which had just been treated), especially public ones, where calumniators and penalties are dealt with. Burdens, moreover, are as it were penalties, and in taxes and fiscal law informers commonly intervene, who are not unlike calumniators. Next, because honours and offices, which are rendered to Caesar, whether honorary or salaried in peace and in war, cannot be supplied unless taxes are first in place, as the sinews of the state. There is also a third reason: that nothing has yet been said about burdens, while about honours it is in lib.1. but by reason of jurisdiction, not of the treasury or of Caesar. Therefore it is not unreasonably placed last, concerning honours or magistracy.

units.la: Adhuc de primo ordine Codicis de librorum scilicet inter se collatione est explicatum. Proximum est, ut de altero ordine, qui est titulorum inter se, videamus.
units.tr: So far, concerning the first order of the Code, that is, the arrangement of the books among themselves, has been explained. Next, let us see concerning the second order, which is that of the titles among themselves.

units.la: ICTUM est supra jus publicum, quod in sacris & sacerdotibus & magistratibus consistit lib.1 tractari: & primum quidem sacra, deinde sacerdotes tum magistratus. Ex sacris autem duo maxime hic adferuntur, unum de fide ipsa, seu de doctrina fidei, alterum de Ecclesiis earumq; jure: nam & Ecclesiæ ritum conservare inter sacra connumeratur. Illud admonendum Ecclesiæ verbum hic esse ambiguum: proprie valet ipsum coetum Christianorum, minus proprie pro æde sacra ponitur. Utraq; notio hoc intelligenda ut. de SS. Eccles. ut videre est mi.1.& 2.d.tit. Ex his duobus rebus sacris, fide & Ecclesia prius agitur de fide, tit.1. deinde de Ecclesiis tit 2. quia fides ad ipsum Deum & ejus cognitionem pertinet: Ecclesiæ tractatio ad praxin & usum potius, multaq; humana Ecclesiastica tamen continet. Prius est plane divinum, alterum Ecclesiasticum & proinde posterius. Sacra proxime sequuntur sacerdotes. tit. 3.de Ep.scop.& Cler.& tit.4.de Episcop.audient. Ratio ordinis expositae est supra. Et tit quidem 3.de Episc. creatione & privilegiis. tit.4 est de eorum variis officiis. Ratio ordinis est perspicua ut prius sit Episcopus, quā quid gerat aut administret quemadmodum prius de tutoribus institutenda, quam de eorum auctoritate & administratione agitur. His de vera & Catholica fide Ecclesiis de sacerdotibus, &c. jam expositis: quia legis virtus non tantum est in jubendo quod rectum, sed & in vetando quod vitiosum est, adjungitur statim titulus de prava fide, sive religione, sive de iis qui falsam fidem confitentur. Cum autem eorum quatuor fere sint genera: Hæretici, Apostatæ, Judæi & Pagani de omnibus singulatim eoq; ordine agitur. Et I. de hæreticis tit.5. quia cum hæretici sint Christiani reliquis tribus qui non sunt, videntur meliores. Huic tituloadhæret tit.6. ne sacrum Baptisfter. Nam & Baptismum iterare est hæresis. Cur autem de hac hæresi sive de hoc errore separatim agatur, hæc videtur ratio, tū quia hic error etiā in Catholicis multis suerit, ut in Cypriano, tū quia ea ætate, qua LL. sub hoc titulo fuerunt late, ac etiā sub Justiniano, & post graviter in Aphrica Donatistæ, (quorum magnus erat numerus & audacia) rebaptizates à Catholicis Baptizatos. Propter has causas singulares proprius est tit. ei attributus & specialiter prohibetur l.3.§.ait prætor Naut.caup.stab.&c. Hæreticis similes sunt Apostatæ, in eo qut hæretici à Catholica fide ad Hæresim & errorem defecedunt ita Apostatæ à religione Christiana deficiant ad non Christianā, ut Judæorum aut paganorū. Hujus igitur similitudinis rōe adjungitur tit.7. de Apostat. Hunc sequitur tit.8. Nemini licere signum Sal.&c. Nā & hic est error, quia non tamen est in religione, quā in quadam re externa & non est plane hæresis, ideo separatim de eo agitur. Adhuc de erroribus Christianorum sive hæreticis, & de A postatis & eorum cognatis. Nunc de Judaeis de quib. est tit. 9. Judaeorū. n. error, quia paganico tolerabilior videtur, priore loco de Judaeis agitur, q; de Paganis tit. 10. ne Christianum mancipium, &c. Ratio est, quia licet hodie ad omnes errantes pertineat, q; sub eo tit. cōtinetur, haereticos, inq;, Judaeos & paganos, primū tamen id contra Judaeos fuit introductū à Constantino Imperatore, teste Eusebio lib. 4. de vita Constantin. Restant pagani de quib. ut pestimis, ob pestimam eorū religionem agitur ult c. tit. 11. de pag. Tādem hunc sequitur t. 12. de his qui ad Eccl. confug. quia hoc jus asyli & profugij, de quo hic agitur, commune est, & patet, non tantū orthodoxis, sed etiā errantibus haereticis Judaeis, &c. Prius ergo quae propria sunt Catholicorū, haereticorū, &c, distincte & separatim sunt explicata, deinde q; eorū communia, ut jus asyli, adjunguntur, q; & alias factum admonuimus jā supra ad Institut. Postremo adjungitur tit. 13. de hu qui in Eccl. manum. Nam & hoc propter Ecclesias pertinet ad hoc caput de jure divino. Quia tamen manumissio est status civilis potius q; divinus & quia est servorum, quorū ultima & infima est conditio, merito ultimo loco de ea agitur. Convenit quoq; hic tit. 13. priori titulo de his, qui ad Eccl. confug. Nam servi plerunq; & ad Ecclesias cōfugere solent. Et haec hactenus de jure divino, sive de duab. juris publici partibus, sacris & sacerdotib. sint explicata. Reliqua est pars tertia de magistratu, quae proprie est juris publici, si proprie jus publicū acceipias. Tum n. differt jus publicū à divino & privato, l. ut in ter, C. de SS Eccl. Ut aut in illis duab. juris divini partib. prius de fide ipsa sive differentia fidei, deinde de ministris sive Episcopis eorumq; officio dictum est, ita & in hac parte prius de jure & legibus ipsis postea de magistratibus eorumq; officiis explicatur quo ipsoordine & Episcopi de recta fide, & magistratus de jure ac legib. admoneantur, nihil ut agant q; verae fidei vel legib. ac juri sit contrarium. Haec una est causa, cur post illas duas partes non statim de ipsis magistratib. sed prius de jure ac legib. agatur, tit. 14. de leg. b. & seqq. usq; ad tit. 20. Est & altera causa sive ratio, q; scil. huic operi hoc est, Codici propositū sit, maxime jus humanum, tam publicum quam privatum; convenies sit ut etiam de ipso jure, ejusq; natura, partibus & origine velut principiā quaedam hujus operis statim initio pertinentur, quod & in Instit. & in ff. item factitatur. Partes autē Juris scripti cum sint 6. Lex Plebiscita, Senatusconsulta, Edicta praetorum, mandata principum, responsa prudentum, de tribus videtur conceptus tit. 14. de leg. bus aut certe ad eas allusum est. Nam ahoqui Edicti verbum in eo titulo ad Imp. Edicta referri possit, nō praetorū l. 3. C. de leg. b. ut & totus ille tit. ad LL. Impp. fere pertinet. Quae est quoq; ratio, cur hic tit 14 intereos, qui de juris partibus sunt, primum locum obtineat: quia de Imp Constitutionibus agat. Est & altera ordinis causa, q; hujus tituli pars sit generalis, ad omnes juris partes pertinens, sive ad omne Jus, d. l. 3 Et ita quoq; in ipso tit. del. gib. haec clausula de legib generaliter accipienda videtur. Hunc tit. statim sequitur
units.tr: It has been said above that the public law, which consists of sacred things, priests and magistrates, is treated in lib.1: first the sacred things, then the priests, then the magistrates. Two sacred matters are chiefly brought forward here: one concerning the faith itself, or the doctrine of the faith, and the other concerning the Churches and their law, since keeping the rite of the Church is also counted among sacred things. It should be noted that the word Ecclesia is ambiguous here. Properly it means the assembly of Christians; less properly it is used for the sacred building. Both senses must be understood in this way, as can be seen in ut. de SS. Eccles. and mi.1.& 2.d.tit. Of these two sacred matters, faith and Church, the faith is treated first, in tit.1., and then the Churches, in tit 2., because faith pertains to God himself and to the knowledge of him, whereas the treatment of the Church pertains more to practice and use, although it also contains many human, ecclesiastical matters. The former is wholly divine, the latter ecclesiastical and therefore posterior. Sacred things are followed closely by priests, in tit. 3.de Ep.scop.& Cler. and tit.4.de Episcop.audient. The reason for this order has been set out above. tit.3. concerns the creation and privileges of bishops, and tit.4 concerns their various duties. The order is plain: the bishop must first exist before we consider what he does or administers, just as guardians must be appointed before their authority and administration are discussed. Having now set out the true and Catholic faith, the Churches, the priests, and so on, the title on depraved faith, whether religion or those who profess a false faith, is added at once, because the force of a law lies not only in commanding what is right but also in forbidding what is wrong. There are about four kinds of such people: heretics, apostates, Jews and pagans, and these are treated individually and in that order. First, concerning heretics, in tit.5., because heretics are Christians, and among the other three, who are not Christians, they seem to be the better. Joined to this title is tit.6. ne sacrum Baptisfter., for to repeat baptism is also a heresy. Why this heresy, or this error, is treated separately seems to be for two reasons: first, because this error was common even among Catholics, as in Cyprian; second, because at the time when the laws under this title were widely issued, and also under Justinian, and afterwards in Africa, the Donatists (who were numerous and bold) rebaptized those baptized by Catholics, and this was seriously troubling. For these special reasons a title of its own was assigned to it, and it is specially prohibited in l.3.§.ait prætor Naut.caup.stab.&c. Similar to heretics are apostates, in that heretics fall away from the Catholic faith into heresy and error, while apostates fall away from the Christian religion into a non-Christian one, as Jews or pagans do. For this reason of similarity, tit.7. de Apostat. is added. This is followed by tit.8. Nemini licere signum Sal.&c., for this too is an error, but since it concerns not religion itself but some external matter, and is not plainly heresy, it is treated separately. So far, concerning the errors of Christians, or heretics, and concerning apostates and their kin. Now concerning the Jews, of whom tit. 9. treats: since the error of the Jews seems more tolerable than that of the pagans, the Jews are treated first, before the pagans in tit. 10. ne Christianum mancipium, &c. The reason is that, although today the title applies to all who err, which it contains (heretics, apostates, Jews and pagans alike), it was nevertheless first introduced against the Jews by the Emperor Constantine, as Eusebius testifies in lib. 4. de vita Constantin. There remain the pagans, who are treated last, as the most pestilential, because of their pestilential religion, in tit. 11. de pag. Finally, this is followed by t. 12. de his qui ad Eccl. confug., because the right of asylum and refuge, of which this title treats, is common and clearly extends not only to the orthodox but also to erring heretics, Jews, and so on. Thus, what is proper to Catholics, heretics, and the rest has first been explained distinctly and separately, and then what is common to them, such as the right of asylum, is added, as we have already noted elsewhere above on the Institutes. Lastly, tit. 13. de hu qui in Eccl. manum. is added, for this too, on account of the Churches, belongs to this chapter on divine law. Yet because manumission is a civil status rather than a divine one, and because it concerns slaves, whose condition is the last and lowest, it is rightly treated in the last place. This tit. 13. also fits well with the earlier title de his, qui ad Eccl. confug., for slaves often also take refuge in the Churches. And so far, concerning divine law, or the two parts of public law, sacred things and priests, has been explained. The third part remains, concerning the magistrate, which properly belongs to public law, if we take public law in its proper sense. For public law differs from divine and private law, l. ut in ter, C. de SS Eccl. And just as in those two parts of divine law the faith itself, or the difference of faith, was discussed first, and then the ministers or bishops and their office, so in this part too the law and the laws themselves are explained first, and afterwards the magistrates and their offices. In this order, bishops are reminded of the right faith and magistrates of law and statutes, so that they do nothing contrary to true faith, or to law and right. This is the one reason why, after those two parts, it is not at once the magistrates themselves but first the law and laws that are treated, in tit. 14. de leg. b. and following, down to tit. 20. There is also a second reason or cause: this work, that is the Code, aims chiefly at human law, both public and private, so it is fitting that certain foundational matters, namely the law itself, its nature, parts and origin, should be set out at the very start, as is also done in the Institutes and in the Digest. Since the parts of written law are six (statutes, plebiscites, decrees of the Senate, edicts of the praetors, mandates of the princes, and opinions of jurists), the concept seems to be taken from three of these in tit. 14. de leg. bus, or at least to allude to them. For otherwise the word Edicti in that title could be referred to imperial edicts, not to those of the praetors, l. 3. C. de leg. b., and indeed that whole title pertains mostly to the laws of the emperors. This is also the reason why this tit. 14 holds the first place among those that concern the parts of law: because it treats of imperial constitutions. There is also a second reason of order: that part of this title is general, pertaining to all parts of law, or to all law, d. l. 3. And so in the title itself, del. gib., this clause should be taken generally concerning laws. The title immediately following this one is

units.la: tit.ff.de mand.princip. Ratio est: quia cum priore titulo de consl.t principi sit dictum generaliter, recte jam adjungitur titul.de mandatis eorum, quae sunt constitutiones speciales, vel certè, ut praesidibus Provinciarum dari solent: Proximus est tit.16.de Senatusconsultis, quia & haec pars juris proximam constitutionibus vim & potestatem habet, imo & ipsa Senatusconsulta potius reipsa sunt constitutiones. & nomine tantum Senatusconsulta Restant prudentum respōsa, de quibus postremo locoagitur. quia olim eorum minima esset auctoritas ratione aliarum partium sed ea nunc confirmantur. ff. eiusdem.
units.tr: tit. ff. de mand. princip. The reason is that, since the previous title de consl. t principi was stated in general terms, it is rightly followed by the title on the mandates of the princes, which are special constitutions, or at least those usually given to governors of provinces. Next is tit.16.de Senatusconsultis, because this part of law has a power and authority next to the constitutions, and indeed decrees of the Senate are in reality rather constitutions, and are called Senatusconsulta only in name. What remains are the opinions of jurists, which are treated in the last place, because in former times their authority was least in comparison with the other parts; but now these are confirmed. ff. eiusdem.

units.la: fa, l.ult.de jurevat gent.&c.ti.17.de vel jur.enucl.His partibus juris jam expositis adjungitur tit.18.de jur.& fact ignor. tantum similitudinis gratia. Ut enim alii ad scientiam, ita hicad ignorantiam pertinet, qui in ff alio loco, puta ubi de probationibus, ponitur, sed alia ratione, de qua ibi Jam vero quia constitutiones quarum causa factus est Codex vel sunt generales, vel speciales & de generalibus, ut ordine priorib jam dictum est: Proximū nunc est, ut de specialibus agatur quae plerunq; rescripta dicuntur, & interdum pragmaticae sanctiones: si videlicet nō uni personae sed corpori & collegio impetrētur, ut inf de diversis reser.& pragm.sanct. Sed hae speciales constitutiones, quia precibus principi oblatis impetrātur prius agitur de precib. & rursus, quia preces vel sunt verae vel obreptitiae seu falsae, prius de illis, justa ratione
units.tr: fa, l. ult. de jure vat. gent. etc. tit. 17 de vel jur. enucl. Now that these parts of law have been set out, there is added tit. 18 de jur. & fact. ignor., merely for the sake of resemblance. For as the former pertains to knowledge, so this pertains to ignorance, which in the Digest is placed in another position, namely where proofs are discussed, though for a different reason, which is explained there. Now, since the constitutions for whose sake the Code was made are either general or special, and the general ones have been treated first, as already said, the next task is to deal with the special ones, which are commonly called rescripts and sometimes pragmatic sanctions, if they are granted not to a single person but to a body or corporation, as below in de diversis reser. & pragm. sanct. But since these special constitutions are obtained by petitions offered to the prince, the treatment of petitions comes first; and again, since petitions are either true or obreptitious, that is, false, the true ones are rightly treated first.

units.la: Itaq; primum de precibus justis generalis est tit.19 de precib Imp.off. deinde speciali ter de precibus ad litem pertinentibus Generalia enim sunt speciali bus priora ut supra dictum. Et tit.quidem 20 quando libel.Cofari,&c. prior est,tit 21.ut lite pendēte posterior est quia agit nō de initio judicij, sed de medio ut lite pendente puta de litis contestatione, & de fine judicij ut sententia & appellatione. Post justas statim adjūgitur de injust's. tit 22.ficotrajus veluti. quemadmodū & in Inst prius de utilib.post de inutilib stipulationibus Super n.deteriora sive irrita in posteriore locū sunt rejicieda. Preces jā expositas statim sequuntur rescripta tit 23. Ratio est dictafup. Nam hūc tit. esse de specialibus & personalibus constitutionibus aperte indicat.l.2.5.ejusdem tit Eum sequitur tit.24.de flatuis & imag Ratio tantū est propter similitudinē. Nam ut rescripta sunt principis quaedā beneficia tit.23.l 4.ita & hic titulus beneficiū continet speciale, quo Princeps permittit civitati ut statuā erigat, id dicitur Impatoris beneficiū. l.1.hoc tit. Cui mox adjūgitur tit.25.de his qui ad statuas confug. Nā & hic tit. infigne jus & beneficiū asyli ad statuas Principi continet & recte sequitur priorem Nam statuae erectio prior est asylo & perfingioad statuā. Illud notandum. priusquā transfeatur ad magistratus (quae est tertia pars juris publici) haec principia de jure & legib cōcludi asylo, ut & jus divinū sup.tit.12.de his,qui ad Eccl.cōfug. Videntur n.hi tituli de jure & de precib.ab Imp.ptinere,ut&de ejus quodāmodo officio ante magistratus qdā afferatur. & ut sit tanq; medius Imp.inter tit.de jure divino & jure humano, aut certe sumus aut primus magistratus. Veniēdū est nūc ad partem, téquæ est de magistratibus, quæ in C copiose explicatur, in locis, utjá supra dictum est duobus. Primum hic lib. 1. tit. 26. de off. pref. pretor. &c. & seqq. usque ad finem libri, deinde toto lib. 12. infra Sed quod diligenter observandum, ut supra dixi: quia juris maxima pars ad jus privatum pertinet, cujus finis est jurisdictio, & huic jurisdictioni præest magistratus initio, hoc est, libro hoc primo explicantur ea officia magistratuum quæ ad jurisdictionem pertinent, sive ad judicia & alia; ut passim videre licet, in legibus horum titulorum. Nam de aliis magistratuum officiis extra jurisdictionem, & dignitate ac gradu alio in loco explicatur putal b. 12. infra. Quod ad hunc locum de magistratibus attinet duo ejus summa sunt membra: unum de magistratibus publicis Imperii, seu P. R. alterum de magistratibus municipalibus, & hoc est posterius, de quo infra tit. de defensor. civit. & seqq. Ratio est facilis quia major est dignitas publicorum quam municipalium. De publicis quoq; prius ipsis: posterius vero de eorum Vicariis & ministris justa ratione agitur de Vicariis tit. 48. de off. & c. & tit. seq. idque separatim: Primum, inquam, de ipsis magistratibus & eorum ministris, postea communiter de utrisq; tam de magistratib. quà ministris, tit. de annonis, tit. 2. & seq. Ratio ordinis perspicua est, & infra dicetur. Rursus, quod ad ipsos magistratus attinet duplex quoq; est ordo. Primum de singulis magistratibus speciales sunt tituli deinde generales tituli de off. civ. jud. &c. & 4. seqq. Ratio ordinis eadem est, quæ in Instit. ubi de tutoribus & curatoribus prius distinctè de singulis eorumq; officiis: postea, quæ eorum sunt communia, exponuntur. Quod ad singulos attinet, id admonendum initio ordinem in iis servari dignitatis. Nam cum tres sint dignitatis gradus in jure, illustres, spectabiles & clarissimi; Duaren. l. 2. d. s. c. r. Nov. 7. Primo magistratus illi exponuntur, qui illustres: Secundo, qui spectabiles, tit. 34. de off. proconsul. & 4. seqq. Postremo, qui clarissimi, tit 40. de off. pretor. cum 3. seqq. Ergo ex magistratibus primus locus datur præfectis prætorio de quibus est tit. 26. & 27. Ratio est tum quia horum maxima est potestas, & latissime patet, ferè ut Imperatoris quia & ipsi quasdam ll. condunt, quæ formæ dicuntur l. 2. tit. 26 Ideo proximis titulis, ubi de legibus actum rectè hicadjugitur. Cur autem prius de officio præfecti, pretorio Orientis & Illyrici t. 26. & posterius de præfecto prætorio Africæ agatur titul. 27 Ratio est, quia hic illis est recentior, ut à Justiniano demum introductus. Fuerat autem & alius præfectus prætorio Italiæ, sed desierat Italia à Gothis occupata, & temporibus Cod. nondum recuperata à Justinian. Hos titulos statim sequitur tit. 28. de offic. præfect. urb. quia hujus maximè erat dignitas, ut qui esset tanquam Vicarius Cæsaris & in Consistorio primum locum obtineret post 'mperatorem. Proximus est tit. 29. de offic. magistr. milit. quierat Cæsaris velut generalis Vicarius in re militari; ut in jure dicundo præfectus urbi. Sed urbana militaribus præferri solent, quæ est ratio, cur prius de præfecto urbi, quam de præfecto militari agatur. Est & altera quia præfectus urbi est antiquior, à Regibus Romanis institutus, & ab Augusto revocatus in usum, l.2. §. & hac omnia, de orig. jur. Magister militum est recentior institutus à Constantino Magno teste Sozimo lib.1. Alioqui horum trium præfecti prætorio, præfecti urbi, & magistri militum par, & æqualis dignitas esse dicitur, leg.1. de præfect. prætor. lib.12.
units.tr: Accordingly, the first thing is the general title tit. 19 de precib. Imp. off. on just petitions, and then the special titles on petitions relating to a lawsuit. General matters come before special ones, as said above. Tit. 20 quando libel. Cofari, etc. comes first, and tit. 21 (on what happens while a suit is pending) comes after it, because it deals not with the beginning of a trial but with its middle, such as the joinder of issue while the case is pending, and with its end, such as sentence and appeal. After the just petitions, the unjust ones are dealt with straight away in tit. 22 si contra jus, veluti, just as in the Institutes the useful stipulations come first and the useless ones afterwards. The void or invalid matters are to be set aside to a later place. Next after the petitions already set out come rescripts, tit. 23. The reason is what was said above: this title plainly indicates that it concerns special and personal constitutions, l. 2, 5 of the same title. It is followed by tit. 24 de statuis & imag., and the reason is merely resemblance. For just as rescripts are certain benefits of the prince tit. 23, l. 4, so this title also contains a special benefit by which the Prince permits a city to erect a statue; this is called the Emperor's benefit, l. 1 of this title. Immediately after it comes tit. 25 de his qui ad statuas confug. For this title too contains the remarkable right and benefit of asylum at the statues of the Prince, and it rightly follows the former, since the erection of a statue comes before asylum and the flight to a statue. This is to be noted: before passing to the magistrates, which is the third part of public law, these principles concerning law and laws are concluded with asylum, as also divine law above in tit. 12 de his qui ad Eccl. confug. For these titles on law and on petitions to the Emperor seem to pertain to the Emperor, and something of his office in a way is set forth before the magistrates, so that he may be, as it were, a middle term between the title on divine law and the title on human law, or else the first of the magistrates. Now we must come to the part concerning magistrates, which is treated at length in the Code, in the places that, as has been said, are two. First here, lib. 1, tit. 26 de off. pref. pretor. etc. and following, to the end of the book; then throughout lib. 12 below. But this must be carefully observed, as I said above: since the greatest part of law pertains to private law, whose purpose is jurisdiction, and the magistrate at the outset presides over this jurisdiction, the duties of the magistrates that pertain to jurisdiction, whether to judicial proceedings or other matters, are explained in this first book, as can be seen everywhere in the laws of these titles. For the other duties of the magistrates outside jurisdiction, and their dignity and rank, are explained in another place, for example b. 12 infra. As far as this place concerns magistrates, its main content has two parts: one concerning the public magistrates of the Empire, or of the Roman people, and the other concerning municipal magistrates, which is the later, treated below in tit. de defensor. civit. & seqq. The reason is easy: the dignity of public magistrates is greater than that of municipal ones. Among public magistrates too, the former are treated before the latter, and the deputies and ministers of these are treated with good reason: the deputies in tit. 48 de off. etc. and the following title, and these separately. First, I say, the magistrates themselves and their ministers, and afterwards in common both magistrates and ministers, tit. de annonis, tit. 2 and seq. The reason for this order is clear, and it will be explained below. Again, as far as the magistrates themselves are concerned, there is also a double order. First, there are special titles on the individual magistrates, then general titles de off. civ. jud. etc. and 4 seqq. The reason for the order is the same as in the Institutes, where concerning tutors and curators the individual ones and their duties are first set out distinctly, and afterwards what is common to them is expounded. As for the individual magistrates, this must be noted at the outset: the order among them is observed according to dignity. For since there are three grades of dignity in law, illustrious, respectable and most distinguished, (Duaren. l. 2 d. s. c. r.; Nov. 7), the magistrates of the first rank, the illustrious, are set out first; second, those of the respectable rank, tit. 34 de off. proconsul. & 4 seqq.; last, those of the most distinguished rank, tit. 40 de off. pretor. cum 3 seqq. Therefore among the magistrates the first place is given to the praetorian prefects, concerning whom are tit. 26 and 27. The reason is both that their power is greatest and extends most widely, nearly like that of the Emperor, since they too issue certain laws which are called formulae, l. 2 tit. 26. Hence it rightly follows, in the nearest titles, where laws are discussed, and is added here. But why the office of the praetorian prefect of the East and of Illyricum, tit. 26, is treated before that of the praetorian prefect of Africa, tit. 27, the reason is that the latter is more recent, having been introduced only by Justinian. Moreover there was also another praetorian prefect of Italy, but Italy had ceased to be such because it had been occupied by the Goths, and in the time of the Code it had not yet been recovered by Justinian. The titles are immediately followed by tit. 28 de off. praef. urb., because the dignity of this office was chiefly the highest, as he was like a deputy of Caesar and held the first place in the Consistory after the Emperor. Next is tit. 29 de off. magistr. milit., which was like a general deputy of Caesar in military affairs, as the prefect of the city was in administering justice. But civil matters are usually preferred to military ones, and this is the reason why the prefect of the city is treated before the military prefect. There is also another reason: the prefect of the city is older, instituted by the Roman kings and restored to use by Augustus, l. 2 §. & haec omnia, de orig. jur. The master of the soldiers is more recent, instituted by Constantine the Great, as Zosimus attests, lib. 1. Otherwise the praetorian prefects, the prefect of the city and the masters of the soldiers of these three are said to have equal and like dignity, l. 1 de praefect. praetor. lib. 12.

units.la: His tribus proximè adjicitur Quæstor, tit.30. de officio quæst. tum quia dignitas sive officia quædam militaria, quæ magister militum, de quo modo dictum, usurparat, reddita sunt quæstori: tum quia nemo prioribus tribus exceptis fuerit qui prior esse posset. Nam magister officiorum de quo tit.31. etli dignitate non erat inferior quæstore, tamen ut morum & disciplinæ cura, quæ ad magistrum officiorum pertinebat cedit legibus & consilio, quorū cura erat quæstoris: ita & non immerito quæstori prior datur locus. Recte autem hi duo conjunguntur, quia uterq; Principi inservit sive paret. His adjunguntur & alii tres, qui item inserviunt Principi, sed ex prioribus quæstor legum consilio & exemplis, magistermoribus ac disciplinæ, tres reliqui bonis: ac proinde posteriores. Primus est comes sacrarum largitionum, de quo titul. 32. Alter est comes rerum privatarum, de quo tit.33. Tertius est comes patrimonii de quo tit.34. Ratio ordinis, quia primus curat bona Principis publica & fiscalia: Secundus curat privata, tertius tantū cur mensam sive ea, quæ mensæ principum sunt assignata: & proinde cum sit specialis hic tertius ultimo loco ponitur. Adhuc de primo gradu magistratuum illustrium scilicet, qui item vel palatio serviunt, ut quinque posteriores, vel serviunt universo Imperio, ut tres priores, quorum unus est urbanus & militaris, ut præfectus prætorio, alter urbanus tantum, ut præfectus urbi: tertius militaris tantum, ut magister militum. Nunc de altero gradu, sive spectabilium, qui Provincias tantum regunt, afferuntur quatuor principales, 1. Proconsul tit.35. de offic. proconsul. & leg. Ratio est, propter antiquitatem. Notum est enim jam ante Imperatores fuisse institutos, cum reliqui tres ab Imperatoribus sint instituti. Sed observandum tempore Justiniani hunc magistratum sive ejus nomen fere extinctum fuisse, & tantum in una Africæ parte remansisse, circa urbem Carthaginem: quæ regio ab eo per excellentiam in jure & alibi ab Historicis dicitur proconsularis. Legatus est quidem magistratus, sed non principalis. Est enim Vicarius proconsulis, ideoq; titulus concipitur de offic. proconsul. & legati tam hic quam in ff.
units.tr: Immediately added to these three is the quaestor, tit. 30 de officio quaest., both because certain military dignities or offices, which the master of the soldiers, mentioned just above, had usurped, were given back to the quaestor, and because no one, apart from the first three, could have precedence over him. For the master of the offices, concerning whom is tit. 31, although not inferior to the quaestor in dignity, yet, since the care of morals and discipline, which pertained to the master of the offices, yields to the laws and to counsel, whose care belonged to the quaestor, so the quaestor is not unreasonably given the prior place. These two are rightly joined, because both serve or attend upon the Prince. To these are also added three others, who likewise serve the Prince, but whereas the quaestor serves him with law, counsel and examples, and the master of the offices with morals and discipline, the three remaining serve him with goods; and therefore they come later. The first is the count of the sacred largesses, concerning whom tit. 32. The second is the count of the private estates, concerning whom tit. 33. The third is the count of the patrimony, concerning whom tit. 34. The reason for the order is that the first looks after the Prince's public and fiscal goods, the second his private ones, and the third only the table, or those things which are assigned to the tables of the princes; and therefore, since this third is a special office, it is placed last. So far concerning the first rank of illustrious magistrates, namely those who either serve the palace, as the five later ones do, or serve the whole Empire, as the three earlier ones do, of whom one is civil and military, like the praetorian prefect, another civil only, like the prefect of the city, and the third military only, like the master of the soldiers. Now concerning the second rank, that of the respectable, who govern only provinces, four principal ones are set out. 1. The proconsul, tit. 35 de off. proconsul. & leg. The reason is antiquity: for it is well known that he was instituted even before the Emperors, whereas the other three were instituted by the Emperors. But it must be observed that in the time of Justinian this magistracy, or its name, had nearly disappeared, and remained only in one part of Africa, around the city of Carthage; that region is called proconsular by the jurists by preeminence, and by the historians elsewhere. The legate is indeed a magistrate, but not a principal one. For he is the deputy of the proconsul, and therefore the title is framed de off. proconsul. & legati, both here and in the Digest.

units.la: Alterum locum obtinet comes Orientis. Tertium præfectus Augustalis: Ultimum Vicarius. Ratio ordinis dependet à tempore quod comes Orientis ab Imperatorib primum fit introductus. Proconsul autem institutus, ut jam dixi stante adhuc republica Cur autem præfectus Augustalis, cum sit antiquior comite Orientis, tamen ei postponatur, hæc est ratio: quia major esset comitis orientis potestas. Ille enim præfectus Augustalis, uni Provinciæ Ægypto: hic ut totius, inquam, Orientis Provinciis præerat. Ratio autem cur Vicarius (quod speciale nomen hic est) ultimum locum hic obtinet, est, quia praefecti praetorio vicem gerit, & ideo prioribus tanquam principalibus postponitur. Et haec de altero gradu magistratuum.
units.tr: The count of the East holds the second place, the Augustal prefect the third, and the vicar the last. The order depends on the time when the emperors first introduced the count of the East. The proconsul, however, was instituted, as I have already said, while the republic still stood. As to why the Augustal prefect, although older than the count of the East, is nonetheless placed after him, the reason is this: the power of the count of the East was greater. The Augustal prefect presided over a single province, Egypt, whereas the count presided over the provinces of the whole East, I say. The vicar (a special name here) holds the last place because he takes the place of the praetorian prefect and is therefore placed after the earlier officials, who are the principals. This is said of the second grade of magistrates.

units.la: Tertius statum sequitur, qui est Clarissimorum qui est ultimus Senatorii dignitatis gradus. Et primo quidem de urbanis, quorum unus tantum hic adfertur, Praetor tit. 39. deinde Provinciales exponuntur. Rationem saepe dixi: quia urbana praeferuntur militaribus & peregrinis. Sunt autem hi Provinciales Vicarii, ut Praesides, Consulares, Correctores, de quibus hic unus titulus 40. de officio rectoris provinciae. His Provincialibus jam expositis adjungitur tit. 41. ut nulli patriae sua, &c.
