Hactenus de ordinariis magistratibus in tres, ut dixi, dignitatis gradus distinctis: Hos sequuntur extraordinarii, praefectus annonae, de quo tit. 42. & praefectus vigilum, quae Cassiodor. vocat obscurum, & grassatorum observatorum, de quo tit. 43. Quare & praefectus annonae Principem appellare solet: Praefectus vigilum appellabat Praefectum urbi, tit. ult. quod cum eo quis &c. Admonendum est in quibusdam manuscriptis etiam hunc tit. reperiri: de quadrimestribus brevibus ante tit. de praefecto annonae: rectius tamen omittendus, tum quia de his brevibus sup. est explicatum, l. ult. de off. mag. off. & l. t. de off. com. sacr. larg. Atque ita de hoc tit. de quadr. brev. Cuiac. quoque exstimat in Paratit. (licet aliter Contio videatur) quem, credo, movet auctoritas lib. manuscripti, & etiam auctoritas Graecorum Juris interpp. ex quibus intelligitur tit. aliquem in vulgatis libris Cod. desiderari hic, hb. 1. quare de coreperiendo valde laborat Anto Augustinus in notis ad Cod. & Contius putat hunc esse, de quadr. brev. Cujac. putat esse alium, quem ipse primus in lucem prodidit, puta de off. tribun. & comitus rei milit. non tamen indicat, ubi eum reperit. de quo paulo infr. Et hactenus expositae sunt species magistratuum pro gradibus dignitatis: Speciales sit. jam sequuntur generales, cujus ordinis ratio jam saepe est expositi, quorum primus est de off. civil. jud. tit. 44. alter est de off. milit. jud. tit. 45. Ratio est, quia major est semper dignitas civilium, quam militarium, ut major quoque est dignitas urbanorum, quam Provincialium Judicum. Et hos titulos sumpsit Tribun. ex C. Theod. quem plerumque sequitur in dispositione h. Cod Huic tit. de off. mil. jud. adjunguntur duo alii tit. 46. de off. trib. & com. rei mil. & tit. 47. ne res milit. comit. &c. qui duo tituli, etsi non sunt ita generales ut duo priores, tamen propter similitudinem argumenti adjiciuntur titulo generali, de off. mil. jud. His tandem adjungitur titulus maxime generalis & proinde recte post priores collocatur. Puta tit. 48. de off. div. jud. qui tit. est de omnib. judicib. tam civilib. seu urbanis, quam militaribus. Ejusdem generis est tit. proximus 49. ut omnes jud. tam civ. &c. Ratio a cur hic posterior sit est, quia agit de magistratuum officio jam finito, & proinde ad finem est reservatus. Hunc sequitur tit. 50. de off. eius qui vicem, &c. Dicet aliquis, tractatum de judicib. jam finitum esse, & tamen hic rursum de officiis agi Sed jam sup. dictum est, totum de magistratib. tractatum in 2. capita tribuendum, ut priore de ipsis magistratib. altero de iis, qui magistratib. inserviunt, agatur, in quo sunt magistratuum alleffores, comites & ministri. Et primum quidem de Vicariis dicitur tit. 30. de off.ejus,qui vicem, &c. deinde de assessor. lib. tit. 31. Ratio ordinis cur Vicarius prior sit assessore, est, quia est loco ipsius magistratus, cui assidet, & consilium administrat assessor. Hos sequuntur 2. tituli valde generales, communes tam ipsorum magistratuum, quam comitum sive ministrorum Ratio jam saepe dicta, qui generales officiorum tituli plerunque sunt posteriores.
units.tr: The third rank follows, that of the Clarissimi, which is the last grade of senatorial dignity. First, the urban officials are set out, of whom only one is cited here: tit. 39. Praetor. Then the provincial officials are explained. I have often given the reason: urban officials are preferred to military and foreign ones. The provincial officials are the vicars, the presidents, the consulars and the correctors, on whom this one title, tit. 40. de officio rectoris provinciae, treats. To these provincial officials, now explained, is added tit. 41. ut nulli patriae suae, and so on. So far concerning the ordinary magistrates, divided, as I said, into three grades of dignity. These are followed by the extraordinary officials: the prefect of the grain supply, on whom tit. 42. treats; the prefect of the watch, whom Cassiodorus calls the unclear office, and the prefect of the observers of the bandits, on whom tit. 43. treats. That is why the prefect of the grain supply is accustomed to be called the Prince, and the prefect of the watch was called the prefect of the city, tit. ult. quod cum eo quis, and so on. It must be noted that in some manuscripts this title is also found: de quadrimestribus brevibus, placed before the title de praefecto annonae. It is more rightly omitted, both because these short registers were explained above, l. ult. de off. mag. off. and l. t. de off. com. sacr. larg., and because of this, Cujacius also thinks, in the Paratitla (although Contius seems otherwise), that the title de quadr. brev. is not the one meant. I believe he is moved by the authority of a manuscript, and also by the authority of the Greek interpreters of the law, from whom it is understood that some title is lacking in the printed books of the Code here, in book 1. Therefore Antonius Augustinus labours greatly in his notes on the Code to find what is missing, and Contius thinks it is de quadr. brev. Cujacius thinks it is another, which he himself was the first to bring to light, namely de officio tribunorum et comitibus rei militaris, though he does not indicate where he found it, as I shall say a little below. So far the kinds of magistrates have been set out according to grades of dignity; now follow the general ones, whose order has also often been explained. The first of these is tit. 44. de officio civilis judicis, the second tit. 45. de officio militaris judicis. The reason is that the dignity of civil officials is always greater than that of military ones, just as the dignity of urban judges is greater than that of provincial judges. Tribonian took these titles from the Theodosian Code, which he generally follows in the arrangement of this Code. To this title de officio militaris judicis are added two other titles, tit. 46. de officio tribuni et comitis rei militaris and tit. 47. ne rei militaris comites, and so on. These two titles, though not so general as the two preceding, are nevertheless added to the general title de officio militaris judicis on account of the similarity of subject. Finally, to these is added a title that is most general, and so is rightly placed after the earlier ones: tit. 48. de officio diversorum judicum, which treats of all judges, civil or urban as well as military. Of the same kind is the next title, tit. 49. ut omnes judices, both civil and so on. The reason this one comes later is that it deals with the duty of magistrates once their office has ended, and so it is reserved for the end. It is followed by tit. 50. de officio eius qui vicem, and so on. Someone will say that the treatment of judges is already finished, and yet here again duties are treated. But it has already been said above that the whole treatment of magistrates is to be divided into two chapters, so that in the first the magistrates themselves are dealt with, and in the second those who serve the magistrates, among whom are the assessors, companions and ministers of magistrates. First of all, the vicars are discussed in tit. 30. de officio eius, qui vicem, and so on; then de assessoribus, lib. tit. 31. The reason for the order, that the vicar comes before the assessor, is that the vicar stands in the place of the magistrate beside whom the assessor sits and gives counsel. These are followed by two very general titles, common both to the magistrates themselves and to the companions or ministers. The reason has often been given: the general titles on duties are generally placed later.

units.la: Ex his duob. prior est tit. 52. de anno. & capitatione, &c. posterior est tit. 53. de contractib. jud. & ear. &c. Ratio est, quia prior de annonis est de stipendio, hoc est, de re favorabili tum quia est de permittendo & donando quod ite est favorabile: sed alter est de prohibitione rei, quae ad delictum invitare possit: quod odiosum est, & proinde posterius. Ultimus titulus de magist pub. Pop. Rom. putat tit. 54. de modo multarum. Ratio ordinis est cur inquam, hic tit. sit ultimus: quia est quodammodo poenalis: At poenalia & criminalia in ultimum rejicere solent locum. Expositis igitur jam iis quae ad magistr. pub. pertinent, ratio dictat, ut jam agatur de altera magistratuum specie, hoc est, de magistratib municipalib. de quibus primus est tit. 55. de defens. civit. Nam & hi ad civitates pertinent, licet proprie distinguantur a magistrat. civitatum de quibus est tit. 6. de magistr. municip. Ratio ordinis, cur prius de defensoribus agatur, est quia defensorum potestas fuit latior: & sunt ipsi tanquam vice praesidum Nov. 15. & 18. Hunc titulum 36. de magistr. municip. &c. Sequitur statim tit. 57. de offic. jurid. Alex. qui est titulus ult. lib. 1. Cod. Ratio est quia speciem tantum magistratuum municipalium continet.
units.tr: Of these two, the first is tit. 52. de annona et capitatione, and so on; the second is tit. 53. de contractibus judicum et earum, and so on. The reason is that the first, on the grain supply, concerns a grant, that is, a matter that is favourable, both because it concerns permitting and bestowing, which is itself favourable; but the second concerns the prohibition of a thing that could invite to wrongdoing, which is odious, and therefore comes later. The last title, concerning the public magistrates of the Roman people, is thought to be tit. 54. de modo multarum. The reason for this order, I say, is that this title is the last because it is in some way penal; and penal and criminal matters are customarily placed in the last position. Having now set out what pertains to the public magistrates, reason dictates that we now deal with the other kind of magistrate, namely the municipal magistrates. Of these the first is tit. 55. de defensoribus civitatis. For these too pertain to the cities, although they are properly distinguished from the magistrates of the cities, of whom there is tit. 56. de magistratibus municipalibus. The reason why the defenders are treated first is that the power of the defenders was wider, and they stand, as it were, in the place of the presidents, Nov. 15. & 18. This title is followed at once by tit. 57. de officio juridici Alexandriae, which is the last title of lib. 1. Cod. The reason is that it contains only a species of municipal magistrate.

units.la: Lib. II. Codicis.
units.tr: Lib. II. Codicis.

units.la: HACTENUS de jure publico, quod in sacris sacerdotibus & magistratibus consistit, explicatum. proximum est caput de jure privato. Hujus explicationem oritur Imp. a lib. 2. & pertexit usque ad lib. 10. ut jam supra diximus. Jus igitur privatum, & civile, quia maxime in judiciis & actionibus versatur, ut jam supra dictum est. ubi de ordine librorum codicis ideo jam afferuntur ea, quae ad judiciorum primas partes & initia pertinent: principium autem judiciorum, & omnium actionum est in jus vocatio. f. omnium inst. de poen. tem. litig. recte igitur hic statim ponitur tit. 2. de in jus voca. sed eum tamen praecedit tit. de edendo, quia est primus libri secundi, quia olim (saepe autem in C jus vetus & olim usitatum servatur, & saepius quam in ff.) editio actionis praecedebat in jus vocationem, ut dicetur ad ff. Hos 2. titul. statim sequitur 3. de pact. eumque 4. de transact. Ratio ordinis dicetur infra ad ff. ubi idem est ordo. Namid hoc loco admonendum,
units.tr: Thus far the public law, which consists in sacred matters, priests and magistrates, has been explained. The next chapter concerns private law. Imperial law begins its exposition of this in book 2 and runs on to book 10, as we have already said above. Private and civil law, because it is chiefly concerned with judicial proceedings and actions, as has already been said above, when the order of the books of the Code was discussed, is therefore introduced at this point with those matters which pertain to the first parts and beginnings of judicial proceedings. The beginning of all judicial proceedings and actions is the summons to court (in jus vocatio), cf. Inst. de poenis temere litigantium, rightly therefore title 2, De in jus vocando, is placed here straight away. But it is preceded by the title De edendo, because it is the first of book 2, since formerly (and the old law, still in use, is often preserved in the Code, more often than in the Digest) the production of documents (editio actionis) came before the summons to court, as will be said at the Digest, on the second title there. Straight after that follows title 3, De pactis, and then title 4, De transactionibus. The reason for this order will be given below at the Digest, where the order is the same. For now it must be noted here, lest the same thing be repeated twice, since both in the Digest and the Code...

units.la: { } Tit. I. Tit. II. Tit. III. Tit. IV. Tit. LVI. Tit. LVII. Tit. LVIII. Tit. LIV. Tit. LV. Tit. LVI. Tit. LVII. (marginal references, left margin) ter dum, nos ne idem bis iteretur, cum in ff. & C. idem erit ordo, rationem ordinis ad ff. rejectutos, brevitatis causatitulo 4. de transfacl. adjungitur s. de errore calculi, hac ratione, quia error calculi semper possit retractari: nisi de eo sit transfactum vel judicatum. Post hos tres titulos (depacl. de transact. de errore calc.) velut interjectos, redit Imp. ad ordinem judiciorum, qui est ut in jus vocatus, nisi transfigat, cogatur in jus venire. l. 22. §. 1. de in jus voc. sed quia hodie in jus venire non cogitur, ipse, sed per aliu defendi poterit, recte & ordine jam de iis statim agitur, per quos agere quis, aut defendi possit: quorum 2. cum sint genera, advocati & procuratores. de utroque genere hic explicatur. titulo 6. de postul. & 12. tit. seqq. Prius autem de advocatis, quia longe major advocati est dignitas, quam procuratoris. De advocatis igitur est titulus 6. 7. 8. 9. & 10. quo etiam pertinet 11. Curatem titulus 6. de postulando prior sit titulo de advoc. diverf. jud. qui est titulus 7. (perperam autem in vulgatis libris hic titulus induos titulos est tributus: perperam inquam, qui contra libros veteres & auctoritatem Graecorum, ut & ipse ordo LL. convincit) ratio est, quia titulus 6. est generalis, tum quia est antiquior, pertinens ad edictum: tum etiam quia de prohibitis est, qui non possunt esse advocati. Prohibitoria autem primum sunt collocanda, ut & generalia. At titulus 7. de advocatis magis est specialis, utpote fere totus de advocatis provincialibus & municipalibus: est & recentior, quia jura continet praecipue ex constitutionibus principum prolata: quia autem advocatus fisci est plane specialis, & quaedam in eo sunt specialia, nemo quoque is esse potest, nisi prius fuerit in ordine advocatorum ideo separatim & posteriusde hoc agitur. tit. 8. de advoc. fisc. Huic adjunguntur 2. tituli 9. de errore advoc. &c. & tit. 10. ut quae desunt advocatis, &c. qui sunt ultimi de advocatis. Ratio, quia vicia & errata in ultimum titulum rejiciuntur, sed cur tit. 10. ut quae desunt advocatis, &c. sit posterior, hoc est ratio, quia agit de judice, de quo postremum, & non nisi post advocatos quaeritur, postquam videlicet advocati sua jam allegarunt, an judex postea ab advocatis omissa supplere possit. His autem tit. de postulando, sive de advocatis adjungitur. tit. 11. de causis ex qu. b. infam. alicui irrog. quia scil. infamia notati prohibentur pro aliis postulare. lib. 1. ff. de postul. ut in ff. Post advocatos ponitur tit. de procurat. 12. Ratio jam dicta est. Ad eos autem pertinet quoque tit. 13. Ne liceat potentiorib. &c. Nam h. tit. prohibentur potentiores, procurationes & patrocinia suscipiendo, aliorum actiones inse transferre, quod delictum, quia interest Reipubl. puniri, de eo hic proprius est tit. sumptus ex C. Theod. ut & tit. proximus 14. de his qui potentiorum, in quo delictum priori similimum continetur. Nam & priore titulo prohibetur procuratio potentiorum, ita in hoc 14. prohibentur potentiorum tituli, qui sunt tabulae quaedam affixae praediis, de quibus videtur Duar. lib. 1. disput. cap. 4. & Cujac, in Parat. & Nov. 14. quæ similitudo delicti per potentiores perpetrandi facit ut hic titulus 14. de titulis, licet hic alienus, tamen inseratur ut & tit. 15. ut nemo privatus, & c. & 16. ut nemini liceat, & c. quia & hi duo sunt de titulis five signis, sed prior est de rebus immobilibus five prædiis, quorum proprie sunt tituli five tabulæ, ut mobilium propriasunt signa. Nov. 164. prædiorum autem & rerum soli major est æstimatio, & proinde ille tit. prior loco positus est. Hos titulos sequitur recte tit. 17. ne fisc. vel Respubl. Ut enim modo, de prohibita procuratione potentiorum dictum est, ita nunc quoque de prohibita procuratione fisci aut Reipublicæ recte prioriadjungitur. Et hæc de procuratoribus, quibus quia negociorum gestores sunt persimiles, utrique enim negotia aliena gerunt, sed procurator cum mandato, negociorum gestor sine mandato. l. 1. de procurat. & init. tit. 1 §1. de obl. quæ ex qua. contract. recte titulo de procuratoribus. adjungitur decimusoctavus de negot. gest. tam hic in C. quam in ff. Jam vero quia procurator defensor non est idoneus sine satisdatione. §. ult. de satisd. proximum erat, titulo de procuratoribus tit. de satisdationib. (ut fit in initio) adjungere. Sed hic ante titulum de restitutionibus duo interponuntur restitutio in integrum & arbitrium. Ratio, cur hæc duo interponantur, & adjungantur prioribus tit. de advoc. & procurat. est hæc, tum quia titulo de negot. gest. quæ vi gesta sunt (quod ad verbum gestum) aliquatenus respondent, ut recte hic Cujac. tum quia sæpe ad hæc duo decurrere solent in jus vocati, ut liberentur ab ipso judicio persequendo vel accipiendo. Sæpe enim jus vocati vel laborant, ut in integrum restituantur, & non cogantur litigare: sæpe etiam ad arbitrium ire malunt, & arbitrio rem componere, quam incerto litis eventui rem committere. Plato libro undecimo, de LL. Greek text. Cur autem de restitutione prius agatur, quam de arbitrariis, ratio explicabitur infra ad ff. Nam ibi idem est ordo. Itaque tit. de neg. gest. sequitur titulus decimusnonus, de his quæ vi, &c. Cum autem restitutionis species sint sex, metus, dolus, ætas absentia, status mutatio, & justus error, l. 1. & 2. de in integr. rest. Ex iis tantum priores quatuor hic in C. adferuntur. Hac fortasse de causa, quod reliquæ duæ in ff. satis sint explicatæ: & nulla forte constitutio extaret, quæ de his duabus reliquis, puta de status mutatione & errore aliquid novi contineret. Inter has igitur species metus primo loco ponitur tit. 19. de his quæ vi, &c. Secundo dolus. tit. 20. de dolo malo. Tertio ætas, tit. 21. de in integ. rest. min. Quarto absentia. tit. 50. 51. & 53. Ratio ordinis infra in ff. in quibus idem est, auferetur. Sed de ætate cum in ff. uno titulo, in C. 30. titulis agatur, eorum ratio & ordo hic explicanda. Puto igitur hos titulos de ætate ad tria capita {a}capitare vocari posse, quorum primum sit de hac ipsa restitutione propter ætatem, hoc est, an & quibus de causis. & contra quos ea detur, aut non detur, alterum sit de modo, sive de processu, ac ratione ejus impetrandæ tit.46. posterum de fine & interitu restitutionis tit. 52. Ratio ordinis inter hæc tria capita est facilis. Nam natura prius est quærere, an detur, posterius quando detur, posterius quando finiatur. Quod ad primum caput attinet, id quia late patet, trimembre esse videtur: Nam restitutio vel datur: quia scilicet sit necessaria: & quia justæ sunt causæ, de quo membro itu!.21.de minor.restit.& tit.17.seqq. vel non datur, idque aut quia non sit necessaria, de quo tit. 40. in quib. caus. in integr. &c. aut quia causæ non sunt justæ, ut detur, de quo membro est tit. 41. qui & adversus quos, &c. & 4. tit.seqq. Horum autem trium membrorum ordo hanc habet rationem: hoc est, cur prius de danda, posterius de non danda restitutione agatur: tum quia ex datione, restitutionis natura melius intelligitur tum quia datio est magis favorabilis, quam denegatio. Non datio aut denegatio duo, ut dixi, membra continet. Vel enim non datur, quia non est necessaria, vel quia non est justa causa, illa priore loco ponitur: quia illam causam habet, ut & datio, ideoque; illa dationi, quæ primo loco ponitur, similior & proximior est. Ergo datur restitutio minori læso, ut generaliter dicamus. Et de hoc est tit. generalis, ac proinde primus, puta 21. de in int.restit. sed quæri solet, an etiam detur parenti, & fidejussori minoris, ad parentem pertinet titulus 22. de filiofam. minore ad fidejussorem pertinet titulus 23. de fidejuss.min. Huic adjungitur titulus 24. si tutor vel curat. ubi quæritur, an minori detur restitutio, si tutor vel curator intervenerit, an, inquam, detur minori tutore præsente. quod vix admittendum videbatur. sed tamen & hoc casu datur. Adjunguntur & aliæ causæ, in quibus etiam difficulter datur hæc restitutio, sed tamen datur propter favorem minorum. Sed huic titulo vigesimoquarto, prius adjungitur titulus 25. si in communi eadem causa, &c. Nam ut in priori tit. 14. ita & hoc 25. non videbatur danda minori propter majorem. Huic tit. 25. jam subjunguntur causæ, propter quas datur restitutio, sed difficillime. Et hæc est causa, cur hæ explicentur nominatim. Nam etsi magnus est favor ætatis, qui induxit hanc restitutionem. l. 1. de min. restit. tamen omnis ægre concedi solet, hac de causa quia omnis restitutio est contra jus. l.in honorariis. 25. d: oblig.&a. f. rursus de act. Et sunt quædam causæ quæ ipsæ sunt favorabiles, nec facile relcindi debent, qualis est res judicata, & proinde primus titulus est de his qui adversus rem jud. tit. 26. Huic titulo adjungitur titulus 27. si adversus venditionem, &c. Nam venditioni si accedat jusjurandum, quod rei judicatæ est simile: plane denegatur restitutio. l. 1. hoc titulo. Hunc titulum sequitur tit. 28. si adversus vend. pign. Est enim species prioris tit. & F 1
units.tr: { } Tit. I, II, III, IV, LVI, LVII, LVIII, LIV, LV, LVI, LVII (marginal references, left margin). Lest the same thing be repeated twice, since the order in the Digest and the Code is the same, the reason for the order is left to the Digest. For the sake of brevity, de transact. (title 4) is joined by the title de errore calculi, for this reason: an error in calculation can always be reopened, unless it has been settled by agreement or adjudged. After these three titles (de pact., de transact., de errore calc.), which are inserted as it were between, the Emperor returns to the order of judicial matters, which is that a man summoned to court, unless he settles, must be compelled to come to court. L. 22, §1, de in jus voc. But because today a man is not compelled to come to court himself, but may be defended through another, it is rightly and in good order now treated at once of those through whom a man may act or be defended. There are two kinds of these, advocates and procurators, and both kinds are explained here, in title 6, de postulando, and the twelve following titles. Advocates come first, because the dignity of an advocate is far greater than that of a procurator. So the titles on advocates are 6, 7, 8, 9 and 10, to which also belongs title 11, de causis ex quibus infamia alicui irrogatur. Title 6, de postulando, precedes de advocatis diversorum judiciorum, which is title 7. (In the printed books this title has been wrongly divided into two titles, wrongly, I say, as the old manuscripts and the authority of the Greeks, and the order of the laws itself, prove.) The reason is that title 6 is general, both because it is older and pertains to the edict, and because it deals with prohibitions, persons who cannot be advocates. Prohibitions ought to be placed first, as also general matters. But title 7, de advocatis, is more special, being almost wholly about provincial and municipal advocates; it is also more recent, since it contains laws drawn chiefly from imperial constitutions. Because the advocate of the treasury (advocatus fisci) is wholly special, and certain things in it are special, and no one can be such unless he has first been in the order of advocates, this is treated separately and later, in title 8, de advocatis fisci. To this are joined two titles, 9, de errore advocatorum, etc., and title 10, ut quae desunt advocatis, etc., which are the last on advocates. The reason is that faults and errors are put in the final title. But why title 10, ut quae desunt advocatis, etc., comes later is this: it deals with the judge, who comes last, and it is asked only after the advocates, namely once the advocates have already pleaded their cases, whether the judge may afterwards supply what the advocates have omitted. To this title de postulando, or on advocates, is added title 11, de causis ex quibus infamia alicui irrogatur, because those branded with infamy are forbidden to plead for others. L. 1, ff. de postulando, as in the Digest. After the advocates comes title 12, de procuratoribus. The reason has already been given. To these also belongs title 13, Ne liceat potentioribus, etc. For in this title the more powerful are forbidden to take on procurations and patronage, and to transfer to themselves the actions of others; this is a crime which it is in the public interest to punish, and about it this title is more fitting here, taken from the Theodosian Code, as is the next title, 14, de his qui potentiorum, in which a crime very like the former is contained. For in the previous title the procuration of the powerful is forbidden, and so in this 14th the titles of the powerful are forbidden, which are certain tablets fixed to estates; concerning these see Duaren, lib. 1 disput. cap. 4, and Cujas, in Parat. & Nov. 14. This likeness of a crime committed by the powerful makes this title 14, de titulis, although foreign here, inserted, as also titles 15, ut nemo privatus, etc., and 16, ut nemini liceat, etc., because these two too are about titles or signs; but the former concerns immovable things or estates, whose proper titles or tablets they are, as signs are proper to movables. Nov. 164. But greater value attaches to estates and land, and therefore that former title is placed first. Rightly these titles are followed by title 17, ne fisc. vel Respublica. For just as the forbidden procuration of the powerful was discussed a moment ago, so now the forbidden procuration of the treasury or the commonwealth is rightly added to the former. And so much for procurators. Since agents of affairs (negotiorum gestores) are very like them, both indeed manage the affairs of others, but the procurator with a mandate, the agent without one (L. 1, de procurat.; and the beginning of title 1, §1, de obl. quae ex quasi contractu), rightly to the title de procuratoribus is added the eighteenth, de negotiis gestis, both here in the Code and in the Digest. Now, since a procurator is not a suitable defender without security (§ ult. de satisd.), the next thing was to add, to the title de procuratoribus, the title de satisdationibus (as is the practice at the beginning). But here, before the title de restitutionibus, two are interposed: restitution in integrum and arbitration. The reason why these two are interposed and joined to the former titles de advocatis et procuratoribus is this: partly because the things done by force (which the Greek term corresponds to, as Cujas rightly notes here) correspond in some degree to the title de negotiis gestis; and partly because those summoned to court often have recourse to these two, to be freed from pursuing or accepting the judgment itself. For those summoned to court often labour to be restored in integrum, and not to be compelled to litigate; often too they prefer to go to arbitration and settle the matter by arbitration rather than entrust it to the uncertain outcome of a suit. Plato, in book eleven of the Laws (Greek text). Why restitution is treated before arbitrations will be explained below, in the Digest, for there the order is the same. So after the title de negotiis gestis follows title 19, de his quae vi, etc. Since there are six kinds of restitution, fear, fraud, age, absence, change of status, and just error (L. 1 and 2, de in integrum restitutione), only the first four are treated here in the Code. Perhaps the reason is that the other two are sufficiently explained in the Digest, and perhaps no constitution exists containing anything new on those other two, namely change of status and error. Among these kinds, therefore, fear is placed first, in title 19, de his quae vi, etc.; second, fraud, in title 20, de dolo malo; third, age, in title 21, de in integrum restitutione minorum; fourth, absence, in titles 50, 51 and 53. The reason for the order will be dropped below in the Digest, where it is the same. But since in the Digest the matter of age is treated in one title, and in the Code in thirty titles, their reason and order must be explained here. I think therefore these titles on age may be called three heads: the first about this very restitution on account of age, that is, whether it is granted and on what grounds, and against whom it is or is not granted; the second about the mode, or the procedure, and the manner of obtaining it, title 46; the third about the end and extinction of restitution, title 52. The order among these three heads is easy. For it is more natural to ask whether it is granted before asking when it ends. As to the first head, since it extends widely, it seems to have three parts: restitution is either granted, namely because it is necessary, and because the causes are just (on this member see tit. 21, de minorum restitutione, and titles 17 onwards); or it is not granted, and that either because it is not necessary (on which see title 40, in quibus causis in integrum restitutio, etc.), or because the causes are not just for it to be granted (to which part belongs title 41, qui et adversus quos, etc., and titles 42 onwards). The order of these three parts has this reason: that is, why the grant of restitution is discussed first and its refusal afterwards; partly because the nature of restitution is better understood from the grant, and partly because the grant is more favourable than the refusal. Non-grant or refusal, as I said, contains two parts. For either it is not granted because it is not necessary, or because there is no just cause; the first is placed first, because it has the same ground as the grant, and so it is more like and nearer to that first-placed grant. Therefore restitution is granted to a minor who has been injured, to put it generally. And of this there is the general title, and so the first, namely 21, de in integrum restitutione minorum. But it is commonly asked whether it is also granted to a parent and to a surety of a minor. To a parent belongs title 22, de filiofamilias minore; to a surety belongs title 23, de fidejussoribus minorum. To this is added title 24, si tutor vel curator interveniat, where it is asked whether restitution is granted to a minor if a guardian or curator has intervened, that is, I say, whether it is granted when the minor's guardian is present, which seemed hardly admissible. Yet even in this case it is granted. Other causes are also added, in which this restitution is again granted with difficulty, but nevertheless it is granted on account of the favour shown to minors. But before this title 24 comes title 25, si in communi eadem causa, etc. For, as in the earlier title 14, so here in 25 it did not seem to be granted to a minor on account of a major. After this title 25 come the causes on account of which restitution is granted, but with the greatest difficulty. And this is the reason why these are explained by name. For although the favour of age, which introduced this restitution (L. 1, de minorum restitutione), is great, nevertheless all such grants are usually made with reluctance, for the reason that every restitution is against the law (L. in honorariis 25, de obligationibus et actionibus; further, de actionibus). And there are certain causes which are themselves favourable and ought not easily to be rescinded, such as a thing adjudged; and so the first title is de his qui adversus rem judicatam, title 26. To this title is added title 27, si adversus venditionem, etc. For if an oath is added to the sale, which is like a thing adjudged, restitution is plainly refused (L. 1, this title). The title that follows this is title 28, si adversus venditionem pignoris. For it is a species of the earlier title, and here too restitution is granted with difficulty, on account of the solemn sale of a pledge. To the sale is joined a gift, title 29, si adversus donationem. The reason is that both are here presented as done with the guardian's authority, and that in both the ownership is here transferred; for in both a traditio is understood to have been made.

units.la: in hoc quoque difficulter datur restitutio, propter solemnem venditionem pignoris. Venditioni adjungitur donatio. tit. 29. si adverf. donat. Ratio est, tum quia utraque hic proponitur facta tutore auctore, tum quia utraque hic transfertur dominium: Nam in utraque intelligitur traditio mulfacta. Donationi proxima causa est libertas. tit. 30. si adverf. libert. quia libertatis donatio est quaedam species beneficii, & quidem summi, ut ait Terent. Notum quoque est libertatem revocari difficillime. §. semel. inst. ex quibus causis, &c. Huic adjungitur titulus 31 si adverf. transact. &c. Nam & illa difficilime revocatur leg. 20. C. de transact. & continet aliquid dominio non absimile. Nam transactione aliquid remittitur: licet tamen contra etiam quid recipiatur. l. 33. transactio. C. de transact. Divisio vero transactione fieri solet: unde & pactum divisionis dicitur. l. 7. si fides. C. communia utrinsque judic. transactioni similis est solutio, & proinde eam subsequitur, quae est ipsa favorabilis, & proinde non tam facile rescinditur, de quo est titulus 32. si adverf. solut. Adjicitur dos. titulus 33. si adversus dotem. Nam haec quia favorabilis, non semper datur ejus nomine restitutio. Cur autem dos sequatur ratio est, quia in his duobus titulis proponitur solutio facta per alium, per curatorem licet minoris: ut & dos per alium, puta per tutorem minoris puellae. Tandem est titulus trigesimus quartus, si adverf. delict. &c. Nam ut saepe dictum, vicia & delicta in ultimum titulum rejiciuntur. Cur igitur dicat aliquis, post hunc titulum ponitur alius titulus trigesimus quintus, si adverf. usucap. &c. quae cum sit adquisitio dominii videbatur prope titulum si adversus donationem potius collocandus? Ratio ordinis haec est, quia haec causa differt ab omnibus prioribus in eo, quod in illis factum aliquod, ut vendere, donare, &c. in usucapione nullum factum minoris sed non factum, hoc est, negligentia versetur, sive patientia socors. l. alienationis ff. de verb. signif. quae causa quoque est, cur & haec restitutio ob usucapionem fit difficilior. Est & altera ordinis ratio, quia quaedam species delicti hic versatur, puta animia negligentia, & proinde tit. si adverf. delict. recte adjungitur huic tit. si adverf. usucap. Huic adjungitur tit. 36 si adverf. fiscum, vel quia post restitutionem adversus privatos, ratio postulat, ut etiam de ea agatur, quae adversus fiscum, Nam & haec difficilis est propter furorem fisci. Et haec ratio indicatur, l. 2. hoc tit. vel quia in hoc tit. l. ult. asseritur de praescriptione quinquennii quae pertinet ad usucapionem, de qua priore tit. quare & in instit. §. ult. de usucap. idem ponitur, quod hic inl. ult. tit. si adverf. fiscum. Hunc titulum sequitur tit. 37. si adversus creditorem. Ratio est, quia hactenus dictum est de restitutionibus ex hac causa, si minor aliquid amittat ex propriis bonis proximum est, ut agatur de iis qui nihil alienant, vel amittunt ex suis bonis. Quo pertinet titulus ist e 37. si adverf. credit. &c.
units.tr: In this case too, restitution is granted only with difficulty, on account of the formal sale of a pledge. Sale is followed by gift: title 29, "If against a gift." The reason is that both are here treated as transactions done with a guardian's authority, and both transfer ownership, since in each a delivery by hand is understood to have taken place. Closest to gift is liberation: title 30, "If against a manumission," because the granting of freedom is a kind of benefit, and indeed of the highest kind, as Terence says. It is also well known that liberation is revoked with the greatest difficulty (§ semel, Inst. "From what causes..."). To this is joined title 31, "If against a settlement," for that too is very hard to revoke (L. 20, C. "On settlements"), and it contains something not unlike ownership. For in a settlement something is given up, though on the other side something may also be received (L. 33, "Settlement," C. "On settlements"). Division of property is usually effected by settlement, whence it is also called a pact of division (L. 7, "If there is good faith," C. "On the common property of both judgments"). Payment is similar to settlement, and so it follows it. Payment is itself favoured, and therefore is not so easily rescinded; this is the subject of title 32, "If against a payment." Dowry is added: title 33, "If against a dowry." For this, since it too is favoured, restitution is not always granted on its account. The reason dowry follows is that these two titles deal with payment made through another, a curator of a minor, as also a dowry given through another, for instance through the guardian of a minor girl. Last is title 34, "If against a wrong," and so on. For, as has often been said, defects and wrongs are placed in the last title. So someone may ask why, after this title, another title 35 is placed, "If against usucapion," which, since it is an acquisition of ownership, seemed rather to belong close to "If against a donation." The reason for the order is that this cause differs from all the earlier ones in this respect: in those some act was done, such as selling or giving, whereas in usucapion there is no act of the minor, but a non-act, that is, negligence or slothful acquiescence (L. "Alienation," D. "On the meaning of words"). This is also why restitution on account of usucapion is harder to obtain. There is also a second reason for the order: a certain species of wrong is involved here, namely minor negligence, and so title "If against a wrong" is rightly joined to "If against usucapion." To this is joined title 36, "If against the treasury." This is either because, after restitution against private persons, reason requires that the case against the treasury also be treated; for this too is difficult on account of the treasury's fury, and this reason is indicated in L. 2 of this title; or because in this title, in the last law, prescription of five years is asserted, which belongs to usucapion, the subject of the earlier title. Therefore also in the Institutes (§ last, "On usucapion") the same point is made as in the last law of this title, "If against the treasury." This title is followed by title 37, "If against a creditor." The reason is that, so far, it has been discussed what restitutions arise from this cause, when a minor loses something from his own goods. Next comes treatment of those who alienate nothing, or lose nothing from their own goods. To this belongs title 37, "If against a creditor," and so on,

units.la: . credit. & 2 tit. feqq. quæ ratio ordinis indicatur in tit. 39. d. si at omissam. Et hu-jus generis est cautio sive obligatio: ut si mutuû acceperit minor, nihil alienat de suo sed accipit potius alienum: & tamen datur restitutio, quia se obligavit ad alienandum, hoc est reddendum mutuum. Ejusdem generis est hereditas minori obveniés, de qua 2. sunt tituli, prior est tit. 38. si minor ab hereditate se abstineat, &c. alter est tit. 39. si ut omissam hereditatem. Nam in hereditate minor bifariam leditur, aut in adeunda aut in omittenda. Ratio ordinis est; hoc est, cur tit. si minor ab her. se abst. &c. de additione fit prior: tũ quia hoc casu, (quo minor jam adijt, seque creditor ibus obligavit adeundo f. beres. institut. de oblig. quae ex q. contr. & posteaad versus aditionem restitui velit, ut se abstineat rursus ab hereditate) creditores sint convocandi, quorum scilicet interest. Nov. 111. Et proinde huic tit. si minor ab hereditate, &c. recte adjungitur tit. si ut omiff. &c. tum quia aditio natura prior est omissione, ut habitus prior est privatione. Et haec de primo membro restitutionem, hoc est ex quibus causis detur restitutio licet ex multis egre. Alterum est de causis ex quibus non detur, quia non sit necessaria de quibus est tit. 40. in quibus causi. in integr. rest. &c. Proximum est tertium de iis causis, ob quas minime datur restitutio: ut quia sunt nullæ, & injustæ, quo pertinet tit. 41. qui & adversus quos. &c. 3. feqq. Ille quidem qui & adverf. &c. quia generaliter est conceptus, licet specialiter tamen unam & alteram tantum causam continet. Huic adjungitur tit. 42. si minor se major: &c. Nam ut prior casus est inductræ minoris ad denegandam restitutionem: ita hic est ejus malitia sive malitiosa & fraudulenta inductria. Alius casus adfertur tit feq. 43. si septimus &c. posterior illis hac ratione quia illi de prima restitutione, hic agit de secunda, & iterata. Cui casui proximum tit. obtinet alius, puta impetratio veniæ ætatis, de quo est tit. 44. de his qui veniam, &c. qui casus est ult. Et recte ei adjungitur tit. 45. si major facti. Nam ut priores tituli omnes sunt de minore, ita hic titul. 45. est de majore & proinde posterior: Major autem similis est ei, qui veniam ætatis impetrat, de qua est tit. 44. de his qui veniam. Hactenus de primo capite restitutionis, eoque trimembri, quando & quibus ex causis detur restitutio & quibus non, proximum est caput alterum de modo processu restitutionis impetrandæ, ad quod pertinet tit. 46. & tres feqq. Et primum quidem de judice, apud quem restitutio impetretur d. titul. 46. ubi & apud quem cognitio restitutionis agitanda sit. Nam ut in judiciis, ita & in restitutionibus, quæ cum judiciis similitudinem habent, primum quæritur de ipsa jurisdictione & magistratu. Huic adjungitur tit. 47. de reputatur: Nam ut restitutio fit apud magistratum, ita & reputatio contra minorē. Ad initium quoque sive ad petendam restitutionem pertinet titul. 48. etiam per procuratorem, &c. Nam ut in judiciis, ita & hic primum de magistratibus, deinde de partibus eorumque procuratore constare debet. Hunc sequitur, tit. 49. in integr. rest. post. &c. Ratio, quia priores tituli sunt de postulanda, & tit. XLIX hic jam de postulata, & proinde ultimus. Restat tertium caput, quod est de interitu restitutionis de quo est tit. 52. de temp. in integr. & c, sed ante eum titulum interjiciuntur tituli, de militibus & de militum restitutione, & uxorum militum, tit. 50. de reft. milit. & titul 51. de uxor. milit. quae tamen tractatio de militibus & absentibus Reip. causa propriè pertinebat ad quattam restitutionis speciem propter absentiam Reip. causa, de qua tit. 53. Ratio tamen, cur de his sint interjecti hic 2. tituli, nbi de minoribus agitur, est haec, quia miles absens Reip. causa minoribus sint similes in eo, quod ut minorum, ita & horum restitutio eodem tempore duret: puta olim anno utili, & hodie quadriennio, cum aliud tempus aliis restitutionibus quibusdam etiam perpetuum sit constitutum. Atque ita commode hic adjungitur tit. 52. de temp. in integr. reft. &c. quod est tertium & ultimum caput de restitutionibus propter aetatem. Est & hic titulus communis tam minorum quam militum, & Reip. causa absentium. Et haec de tertia specie restitutionum propter aetatem fcil. Eam proxime sequitur 4. species, quae est propter absentiam: de qua est titul. 53. qu. b. ex caus. major. &c. Ratio, quia ut prior est de minoribus, quorum aetas tempore est prior, ita & haec quarta de majoribus. Ad hanc majorum restitutionem pertinet titul 54. de alienatione judic. mut. caus. &c. sed quia restitutio datur sub eo titulo propter delictum. l. 7. de alien. judic. mut. &c. merito ultimum in locum rejicitur. Dictum est supra judiciorum ordinem interrumpi hoc libro, duobus tractatibus interjectis restitutionum & arbitrorum: itaque illo jam explicato accedit Imper. ad alterum, de quo est titul. 55. de recept. arb. His igitur duobus jam consectis redit Imper. ad ordinem, qui ut intelligatur, meminisse oportet, ante duos illos tractatus actum fuisse de advocatis & procuratoribus. Hi autem quia sine satisdatione non sunt idonei, statim adjungitur tit. 56. de satisdando, ut & in institut. lib 4. est dictum. Tandem novo jure concludit haec initia judiciorum: ita namque solet jus novissimum ponere loco novissimo, ut in instit. tit. de leg. at. tit. de inutil. stip. de interdict. juris novi duo capita hic adferuntur: de formulis actionum, de jutejurand. calumniae. De illis prior est tit. postea 57. de formulis act. & c. de hoc tit 58. de jurejurand. propter calum. Ratio, cum quia jus novum hoc de jurejurando est recentius priore, ut potea Justiniano introductum: cum prius de formulis fit ab aliis Impp. tum quia in processu sive ordine judicij formularum impetratio prior est jurejutando calumniae, quod in ipsa litis contestatione pierunque interponitur: cum formularum impetratio etiam fieret ante editionem statim initio. Est tertia ratio, quia tit. 57. exceptionem habet non impetratae formulae, sed haec sublata est, illa non item.
units.tr: ...creditor, and the two following titles, whose order is indicated in title 39, "If as to an omitted matter." Of this kind also is a caution or obligation: if a minor has received a loan, he alienates nothing of his own but rather takes on what belongs to another; yet restitution is granted, because he bound himself to alienate, that is, to repay, the loan. Of the same kind is an inheritance falling to a minor, for which there are two titles. The first is title 38, "If a minor abstains from an inheritance, etc." the second is title 39, "If an inheritance was omitted." For in inheritance a minor is harmed in two ways, either in accepting or in omitting. The reason for the order, that is, why title "If a minor abstains from an inheritance, etc." on acceptance comes first, is this: in that case, where the minor has already accepted and has bound himself to creditors by accepting (Institutes, "The heir," On obligations arising from contract), and afterwards wishes to be restored against the acceptance so as to abstain again from the inheritance, the creditors must be summoned, since their interest is involved (Nov. 111). Therefore to this title "If a minor from an inheritance, etc." is rightly joined the title "If an omitted matter, etc." both because acceptance is by nature prior to omission, as possession is prior to deprivation. So much for the first part of restitution, that is, from what causes restitution is granted, though from many it is granted with difficulty. The second part concerns the causes from which it is not granted, because it is not needed; this is the subject of title 40, "On what causes, in integral restitution, etc." The next is the third part, concerning those causes on account of which restitution is by no means granted, as when they are null and unjust. To this belongs title 41, "And against whom, etc." (3 following). The first of these, "And against whom, etc." because it is conceived in general terms, though in particular it contains only one or two causes. To this is joined title 42, "If a minor pretends to be of age, etc." For as the earlier case is the inducement of a minor to deny restitution, so here is his malice, or malicious and fraudulent inducement. Another case is brought in title 43 following, "If a seventh, etc." which is later than the former for this reason: those treat of the first restitution, while this one treats of a second and repeated restitution. Next to this case stands another title, namely the obtaining of a grant of age, the subject of title 44, "On those who obtain a grant of age, etc." which is the last case. And rightly title 45, "If a major, etc." is joined to it. For as all the earlier titles concern a minor, so this title 45 concerns a major and is therefore later. A major, however, is similar to one who obtains a grant of age, the subject of title 44, "On those who obtain a grant." So far on the first head of restitution, which has three parts: when and from what causes restitution is granted, and when not. The next head is the second, on the mode of procedure in obtaining restitution. This concerns first the judge before whom restitution is sought, title 46, where also it is to be determined before whom the hearing of restitution is to be conducted. For as in judgments, so also in restitutions, which have a likeness to judgments, the question first concerns jurisdiction itself and the magistrate. To this is joined title 47, "On the reckoning," for as restitution is sought before the magistrate, so also is the reckoning against the minor. Title 48, "Even through a proxy, etc." also pertains to the beginning, or to the seeking of restitution. For as in judgments, so here too the magistrates must first be established, then the parties and their proxies. This is followed by title 49, "On integral restitution after, etc." The reason is that the earlier titles concern the seeking of restitution, and title XLIX now concerns the sought restitution, and is therefore last. There remains the third head, which concerns the lapse of restitution, the subject of title 52, "On the time for integral restitution, etc." But before that title are interposed titles on soldiers, on the restitution of soldiers, and on soldiers' wives: title 50, "On the restitution of soldiers," and title 51, "On soldiers' wives." This treatment of soldiers and of those absent on account of the state properly belongs to a certain species of restitution, on account of absence for the state, the subject of title 53. The reason, however, why these two titles are inserted here, where minors are treated, is this: a soldier absent for the state is similar to minors in this, that his restitution, like theirs, lasts for the same period, namely formerly the useful year, and today four years, although for certain other restitutions a different time, even a perpetual one, has been established. And so title 52, "On the time for integral restitution, etc." is conveniently joined here, which is the third and last head of restitutions on account of age. This title is common both to minors and to soldiers and to those absent for the state. So much for the third species of restitutions, on account of age. This is followed closely by the fourth species, which is on account of absence, the subject of title 53, "Whether, etc., from which cause of majority." The reason is that, as the earlier species concerns minors, whose age is earlier, so this fourth concerns majors. To this restitution of majors belongs title 54, "On alienation of a judgment, by mutual cause, etc." but because restitution is granted under that title on account of a wrong (L. 7, "On alienation of a judgment by mutual cause"), it is rightly placed in the last position. It has been said above that the order of judgments is interrupted in this book by two treatises interposed, on restitutions and on arbitrations. So, with that now explained, the Emperor passes to the other, the subject of title 55, "On receiving arbitration." With these two now finished, the Emperor returns to the order, which, to be understood, one must remember that before those two treatises there was discussion of advocates and proctors. And since these are not fit without security, title 56, "On giving security," is immediately joined, as also was said in the Institutes, book 4. Lastly, by the newer law, these beginnings of judgments are concluded; for the newest law is in the habit of placing things in the last position, as in the Institutes, titles "On legacies," "On useless stipulations," "On interdicts." Here two heads of the new law are brought in: on the formulas of actions, and on the oath against calumny. Of these the first is title 57, "On the formulas of actions," and then title 58, "On the oath, on account of calumny." The reason is that this new law on the oath is more recent than the earlier one, as it was introduced later by Justinian; and the earlier one, on formulas, was made by other emperors. Also, in the process or order of a trial, the obtaining of formulas comes before the oath against calumny, which is for the most part interposed at the very contestation of the suit, whereas the obtaining of formulas was done even before the issuing of the summons, at the very beginning. There is a third reason: title 57 has an exception of a formula not obtained, but this has been removed, whereas that exception has not.

units.la: Liber III. Codicis.
units.tr: Book III of the Code.

units.la: ETHaec est analysis titulorum lib. 2.in quo diximus contineri initia judiciorum, quæ græce Ϭ ᾱρχαὶ dicuntur. Ordinis nunc ratio postulat, ut de ipsis judiciis explicetur. Itaq; duo potissimum de iis tractantur. I. quæ ad formam, sive ut vulgo loquuntur, ad processum pertinent. II. Ipsæ judiciorum species. Sed pars prior, quia est bimembris, vt partim ad ipsam judiciorum constitutionem, partim ad finem pertineat: hunc ordinem tenuit Tribunianus tam in C. quam in ff. vt membrum de judiciis constituendis priore loco: alterum de finiendis (enumeratione singulorum judiciorum interposita) posteriore poneretur, ut supradictum ubi de lib. Cod. In hoc igitur lib. 3. tria fere continentur. I. Illud membrum de judiciis constitu-endis. II. Species judiciorum sive actionum in rem exponuntur tit. 28. & 3. seqq. & tandem quaedam accessoria sive extraordinaria tit. 40. & 3. seqq. ꝟ sque adsitum libr. Quod ad primum caput hujus libri attinet de ipsis judiciis eorumque constituendorum, & exercendorum processu, adtria quoque id membra revocari potest, ut res fit dilucidior. Primo namque de personis judicum & litigantium agitur titulo primo & sex seqq. Alterum membrum est de iis, quae ad constitutionem judiciorum ipsam pertinent, de quo est tit. 8. & 4. seqq. Tertium est de foro competente, de quo tit. 13. & 15. seqq. De primo, hoc est, de personis, cur primo loco agitur, ratio est perspicua propter dignitatem, sed cur agatur postremo de foro competente, ratio est, quia ab eo membro tertio facilior fiat transitio ad secundum caput libri 3. quod continet singulas judiciorum species in rem. Nam & hoc membrum de foro competente tractatur per multas judiciorum species. Forum variat pro differentia judicii. Quod igitur ad primum membrum de personis attinet, primum de ipsis judicibus eorumque officio generaliter agitur tit. 1. Tit. I. de judiciis, de quo tamen titulo dicetur latius in ff hoc titulo. Nam & hic videtur generalis, quo ad naturam & proprietatem judiciorum. Multa enim sub eo hic exponuntur, quae non ad judicum personas, sed ad naturam judiciorum pertinent, ut inl. 1. 2. 3. 4. 7. & 8. Huic adjungitur ti-tulus 2 de sportulis, &c. Ratio, quia in l. ult. tit. 1. facta sit mentio executorum, quibus dari solent sportulae, hac occasione statim l. ult. tit. 1. additur titulus secundus de sport. Post hunc titulum secundum statim redit ad ipsos judices. Et primo quia egit de omnibus judicibus & maximè de majoribus, adjungitur jam tit. de minoribus tit. 3. de pedan. judic. Hujus tituli pars videtur titulus 4. qui prostiajuri sdicit. &c. aut certe communis est hic totus titulus titulo 1. & 3. Nam agitur de pedaneis judicibus quinam tales esse possint, & à quib. dentur, five qui eos dare possint, putamajores. Sic & tit. 5. ne quis in sua causa, &c. item est communis tam majori, qui proprie jus Tit. V.
units.tr: This is the analysis of the titles of Book 2, in which we said the beginnings of judicial proceedings are contained, which in Greek are called [αἱ ἀρχαί]. The order of the material now requires that the judicial proceedings themselves be explained. Two main things are treated concerning them: I. what pertains to form, or, as people commonly say, to procedure; II. the kinds of judicial proceedings themselves. But the first part has two members, since it concerns partly the establishment of the judgment itself and partly its conclusion. Tribonian kept this order both in the Code and in the Digest, placing the member on establishing judgments first and the member on bringing them to an end second, with the enumeration of the individual judgments inserted between them, as was said above where we discussed the Book of the Code. In this third book, then, roughly three things are contained. I. That first member, on establishing judgments. II. The kinds of judgments or actions in rem are set out in title 28 and following; and finally certain accessory or extraordinary matters in title 40 and following, right to the end of the book. As for the first head of this book, concerning the judgments themselves, their establishment and the conduct of the procedure, this too can be traced back to three members, to make the matter clearer. First, the persons of the judges and of the litigants are treated, in title 1 and the six following. The second member concerns what pertains to the establishment of the judgments themselves, and this is in title 8 and the following, from 4. The third is on the competent forum, in title 13 and 15 and following. As for the first member, on persons, the reason it is treated first is plain, on account of their dignity. But the reason the competent forum is treated last is that this third member makes the transition to the second head of Book 3 easier, which contains the individual kinds of judgments in rem. For this member on the competent forum is also treated under many kinds of judgments, since the forum varies according to the kind of judgment. So, as to the first member, on persons, the judges themselves and their office are first treated in general, in title 1, De judiciis, though this title will be discussed more fully in the Digest. For this title also appears general as to the nature and property of judgments. Many things are set out under it that pertain not to the persons of the judges but to the nature of judgments, as in laws 1, 2, 3, 4, 7 and 8. To this is joined title 2, De sportulis, etc. The reason is that in the last law of title 1 mention was made of the officials to whom fees are customarily given, and on this occasion the last law of title 1 is immediately followed by the second title, De sportulis. After this second title, the discussion returns at once to the judges themselves. And since it first dealt with all judges, and especially with the greater ones, there is added now the title on the lesser judges, title 3, De pedaneis judicibus. Part of this title seems to be title 4, Qui prosunt iuri dicendo, etc., or certainly this whole title is common to titles 1 and 3. For it treats of which pedaneous judges may be appointed, and by whom they are given, or who may give them, namely the greater judges. So too title 5, Ne quis in sua causa, etc., is common to both the greater judges, who are properly said to declare the law, and the pedaneous judges, who properly judge. And therefore these titles, as common ones, are placed in a later position.

units.la: 4. dicere dicuntur, quam pedaneorum, qui proprie judicare. Et proinde hi tituli ut communes posteriore loco ponuntur. Post judices quaeritur de ipsis litigantibus, ad quos tit. 6. pertinet, qui legit. person. &c. & tit. 7. ut nemo invitus &c. Ratio inter hos 2. tit. est, quia prius cogitare debet, an agere quis possit, quam cogi possit. Siniste enim cogerentur, qui etsi velint, agere non possent. Nunc de ipso processu, sive judicij forma & ritu, quo pertinet titulus octavus, de ord. Judic & 4. seqq. ut supra dictum. Ratio, cur ille titulus prior loco ponatur, est, tum quia verba sunt generalia, tum quia constare debet de ipsa quaestione, de qua sit judicium, quam ulterius de ejus processu agatur. Hunc sequitur titulus nonus, de l. tu conteft. cum ante litis contestationem potius sit controversia quam lis, ut indicat l. 1. de lit. contest. & l. 2. de edo. supra, quae duae LL. sunt conjungendae. Huic tit. de litis contest adjungitur tit. 10. d. plus petit, huic 11. de dilat. Ratio est, quia dilationem plerunque sunt causae, instrumenta sive probationes. ut aist l. 1. At probationes plerunque post litem contestatam fieri solent. Huic adjungitur tit. 12. de feriis, quia & feriae tribuunt dilationem ipso jure: sed dilationes sunt auctoritate judicis. Alius tamen est ordo in ff. & C. Theodof. in quibus hi duo tituli longe anteponuntur ante pacta. Ratio infra exponetur ad ff. Expositis jam duobus membris, de personis & ipso processu, aut saltem de parte ejus prima, nam judicij seu processus pars ultima de sententia & exsecutione rejecta est n libro 7. reliquum nunc est tertium membrum, de foro competenti. De quo titulus generalis 13. de jurisd. omn. jud. & proinde primum obtinet locum: sub quo generalis est reg. ne quis ad alienum judicem se su forum non competens vocetur, ne quis de me vel ad principem. Excipiuntur quaedam personae de quibus tit. 14. quando Imp. inter pupillos, &c. Et hi duo sunt generales tituli de foro competent. Nunc eos sequuntur speciales quorum tres sunt species. Nam 1. agitur de judicijs publicis, propter eorum dignitatem, de quib tit. 15. ubi de criminibus, &c. Hunc statim sequitur tit. 16. ubi de possess. agi. Nam & in hac quaestione de possessione, inest judicium publicum. Eo quoq; pertinet tit. 17. ubi fideicommiss. pet. Non quia fideicommissorum sit publicum judicium, sed qu pertineat ad possessionem. Nam fideicommissorum potius possessio quam dominium peti solet. l. 3. ff. infuf. pet. Secunda species est de privatis judicijs ad quam pertinet tit. 18. ubi conveniatur, & c. & 3. seqq. privata autem judicia, vel sunt in personam, vel in rem. 6. actionum. 1. inst. de act. & prius quidem hic de in personam agitur, ideoq; propter similitudinem privata in personam, illis statim subjungitur. Alioquin prius tractari solet actiones in rem q in personam ut infra dicetur. Cur aut tit. ubi in rem actio exercere idebeat, praecedat titulum de hereditate, ratio videtur esse, quia tit. 19. est generalis de omnium in rem actione, est proprie tamen magis de rei tantum vindicatione agere videtur. At tit. 20. ubi de hereditate agitur, & ubi heredes, &c. est plane specialis, hoc est, de petitione hereditatis quae est species actionis in rem. Specialia autem esse de peti-
units.tr: After the judges, the litigants themselves are inquired into, to whom title 6, Qui legitimam personam standi in iudicio habere non possunt, etc., pertains, and title 7, Ut nemo invitus agere cogatur, etc. The reason for these two titles is that one must first consider whether someone can sue before considering whether he can be compelled to do so. For otherwise those who, even if they wished, could not sue would be compelled in vain. Now we come to the procedure itself, or the form and manner of the judgment, to which title 8, De ordine iudiciorum, and the following titles from 4 pertain, as said above. The reason this title is placed first is that its words are general, and that it must be established what the question is about, on which the judgment is given, before its procedure is discussed further. This is followed by title 9, De litis contestatione, since before the joinder of issue there is a controversy rather than a lawsuit, as law 1, De litis contestatione, and law 2, De edendo, above, indicate; these two laws are to be read together. To this title, De litis contestatione, is added title 10, Si plus petatur, and to this title 11, De dilationibus. The reason is that delays are mostly caused by documents or proofs, as law 1 shows. But proofs are usually produced after the joinder of issue. To this is added title 12, De feriis, because holidays also grant a delay by law itself, whereas delays otherwise depend on the authority of the judge. The order in the Digest and in the Theodosian Code is different, in which these two titles are placed well before De pactis. The reason will be explained below under the Digest. Now that the two members, concerning persons and the procedure itself (or at least its first part, since the last part of the judgment, concerning sentence and execution, was set aside in Book 7), have been set out, what remains is the third member, on the competent forum. To this pertains the general title 13, De iurisdictione omnium iudicum, and therefore it takes first place. Under it is the general rule that no one may be summoned before a judge who is not his competent judge, ne quis de me vel ad principem. Certain persons are excepted, dealt with in title 14, Quando imperator inter pupillos, etc. These are the two general titles on the competent forum. Now they are followed by the special ones, of which there are three kinds. For first, public judgments are treated, on account of their dignity, in title 15, Ubi de criminibus, etc. This is immediately followed by title 16, Ubi de possessione agi, since in this question about possession a public judgment is also involved. To this too pertains title 17, Ubi fideicommissa petantur, not because trust-bequests are a public judgment, but because it concerns possession, for it is usually possession of trust-bequests rather than ownership that is claimed, law 3, Ff. Si quis infra petitionem. The second kind is private judgments, to which title 18, Ubi conveniatur, etc., and the following titles from 3 pertain; private judgments are either in personam or in rem, Inst. De actionibus 6. Here the actions in personam are treated first, and therefore, on account of their similarity, private actions in personam are immediately appended to them. Otherwise, actions in rem are usually treated before actions in personam, as will be said below. Why title 19, Ubi in rem actio exerceri debeat, precedes the title on inheritance seems to be that title 19 is a general title on the action in rem of everything; yet it seems to deal more properly only with the vindication of a thing. But title 20, Ubi de hereditate agitur, et ubi heredes, etc., is plainly special, that is, concerning the claim of an inheritance, which is a kind of action in rem. That special titles are posterior to general ones has been said often enough. To this title is added title 21, Ubi de rationibus, etc. The reason for this order is that, since public and private judgments have already been discussed separately, it is fitting to add at the end a title in which, in common, both...
