The reason is that, both in the Perpetual Edict and, I think, in the Code, the same order was followed, so that the action for the services of a freedman followed the action for theft. The reason seems to be twofold: first, because the conditions of slave and freedman are close, and the one follows the other, since a manumitted slave becomes a freedman; second, because the refusal of services is a kind of theft. This is the reason for the order in tit. 3., de Tit. III. oper. libert. in the Code. In the Digest (where Tribonian often departs further from the reasoning of the Perpetual Edict) this action of services is placed elsewhere and for another reason. To this title on the services of freedmen Tribonian joins other titles pertaining to freedmen and to the rights of patrons, and for this reason, if I am not mistaken, all the rights of patrons pertaining to freedmen are explained in the same place. There are about three rights of a patron which come to him from his freedman: services, goods, and obsequium or reverence. Services are treated in tit. 3., as already said; goods are treated in tit.4. de bon. liber. The reason why services are treated first and goods later is: first, because the refusal of services is like theft, which was treated earlier; second, because services are owed to the patron altogether, if they have been promised, whereas goods are not often owed, nor all of them; and finally, because a new law concerning goods is introduced, and therefore it comes later. To this title on the goods of freedmen belongs tit.5. si in frau. patr. &c., Tit. V., for it concerns the alienation of goods. But tit.14. is general and therefore earlier. As there is an action for services concerning services, so there is the Faviana or Calbisiana action concerning goods, if they are alienated to defraud. This has been said of services and of goods. The third is obsequium, on which is tit. 6. de obseq. &c.; because it is the least, it holds the last place. For obsequium is merely a duty of reverence, l.5. hoc tit. To that which we have just passed over belongs tit.7. d. liber., Tit.VII. eor. liber., which title is not so general as its words sound, but is rather special, namely concerning ungrateful freedmen, where there is also an action against ungrateful freedmen and their children. As the crime of ingratitude deserves it, it holds a later place. But the last place in this second chapter, which concerns the action for ingratitude and freedmen, is held by tit.8. de jure aureorum annulorum, &c., Tit. VIII. The reason is that it pertains to the release from the status of freedman. For there are two modes by which one ceases to be a freedman and is released from those three obligations: services, goods, and obsequium; namely the right of gold rings and the restoration of freeborn status. III. The third chapter of this book concerns possession of goods (bonorum possessionibus), which is contained here in twelve titles. Why possession of goods is treated in this place is to be taken from the order of the Edict, in which, after the civil actions (of which in book 3, chapter 4), the praetorian ones were arranged as said above, and in such a way that the Edicts on possession of goods followed the action for theft, so that possession of goods nearly held the first place among the praetorian matters. Why so? Because they embrace a whole estate: universal matters take precedence over particular ones, as said above. What is said about the order of the Edict is confirmed by book 6 of Paul's commentary on the Edict and by books 2 and 3 of the Sentences of Paul. In this third chapter on possession of goods, therefore, the first title is rightly tit. 9. qui admitti ad bonorum possessionem possunt, §.intra quod tempus. Next comes the general title, of which tit.10. quando non petentium, &c. is as it were a part, for it treats of the right of accrual, which has place only among several possessors of goods. In the Digest this right of accrual is included under the general title de bon. poss. After these two general titles follow others that are special: the first is tit. 11. de bon. poss. sec. tab., and this is tit. 12. de bon. poss. cont. tab. In the Digest and Institutes the order is reversed; the reason for the Digest will be given below. In the Code, the reason for the order seems to be this: why possession according to the tablets comes before possession against the tablets; first, because possession according to the tablets is more favoured, while possession against the tablets is more hostile, as it attacks the will; second, because tit.13. de poss. cont. tab. liberti, which is granted to patrons or their children. tit.12. agrees very well with this, for both contain possession against the tablets: one, which is granted to children against the tablets of their parents, tit.12.; the other, which is granted to patrons and their children against the tablets of a freedman, tit.13. To this is joined tit.14. Unde liberi., then 15. Unde legitimi, and unde cognati, and to this 16. de successorio edicto. The reason will be explained at the Digest, where the order is the same. To this tit.16. is joined 17. de Carboniano edicto, merely on account of the mention of the Edict in each title, as I think. Finally is joined tit.18. Unde vir et uxor, because among the four possessions on intestacy this is the last, by the reason of law. It is followed by tit. 19. de repud. bon. poss. The reason for the order is that it is first to treat of the nature of possession of goods, and afterwards of acquiring it, and then of renouncing it. The last title in this third chapter is 20. de collationibus, because collation is made only after possession of goods has been sought, l.11. hujus tit. But here Tribonian departed from the order of the Edict, of which more below. And this is said of the third chapter of this sixth book. IV. The chapter on inheritance, which we divide into three parts, is either on inheritance by testament, of which is tit.21. and 15. seqq.; or on legacies and fideicommissa, of which are tit.37. and 17. seqq.; or third, on inheritance on intestacy, of which is tit.55. de suis et legitimis and 4. seqq. As for the reason of the order, namely why possession of goods (of which chapter 3 of this book) is placed before inheritance (of which this fourth chapter), it depends on the Perpetual Edict, in which the order was that possession of goods was treated before testaments. The reason for the Edict, though more obscure, seems to me to be this: that testaments are for the most part civil and depend on the laws of the Twelve Tables, namely those words: Uti quisque legassit, &c. It was said above that in the Edict the first place was given to praetorian matters, among which possession of goods holds the chief place. There were indeed some matters in the Edict pertaining also to testaments, but few, and those which can be adapted to and serve possession of goods, such as the Edict si quis omissa causa testamenti, &c., ut cautio legatorum, &c., l.6. ut quis omissa causa testamenti, &c., and the Edict de testamentis aperiendis, which the Edict on possession of goods could not be sought without an opened testament. And therefore in the Perpetual Edict, tit. de bon. poss. was immediately followed by the Edict or title de tab. test. aperiendis, because, as just said, possession of goods cannot be sought or renounced unless the tablets are opened. And this is the reason for the order of this chapter, which I said is threefold: on testament, on legacies, and on the cause of intestacy. The reason for the order among these three parts has partly been explained above on the Institutes and partly is to be understood from what follows. Now let us look at the titles of this three-part chapter, which are thirty-nine in number, one by one. As for the first part, concerning testaments, the first in it is tit. 21. de test. milit., next to it being tit. de collat., of which we have already spoken. The reason why in this part on testaments the title is de test. milit., though the order in the Institutes and the Digest is different, is that, as often said already, Tribonian in the Code especially follows the order of the Perpetual Edict, in which Edict there was a species of possession of goods called that arising from a soldier's testament. Accordingly this title immediately follows the earlier treatment de bon. poss. You may ask why, then, he does not refer this title to the third chapter, which is on possession of goods, but to the fourth chapter, which is on inheritances or testaments? The reason is that Tribonian adapted it and inscribed it de testamento, and not de bon. poss. ex testamento militis. He therefore looked to the order of the Edict, though not to the matter, which is possession of goods, but to the inheritance. To this is joined tit. 22. qui testamenta facere possunt, and with it tit. 23. de testamentis. The order of this will be explained at the Digest. For first comes the treatment of testaments themselves, that is, of their making and form; next are heirs, l.2. ff. qui test. fac. poss. Therefore these two titles (which in the Digest are one) are immediately followed by tit. 24. de hered. instit. and five subsequent titles, all concerning heirs, of which the first, as I said, is the general one on the institution of heirs. To this is subjoined tit. 25. de instit. et substit., for this treats of heirs instituted or substituted under a condition; the earlier title is on heirs purely instituted. For conditional institution is fuller and more perfect, and therefore comes first. This is followed by tit. 26. de impub. et al. subst.; the order is explained in the Institutes. Next is tit. 27. de necess. hered., for the reason of dignity requires that first be treated the free heirs and afterwards the servile heirs. Finally, this is followed by tit. 28. de lib. praeter. et exher. The reason is that the earlier titles concern institution, while this concerns disinheritance, which is odious and therefore later. The last title on heirs is tit. 29. de posthum. hered. instit., because posthumous children are nothing other than descendants. This title de posthumis heredibus is rightly joined to the earlier de lib. praeter., because this too concerns children, but the earlier concerns those already born and this one those not yet born, that is, posthumous children; and because disinheritance pertains to both born and posthumous children, but not to strangers as heirs. In this first part we have treated the testator, the form of the testament, and the heir. The third part of this section remains, concerning the inheritance under the testament itself, because it is the effect of the testament; and so this part comes later. First the acquiring or entering upon the inheritance is treated, and it contains the form or species of forbidden marriages, namely between a ward and her guardian. This is followed by tit. 7. si quacunque praed. tut. sp. esse &c., which contains another species of void marriages, namely between a governor of a province and a woman of the province. The reason why this species comes after that between guardian and ward is that the species between guardian and ward is likewise incest, in that the guardian and the ward are as it were one person. To this tit. 7. is joined tit. 8. si nuptiae exceperint, &c. The reason is that the species of void marriages must be explained before the claims arising from them, for substance precedes accident. The third part concerning marriages pertains to second marriages, of which is l.9. d. secund. nupt.; the reason is plain, since first come the first marriages and then the second. To this belongs also tit. 10. Si cum alio nuptae erit mulier, &c. But in this the special law concerning second marriages of women is contained. The earlier title is general and therefore earlier. And this is said of the first and second chapters on the action concerning dowry, that is, betrothals and marriages. IV. The dowry itself and the action for it, which is the principal chapter, is more fully explained in tit. 13., as said above, the first of which is tit. 11. de dotis promissione. The reason is that a dowry cannot exist unless it has been promised, and from that promise both the dowry and the action for the dowry afterwards arise. Immediately therefore follows tit. 12. de jure dotium, in which the nature of the dowry and the action for the dowry as the effect of that promise is treated. To this is joined tit. 3. de rei uxoriae actione, for this too concerns the nature of the dowry and the action for the dowry, but contains new law and is therefore later. Also rightly following this is tit. 14. de pactis conventis, &c., because the action for the dowry is sometimes changed and reformed by agreements. The same order is followed above in the contract of sale or the action of sale, at the title de pactis inter emptorem et venditorem; for agreements, especially those added at once, usually change and reform the action, l.7. Jur. gentium. §. adeo. de pact., l. nuda. §. penult. de praescript. verb. Moreover, tit. 13. de rei uxoriae actione, a law or imperial constitution, changed the action; tit. 14., the agreements of private persons, likewise change it. A law, however, is stronger than and prior to private agreements. The action for the dowry is followed by the exception de dote causa, &c., tit. 15., the reason being plain: the exception follows the action, as in the Institutes. To this is joined tit. 16. de donationibus inter virum et uxorem. The reason for the order is that here too there is a retention, which, if it is similar to an exception, is afterwards a retention on account of things given by the husband to the wife; and so a retention is sometimes granted against a wife claiming her dowry, in those excepted cases which were formerly six, according to Ulpian, §. retentiones lib. reg., although today such retentions have nearly all been abolished by Justinian, l. unica. ff. tacet. supra de rei ux. act. There was one kind of retention, on account of gifts, which is the subject of this title 16; another was on account of conduct, which is tit. 17.; another on account of things removed, which is tit. 21. Although these three kinds, and others such as for expenses, etc., have today been abolished, as said, because husbands are now provided for by another way than retention, yet, since the very causes of retentions have been abolished, Tribonian still retains the old order in arranging the Code and the Digest concerning retentions, which, as said, are similar to exceptions. After this title de donationibus inter virum et uxorem follows tit. 17. de repudiis et judicio de moribus, &c., partly because it pertains to the other cause of retention, on account of conduct, as already said; and partly because donations between husband and wife are generally prohibited, but are valid for certain causes, among which is divorce. Therefore after the general title de donationibus there immediately follows the title de repudiis, as afterwards tit. 18. soluto matrimonio, &c. Both concern divorce, but the first treats of its causes and form, that is, of the nature of divorce itself; the other, tit. 18. namely, concerns what is done by divorce, such as the recovery of the dowry, which can be sought only once the marriage is dissolved. Hence the rule of which tit. 8. speaks is followed at once by the exception of which tit. 19. speaks, de fundo dotali constante matrimonio. This is followed by tit. 20. Ne fidejussor vel mandator dotis, &c. The reason for the order is that a guarantor is very useful for the recovery of the dowry treated in the earlier title, for example, so that if the husband from whom the dowry is recovered is insolvent, it may be recovered at least from his guarantor. And it is rightly treated first of the marriage and afterwards of the guarantor. To this is joined tit. 21. rerum amotarum. The reason for the order is twofold: first, because this too was a kind of retention, on account of things removed, as said above in Ulpian, ff. retentiones; second, because women who are contemplating divorce are often accustomed to remove a good deal. Therefore after divorce this title is placed, l. 2. hujus tit. There is also a third reason: tit. 20. ne fidejussor spares the husband or his honour, while this tit. 21. spares the honour of the woman. Next to this is tit. 22. ne prod. te, &c., partly because this too spares the reputation of the husband, since this title treats of the execution of the action, and therefore is last, as is the execution in proceedings, except for one title, tit. 23. de fundo dotali. The reason why this is the last of all in this treatment of dowry, or of the action for the dowry, is that all the earlier titles concern the action for the dowry in its universal character, that is, the dowry as a whole, while this one alone is particular, namely concerning the dotal estate, and therefore comes last. And this is the end of the fourth chapter. V. The chapter concerning children, of which is tit. 24. divortio facto apud, &c. and tit. 25. de alend. libr. et part. Why the first is before the second: the reason is, first, because the former is more similar to the earlier titles, in that just as the earlier ones concern divorce and what pertains to divorce, so too does this one, divortio facto, &c.; second, because it must first be asked whether and where the children are to be brought up, and by whom they are to be supported. Moreover, the later title is not only about children but also about parents. The treatment of parents does not pertain to marriage but to children, who are the fruit of marriage. So also below, where guardianship is treated, the title ubi pupilli educari debeant comes before the title on the maintenance of the children themselves, namely tit. 49., tit. 50. infr. h. lib. 5.; and the last title is partly about concubines, tit. 26. de concubinis, and partly about natural children, tit. 27. de lib. naturalibus. The reason why concubines come first among these two titles is that the law of concubines is an ancient law, while the law of natural children is much more recent, introduced by the Emperor Constantine, Nov. 89.; and because natural children are those born of concubines or of maidservants. But an effect is later than its cause. Besides, the action for the dowry has been treated, which is the first part of this book, 5, and arises from equity and good faith, as said above. Now the action of guardianship is joined to this, which is the second part of this book, arising from a quasi-contract, that is, from the administration of guardianship, ff. tutor. Institut. de obligat. which arise from quasi-contract. The reason is explained in the Digest. But as in the action for the dowry, concerning marriage and other things suitable for constituting a dowry, so here all matters concerning guardianships are carefully explained, tit. 48., as said above. To make their order clearer, they are to be recalled under nine heads. I. Concerns the kinds of guardianship, of which tit. 28. and 8. seqq. II. Concerns the administration or office of guardians, of which tit. 37. and 13. seqq. III. Concerns the action of guardianship itself, of which tit. 51. and 7. sequentibus. IV. Concerns the authority of guardians, tit. 59. V. Concerns the ending of guardianship, tit. 60. and following. VI. Concerns the excuse of guardians, tit. 62. and 7. seqq. VII. Concerns the curator of a madman, tit. 70. VIII. Concerns the estates of minors, tit. 71. and 3. seq. IX. And last, concerns the summoning of magistrates, tit. 65. and the last of this title. In the Digest the order is somewhat different, and the reason for it will be explained in both places. First, then, concerning the order among the nine chapters: why the kinds of guardianship are set out first. The reason was given above at the Institutes, where the second chapter was also discussed under the title on the authority of guardians. The reason for the third chapter, which concerns actions, is that the action is an effect of administration, which is a quasi-contract, from which this action arises. Concerning the relations of kinship, the chapter will be discussed further below, at the end of this chapter too. As for the individual titles: first is tit. 28. de testamentaria tutela, with the reason set out in the Institutes. To this is joined tit. 19. de confirmando tutore, the reason for which will be given in the Digest. Following it immediately is tit. 30. de legitima tutela, for this is the second kind of guardianship; why it is so has already been said in the Institutes. This is followed by the third kind, which is dative, to which pertains tit. 31. and 5. seqq. Among these four titles on dative guardianship, the first is tit. 31. qui petant tutorem. Why it is placed first here is that a guardian must be sought before he is given. To the seeking also pertains tit. 32. ubi petantur tutores, &c., for first comes the treatment of the one who seeks, and then of the one before whom or where he is sought. The remaining two titles deal with the dative guardians themselves, who are sought or given. Of these, the earlier is tit. 33. de tutoribus vel curatoribus alienis, on account of the dignity of the ward's person; the later is tit. 34. qui dare tutores, etc., in which is treated not only the guardians who are given, but also the magistrate who gives them; and this too is the reason why this one is later, because it contains two matters. To this is joined tit. 35. quando mulier, &c. For up to this point we have spoken of the guardian as a male office, since guardianship is a man's duty, by the law de reg. jur.; but here an exception is added, which is a later rule, because sometimes a mother and a grandmother discharge the office of guardianship under newer constitutions. This is followed by tit. 36. in quibus causis. The reason is that the earlier titles all concern the first guardian, while this one concerns the second guardian, and therefore it comes later, as said above of the titles de restitutione in integrum and si saepius in integrum. And this is said of the first chapter. The next chapter is on the office of the guardian, which is placed under administration. To it pertains tit. 37. de administratione tutorum, which is first in this chapter, because it is general; to it is joined tit. 38. de periculo tutorum. The reason is that from administration, or sometimes even without it, there is danger to the guardian: danger, as it were, clings to administration. So in the Digest both are under the same title. This is followed by tit. 39. quando ex facto, &c. For this title is as it were a species of the earlier title, which concerns every danger, that is, only the action; and the earlier concerns only the danger to the guardian, while this one concerns the danger and advantage of the ward. Likewise the next title, 40. si ex pluribus tutoribus, &c., contains a species of tit. de administratione and de periculo tutorum. For it concerns the action; but as the earlier tit. 39. concerns the action which the ward brings or receives in his own name, so this tit. 40. concerns the action which the guardian brings or receives in the name of the ward. For the action which a minor brings against the guardian, which is the action of guardianship, will be discussed below. The bringing of this action, or the defence of the ward, is part of administration. To this title is joined tit. 41. ne tutor vel curator, &c., which, being prohibitory, is therefore later. This prohibition pertains to administration, for the reason, namely, that the guardian may discharge his office better. So too tit. 42. de tutoribus et curatoribus qui fieri, &c. is prohibitory, because a guardian who has not previously given security is altogether forbidden to administer. To this is joined tit. 43. de suspectis tutoribus et curatoribus. For this too is prohibitory: indeed a suspected guardian is not only forbidden to administer until he gives security, but is entirely removed, sometimes with infamy, which, being a punishment, is why this title is later. Indeed, the order among these prohibitory titles is understood from this gradation: in tit. 41. the guardian is forbidden to administer but to alienate; in tit. 42. he is also forbidden the pupillary estate, which is more serious; in tit. 43. he is forbidden altogether, which is most serious. This title is followed by tit. 44. de in litem dando tutore, &c. The reason is that administration is either of affairs, of which we have so far spoken, or of lawsuits, of which this speaks. To this is joined tit. 45. de eo qui pro tutore, &c. The reason is plain: so far we have spoken of the administration of a true guardian, and now of that of a false one. This is followed by tit. 46. si mater, &c. The reason is that this title too pertains to the title on administration, for example if the mother or another relative has promised indemnity. To this is joined tit. 47. si contra matris, &c., which is added only because of the mention of the mother already made concerning the danger of administration. For otherwise this title si contra matrem, &c. does not properly belong here; it is rather about the removal of a guardian than about administration. This is followed by tit. 48. ut cause post pub. &c., for the reason that so far we have spoken of administration while the guardianship continues, and now of that which has ended, that is, after puberty. The last place in this chapter on the office of the guardian is held by education and the provision of maintenance, of which there are two titles: tit. 49. ubi pupilli educari debeant and tit. 50. de alimentis pupillo praestandis. The reason for the order, why this part of the office, concerning the education of the ward, is placed last, is that it is as it were a species or part of the office. The earlier titles are general, and specials come after generals. There is also a second reason: the administration of affairs and of lawsuits always lies upon guardians, whereas education is not always committed to them, but often to the mother and other relatives. l.1. C. h. tit. Between these two titles, why ubi pupilli educari debeant comes before de alimentis praestandis: the reason is that it is always first treated where a thing is done, before the matter itself, as may be seen in the title de judiciis, where first is asked about the competent judge, that is, where one must sue and where actions are to be brought, and afterwards the actions themselves are treated. And so far concerning the first and second parts of this treatment of guardianship; afterwards concerning the guardian himself and his office, of which a part, de auctoritate tutorum, pertaining here, is nevertheless deferred to tit. 59. below, where the reason will be indicated. III. The third chapter on guardianships concerns the action of guardianship itself. The reason was explained above. For this action is, as it were, the effect of administration, and therefore later; of this action is tit. 51. arbitrium tutelae. This is followed by tit. 52. de divisione tutelae. The reason for the order is that the earlier title is general, on the nature of this action, while this one is special, namely whether, if there are several guardians, all are liable to that action. The same order is followed in the Digest under the title de duobus reis, which title follows the general title de verborum obligationibus. To this action of guardianship pertains tit. 53. de in litem jurando. The reason is that the earlier titles concern this action, or its nature, against whom it is given; this one now concerns how it is to be carried on, namely whether the oath in litem is to be taken in it. I ask why this title on the action of guardianship is placed here in the Code, since the oath in litem also pertains to other actions. The reason is that the oath in litem in an action of guardianship is especially exacted against the guardian's heirs, l.1. Cod. de in lit. jur. And therefore tit. 54. de heredibus tutorum is joined here; for after treating of the guardian himself, who is liable to this action of guardianship, it is next to explain his heirs. Thus these two titles, 53 and 54, are rightly joined here. The former, however, is de in litem jurando, because this oath, although generally exacted against the heir, is sometimes also exacted against the guardian himself, l.2. C. hoc tit. To this title, ne heredibus tutorum, is now joined tit. 55. si tutor non gesserit. For this too pertains to the action of guardianship; but since we must first treat of the guardian who acted, and whether he is liable to this action, it is rightly followed by the guardian who did not act, for he too is liable. To these titles on actions are joined two accessory titles, namely tit. 56. de usuris pupillorum and tit. 57. de fidejussoribus tutorum, &c. It is well known that interest and guarantors are by law called accessories. Accessories, however, come after principal matters. Why the title de usuris comes before that de fidejussoribus: the reason is that, just as the earlier titles pertain to the guardian but concern the principal matter, that is, the property of the wards, so this title also pertains to the guardian, but concerns interest. The reason requires that the guardian, that is, the principal debtor, be treated first, rather than the accessory, that is, the guardian's guarantor. This title de fidejussoribus tutorum is followed by tit. 58. de contraria tutela. For first the direct action had to be treated, afterwards the contrary action of guardianship, as the Digest order also requires. And this is said of the third chapter. IV. Concerns the authority of guardians, of which only tit. 59. de auctoritate praestanda treats. The reason for the order is more obscure, because since authority is a certain part of the office, this title seems more properly to pertain to the second chapter, where administration is treated, and so…

units.la: Tit.II. Tit.III. Tit.IIII. Tit.V. Tit.VI. Tit.VII. Tit.VIII. tate tutorum, de qua tantum est tit. 59. de auctor. praestand. Ratio ordinis obscurior est, quia cum auctoritas sit pars quaedam officii, rectius ad caput secundum, ubi de administratione, hic titulus pertinere videtur, ut & in ff. Ratio tamen hic in Cod. est, tum quia auctoritas differt ab administratione, ut est apud Ulp. infrag. tit. II. ff. tutoris; tum quia auctoritas tutoris necessaria est non tantum in negotiis & litibus, sed etiam in ipsa actione tutelae instituenda. l. pen. C. si adversus remjudic. & c. tum quia auctoritas non interponitur in eo, quod finit tutelam. l. ult. verf. sed & omnia, C. hoc tit. Et proinde hic tit de auctoritate rectè anteponitur capiti. V. quod est de finienda tutela, sub quo est tit. 60. quando tut. vel curat. esse desin. Hunc quoque pertinet tit. 61. de actore tut. dand. Nam in locum tutoris non quidem finita, sed tantum quasi finita tutela. hoc est, in locum tutoris impediti ad administrandum, solet hic actor dari, ff. ultim. Instit. de tut.
units.tr: Titles II through VIII, and the authority of guardians, of which only title 59, de auctoritate praestanda, deals. The order is rather obscure, because authority is a part of the guardian's office, so this title might seem more fitting under the second chapter, where administration is treated, as it is also in the Digest. There is a reason for the arrangement in the Code, however. First, authority differs from administration, as Ulpian says in infrag. tit. II. ff. tutoris. Second, a guardian's authority is needed not only in transactions and lawsuits but also in bringing the action of guardianship itself, l. pen. C. si adversus remjudic. & c. Third, authority is not interposed in what brings the guardianship to an end, l. ult. verf. sed & omnia, C. hoc tit. Therefore this title on authority is rightly placed before the fifth chapter, which concerns the ending of guardianship and includes title 60, quando tut. vel curat. esse desin. To this chapter also belongs title 61, de actore tut. dand. For an actor is given not in place of a guardian whose office has ended, but only as though it had ended, that is, in place of a guardian who is prevented from administering, ff. ultim. Instit. de tut.

units.la: V I. Caput vocavimus de excusatione tutorum, quod prioribus capitibus de finienda tutela statim adjungitur, hac ratione, quia excusatio est quaedam species finiendae tutelae. ff. ult. Inst. quib. mod. sin. tut.
units.tr: We called the sixth chapter the one on excusing guardians. It is joined immediately to the preceding chapters on ending guardianship, for this reason: excuse is a kind of ending of guardianship, ff. ult. Inst. quib. mod. sin. tut.

units.la: In hoc autem capite tit. 62. de excus. & temporib. earum, est primus, quia generalis: Cui adjungitur tit. 63. si falsò & c. Nam & hic est generalis: sed ille posterior: quia ille est de natura excusationum & de verbis causis sive allegationibus, hic est de falsis. Hos sequuntur tituli speciales quorum 1. est tit. 4. Si tutor vel curator Reip. abs. & c. Ratio est quia haec species five causa excusationis, puta absentia Reipub causa, est publica. Cui adjungitur tit. 65. d. excusa veteran. & c. Nam militia est velut absentia Reip. causa. Huic proximus est tit. 66. quinum. lib. se excus. & c. Ratio quia & haec excusatio ut 2. priores, valde est favorabilis, & ad utilitatem publicam pertinet liberorum procreatio. Sic & morbus est causa favorabilis, sed posterior, quia privata de quo est tit. 67. qui morbo se excus. Cui adjungitur tit. 68. qui aetate, & c. hoc est senectute se excusant, quae & ipsa est velut morbus, ut vulgo dicitur, Aristoteles f. de gener. an. cap. 4. & quia ad mortem accedit rectè prioribus causis est posterior. Ultimum locum hic obtinet excusatio, propter tres tutelas sive numerum tutelarum, tit. 69. qui numero tutelarum, tum quia haec causa differt ab aliis prioribus in eo, quod priores excusent ab omni tutela, haec tantum excusat à quarta, tum quia haec non semper excusat, ne à quarta quidem. si quis tres affectarit, sive affectatione suscepreit. Sic enim legendum est hic ubi vulgo est defunctorie, l. 15. §. ult. de excus. tut. & haec de sexto capite. Ad VII pertinet tit. 70. de curat. furiof. Ratio est, quia priora sex capita sunt de tutore vel curatore pupillorum vel minorum: hoc caput est de curatore furiosi aut prodigi, qui curatores sunt majorum: & proinde posteriores, ut ipsa aetas major posterior minore. IIX. Caput de praediis minorum non alienandis sine decreto judicis in ff. contrarius est ordo. Ubi ratio ordinis exponetur. Hujus igitur capitis de praediis primus titulus est tit. 71. de praediis, & aliis rebus minorum sine decreto non alien.vel oblig.qui est generalis, quê sequitur tit.72.quando decreto opus non sit,&c. Ratio est, quia prior est de eo, quâdo est opus, hic quando nô. Affirmatio autem natura est prior negatione, ut sup. dictu adlib.2.tit. 40. Et velut exceptio quædam h.titu.72. continetur, & proinde tanquam generalis ponitur ante tit.73, si quis ignorans, rem minoris esse sine decreto, copra averit, quotantum species exceptionis adfertur. Hunc sequitur tit.74. si major factus,&c. quo etiam velut exceptio adfertur, qua alienatio absq; decreto facta valeat, seu rata maneat. Restat nonû & ultimum caput de tutelis, quod est de actione subsidiaria, de quo capite est tit.75. de magistrat. conven. Ratio exponetur infra ad ff. Et hæc de titulis Libri V.Codicis.
units.tr: In this chapter, title 62, de excus. & temporib. earum, comes first, because it is general, and it is followed by title 63, si falsò & c. This also is general, but it comes later, because the first deals with the nature of excuses and the grounds or pleas put forward, while the second deals with false ones. These are followed by the special titles. The first of these is title 64, Si tutor vel curator Reip. abs. & c., because this kind of excuse, namely absence on account of the commonwealth, is a public one. To it is joined title 65, d. excusa veteran. & c., for military service is, as it were, absence for the sake of the commonwealth. Next to this is title 66, quinum. lib. se excus. & c., because this excuse, like the two before it, is highly favoured and serves the public interest, since the procreation of children does. Illness is also a favoured ground, but a weaker one, because it is private; it is dealt with in title 67, qui morbo se excus. To this is joined title 68, qui aetate, & c., that is, those who excuse themselves by old age, which is itself, as people commonly say, like an illness (Aristotle, f. de gener. an. cap. 4.). And since old age leads to death, it rightly comes after the earlier grounds. The last place is held by the excuse on account of the number of guardianships, title 69, qui numero tutelarum. This is because this ground differs from the earlier ones in that they excuse from every guardianship, whereas this one excuses only from a fourth; and also because it does not always excuse even from a fourth, if someone has undertaken three by his own eagerness, sive affectatione suscepreit. For so this passage should be read, where the common text has defunctorie, l. 15. §. ult. de excus. tut. And this is what I have to say about the sixth chapter.

units.la: Lib. VI. Codicis.
units.tr: Lib. VI. Codicis.

units.la: NUnc de libro sexto videamus. Cujus lib.ti.62. possunt commodè ad s mebrare vocari I. est de actione furti. II. de actione operarû aliisq; ad jura patronorû & libertorû pertinentib. III. de bonorû possessione. IV. est de hereditate, tâ ex testamento, q̄ ab intestato. V. est accessorium Ordo horum capitû atq; totius libri satis obscurus quëq; multi non assequuntur. Ex ordine Edicti pretoris intelligi potest q̄ Edictum Tribun. in Cod. magis q̄ in ff. sequitur, ut jâ ante dictum. Ordo igitur edicti fuit iste. (res.n.paulo altius et repetenda) ut in edicto primû ponerêtur civilia, deinde prætoria jura & judicia quia civilia prætoriis sunt præstantiora ut & alias dictû Et hûc ordinem tenuit Trib.tâ in ff.q̄ in Cod. licet interdû ab eo discedat, ut supra admonuimus. Ea a. judicia q̄ hactenus expositum, pleraq; sunt civilia, exceptis paucis prætoriis q̄ propter similitudinê fuerunt civilibus adjuncta. Nûc ratio postulat, ut explicatis civilib. transeamus ad ptoria: quorû initiû fuit in edicto ab actione furti, aut certê à bonorû possessione. Actio furti est quodâmodo media partim civilis de furto nec manifesto, partim ptoria, de furto manifesto. §.fi, sunt autê, Inst.de nox.act. Sed in his prætoriis judiciis persequendis, & ordine tractandis sæpe Trib. discedit ab ordine edicti perpetui, multaq; interjicit certis de causis, quas suo loco exponemus. Ex his jâ intelligitur, cur hoc libro de actione furti statim initio hujus lib. tit.2. de furtis & servo corrupt. agatur. Ratio est, quia actio furti actioni rationib.distrahêdis, q̄ ad tutelas pertinet, valde est similis, adeo ut tutor, si res pupilli distrahat animo furandi nō tantum actioue rationib.distrahendis, sed etiâ furti teneatur, l.1.§.pen.l.2.de tut.& ratio.distrah. Et hunc ordinem, ut actione rationib. distrahendis, statim sequeretur, actio furti fuisse in Edicto perpetuo, itê id, q̄ dixi supra in Edicto primo, civilia post prætoria fuisse collocata, perspicuû est ex legib. Caji & Pauli ad Edictum, & etiâ ex Paulo lib.2.sent.tit.30.& seq.
units.tr: Now let us look at the sixth book. Its sixty-two titles can conveniently be grouped under five heads. (I) The action for theft. (II) The action for services owed by workmen, and the other matters that concern the rights of patrons and freedmen. (III) Bonorum possessio. (IV) Inheritance, both by testament and on intestacy. (V) An appendix. The order of these chapters, and of the whole book, is rather obscure, and many people do not grasp it. It can be understood from the order of the praetor's Edict, which the Tribunian compilation in the Code follows more closely than the Digest, as I said earlier. The order of the Edict was this (I must go back a little further for this): first the civil law was placed in the Edict, then the praetorian rights and judgments, since civil law is superior to praetorian law, as I have said elsewhere. Tribonian kept this order in the Digest as well as in the Code, although he sometimes departs from it, as I noted above. The judgments treated so far are mostly civil, with a few praetorian exceptions that were attached to the civil ones because of their similarity. Now reason requires that, having dealt with the civil matters, we pass to the praetorian. The beginning of these was, in the Edict, the action for theft, or at least bonorum possessio. The action for theft is in a way intermediate: partly civil, concerning theft that is not manifest, and partly praetorian, concerning manifest theft. §.fi, sunt autem, Inst. de nox. act. But in pursuing these praetorian judgments and arranging them, Tribonian often departs from the order of the perpetual Edict, and inserts many things for certain reasons, which we shall explain in their place. From this it is already clear why, in this book, the title de furtis & servo corrupto is treated right at the start of the book. The reason is that the action for theft is very similar to the action for an accounting of administration, which belongs to guardianships. So much so that a guardian who sells his ward's goods with intent to steal is liable not only to the action for accounting but also for theft, l.1. §.pen. l.2. de tut. & ration. distrah. That the action for theft followed immediately after the action for accounting in the perpetual Edict, and that the civil matters were placed after the praetorian (as I said above of the first Edict), is evident from the books of Gaius and Paul on the Edict, and also from Paul, lib.2. sent. tit.30. & seq.

units.la: Cur autem titulus, de furt. hic præcedat tit.de serv.fugitiv.& c. qui est primus hujus libri, hæc est ratio, quia furtum est plerunq; servorû. Duo enim sunt servorum vitia frequentia & conjuncta, fuga & furtum. & fugaest prior, quia docet furtum quod est velut discipulus fugæ, ut elegantèr Martialis: Huicquoq; est q olim in servorum venditionib. cautio adhiberi solet, fugitivũ, furé non esse l.1. de edil. edict. ut & Cujac. in Para. Cur autem subtit. 2. adjungatur de servo corrupto, ratio est, ppter similitudinem argumenti. Nam & fuga & furtum sunt vitia & corruptela servorum. ut modo dictum. Et hæc de primo capite hujus libri q est de actione furti, & de actione servi corrupti, q duæ actiones in ff longo intervallo disjunguntur. Alterum caput est de actione operarum, de quo est tit. 3. cũ s. seqq. Ratio quia & in Edicto perpetuo, q & in C. diligenter imitatur, idem fuerit ordo, ut actionem furti sequeretur actio operarum libertí. Ratio videtur, tũ quia servi & liberti conditiones sunt vicinæ, & hic illũ sequitur: quia ex servo manumissus, fit libertus, tum quia operarum negatio, est velut furti species. Et hæc est ratio ordinis ad tit. 3 de oper. libert. in Cod. Nam in ff (in quib. Tribunianus sæpè longius discedit à ratione Edicti perpetui) & alio loco & alia ratione hæc actio operarum ponitur. Huic titulo de oper. liber. adjungit Tribun. alios titulos ad libertos & jus patronorum pertinentes: hac ni fallor ratione, ut omnia patroni juraad libertos ptinentia uno eodemq; loco explicetur. Sunt aut 3. ferè jura patroni, q ei à liberto veniunt, operæ, bona, & obsequiũ sive reverentia. De operis agitur tit. 3. ut jã dictum de bonis agitur tit. 4. de bon. liber Ratio cur primus de operis, posterius de bonis agat est, tum q a operarum negatio est similis furto, de quo prius: tũ quia operæ omnino patrono debetur intellige, si promisse sunt, bona non sæpè nec omnia tũ deniq; quia de bonis novũ jus adfertur, & pinde posterius. Ad hunc tit. de bon. liber pertinet, tit. 5. sin. fam. pair. Nã est de alienatione bonorũ. Sed tit. 14. est generalis, ideoq; prior. Ut aut de operis est actio operarum ita & de bonis est actio Faviana vel Calbisiana, si alienentur in fraudé. Dictũ est de operis, & de bonis. Tertiũ est obsequiũ, de quo est tit. 6. de obseq. q nia minimum est, postremum locũ tenet. Nam obsequiũ est tantum reverentiæ munus l.5. hoc tit. Et primus est tit. 7. d. liber. & liber. qui tit nõ est ita generalis, ut verba sonãt sed est potius specialis, de libertis scil. ingratis ubi & actio est contra ingratos libertos eorumq; liberos, q velut crimen ingrati meritò posteriorem locum tenet. Sed ultimũ tamen locum in hoc capite secundo, quod est de actione ingrati, & libertis tenet tit. 8. de jure aureorum annulorum, &c. Ratio est, quia ad finiendã libertinitatẽ pertinet. Duo n. sunt modi, quib. definit esse libertus & liberatur illis tribus: operis, bonis & obsequiis puta jus aureorum annulorum, & natalium restitutio. III. Hujus libri caput est de bonorum possessionib quod hic in tit. continetur: Cur aut hoc loco de bonorum possessionibus agatur, ratio ordinis ex Edicto sumenda est, in quo post civilia, (de quibus lib. 3. & 4.) Prætoria erant dispositæ ut supra dictum, & ita quidem, ut actionem de furto sequerentur Edicta de bonorum possessionibus, adeo ut primum fere inter prætoria locũ haberent bonorum possessiones. Quid ita? quia universitatem cũtimento aperto. Atque ideo in Edicto perpetuo tit. de bon. poss. statim sequebatur Edict. sive tit. de tab. test. aperr. quia ut modo dictum, bonorum possessio peti aut repudiari non potest, nisi tabulae aperiantur. Et hac de ratione ordinis ad hoc caput, quod dixi esse trimembre, de testamento, de legatis, de causis intestati. Ratio autem ordinis inter haec tria membra, partim jam supra est expositaad Institut partim ex iis, quae infra intelligetur. Nunc de singulis, huius trimembris capitis titulis, qui sunt 39. videamus. Quod ad primum membrum de testamentis attinet, in eo primus est tit. 21. de testa. milit. proximus scilicet tit. de collat. de quo jam dictum. Ratio, cur hoc in membro de testamentis titulus sit de testa. milit. cum alius sit ordo in Inst. & ff haec est, quia ut saepe jam dictum Tribun. in C. maxime sequitur ordinem, edicti perpetui, in quo Edicto species bonorum possessionis fuit, quae dicitur ex testamento milit. Et proinde hic titulus statim sequitur priorem tractatum de bon. poss. Dices, cur ergo hunc titulum non refers ad caput tertium, quod est de bonorum possessionibus sed ad caput quartum, quod est de hereditatibus sive testamentis? Ratio est, quia Tribunianus eum ita accommodavit, & inscripsit de testamento, & non de bonorum poss. ex testamento militis Ordinem igitur Edicti spectavit, licet rem non spectet, hoc est bonorum possessionem, sed hereditatem. Huic adjungitur tit 22. qui testamenta fac. poss. & eum titu. 23. de testamentis. Ratio ordinis exponetur ad ff. Primo enim de ipsis testamentis, hoc est, de testatione & forma agitur, proximum est de heredibus, l. 2. ff. qui test. fac. poss. Itaq; hos duos titulos (qui in ff uno continentur) statim sequitur tit. 24. de hered. instit. & 5. tituli seqq, qui omnes sunt de heredibus, quorum primus est, ut dixi, de heredibus instituendis generalis. Huic subjungitur tit. 25. de instit. & substit. hac ratione, quia hic agitur de heredibus sub conditione institutis aut substitutis: Prior autem titulus est de heredibus pure institutis. Puta, conditionali institutione est plenior & perfectior, ideoque prior. Hunc sequitur tit.26. de impub. & al. subst. Ratio ordinis ad Instit. est expositaProximus est tit 27. de neces. hered. & c. Ratio enim dignitatis postulat, ut prius de heredibus liberis, posterius de heredibus servis agatur. Tandem hunc sequitur tit.28. de lib. praeter. & exher. Ratio est, quia priores tituli sunt de institutione, hic est de exheredatione, quae est odiosa, & proinde posterior. Ultimus de heredibus est tit. 29. de posthum. hered. instit. quia posthumi nihil aliud sunt, quam postremi. Recte autem hic titulus de posthumis heredib. adjungitur priori titulo, de lib praeter. quia & hic titulus est de liberis, sed prior est de jam natis, hic de nondum natis, hoc est, posthumis: Et quia exheredatio pertinet ad utrosque natos & posthumos, sed non ad heredes extraneos. Dictum est in hoc primo membro de testatore & forma testamento & herede: Restat tertia hujus membri pars de ipsa hereditate ex testamento, quia scilicet est effectus testamenti. & proinde haec pars est posterior. Et primo quidem de hereditate adeunda sive adquirenda agitur, puta tit.30. de iure delit. & adiunda hered. &c. quem sequitur tit. 31. de repudianda. Naturali enim ratione aditio & adquisitio prior est & potior repudiatione. Curautem sub uno tit.30. duo simul contineantur & jus deliberandi, & aditio hereditatis, quoniam in ff habent 2. separatos tit. Ratio est propter brevitatem, & quia jus deliberandi cum aditione recte conjungi potest. Aditurus enim hereditatem prius deliberat. Proximus est tit. 32 quem admodum
units.tr: Why the title de furtis precedes the title de servis fugitivis and the others, which is the first title of this book, the reason is that theft is mostly the work of slaves. For there are two frequent and connected faults of slaves: flight and theft. Flight comes first, because it teaches theft, which is, as Martial neatly puts it, like a pupil of flight. To this is added the caution usually taken in sales of slaves, that the slave is not a runaway or a thief, l.1. de edil. edict., as also Cujacius says in Paratitlis. Why the second title, de servo corrupto, is joined to the first is because of the similarity of the subject. For both flight and theft are faults and corruptions of slaves, as just said. And these are the matters of the first chapter of this book, which concerns the action for theft and the action concerning a corrupted slave. These two actions are separated by a long interval in the Digest. The second chapter concerns the action for services, which is title 3, de operis libertorum, with the following titles. The reason it seems the same order was followed in the perpetual Edict, and in the Code as well, is that the action for services followed the action for theft: first, because the conditions of slave and freedman are close, and the one follows the other, since a manumitted slave becomes a freedman; second, because refusing services is a sort of theft. This is the reason for the order of title 3, de operis libertorum, in the Code. In the Digest (where Tribonian often departs far from the reasoning of the perpetual Edict), this action of services is placed elsewhere and for other reasons. To this title de operis libertorum Tribonian adds other titles concerning freedmen and the rights of patrons, I suspect for this reason: so that all the rights of patrons concerning freedmen are explained in one and the same place. There are about three rights of a patron which come to him from the freedman: services, goods, and obsequium or reverence. Services are treated in title 3, as said, and goods in title 4, de bonis libertorum. The reason why services are treated first and goods afterwards is partly that refusing services is like theft, which was treated first, and partly that services are owed to the patron absolutely (if they have been promised), whereas goods are not always owed, nor all of them; and lastly because a new right is introduced concerning goods, and so it comes second. To this title de bonis libertorum belongs title 5, si in fraudem patroni, for it concerns the alienation of goods. But title 14 is general, and therefore comes first. Just as there is an action for services, so there is an action for goods, the Favian or Calvisian action, if they are alienated to defraud. This has been said of services and of goods. The third is obsequium, treated in title 6, de obsequiis; because it is the smallest, it holds the last place. For obsequium is only a duty of reverence, l.5. hoc tit. And the first is title 7, de libertis et eorum liberis, which is not as general as its words suggest, but is rather special, concerning ungrateful freedmen, for which there is an action against ungrateful freedmen and their children; since this is like the crime of ingratitude, it rightly holds the later place. But the last place in this second chapter, which concerns the action for ingratitude and freedmen, is held by title 8, de jure aureorum annulorum, etc. The reason is that it pertains to the ending of freedom. For there are two ways by which a freedman ceases to be a freedman, and he is released from those three things: services, goods, and obsequium; for example the right of the gold rings, and the restoration of birth. III. The third chapter of this book is on bonorum possessiones, which is contained here in the titles. The reason for the order of this chapter, why bonorum possessiones are treated in this place, must be taken from the Edict, in which, after the civil matters (treated in books 3 and 4), the praetorian matters were arranged, as said above; and indeed in such a way that the Edicts on bonorum possessiones followed the action for theft, so that bonorum possessiones held almost the first place among the praetorian matters. Why so? Because they concern the whole estate, which is opened by the will. And for this reason in the perpetual Edict, under the title de bonorum possessionibus, there immediately followed the Edict de tabulis testamenti aperiendis; because, as just said, bonorum possessio cannot be sought or renounced unless the tablets are opened. This is the reason for the order of this chapter, which I said is threefold: concerning testaments, concerning legacies, and concerning causes of intestacy. The reason for the order among these three parts is partly explained above in the Institutes, and partly from what will be understood below. Now let us look at the titles of this threefold chapter one by one, which are thirty-nine. As for the first part, concerning testaments, the first in it is title 21, de testamento militis, followed by the title de collatione, already discussed. The reason why the title de testamento militis stands in this part on testaments, although the order in the Institutes and the Digest is different, is that, as often said already, Tribonian in the Code especially follows the order of the perpetual Edict, in which the form of bonorum possessio called from a soldier's testament existed. And so this title immediately follows the earlier treatment de bonorum possessionibus. You may ask why then do you not refer this title to the third chapter, which concerns bonorum possessiones, but to the fourth chapter, which concerns inheritances or testaments? The reason is that Tribonian adapted it in this way, and headed it de testamento, not de bonorum possessione ex testamento militis. He thus regarded the order of the Edict, although he did not regard the matter, which is bonorum possessio, but the inheritance. To this is joined title 22, qui testamenta facere possunt, and title 23, de testamentis. The order of these will be explained in the Digest. For first there is treatment of testaments themselves, that is, of their making and form; next comes the matter of heirs, l.2. ff. qui test. fac. poss. Therefore these two titles (which in the Digest are contained in one) are immediately followed by title 24, de heredibus instituendis, and the five following titles, all of which concern heirs. The first of these, as I said, de heredibus instituendis, is general. To this is added title 25, de institutionibus et substitutionibus, for this reason: because here it is treated of heirs instituted or substituted under a condition; and the earlier title concerns heirs instituted purely. A conditional institution is, so to speak, fuller and more perfect, and therefore comes first. Next follows title 26, de impuberum et aliis substitutionibus. The order of this in the Institutes has been explained. The next is title 27, de necessariis heredibus, etc. For the dignity of the matter requires that first the free heirs be treated, and afterwards the servile heirs. Finally, this is followed by title 28, de liberis praeteritis et exheredatis. The reason is that the earlier titles concern institution, and this one concerns disinheritance, which is odious, and therefore later. The last title on heirs is title 29, de postumis heredibus instituendis, because posthumous children are nothing other than the last-born. This title de postumis heredibus is rightly joined to the earlier title de liberis praeteritis, because this too concerns children, but the earlier concerns those already born, and this concerns those not yet born, that is, posthumous children. And because disinheritance pertains both to born and posthumous children, but not to outside heirs. This completes what was said in this first part about the testator, the form of the testament, and the heir. The third part of this section remains: the inheritance itself under the testament, since it is the effect of the testament, and therefore this part comes later. And first, the acceptance or acquisition of the inheritance is treated, in title 30, de jure deliberandi et adeunda hereditate, etc., which is followed by title 31, de repudianda hereditate. For by natural reason acceptance and acquisition come before and are stronger than renunciation. Why two things, the right of deliberation and the acceptance of the inheritance, are contained together under one title 30, although in the Digest they have two separate titles, is for brevity, and because the right of deliberation can rightly be joined with acceptance; for one who is about to accept an inheritance first deliberates. The next is title 32, quemadmodum testamenta aperiantur

units.la: test. aper. Ratio infra ad ff. quem sequitur tit. 33. de Edict. Diu. Hadr. toll. &c. quia hic tit est de heredis missione in possessionem, quae missio fit demum post aditam hereditatem. Pars 4. primi membri hoc cap. de hereditate ex testamento, continet quaedam poenalia, & proinde est ultima. Ad eam igitur partem pertinet tit.34. si quis aliquem, &c. & tit 35. de his quib. ut, &c. Sed ordo hic perversus videtur in eo quod tit.35. est generalis continens causas, ex quib. hereditates confiscantur, sive auferuntur heredib. aut indignis, & transferuntur ad fiscum tit.34. est specialis, unam scil. causam talem continens, puta si heres coegerit testatorem, ei heredi aufertur hereditas. Perversus ergo, seu praeposterus est ordo quia generalis tit. postponitur, & rectus est in ff ubi praeponitur. Ratio ordinis in hoc loco est quia titul. 33. de Ed. Diu. Hadr. toll. &c. continet sive agit de constitutione divi Hadriani. Nam & illa causa, de qua in hoc tit 34. inducta est ab Hadriano. l. 1. si quis quem, &c. Ad hoc primum membrum & codicilli pertinere videtur l. quidam. 15. de iure codicill. ideo q; hic subnectitur tit.36. de Codicillis. Et hoc de primo membro quarti capitis, quod membrum est de ipso testamento. Alterum huius capitis quarti membrum est de legatis & fideicommissis. Cur autem prius de testamentis, quam legatis agatur, dictum est ad Inst. Et ad hoc secundum membrum pertinent 18. tituli, quorum primus est tit.37. de legatis, quia generalis, sed quia legata quaedam continent, de quib. dubitari posset propter formulas verborum, ideo cojungitur illi statim tit.38. de verb. signif. Hunc sequitur tit 39. si homo ... fuerit. &c. qui item ad legata pertinet. Sed quia continet fraudem & delictum, merito posterior est, licet sit generalis de omni legato titul. 40. specialis est de legato, quod relictu est sub conditione viduitatis. de ind. et vidua. & leg. Cui adjungitur tit. 41. de his quae poena, &c. Nam & hic tit de poena legato adscripta agit, sed est posterior quia haec poena est plane privata. At poena tit. superioris est publica, aut certe lege publica confirmata, per legem scilicet Juliam Miscellam. Et haec de legato separatim. Nunc item de fideicommissis separatim, de quibus est tit. 42. de fideicomm. Cur prius agitur de legatis quam fideicommissis, dictum est ad Inst. Et haec de iis titulis qui sunt proprii primum legatorum, post fideicommissorum, sed certa de causa in inferiorem locum rejecti: quae causa infra exponetur, in prin. tit. 49. & 50. proxime aut tit. proprios sequuntur communes, ut jam saepe dictum est in princ. lib. 4. de reb. & (illis exceptis sc 49. & 50.) alii ones, usq; ad tit.55. de iuis & legit. Inter omnes aut primus est tit. 43. communia de legat. &c. qui est generalis. Huic deinde ti. 44. defalfa causa adjecta legato velfideicommiffo adjungitur, & huic tit. 45 de his quae sub modo, &c. & huic deniq; tit. 46 de condit.infert. Ratio ut intelligatur, meminisse oportet quatuor esse, quae legatis aut fideicommissis inferi solet, causa, demonstratio, modus & conditio, ut videre est in tit. de condit. & demonstr. De his quatuor tres tituli hic afferuntur quia sub causa continetur demonstratio. Cur autem prius de causa agatur putat titul 44. ratio est, cum quia tit. 43. & omnes priores tituli de legatis, sunt de legatis & fideicommissis puris. Legatum autem cum causa, est purum, sed legatum cum conditione non est purum, & proinde titul. de condit. est posterior tit. 46. Inter haec duo, causam & conditionem medius est modus de quo est tit. 45. Modus enim interdum conditionem valet, interdum non. l. ea. de condit. & demonstr. Hunc titulum de conditionib. sequitur tit. 47. de usur. &c. Namut illa conditio, modus &c. adjiciuntur legatis & fideicommissis, ita & usura fructusque sunt adjectiones, & accessiones legatorum, & omnino accessiones, ideoque priorib. posteriores. Hic adjungitur tit. 48. de incert. perf. qui tamen in exeplaribus emendatis minus confusus est cum tit. seq. ad Trebel. cum quo nihil habet simile. Nam hic tit. de incertis personis est, ut & priores, communis tam legatorum quam fideicommissorum. f. incertis Inst. de legat. At titulus de SC. Trebell. non est communis sed proprius, puta fideicommissorum; & ita quoque hic titulus de incertis personis, distinguitur in veteribus libris a titulo ad Trebell. qui est tit. 49. Dixi supra duos titulos proprios inseri tractationi titulorum communi, & hi sane sunt isti duo, tit. scil. 49. ad SC. Trebell. & tit. 50. ad leg. Falcid. Et primo quidem, cur hoc loco interjiciantur, ratio est, quia priores tituli omnes pertinent tam proprii quam communes ad formam & essentiam legatorum & fideicommissorum, quibus nunc adjunguntur tituli, qui ad effectum pertinent, & proinde sunt posteriores, hoc est, ad legatorum & fideicommissorum adquisitionem. Quia autem legata & fideicommissa antequam adquirantur (quod fit additione & agnatione) solent saepe diminui, & vel prorsus intercidere, primum agitur, quibus legata vel fideicommissa vel delibantur, hoc est diminuuntur, vel prorsus pereunt. Delibantur autem senatusconsulto aut lege. Peribant olim lege Papia, hodie non item. Et haec est ratio, cur jam hic agatur de SC. Trebell. & de leg. Falcid. quia iis modis delibantur legata & fideicommissa & etiam cur agatur de caduc. toll. qui titulus est de modo, quo plane peribant, & intercidebant legata. Deinde cur prius ponatur titulus 49. ad Trebell. posterius titul 50. ad Leg. Falcid. contrario atque in Instir. atque ff. ordine, ratio est, quia universalia singularibus sunt priora. SC. Trebell. est de fideicommisso universali, Lex Falcid. est de legato singulari. Huic jam proximus est titul. 51. de caduc. toll. qui rursus est communis tam legatorum quam fideicommissorum Ratio ordinis item dicta est, quia priores tituli tantum deminuunt, hic plane tollitur legatum aut fideicommissum. Sed quia jus novum continet, & caducaeo tolluntur, posteriore loco ponitur. Cui adjungitur tit.s2.de his quiante apert.tab.&c. Eftenim velnt pars prioris tituli ut videre est in illo titulo priore §.innovissimo, verf.hereditatem, ubi de transmissione hereditatis agitur, quae transmissio hunc titulum statim sequitur, & hoc tit. cum exceptione quadam distinguitur. Huic titulo s2.qui ante,&c. adjungitur tit.s3.quando dies leg.&c. etiam communis. Ratio, quia hic titulus agit de die sive cessione diei, de qua & sub illo titulo, de caduc.toll. multa erant exposita. Est& haec ratio, quia cessio ad effectum quoq; pertinet & ad transmissionem, de qua modo dictum. Nam non transferuntur sive transmittuntur legata sive fideicommissa, nisi prius dies eorum cesserit.l.3.quando dies legat.&c. Hunc sequitur tit.s4. & ultimus huius membri, de legatis, item communis puta,ut in possef.legat. Ratio cur sit ultimus est, quia agit de missione in possessionem, & de cautione. Missioautem in possessionem est ultimus effectus: cautiones sunt accessoriae, & proinde in posteriorem titulum rejici solent. Et haec de quarto capite huius libri sexti membris duobus, de testamento scilicet & de legatis & fideicommissis. His proximum est tertium membrum de intestato: ad quod pertinent s. tituli, quorum quatuor priores propria continent, ultimus communia. Inter proprios tit.ss.de suis & legit. est primus, quia cum duo sint gradus succedentium ab intestato, suorum scilicet & legitimorum, de quo est d. titulus de suis& legitim. de suorum successione priore loco tractandum, quia gradus suorum prior est. (cur sit prior gradus suorum, explicatum ad Instit.) Huic gradui suorum adjunguntur hi duo tituli puta tit.s6. ad SC.Tertul.& tit.s7. ad SC.Orficia. contrario ordine atque in Instit.ubi hi duo tituli adjunguntur gradui cognatorum. Ratio differentiae dicetur ad ff. Cur hic titulus ad Tertull. sit prior tituload Orficiam. Ratio est quia Tertull.prius est Orfic.tempore, ideoque etiam ordine, ut ad Instit.supra dictum. Gradum suorum sive liberorum priorem sequitur secundus agnatorum sive legitimorum, de quibus est tit. s8.de legit.hered. Ultimus titulus hujus tertij membri est tit s9.communia de success. Propriis enim communia sunt posteriora, ut saepe dictum. Et hic titulus continet communia scilicet ab intestato, non communia etiam ex testamento, quod ex legibus hujus tituli intelligitur. Et haec de quarto capite. Restat quintum & ultimum hujus libri sexti, quod, ut dixi, est accessorium, quia in eo quaedam prioribus adjiciuntur quaedam similitudine, & occasione. Nam cum tria in eo capita sint sive tituli, duo priores tituli 60. & 61. occasionel.ult. tituli superioris, putas9.communia de success. sunt his adjecti. Inter hos autem duos tit.60. de bonis mat.&c. & tit.61. de bon.quae lib.&c. ratio ordinis est, quia jus de bonis maternis tempore prius est jure de bonis quae liberis & matrimonio,&c. illud induxit Constantinus, hoc Theodorius & Valentinianus. Ultimus titulus est 62.de hereditibus Decurionum &c. Ratio est, quia aut in prioribus 2. ita & hic est quaedam adquisitio, & quasi successio five hereditas extraordinaria. Est autem hic titulus ultimus, quia agit de eo casu, quo decuriones, &c sine herede nullo moriuntur: quo casu illorum bona, velut ad ultimum successorem fiscum recidunt: reliquorum de quibus hic titulus ad fiscum non recidunt speciali privilegio: sed decurionum bona recidunt ad curiam. Atque hæc de titulis libri sexti.
units.tr: test. aper. The reason for this is given below, under the title quem sequitur, and the next title, 33, de Edict. Diu. Hadr. toll. &c., because this title concerns the putting of the heir into possession, which takes place only after the inheritance has been accepted. The fourth part of the first member of this chapter, on the inheritance under a will, contains some penal provisions, and for that reason it comes last. To that part belong title 34, si quis aliquem, &c., and title 35, de his quib. ut, &c. But the order here seems inverted, in that title 35 is general, containing the causes by which inheritances are forfeited, or taken away from heirs who are unworthy and transferred to the treasury, while title 34 is special, containing one such cause only, namely, if an heir has compelled the testator, the inheritance is taken from that heir. The order is therefore perverse or back to front, since the general title is placed after the special one, whereas in the Digest the order is correct, with the general title first. The reason for the order in this place is that title 33, de Edict. Diu. Hadr. toll. &c., deals with, or treats of, the constitution of the divine Hadrian. For that cause, too, which is discussed in title 34, was introduced by Hadrian, l. 1. si quis quem, &c. The law l. quidam. 15. de iure codicill. also seems to pertain to this first member, on codicils, and so title 36, de Codicillis, is appended here. This is what I have to say about the first member of the fourth chapter, which concerns the will itself. The second member of this fourth chapter concerns legacies and fideicommissa. Why the will is treated before legacies has been explained in the Institutes. To this second member belong eighteen titles, of which the first is title 37, de legatis, since it is general; but because it contains certain legacies about which doubts might arise on account of the forms of words, it is joined immediately to it title 38, de verb. signif. Next follows title 39, si homo ... fuerit. &c., which likewise pertains to legacies. But because it deals with fraud and wrongdoing, it is rightly placed later, although it is general, covering every legacy. Title 40 is special, concerning a legacy that is left under the condition of widowhood, de ind. et vidua. & leg. To this is added title 41, de his quae poena, &c., for this title too treats of a penalty attached to a legacy, but it comes later because this penalty is purely private. The penalty of the preceding title, however, is public, or at least confirmed by public law, namely by the Lex Julia Miscella. This is what I have to say about legacies taken separately. Now, likewise, about fideicommissa taken separately, which is the subject of title 42, de fideicomm. Why legacies are treated before fideicommissa has been explained in the Institutes. These are the titles that belong properly first to legacies and then to fideicommissa, but for a certain reason they have been thrown into a lower place; that reason will be explained below, at the beginning of titles 49 and 50. Next after the proper titles come the common titles, as has often been said at the beginning of Book 4 concerning things, and (with the exception of 49 and 50) the others, down to title 55, de iuis & legit. Among all of these, the first is title 43, communia de legat. &c., which is general. To this is then added title 44, de falsa causa adjecta legato vel fideicommisso, and to this title 45, de his quae sub modo, &c., and finally to this title 46, de condit. infert. To understand the reason, one must remember that there are four things which are usually attached to legacies or fideicommissa: cause, demonstration, modus and condition, as may be seen in the titles de condit. & demonstr. Of these four, three titles are brought in here, because demonstration is contained under cause. Why title 44 treats the cause first is for this reason: titles 43 and all the earlier titles on legacies deal with pure legacies and fideicommissa. A legacy with a cause is pure, but a legacy with a condition is not pure, and therefore the title on conditions, title 46, comes later. Between these two, the cause and the condition, lies the modus, which is the subject of title 45. For a modus sometimes has the force of a condition, and sometimes not, l. ea. de condit. & demonstr. This title on conditions is followed by title 47, de usur. &c. For just as the condition, the modus, and so on, are added to legacies and fideicommissa, so interest and fruits are additions and accessions to legacies, and indeed accessions in general, and therefore they come after the earlier titles. Here is added title 48, de incert. perf., which, however, in the corrected copies is less confused with the following title, ad Trebel., with which it has nothing in common. For this title, de incertis personis, is, like the earlier ones, common to legacies and fideicommissa alike, f. incertis Inst. de legat. But the title de SC. Trebell. is not common but proper, namely to fideicommissa; and so, too, this title on uncertain persons is distinguished in the old books from the title ad Trebell., which is title 49. I said above that two proper titles are inserted into the treatment of common titles, and these are certainly those two, namely title 49, ad SC. Trebell., and title 50, ad leg. Falcid. The reason why they are placed here first is that all the earlier titles, both proper and common, pertain to the form and essence of legacies and fideicommissa, and to these are now added titles which pertain to effect, and which therefore come later, that is, to the acquisition of legacies and fideicommissa. But because legacies and fideicommissa, before they are acquired (which happens by addition and accrual), are often diminished, and sometimes altogether lost, the titles first deal with the means by which legacies or fideicommissa are reduced, that is, diminished, or perish altogether. They are reduced by a senatus consultum or by a law. They used to perish by the Lex Papia, but not so today. This is the reason why the Senatus Consultum Trebellianum and the Lex Falcidia are now treated here, since by these means legacies and fideicommissa are diminished; and also why the title de caduc. toll. is treated, which is the title on the manner in which legacies were wholly lost and perished. Next, the reason why title 49, ad Trebell., is placed before title 50, ad Leg. Falcid., in the reverse of the order in the Institutes and the Digest, is that universal matters come before particular ones: the Senatus Consultum Trebellianum concerns a universal fideicommissum, while the Lex Falcidia concerns a particular legacy. Next to these comes title 51, de caduc. toll., which again is common to legacies and fideicommissa. The reason for this order has also been given, namely that the earlier titles only diminish, whereas this one wholly removes the legacy or fideicommissum; but because it contains new law, and such things are removed by lapse, it is placed in a later position. To it is added title 52, de his quae ante apert. tab. &c. For this is part of the earlier title, as may be seen in that title, in the § innovissimo, verf. hereditatem, where the transmission of an inheritance is treated; and this transmission immediately follows this title, and this title is distinguished from it by a certain exception. To this title 52, qui ante, &c., is added title 53, quando dies leg. &c., also common. The reason is that this title deals with the day, or the cession of the day, about which many things were set out under that title de caduc. toll. There is also this reason: cession pertains to effect as well as to transmission, which has just been mentioned. For legacies or fideicommissa are not transferred or transmitted unless first their day has come, l. 3. quando dies legat. &c. Next follows title 54, ut in possef. legat., and the last of this member, on legacies, also common: it concerns the putting into possession and security. The reason it is last is that it deals with the putting into possession, which is the final effect; securities are accessory, and therefore they are usually thrown into a later title. This is what I have to say about the fourth chapter of this sixth book, with its two members, on the will and on legacies and fideicommissa. Next to these is the third member, on intestacy, to which belong five titles, of which the first four contain proper matters and the last common matters. Among the proper titles, title 55, de suis & legit., comes first, because, since there are two degrees of those who succeed on intestacy, namely the children (sui) and the legitimate kin, and the title de suis et legitimis deals with these, the succession of the children must be treated first, since the degree of the children is prior. (Why the degree of the children is prior has been explained in the Institutes.) To this degree of children are added these two titles, namely title 56, ad SC. Tertul., and title 57, ad SC. Orficia., in the reverse order from the Institutes, where these two titles are attached to the degree of cognates. The reason for the difference will be given in the Digest. Why this title ad Tertull. comes before the title ad Orficiam is that the Tertullian senatus consultum came earlier in time, and therefore also in order, as was said above in the Institutes. The second degree, of agnates or legitimate heirs, follows the prior degree of children or descendants, and concerns title 58, de legit. hered. The last title of this third member is title 59, communia de success. For common titles come after proper ones, as often said. This title contains the common matters of intestate succession, not common matters also of succession by will, which is understood from the laws of this title. This is what I have to say about the fourth chapter. What remains is the fifth and last chapter of this sixth book, which, as I said, is accessory, because in it certain matters are added to the earlier ones by similarity and occasion. For although there are three chapters or titles in it, the two earlier titles, 60 and 61, have been added on the occasion of the last law of the preceding title, namely title 59, communia de success. As for the order of these two titles, title 60, de bonis mat. &c., and title 61, de bon. quae lib. &c., the reason is that the right concerning maternal goods came earlier in time than the right concerning the goods which belong to children and marriage, and so on. The former was introduced by Constantine, the latter by Theodosius and Valentinian. The last title is 62, de hereditibus Decurionum &c. The reason is that, as in the two earlier titles, there is here also a certain acquisition, and as it were an extraordinary succession or inheritance. This title is last because it deals with the case in which decurions and others die without any heir; in that case their goods fall, as to the ultimate successor, to the treasury, whereas the goods of the others, which are the subject of this title, do not fall to the treasury by special privilege, but the goods of decurions fall to the curia. And so much for the titles of the sixth book.

units.la: Liber VII. Codicis.
units.tr: Book VII of the Code.

units.la: NUnc de libro septimo videamus, cujus tituli 7 ad tria capita revocari commode possunt. I. de manumissionibus sive de liberali causa. II. de usucapionibus & præscriptionibus. III. de judiciorum posterioribus, hoc est, sententia, appellatione & executione. Ratio autem ordinis inter hæc tria capita, & hujus libri cum priore sexto perdifficilis & obscura, explicabitur infra ad ff. Quod igitur ad primum caput, id facio trimembre. Nam primo, de ipsa libertate, ejusque causis, sive de manumissionibus, pertinent primi tituli 15. in hoc libro 7. in quibus libertatis causæ sive manumissiones primò separatim, deinde communiter tractantur, ordine jam usitato. Manumissionis autem modi cum hodie tantum sint 2. vindicta & testamentum, ad primum pertinet tit 1. de vindict. & libert. &c. ad testamentum pertinet tit. 2. de testamentar. manumiss. Ratio infra ad ff. Ad manumissiones testamentarias, pertinet lex Fufia Caninia, ideoque titulo secundo statim adjungitur tit. 3. de leg. Fuf. Can. toll. Eodem quoque pertinet libertas fideicommissaria. tit. 4. de fideicommiss. libertat. bus. Nam fideicommissa plerunque testamentis relinquuntur, sed ratio postulat, ut prius directa libertas, puta vindicta, aut testamento, hoc est, legato, quod semper testamento relinquitur, posterius fideicommissaria explicetur, quia directa est antiquior & plenior. Huic titulum 4. de fideicomm. lib. sequitur tit. 5. de Deditit. libert. &c. eum tit. 6. de latin. libert. &c. Ratio, quia priores tituli agunt de vera & perfecta libertate hi duo continent libertatis species minus perfectas, & proinde sunt posteriores.
