Est & altera ratio, quia quæ tolluntur, posteriora esse solent Hos sequitur tit. 7. de communi serv. manum. Ordo ut intelligatur admonendum est eos tantum servos recte manumitti, qui sunt veri aut proprii, & horum manumissio est justa & vera: de qua hactenus, nunc de iis servis qui non sunt ita proprii, & quorum manumissio vel est dubia vel inutilis. Inter hos primus est servus communis, quia & hic licet non totus, saltem ex parte est proprius & proinde prioribus tit ulti. de proprio, hic est tit. proximus cui adjungitur titul 8. de servo pig. dat. man. Et hic servus, pignori datus vel etiam in dotem datus, licet maneat proprius, quia tamen pignori aut doti est datus, quodammodo videtur alienus, & proinde manumissio talis servi magis prohibetur, quam servi communis. Sic & servus civitatis non poterat olim manumitti ab ordine sive curia: quia servus iste non est ordinis sive curiæ, sed civitatis potius. Et hæc est ordinis ratio ad titulum 9. de serv. retp. man. Cui recte adjungitur {*} 10 de bis qui anon dom. &c. qui titulus est de servo prorsus alieno & proinde ejus manumissio prorsus est prohibita & inutilis. Atque ita primum de servis propriis deinde de partim propriis, partim alienis, tandem de prorsus alienis: sive prius de manumissionibus utilibus ac permissis postea de inutilibus aut dubiis ac prohibitis. His titulis accedunt & aliæ duæ manumissiones prohibitæ, quæ ultimum locum tenent, quia causa prohibendi est delictum Prioris prohibitionis causa est fraudatio creditorum, de qua est tit. 11. qui manu non poss. posterior est sub titul. 12. qui non possit ad libert. pervenire, ut si servus ob delictum in perpetua vincula damnatus fuerit. Ratio ordinis est, quia hæc posterior prohibitio est ob grave & verum delictum: prior est obvius, puta ob fraudationem creditorum. de qua est titulus 11. Huic tit. adjungitur 13. proquib. cau. serv. &c. Ratio est, quia ordinariam libertatis consequendæ rationem sive viam ex vindicta vel testamento, sequi debeat extraordinaria beneficio principis. Hunc sequitur titul. 14. de ingen. manum. fl. Ratio est, quia hactenus de servorum manumissione quæ est usitata & efficax, nunc de ingenuorum, sive liberorum hominum manumissione, quæ est inusitata & inefficax & proinde posterior. Et hactenus titulide manum. proprii, quibus unusadjungitur communis, puta titul. 15. communia de manum. Et hæc de primo membro hujus capitis, hoc est de causa libertatis sive de ipsa libertate. Alterum est de actione sive judicio, quod liberale & liberalis causa dici solet unde titul. 16. de liberali causa. Primum locum obtinet quia est generalis & præcipuus, ejus velut pars quædam est titulus 17. de advert. toll. Nam in hoc judicio exercendo olim necessaria erat assertio, quæ jam tollitur hoc titul. 17. Cui recte adjungitur titulus 18. quib. ad libert. proclam. non licet. Ratio est, quia prius agendum fuit de iis qui hoc judicio uti possunt, hoc est quibus proclamare licet, quam de iis, quibus non licet. Hunc titulum sequitur titul. 19. de ordine cognition. qui item pertinet ad hoc judicium liberale, in quo agitur de concursu hujus judicii cum aliis, & exponitur, quis ordo in hoc judiciorum sive cognitionum concursu sit servandus. Et semper hujus causæ liberalis cognitio præfertur, unde & præjudicialis actio dicitur, sive præjudicium. §. præjudic. ales. Inst. t. de Act. Huic titulo similiter conceptus est titul 8. supra de ord. judic. lib. 5. sed ille est generalis, hic est specialis sive proprius judicii liberalis concurrentis cum aliis. Pertinet quoque ad judicium liberale titul. 20. de collusione detegenda. Nam collusio nihil est aliud, quam judicium non serium, hoc est periculosorum & inutile. Ratio autem ordinis postulat, ut prius de utili, de quo antea posterius de inutili agatur. Et hæc de judicio sive actione liberali. Nunc duæ exceptiones contra eam actionem exponuntur. Actionem exceptione priorem esse, notat est. Prior exceptio est præscriptio quinquennii, de qua tit. 21. vide ne de statu defunct. &c. Altera exceptio est præscriptio longi temporis, de qua est titulus 22. de long. temp. præscript. Ratio autem ordinis, cur ille sit prior, est tum quia quinquennium prius est decennio: tum quia exceptio quinquennii convenit titulo de coll.dotis. Et hæc de secundo membro, sive de judicio, aut actione liberali. Tertium appellavimus accessorium, & proinde ultimum, quod tribus continetur quorum primus est titul. 23 de pecu- liove jus qui liberi, &c. quo titulo quæritur an peculium sit accessio manumissionis, sive an testator servum jam manumissum, de quo est §. peculium. Inst. de leg. Hunc titulum sequuntur duo alii, puta titul. 24. de Senatusconsulto Claud. toll. & titul. 25. de nudo jur. Quir. &c. qui sunt ultimi hujus capitis primi de libertate, tum quia odiosa, tum quia abroganda & tollenda continent. Cur autem titulus Senatusconsulto Claud. prior fit titulo de nudo jure Quirit. &c. ratio est quia titulus de SC. Claud proprie & solum pertinet ad hoc caput I. hoc est, ad servos & libertos, sed titulus de nudo jure Quirit. &c. pertinet non tantum ad servos, sed & alias quaslibet res. Et quia hic titulus de nudo iure agit de duplici dominio, ex jure Quiritum, & bonis commoda fit transitio ab hoc titulo ad proximum caput secundum de usucapionibus, qui est modus adquirendi dominii. Et hæc de primo capite hujus libri septimi quod est de libertate & servitute. Alterum caput dixi esse de usucap. & præsc. idq; est trimembre, & continetur titulis 16. Et primum quidem membrum est de usucapione altera de præscriptione, tertium accessorium. Ratio inter hæc membra est facilis, tum quia usucapio est antiquior, tum quia est efficacior præscriptione. De usucapione igitur, sive de primo membro hujus secundi capitis sunt 6. tituli quorum 4. priores sunt proprii, sive continent 5. species usucapionis, inter quas primus titulus est 26 de usucap. pro empt. qui est duplex, sive duas continet species. Hunc sequitur titul. 27. de usucap. pro donato & eum titul 28. de usucap. pro dote. eum denique tit. 29. de usucap. pro herede. Ratio exponetur ad ff. ubi idem fere est ordo. Hos proprios titulos sequitur communis titulus 30. communia de usucap. Ratio est nota. Ultimus de usucapionibus titulus est, tit. 31 de usucap. transform. Ratio est, tum quia jus novum continet & quædam tollit tum quia hic titulus est velut communis usucapionis de qua jam dictum, & præscriptionis sive longi temporis, de qua jam dicetur. Atque ita ab usucapione fit commoda transitio ad præscriptionem. sic & titul. 32. de adquir. & retin. poss. est item communis & velut medius titulus. Possessio enim tam in usucapione, quam in præscriptione requiritur. Nos tamen ordinis gratia hunc titulum 32 potius referimus ad præscriptionem, quia usucapione dominium, præscriptione tantum possessio adquiratur unde & longi temporis præscriptio dici solet. Expositio igitur priore membro de usucapione proximū nunc est membrum secundū de præscriptione, quod continetur 10. titulis, quorū primus est hic titul. 31. Est enim generalis & plures modos adquirēdæ & retinendæ possessionis continet cum reliqui eum sequentes tituli sunt speciales, unum duntaxat modum, puta tempus continentes. Hunc igitur titulũ, de adquir.poss. sequitur tit.33. de præscr.longi temp. quæ præscriptio inter species præscriptionum, de quibus hic agitur, est antiquissima, & proinde prima. Ad quam quoq; pertinet tit.34. in quib.ca seccssat.&c. Prius enim est videre, in quibus causis locum habeat titu.33. posterius in quibus non habeat.
units.tr: Now let us look at the seventh book. Its titles can conveniently be reduced to three heads: I. on manumissions, or on the cause of liberty; II. on usucapions and prescriptions; III. on the later stages of judgments, namely sentence, appeal and execution. The order among these three heads, and between this book and the preceding sixth, is very difficult and obscure, and will be explained below at the Digest. As for the first head, I divide it into three parts. First, concerning liberty itself and its causes, or manumissions, the first fifteen titles of this seventh book apply. In them the causes of liberty, or manumissions, are treated first separately and then in common, in the order now customary. Since there are today only two modes of manumission, the rod (vindicta) and the will, the first belongs to title 1, On the rod and liberty, and the second to title 2, On testamentary manumissions. The reason is given below in the Digest. To testamentary manumissions belongs the Lex Fufia Caninia, and so title 3, On the Lex Fufia Caninia repealed, is joined directly to title 2. To the same head belongs fideicommissary liberty, title 4, On fideicommissary liberties. For fideicommissa are for the most part left in wills, but reason requires that direct liberty, whether by the rod or by will (that is, by legacy, which is always left in a will), be explained first, and fideicommissary liberty afterwards, because direct liberty is older and fuller. Title 4, On fideicommissary liberties, is followed by title 5, On dediticii freedmen, and title 6, On Latin freedmen. The reason is that the earlier titles deal with true and perfect liberty, whereas these two contain less perfect kinds of liberty, and so come later. There is also a second reason: things that are abolished tend to come later. These are followed by title 7, On the common manumission of slaves. To understand the order, it must be noted that only those slaves are rightly manumitted who are true or proper slaves, and the manumission of these is just and valid. That has been dealt with so far; now we turn to those slaves who are not wholly proper, and whose manumission is either doubtful or invalid. Among these the first is the common slave, for this slave, though not wholly, is at least partly proper, and so comes after the earlier titles on the proper slave. This is the next title, and it is joined to title 8, On a slave given in pledge. Such a slave, given in pledge or even given in dowry, though he remains proper, seems in some way alien, and so his manumission is more forbidden than that of a common slave. So too the slave of a city could not formerly be manumitted by the order or curia, because that slave belongs not to the order or curia but rather to the city. This is the reason for the order at title 9, On the manumission of slaves of the public treasury. To this is properly joined {*} title 10, On those who manumit what is not their own, and so on. That title concerns a slave who is wholly alien, and so his manumission is entirely forbidden and invalid. Thus the order runs: first concerning proper slaves, then partly proper and partly alien, and lastly wholly alien; or first concerning valid and permitted manumissions, and afterwards invalid, doubtful and forbidden ones. To these titles are added two other forbidden manumissions, which hold the last place, because the cause of the prohibition is a crime. The cause of the former prohibition is fraud against creditors, treated at title 11, On those who cannot manumit. The later one is under title 12, On those who cannot attain liberty, as when a slave has been condemned for a crime to perpetual chains. The reason for this order is that the later prohibition rests on a grave and real crime, the former on an obvious one, such as fraud against creditors, which is title 11. To this title is joined title 13, On the causes for which slaves.... The reason is that the ordinary way of obtaining liberty, by the rod or by will, ought to be followed by the extraordinary way, by the favour of the prince. It is followed by title 14, On the manumission of freeborn persons. The reason is that so far we have discussed the manumission of slaves, which is customary and effective; now we discuss the manumission of freeborn or free men, which is unusual and ineffective, and so comes later. So far the titles on the manumission of proper slaves, to which one common title is joined, namely title 15, On common manumissions. This is what I have to say about the first part of this head, that is, about the cause of liberty, or liberty itself. The second part concerns the action or judgment, commonly called liberale and liberalis causa, whence title 16, On the liberal cause. It holds the first place because it is general and principal. Title 17, On the removal of advertisement, is in a way a part of it, for in conducting this judgment an assertion was formerly necessary, which is now abolished by this title 17. To this is rightly joined title 18, Who may not proclaim to liberty. The reason is that it was necessary to treat first of those who can use this judgment, that is, who may proclaim, before those who may not. Title 18 is followed by title 19, On the order of cognition, which likewise pertains to this liberal judgment, in which the concurrence of this judgment with others is treated, and it is set out what order is to be observed when these judgments or cognitions concur. The cognition of this liberal cause is always preferred, whence it is also called a preliminary action, or a prejudgment (Inst. §. praejudiciales, Inst. de actionibus). A title similar to this was framed above at title 8 of book 5, On the order of judgments, but that one is general, whereas this one is special, or proper to the liberal judgment as it concurs with others. Title 20, On the detection of collusion, also pertains to the liberal judgment, for collusion is nothing other than a judgment that is not serious, that is, dangerous and useless. The order of reason requires that the useful be treated first, and then the useless, which was treated before. And this is what I have to say on the liberal judgment or action. Now two exceptions against that action are set out. It has been noted that the action comes before the exception. The first exception is prescription of five years, treated at title 21, see On the status of the deceased, &c. The second exception is prescription of long time, the subject of title 22, On prescription of long time. The reason for the order, why the former comes first, is both that the five-year period is earlier than the ten-year, and that the exception of five years fits the title On the collation of dowry. This is what I have to say on the second part, that is, on the judgment or liberal action. I have called the third part accessory, and therefore last, and it is contained in three titles. The first of these is title 23, On peculium, and whether the free..., in which it is asked whether the peculium is an accessory of manumission, or whether a testator may bequeath a slave already manumitted, of which there is the §. peculium, Inst. de legatis. Two other titles follow this one, namely title 24, On the Senatus consultum Claudianum repealed, and title 25, On bare Quiritary right, &c., which are the last of this first chapter on liberty, both because they contain matters that are odious and matters that are to be abrogated and abolished. As to why the title on the Senatus consultum Claudianum comes before the title on bare Quiritary right, the reason is that the title on the Senatus consultum Claudianum properly and solely concerns this first head, that is, slaves and freedmen, whereas the title on bare Quiritary right, &c., concerns not only slaves but any other things whatever. And because this title on bare right deals with the twofold ownership, by Quiritary right and by good faith, the transition is made from this title to the next, the second chapter, on usucapions, which is a mode of acquiring ownership. And this is what I have to say about the first chapter of this seventh book, which concerns liberty and servitude. I said the second chapter concerns usucapion and prescription, and it has three parts, contained in sixteen titles. The first part is on usucapion, the second on prescription, and the third is accessory. The reason for the order among these parts is easy: usucapion is older, and it is more effective than prescription. So for usucapion, that is, the first part of this second chapter, there are six titles, of which the first four are proper, that is, they contain five kinds of usucapion. Of these the first title is title 26, On usucapion for purchase, which is double, that is, it contains two kinds. It is followed by title 27, On usucapion for gift, then title 28, On usucapion for dowry, and finally title 29, On usucapion for heir. The reason will be explained in the Digest, where the order is almost the same. These proper titles are followed by the common title 30, On common usucapions; the reason is well known. The last title on usucapions is title 31, On the transformation of usucapions. The reason is that it contains new law and abolishes some things, and also because this title is, as it were, common to usucapion, already discussed, and to prescription, or long time, which will be discussed next. So from usucapion there is a convenient transition to prescription. Likewise title 32, On acquiring and retaining possession, is also a common and, as it were, middle title, for possession is required both in usucapion and in prescription. Nevertheless, for the sake of order, we refer this title 32 rather to prescription, because by usucapion ownership is acquired, but by prescription only possession, whence it is also commonly called prescription of long time. Having explained the first part on usucapion, the next is the second part, on prescription, which is contained in ten titles. The first of these is title 31 here, for it is general and contains several modes of acquiring and retaining possession, whereas the remaining titles that follow are special, each containing only one mode, namely time. So after this title, on acquiring possession, comes title 33, On prescription of long time, which among the species of prescription treated here is the most ancient, and therefore first. To it also pertains title 34, In which cases it ceases, &c., for one must first see in which cases title 33 has effect, and afterwards in which it does not.

units.la: tit.34. Hujus velut pars est tit.35. quib.non obuir.long.temp &c. Nam & hic tit. causam continet, quia cessat: sed est causa singularis puta ob privilegium militiæ, & proinde posterior. Sic & titul 36. si a uterf.credit.&c. est de singulari persona puta creditoris, ut prior titulus est de persona potissimum creditoris vel absentis Reip.causa, an eis, creditori inquam & militi noceat præscriptio, an verò cesset. Præscriptionem longi temporis sequitur altera species præscriptio quadriennii, quæ est recentior, & proinde posterior ordine. Ad quâ pertinet tit.37. de quadriennii præscr. quamquam & ad præscriptum longi temporis hæc præscriptio quadriennii pertineat. Nam in aliis quidem rebus possessor est tutus præscriptione longi temporis in reb fisci, & in reb. Cæsaris possessor est tutus præscriptione quadriennii. Et hinc est, quod in Inst.tit.de usucap §.ult.ponatur quod hic sub alio tit. Hunc tit.37.
units.tr: Title 34 is, as it were, part of this one. Title 35, quib.non obuir.long.temp &c., also deals with a cause, namely the cessation of prescription, but it is a particular cause, the privilege of military service, and so it comes later. Likewise Title 36, si a uterf.credit.&c., concerns a particular person, the creditor, whereas the earlier title concerns chiefly the person of the creditor or of one absent on public business: whether prescription harms them, the creditor and the soldier I mean, or whether it ceases. After the prescription of long time comes another species, the prescription of four years, which is more recent and so later in order. To it belongs Title 37, de quadriennii præscr., although this prescription of four years also pertains to the prescription of long time. For in other matters the possessor is protected by the prescription of long time when the property is the fisc's, while in matters belonging to Caesar the possessor is protected by the prescription of four years. This is why, in Inst. tit. de usucap. §ult., it is placed under another title; this title 37.

units.la: statim sequitur tit.38. Ne res dominicæ, vel templor.vind.&c. tantum hic adjectus occasione mentionis factæ rerum Cæsaris in l.ult.supra cit. proximo Nâ & hic titul ad res Cæsaris pertinet quo planè prohibetur præscriptio rerum Cæsaris Est autem hic tit. posterior quia prohibitorius. Eum sequitur tit.39. de præscr.30.vel 40.ann. quæ est tertia species, & ultima, quia est novissimi temporis. Tertium membrum hujus secundi capitis libri 7. vocavimus saccessorium, in quod varia sunt conjecta prioribus tamen agnata & affinia & primo quidem est tit.40. de annal.excep. sub quo tit. varia de præscriptionib, continentur, & initio tollitur quædam species præscriptionis quæ vocatur annalis exceptio contractus Italici. Et quia hic titulus continet aliquid, quod tollitur, est posterior, cui adjungitur titu.41. de alluu. & palud.&c. propter similitudinem præscriptionis & alluvionis Nam ut in præscriptionib. & usucapionibus, ita & in alluvione dominium adquiritur paulatim tempore. Et hæc de secundo capite eoq; trimembri lib.7. Tertium caput. est de fine judiciorum. & continetur 34.titulis usque ad finem hujus libri septimi. Quod ipsum caput item est trimembre: nam I.agitur de sententia & rejudic.II.de appellationibus. III. de bonis possid. Ad primum membrum pertinent tituli 19. quorum 10. ad sententiam 9. pertinent ad rem judicatam.
units.tr: Immediately follows Title 38, Ne res dominicæ, vel templor.vind.&c., added here only on the occasion of the mention of Caesar's property in l.ult.supra cit. just above. For this title too concerns Caesar's property, and it plainly forbids prescription of Caesar's property. This title is later because it is prohibitory. It is followed by Title 39, de præscr.30.vel 40.ann., which is the third species and the last, because it belongs to the most recent period. We have called the third member of this second chapter of Book 7 the accessory part, into which various matters have been gathered that are nonetheless akin and related to the earlier ones. First is Title 40, de annal.excep., under which various matters concerning prescription are contained, and at the outset a certain species of prescription, called the annual exception of an Italian contract, is abolished. And because this title contains something that is abolished, it is later. To it is joined Title 41, de alluu. & palud.&c., on account of the similarity between prescription and alluvion: for just as ownership is acquired gradually over time through prescriptions and usucapions, so also in alluvion. And so much for the second chapter of Book 7, which has three members. The third chapter concerns the end of judgments and is contained in 34 titles down to the end of this seventh book. This chapter too has three members: for I. it deals with sentences and res judicata, II. with appeals, III. with possession of goods. Titles 19 belong to the first member, of which 10 concern sentences and 9 concern res judicata.

units.la: Primum igitur locum obtinet tit.42. de sent.pref.prætor. propter dignitatem judic.cui proximus est tit.43. quomodo & quàdoju d.&c. qui titulus est de forma sententiæ latæ (scilicet parte præsente. Ratio est. quia statim id initio occurrit judici. ut sub partium adspectu & præsentia ferat sententiam. Sic & in hoc initio judex sententiam laturus, curare debet, ut sententiam scribat, deinde ferat ac recitet unde tit. 44. de sententiis ex periculo recitandis. Hos sequuntur & alii ad formam pertinentes tituli, sed ea cōtinentes quae non statim initio occurrunt & curanda sunt ut est tit. 41. de sent. & interlocut. quittulus est velut generalis, ideoq; videbatur primo loco collocando. Ratio tamen, cur posterius ponatur, haec est tum quia illa, quae dixi, statim initio occurrunt & curanda sunt, & antequam ferat sententiam, puta ut partes sint praesentes, & sententiam scribat. tum quia hic titulus non tantum de sententiis agat, sed etiā de interlocutionibus quae nō habent vim sententiae. Hunc sequitur tit. 46. de sent. quae sine certa quantit. prolata est. Ratio est, quia adhuc de sententia legitima & recte lata, nunc de non recte prolata, hoc est, non bona seu mala forma, verbi gratia si sententia proferatur sine certa quantitate. Ratio enim postulat, ut posterius de inutilibus agatur. Hujus tituli velut pars quaedam est titul. 47. de sent. quae pro eo quod interest, &c. Prior enim est de sententia incerte quantitatis. Id autem quod interest, plerumque est incertum. Et hoc loco definit Imperator & certum reddit quo dammodo id, quod interest. Inutilis quoque est sententia à non competente judice lata, & proinde priores recte subsequitur titul. 48. si a non compet. jud. &c. quod vicium incompetentiae ut vocant, non est abs similie priori vitio incertitudinis. Nam ut illic judicatur incertum, ita hic judicatur aliud ab alio Judice, quod est prorsus inutile, ideoque hoc vicium priore est posterius. Ultimum de sententiis istis inutilibus locum tenet tit. 49. de poenā jud. qui male jud. &c. Ratio est facilis, quia agit de poena. Poenalia autem solent esse ultima, ut odiosa. Huic adjungitur titul 50. sent. ntiam re scindi non posse. Nam tametsi hic titulus, videatur potius pertinere ad vim & effectum (ut scilicet sententia maneat rata & firma) quam ad formam sententiae, de qua hactenus egimus. Nos tamen hunc titulum accommodamus ad formam, eo quod hic titulus velut secunda quaedam sententia continetur, quā scilicet prior rescindatur vel ab ipso judice vel à principe. Ad formam quoque pertinet titul. 51. de fruct. & lit. expens. Nam sententia judicis est non tantum de re principali, sed etiam de accessoria, ut de fructibus rei, & de expensis, in litem ipsam factis. Et haec est ratio, cur hic titulus inter eos, qui sunt de sententia, sit ultimus quia de accessionibus agat ut jam dictum. Cur item hic titulus posterior sit tituli sententiam rescindi, &c. Ratio est quia de expensis demum agatur terminato iam negotio, & sententia rata manente, sive non rescissa. Hunc sequitur titul. 52. de re jud. Ordinis ratio ut intelligatur admonendum hic breviter, haec duo verba, sententiam, & rem judicatam veteribus idem valere, qui amant haec dicendi genera, ut rem militarem, rem rusticam, rem judicatam. Quare & in ff unus est titul. de re jud. sed hic alius est de sententiis, & alius de re judic. & aliquot tituli ad sententias, de quibus jam dictum aliquot ad rem judic. Videtur enim in C. sententia esse ipsa argumentatio jud. causam definiētis. Res judicata videtur esse decisio, sive de- K 3 finitio causæ, sive causa ipsa, & lis decisa sive terminata: ut sententia sit velut causa, & res judicata sit velut effectus. Videntur & Glossographi suam quoque doctrinam inter hæc duo hinc mutuati. Sed ea tamen non est recipienda, ut in jure plane ignota, qua sententiam distinguunt à re judicata, ut ea proprie sit sententia, à qua sit appellatum, vel frustra, vel utiliter. Itaque hujus membri quod primum dixi cap.3 Videntur duas partes esse, prior de sententiis posterior de re judicat ad quam pertinet titulus 52. quia est generalis, & agit de firmitate rei judicatæ. Ei proximus est tit. 53. de execut. rei jud. Nam id ratio judicii postulat, ut res judicata, quæ firma manet, mandetur executioni. Hunc titul. 54. de desfur. res jud. sequitur. Ratio est quia prius est, ut de principali exequenda, posterius de accessoria, hoc est de usuris agatur. Reus enim, si non pareat judicato intra spatium mensium 4. contra eum postea fit executio, eaque fit non tantum rei principalis, in quam est condemnatus, sed & usurarum nomine, quas debet gravissimas, hoc est, centesimas, post tempus judicati faciendi. Hunc sequitur titul. 55. si plures una sententia, &c. qui & ipse pertinet ad executionem, quemadmodum scil. ea fit facienda contra plures judicatas. Prius enim semper de executione in genere posterius de executione duorum aut plurium considerandum. Sic & alias sæpè ut ad titulum, de duobus reis, &c. dictum supra ad Institut. Huic adjungitur titul. 56. quibus res judicata non nocet. Nam & hic agit de re judicata ad plures pertinente, ut ad plures fratres aut coheredes, sed quia res judicata de qua hic agitur, ex parte nocet hoc est, utilis est, ex parte non nocet hoc est, inutilis est, hoc est, si contra unum ex coheredib. fit judicatum, & alii non adfuerint, merito hic titulus est posterior, ut de inutili re judicata, quem sequitur tit. 57. Comminationes, Epistolas, &c. recto ordine. Nam ut modo dictum de re judicata, partim utili, ita nunc de plane inutilibus sive de iis quæ similitudinem habentes judicatæ, sed tamen veram auctoritatem non habent, ut sunt Comminationes. Huic adjungitur tit. 58. si ex falsis instrumentis. Ratio est, quia & hic tit agat de judicio non vero, sed falso & quia delictum continet, falsi vel perjurii merito posteriorem locum tenet, quem sequitur titul. 59. de confessis. Ut enim priores duo tituli agunt de iis, quæ differunt à re judicata, ita hic agit de iis, qui similes sunt judicatis, & proinde titulus de confessis, distinguitur à titulo, de judicatis, tàm hic, quàm in ff. Tandem ponitur tit. 60. res inter alios, &c. qui est ultimus hujus membri hac ratione, quia hic titulus non tantum de re judic sed etiam de aliis, ut de solutione, transactione, pactione agat: imo potissimum de aliis, & non vere de re judicata. Cur autem de aliis hic agatur, in causa est similitudo: Plerunque enim solet quæri, an res judicata inter alios [noceat aliis. Sic & interdum quæritur, an res inter alios transacta noceat aliis. Putat Cujac. hic in Parat. verbum vel judicatas, delendum, quia inquit, hic titulus non agat de judicatis rebus, sed tantum de aliis. Puto tamen nihil mutandum, tum quia libri veteres repugnant, tum quia l.alt.b.tit. non tantum de aliis, sed etiam de re judicata videatur agere, in his verbis, paciscendo vel agendo: id tamen verum de aliis hic potissimum agi, quia de re judicata, an noceat alibi jam supra satis fuerat explicatum, tit.52. de rejudic. Et haec de primo membro tertii capitis hujus lib. 7. Alterum hujus capitis membrum est de appellationibus, ut jam supra dictum, ubi tamen omissa Ano bis ratio inter haec membra, eoque perfacilis haec est cur inquam prius ponatur tit. de sententia, posteriusque tit. de appellationibus, quia hic est ordo judiciorum, ut sententia prior sit appellatione & rursus appellatio prior sit missione in bonorum possessionem, ad quam pertinet tertium membrum. Hoc autem secundum continetur 10. titulis, quos fere Tribun. sumpsit ex Cod. Theodof. l.b.11. Eorum primus est tit. 61. de relationibus, alter est 62. de appell. & consult. Tit. LXI. Cur autem prior sit titulus de relationib. cum tamen titulus 62. generalis Tit. LXII. sit, ratio est, tum propter dignitatem Principis, ad quem si vel ad cujus comitatum & consistorium solent fieri relationes, tum quia relationes saepe ante appellationem, imo ante sententiam fiunt. Relatio autem idem valet, quod consultatio; Cur ergo dicat aliquis, bis agitur de eodem, puta tit. de relat. & tit. de appellat. & consultat. Respond. in titul. de relationib. tantum ea tractari, quae pertinent ad officium referentis, sive consultantis magistratus & judicis, & agi de consultationibus iis, quae fiunt ante sententiam potissimum, sed in tit. de appellat. agi de iis potissimum consultationibus, quae fiunt post sententiam judicis ut & appellationes, & proinde sub eo titulo continentur: agi quoque de iis, qui pertinent ad officium eorum, ad quos fiunt consultationes, ut sunt proceres consistorii. Cujac. in Parat. etiam adfert distinctionem inter titul. de relat. & de appellat. putatque verb. consultationis non semper idem valere, sed interdum poni pro consultatione seu relatione, hoc est, pro eo quod referturad Principem: iuterdum pro eo quod a Principe respondetur, sive a consistorianis, & ita posterius accipi in titul. de appellationibus sed non probat. nec puto consultationis verbum, vel pro sententia ad consultationem facta usquam reperiri Et haec de titulo 61. & 62. Cui proximus est tit. 63. de tempor. & repar. & c. Cujus ratio, ut intelligatur, memi- Tit. LXIII. nisse oportet, in appellationibus certa esse tempora interponendae appellationis de quibus jam est dictum tit. 62. hic titul. 63. est de temporibus exercendae. Prius autem interponitur posterius exercetur appellatio. Huic titulo proximus est tit. 64. quando provoc. necess. non sit. Nam ut supradictu in tractatu restitutionum in integrum, priusde causis. propter quas no est necessaria, ita & hic de appellatione prius quando est necessaria (de qua hactenus) posterius, quando non est necessaria de qua tit 64. Huic adjungitur titu 65. Tit. LXV. quorum appellationes non recip. idem quod in tractatu restitutionis; Primo de necessaria secundo de non necessaria tertio de prohibita ibi quidé restitutione, hic vero de appellatione ordine ac denique agitur. Huc sequitur tit. 66. si pen.
units.tr: First, then, the title de sententia praefecti praetorio (tit. 42) holds the first place, on account of the dignity of the judge. Next to it is tit. 43, quomodo et quando iudex sententiam ferre debeat, which concerns the form of a sentence once pronounced (namely, with the parties present). The reason is that this is the first thing that falls to the judge, who must pronounce sentence in the sight and presence of the parties. So too at the start of this, the judge who is about to pronounce sentence must take care to write the sentence, then to deliver and read it aloud. Hence tit. 44, de sententiis ex periculo recitandis. These are followed by other titles that concern form, but which contain matters that do not fall at the very beginning and must be attended to later, such as tit. 41, de sententiis et interlocutionibus. That title is, as it were, general, and so it seemed it ought to be placed first. The reason it is placed later is this: the matters I have mentioned fall at the very beginning and must be attended to before the sentence is pronounced, for instance that the parties be present and that the sentence be written down; and also because this title deals not only with sentences but also with interlocutions, which do not have the force of a sentence. It is followed by tit. 46, de sententia quae sine certa quantitate prolata est. The reason is that, having dealt with a sentence that is lawful and rightly pronounced, we now turn to one not rightly pronounced, that is, one defective in form, for example if a sentence is pronounced without a certain amount. For reason requires that the defective be treated after the valid. Part of this title is, as it were, tit. 47, de sententia quae pro eo quod interest, etc. For the former concerns a sentence of uncertain amount, and the interest is generally uncertain; and in this place the Emperor defines it and makes clear, in a certain way, what the interest is. A sentence pronounced by a judge who lacks competence is also void, and so tit. 48, si a non competente iudice latum sit, rightly follows the former. This defect, which they call incompetence, is not unlike the former defect of uncertainty. For just as there an uncertain thing is judged, so here something other than what the judge is competent to judge is judged, which is wholly void; therefore this defect comes after the former. The last place among these void sentences is held by tit. 49, de poena iudicis qui male iudicavit, etc. The reason is easy: it treats of a penalty. Penal matters are usually placed last, as odious. To this is joined tit. 50, sententiam rescindi non posse. For although this title seems rather to pertain to the effect and force of a sentence (namely, that it remain valid and firm) than to the form of the sentence, of which we have treated hitherto, nevertheless we assign this title to form, because it is contained as a kind of second sentence, by which the former is rescinded, either by the judge himself or by the prince. Tit. 51, de fructibus et litis expensis, also pertains to form. For a judge's sentence concerns not only the principal matter but also the accessory, such as the fruits of the thing and the expenses incurred in the suit itself. This is the reason why this title is the last among those that concern sentences: it deals with accessories, as has already been said. Likewise the reason this title comes after the title sententiam rescindi non posse is that expenses are dealt with only once the business is concluded and the sentence stands unrescinded. It is followed by tit. 52, de re iudicata. As to the order, it should be briefly noted here that these two words, sententia and res iudicata, meant the same to the ancients, who liked such modes of speaking as res militaris, res rustica, res iudicata. Hence in the Digest too there is one title, de re iudicata; but here there is one title de sententiis and another de re iudicata, and some titles concerning sentences have been discussed, and some concerning res iudicata. For in the Code a sentence seems to be the very reasoning of the judge defining the cause. A res iudicata seems to be the decision, or definition, of the cause, or the cause itself, and the dispute decided or ended: so that the sentence is as it were the cause, and the res iudicata as it were the effect. The Glossators too seem to have borrowed their own doctrine from these two notions. But that doctrine is not to be accepted, since it is plainly unknown in law, which distinguishes sentence from res iudicata so that the sentence is properly that from which an appeal is made, either in vain or with profit. Accordingly, of the first member of this chapter, which I mentioned first in chapter 3, there seem to be two parts: the former concerning sentences, the latter concerning res iudicata, to which belongs tit. 52, because it is general and treats of the firmness of res iudicata. Next to it is tit. 53, de executione rei iudicatae. For the nature of judgment requires that a res iudicata, which remains firm, be committed to execution. It is followed by tit. 54, de usuris rei iudicatae. The reason is that it is first proper to deal with execution of the principal, and afterwards with the accessory, that is, with interest. For if the defendant does not obey the judgment within four months, execution is then carried out against him, and this is done not only for the principal thing for which he was condemned, but also in the name of the usury, which he owes at the most grievous rate, that is, at one per cent per month, from the time the judgment ought to have been made. It is followed by tit. 55, si plures una sententia, etc., which also pertains to execution, namely as to how it is to be carried out against several persons under one judgment. For the general matter of execution must always be considered first, and afterwards the execution against two or more. So also, as often elsewhere, as to the title de duobus reis, etc., mentioned above on the Institutes. To this is joined tit. 56, quibus res iudicata non nocet. For this too deals with res iudicata affecting several persons, such as several brothers or coheirs; but since the res iudicata here treated harms in part, that is, is useful in part, and does not harm in part, that is, is useless, namely if judgment has been given against one of the coheirs and the others were not present, this title rightly comes later, as concerning a useless res iudicata. It is followed in proper order by tit. 57, comminationes, epistolas, etc. For just as what has just been said concerns a res iudicata that is partly useful, so now the subject is things that are wholly useless, or those that resemble a res iudicata yet do not have true authority, such as threats. To this is joined tit. 58, si ex falsis instrumentis. The reason is that this title deals not with a true but with a false judgment, and because it contains a crime, of forgery or perjury, it rightly holds a place later, and it is followed by tit. 59, de confessis. For just as the two preceding titles deal with those things that differ from res iudicata, so this one deals with those that resemble judgments; and therefore the title de confessis is distinguished from the title de iudicatis, as much here as in the Digest. Finally tit. 60, res inter alios, etc., is placed, which is the last of this member, for this reason: that this title treats not only of res iudicata but also of other matters, such as payment, compromise and agreement; indeed chiefly of other matters, and not truly of res iudicata. But the reason why other matters are treated here is the similarity: it is commonly asked whether a res iudicata harms others, and so sometimes it is asked whether a matter transacted between others harms them. Cujacius, in his Paratitla on this place, thinks the words vel iudicatas should be deleted, because, he says, this title does not treat of judged matters but only of others. I think nothing should be changed, both because the old books oppose it, and because the law at the end of the title seems to treat not only of others but also of res iudicata, in these words, paciscendo vel agendo. Yet that chiefly other matters are treated here, because whether res iudicata harms others had already been sufficiently explained above, in tit. 52, de re iudicata. And this is what I have to say about the first member of the third chapter of this seventh book. The second member of this chapter concerns appeals, as has already been said above, where, however, the reason for the order between these members was omitted; and it is very easy: why, I say, the title de sententia is placed first, and the title de appellationibus afterwards, is that this is the order of judicial proceedings, namely that sentence comes before appeal, and again appeal comes before the grant of possession of goods, to which the third member pertains. This second member, however, is contained in 10 titles, which the Tribonian compilers took almost entirely from the Theodosian Code, book 11. The first of these is tit. 61, de relationibus; the second is tit. 62, de appellationibus et consultationibus. Tit. LXI. Why the title de relationibus comes first, although tit. 62 is general, Tit. LXII. the reason is, partly, on account of the dignity of the Prince, to whom, or to whose council and consistory, reports are usually made, and partly because reports are often made before an appeal, indeed before a sentence. Now relatio means the same as consultatio. So if someone asks why the same matter is treated twice, namely in the title de relationibus and in the title de appellationibus et consultationibus, the answer is that in the title de relationibus only those matters are treated which pertain to the duty of the reporting, or consulting, magistrate or judge, and consultations that take place chiefly before sentence are dealt with; but in the title de appellationibus the consultations chiefly dealt with are those made after the judge's sentence, as are appeals, and therefore they are contained under that title; and matters are also dealt with that pertain to the duty of those to whom the consultations are made, such as the nobles of the consistory. Cujacius, in his Paratitla, also draws a distinction between the titles de relationibus and de appellationibus, and thinks that the word consultatio does not always have the same meaning, but sometimes stands for a consultation or report, that is, for what is referred to the Prince, and sometimes for what is answered by the Prince or by the consistorians; and so the latter is understood in the title de appellationibus; but he does not prove it. Nor do I think the word consultatio is found anywhere for a sentence made upon consultation. And this is what I have to say on titles 61 and 62. Next to these is tit. 63, de temporibus et reparationibus, etc. To understand its reason, it must be remembered that in appeals there are fixed times for interposing an appeal, of which we have already spoken under tit. 62; this tit. 63 concerns the times for pursuing it. The appeal is interposed first, and afterwards it is pursued. Tit. LXIII. Next to this title is tit. 64, quando provocatio necessaria non sit. For as was said above in the treatise on restitution in integrum, the causes for which restitution is not necessary come after those for which it is, so here too, concerning appeal, the cases where it is necessary (of which we have spoken hitherto) come first, and afterwards the cases where it is not necessary, which is tit. 64. To this is joined tit. 65, Tit. LXV. quorum appellationes non recipiantur, which in the treatise on restitution is the same, there treated first of the necessary, secondly of the non-necessary, thirdly of the forbidden; but here, in the matter of appeal, the order is the same and finally treated. This is followed by tit. 66, si pendente.

units.la: {Tit.LXI} Tit. LXII. Tit. LXIII. Tit. LXIV. Tit. LXV.
