units.la: 66.si pendente appellatione,&c. Ratio ordinis est, quia hactenus de ipso, qui coepit appellationem exercere nunc de eius herede,cui proximus est tit.67. de his qui propt. met. jud. Ratio haec est,quia hactenus dictum est de iis, qui appellant nunc de iis,qui non appellant,quod natura est posterius. Quemadmodum autem saepe jam dictum est, maxime ad titul. de duob. reis. Instit. prius temperagi de uno, posterius de pluribus: ita hic eadem est ratio ordinis ad tit.68.si unus ex plurib. quem sequitur tit 69.si de moment.poss. &c. qui titulus cur in tit.de appell. sit penultimus, rationem aliam non video, quam vel quod priores omnes tituli sunt de proprietate, quae est potior: hic vero de possessione, vel quod sit prohibitorius nt& titulus proximus, qui est ultimus,prohibitoria ultimum in locum rejici solent. Sed in Cod. Theodos. ex quo fere hi tituli sunt sumpti,paulo alius est ordo.Ultimus est titulus,ut modo dictum est tit.70. ne liceat in una &c. Ratio ordinis est, tum quia hic titulus est prohibitorius, tum maxime, quia agit de secunda & tertia appellation.quae posteriores sunt,prima de qua hactenus dictum. Secunda & tertia postremum semper locum tenent. Restat tertium & ultimum hujus cap. tertij membrum, ad quod pertinet tit.71.qui bon.ced.poss. & tres seqq. usque ad finem libri septimi. Ratio ordinis ad titul 71.qui bon.ced.poss. Cur, inquit, appellationem sequatur statim cessio bonorum, est, quia reo condemnato duo sunt remedia. unum ordinarium appellatio, alterum extraordinarium & miserandum. cessio bonorum,tandem venitur ad bonorum venditionē, ac missionem in possessionem. Nam reus non tantum in priore judicio, sed etiam in judicio appellationis victus.si velit uti judicio cessionis, potest, si non ducitur in carcerem,& nihilominus bonaejus auctoritate magistratus dantur possidenda victori,& posita vendenda,qui est ordo judicialis.Et iste ordo tenetur in his titulis,puta dict. tit 71.& tit.72.de bon. auct. jud.poss. ad quem titulum pertinet quoque tit.73.de privil.fisc. & tit.74.de privil.dot. Ratio est, quia in missione in bonorum possessionem.& in venditione bonorum creditoris, qui mittuntur, non omnes eodem sunt jure, sed quidam sunt meliore,hoc est privilegium habent. Duo hic tantum commemorantur fiscus & mulier dotis caula, quia haec duo sunt maxima & celeberrima. Prius autem de fisco agitur,quia publica privatis praeferuntur Ultimus libri 7.titulus est de revocat. his quae infr. &c Ratio ordinis, quia & hic titulus ad bona eorum,sed in fraudem alienata pertinet:&quia fraudem sive delictum continet in ultimum locum est rejectus. Et haec de libro septimo.
units.tr: 66. si pendente appellatione, &c. The reason for the order is this: until now the discussion has concerned the one who began the appeal, and now it turns to his heir, to whom title 67 de his qui propter metum judicii is closest. The reason is that until now the discussion has been about those who appeal, and now it is about those who do not appeal, which comes naturally later. As has often been said already, especially under the title de duobus reis in the Institutes, one should first treat of one party and then of several. So here too the reason for the order is the same as for title 68 si unus ex pluribus, which is followed by title 69 si de momentanea possessione, &c. I see no other reason why this title should be next to last in the title de appellationibus than that all the earlier titles deal with ownership, which is the stronger right, whereas this one deals with possession; or else that it is prohibitory, and the title next to it, which is the last, is prohibitory too, and prohibitory titles are usually placed in the last position. But in the Theodosian Code, from which these titles were mostly taken, the order is somewhat different. The last title is, as just said, title 70 ne liceat in una, &c. The reason for this order is both that this title is prohibitory and, above all, that it deals with the second and third appeals, which come later, while the first appeal is the one discussed so far. The second and third always hold the last place. There remains the third and last member of this chapter, to which title 71 belongs, qui bonis cedere possunt, and the three following titles, to the end of the seventh book. As for the order of title 71 qui bonis cedere possunt: why, he says, the cession of goods immediately follows the appeal is that a condemned defendant has two remedies. One is ordinary, the appeal; the other is extraordinary and pitiable, the cession of goods. Finally one comes to the sale of the goods and the putting of the creditor into possession. For the defendant, if he is defeated not only in the first trial but also in the appeal, may, if he wishes, use the procedure of cession, provided he is not led off to prison; and nonetheless his goods, by the authority of the magistrate, are handed over to the victor to be held and put up for sale. This is the judicial order. And this order is observed in these titles, namely the said title 71 and title 72 de bonorum auctoritate judicis possidendorum, to which title also belongs title 73 de privilegio fisci and title 74 de privilegio dotis. The reason is that in the putting of goods into possession and in the sale of the goods of a debtor, not all creditors stand on the same footing; some have a better right, that is, they enjoy a privilege. Only two are mentioned here, the fisc and the wife for the sake of her dowry, because these two are the greatest and most celebrated. The fisc is treated first, because public claims are preferred to private ones. The last title of the seventh book is de revocandis his quae infra, &c. The reason for the order is that this title also concerns their goods, but goods alienated in fraud; and since it contains fraud or wrongdoing, it has been placed in the last position. And so much on the seventh book.

units.la: Lib. VIII. Ccdcis,
units.tr: Book 8 of the Code

units.la: NUncde libro 8. videamus,cujus tituli sunt 58. vulgo numerantur 59. sed non recte,ut infra dicetur ad tit.10. & 11: videntur autem hi tituli 58. commodè revocari ad 4. capita, quorum primum est de interdictis dictis,tit.1.&c. Secundum est de pignoribus,titul.13.&c. Tertium est de accessionibus obligationum & actionum,tit.35. Ultimum est varium & accessorium,titul.46. usque ad finem libri. Ratio ordinis, & sane difficilis explicabitur inf.ad edicta perpetua. Quod ad primum c.attinet de interdictis id cötinetur tit.12. quorum primus est tit. 1. de interdictis, quia est generalis, cui adjungitur statim tituli speciales. Sūt enim interdictorum tres species, restitutoria, prohibitoria & exhibitoria. Et primo quidem loco ponuntur restitutoria. Ratio exponetur ad ff ut est interdictum quorum bonorum, titul.2. quorum bonorum, quod primo loco ponitur quia est universale. Ejusdem generis est interdictum quorum legatorum, titul.3. quo legatorum. Ratioordinis, quia legata cum bonorum possessionibus & hereditatibus cognationem habent. Huic additur titul.4. unde vi. Ratio est, quia inter singularia intetdicta hoc est gravissimum, propter vim. Ejus tituli pars est titul f.siper vim vel al omodo,&c. Nam & hic titulus est de vi sedeftantum de vi facta absenti in qua vi, quia multa sunt singularia, merito proprius de ea est titulus. Et autem hoc interdictum de vi etiam restitutorium: sed interdictum uti possidetis, est prohibitorium, de quo est titul.6. uti possidetis. Nam titulis 2.3.4.& 5.expositis restitutoriis, transit Imperator ad prohibitoria, tandem ad exhibitoria,ut est interdictum de tab.exhib. tit.7. & interdictum. de liber.exhib. titul.8. Ratio autem, cur illud priore loco ponatur, est, quia ad testamentum sive universitatem pertinet. Universalia autem singularibus sunt priora. Proximus est titul. 9. deprecario, & de Salviano interdicto, quod tamen utrumque interdictum est restitutorium. Ratio ordinis exponetur infra ad Pand. Nam & ibi in posteriorem locum rejiciuntur haec duo, & Salvianum maxime, quod est plane ultimus titulus 33 ff. de interdict. libr. 43. Quod interdictum Salvianum in ff. statim postponitur interdicto,de migrando. Utrumque enim & de migrando & Salvianum, pertinet ad aedificia & villas quae inhabitantur ab inquilinis & colonis.
units.tr: Now let us consider Book 8, which has 58 titles. They are commonly numbered 59, but not correctly, as will be said below at titles 10 and 11. These 58 titles may conveniently be traced back to four chapters. The first concerns the interdicts, tit. 1 etc. The second concerns pledges, tit. 13 etc. The third concerns the accessions of obligations and actions, tit. 35. The last is miscellaneous and incidental, tit. 46 to the end of the book. The reason for the order, which is certainly difficult, will be explained below, under the Perpetual Edict. As for the first chapter, on interdicts, it is contained in titles 1 to 12. The first is title 1, de interdictis, because it is general, and special titles are added to it at once. For there are three kinds of interdicts: restitutory, prohibitory and exhibitory. The restitutory come first. The reason will be set out under the Digest, in the interdict quorum bonorum, title 2, quorum bonorum, which is placed first because it is universal. Of the same kind is the interdict quorum legatorum, title 3, quo legatorum. The reason for the order is that legacies have a kinship with possessions of goods and with inheritances. To this is added title 4, unde vi. The reason is that among the individual interdicts this is the most serious, on account of the force involved. Part of this title is title 5, si per vim vel alio modo, etc. For this title too concerns force, but only force used against someone absent, and since there are many particular cases, it is rightly given a title of its own. This interdict de vi is also restitutory. But the interdict uti possidetis is prohibitory, and it is the subject of title 6, uti possidetis. For after setting out the restitutory titles 2, 3, 4 and 5, the Emperor passes to the prohibitory ones, and finally to the exhibitory, such as the interdict de tabulis exhibendis, title 7, and the interdict de liberis exhibendis, title 8. The reason why the former is placed earlier is that it concerns a testament or universal succession. Universal matters, however, come before particular ones. Next is title 9, de precario, et de Salviano interdicto, although both these interdicts are restitutory. The reason for the order will be explained below under the Digest. For there too these two are placed in a later position, and the Salvian interdict especially, which is plainly the last title, 33, of de interdictis, Digest Book 43. The Salvian interdict in the Digest is placed immediately after the interdict de migrando. For both the interdict de migrando and the Salvian one concern buildings and farms which are lived in by tenants and coloni.

units.la: Atque hujus interdicti Salviani occasione hic positi in Cod adjungitur ei titul.10. de ædif.privat. Cujacius in Parat. aliam rationem adfert, cur hic titulus de ædif. privat, hic inter titulos interdictorum ponatur: quia inquit, & de aedificijs sunt interdicta quaedam, ut quod vi aut clam, &c. & eadem. inquit, ratione titulum 10. de ædif. privat. sequitur titul.11, de operibus publicis, quia & de his sunt quaedam interdicta, sed etsi verum est, de illis esse interdicta quaedam, tamen sub his titulis non agitur de interdictis, neque ulla interdicti fit mentio, sub titul. 10. & 11. Quare potius interdicti Salviani & de migrando occasione (licet hoc loco id sit omissum) positus videtur hic titul.10. de ædif.priv.
units.tr: On the occasion of this Salvian interdict, which is placed here in the Code, title 10, de aedificiis privatis, is added to it. Cujacius, in his Paratitla, gives another reason why this title, de aedificiis privatis, is placed here among the titles on interdicts: namely, he says, that there are certain interdicts concerning buildings too, such as those for works done by force or secretly, etc. And for the same reason, he says, title 11, de operibus publicis, follows title 10, de aedificiis privatis, because there are also certain interdicts concerning these. But although it is true that there are certain interdicts concerning those matters, nevertheless under these titles 10 and 11 there is no discussion of interdicts, and no mention of any interdict is made. Therefore it seems more probable that title 10, de aedificiis privatis, is placed here on the occasion of the Salvian interdict and of de migrando (although this has been omitted in this place).

units.la: Eaque occasione aedificiorum adjungitur tit 11. de operibus publ. ut omnia scilicet aedificia, eodem loco ponantur. Cur autem titulus de ædific.privat. prior sit titulo de operibus public. cum tamen publica privatis sint potiora. ratio est qua priores tituli (ut omnes ferè hujus libri) sunt de jure & rebus privatis, ut & illa interdicta de migrando & de Salviano ad privata ædificia & villas pertinent. Recte igitur ei titulo 9. ac præcar. & salv. Itaque adjungitur titulo 10. de ædif. priv. & ædificiorum ratione huic titul. 11. de operib. publ. Cujus pars est tit. 12. de rationibus oper. publ. & c. Ratio, quia operibus jam factis demum excutiuntur rationes operum. Et hæc de primo capite, scilicet de interdictis.
units.tr: And on the occasion of buildings, title 11, de operibus publicis, is added, so that all buildings are placed together in one place. Why the title de aedificiis privatis comes before the title de operibus publicis, although public matters are superior to private ones, is explained as follows. The earlier titles (as almost all of this book) concern private law and private affairs, and so do those interdicts de migrando and de Salviano, which pertain to private buildings and farms. It is right, therefore, that title 10 de aedificiis privatis follows title 9, de precario et Salviano. And on account of buildings, title 11, de operibus publicis, is added to title 10. Title 12, de rationibus operum publicorum, belongs to it, because the accounts of public works are examined only once the works are completed. And so much for the first chapter, namely on interdicts.

units.la: Alterum membrum hujus lib. 8 est de pignoribus ac titulis 12. continetur estque quadrimembre. I enim agitur de pignore contrahendo & contituendo. I I. de eo finiendo. I I I. de eo vendendo. I V de jure novo. Ratio ordinis inter hæc membra exponetur infra, partim ad ff. ubi fere idem est ordo. Ad primum membrum de pignore contrahendo pertinet 12. tituli quorum 1. est titulus 13. de pignor. & hypoth. Est enim generalis, quem sequitur titulus 14. in quibus causis pign. &c. eumque sequitur tit. 15. si alienaverit pignori, &c. & hunc tit. 16. quæ res pignori obligari, &c. hunc denique t. 17. qui potiores sint in pignore, &c. Ratio oi dinis exponetur infra ad ff. Huic adjungitur titulus 18. de his, qui in prior. cred. &c. qui pertinet ad titulum priorem, quam partiar, &c. Nam & hic de pluribus quæ litem. quis sit potior, sed titulus prior est de creditoribus principalibus, hic est de successoribus in eorum locum, & proinde est posterior. Huic subjicitur tit. 19. pignus. antiquior cred. torpignus, &c. quia pignus vendi non potest ante contractum. Eum sequitur titulus 20. si communis res pignori,&c. ratione similitudinis ni fallor, quia scilicet, ut priores tituli sunt de communi pignore, sive de pluribus oppignoratis: ita & hic titulus est de communi re oppignorata vel uni vel pluribus.
units.tr: The second part of this Book 8 concerns pledges, and it is contained in twelve titles. It has four parts. The first deals with contracting and constituting a pledge; the second with extinguishing it; the third with selling it; the fourth with the new law. The order among these parts will be explained below, partly under the Digest, where the order is almost the same. To the first part, on contracting a pledge, belong the twelve titles, of which the first is title 13, de pignoribus et hypothecis. For it is general, and it is followed by title 14, in quibus causis pignus, etc., and that by title 15, si alienaverit pignori, etc., and this by title 16, quae res pignori obligari, etc., and finally title 17, qui potiores sint in pignore, etc. The reason for the order will be explained below under the Digest. To this is added title 18, de his qui in priorum creditorum locum succedunt, which pertains to the earlier title, qui potiores. For that too concerns the priority of claims in a dispute, but the earlier title concerns the original creditors, and this one concerns those who succeed into their place, and so it comes later. Under this is placed title 19, pignus antiquius creditori tornatur, etc., because a pledge cannot be sold before the contract. It is followed by title 20, si communis res pignori, etc., by analogy, unless I am mistaken: just as the earlier titles concern a common pledge, that is, several things pledged together, so this title concerns a common thing pledged to one person or to several.

units.la: Illud hic admonendum pignus in jure triplex esse, testamentarium conventionale & prætorii. De testamentario & de conventionali simul sub hisce titulis agi solet: sed tamen in prioribus titulis tantum de conventionali agitur quia testamentarium est rarissimum. Expolito eo conventionali proximum est, ut de prætorio agatur, de quo est titulus 21. de prætorio pignore. Cur prius de conventionali? Ratio est, quia id est ordinarium & quotidianum: prætorium est rarius, & extraordinarium: Cujus species videtur judiciale pignus, quod tamen à prætorio proprie dicto in multis rebus differt.
units.tr: It must be noted here that in law a pledge is threefold: testamentary, conventional, and praetorian. The testamentary and the conventional are customarily treated together under these titles. But in the earlier titles only the conventional is discussed, because the testamentary is very rare. Once the conventional has been set out, it is next that the praetorian should be discussed, which is the subject of title 21, de pignore praetorio. Why is the conventional taken first? The reason is that it is ordinary and everyday, whereas the praetorian is rarer and extraordinary. A species of it seems to be the judicial pledge, which nevertheless differs from the praetorian pledge properly so called in many respects.

units.la: Differentias exponit Cujacius in Parat. & de hoc judiciali pignore est tit. 22. sin causa judicati, &c. Hunc sequitur titulus 23 si pig. pig. dat. sit. Ratio est perspicua: Prius enim de primo genere, posterius de secundo, quod pignus pignoris dicitur agendum. Ei adjungitur titulus 24. de partu pignoris & omnis causa. Est enim hic titulus de accessione pignoris & proinde ultimum locum in hoc primo membro de contractu & actione pignoris tenet.
units.tr: Cujacius, in his Paratitla, sets out the differences, and the judicial pledge is the subject of title 22, si in causa iudicati, etc. This is followed by title 23, si pignus pignori datum sit. The reason is clear: the former deals with the first kind, the latter with the second, which is called a pledge of a pledge. To it is added title 24, de partu pignoris et omni causa. For this title concerns the accessories of a pledge, and so it holds the last place in this first part, on the contract and action of a pledge.

units.la: Nunc de secundo membro, quod est de finiendo pignore, quo pertinent duo tituli, quorum prior est titulus 25. de remissione pignoris alter est titul. 26. Etiam ob Chirographariam, &c. Ratio ordinis, quia ille modum finiendi pignoris per pactum continet celeberrimum: hic alium minus celebrem & infrequentem per novationem. Sunt & alii modi finiendi pignus, de quibus est titulus ff. qui h. mod. pign. v hypoth. solv. Tertium membrum est de pignore vendendo sive distrahendo ad quodac commodari possunt 6. tituli Cujacius in parat. distractionem ponit inter modos finiendi pignoris, fortasse non malè, quia & venditio finit, sive tollit pignus. & tum hi tituli ad distractionem pignoris pertinentes, ad membrum secundum accommodarentur: quia tamen in ff. perspicuè distinguitur distractio pignoris à modis finiendi, & quia hic articulus de pignore distrahendo est valde celebris in tractatu piguoris, rectius fortasse facere videbitur, qui hoc membrum de distractione distinguat à priore definiendo pignore. Contrario atque in ff ordine ratio hæc est, quia in hoc tractatu five capite de pignoribus ultimum membrum de impetrando dominio pignoris, quæ impetratio pignoris venditioni commodè adjungitur: Nam si creditor pignus non posset vendere aliis (sibi non potest) solet tandem à Principe dominium pignoris ipse sibi impetrare. Atque ita à venditione fit commoda transitio ad impetrationem domini. hoc est, à tertio membro ad quartum. Alia est ratio in ff ubi quartum illud membrum nō habetur. quia est ex novo jure Jurisconsultis ignotum. dico, quòad formam novam ab Imperatore Justiniano introductam, l. 31. de jure domini impetr. Horum igitur sex titulorum ad venditionem pignoris pertinentium primum locum obtinet. titulus 27. de distr. pign. quia est generalis, huic adjungitur titulus 28. De torem vend. pignoris imped. non posse; quia est velut pars tituli prioris. Hunc sequitur titulus 29. si vendito pignor. ag. Ratio est quia modo dictum est de pignore vendendo: eo autem vendito interdum actio datur debitori propter rei suæ hoc est, pignoris venditionem non recte factam. Huic adjungitur titulus 30. de luit. p. gu. occasione actionis, de quamodo dictum est. Nam ut ibi propter venditionem pignoris debitor interdum habet actionem. ita & propter luitionem pignoris debitoractionem habet ad pignus recuperandum. Recte autè huic titulo 30. adjungitur statim titulus 31. si unus ex pluribus heredi. Nam & hic titulus est de actione propter luitionem, sed est de heredibus, hoc est, de actione, quæ datur heredibus vel debitoris, vel creditoris: debitoris quidem pignoratitia; creditoris autem hypothecaria. Sic & titulus 32. si pignoris conventionem, etc. ad actionem pertinet: sed priores tituli sunt de vero pignore, ex quo & utrinque vera datur actio: sed hic titulus est de pignore irrito, & per mendacium accepto, & proinde merito est posterior. Et hæc de tertio membro, hoc est, distractione pignoris. Restat quartum membrum, quod quia est de jure novo in pignoribus, merito est ultimum, quo pertinet titulus trigesimus tertius de jure domini impetr. Ratio ordinis quia impetratio dominii proxima est venditioni pignoris de qua modo fuit dictum. Eodé
units.tr: Now to the second part, on extinguishing a pledge, to which two titles belong. The first is title 25, de remissione pignoris, and the second is title 26, etiam ob chirographariam, etc. The reason for the order is that the former contains the most common way of extinguishing a pledge, by agreement, and the latter another, less common and less frequent, by novation. There are also other ways of extinguishing a pledge, which are the subject of the Digest title qui potiores, qui hoc modo pignus vel hypotheca solvitur. The third part concerns selling or distraining a pledge, to which six titles may be adapted. Cujacius, in his Paratitla, places distraction among the ways of extinguishing a pledge, perhaps not badly, since sale also ends or removes a pledge. And these titles concerning the distraction of a pledge might then be adapted to the second part. But because in the Digest distraction of a pledge is clearly distinguished from the ways of extinguishing it, and because this topic, the distraction of a pledge, is very famous in the treatise on pledges, he who distinguishes this part, on distraction, from the earlier one, on extinguishing, will perhaps seem to act more rightly. The order is the reverse of the Digest's, and the reason is this: in this treatise, or chapter, on pledges, the last part concerns obtaining ownership of a pledge, and the obtaining of a pledge is conveniently joined to its sale. For if a creditor could not sell the pledge to another (he cannot sell it to himself), he is in the end accustomed to obtain ownership of the pledge for himself from the Prince. And so there is a convenient transition from sale to the obtaining of ownership, that is, from the third part to the fourth. The order is different in the Digest, where that fourth part is not found, because it arises from new law unknown to the jurists: I mean the new form introduced by the Emperor Justinian, l. 31, de iure dominii impetrando. Of these six titles concerning the sale of a pledge, the first place is taken by title 27, de distractione pignorum. Because it is general, it is followed by title 28, de tutore vendente pignus impetrare non posse, which is as it were part of the preceding title. This is followed by title 29, si vendito pignore agatur. The reason is that, as has just been said, a pledge is to be sold, and once it has been sold, an action is sometimes given to the debtor on account of his own thing, that is, because the sale of the pledge was not properly carried out. To this is added title 30, de luitione pignoris, on the occasion of the action just mentioned. For just as on account of the sale of a pledge the debtor sometimes has an action, so on account of the redemption of a pledge the debtor has an action to recover the pledge. Rightly, moreover, title 31, si unus ex pluribus heredibus, is added at once to title 30. For this title too concerns an action arising from redemption, but it concerns heirs, that is, the action given to the heirs either of the debtor or of the creditor: the debtor's heirs have the pledging action, the creditor's the hypothecary action. Likewise title 32, si pignoris conventio, etc., belongs to the action. But the earlier titles concern a true pledge, from which a true action arises on both sides, whereas this title concerns a void pledge, obtained by falsehood, and so it rightly comes later. And so much for the third part, that is, the distraction of a pledge. There remains the fourth part, which, because it concerns new law on pledges, rightly comes last. To it belongs title 33, de iure dominii impetrando. The reason for the order is that obtaining ownership is closest to the sale of a pledge, of which we have just spoken. Of the same kind, the last place is held by the prohibitory character, because it is prohibitory and contains both a seizure and a fraud: the law Commissoriae, which the Emperor Constantine abolished absolutely, the so-called commissory law or pact. Today it has been abolished only in the case of pledges, not in sales. And so much for the second…

units.la: óiatu pignorum sit ultimus, est quia est prohibitorius, & delictum continet sive captionem & fraudem l. Commissoriæ, quam legem sive pactum Commissoriû sustulit Cõstantinus omnimodo: sed hodie tantum in pignoribus sublata est, in venditionibus non item. Et hæc de secundo capite hujus libri 8. hoc est, de pignoribus. Tertio capite diximus, contineri accessiones quasdam actionum & obligationum ex jure prætorio. Nam & pignoratitia sive hypothecariaactio est juris prætorij, §. autem Serviana, de actionibus. Hujus generis sunt exceptiones, fidejussiones, stipulationes prætoriæ. Dices, pignora quoq; esse accessiones, quod verum est eaq; de causa in Edicto perpetuo tractatio de pignoribus, exceptionibus & stipulationibus prætorijs suerunt conjunctæ, ut dicetur infr. ad ff. sed nos hunc tractatum de pignoribus distinximus à reliquis accessionibus secuti Tribun. in ff. etiam cómoditatis gratia, quia hic tractatus de pignoribus alioqui per se est prolixus & proinde proprio loco dignus. Ad hoc autem caput 3. pertinent 11. tituli, quorum primus est tit. 35. de except. & præscript. Ratio ordinis, cur pignoribus proximè ponantur exceptiones, est, quia hic ordo erat Edicti, quem sequitur Tribun. & quidem in C. magis, quam in ff. Cur autéinter accessiones & hæc prætoria hic fuerit ordo Edicti, dicetur infra ad Edictaperpetuà. De exceptionibus igitur erit primus hic titul 35. quia est generalis: Nam titul 36. de litigiosis est speciales, sive continet speciem exceptionis, quæ dicitur exceptio litigiosi. Hnic adjungitur titul. 37. de cõrahend. & committ. stipulat. Ratio ordinis pendet ex edicto: in quo primum pignora, deinde stipulationes prætoriæ planè erant in ultimum locum rejectæ. Sic & hic primò de pignoribus latè, deinde habetur de except. & nunc tandem de stipulationibus prætorijs. Sed hac occasione non tantum de prætorijs, sed etiam de civilibus stipulationibus agitur, ut & in ff. Quare etiam titul. 37. de contrahend. & commit. stipul. qui est generalis, primo ponitur. Hunc sequitur titulus 38. de inutil. stipul. Ratio est nota ex Instit. Prius enim utilia posteriusinutilia, aut irrita aut prohibita collocantur. Huic proximus est titul. 39. de duobus reis stip. & huic tit 40. de fidejussoris. Ratio ordinis expositæ est ad Instit. quia sicet fidejussor (qui etiam accessio est, ut pignus) fieri solet stipulatione: sic & novatio, quæ est modus tollendæ obligationis, fit stipulatione, & proinde huic quoque subjungitur titul. 41. de novat. Eiautem adjungitur titul. 42. de solut. quia ut novatio, ita & solutio est modus tollendæ obligationis. Hunc sequitur tit. 43. de acceptilatione. Cur autem inter hos tres modos tollendæ obligationis novatio hic primo ponatur, & in Instit. ultimo. Ratio hæc est, quia hic agitur de stipulatione. Et hac de causa dixi positum esse titulum de novation. quia & ipsa fiat per stipulationem. Reliqui duo modi, solutio & acceptilatio, tantum hic sunt positi propter novationem, hoc est, ut quia unius modus tollendæ obligationis hic ponitur, ponantur & alij. Et hæc de stipulationibus in genere, quæ tamen tantum propter stipulationes prætorias
units.tr: That the title on the sale of pledges comes last is because it is prohibitory and involves both seizure and fraud (see the law Commissoriae). Constantine abolished that law, or agreement, of forfeiture (pactum commissorium) entirely, though today it has been abolished only for pledges and not for sales. This is what I had to say on the second chapter of this eighth book, that is, on pledges. In the third chapter, I said, certain accessions of actions and obligations arising from the praetorian law are contained. For the pledge action (actio pignoratitia or hypothecaria) is also of praetorian origin (§ autem Serviana, de actionibus). Of this kind are the exceptions, the sureties, and the praetorian stipulations. You may object that pledges too are accessions, which is true, and for this reason in the perpetual Edict the treatment of pledges was joined with the praetorian exceptions and stipulations, as will be said below in the Digest. But we have separated this treatment of pledges from the other accessions, following Tribonian in the Digest, also for convenience, because the treatment of pledges is otherwise lengthy in itself and so deserves its own place. Eleven titles belong to this third chapter, of which the first is title 35, de exceptionibus et praescriptionibus. The reason why exceptions are placed immediately after pledges is that this was the order of the Edict, which Tribonian follows, and indeed more in the Code than in the Digest. Why this order of the Edict places praetorian accessions here will be said below, in the commentary on the perpetual Edict. So the first title here is title 35, on exceptions, because it is general. For title 36, on litigious matters, is specific: it contains a particular kind of exception, called the exception of litigiousness. To this is joined title 37, de contrahenda et committenda stipulatione. The reason for this order depends on the Edict, in which pledges came first and the praetorian stipulations were plainly put in the last place. So here too, first the treatment of pledges at length, then exceptions, and now at last the praetorian stipulations. But on this occasion not only praetorian but also civil stipulations are discussed, as in the Digest; so title 37, de contrahenda et committenda stipulatione, which is general, is placed first. It is followed by title 38, de inutilibus stipulationibus. The reason is known from the Institutes: useful matters come before useless ones, and void or prohibited ones are placed last. Next to this is title 39, de duobus reis stipulandi, and next to that title 40, de fidejussoribus. The order explained is that in the Institutes, because a surety (who is also an accession, like a pledge) is usually created by stipulation, novation, which is a mode of extinguishing an obligation, is also made by stipulation; so title 41, de novationibus, is also added here. To this is joined title 42, de solutionibus, because, as novation, so also payment is a mode of extinguishing an obligation. It is followed by title 43, de acceptilatione. Why, among these three modes of extinguishing an obligation, novation is placed first here and last in the Institutes: the reason is that here the subject is stipulation, and for this reason I said that the title on novation is placed here, because novation too is effected by stipulation. The other two modes, payment and acceptilation, are placed here only on account of novation, that is, since one mode of extinguishing an obligation is placed here, the others are placed too. And this is what I have to say on stipulations in general, which nevertheless are placed here only on account of the praetorian stipulations.

units.la: torias toriàs huc sunt positæ. Nam ut supra dictum, tantum prætoria hic ponuntur, ut pignora, ut exceptiones, ut stipulationes prætoriæ. Sed hic in C. tantum una ponitur exceptio prætoria; in ff. multæ hæc una dicitur exceptio evictionis, de qua est tit 44 de evict. Cujus pars est tit. 45. creditorem evictionem, &c. qui tit. est speciali de evictione pignoris. Et hæc de tertio c.lib. 8. Restat ultimum caput, quod est variuum, in quo tamen hæc potissimum continentur: de patria potestate, de adoptione, de donationibus. Ratio ordinis perobscura & ad explicandum difficilis. Diximus jam sæpè Tribun. diligentius in C. quam in ff. tenuisse ordinem Edicti perpetui, aut certè Interpretû edicti. Nunc certum est aut in edicto ipso, aut certè in libris Jurisconsultorum hunc fuisse ordinem, ut post tractatum de prætoriis stipulationibus, de quo modo est dictum alia quædam fuerint posita, ut de adoptionibus, de legitimis heredibus, & donationib.; quod in ff infra latius explicabitur. Quare & hic in C. post tractatum de stipulationibus statim ponuntur hi varii tractatus. Et primum quidem de patria potest. tit. 46. hac, ni fallor, ratione, quia jus personæ, quoad dignitatem prius est jure rerum. Cui adjungitur tit. 47. de adopt. & ei tit. 48. de emancip. qui ordo est, & in lib. Inst. ubi ratio jam est exposita. Hunc sequitur tit. 49. de ingratis liber. Est & hic titulus velut pars tituli prioris de emancip. lib. quæ emancipationes interdum rescinduntur, puta, si liberi sint ingrati. Hunc sequitur tit. 50. de postlim. Ratio ordinis ex Cod. Theod. & libris prudentû, quos hic imitatur Tribun. peti poterit. Nam, ut dixi, in illis libris prudentum postremum locum tenet tractatus de legitimis heredibus, & in eo tractatu ultimum locum tit. de bon. & hered. mil. ut sup. dictum lib. 6. titulo ultimo id perspicuum est ex Cod. Theod. lib. 5. Et hac occasione, hereditatis scil & bonorum militarium adjungebatur tit. de postlim. reverf. Nam postliminium ad milites maxime pertinet: ac de bonis ac hereditate militum ab hostè captorum tractatio, rectè priori de bonis militum conjungitur. Dices, cur ergo hic tit. de post. reverf. non ponitur sup. li. 6. ubi est tit ult. de hered. mil. quemadmodum in Cod. Theod. est positus, sed ponitur hic in fine lib. 8. Ratio est, quia Tribun. successionem sive hereditatem legitimam in Cod. posuit alio in loco, quam erat in libris prudentum, & in C. Theod. puta. posuit eum sup lib. 6. ut scilicet duæ species hereditatis ex testamento & ab intestato eodem in loco & libro conjungeretur: hunc autè tit. de postlim. reliquit in loco antiquo: quia proprie non est hereditas liberorum, de quibus potissimum hic agitur. Patern filii militis capti ab hoste, & redeuntis, aut non redeuntis post mortem filii occupat non ut hereditātem, sed ut peculium, l. bona, de captiv. & post l. & dictum est ad §.1. Inst. it. per quas perf. nob. acquir. Rectè autem hic titulus de postliminio conjungitur superioribus, qui sunt de patre & de liberis, quia & hic titul. maxime agit de liberis ab hoste captis, & postliminio revertentibus: quamvis tamen & de aliis quoque agat. Hunc titulum sequitur tit. 51. de infant. expos. & istum tit. 52.
units.tr: For, as said above, only the praetorian matters are placed here: pledges, exceptions, praetorian stipulations. But here in the Code only one praetorian exception is placed; in the Digest there are many, and this one is called the exception of eviction, on which is title 44 de evict.. Part of it is title 45 creditorem evictionem, &c., which title is specific to the eviction of a pledge. And this is what I have to say on the third chapter of book 8. There remains the last chapter, which is miscellaneous, though it chiefly contains these matters: on paternal power, on adoption, on donations. The order here is very obscure and hard to explain. I have said many times already that Tribonian followed the order of the perpetual Edict, or at least of the interpreters of the Edict, more carefully in the Code than in the Digest. Now it is certain that this order was either in the Edict itself or at least in the books of the jurists: after the treatise on praetorian stipulations just mentioned, certain other matters were placed, such as adoptions, legitimate heirs, and donations, which will be explained more fully below in the Digest. So here too in the Code, after the treatise on stipulations, these miscellaneous treatises are placed at once. And first de patria potest. tit. 46., for this reason, unless I am mistaken: the right of a person is prior in dignity to the right of things. To this is joined tit. 47. de adopt., and to that tit. 48. de emancip., which is the order also in the Institutes, where the reason has already been explained. It is followed by tit. 49. de ingratis liber. This title is also, as it were, part of the preceding title de emancip. lib., since emancipations are sometimes rescinded, for instance if the children are ungrateful. It is followed by tit. 50. de postlim. The reason for this order may be sought from the Theodosian Code and the books of the jurists, whom Tribonian imitates here. For, as I said, in those books of the jurists the treatise on legitimate heirs holds the last place, and in that treatise the last title is tit. de bon. & hered. mil., as said above in book 6; this is clear from the Theodosian Code, book 5, title last. On this occasion the title de postlim. reverf. was joined to the inheritance and goods of soldiers. For postliminy pertains chiefly to soldiers, and the treatment of the goods and inheritance of soldiers captured by the enemy is rightly joined to the earlier one on soldiers' goods. You may ask why then the title de post. reverf. is not placed above in book 6, where the last title is de hered. mil., as it is placed in the Theodosian Code, but is placed here at the end of book 8. The reason is that Tribonian placed legitimate succession or inheritance in the Code in a different position from that in the books of the jurists, and in the Theodosian Code too: he placed it above in book 6, so that the two kinds of inheritance, by testament and on intestacy, would be joined in the same place and book. But he left the title de postlim. in its old place, because it is not properly an inheritance of children, which is chiefly what is treated here. The father of a son captured by the enemy, whether the son returns or does not return after his death, takes possession not as an heir but as a peculium (law Bona, de captivis, and post l.), and this was said on §1 of the Institutes, per quas personas nobis acquiritur. Rightly, however, this title on postliminy is joined to the preceding ones, which concern the father and the children, because this title too chiefly deals with children captured by the enemy and returning by postliminy, although it also treats of others. This title is followed by tit. 51. de infant. expos., and that by tit. 52.

units.la: Tit. XLIV-XLVIII, L, LI, LII: marginal references to titles of the Code. quae sit longa consuetudo. Et hic quoque Tribun. Cod. Theod. imitatur ut videre est l. 1. tit. 7. §. 8. & nlt. Ratio ordinis autem ad d. tit. 7. de insp. ant. expos. est similitudo inter hunc & priorem de postliminio. Nam ut illic militi capto ab hoste, & postea reverso vel redempto, non nocet ad libertatem sive ingenuitatem captum semel fuisse, & pro servo habitum: ita & hic non nocet infanti expositio, si sit liber, non nocet inquam, ad libertatem ejus habitu, & educatum ipsum fuisse pro servo. Ratio autem ordinis ad titulum 52. quae sit longa consuetudo est obscurior. Cujac. in Parat. hanc adfert, quia longa, inquit, consuetudinis mentio paulo ante facta fuit puta l. 2. tit. 48. & proinde adjungitur jam titulus 51. quae sit longa, &c. quae ratio ordinis fortasse non est contemnenda. Videtur tamen vera ratio altius repetenda, ex libris prudentum. Autem in ultimis suis libris ff. qui erant accommodati adjectus, ut Julianus, ut Celsus, ut Marcellus viderunt in iis libris tractasse etiam de longa consuetudine, ut videre est in l. qu. b. ff. de legib. Cur autem de consuetudine agerent ultimo fere loco, ratio vix reperiri potest propter amissos libros, nisi forte dicamus, prius illos egisse de jure scripto, posterius de jure non scripto, hoc est, de consuetudine. Huic proximus est titulus 53. de donat. quia est generalis, cui adjungitur tit. 54. de dona tomb. quae sub modo, &c. Ratio enim postulat ut prius de donationibus pure, postea de conditionali bus agatur, ut & sup. factum de Instit. haered. & legat. lib. 6. Huic proximus est tit. 55. de revoc. donat. Ratio est per specialia. Donatio enim prius fit, posterius revocatur jam ante facta. Cujus autem donationum duae praecipue sunt species, inter vivos & mortis causa: Prius agitur de inter vivos, quia est perfectior & ad eam pertinent tituli jam expositi, quos recte jam sequitur titul. 56. de don. mort. causa, quae est altera species, sed posterior. Dices, curin Instit. est prior. Ratio haec est, cur inter vivos ibi est posterior, quia de ea ibi multa & nova pleraque explicantur. Nova autem posteriora esse solent: Proximus huic est tit. 57. de inoff. test. & tit. ultimus 58. de jure liberor. uterq; sumptus est ex Cod. Theod. lib. 8. post tit. de donat. ut & hic ratio ordinis obscurior, tamen cognoscitur potest ex ordine veteri in libris Jurisconsultorum, in quibus libris post tractatum de donationibus & de legitimis heredibus videtur quoque fuisse tractatus de jure fisci ut videre licet apud Paul. lib. 5. sent. tit. 11. & 12. Jam vero ad jus fisci pertinebat olim Lex Papia, quae poenam irrogabat coelibi & orbo. Sed haec Lex, quia hic tollitur, merito in posteriorem locum rejecta est. Potest & alia ratione hic titulus de inoff. poen. coel. b. accommodari prioribus, qui agunt de donationibus, qui tractatus de donationibus maxime propter donationes causa mortis olim a Jurisconsultis positus in ultimis libris ff. quia haec donatio causa mortis, est similis legato: de quo, ut & legitimis heredibus in illis ultimis ff. libris agebatur. Jam igitur Lex Papia, quae, ut dixi poenam irrogabat coelibi & orbo prohibes scilicet eos capere legata, ut alia testamento relicta, etiam loco habebat in donationibus causa mortis, ne recte hic admonuit in Parat. Cujacius ex l.35. Senatus, de mort. caus. donat. Tandem huic titulo adjungitur titulus ultimus de jure liberor. Ratio ordinis est, quia legis Papiae poena cessabat in quibusdam casibus, inter quos est jus liberorum, esse Ulpiano in lib. reg. tit. 16. Et haec de libro octavo.
units.tr: Titles XLIV–XLVIII, L, LI, LII: marginal references to titles of the Code. What is a long custom. Here too the Theodosian Code imitates the earlier work, as can be seen in l. 1. tit. 7. §. 8. & nlt. The reason for the order, with respect to tit. 7. de insp. ant. expos., lies in the similarity between this title and the earlier one on postliminy. For just as there, it does no harm to a soldier captured by the enemy and later returned or ransomed that he was once captured and treated as a slave, so that his freedom or freeborn status is not affected; so here too, the exposure of an infant does not harm his freedom if he is free, and it does not harm his freedom that he was treated and brought up as a slave. The reason for the order with respect to titulum 52. quae sit longa consuetudo is more obscure. Cujacius, in Parat., offers this: because mention of long custom was made shortly before, namely in l. 2. tit. 48., the title titulus 51. quae sit longa, etc., is therefore added next. This reason for the order is perhaps not to be scorned. Yet the true reason seems to be traced from further back, from the books of the jurists. In the last books of the Digest, which were arranged in an appended form, as Julian, Celsus and Marcellus saw, they treated of long custom as well, as can be seen in l. qu. b. ff. de legib. Why they treated of custom almost in the last place can hardly be discovered, because the books are lost, unless perhaps we say that the earlier ones dealt with written law and the later with unwritten law, that is, with custom. Next to this is titulus 53. de donat., because it is general, and to it is joined tit. 54. de dona tomb. quae sub modo, &c. For reason requires that gifts made outright be treated first and conditional gifts afterwards, as was also done above, de Instit. haered. & legat. lib. 6. Next to this is tit. 55. de revoc. donat. The reason is that the specific comes after the general. For a gift is made first and is revoked afterwards, having already been made. Of gifts there are two chief kinds, inter vivos and mortis causa. The inter vivos kind is treated first, because it is the more perfect, and the titles already explained pertain to it, which titul. 56. de don. mort. causa rightly follows; this is the other kind, but the later one. You may object that in the Institutes it comes first. The reason is this: the gift inter vivos is placed later there because many new matters are explained about it there, and new matters tend to come later. Next to this is tit. 57. de inoff. test., and the last title, 58. de jure liberor., both taken from the Theodosian Code, lib. 8., after the tit. de donat. Here too the order is more obscure, yet it can be recognised from the old order in the books of the jurists, in which, after the treatise on gifts and on legitimate heirs, there seems also to have been a treatise on the right of the fisc, as can be seen in Paulus, lib. 5. sent. tit. 11. & 12. Now the Papian Law, which, as I said, imposed a penalty on the unmarried and childless, formerly belonged to the right of the fisc. But since this law is here abolished, it was rightly placed in a later position. This title, de inoff. poen. coel. b., can also be fitted to the earlier ones, which deal with gifts, by another reasoning: the treatise on gifts was set down by the jurists, chiefly on account of gifts mortis causa, in the last books of the Digest, because a gift mortis causa is similar to a legacy, and that was discussed in those last books of the Digest, as were legitimate heirs. Thus the Papian Law, which, as I said, imposed a penalty on the unmarried and childless, that is, forbade them to take legacies, as well as other things left by will, was also regarded as applying to gifts mortis causa, as Cujacius rightly noted in the Parat., from l. 35. Senatus, de mort. caus. donat. Finally, the last title, de jure liberor., is added to this one. The reason for the order is that the penalty of the Papian Law ceased in certain cases, among which, according to Ulpian in the lib. reg. tit. 16., is the right of children. And so much for the eighth book.

units.la: Liber IX. Codicis.
units.tr: Book IX of the Code.

units.la: TAm vero liber nonus, qui est de criminibus & delictis titulos habet xl quos licet complecti quatuor capitibus. I. Est de criminibus sive publicis judiciis initio instituendis. II. Ipsae judiciorum publicorum species continentur. III. Judiciorum privatorum, sed ex delictis, tamordinariis, quam extraordinariis. IV. Ea continentur, quae pertinent ad haec judicia jam coepta & instituta persequenda & exercenda. Ratio ordinis inter haec capita, tam est perspicua, ut non sit opus verbis. Et plane est idem hic ordo in publicis judiciis, qui explicatur uno hoc libro ordo in qua tractationis qui fere est in judiciis privatis, de quibus dictum est. lib. 2. ff. seqq. Quod ad primum caput attinet de instituendis sive incipiendis his judiciis criminalibus, id continetur sex titulis: quorum primum locum obtinet tit. 1. de hu. qui accusare non poss. Ratio ordinis est quia cum accusatio & inscriptio sint necessaria ad haec judicia primum instituenda: accusatio autem fieri non potest nisi a legitimo accusatore primo loco agitur de eo qui accusator legitimus esse potest, qui non id est, prius de persona accusantis: deinde de ipsa accusatione, sive ejus ordine & forma, tit. 2. de accus. & inscript. ut & supra l. 6 prius de persona testatoris, tit. 22. deinde de forma testamenti, tit. 23. Hinc ponitur tit. 3. de exhib. & transmit. rei: hac ratione tum quia accusationem sequitur exhibitio rei & remissio, tum quia prius de accusatore, tit. 1. 2. Posterius de reo, tit. 4 agendum. Hunc tertium sequitur tit. 4. de custod. reorum. Nam reus jam exhibitus, statim detineri solet in custodia sive carcere: Cujus occasione oritur & tit. de pr. v. carc. inh. qui titulus est posterior quia titul quartus est de carcere publico, & de carcere licito, sed tit. 5. est de carcere privato & prohibito, ideoque merito est posterior. Dictum est separatim de accusatore & de reo: nunc communiter de utroque; est tit. 6. sireus vel accus. & c. Ratio ordinis est nota, tum quia hic titulus est communis, tum quia de morte agit, & proinde ultimus in hoc primo capite. Secundum caput de ipsis criminibus publicis continetur 25 titulis, quorum primus est tit. 7. si quae Imp. maledix. Ratio ordinis inter ea crimina per totum hoc secundum caput petenda est ex criminis magnitudine ut & supra dictum ad Institut. tit. ult. Quare crimen perduellionis & majestatis, cum sit maximum & gravissimum, de eo primum agitur puta tit. 7. & 8. ad Leg. Jul. majest. Inter hosantem titulos ordinis ratio est, quia titulus 7. agit tantum de ipso Imperio, tit. 8. de iis potissimum, quae fiunt contra Imperium: tum quia tit. 7. est de dictis sive convictis. titulo 8. de factis. Imperator potior est Imperio, & plerunq; dicta factis sunt potiora, & priora. Et hic quoq; est ordo in Cod. Theod. lib.9.tit.4. &5. Crimen majestatis sequitur crimen adulterii, de quo est tit.9. ad leg.Jul. de adult. Ratio exponetur ad ff. Ejus pars est tit.10.si quis eam, cujus tutor etc. Sed quia crimen hoc tutoris in pupillam quoddam habet singularia, merito proprium habet titulum, quem sequitur tit.11.de mulieribus, quae se propr.serv.junx. Nam & hic titulus ad idem crimen adulterii aut stupri pertinet: sed quia est cum servo, posteriorem locum tenet. Tertium crimen est vis, de quo est tit.12. ad leg.Jul. de vi publ. Ratio infra ad ff. Ejus quoque velut pars est tit.13. de rapt. virg. Sed ille est generalis, hic est specialis, & proinde posterior. Raptus est species vis, vim sequitur homicidium. Ratio infra ad ff. Ad quod crime homicidii pertinent tres tituli puta tit.14. de emend.serv. & tit.15. de emend. preping. & tit 16. ad leg.Cornel. de sicar. Duo priores sumpti sunt ex lib.9. tit.8. & tit.9.C.Theod. Cur autem sint priores, ratio esse videtur, tum quia emendatio tam servorum, quam liberorum non semper est prohibita, tum quia haec jura de emendatione ab Imper. sunt constituta. Quae causa quoq; est, cur titulus, de emendatione propinquorum sit posterior titulo, de emendat. serv. ratio seu causa est in tempore. Nam auctor legis subtitulo, de emend.serv. antiquior est, sive prior, puta Constantinus: auctores legum subtitulo, de emendat.propinq. sunt recentiores, puta Valentinus & Valens. Et haec de homicidio, quod est quartum crimen, cui adjungitur parricidium, quod est velut species homicidii, de quo est titul.17.de his, qui parentes vel liberos. Quem sequitur tit.18.de malef. & Mathem. quod est aliud crimen, puta Magiae, quoniam etiam hic homicidii quaedam species; puta per venenum continetur: Et hinc ratio est fumenda. Cui adjungitur tit.19.de sepulch.viol quod est crimen sepulchri violati. Ratio ordinis est, tum quia maleficio & Magiae saepe conjunctum est. Solent enim saepenumero Magi & incantatores infestare mortuos & sepulchra; ut videre est apud Lucanum de Appio, & apud Horat. in Epod. de Canidia. Et idem ait Apuleius lib.2. Metam. tum quia hoc crimen sepulchri violati magnitudine & gravitate proximum est priori magiae: quamvis in ff. hoc crimen sepulchri violati inter extraordinaria delicta collocetur, ut infra dicetur. Hunc de sepulchro viol. sequitur titulus vigesimus ad l. Fabiam de plagiariis, tum quia crimen plagii magnitudine non est impar priori tum quia utrumque; & sepulchri violati, & plagium, est velut quaedam species furti. Huic proximus est tit.21. ad l. Vifellium. Nam ut prior titulus est de statu personae: ita & iste. Plagium enim est crimen, quo liber homo venditur, abducitur. Crimen hoc l. Visellia, quod est ἀνδραποδισμός est crimen, quo non ingenuus, hoc est, libertinus se gerit pro ingenno, & ita statum suum mentitur. Atque ita hoc crimen l. Visellia, est species quaedam falsi, itaque ab hoc titulo 21.ad l.Vifell. commodè fit transitio ad tit. 22. ad l. Cornel.
units.tr: The ninth book, which deals with crimes and offences, has 40 titles, which may be grouped under four heads. I. The first concerns the initiation of criminal trials (publica judicia). II. The kinds of public trials themselves are set out. III. Private trials arising from offences are treated, both ordinary and extraordinary. IV. The matters that pertain to pursuing and conducting these trials once begun are covered. The reason for the order among these heads is so clear that it needs no words. The order within the public trials is plainly the same as the order of treatment in this one book, which is nearly the same as the order in private trials, discussed in book 2 of the Digest and following. As to the first head, on initiating or beginning these criminal trials, it is covered by six titles. The first of these is tit. 1, de his qui accusare non possunt (on those who cannot bring an accusation). The reason for this order is that accusation and inscription are necessary to begin these trials, but an accusation cannot be made except by a lawful accuser. So the first question is who may be a lawful accuser, that is, the person of the accuser, and then the accusation itself, its order and form, in tit. 2, de accusationibus et inscriptionibus, just as above in law 6 the person of the testator came first (tit. 22), and then the form of the will (tit. 23). Hence tit. 3, de exhibendis et transmittendis reis (on producing and transferring the accused) is placed here. The reason is twofold: first, because the production and release of the accused follow the accusation, and second, because the accuser is treated first (tit. 1, 2) and the accused afterwards, in tit. 4. The third title is followed by tit. 4, de custodia reorum (on the custody of the accused). For an accused person once produced is usually held at once in custody or prison. On this arises also tit. de privatis carceribus inhibendis, which is later, because title 4 concerns the public prison and the lawful prison, while tit. 5 concerns the private and forbidden prison, and so it rightly comes later. The accuser and the accused have been treated separately; now both together: tit. 6, si reus vel accusator decesserit (if the accused or the accuser dies). The reason for this order is plain: this title is general, and it deals with death, and therefore comes last under this first head. The second head, on the public crimes themselves, is covered by 25 titles, the first of which is tit. 7, si quis imperatori maledixerit (if anyone has cursed the emperor). The order among these crimes throughout this second head is to be sought from the gravity of the crime, as was said above on the last title of the Institutes. So the crime of treason and of majesty, being the greatest and most serious, is dealt with first, in tit. 7 and 8, ad legem Juliam maiestatis. The reason for the order between these two titles is that title 7 deals only with the emperor himself, and title 8 with those acts chiefly which are done against the empire; and also that title 7 concerns words or utterances, title 8 deeds. The emperor is greater than the empire, and words are generally weaker and earlier than deeds. The same order is found in the Theodosian Code, book 9, titles 4 and 5. The crime of majesty is followed by the crime of adultery, on which is tit. 9, ad legem Juliam de adulteriis. Its explanation will be set out at the Digest. Part of it is tit. 10, si quis eam, cuius tutor etc. But because this crime of a guardian against his ward has certain peculiar features, it rightly has its own title, which is followed by tit. 11, de mulieribus quae se propter servitutem iunxerunt (on women who joined themselves to slaves). For this title too pertains to the same crime of adultery or stupration, but because it concerns a slave, it holds a later place. The third crime is violence, on which is tit. 12, ad legem Juliam de vi publica. Its explanation is below in the Digest. Part of it, as it were, is tit. 13, de raptu virginum. But the former is general, the latter special, and so comes later. Rape is a species of violence, and homicide follows violence. The explanation is below in the Digest. Three titles pertain to this crime of homicide, namely tit. 14, de emendatione servorum, tit. 15, de emendatione propinquorum, and tit. 16, ad legem Corneliam de sicariis. The two former are taken from the Theodosian Code, book 9, titles 8 and 9. As to why they come first, the reason seems to be that the chastisement of slaves as well as of free persons is not always forbidden, and because these laws on chastisement were enacted by the emperors. This is also the reason why the title de emendatione propinquorum comes after the title de emendatione servorum: the reason lies in time. For the author of the law under the title de emendatione servorum is older, or earlier, namely Constantine; the authors of the laws under the title de emendatione propinquorum are more recent, namely Valentinian and Valens. So much on homicide, which is the fourth crime, to which parricide is joined, as a kind of species of homicide, on which is tit. 17, de his qui parentes vel liberos occiderint (on those who kill parents or children). It is followed by tit. 18, de maleficis et mathematicis (on sorcerers and astrologers), which is another crime, namely magic, since this too is a kind of homicide, as it includes poisoning; and the reason is to be taken from this. To it is joined tit. 19, de sepulchro violato (on the violation of tombs), which is the crime of violating a tomb. The order is explained both because it is often joined with sorcery and magic, for magicians and enchanters are wont very often to molest the dead and the tombs, as may be seen in Lucan on Appius, and in Horace in the Epodes on Canidia, and Apuleius says the same in book 2 of the Metamorphoses; and because the crime of violating a tomb is next in magnitude and gravity to the earlier one of magic, although in the Digest this crime of violating a tomb is placed among the extraordinary offences, as will be said below. The de sepulchro violato is followed by titulus vigesimus ad legem Fabiam de plagiariis (title twenty, on the Fabian law concerning kidnappers), both because the crime of kidnapping is not inferior in magnitude to the former, and because both the violation of a tomb and kidnapping are, as it were, a certain species of theft. Next to this is tit. 21, ad legem Viselliam. For as the earlier title concerns the status of a person, so does this one. For kidnapping is the crime by which a free man is sold or carried off. The crime of the Visellian law is andrapodismos [ἀνδραποδισμός], that is, the crime by which a person who is not freeborn, that is, a freedman, poses as freeborn and so falsely claims his status. And so this crime under the Visellian law is a certain species of forgery, and thus from this tit. 21, ad legem Visellam there is a convenient transition to tit. 22, ad legem Corneliam.

Ratio a. cur hic tit. de publ fit posterior, & ille de privata fit prior. hæc est, tum quia tit. 42. etsi proprie agit de priv. abolit. tamen generali verbo de abolit. conceptus est. tum quia privata abolitio est frequentior: publica est rarior & extraordinaria;
units.tr: The Cornelian law on forgery (lex Cornelia de falsis) concerns a tenth crime, namely forgery, to which is attached title 23, de his qui sibi adscribunt, and so on. To understand the order, one must remember that the Cornelian law on forgeries had two parts, the testamentary and the monetary. The title that belongs to the first part on wills is title 23, which deals with one who has a bequest written in his own favour in a will, even though the testator wishes it; by that writing he commits what is in effect forgery. But if he wrote it while the testator was still alive, he would commit true forgery, and he is punished under the Cornelian law as for forgery, and punished under the Senatus-consultum Tribunicium. Concerning this senatus-consultum there is title 2 of this book; on the true forgery, see 24, de falsa moneta. For the best reason, since the first part of the Cornelian law on testaments has been explained, the next part to be treated is the second, on money or coin. I ask: why is the testamentary part treated before the monetary? Because the testamentary part concerns a whole universitas, while the monetary part concerns a single thing, namely a coin. To this crime of forgery belong not only the three titles already explained, 22, 23 and 24, but also title 25, de mutatione nominis. Hence the reason for the order is easily understood. For the Cornelian law, as it dealt with the two kinds of forgery, testaments and coin, but there are also many other kinds of forgery, which were later included and added by senatus-consulta, among which is the alteration of a name, treated in this title. There follow title 26, ad legem Iuliam de ambitu, and title 27, ad legem Iuliam repetundarum. For these two crimes are lighter than the earlier ones and are punished more mildly. Why bribery (ambitus) comes before extortion (repetundae) has this reason: bribery is committed before a magistracy and its administration, extortion in the magistracy itself and in its administration. In the Digest, however, the order is somewhat different, and not without reason, which will be explained at the Digest. To this is attached title 28, de crimine peculatus. The reason for this order is that, just as extortion, of which we have just spoken, is a kind of public theft, so too is peculation; but they differ in that extortion is committed only by magistrates, peculation by anyone; and extortion occurs only in the provinces, peculation also at Rome. To this is attached title 29, de crimine sacrilegii. For this crime too is a kind of theft, but of sacred things. And since under the word publicum the sacred is also generally included, not only the public, law 1, §6 of this title, de iustitia et iure. Hence it has come about that under the name of peculation the sacrilege is also contained, and under the same title in the Digest both are explained. Because sacrilege is a kind of peculation, law 4, ad legem Iuliam peculatus, therefore peculation is treated first, as of the genus, and sacrilege later, as of a species. Next to this is attached title 30, de seditiosis, which title is taken from the Theodosian Code, book 9, title 24, and which contains an extraordinary crime; therefore it is placed last among the crimes, namely the crime of sedition and tumult, which Cujacius says is not unlike sacrilege, of which we have spoken; but this crime too is punished by the Julian law on majesty and the Julian law on violence, and it is ordinary. There follows title 31, quando civilis actio criminali praeiudicet. The order is elegant: since the kinds of criminal actions have now been set out, before passing on to offences, that is, to private actions arising from offences, the author has interposed this title as a middle point, since it treats both of criminal and of private or civil action. And these matters concern the second part of book 9. The third part concerns the private crimes, that is, delicts, which are contained in title 8. The first is title 32, de crimine expilatae hereditatis. The reason is that among delicts theft holds the first place, of which the species is the plundering of an inheritance. The reason why theft is placed first among delicts has been explained at the Institutes. But here in the Code it is treated of theft elsewhere, namely in book 6, title 2, where the reason was set out. Now the plundering of an inheritance is placed here as a species of theft, so that some order may be kept among these private delicts or offences. Next is title 33, de bonis vi raptis. For robbery is close to theft, or is wicked theft. To this is attached title 34, de crimine stellionatus, which seems to be placed here in the place of that delict which is called damage by injury under the Aquilian law. For stellionate is damage of another kind, but the damage by injury itself has already been explained in book 3, title 35, ad legem Aquiliam. There is also another reason why this crime of stellionate is placed here: as plundering and robbery, of which we spoke before, harm a person's property, so does stellionate; but injury harms not property but also reputation, as was said above at the Institutes. Injury therefore holds the next place, title 35, de iniuriis, as also in the Institutes, where the reason was set out. A part of this title is title 36, de famosis libellis. But since the former is general, and this title contains only a specific kind of injury, it is rightly placed later here. To this title are attached title 37, de abigeis, and to this title 38, de nili aggeribus non rumpendis. These two are extraordinary crimes, namely cattle-rustling and the breaking of the embankments of the Nile, and therefore they come later. Why cattle-rustling, however, is placed first among the crimes here, the perhaps reason is that cattle-rustling is a general crime, that is, it occurs everywhere, but the breaking of embankments only in Egypt, though its use might nowadays be extended to other regions as well. Receiving and concealing stolen goods is also an extraordinary crime, wherefore it is treated in title 39, de his qui latrones occultant, etc. Why this last title of the book stands among the private crimes is because this title is common to all the preceding ones, both public and private crimes or delicts. And these matters concern the third part of this book, on the kinds of private crimes or delicts. For the second part concerned public crimes, and the first concerned the instituting of proceedings, as they are called. There remains now a fourth and last part, which concerns the prosecution, execution and conduct of criminal procedure, and this part is contained in the last twelve titles of book 9. First is title 40, de requirendis reis. For here is the order of public trials, or the procedure, namely that the accused is first accused, and afterwards the defendant, once accused, presents himself for trial; but since defendants often lie hidden, the title on the seeking out of defendants has been placed here, which fits well with the earlier one on the concealers of hidden defendants, or at least of criminals. Then follows title 41, de quaestionibus, for two reasons: first, because the seeking out of a defendant resembles a question in its name; and second, because this is the order of public trials, that proof be made against the defendant now present, in place of which, in criminal cases, questions (torture) are often interposed. Next comes title 42, de abolitionibus, to which belong also the four following titles. The reason for the order is that these criminal trials are not brought to an end either by abolition or by desertion. Therefore to abolition belongs title 42, which is a general title and therefore first. But abolition is either general and public, or special or private; the private kind is treated in title 42, and the general in title 43, de generali abolitione. The reason why the title on public abolition comes later, and the one on private abolition earlier, is this: because title 42, although it properly treats of private abolition, is nevertheless worded generally, as concerning abolition; and because private abolition is more frequent, while public abolition is rarer and extraordinary.

units.la: Proximus est tit. 44. ut intra cert. tēp. &c. Ratio ord est, qa ut modo dictum judiciū criminale interdū nō ,pducitur ad finēs nō terminatur: idq; 2. modis fit abolitione & desertione, ut modo d. De abolitione dictū est jam restat desertio, de qua est tit. 45. ad SC. Turp. sed anteeū ponitur d. tit. 44. ut intra cert. tēp. Ratio ordinis, q judiciū criminale deseritur aut negligētia quadā & morā, aut cōsilio & deliberato. & hic q cōsilio deserit, proprie desertor & tergiversator dicitur, isque punitur hoc SC. Turpill. qui negligētia, moratorpotū°, quā desertor est q nō punitur, & pinde de moratore pri° agitur, d. t. 44. de desertore tit. 45. ad Turpill. Putat tamē Cuj. moratoris nomē gravius esse quàm desertoris qa; inquit, gravi° punitur morator. l. 1. d. tit. 44. Sed moratoris crimē videtur levius qa negligētia & culpa leviore dolo, s. proæresi & cōsilio, putoq; gravius puniri desertoré, cuj° pœna est extraordinaria. l. 1. tit. 45. l. 5. s. pen. de pœn. l. 3. s. 1. Et hæc de moratore & desertore, s tergiversatore: q b° nō absimiles sūt calumniatores, sed illi vera crimina, hi falsa intētāt. l. 1. nad Turpill. quare tit. 44 & 45. sequitur recte tit. 46. de cal. Huic prox. deinde est tit. 47. de pœnis. Nā h e ordo judicii criminalis sc. si judiciū nō deseratur, sed legitimè terminetur sētētia cōtra reū lata, ut tandē ad executionē veniatur. h e ,ad pœnā sētētia cōprehēsā. Eodē pertinet tit. 48. ne sin. jufs. Nā cōfiscatio est species pœnæ, sed prior est tit de pœnis. q a est generalis. Huc quoq; pertinet tit. 49. de bo. pros. Nam & h. tit. est de confiscati. Caeterū ille sit prior. hic posterior. ratio ord est qa illē est de ipso judice, sive magist & ,p inde prior ,ppter d̃gnitatē, & ,ppter ordinē h. tit. 49. est de ipsis bonis cōfiscandis. Eodē pertinet t. t. 50 de bō. eor. qui mort. sibi cōsc. Nā & h e de cōfiscatione. Est aut̄ specialis h tit (Nā est de eo tātum s. de cōfiscatione ej°, q mortē sibi cōscivit nō de cōfiscatione generali sive cujuslibet, ut prior) & iccirco est posterior.
units.tr: The next is title 44, ut intra certum tempus, etc. The reason for the order is that, as has just been said, a criminal trial is sometimes not carried through to its end and is not concluded; and this happens in two ways, by abolition and by desertion, as just mentioned. Abolition has been dealt with; there remains desertion, of which title 45, ad Senatus-consultum Turpillianum treats. But before this is placed the said title 44, ut intra certum tempus. The reason for the order is that a criminal trial is deserted either through a certain negligence and delay, or through deliberate purpose. The one who deserts on purpose is properly called a deserter and a shuffler, and he is punished under this senatus-consultum Turpillianum; but the one who deserts through negligence and delay is not punished as a deserter. Therefore the delayer is treated first, in the said title 44, and the deserter in title 45, ad Turpillianum. Cujacius, however, thinks that the name of delayer is more serious than that of deserter, because, he says, the delayer is punished more severely, law 1 of the said title 44. But the crime of the delayer seems the lighter, since it arises from negligence and a lighter fault than from malice, that is, from deliberate choice and intention; and I think the deserter is punished more severely, whose penalty is extraordinary, law 1, title 45, law 5, last paragraph, de poenis, law 3, §1. And these matters concern the delayer and the deserter, or shuffler; to whom calumniators are not unlike, but the former bring true charges and the latter false ones, law 1, ad Turpillianum. Wherefore titles 44 and 45 are rightly followed by title 46, de calumniatoribus. Next to this is title 47, de poenis. For this is the order of a criminal trial, namely, if the trial is not deserted, but the sentence passed against the defendant is lawfully brought to an end, so that at last execution follows; that is, the sentence concerns the penalty. To this belongs title 48, ne liceat sine iudice. For confiscation is a kind of penalty, but the title on penalties, which is general, comes earlier. To this also belongs title 49, de bonis proscriptorum, for this title too is about confiscation. But the one comes earlier and this one later. The reason for the order is that the former concerns the judge himself, or the magistrate, and therefore comes first on account of its dignity; while title 49 concerns the goods themselves to be confiscated. To this also belongs title 50, de bonis eorum qui mortem sibi consciverunt, for this too concerns confiscation. But it is a special title, for it treats only of the confiscation of the goods of one who has taken his own life, and not of general confiscation, as the earlier title does; and for that reason it comes later.

units.la: Ultim° tit. huj° lib. 9. est tit. 51. de sēt. pass. Ratio ord. qa cum adhuc dictū sit de ord. judicii crim. ab initio h. e., accusat., usq; ad finē. h. e. usq; ad sētiā & executionem (q est ordo legitim° & ppetuus ut sentētiā sequatur executio, si modo sentētia sit recta & legitima.) Adjungitur h. 1. tit. qno interdum extra ordinē rescindituria criminalis puta p rest. in integrū à principe impetrādā. Ex quo ratio ord. satis intelligitur, tum quia rata & legitima sunt pronūnciatio tum quia hęc restitut. est beneficium princip. extraord.: & ,pinde ultimum, & hæc de libro 9.
units.tr: The last title of this ninth book is title 51, De sententiis passis. The reason for this order is that, since the order of criminal judgment has already been treated from its beginning, that is, from the accusation, to its end, that is, to sentence and execution (which is the lawful and continuous order, so that execution follows sentence, provided the sentence is right and lawful), there is added this title, in which a criminal sentence is sometimes annulled outside the ordinary course, for instance by restitution in integrum to be obtained from the prince. From this the reason for the order is sufficiently clear: partly because the pronouncements are ratified and lawful, and partly because this restitution is an extraordinary benefit of the prince; and therefore it comes last. And these are the matters of book 9.
