units.tr: I now turn to the remaining three books of the Code, which correspond to the last two books of the Digest, 49 and 50. The order is difficult, because these titles were not in the Perpetual Edict but only in the Code, and Tribonian often changes their order in these three books. The titles of these three books are contained there in eight, namely 6, 7, 8, 10, 11, 13, 14 and 15. As for the order of the books, that has already been explained, and here we treat of the titles. This tenth book contains 77 titles, which can conveniently be recalled under three chapters: I. On the right of the fisc. II. On the right of the cities. III. On accessories. I. The chapter on the right of the fisc contains 30 titles. The first of these is the title On the right of the fisc, because it is general. This general title is followed by other special titles, which can be divided into four parts. I. On the debts and contracts of the fisc. II. On goods falling to the fisc. III. On treasures. IV. On the annona and taxes. The first part, as we said, concerns the fisc's contracts and debts, and to it belong titles 2 and 7 et seq. The reason for this order is that things which already belong to the fisc, or are owed to it under a contract, had to be treated first, before those which may at some time be acquired by the fisc. Here belong title 1 and title 2, on agreements with the fisc, and title 3, on the good faith and the law of the fiscal auction, etc. Both are taken from book 9 of the Theodosian Code. The reason for this order is that title 2 concerns agreements about debts and title 3 the sale of goods, and an agreement precedes a sale, as was said under the title on the distraint of pledges, book 8. These are followed by title 4, on the sale of fiscal property, etc. For this title too belongs to sales, but the earlier one is title 3, because it concerns the sale of things belonging to the fisc alone, whereas title 4 concerns the sale of common things, that is, things partly belonging to the fisc and partly to private persons. Title 5 also belongs to sales, ne res quae venditur, etc., but the earlier titles concern the contracting of a sale, that is, the undoing of a sale already made, and so it comes later. Next follows title 6, on those who owe to the public accounts, etc. This title is taken from title 44 of book 10 of the Theodosian Code, On those who contracted with the agents. The reason for the order is that first the lawful contracts with the fisc are treated, and then the unlawful and prohibited ones, as in this title on the prohibited loan. Next to it is title 7, on the fisc's claims for penalties being preferred to other creditors. The reason is that so far we have spoken of the right of the fisc and its privilege, and of accessories [ἀκόλουθα] in an obligation or principal contract, that is, the principal sum. Now we turn to the accessory, in which the fisc has no privilege but other creditors are preferred to it. Accessions are here of two kinds, penalty and interest. Of the penalty we treat first, in title 7; of interest, later, in title 8, on the fisc's interest. The reason for this order is that a penalty is sometimes like a principal, as when a fiscal procurator imposes a fine on someone, and also because the question is whether interest equal to the amount of the principal and penalty can be exacted from the fisc, which is denied in law 1 of this title 8. This is followed by title 9, on sentences given against the fisc, etc., which deals with the retracting and rescinding of judgments given against the fisc. This last title is placed at the end of this first part, because such things are useless, subject to retraction and prohibited, and it is customarily placed last, as in the last title of book 7 of book 9. Second, I said that the second part of this first chapter concerns goods falling to the fisc. The reason why this comes first is that these goods, caduca and vacantia, having no owner, are at once by law the fisc's own. Although the third and fourth parts treat of the modes by which goods are acquired by the fisc, this first part is more frequent than the others, for example when goods without an owner fall to the fisc, which the Greeks call adespota [ἀδέσποτα]; of these the law has various kinds, such as caduca, vacantia, etc. To this first part therefore belongs, of this kind, title 10, On vacant goods. The reason is that this title is general, although it bears a special inscription, for under it is treated not only vacant goods but also others, such as those from confiscation, from tacit trust, etc., which pertain to these; and also because this title treats of the very acquisition of goods, by law itself, by which goods are acquired by the fisc, for example because they are vacant, because they are confiscated, because they are forfeited, because they are caduca, etc. Now this title 10 is double, namely on vacant goods and on incorporation. These two parts have distinct titles in the Theodosian Code, namely book 10, titles 8 and 9, whereas here two distinct titles, 11 and 12, are contained in one, namely title 10 of book 10 of the Theodosian Code. Goods that have returned to the fisc and begun to belong to it are usually announced to the fisc by informers. This is the reason why I follow title 10, on vacant goods, with title 11, on informers. Often such goods are sought by private persons from the emperor, at once as soon as they have been reported, and often even before. These are called petitions for goods, and are forbidden in title 12, on the petition for goods taken away. This is also the reason for this title, since reported goods are usually sought at once, as has been said, and sometimes before the report. Hence in the Code the petition is put first, as in title 10 of the Theodosian Code, On petition, and on an informer voluntarily given. Informers also belong to title 13, On those who denounce themselves. The reason for the order is clear, since the title on informers is general and concerns chiefly those who denounce others, whereas this title 13 concerns informers who denounce themselves, who are not properly informers; and so they come after the earlier ones. Next follows title 14, If a freedman or partner of the emperor, etc., for this too concerns vacant goods, but it contains a special case, and so it is distinct from and later than the earlier titles: in those the fisc succeeds, in this it does not succeed. And so much for the second part. To the third part belong the titles on treasure, De thesauris. The reason why this is the third part is that, as the second concerns vacant goods, that is, adespota, so treasures are money without owner. But vacant goods always belong to the fisc, and all of them do, except in the case of title 14; treasure, of which title 15 treats, does not always belong to the fisc, as also in the Institutes, under On treasure, De rerum divisione. IV. We said that the fourth part of this chapter concerns taxes. The reason why this is the title is that taxes do not belong to the fisc, so that the earlier goods (for taxes are usually imposed only by judicial decision), and also

Sed hoc in C. ex illis decerpt. z, quarum collationum t. est coemptio f. ... Et a. hæc species collationis, cum frumetum hordeum vinum, havena, panis, caro, lardum &c. ad us' militares jussu principis coemuntur, qu uno nomine species dicuntur, quas coguntur provinciales & subditi pendere principi, sed justo precio soluto. Et hunc pertinet tit. 26. de coë an publ. horr. & tit. 27. ut nemini liceat in coëpt. spec. Maximè ad hæc coemptionè pertinet tit. 27. Nam tit. 26. nō est proprie de coemptione speciem, sed de cōditis speciebus l. de iis, quæ jam sunt recōdite in horreis publicis. ¶ Ea a. cōdita, qa prius expedi & abfumi debent, quā nova coëmi, pterunt. de cōd. & c. prior est tit. de coempt. Ratio ord. qa ut modo dictum species quedā collationum hic ordine exponuntur. Prim' est coemptio. de qua jā d. tit. 26. & 27. altera est collatio donatorum, de qua est tit. 28. prior ht in specieb. ut fru mēto, oleo & c. Hæc altera fiebat fere in auro & arg. l. i. C. The. hujus t. t. Cui recte adjungi. 3. quæ est collatio æris & quæ est auro & arg. vili, & proinde posterius, d. tit. 29. Cui adjungitur tit. 30. de disjunct. q est ult. in h. art. detributus, & collationib, hac rōe qa priores oës sūt de tribut. solvēdis, & præstādis: h. e. de tributis jā solutis. Nā dilcuissor, cuj' munis est rōes tributorias l. collationum discutere & examinare, demum facta collatione intervenire solet. Et hæc de primo capite hujus libri 10. quod est de Jure fisci, ut supra dictum.
units.tr: Titles VII, VIII, IX, X, XI, XII, XIII, XIV and XV (marginal references to the titles), because taxes seem to be more extraordinary, although many of them have now become canonical and ordinary and customary. ¶ To this section belong titles 15 to 17 and 18. The first of them is 16, de annonis et tributis, because it is general, and to it is joined title 17, de susceptoribus et collatoribus; then title 18, de superindictione. These titles are mostly taken from the Theodosian Code, book 11. The reason for the order is that first comes the matter of the taxes themselves, who and to what extent they must be paid; then, since this is usually done by indictions, that is, from the beginning of September, and this is title 7, de susceptoribus. For indictions are nothing other than taxes to be paid at fixed times. Hence the use of indictions began to be carried over to the years. The beginning of the indictions was 1 September, which was instituted not by Tiberius, as Cedrenus thinks, nor by Augustus, as the astrologers and notaries commonly think, but by Constantine the Great. This can be confirmed, first, from the Greek calendars, which Onuphrius cites, in which the beginning and origin of the indictions are expressly referred to Constantine and Licinius; second, from the ancient synods and the books of the Code. There is no mention of indictions before Constantine, but mention of them is frequent immediately after him and long before. In the Theodosian Code, book 6, the fourth indiction is mentioned under the emperors Constans and Constantius, and in the synod of Jerusalem in Athanasius. So also the fifteenth indiction is mentioned under the emperors Valentinian and Valens in a law of the Theodosian Code, book 13, title de naviculariis. But these matters... are in the said title. Title 18, de superindictione, follows rightly after 17, since it is nothing other than an increase of the indiction or of the tax. After it follows title 19, de exactionibus tributorum. For the reason demands that first the taxes themselves be treated, both whether and when they are to be paid, and then the collecting of them and their collectors. To this is joined title 20, de superexactionibus. Following the example of indictions and superindictions, here the exactions are set first and then the superexactions. An exaction is lawful, a superexaction unlawful, and therefore later. After this comes title 21, de capiendis et distrahendis pignoribus, and so on. For if a contributor or taxpayer does not submit to the exaction, the collector is accustomed to seize the goods of the contributors as pledges and to sell them. Next follows title 22, de apochis publicis. The reason for the order is that the earlier titles concern the taxes to be paid and collected; this one concerns those already paid and collected. If a contributor shows the receipts for these already paid to a new collector, he will be safe from a new exaction, and these are called public receipts because they are receipts for public taxes. After this comes title 23, de canonibus largitionalibus. The reason for the order is that up to this point the taxes have been discussed in general; now certain species of taxes or contributions are set out, although this species is rather a special use than a proper kind of tax. For the earlier titles concern the general use of taxes, while this one concerns the private treasury of the prince, from which he provides gifts and donations (here he is called largitionales, that is, the taxes and gifts of the prince), and what is necessary for the household, as in law 2 of the de metallis title. After this comes title 24, ne operae a collatoribus exigantur. The reason for the order is that up to this point it has been said what is lawful, that is, what taxes may be demanded, such as the kinds: grain, barley, salt, meat, lard, oil, gold and silver, clothing, and so on. Now the things that are unlawful, which may not be demanded from subjects, such as labour services, are treated. The unlawful and forbidden things come later. Next comes title 25, de immunitate nemini concedenda. The reason for the order is that, as title 24 is prohibitory concerning services, so this one is prohibitory concerning immunity. The reason why the former comes first is that the services belong to the kinds of tax, of which kinds the discussion has already taken place. And this is almost all in general concerning taxes. Now, indeed, the species of contributions or taxes are set out, of which many things are found in the Theodosian Code, book 11, but in this Code they have been selected from those. Of these contributions the first is the purchase (coemptio), in which grain, barley, wine, oats, bread, meat, lard and so on are bought for military uses by order of the prince, and these are called by one name, species, which the provincials and subjects are compelled to pay to the prince, but at a fair price paid. To this belongs title 26, de coemptionibus publicorum horreorum, and title 27, ut nemini liceat in coemptione species. Title 27 pertains most of all to this purchase. For title 26 is not properly about the purchase of the species, but about stored species, that is, those that have already been stored in public granaries. But stored goods, since they must first be spent and used up before new ones can be bought, come before. The title de coemptione is prior. After these two follows title 28, de collatione donatorum, and this title 29, de collatione aeris, and finally title 30, de discussoribus. The titles have been taken from the Theodosian Code, book 11. The reason for the order is that, as has just been said, certain species of contributions are set out here in order. The first is the purchase, which was discussed in titles 26 and 27. The second is the collection of gifts (donativa), with which title 28 deals. The former has species such as grain, oil and so on; this second was made almost always in gold and silver, law 1 of the Theodosian Code, this same title. To this is rightly joined a third, which is the collection of bronze and of base gold and silver, and therefore comes later: title 29. To this is joined title 30, de discussoribus, which is the last in this article on taxes and contributions. The reason is that all the earlier titles concern taxes to be paid and furnished, that is, taxes already paid. For the examiner, whose office is to discuss and examine the tax accounts and contributions, usually comes in after the contribution has been completed. And this is what concerns the first chapter of this book 10, which is on the right of the fisc, as said above.

units.la: Alterum c. ut dixim', est de jure civitatum, quo illo est posterius optima rōe: qa civitates sunt privatorum loco: fiscus est principis: & proinde prior dignitate. Hoc a. caput de jure civitatum est bimēbre. Nā prius membr. est de Decur. on. posterius de munerib. Ratio ordinis ad hæc duo membra exponetur ad if. ubi idem est ordo. Ad prius igitur memb. pertinet tit. 7. ex iis l. est tit. 31. de Dec. nr. & fi. lis eorū, &c. qa est generalis omnia fere jura Decurionum coplectitur, maximē de psonis, q Decuriones esse possint q nō possint. Hunc sequitur tit. 32. si jure. aut libert. ad Decur. &c. Nā & hic tit. est de psonis. q non possunt esse Decuriones de quib. separatim & posterius agitur qa iunt viliores, & qa deliètum hic tit. cōtinet, puta quia hi adspirant eō, quo nō denunt, ideoq; puniuntur. Et hæc de plonis potissimum Decurionum. Nunc de reb. & bonis eorum ad q pertinet tit. 33. de præd. Decur. &c. Nā prius de psonis, q de reb. agi solet. Ad ea quoq; ptinet tit. 34. quan. & quib. deb. &c. sed tit. 33. est de actu inter vivos, ut de vend. bonor. tit. 34. est de testam. aut successione ab intestat. & pinde est posterior. Cuj' velut pars est tit. 35. de impon. lucr. defc. Nā ut tit. 34. ita & hic 35. ad inccellliones ptinet. ¶ Hoc. n. tit. imponitur heredi Decurionis onus qdā, aut et aliis, q bona Decurionis nati fuerint, ex causa lucrativa, ut legato donoe, &c. Et h onus hic dicit de scii ptio lucrativorū Hi quoq; tit. funtex C. Th. Sed ex li. 12. ex quo est ti. 36. dcph. sal. qui tit. qa est phibitorius, nā prohibētur salaria dare decurionesfine mand. principis, pterea posteriore locū tenet, ut &tit. 37. si curiat. rel. crv. & c. Nā & hic est phibitorius, sed prior est tit. ex parte phibitori, & ptinet ad bona: ideoq; prior est tit 37. q est omnino phibitor. ideoq; planè ult in h. membro, c. 2. q mēbrū esse diximus de Decurionū, sive curialib. Alterū hujus cap. membrū, q de munerib. & honorib. diximus, cōtinet 32. tit. quorū 1. est tit. 38. de munī. & c. & alter est tit. 39. de incolis, & ubi q domi, & c. q 2. tit. sunt tit. tūqa sunt de psonis ipsis ad munera gerēda vocādis sunt aptis: tū qaeas cōtinēt, ex quib. intelligatur, qs & obi debeat fungi munere & honore. Recte a municipes incolis pferunt: quamu nicipes sunt cives, incolæ nō ité His iā ,primus est tit 40. d. munn. & hon. & c. Nā & hic tit ad psonas ptinet P. & F. sed priores sunt de munerib. primū incipiendis, hic decōtinuādis: &c, pinde posterior. Huic additur iā tit. 41. de mun. pat. Ratio ordinis. qa psonarū tractāsem ordine seqr tractatio de re ipsa, li e. de munerib sed munera qa partim sunt psonalia, partim patrimonialia, omisso priore mēbro (fortasse quia & in ff. & c. sub ti, plixo de Dicur. satis actū) de munerib. patrimoniorū hic agitur: reliquit, tit. ut & priores ptinēt nō tm ad patrimonialia sed ét ad psonalia munera, ut est tit. 42. quemad. civ. mun. &c. Ratio ordinis ad hunc tit. est, tū qa priusagēdū de re aut munere ipso; ut tit. 41. posteriusde modo, ut hic, tū qa hic tit. 42. agit potissimū de munerib. his iteratis ac 2. aut iterata, sunt posteriora. Hunc tit. sequitur tit. 43. de his qui sunt ont. &c. Ratio ordinis hæc est: qu munera publica alij cogātur subire de quib. hactenus alii nō cogātur subire sed tū subeūt sua spōte de quib est hic tit. alij neq; cogūtur subire. neq; ēt subeunt, puta quia sunt immunes quo ptinēt ét ij qui, phibēt, ut infames, rei, exules, mulieres, de quib j. Et hic ordo minime cōsentaneus est ut prius de administratib posterius de nō administrationib. agatur. Administrantiūaut ut dictū duo sūt genera: partim q coacti & necessārio partim q sponte: administrātiū item 2. sūt genera: partim q immunitate & excusatione habēt, partim q prohibentur. Qui a. immunitate habēt, eā vel ā principe impetrāt, quæ videt vacatio munerū, vel excusationis aliq causā habēt. De vacatione priusagit, pterdignitate principis, à quo impetrāt. Et huc (ad vacatione in q munerū) ptinet tit. 44. de his a princip, &c. & tit 45. de vac. publ. mun. prior tit exponit, à quo lit impetranda, & quib excausis: posterior exponit, q dnā eā vacatione cōtineat h.e, agit de effectu & pinde est posterior. Ad q rēm quoq; ptinet tit. 46. de dec. decur. priores 1. sūt de vacatione à principe; sed h. de vacatiōe à Decurionib impetranda, quæ phibetur exceptis, pfessorib bonarū artiū. Impetratione immunitatis jam seqtur excusatio à muerib: quo ptinent 14. tit. quorū 1. est tit. 47. de excus. mun. Tit. XLVI. q a generalis est, cuj tit velut pars est, tit 48. de quib. munerib. vel pfessionib. &c. nā & h. e. generalis, sed est posterior: q a munera alia sunt. de q b. licet se excusare, de q b. est prior: alia de quib. nō licet, ad quæ ptinet h. tit. Hos generales tit seq. speciales, in quibus causæ excusationū à munerib exponunt. Cōmuniter a alie sunt justæ, alie injustæ. De justis prī agit justa rōne. Inter has 1. locum obtinet ætas, de quā est tit. 49. ætate, &c. Ratio ord. est hæc fortasse qa hæc causa est maxime generalis, & frequētior. Altera causa est morb, de qua est tit 50. quorbo, &c. Nā & hæc causa est satis cōmunis sive generalis: sed odiosior & ad morte ppior, ac pinde posterior 3 4. caæ sunt num. liber. & paupertas tit. 51. de iis qui nu. lib. paup. &c. Ratio ordinis tum quia hæ cā nō sunt ita generales & frequentes, tū quia speciali privil. cā hæc de nume liberor est indūcta. Hunc sequit tit. 52. de profes. & med. q cā liberal. artium in paucis cadit; eoq; ut valde specialis posterior est. Hūjus tit. velut pars est tit prox. 53. de Athl. Nā & Athletæ est ars, sed est corporis: at priores sunt animi; quare hęc cā artis Athleticæ à reliquis distingui pōt. VII. cā est militia, ad q pertinent 2 tit putat. 54. de his, quæ nō impl. Tit. LV. personalibus: quam patrimonialibus, sed hic tantum pertinet ad immunitatem personalium. l. 3. §. up. de munerum patrum. Hunc sequitur tit. 66. de postiorib. ad munn.nominan. Cur autem de hac nominatione ad extremum agatur, est haec ratio, quia priores causae excusationum valent per se haec valet propter alium. Ea enim quae per se potiora sunt illis, quae propter aliud. Cui titulo adjungitur tit. 67. si propter inimicit. creat. &c. Nam & haec causa excusationis non est propter se, sed propter alterius quasi delictum, qui suam inimicitiam & odium explere velit, & non consulere Reip. in munere alicui deferendo, quod quia quasi delictum est, posteriorem locum obtinet hic tit. 67. quem sequitur tit 68. de sumpt. recuper. Ratio ordinis est, quia excusatione indicata & non accepta, poterit quis appellare, & sumptibus in eam appellationem factis si juste appellaverit nominatur ad munus, à quo se excusaverat, recuperabit à nominatore, qui excusationem accipere noluerat. Ultimum locum obtinet tit 69. si post creationem, &c. quia scilicet de morte agatur hic tit. nominati ad munus & quidem de ea morte, quae post creationem accidit. Et haec de secundo c. hujus libri. Tertium & ultimum caput accessorium vocavi, quia de ministris sive officiis, hoc est officiarijs agit, qui operam praestat fisco in vectigalibus & curijs, & civitatibus de quibus supra dictum Comitetur hoc c.8. titulis, quorum i. est tit. 70. de tabularis Ratio est quia hic titulus est de ijs officijs, quae serviunt partim fisco, partim civitatibus sed tit. proximus est 71. de fulcep. praepof. ad ea pertinet officia quae tantum fisco serviunt: proinde tit. 70 est prior & communior, tit. 71. est posterior, ut speciális. Cui adjungitur tit 72. de ponderat. & auri illatione. Nam & hi fisco serviunt in vectigalibus maxime tamen in una vectigalium specie, puta in pecunia, solidis sive aureis. Et haec quoque est ratio, cur hic tit de ponderat. statim sequitur priorem titulum 71. Sub eo titulo 71. in l. ult. agitur de auro & argento & de ponderum iniquitate ut recte statim adjungatur de ponderatoribus. tit. 72. quem sequitur tit. 73. de auri publ. perfecut. Ratio ordinis est perspicua prius enim aurum sive solidi vectigales ponderantur, posterius ad fiscum & principem deportantur per persecutores. Huic tit. adjungitur titulus 74. de his, quae ex publ. &c. & hunc sequitur tit. 75. de auro coronario. Ratio ordinis videtur obscurior. Nam prioribus titulis de auro videatur potius hic tit. de auro coronario, adjungendus statim, quam ille, de his, quae ex publ &c. & tamen hic prior est titulus de auro coronar. etiam in Cod. Theod. id quod hac de causa, quia sub titul. 73. de auri publ. perfect. id maxime agitur, ut persecutores, qui aurum collatum à Provincialibus & jam ponderatum, quasi interdum retinebant, in posterum prohibeantur, id diutius retinere. Cui prohibitioni de non retinendo auro adjungitur alia prohibitio, de non usurpando vectigali, vel etiam alio quolibet tributi genere. Usurpare inquam, hoc est, vel mutuo fumere, vel in suos usus convertere. Poteare edit Tribun. ad auri de quo jam egerat in fine tit. 71. & tit. 72. & 73. atque adjungit jam titul. 75. de auro coroTheod.tit.de argenti pretio &c. Sed eum titulum Tribun.ex Cod.Theod. in hunc nostrum Cod. transtulit, ante hunc tit.de aur.lustral. &c. eumque posfuit ultimum in libro priori; Hac, ni fallor, de causa, ut non longe absit ab hoc ipso titulo & etiam, quia ille titulus, de argenti pretio, &c. non pertinet ad collegia, & proinde remotus est ab hoc libro 11. qui initio agit de collegijs Itaq; secundus jam titulus hujus lib. 11. est de navicularijs sive naucleris publ.&c. quo ti continetur alterum corpus generale puta navicularium. Et ad hoc caput pertinet tit. 2 & 4. seqq Titulus 2 ut generalis est idcirco inter hos titulos de navicularijs, primum locum tenet: quem sequitur statim titul.3.de prædiis, & omnib.reb.navic. Ratio ordinis est quia prius de personis, posterius de rebus & prædijs fit agendum Ut enim ipsi navicularij ita & prædia eorum sunt obnoxia ad hoc onus & functionem navicularium sustinendum. Hunc sequitur titul.4.de navib.non excus. qui titulus est prohibitorius, ut & tit.5.ne quid oneri publ.impon. idcirco sunt posteriores. Cur autem titulus, de navib, sit prior titulo, ne quid, &c. ratio est quia titul.2. & 3. sunt de navibus publicis, quos sequitur recte tit.4 qui est de navibus priv. Nam ut naves collegij navicularium sunt obnoxiæ, tanquam publicæ, ad species & onera publica deportanda, ita & naves privatorum postulante necessitate non excusantur ab ijsdem oneribus deportandis. Jam tit.6.de naufrag. inter hos titul. nauticos, ultimum locum tenet, quia naufragium est velut mors, hoc est, interitus navium & sæpe navicularioru Et hæc de primo membro, quod est corporum valde generalium duorum. Secundo membro diximus, continet corpora magis speciali, ut Principi & fisco magis addicta, atq; conditionalia, hoc est, quæ non omnino libera sunt. Et hinc intelligitur ratio, cur hoc membrum prioris illo est posterius, quia scilicet speciale est. Multa autem Principi deservientia fuerunt, ut murilegulorum & gymeciar.&c. metallarios quoque eò refero. Nam metalla sunt Principis, saltem ea, de quibus hic agitur. Et ad hoc membrum pertinet titul.7.de metallariis & metallis, & Procuratoribus metallorum, & reliqui usque ad titul 14. Cur autem tit de metallariis, sit primus in hoc secundo membro, ratio hæc est: tum quia metallarij sunt honestiores interdum quam reliquorum collegiorum socij, qui semper sunt servi aut semiservi. cum metallici sæpe sint liberi tum quia metalla sunt res valde cara & pretiosa.
units.tr: The second chapter, as I said, concerns the law of cities. It rightly follows the one on the fisc, because cities stand in the place of private persons, whereas the fisc belongs to the prince, and so it ranks first in dignity. This chapter on the law of cities has two parts. The first concerns the decurions, the second concerns public offices (munera). The reason for this order will be set out at the Digest, where the same order is followed. To the first part belongs title 7, which is general and concerns almost all the rights of the decurions, chiefly who may and who may not be decurions. It is followed by title 32, if by law or by liberty, concerning decurions, which is also concerned with persons who cannot be decurions. These are treated separately and later, because they are of lower rank, and because this title contains an offence: such persons aspire to what they are not allowed, and so they are punished. So much for the persons of the decurions. Now come their property and goods, to which title 33 belongs, concerning the property of decurions. For persons are customarily treated before property. To these also belongs title 34, on the sums due and to whom they are due. But title 33 concerns transactions inter vivos, such as the sale of goods, whereas title 34 concerns wills or succession on intestacy, and so it comes later. Title 35, on the imposition of gain and of the decurion's heirs, is in a sense part of this. For, like title 34, title 35 also concerns successions. This title imposes on the heir of a decurion a certain burden, or on others, if the goods of the decurion were acquired by a gratuitous cause, such as by a legacy or gift. This title speaks of the acceptance of gratuitous bequests. These titles also derive from the Theodosian Code. But from book 12, from which title 36 comes, on the salaries of decurions, which is prohibitive, since decurions are forbidden to pay salaries without the prince's mandate, it holds a later place. Title 37, if the curials..., likewise is prohibitive, but the earlier title is prohibitive on the side of property, and so title 37, which is wholly prohibitive, comes last. Hence this part, chapter 2, which we said concerns decurions or curials, ends clearly here. The second part of this chapter, which we said concerns offices and honours, contains 32 titles. The first of these is title 38, on public burdens, and the second is title 39, on residents, and where each is domiciled. These two titles come first because they concern the persons who are to be called to discharge offices and are fit for them, and then the causes which show who ought to perform the office and honour, and where. Rightly do they bring together the municipes and the residents; for municipes are citizens, but residents are not. Next comes title 40, on offices and honours, which also concerns persons. Here the earlier titles concern the offices as first undertaken, and this one their continuation, and so it is later. To this is added title 41, on the patrimonial burdens. The order is this: after treating the persons, the treatment proceeds to the thing itself, that is, to the offices. But because offices are partly personal and partly patrimonial, the earlier part (perhaps because it was already fully treated in the Digest under the title On decurions) being set aside, the patrimonial offices are treated here. Yet the earlier titles concern not only patrimonial but also personal offices, as title 42 does, in what manner citizens bear offices. The order of this title is this: first the thing or office itself is treated, as in title 41; later the manner, as here; and because title 42 deals chiefly with offices that are repeated, or undertaken a second time, it comes later. There follows title 43, on those who are appointed. The order is this: some public offices are such that people are compelled to undertake them, and so far as these are concerned others are not compelled but undertake them of their own accord, and this is the subject of the present title. Others are neither compelled to undertake them nor do so, because they are immune, and to these belong also those who are forbidden, such as the infamous, the accused, exiles and women, of whom I have spoken. This order is by no means consistent with treating first those who administer and then those who do not. Administrators, as I said, are of two kinds: some are compelled and bound by necessity, others act of their own accord. Administrators are again of two kinds: some hold immunity and excuse, others are forbidden. Those who hold immunity obtain it either from the prince, which is what vacation from offices is, or have some cause of excuse. Vacation is treated first, on account of the dignity of the prince from whom it is obtained. To this (namely, vacation from offices) belongs title 44, on those from the prince, and title 45, on the vacation from public offices. The earlier title sets out from whom it is to be obtained and for what causes; the later sets out what it contains, that is, it treats its effect, and so it is later. To this matter also belongs title 46, on decurions as decurions. The earlier titles concern vacation from the prince; but this one concerns vacation to be obtained from decurions, which is forbidden except for professors of the liberal arts. After immunity comes excuse from offices, to which belong 14 titles, of which the first is title 47, on the excuse of offices. Title 46, which is general, has as its part title 48, on which offices or professions. This too is general, but later, because some offices may be excused and others may not, the former being treated earlier and the latter here. These general titles are followed by special ones, in which the causes of excuse from offices are set out. In general, some causes are just and others unjust. The just causes are treated first, by just reasoning. Among these, age holds first place, treated in title 49, on age. The order is perhaps this: this cause is most general and most frequent. The second cause is illness, treated in title 50, on illness. This cause is also fairly common or general, but more burdensome and closer to death, and so it is later. The third and fourth causes are the number of children and poverty, title 51, on those who are excused by number of children or by poverty. The order here is that these causes are not so general and frequent, and the number of children was introduced as a special privilege. Next follows title 52, on professors and physicians, a cause which applies to few, and so, as very special, it comes later. A part of this title is in a way the next title, 53, on athletes: for athletics is also an art, but of the body, whereas the earlier ones concern the mind. Hence this cause of athletic art can be distinguished from the rest. The seventh cause is military service, to which two titles belong, 54 on those who do not fulfil... Title 55 concerns personal rather than patrimonial burdens, but this one concerns only immunity from personal burdens (l. 3, §. up., on the burdens of the fathers). There follows title 66, on the later nominations to offices. Why this nomination is treated at the end is the following reason: the earlier causes of excuse are valid in themselves, whereas this one is valid on account of another, for those things which are in themselves weightier come before those which are on account of something else. To this title is joined title 67, if on account of enmities a person is created. For this cause of excuse also is not on account of itself but on account of another's quasi-offence, namely of one who wishes to satisfy his enmity and hatred and does not consult the commonwealth in nominating someone to an office. Because this is in a way an offence, this title 67 holds a later place, and it is followed by title 68, on the costs of recovery. The order is this: when an excuse has been declared but not accepted, a person may appeal; and if he has rightly appealed, the costs incurred in that appeal, and the nomination to the office from which he had excused himself, he recovers from the nominator, who had refused to accept the excuse. The last place is held by title 69, if after the creation..., because this title treats of the death of a person nominated to an office, and of that death which occurs after the appointment. So much for the second chapter of this book. The third and last chapter I have called accessory, because it deals with ministers or officials, that is, officers who render service to the fisc in the revenues and in the curiae and cities of which I have spoken above. This chapter has eight titles, of which the first is title 70, on the tabularii. The reason is that this title concerns those offices which serve partly the fisc and partly the cities; but the next title, 71, on those who receive the prefects, concerns those offices which serve only the fisc. Therefore title 70 is earlier and more general, and title 71 later, as more special. To this is added title 72, on the weighing and bringing in of gold. For these also serve the fisc in the revenues, chiefly in one kind of revenue, namely money, in solidi or gold coins. This too is the reason why this title on weighing immediately follows the earlier title 71. Under that title 71 (in the last law) gold and silver are treated, and the unfairness of weights, so that the weighers are rightly added immediately after. Title 72 is followed by title 73, on the public pursuit of gold. The order is plain: first the gold, or the revenue solidi, is weighed; then it is conveyed to the fisc and the prince by the pursuers. To this title is joined title 74, on those things which are from the public..., and it is followed by title 75, on the coronary gold. The order here seems more obscure. For after the earlier titles on gold it would seem that this title on coronary gold ought to be joined immediately, rather than that one, on those things which are from the public. Yet this title on coronary gold is earlier, as also in the Theodosian Code. The reason for this is that under title 73, on the public pursuit of gold, the chief matter is that the pursuers, who used to keep back for a while gold that had been collected from the provincials and already weighed, should be prohibited from keeping it for longer in future. To this prohibition on retaining gold is added another prohibition, on not usurping a revenue or any other kind of tribute. To usurp, I say, is either to borrow or to convert to one's own use. Tribonian edited this, and in title 75 he joins to the gold matter already treated at the end of titles 71, 72 and 73 the title on coronary gold, taken from the Theodosian Code, on the price of silver, etc.. But when Tribonian transferred that title from the Theodosian Code into this our Code, he placed it before this title on the gold of lustral tax, etc., and he could have placed it last in the earlier book. This was done, unless I am mistaken, for this reason, that it should not be far from this very title, and also because that title, on the price of silver, etc., does not concern guilds, and so it is removed from this book 11, which at the outset treats of guilds. Thus the second title of this book 11 is on the shipowners or public shipmasters, etc., under which is comprised the second general body, namely the shipowners. To this chapter belong titles 2 and 4 and those following. Title 2, being general, holds first place among these titles on shipowners, and it is followed immediately by title 3, on the estates and all the property of shipowners. The order is that persons are treated first and things and estates afterwards, since, as the shipowners themselves, so their estates are liable to this burden and to the function of sustaining the shipowners' service. This is followed by title 4, on ships not excused, which is prohibitive, as is title 5, that nothing be imposed as a public burden, and so they are later. Why the title on ships comes before the title that nothing, etc. is because titles 2 and 3 concern public ships, and title 4 rightly follows them, concerning private ships. For as the ships of the shipowners' guild are liable, as public ships, to carry public goods and burdens, so the ships of private persons, when necessity demands, are not excused from carrying the same burdens. Now title 6, on shipwreck, holds the last place among these nautical titles, because a shipwreck is as it were the death, that is, the destruction, of ships and often of shipowners. So much for the first part, which consists of two very general bodies. The second part, as I said, contains more special bodies, more devoted to the prince and the fisc, and conditional, that is, not wholly free. This shows the reason why this part is later than the former, namely because it is special. Many bodies serving the prince were of this kind, such as the purple-dyers and the gynaeceum workers, etc. I also refer the metal-workers here, for the metals belong to the prince, at least those of which this chapter treats. To this second part belong title 7, on metal-workers, metals, and the procurators of metals, and the rest down to title 14. The reason why the title on metal-workers comes first in this second part is twofold: first, because metal-workers are sometimes more honourable than the members of other guilds, who are always slaves or half-slaves, whereas metal-workers are often free; and second, because metals are a very costly and precious commodity.

units.la: Huic titulo 7 proximus est tit.8. De murilegulis & Gynaciariis, qui titulus continet varia collegia seu corpora artificiorum, quæ ad Principis domum & usum proprie pertinent, quæ omnia recte sub unum titulum sunt redacta: ut & ad unum præfectum P.aut comitem largitionum pertinebant. Huic titulo adjungitur titul 9. de vestib.holoberis, &c. qui titulus est velut pars prioris. Nam prior titulus est de infectoribus & textoribus vestium. Et hic titulus est fere prohibitorius, ideoque posterior, quem sequitur titul. 10. de fabricensibus. Ratio ordinis est, quia hoc corpus fabricensium, hoc est
units.tr: Next to this title 7 is title 8, On the murilegulis and gynaciarii, which contains various guilds or corporations of craftsmen that belong properly to the household and use of the Prince. All of these have been rightly brought under one title, just as they formerly pertained to one prefect, the praetorian prefect or the count of the largesses. Attached to this title is title 9, On vestments of holoberis, etc., which is in a sense part of the earlier title. For the earlier title concerns dyers and weavers of garments, and this one is mostly prohibitive, which is why it comes second. It is followed by title 10, On the fabricenses. The reason for the order is that this corporation of the fabricenses, that is, of workmen labouring in public workshops and assigned to making arms, pertains to military use, whereas the earlier corporations pertain to civil use. But civil matters take precedence over military ones, as urban matters do over provincial ones, as has often been said.

units.la: in fabricis publicis laborantium opificum & armis fabricandis deputatum ad usum militarem pertinet priora corpora ad usum civilem. At civilia militaribus, ut urbana Provincialib. sunt priora ut dictum saepe. Huic tit adjungitur tit.11.de vet.numism.potest. & ei tit.12. nulli licere in finanu & equestrib. Huic tandem adjicitur tit.13.de Classicu, in C. Theod. lib.10.tit.22.de fabr.statim adjungitur tit. de Classic. Sed in nostro C.duo tit. interponuntur ut jam dictum. Ratio ordinis & causa hujus interpositionis satis obscura videtur, nam tit.11. de vet.num. potius pertinere videtur ad corpus monetariorum, de quo supra, tit.8. quod ad corpus fabricensium, de quo tit.10. Fortasse tamen haec est ratio ad d. tit.de vet.numism. &c. Cur ille scilicet adjungantur tit.10. ubi de armis, quod arma interdum solent deaurari, ut indicat l.1. C Theod.de fabr. ad deauratationem vero vetera numismata hoc est aurei potius antiqui, quam novi adhibentur. Cui rationi non male congruit titul. proxim. nullis licere, &c. ubi prohibetur margaritarum aptatio, & accommodatio in frenis, in Baltheis militaribus & alia id genus ad arma & militiam pertinentibus. Atq; ita deauratio & margaritarum accommodatio, nō male hic conjungitur, ubi de armis agitur. Ad militiam quoque pertinet tit.13. de classicis, qui sunt milites deputati purgandis fluminibus & proinde viliores. Huc titulum sequitur tit.14. de Decuralib. urbis Romae, quod collegium decuralium Rom. decuralia & alia id genus acta publica scribebat & conservabat, l.1. Codice Theodof.hoc titul. Ratio ordinis perspicua, quia scilicet adhuc expositis collegiis, quae toti imperio aut Principi serviunt, adjungantur specialia quaedam & unius propria collegia, ut urbis Romae, quorum Romā. Collegiorum primum hic ponitur decuralium propter dignitatem, quae certe major est in eo quam in iis, quae adjunguntur. Hunc titulum sequitur tit.15. de privilegiis corporatorum, &c. quod est velut commune quoddam collegiatorum corpus, quam vis proprie corporati dicuntur, specialibus addicti coporibus, ad quos hic tit. proprie pertinere videtur. Cui adjungitur tit.16. de pastor.b. Horum in urbe corpus fuit valde celebre, qui interdum mancipes dici solent. Huic proximus est tit.17. de fabrii & susceptoris, &c. Ratio ordinis ex dignitate singulorum satis patet. Tandem est tit.18. de collegiatis, &c Ratio ordinis est quia collegiati proprie dicebantur, quidam collecti ex variis collegiis & corporibus, erantque deputati ad varios usus maxime incendiorum numerus eorum erat 563. l.3. supra de commerc. & merc. Recte igitur & ordine collegia singula prius sunt exposita, ex quibus velut colluvies quaedam collectitia collegatorum sumatur, quos & ab. 9. Erhymolog. capite 4. Isidorus vocat sordidissimum genus hominum. Cur autem huic collegiatorum collegio adjungatur collegium Chartopratarum, hoc est, Chartam conficientium in Chartopratis, ratio est quia constitutio h. tit. Chartopratarum mentionem facit in fine Et hoc de primo cap. quod est de collegiorum privilegiis. Proximum est ca. 2. de iis quae ad urbem Romam & alias nonnullas pertinét privilegiis. Ratio ordinis est. tum quia priores titulí proximi agút de corporibus urbis Romæ, tũ etiam propter dignitatem hujus urbis. Continetur hoc secundum cap. 11. tit. 15. inter quos primus est hic tit. 19. de studiis lib. urbe Rom. Quod ad ordinis rationem attinet, videri possit, hunc titulũ pertinere ad c. 1. de collegiis, quia & literarũ sive magistrorũ & discipulorũ quoddam collegium videtur: id quod hic ultimo loco sit positũ, hac fortasse de causa vel quia tum non esset proprie collegium, vel quia nõ pertineat ad onera Reip. ut priora collegia. Verũ cum in jure nostro hujus collegii nulla fiat mentio malim hunc tit. de stud. liberal. distinguere & referre ad cap. 2. de privilegiis Rom. Nam & hoc erat ejus privilegium, ut studia liberalia omnia tum Romæ & postea etiam Constantinopoli docerentur. Cur autem in hoc secundo cap. hic tit. 19. fit primus, ratio propter eorum studiorum dignitatem & favorem, quem titulum sequitur titul. 20. de honoratorum vehiculus, honoratorum hoc est, magistratuum vehiculis, quod jus vehiculi propter dignitatem eorũ, quibus id concessum est, proximum est studiis liberalibus. Huic adjungitur tit. 21. de priv. urb. Const priores tit. sunt potissimum de Roma, hic est de Constantinopoli quæ dici solet nova Roma. altera vetus, cui novæ hic dantur omnia privilegia veteris Romæ & proinde hic tit. priorib recte adjungitur. Huic adjungitur tit. 22. de Metrop. hac ratione, quia ut Constantinopoli dătur privilegia nova, ita & huic Berytodarũ novum privilegiũ seu jus Metropoleos Hunc sequitur tit. 23. de Canone frumentario, & annonis civ. Credo, quia priora. ut jus scholæ jus vehiculi, jus metropoleos sunt præstatiora: jus canonis & annonæ est vilius ac inferius, ac proinde inferiori loco explicatur. Ad hoc caput pertinet tit. 23. de canone frumēt. urb. Rom. & deinde tit. 24. de frum. urb. Const. Ac cur prius de canone urbis Romæ, quã de urbis Constantinopolitanæ agatur, cum hæ duæ urbes sint pares, ut supra dictum Ratio est? quia Roma propter antiquitatem loco prior est Constantinopoli, jure & potestate par est. Eodem pertinet tit. 25. de annonis civilib. Annonas vocat panem gradilem oleũ carnem, quæ populo dividi solent irrurbe: ideoq; & civiles dicuntur, ut differant à militaribus. Duo priores tituli, de can. frum puta 13. & 14. agunt fere de modo canonis sive annonæ, atq; de ratione coëmendi: sed hic tit. 25. agit de ratione dividendi, & de iis, quibus dividi debeat canon & annona, ideoq; illis est posterior. Quæ recte sequitur. tit. 26. de mend. validu, hac ratione quia publicæ annonæ ad suble vandã paucum civium inopiam dividuntur, non ad mendicantes validos alédos, qui hic prohibentur. Eum titulũ sequitur tit. 27. ne nautis Tyberinis. Ratio ordinis, ut intelligatur, breviter admonendum, hos titulos ex Cod. Theod. sumptos lib. 4. ut est & tit. de precio pan. Oft. enf. tit. de naut. Tyber. tit. de sacrariis portus Rom. tit. de pronis boreor. potuenf. ex quibus unũ duntaxat hunc tit. de naut. Tyber. retinuit hic Tribun. Nam cum de frumento Romam deportado, & de pane Oftiensi agatur, recte positus quoque fuit titul. de naut. Tyber. qui
units.tr: To this title is added title 11, On old coinage and its power, and after it title 12, That no one may be permitted [to use gold] in the army and cavalry. Finally, title 13, On the classicians is added to this. In the Theodosian Code, book 10, title 22, On the fabricenses, is immediately followed by On the classicians; but in our Code two titles are inserted, as already said. The reason for the order and the cause of this insertion seem rather obscure. For title 11, On old coinage, seems rather to belong to the corporation of moneyers, discussed above at title 8, than to the corporation of the fabricenses, discussed at title 10. Perhaps, however, this is the reason why that title, On old coinage, etc., is joined to title 10, where arms are treated: arms are sometimes gilded, as law 1 of the Theodosian Code, On the fabricenses, indicates, and for gilding old coins, that is, ancient gold pieces rather than new ones, are used. The following title, That no one may be permitted, etc., agrees reasonably well with this reason, since it forbids the setting of pearls and their fitting to bridles, to military belts, and other such things pertaining to arms and soldiering. Thus gilding and the fitting of pearls are not badly joined here, where arms are the subject. Military matters also belong to title 13, On the classicians, who are soldiers assigned to clearing rivers and are therefore of lower rank. This title is followed by title 14, On the decurions of the city of Rome, since the college of Roman decurions wrote and kept the decurial records and other such public acts, law 1 of the Theodosian Code, this title. The order is clear: after the corporations that serve the whole empire or the Prince have been set out, the special corporations belonging to one place alone, such as those of the city of Rome, are added. The college of decurions is placed first here on account of its dignity, which is certainly greater than that of those that are added after it. This title is followed by title 15, On the privileges of incorporated persons, etc., which is as it were a common body of the members of corporations, although strictly speaking those called incorporated are attached to particular bodies, to which this title seems properly to refer. To it is added title 16, On the pastors of the holy [...]. The corporation of these in the city was very famous, and they are sometimes called contractors. Next to this is title 17, On the fabrii and the susceptores, etc. The reason for the order is fairly plain from the dignity of each. Finally there is title 18, On the collegiati, etc. The reason for the order is that the collegiati were properly so called: certain men gathered from various colleges and corporations, and they were assigned to various uses, above all fire-fighting; their number is given in law 3, above, On commerce and merchandise. Rightly and in order, therefore, the individual colleges are set out first, from which a certain mass of gathered collegiati is drawn together, whom Isidore, in Etymologies, book 9, chapter 4, calls the most sordid kind of men. As to why the college of the chartopratae, that is, makers of paper in the chartopratae, is joined to this college of collegiati, the reason is that the constitution of this title mentions the chartopratae at the end. And this is the end of the first chapter, which concerns the privileges of the colleges. The next is chapter 2, on those privileges that pertain to the city of Rome and some others. The reason for the order is both that the preceding titles deal with the corporations of the city of Rome, and also on account of the dignity of this city. This second chapter contains, at the eleventh title of the fifteenth book, among which this title 19, On the studies of the liberal arts in the city of Rome, comes first. As to the reason for the order, it may be thought that this title belongs to the first chapter, on the colleges, since it seems also to be a kind of college of teachers and pupils; that it has been placed here in the last position may perhaps be for this reason, either because it was then not strictly a college, or because it does not belong to the burdens of the state as the earlier colleges do. But since no mention of this college is made in our law, I would prefer to distinguish this title, On the liberal studies, and refer it to chapter 2, on the privileges of Rome. For this too was its privilege, that all the liberal studies were taught both at Rome and afterwards also at Constantinople. As to why this title 19 is first in this second chapter, the reason is the dignity and favour of those studies. This title is followed by title 20, On the carriages of the honorati, that is, of the magistrates, since the right of carriage, on account of the dignity of those to whom it has been granted, comes next after the liberal studies. To this is added title 21, On the privileges of the city of Constantinople. The earlier titles are chiefly about Rome; this one is about Constantinople, which is commonly called the New Rome, the other being the Old. To the new city are here given all the privileges of the old Rome, and therefore this title is rightly added to the earlier ones. To this is added title 22, On the metropolis, for this reason, that just as new privileges are given at Constantinople, so too Berytus receives a new privilege or right of metropolis. This is followed by title 23, On the grain allowance and the civic annona. I think this is because the earlier ones, such as the right of the school, the right of carriage, and the right of the metropolis, are more excellent; the right to the grain allowance and the annona is baser and inferior, and therefore it is explained in a lower place. To this chapter belongs title 23, On the grain allowance of the city of Rome, and then title 24, On the grain of the city of Constantinople. Why is the grain allowance of the city of Rome treated before that of Constantinople, since these two cities are equal, as said above? The reason is that Rome, on account of its antiquity, is prior in place to Constantinople, though equal in right and power. To the same belongs title 25, On the civic annonae. He calls the annonae bread, grilled [bread], oil and meat, which are usually distributed to the people in the city; they are therefore called civic, to distinguish them from the military ones. The two preceding titles, on the grain allowance, that is 13 and 14, deal chiefly with the amount of the allowance or annona and the manner of purchasing it; but this title 25 deals with the manner of distribution and with the persons to whom the allowance and annona ought to be distributed, and therefore it comes after them. This rightly follows title 26, On begging able-bodied [men], for the reason that the public annonae are distributed to relieve the poverty of a few citizens, not to feed able-bodied beggars, who are forbidden here. This title is followed by title 27, That the Tiber sailors [...]. As to the order, it should briefly be noted that these titles were taken from the Theodosian Code, book 4, as were the titles on the price of bread at Ostia, on the Tiber sailors, on the sacred warehouses of the port of Rome, and on the prones of the Boreorum at Puteoli, of which this Tribunian retained only this title on the Tiber sailors. For since the matter concerns grain carried to Rome and bread from Ostia, the title on the Tiber sailors, who carried most of the cargoes, grain, provisions, and so on, from the port of Ostia up the Tiber into the city of Rome, was rightly placed here too. This is followed by title 28, On the grain of Alexandria, for that city too had a grain allowance; it was as it were a Rome in Africa.

units.la: {N} ǂ ex portu Cftiensi pleraq; onera,frumentum, cómeatum, &c. per Tyberim subvehebant in urbem Rom. Hunc sequitur tit. 28. de frum. Alex. Nam & in ea urbe erat canon frumetarius:quæ urbs erat velut Roma in Africa.Preius autem de canone urbis Rom.& Constât.agitur propter dignitatem. Huic adjungitur tit. 29. de Alex. prim. Occasione enim canonis Alexandrinæaliquid etiam de corporatorum ejus urbis privilegiis adjungitur,ut & in Cod. Theod. Et hæc de 1 capite hujus lib. 11. quod est de jure & privilegiis urbis Rom potissimum. Tertium cap. est de jure aliarum civitatum. Ratio ordinis perquam facilis, ut prius de Roma quam de civitatibus, quę ut jam alias dictum, privatorum loco habentur. Et hoc cap. continetur 11.tit 'quorum primus est tit.30.de jure Reip.quia est generalis Sic & tit.31. de administratione rerump. est generalis, quo ad rerum administrationem: sed ille est de ipso jure. Nam prius de re,h. e de ipso jure,quam de accidente,h. e. administratione agitur. Hunc sequitur tit.32.de vend.reb.civ. venditio enim est pars administrationis rerumpubl.cui adjungitur tit.33.debit.civ 1. hac ratione:quia ex administratione sepe fit,ut administrator h.e curator Reip.sive magistratus debitor fiat Reip.& eo pertinet h.tit.de debit.civit. Quem sequitur tit.34. de periculo nominatorum. Dictum est modo,curatore interdum fieri debitorem civitatis:hujus debiti sive obligationis periculum ptinet primum ad ipsum curatorem, sed pertinet quoq; ad alios, si forte curator non esset solvendo, puta ad nominatores h.e. eos qui crearint curatorem aut magistratu, aut etiâ iuterdum ad fidejussores Curator enim civitatis statim initio cogitur dare fidejussores civitati. Et hinc est, quod de hoc periculo primum est tit. 33. qui ad ipsos curatores, deinde est tit.34.qui ad nominatores:III est tit.35.de periculo eorum.qui pro magistratibus intervenerunt q pertinent ad fidejussores. Huic adjungitur tit 36.quo quisq; ordine conveniatur. qui etiâ pertinet ad periculum hujus debiti,sed ut sepe jam dictum,ut in stipulationib prius agitur de uno, posterius deduob. reis stipulandi & promittendi: ita & hic prius agitur de uno curatore sive uniuspericulo & obligatione posterius de duobus simul ficil.creatis & collegiis in magistratu,de quib.quæritur, quo ordine conveniatur illi. An simul ambo ip solidū teneantur nec ne. Hunc sequitur tit.37. N: quisliber invitus,&c. qui tit est de actore,h.e.servo dispensatore Reip. Nā hic actor plerunq; est servus. Potest tamē esse & liber,sed cogi non potest ex hoc tit. Hinc ratio ordinis intelligitur,quia actor curatore est vilior,& quia ei subservit tanquam adjutor in rationib & pecuniis exigedisac fœnerādis. Cui proximus est tit 38.sumptuum injuncti muneris, &c. Ratio ordinis est, quia de sumptibus plerunq;ultimo agitur post finitū officiū,& qnia sumptus viliores,& nō tantū ab ipsis curatoribus sive magistratibus sed & ab actoribus illis interdum fiunt & exiguntur. Idcirco post utrosq; agitur demum de sumptibus quamvis curatio Reip. plerunq; est fine sumptu.l.l.supra quemadmodum civ.mun.indic. Hunc titulum sequitur,tit.39. de his qui ex officio quod administr. ministr. &c. quietsi generaliter conceptus tamen specialiter intelligendus est de usuris, ut ipsa lex indicat, qua curator Reip. ad fortem quidé tenetur, sed nonad usuras, si ϕ damnum ejus culpa accipiat resp. in reip. pecunia feneranda. Usurae enim suntaccessiones & proinde in posteriorem locum hic sunt rejectae Sed posteremum locum in hoc; cap. tenet tit. 4. de folut. & liberat. deb. civ. Nam ut prius de obligatione quatenentur curatores, itanunc de solutione posteremum agitur, quae solutio est finis obligationis. Cap. 4. diximus de ludis & spectaculis. Ratio ordinis est facilis: quia rerum ludicrarum & vilium tractatio in posteriorem locum rejici debeat. Ad hoc cap. pertinent tit. 7. primus est tit. 41. de spectac. & scenic. &c. Ratio ordinis est facilis. Ut tamen intelligatur a monendum est hic adfert quinq; genera ludorum: Circenses, scenicos, gladiatorios, venationem & majumam. De duobus agitur primo, hoc est h. tit. 41. quia illi fiunt in ipsis urbibus, & quia sunt favorabiliores ac minus crudeles. Cur autem lenones sub eodem ti-ponantur, haec est ratio quia scenicae mulieres plerunq; erant turpes & infames: Huc pertinet tit. 42 de expensi lud publ. Nam tametsi hic tit generaliter conceptus est, tamen de expensis ludorum Circensium proprie agit cui adjungitur tit. 43. de aquaeductu. qui tit. ad ludos non pertinet, & tamen hic interjectus est tantum occasione legis tit. prioris, in qua fit mentio praesidis, qui impensas ludorum transtulerat in refectionem murorum. Hac igitur ratione adjugitur tit hic de impensis quae fiunt in aquaeductu publicorum refectionibus, quae impensae olim erant ingentes. Post hunc tit. redit. Tribun ad ludos puta gladiatores, de quibus est tit. 44. de gladiatoribus per. toll. Ratio ordinis tum quia hi ludi cruenti & minus favorabiles, tum quia hic tit. est prohibitorius, & proinde posterior. Cui adjungitur tit. 45. de venat. ferar. Nam hic ludus venationis sive arenae, erat olim gladiatorio non absimilis, nimirum quod in gladiatorio homines inter se, in venatione homines cum beluis pugnabat. Sed videtur hic titulus pertinere tam ad venationem ferarum in sylvis (ita enim haec lex posita sonat) quam ad ludum arenae sive Circi Ultimum locum inter ludos tenet Majuma tit. 46. de Majuma, quia priores tit. & in urbe & in provinciis, sed maxime in urbe Roma at Majuma nunquam in urbe, sed tantum extra urbem; & in provinciis fiebat. Hunc sequitur tit. 47. ut armorum usus non sit ut principe, &c. quia tit. & in Cod. Theod. l. 15. est ultimus ex quo Codice ratio ordinis est petenda ad hunc titulum. Nam & in eodem libro decimoquinto sunt tituli priores de ludis & alij quidem ut tit. de usu fellar. & tit. d. arm. usu. sed inter eos est tit. de infirm. his qua fuh Tyrannis gesta sunt. Ex his tribus retinuit tantum unum Tribun. puta de usu armor. Ratio autem cur in Cod. Theod. esset tit. de usu fellar. &c. est, quia ad scenicos ludos usus sellarum pertineat, & hac occasione etiam de usu armorum adjunctum est. Atque ita in exemplo Cod. Theodosi hic tit. de usu arm. interdicto hic remansit. Et haec de 4. capitibus hujus libri m. Ultimum seu quintum caput est de Agricolis & agris. Ratio ordinis, quia hactenus dictum est de urbe, & de civitatibus ut bono jam ordine agatur de agris. Est autem hoc caput bimębre: prius enim de agricolis, posteriusque agitur de ipsis agris sive prædijs, eorumq; oneribus sive tributis Agricolarū tributa, quia in singula capita erant statuta dicuntur proprie capitationes & interdū capita: agrorum & jugerum tributa, dicuntur proprie census. Ratio ordinis ut prius de agricolis agatur, est perspicua, quia de personis primo, postea de rebus agendum. Prius membrum continetur decem tit., quorum primus est tit. 48. de agr. & cens. fit. quia hic tit. est generalis, agricolarū sunt variæ condiciones, sed duæ propriæ propter quas agricolæ dividuntur in censitos & non censitos. Céliti censum & capitatione præstant. Fisco, & erant verè servi, proprièq; dicuntur adscriptitii, & interdum tributarii. Nam céfiti fisco nihil præstat: sed tatū domino reditū aliqué dant & hi proprie dicuntur coloni, eráūq; liberi. Et hoc est quod ait hic tit. de agris & cens. & colon hoc est, non censitis.
units.tr: From the port of Ostia most of the cargo, grain, provisions and so on, was carried up the Tiber into the city of Rome. This is followed by tit. 28. de frum. Alex. For there too, in that city, there was a grain tax, and that city was, as it were, Rome in Africa. Furthermore, the title concerns the grain tax of the city of Rome and of Constantinople, on account of their dignity. To this is added tit. 29. de Alex. prim. Since the grain tax of Alexandria gave the occasion, something is also added about the privileges of the corporations of that city, as in the Theodosian Code. These are the matters of the first chapter of this eleventh book, which concerns chiefly the law and privileges of the city of Rome. The third chapter concerns the law of the other cities. The order is quite simple: Rome is treated before the cities, which, as I have said elsewhere, are regarded as in the position of private persons. This chapter contains eleven titles, of which the first is tit.30.de jure Reip. because it is general. So too tit.31. de administratione rerump. is general as regards the administration of public affairs, but the former concerns the law itself. For the law of the thing comes first, that is, the law itself, and then what is incidental, that is, administration. This is followed by tit.32.de vend.reb.civ. for sale is part of the administration of public affairs. To this is added tit.33.debit.civ 1. for this reason: because from administration it often happens that the administrator, that is the curator of the commonwealth or the magistrate, becomes a debtor of the commonwealth, and to this belongs tit.de debit.civit. which is followed by tit.34. de periculo nominatorum. It has just been said that a curator sometimes becomes a debtor of the city. The risk of this debt or obligation belongs first to the curator himself, but it also belongs to others, if perhaps the curator should not be solvent: namely to the nominators, that is those who appointed the curator or magistrate, and sometimes also to the sureties. For a curator of a city is forced at the very outset to give sureties to the city. Hence it is that concerning this risk, the first is tit. 33. which concerns the curators themselves; then tit.34. which concerns the nominators; third is tit.35.de periculo eorum.qui pro magistratibus intervenerunt which concerns the sureties. To this is added tit 36.quo quisq; ordine conveniatur. which also belongs to the risk of this debt. But, as has often been said already, just as in stipulations the matter is first treated concerning one party and afterwards concerning two parties who stipulate and promise, so here too the matter is first treated concerning one curator, or the risk and obligation of one, and afterwards concerning two who are created together and share in the magistracy, concerning whom it is asked in what order they are to be sued, and whether both are simultaneously bound for the whole or not. This is followed by tit.37. N: quisliber invitus,&c. which title concerns the agent, that is the slave who manages the affairs of the commonwealth; for this agent is usually a slave. He may however also be free, but he cannot be compelled under this title. The reason for the order is understood from this: the agent is of lower rank than the curator, and he serves him as an assistant in collecting and lending accounts and money. Next to it is tit 38.sumptuum injuncti muneris, &c. The reason for the order is that expenses are usually treated last, after the office has ended, and because expenses are of lesser importance, and are incurred and exacted not only by the curators or magistrates themselves but sometimes by those agents. Therefore the matter of expenses is treated last of all, after both, although the administration of the commonwealth is usually without expense. l.l.supra quemadmodum civ.mun.indic. This title is followed by tit.39. de his qui ex officio quod administr. ministr. which, although conceived in general terms, is to be understood specially of interest, as the law itself indicates, by which the curator of the commonwealth is bound indeed for the principal, but not for interest, if through his fault the commonwealth suffers loss in lending public money. For interest is an accessory, and therefore it is placed here in a later position. But the last place in this chapter is held by tit. 4. de folut. & liberat. deb. civ. For as the obligations by which curators are bound were treated first, so now the discharge is treated last, and discharge is the end of an obligation. In the fourth chapter we treated of games and shows. The reason for the order is simple: the treatment of playful and trivial things ought to be put in a later place. To this chapter belong seven titles, the first of which is tit. 41. de spectac. & scenic. &c. The reason for the order is simple. However, so that it may be understood, it must be pointed out that here he distinguishes five kinds of games: chariot races, stage plays, gladiatorial contests, hunting, and the Majuma. He treats first of two of these, namely h. tit. 41. because these are held in the cities themselves, and because they are more popular and less cruel. Why brothels are placed under the same title is for this reason: stage women were generally base and infamous. To this belongs tit. 42 de expensi lud publ. For although this title is conceived in general terms, it nevertheless properly concerns the expenses of chariot races, to which is added tit. 43. de aquaeductu. which title does not belong to games, and yet is inserted here only on the occasion of the law of the preceding title, in which mention is made of a governor who had transferred the costs of the games to the repair of the walls. For this reason the title concerning expenses incurred on the repairs of public aqueducts is added here, which expenses were formerly enormous. After this title the Tribonian arrangement returns to games, namely gladiators, concerning whom is tit. 44. de gladiatoribus per. toll. The reason for the order is that these games are bloody and less popular, and also because this title is prohibitory and therefore later. To this is added tit. 45. de venat. ferar. For this hunting game, or the game of the arena, was formerly not unlike gladiatorial combat, since in the gladiatorial games men fought with one another, and in the hunt men fought with wild beasts. But this title seems to concern both the hunting of wild beasts in the woods (for this law is so worded) and the game of the arena or circus. The last place among the games is held by the Majuma, tit. 46. de Majuma, because the earlier titles concern both the city and the provinces, but chiefly the city of Rome, whereas the Majuma was never held in the city, but only outside it, and it took place in the provinces. This is followed by tit. 47. ut armorum usus non sit ut principe, &c. which title, and in the Theodosian Code l. 15. is the last, and from that Code the reason for the order is to be sought for this title. For in the same fifteenth book the earlier titles concern games, and others such as tit. de usu fellar. and tit. d. arm. usu. but between them is the title tit. de infirm. his qua fuh Tyrannis gesta sunt. Of these three Tribonian retained only one, namely tit. de usu arm. The reason why in the Theodosian Code there was a title de usu fellar. and so on, is that the use of chairs pertains to stage games, and on this occasion the use of arms was also added. And so in the example of the Theodosian Code this title tit. de usu arm. remained here as a prohibition. And these are the matters of the four chapters of this book. The last or fifth chapter concerns farmers and fields. The reason for the order is that hitherto we have spoken of the city and of the cities, so that now in good order we may treat of the fields. This chapter has two parts: first it treats of the farmers, and then of the fields themselves, or the estates, and their burdens or taxes. Taxes on farmers, because they were imposed on each head, are properly called poll taxes and sometimes heads; taxes on fields and on iugera are properly called census. The reason for the order, that first the farmers should be treated, is clear, because persons come first, and afterwards things must be treated. The first part contains ten titles, of which the first is tit. 48. de agr. & cens. fit. because this title is general. The conditions of farmers are various, but two are special, on account of which farmers are divided into censited and non-censited. The censited pay the census and the poll tax to the fisc; they were truly slaves, and are properly called adscripticii, and sometimes tributarii. For the censited pay nothing to the fisc, but give only some rent to the owner; these are properly called coloni, and they were free. And this is what this title means by "de agris et censitis et colonis", that is, the non-censited.

units.la: Hunc sequitur tit. 49. de capit. cens. exim. Ratio ordinis est, quia prius de iis, qui præstant capitationem ut sunt rustici, censiti posteriusque de iis, qui capitatione non præstant, ut privatio habitu est posterior. Huic subjicitur tit. 50 in quib. cauf. coloni censiti dominos accusare possint qui quia tantū est de censitis, cū priores sint generales, merito hic ut specialis postponitur. Quę sequuntur 3. tit. plane speciales, ut tit. 51. de Colon. Palæst. & tit. 52. de Colo. Thrac. & tit. 53. de Colon. Illyricianis. Ratio ordinis inter hos videtur partim ex situ, hoc est, prius deoriente dicendū, deinde progrediendum occidētem versus, ut à Palestinis ac Thracensib. ad Illyricanos, partim quia sub tit. 52. ac 53. agatur de delicto & pœna receptatoris. Hos sequūtur quatuor tit. prohibitorii & proinde postremi hujus membri prioris: quorum primus est tit. 54. ut nemo ad fuit patrocinium, etc. Ratio est, quia ut tit 52. & 53 receptatores Colonorum puniuntur, ita & hic fuit receptatores eorum prohibentur: quo casu ipsi rustici proprie dicuntur (suscepti hic & tit. 55 ut rusticani ad nullū, etc. quotit. etiam prohibetur vexatio rusticorum ex angariis (Germanice frohnen) Hunc sequitur tit. 56. non licere habitatoribus, etc. Ratio ordinis est quia priores tituli prohibitorii de omnibus sunt rusticis: sed hic tantum de rusticis metrocomicē, & proinde ut specialior ita posterior. Cui adjungitur tit. 57. ut nullus ex vicanis, etc. Ratio ordinis est, tum quia ut prior est de cōvicaneis ita & iste, tū quia priores tit. sunt de oneribus propriis singulorum rusticorum, hic de onere sive debito alieno, hujus rei ut iniquissimæ prohibitio merito ultimū locum tenet. Alterum membrum est de ipsis agris eorumq; jure, & tributis. Continetur 21. tit. Potestautem hoc membrū in duas partes secari. Nam primo agitur de ipsis cōfortibus & infpeētoribus prædiorū: deinde de ipsis prædiis seu fundis. Ad censitores igitur pertinet 1. tit. 58 de censib. & censit. Ratio ordinis quia cum hoc totum membrum secundum sit de jure tributis prædiorum rusticorum potissimum (nam tributa tantum in rusticis prædiis hoc est fundis non urbanis, hoc est, aedibus jure civili imponuntur) Sciri autem nō possit quæ prædia quæ non, & quantum illa tributi fisco præstare debeant, nisi prius illorum conditio, fertilitas aut sterilitas per inspectores & peraequatores fuerit diligenter inquisita: merito hic titulus de inspectoribus prædiorum ponitur ante prædia. Hunc sequitur tit 59. de omni agro deserto, ubi est altera pars eaque præcipua huius secundi membri, de ipsis agris & prædiis. Quæ pars altera videtur item bimembris, generalis & specialis. Nā in hac tota parte, cum fundorum genera, decè exponantur, steriles, limitrophi, limitanei, castellanei patrimoniales rei privatæ, rei dominicæ, sive dominici, tamiaci t:mploru & civitatū: Ex his 4 primi functi ad generales pertinent titulos: reliqui sunt magis speciales Et primum quidem de agris desertis & sterilibus est d.titul.59.de omni agro. &c. Ratio est, tum quia hic titulus est generalis ut & verba ejus, de omni agro, &c. indicant: potuit tamen & hic speciem fundi, puta steriles & desertos agros: sed improprie: tum quia in l.ult. tituli priorum puta 58 agitur de agris desertis à peraequatore traditis alii: & proinde statim adjungitur titul. de agr. defirt. Pars autem hujus tituli his verb. & quando steriles fertilibus imponuntur. intelligenda est de adjectionibus quæ Græcè ἐπίβολαι dicuntur, de quibus est Nov. 166. Est autem ἐπίβολη sive adjectio prædii deserti aut sterilis attributio & assignatio facta consorti cum onere tributi. Videatur Haloand. in praefat. Novell. & Cujac. lib. 4. obs. c. 20. Hunc sequitur tit. 60. de fundis limitroph. &c. quo tria fundorum genera continentur: limitrophi sunt fundi, ex quibus aluntur milites limitanei. Fundi limitanei sunt illi, qui militibus sunt assignati, & eorum proprii. Castellanei fundi sunt iidem illi, qui proprie sunt militum castellaneorum, hoc est eorum qui castella tuentur. Ratio ordinis ad hunc titulum est: tum quia & hic titulus ex parte est generalis (nam limitrophi erant varii, hoc est tam privati quam publici & fiscales & civitatum) tum quia ut prior titulus 59. est de fundis sterilibus quorum tributa sunt exigua, ita & hic titulus est de fundis, quorum nulla sunt tributa, hoc est, qui sunt immunes, utpote militares, aut certè militaribus servientes. Huic adjungitur titulus 61. de pasc. publ. & priv. Ratio ordinis est quia hic titulus est generalis, sed priores sunt de fundis, hic est de pratis & pascuis, quæ ut fundi sunt minora & viliora ita ordine posteriora. Hunc sequitur tit. 62. de fundis patrimonialib. Ratio ordinis est quia expositis jam titulis generalibus fundorum, ordo postulat ut speciales jam tituli collocentur: inter quos primum locum obtinet hic titulus 62. propter dignitatem principis, ad cujus patrimonium pertinent. Sunt aut hic fundorum principis 4. genera: patrimoniales, rei privatæ, rei dominicæ & tamiaci, quæ genera ordine ac deinceps explicantur. Cur aut patrimoniales primo ordine ponantur hæc est ratio, quia hi nunquam mutant dominium, hoc est, venduntur tantum à principe. Ad eundem fundum pertinet titulus proximus, puta tit 63. de mancip. & coloniis patr. Nam mancipia & coloni, sunt velut partes fundorum, ut & servi rustici inter res mobiles praediorum numerantur. l. 4. de diversis temp. praescr. &c. Huic adjungitur tit. 64. de fugitivis col. patrum. Nam ut prior tit est de colonis frugalibus & bonis, ita hic est de colonis nequam, hoc est fugitivis, & proinde posterior. Ad eundem titulum pertinet tit. e f. de collat. fund. patrim. Ratio ordinis, quia priores tituli sunt de jure & proprietate fundorum patrimonialium: hic autem est de eorum onere ac tributo quod ut est odiosius ita est posterius. Et haec de primo genere fundorum principis. Alterum diximus fundos rei privatae, de quibus est tit. 66. de funct. ... pri. Ratio ordinis, cur inter 4. fundorum principis genera, hi rei privatae secundum locum obtineant, est haec: quia duo genera sunt generalia, hoc est, ei viunt principi ad omne usum: puta patrimoniales & rei privatae reliqua duo sunt specialia, quae sic nonad omnem sed ad certum usum pertinent, specialia autem generalibus sunt posteriora. Hunc sequitur tit. 67. de fund. & alib. rei domin. &c. quod est tertium genus fundorum principis. Putat Cujacius in comment. ad hunc tit. fundos rei dominicae esse prorsus eosdem, qui sunt rei privatae eaq; de causa hunc titulum de rebus dominicis esse supervacaneum. Sed est tamen aliqua differentia inter rem privatam principis, & inter dominicam: haec nimirum, quod privata res sit velut totum & dominica sit velut pars rei privatae maximè posita in cubiculo & cellario principis. Fundi igitur rei privatae sunt generaliores, & fundi rei dominicae magis speciales. Hunc sequitur tit. 68. de ag. ut col. & mancip. dom. &c. Ratio jam expositia est supra ad tit. 65. Nam ut ibi titulo de fund. patrim. adjungitur titulus de mancipiis quae sunt fundorum velut partes: ita & hic fundis rei privatae, & fundis rei dominicae adjungitur titulus de mancipiis utriusque generis fundorum: Hactenus de 1.2. & 3. genere fundorum principis dictum. Restat quartum, de quo tit.
units.tr: This is followed by title 49, de capitatione censitorum eximendis (on exempting the registered from the poll tax). The order is this: first come those who pay the poll tax, such as the country folk who are registered, and then those who do not pay it, since privation is posterior to having something. Title 50 follows, in quibus causis coloni censiti dominos accusare possint (in what cases registered tenants may accuse their lords). Since the earlier titles are general and this one concerns only the registered, it is rightly placed after them as the more specific.
