The three titles that follow are wholly specific: title 51, de colonis Palaestinis (on the Palestinian tenants); title 52, de colonis Thracensibus (on the Thracian tenants); and title 53, de colonis Illyricianis (on the Illyrian tenants). The order among these seems partly to follow geography, so that one moves from east to west, from the Palestinians and Thracians to the Illyrians, and partly because titles 52 and 53 deal with the offence and punishment of those who harbour tenants. Four prohibitory titles follow these and so close this first part. The first is title 54, ut nemo ad fugam (vel) patrocinium (that no one shall give refuge or patronage, etc.). The reason is that, as titles 52 and 53 punish those who harbour tenants, so here those who shelter them are forbidden to do so, and in that case the country folk themselves are properly the subject. Title 55, ut rusticani ad nullum (that country people shall not be...), follows, which also forbids the harassment of country folk by forced labour (in German, frohnen). Title 56, non licere habitatoribus (that residents may not...), comes next. The order is that the earlier prohibitory titles concern all country folk, whereas this one concerns only the country folk of the metrocomia, and so, being more specific, it is placed later. To it is joined title 57, ut nullus ex vicanis (that no one of the villagers...). The order is that, as the earlier title concerned fellow villagers, so does this one; and also because the earlier titles concern the personal burdens of individual country folk, whereas this one concerns a burden or debt belonging to another. Since a prohibition of this kind is most unjust, it rightly holds the last place. The second part of this member concerns the lands themselves and their law and taxes. It comprises 21 titles, but this part may be divided into two sections. First the collectors and inspectors of estates are dealt with, and then the estates or farms themselves. Title 58, de censitoribus et censibus (on tax collectors and taxes), belongs to the collectors. The order is this: since this whole second member concerns chiefly the law on the taxes of rustic estates (for taxes are imposed by civil law only on rustic estates, that is, on farms, not on urban properties, that is, buildings), and since it cannot be known which estates are which, or how much tax each ought to pay to the treasury, unless their condition, fertility or sterility has first been carefully investigated by the inspectors and assessors, it is rightly placed here, before the estates themselves, that title on the inspectors of estates. Title 59, de omni agro deserto (on all deserted land), follows this, and it opens the other and chief part of this second member, concerning the lands and estates themselves. This second part also seems to have two divisions, a general and a specific. In this whole part ten kinds of estates are set out: sterile, border, frontier, castle-held, patrimonial, of the private fund, of the lord's household, the lord's own, the tamiaci (the storehouse estates), and those of the temples and cities. Of these, the first four belong to general titles, and the rest are more specific. The first of these, on deserted and sterile land, is the aforesaid title 59, de omni agro, etc. The reason is that this title is general, as its words, de omni agro, indicate. Yet it could also have treated a kind of estate, namely sterile and deserted lands, but this would have been improper. Moreover, in the last law of the preceding title 58 it is treated of deserted lands assigned by the assessor to others, and so the title de agris desertis is immediately joined to it. The part of this title with the words et quando steriles fertilibus imponuntur (and when sterile lands are laid upon fertile ones) must be understood of the additions which are called in Greek epibolai [ἐπίβολαι], of which there is Novel 166. An epibole [ἐπίβολη], or addition, is the attribution and assignment of a deserted or sterile estate made to a co-owner with the burden of tax. See Haloander in the preface to the Novels, and Cujacius, book 4 of the Observationes, chapter 20. Title 60, de fundis limitrophis (on border estates), follows, which contains three kinds of estates. Border estates are those from which the frontier soldiers (limitanei) are maintained. Frontier estates are those assigned to soldiers and held as their own. Castle estates are those which properly belong to the castle soldiers, that is, those who guard the forts. The reason for the order here is, first, that this title too is partly general, for border estates were of various kinds, private as well as public, fiscal and belonging to cities; and second, just as title 59 concerns sterile estates whose taxes are small, so this title concerns estates which pay no tax at all, that is, which are immune, being either military or serving military purposes. Title 61, de pascuis publicis et privatis (on public and private pasturage), is joined to it. The order is that this title is general, but the earlier ones concern estates, whereas this one concerns meadows and pastures, which, as they are lesser and cheaper estates, come later in order. Title 62, de fundis patrimonialibus (on patrimonial estates), follows. The order is that, now that the general titles on estates have been set out, the specific titles must be placed in turn. Among these the first place belongs to this title 62, on account of the dignity of the prince, to whose patrimony such estates belong. There are four kinds of the prince's estates: patrimonial, of the private fund, of the lord's household, and tamiaci, and these kinds are explained in turn and in order. The reason patrimonial estates are placed first is that they never change ownership; that is, they are sold only by the prince. To the same estate belongs the next title, title 63, de mancipiis et colonis patrimonialibus (on slaves and tenants of the patrimonial estates). For slaves and tenants are as it were parts of estates, just as rustic slaves are counted among the movable goods of estates. L. 4 de diversis temporum praescriptionibus, etc. [l. 4 de diversis temp. praescr., etc.]. Title 64, de fugitivis colonis patrimonialibus (on fugitive patrimonial tenants), is joined to it. For as the earlier title concerns useful and good tenants, so this one concerns worthless tenants, that is, runaways, and is therefore later. To the same title belongs title 65, de collationibus fundorum patrimonialium (on the contributions of patrimonial estates). The order is that the earlier titles concern the law and ownership of patrimonial estates, whereas this one concerns their burden and tax, which, being more burdensome, comes later. So much for the first kind of the prince's estates. We have said that the second kind is the estates of the private fund, on which there is title 66, de functionibus ... pri... (on the duties ... of the private fund). The order by which, among the four kinds of the prince's estates, these private-fund estates hold the second place is this: two kinds are general, that is, they serve the prince for every use, namely patrimonial and private-fund estates, while the other two are special, being devoted not to every use but to a particular one; and special things come after general ones. Title 67, de fundis et aliis rei dominicae (on the estates and other property of the lord's household), follows; this is the third kind of the prince's estates. Cujacius, in his commentary on this title, thinks that the estates of the lord's household are altogether the same as those of the private fund, and for that reason this title on the lord's household is superfluous. Yet there is some difference between the prince's private fund and his household fund: namely, that the private fund is as it were the whole, while the household fund is as it were a part of the private fund, placed chiefly in the prince's bedchamber and storeroom. The estates of the private fund are therefore more general, and those of the household more specific. Title 68, de agris et colonis et mancipiis domus divinae (on lands, tenants and slaves of the imperial household), follows this. The reason has already been set out above under title 65: just as there the title on patrimonial estates is joined to the title on slaves, which are as it were parts of the estates, so here the title on slaves of both kinds of estate, the private fund and the household, is joined to the estates of both kinds. So much for the first, second and third kinds of the prince's estates. The fourth remains, to which title

units.la: 69. de praediis Tamiacis quod genus est maxime speciale & proinde ultimum: pertinet hoc genus fundi tantum ad usum Tamii, hoc est, cellarii & culinae principis. De tamiacis videatur Nov. 20. & 30. Huc sequitur tit. 70. de diversis praed. &c. Ratio ordinis est, quia civitatum & templorum praedia praediis principis, ut dignitate ita & ordine sunt posteriora: & haec duo praediorum genera, puta templorum & civitatum, ex 10. praediorum generibus sunt ultima. Ratio jam est expositia. Hunc autem titulum de diversis praed. &c. sequitur tit. 71. de locatione praed. civil. &c. qui est communis praediorum sive fundorum tam principis quam templorum & civitatum, etiam privatorum, & proinde est posterior: quia communia propriis sunt posteriora, ut saepe dictum. Duo autem capita communia hic ponuntur: locatio praediorum quorumlibet & collatio praediorum. De locatione prius agitur, puta tit. 71. 72. & 73. de collatione posterius, puta tit. 74 & 75. Ratio ordinis cur prius de locatione, & posterius de collatione sive tributis agatur, est quia locatio est magis favorabilis: collatio magis odiosa: tu quia collatio praestari solet & solui tributum ab iis, quibus prædia fuerunt locata, hoc est, à conductoribus & idcirco conductores prius esse debent, quam tributum ab iis exigi. Ad locationem igitur pertinet hic titulus 71. pertinet & eodem tit. 72. de conductor. & procura. qui titulus agit quidem de locatione non cujuslibet prædii, verum prædii fiscalis sive principis & proinde est specialior, atque ita priore generali posterior Est & altera ratio: quia hic titulus est prohibitorius quo scilicet prædiorum principis conductor vel actor prohibetur causas agere aliorum & jubetur tantum curare causas & prædia principis Sic & tit. proximus 73. quib. ad conductionem prædior. &c. pertinet ad locationem, sed prædiorum quoque fiscalium duntaxat & idem quoque est prohibitorius, quo scilicet milites Palatini prohibentur conducere prædia principis. Et hi igitur tituli 72. & 73 sunt prohibitorii. Cur autem hic titulus 73. sit posterior, ratio est quia prior est de iis, qui conducere possunt: hic est de iis, qui conducere non possunt. Et hæc de locatione Nunc de collatione. Ad quam pertinet tit 74. de collat. fund. fisc. quem titulum dixi quoque esse communem fundorum principis templorum & civitatum. Ratio ordinis supra exposita. Huc adjungitur tit. 75. de privileg. domus Aug. &c. Ratio ordinis est, quia, hic titulus ut & prior ad collationem pertinet: sed prior est de præstatione, hic de excusatione & rectè in tit. 74. l. ult. dicitur prædia principis non excusari à muneribus & collationibus ordinariis Excusantur autem ab extraordinariis & sordidis de quibus agitur h. tit. 75. quem sequitur tit. 76. de grege dominico Nam ut mancipia ita & greges sunt veluti partes fundorum aut certè accessiones, & idcirco tractatione de fundis jam absolutà, adjungitur hic titulus de greg. domi i co. Huic quoque adjungitur titul 77. dep e'ar is & domib. dominicus. Nam prædia sunt vel rustica aut urbana, ut ædes & domus, de quibus hactenus est dictum vel urbana, ut ædes & domus, de quibus hic est titulus cui tandem adjungitur ultimus hujus libri in titu 78. de cuprefis ex luco Daphneni. qui planè est specialis: agit enim de proprio & certo loco, eoque celebrimo in suburbiis Antiochiæ qui Daphne dicitur. Et hæc de titulis libri II. qui sunt 78 quod supra initio hujus libri prætermissum est.
units.tr: 69. De praediis Tamiacis, which is the most special kind and therefore the last. This kind of estate pertains only to the use of the Tamius, that is, the prince's cellarer and kitchen. On the Tamiac estates see Nov. 20 and 30. There follows title 70, de diversis praediis, etc. The reason for the order is that the estates of cities and temples are, both in dignity and in order, inferior to the prince's estates; and these two kinds of estates, namely those of temples and of cities, are the last of the ten kinds of estates. The reason is now explained. After this title, de diversis praediis, comes title 71, de locatione praediorum civilium, etc., which is common to the estates, or lands, of the prince, of temples and cities, and also of private persons, and therefore comes later; for common matters come after particular ones, as has often been said. Two common heads are set out here: the letting of estates of any kind and the collection of the tax on estates. The letting is treated first, in titles 71, 72 and 73; the collection afterwards, in titles 74 and 75. The reason for treating the letting first and the collection, or taxes, afterwards is that letting is the more favourable matter and collection the more burdensome, since the tax on estates is usually paid and exacted from those to whom the estates were let, that is, from the lessees; so the lessees must come before the tax is demanded from them. To letting, therefore, belongs this title 71; it also belongs, under the same heading, title 72, de conductoribus et procuratoribus. This title deals indeed with the letting not of any estate whatever, but of a fiscal or princely estate, and is therefore more special, and so later than the earlier, general title. There is also another reason: this title is prohibitory, since it forbids the lessee or agent of the prince's estates to conduct the causes of others, and orders him only to attend to the causes and estates of the prince. So too the next title, 73, quibus ad conductionem praediorum, etc., belongs to letting, but only of fiscal estates, and it is likewise prohibitory, since it forbids the soldiers of the palace to lease the prince's estates. Titles 72 and 73 are therefore prohibitory. As to why this title 73 comes later, the reason is that the earlier one concerns those who may lease, and this one concerns those who may not. So much for letting. Now for the collection. To it belongs title 74, de collationibus fundorum fiscalium, which I said is also common to the estates of the prince, of temples and of cities. The reason for the order has been explained above. To this is joined title 75, de privilegiis domus Augustae, etc. The reason for the order is that this title, like the earlier one, belongs to collation; but the earlier one concerns the performance of the tax, and this one concerns exemption. And rightly, in title 74, last law, it is said that the prince's estates are not exempt from the ordinary public burdens and collections. They are, however, exempt from the extraordinary and menial ones, which are treated in this title 75. This is followed by title 76, de grege dominico. For just as slaves, so also herds are as it were parts of estates, or at least accessories; and so, with the treatment of estates now complete, this title, de grege dominico, is added. To this is also joined title 77, de aedificiis privatis et domibus dominicis. For estates are either rural or urban, such as buildings and houses; of the rural ones enough has been said so far, and this title deals with the urban ones. Finally, the last title of this book, title 78, de cupressis ex luco Daphnensi, is added. It is quite special, for it deals with a particular and definite place, and a very famous one, in the suburbs of Antioch, which is called Daphne. And so much for the titles of the second book, which are 78; this was omitted at the beginning of this book, as noted above.

units.la: Liber XII. Codicis.
units.tr: Liber XII. Codicis.

units.la: NUnc de libro 12 & ultimo hujus Cod. videamus, qui continet titulos 62. & conflatus est ex 3. libris Cod. Theo. puta lib. 6. 7. & 8. dim. d. o. Ut autem hic liber 12. conflatus est ex illis 3. libris, ita & in tria capita potest distribui. I. Namque agitur de dignitatibus II. de re militari. III. de ministris & apparitoribus magistratuum Ordinis ratio inter hæc tria capita est facilis. Nam civilia hujus generis sunt priora militaribus justa quoque & perspicua ratione ministri dignitatum & magistratuum. ultimum locum obtinent. Ergo de capite primo illud admonendum, quod & supra jam diSed tum est libr.10. duobus libtis in Cod agi de magistratibus scil lib.1. & hoc lib. ult. sed alia de causa ac ratione. Nam hoc libro 12 agitur de dignitatibus, quatenus & principi inserviant & praestò sint & quatenus ad eorum, qui sunt in his dignitatibus honores, immunitates & privilegia pertinent sed lib.1. agitur de magistratibus quatenus serviunt jurisdictioni. Dignitatum autem summae species tres hic adferuntur, senatoria, equestris & perfectissimatus, quae tria hic ordine ac deinceps explicantur primo senatoria titul.1. & 30.sequentib. Secundo equestris tit.2. Tertio perfectissimatus tit.33. Ratio ordinis inter has species est perspicua: quia senatoria est prima, & equestris est secunda. d.tit.31.l.1. quod ad senatorem attinet, hunc in eaexplicanda tenuit Tribunianus ordinem, ut primo generaliter de ea dignitate, secundo specialiter de singulis ejus membris: prius de majoribus, posterius de minoribus, & tandem eorum velut adjutoribus explicetur.
units.tr: Now let us look at book 12, the last of this Code, which contains 62 titles and is compiled from three books of the Theodosian Code, namely books 6, 7 and 8 (with the dimissive and the other matters omitted). Just as this twelfth book is compiled from those three books, so too it can be divided into three heads. I. For it deals with dignities; II. with military affairs; III. with the ministers and attendants of magistrates. The order among these three heads is easy to follow: civil matters of this kind come before military ones, and the ministers of dignities and magistrates, which rightly and clearly follow from that reasoning, hold the last place. Therefore concerning the first head, it must be noted what was already said above, that in two books of the Code (the first and this last) magistrates are treated, but for a different reason and in a different way. For in this twelfth book dignities are dealt with insofar as they serve the prince and attend upon him, and insofar as they pertain to the honours, immunities and privileges of those who hold these dignities; but in the first book magistrates are dealt with insofar as they serve jurisdiction. Now three chief kinds of dignity are presented here: senatorial, equestrian and most perfect (perfectissimatus), which three are explained here in order and one after another: first the senatorial (titles 1 and 30 following), second the equestrian (title 2), third the most perfect (title 33). The order among these kinds is clear, because the senatorial is first and the equestrian second. As regards the senator, Tribonian kept to this order in explaining him: first to treat that dignity generally, second to treat its individual members specifically, the greater ones first, the lesser ones afterwards, and finally those who are, as it were, their assistants.

units.la: Quare titulus primus hujus libri de dignit. quia est generalis, primum locum obtinet. Sed tamen ita est generalis, ut proprie & perspicue de specie senatoria subeo agatur, quema modum & in n.ff.t.1.t.1.lib.4. de obligat. qua ex del. est generaliter coceptus sed sub eo perspicue agitur de specie delicti, furto, ut & aliàs admonuimus. Huic adjungitur titulus secundus, de praetor. & honore praetura, &c. Ratio ordinis, hoc est, cur post generalem titulum inter species hic fit primus: & de Consule (qui tamen ut & alii, praetorem dignitate superat) sic secundus & posterior: ratio inquam, est, quia praetura quatenus de eahic agitur, erat illo tempore quoddam velut omnis senatoriae dignitatis, putain ludis Circensibus & scenicis exhibendis, ad quos soliti erant sumptus facere praetores. Cogebantur quoque praetores facti ordini senatorio inferre quaedam tributa, sive collationes aut functiones, puta glebae follis, & 7. solidorum: Sed ea hic tolluntur, ludorum onera non tolluntur. Glebaautem interdum dicitur aurum glebale: quia erat species tributi, quod in auro praetores ratione suorum bonorum immobilium sive praediorum, hoc est, glebarum soluebant senatui. Follis autem nummorum sed minutorum species ut solidi majorum. Hunc titulum sequitur titulus tertius de confulib.& nonspargendis, &c. qui titulus et si de plurib concipitur tamen tantum de duobus tractat cosulatu & patriciatu: de reliquis tractatur infra, titulo proximo. Cur autem in ipso titulo sive inscriptione eorum fiat mentio, haec est ratio: quia patricii eam dignitatem non consequuntur, nisi prius aut fuerint Coff. aut praefecti aut magistratus. Et haec quoque est ratio, cur in hoc titulo sive inscriptione primum consul, & postremo patricius ponatur, cum tamen patriciatus dignitas major sit dignitate consulari. Cur autem de Coff. statim agatur post praetores, & ante praesectos pretorio & urbi, qui tamen primum in consessu senatus locum tenet, ut supra dictum lib.1. ratio haec est: tum quia de praetoribus modo dictu est, eos ad ludos & tributa senatui praestanda sumptus & pecuniam conferre solitos(quain re Coll praetoribus quadantenus sunt similes:nam & Coll pecuniam aliáq; missiliacogebantur spargere vulgo,ut notum ex §. pen. Inst. de rer. divis. quorum missilium usus hic interdicitur Coll & jubentur eam pecuniam conferre ad refectionem aquaeductuum publicorum,) tum quia consulatus est antiquissima dignitas,& proinde primo ponitur, tam hic, quam in ff Hunc sequitur tit. 4. de praefect. praetor. sive urbis, &c. quae tres dignitates continentur: praefectura praetorii praefectura urbis, & magistrorum militum quae singulae suos habent titulos supra lib. 1. Huic adjungitur tit. 5. de praepos. fac. cubic. Recte de praepositis: sunt enim duo cubicula Augusta & Augustae: sic & praefecti praetorio sunt plures, & magistri militum sunt duo, praetores sunt 3. Coll 2. praefectus urbi unus. Sed haec disputatio huc non pertinet. Quod ad ordinis rationem attinet ea haec est ad titulum quintum huic: quod ut priores puta Coll praefecti &c. sunt illustres (qui item et tres dignitates gradus est primus) ita & hi praepositi, l. ult. in sin. & h. tit. quae sequitur tit. 6. de quaestorib. & magistr. offic. &c. quo titulo quarto, dignitates continentur quae suum quoq; habent distinctum titulum supra lib. 1. Et sunt hae quoque omnes illustres: sed prioribus minores, ut dictum est libro primo. Unde ratio ordinis intelligitur. Illud mirari quis posset praepositos cubiculi praeferri quaestoribus & magistris officiorum sed saepe ordo dignitatum pendet ex voluntate principis, & non ratione. Hactenus de dignitatibus illustribus: nunc de minoribus quae dicuntur spectabiles. Clarissimae autem dicuntur tam de illustribus quam de spectabilibus. Spectabilium igitur primum locum obtinent primicerii: tit. 7. de primicer. &c. tum quia magna horum erat dignitas, (sunt enim primi secretarii principis qui saepe tribuni & notarii dicuntur, tum quia hi summi notarii erant velut adjutores quaestoris, hoc est, cancellarii de quibus proxime dictum. Huic adjicitur titulus octavus, ut dignit. ordo servetur: imo potius hic interjicitur tantum, occasione l. ult. tit. 7. arrepta, ut perspicuum est ex verbis d. l. in qua Imperator graviter vetat conturbari seriem graduum publicqua, ut dixi, occasione generaliter statim jubentur servari do dignitatum in hoc titulo 8. Alioqui hic titulus ut generalis poterat poni initio hujus libri, ut est positus in Cod. Theod. lib. 6. Inter spectabiles secundo loco ponuntur magistri sacrorum scriniorum, tit. 9. de mag. scrin. Ratio ordinis est quia ut priores, puta secretarii ita & hi magistri scriniorum tractabant scripta, ut pistolas, edicta, rescripta, annotationes principis. Hunc sequitur titulus decimus de comit. consistorianis, qui ite sunt spectabiles, lege secunda, hoc titulo. Ut autem ratio ordinis melius intelligatur admonendum est comitivam dignitatem esse primi ordinis spectabilium, cujus multae sunt species; quae hic ordine aliquot exponuntur, ut hoc titulo decimo. Ratio autem cur comites consistoriani ponantur post magistros scriniorum est, quia magistrorum erat major dignitas, quod ex eo intelligitur, quod hi comites stabant, cum priores, ni fallor, sederent in consistorio principis. Cur autem inter comites primi ordinis ponantur primo hi consistoriani, ratio videtur quia major eorum esset dignitas, utputa quibus pateret aditus ad consistorium principis. Proximus huic est titulus undecimus, de comitib. & tribunis scholarum. Erant olim undecim scholæ, hoc est, corpora sive collegia militum & ministrorum quorundam principis Ratio ordinis, quia ut priores comites intersunt consistorio ita illi epulis principis, quæ non levis erat dignitas, & facultas, sive gratia Eadem & comitibus stabuli, & quibus erat cura palatii, dabatur: idcirco hic tres dignitates conjunguntur in hoc titulo. Hunc sequitur titulus duodecimus, de comit. rei milit. Semper enim civilibus militaria postponuntur. Cui adjungitur titulus 13. de comitibus & Archiatris sacri palatii. Ratio ordinis, cur Archiatri comitiva honorati postponuntur comitibus rei militaris. hæc esse videtur tum quia comites rei militaris interdum vicem gerebant illustrium magistratuum militum, tum quia archiatri non semper comitiva primi ordinis, sed interdum secundi donantur. l. 1. supra de profess. & medic. Hunc sequitur tit. 14. de comit. qui provinc. regunt. Ratio ordinis est, quia principalia civilibus sunt posteriora cui adjungitur titul. 15. de profess. in urbe Const. Ratio ordinis videtur, cur hi inquam prioribus sint posteriores, tum quia isti non nisi tarde & sero, hoc est, post 10. demum annos professionis: sed priores statim, aut certe citius comitivam consequuntur nullo tempore præscripto: tum quia priorum dignitas sive comitiva est actu, hæc professorum tantum est codicillaris illi inquam aliquid agunt, vel apud principem vel nomine principis, hi nihil tale agunt, sed tantum artes profitentur. Codicillaris autem dignitas posterior est ea quæ est actu, l. 5. C. Th. de honorar. codicill. Dictum est hactenus de dignitatibus senatoriis majoribus & minoribus, hoc est, illustrium & spectabilium, quæ sunt duæ partes in hoc primo membro quod diximus de dignitate senatoria. Restat tertia pars, qua continentur aliæ dignitates, quas minimas vocare licet: quæ potius administrat sunt, & adjutrices priorum, quarum minimarum dignitatem aliæ ipsi principi, aliæ majoribus dignitatibus sive magistratibus aderant, & quodammodo serviebant quædine pro dignitatum serie hic exponuntur. Primum igitur est tit. 16. de silentiariis, &c. qui sunt excubitores ad consistorium & cubiculum principis atque ita proximi ei, & intimi in comitatu sive palatio, eaque de causa primi hic ponuntur. Huic proximus est titulus 17. de domesticis & protectoribus. qui silentiarii sunt posteriores, tum quia horum dignitas sive militia erat magis armata tum quia isti non tantum domi, sed etiam foris hoc est in acie aut bello principi adessent. Protectores enim vel domi & in palatio (qui propriè domestici) vel in bello (qui generali nomine dicuntur hic protectores) principis latus tuentur, vulgo stipatores Hunc sequitur tit. 18. de præpos. labbor. quia hi sunt species protectorum. Erat autem vexillum Cæsaris, quod laborum dicitur, & interdum labarum, cui deferendo, deportando, & custodiendæ ftodiendo aliquot ex comitatu Cæsaris præerant. Hunc sequitur tit.19. de proximus sacror.scrinior. Ratio ordinis quia hi sunt prioribus dignitate proximi, quod intelligi potest ex eo ordine, quem hic Tribun.tenet. Nam hæ dignitates ut ita dicam servientes, eo ponuntur ordine, quo dominantes dignitates verb gratia, præfectus prætorio est primus dominantium, eoque longe posterior præpositus cubiculo: Jam magistri sacrorum scriniorum ut & priores puta præpositi laborum &c. pertinent potissimum ad præfectos prætorio. Et hi magistri scriniorum ad eos pertinent, ad præfectos inquam prætorio, & præpositos cubiculo. Sed hi proximi scriniorum pertinent potissimum ad quæstorem palatii, qui quæstor præfecto & præposito cubiculi est inferior. Sic quæstore inferiore est magister officiorum & hinc est, quod proximos scriniorum qui ad quæstorem proximè sequantur agentes in rebus, qui ad magistrum officiorum proprie pertinent de quibus est titul.20. de agent. in rebus qui & inde dicuntur magistriani. Ad has autem agentes in rebus pertinent quoq; tit. 21 de præpos.agent. in reb. & tit.22. de princ. agent. in rei. qui duo tituli differunt: hoc est, differt præpositus à principe: nam præpositus erat ipsorum caput, quod tamen caput suberat superiori capiti, puta magistro officiorum. Sed principis sive principatus agentium in rebus tantum erat honos, seu titulus, qui dari solet his agentibus officio defunctis tanquam præmii loco, quemadmodum veterani dicuntur functi militia: plus igitur præpositura, & munus erat principatus: idcirco titulus, de præpositis prior est, tit. de princip. &c. Ad hos agentes in rebus pertinet quoq; tit 23. de curiof. & statione. Nam & hi sunt numero agentium in rebus, & velut species eorum Curabant enim isti tantum cursum publicum. Hos 4. titulos de agentibus in rebus sequitur tit.24. de palat. sacrar. largit. Ratio est, quia ut comites sacrarum largitionum & comites rei privatæ sunt posteriores dignitate quæstore & magistro officiorum, ut supra dictum lib.1. tit.30. & 4.legg. ita & paulatim isti, puta sacrarum largitionum, hoc est, illi qui comitib. illis inserviunt, quodammodo sunt posteriores illis, qui pertinent ad curam quæstoris & magistri. Recte autem hic dicuntur Palatini sacrarum largitionum. Nam sunt & alii Palatini, hoc est, nomen Palatini interdum est generale & commune omnium dignitatum servientium in palatio principis. Hunc titulum sequitur tit. 25. de stratorib. Ratio ordinis est, quia hactenus dictum est de illis officiis, quæ sunt civilia & urbana: nunc de iis, quæ sunt provincialia, ut est officiū stratorum qui pertinent ad præsides provinciæ & gerebant curam equorum. Huic adjungitur tit.26. de Castrenfianis & ministerianis. Ratio ordinis est, quia priores omnes pertinent & serviunt dignitatib. illustribus & superioribus sed hi serviunt inferioribus, puta cuidam qui dicitur Castrensis sacri palatii: & erat tantum spectabilis hic Castrensis: unde & Castrēsiani dicūtur, qui quia varia ministeria in palatio principis obibat, & ministeriani sūt dicti, ut pinacernæ pistores, coqu, vestitores, pares, pædagogia, sive pueri pædagogiani. Horum quoque ministeriorum in numero erant decani hoc est fuerunt curatores qui alias latinè Vespillones, & interdum Græco vocabulo κοσμάτω dicuntur, ad quos pertinet tit. 27. de Decanis. Mensores quoque agrorum erant in numero ministerianorum, de quibus hic est tit. 28. de mensoribus. Cur autem de decanis & mensoribus agatur ultimo loco, & generaliter de ministerianis, ratio est, quia ministeriani erant fere viliores, & decani curabant funera & mortuos, propterea & sunt posteriores. Ultimi autem sunt mensores quia mensorum officium ad agros pertinet: rustica autem urbanis sunt posteriora. Hactenus expositi sunt tituli de singulis dignitatibus, maximis, mediis & minimis, dico ad senatoriam dignitatem pertinentibus, species inquam illarum singulatim sunt expositæ. Eos igitur titulos speciales sequuntur 3 tituli omnium illarum dignitatum communes. Specialibus enim & propriis communia sunt posteriora ut scæpè dictum est. Ex his titulis communibus primum locum tenet tit. 29. de privileg. eor. qui in fatro palat. mil. Ratio est quia hic titulus est planè generalis planeq; communis omnium, puta officiorum palatinorum. Quæ sequitur tit 30. de privilegiis scholarum. Ratio ordinis est maximè propter militudinem, videlicet de privilegiis: ut enim prior titulus, ita & hic agit de privilegiis: sed prior est de privilegiis palatinorum, hoc est eorum qui in officiis dignitatum sunt: hic titulus 30. est de privilegiis scholarum. Differunt autem scholares à palatinis, l. 2. supra tit. 28. Communis quoque est tit. 31. de Castrensi omnium palat. pecul. Ratio ordinis est, quia ut titulus 29. est maximè generalis puta de omnibus palatinis, & de omnibus eorum privilegiis, ita & hic titulus 31. est generalis quidem de omnibus Palatinis, sed tantum de uno privilegio puta de eorum peculio castrensi: alioqui peculiū castrense proprium est militum: sed hoc privilegium datur etiam palatinis: quia & ipsi sunt milites. Est enim duplex militia: armata, quæ proprie; & urbana sive palatina, quæ minus proprie. Et hæc est ratio ordinis, cur hic titulus 31. inter communes sit ultimus, quia de una specie privilegii agat: tum quia agat de peculio. At peculium est accessio quædam, & proinde posteriori loco poni solet. Hactenus de primo membro hujus primi capitis (quod membrū de senatoria dignitate tributum in dignitates majores, minores & minimas) explicatum est. Alterum hujus primi capitis membrum diximus de equestri dignitate, quo pertinet tit. 32. de equestri dignitate. quem sequitur ti. 33. de perfectissimatus dignitate, qui titulus dignitatis ut & alii (puta egregiatus, l. 1. C. Th. de murilegulis) priorib. dignitatib. (puta senatoria & equestri) & dignitate & gradu & origine. (Nam à Constantino hic titulus introductus videtur) est posterior: & proinde in hoc capite primo ultimum locum tenet. Proximum nunc est alterum caput de arte militari quod 16. titulis continetur. Eorum i est tit. 34. qui militare possent vel non. Ratio ordinis est, quia prius de peditibus quam de re sit agendum, ut & alias dictum ad titulum 22. supra libri 6. Ad personas quoq; pertinet tit.35. Negotiatores ne militent qui titulus est (specialis hoc est, negociatorum proprius, & quia est prohibitorius, merito est posterior illo. Quem sequitur tit.36. de re militari. Personarum enim tractatione, sequitur jam altera de re ipsa, & hic titulus est plane generalis, quae sequitur tit. 37. de Castrensi peculio, militari & praefectiani. (ita apparitores praefecti praetorio & praefecti urbi dicuntur.) Ratio ordinis est, quia peculium Castrense colligitur ex stipendiis & donativis de quibus stipendiis dictum est titulo priori. 36. Hunc titulum 37. sequuntur sex tituli, de his, quae militibus praeter stipendia solent deberi aut dari, ut sunt annonae militares, vestes, hospitii, salgamu & commeatus. De annonis primum agitur, puta tit. 38. de rogat. mil. annona. Ratio est, quia alimentorum (annonae enim hic sunt panis, vinum, acetum, caro, lardum & aliae id genus species) usus militi ad vitam maxime est necessarius & primus. Ad annonas quoq; pertinet tit. 39. de exactione, collation. & translation. milit. annonar. sed prior est generalis, hic est specialis, tantum de exactione & proinde posterior. Altera sequitur vestis, tit. 40. de militare vestes quia ejus proxima est necessitas. Inde hospitium tit. 41. de metatis & Epidemeticis. Metata sunt hospitia, quae metatores die Iuriter militibus adsignant. Sed quidam provinciales, ne milites in domos suas reciperent, solent saepe se pecunia redimere, data clam pecunia metatoribus quam pecuniam hic Epidemetica, quasi hospitale dicas, sed ea Epidemetica hic prohibetur l. ult. Ad hospitium quodammodo etiam pertinet tit. 42. de salgamo hospitis, b. non praestando, &c. Salgami nomine continentur herbae conditae, ut brassica, beta enula, &c. sed milites eo nomine non herbas, sed alia ab hospitibus exigebant puta culcitras oleum &c. quod hic prohibetur. Atq; hic titulus est prohibitorius & proinde posterior. Tandem agitur de commeatu tit. 43. Ratio ordinis est quia commeatus est quasi finis & dimissio militiae. Dico quasi, quia verus finis dicitur missio sed commeatu miles tantum ad tempus dimittitur & potestatem accipit visendi suos, curandi sua, &c. Hunc titulum sequitur tit. 44. de Tyronib. Ratio ordinis est quia in scholis militum semper Tyrones posteriore loco ponuntur, inquit l. ult. hoc ti. Cui adjungitur tit. 45. de littor. & stin. custod. Ratio est quia custodia littorum per milites fiebat, sed hoc titulo prohibetur delictum quoddam quo mercesillicitae ad barbaros deferuntur, de quo delicto supra lib. 4 t. 63. & t. 41. Quare cum sit prohibitorius, & agat de militib. littoru custodibus (quae sunt inferiores militibus in acie versantibus, de qb. sup.) merito illis postponuntur. Huic adjungitur tit. 46 de defens. & occult. eor. de militibus agunt. Ad rem tamen militarem etiam pertinet tit. 47. de veteranis Ratio est, quia priores tituli sunt de his qui militant hi est de iis qui militarunt. Cui adjungitur tit 48. de filiis officialium militarium, &c. Ratio ordinis est perspicua: priores enim tituli sunt de militibus & veteranis hi de eorum jam defunctorum filiis, ut parentum praedia & officia, sive militias assequantur. Est & altera ratio, quia hic titulus agit de
units.tr: Therefore the first title of this book, On dignities, since it is general, holds the first place. Yet it is so general that it deals properly and clearly with the senatorial rank, just as in n.ff.t.1.t.1.lib.4. On obligations arising from delict was conceived in general terms, but under it the species of delict, theft, is dealt with clearly, as we have also noted elsewhere. To this is joined the second title, On the praetors and the praetorship, etc. The reason for the order, that is, why after the general title the first of the species is placed here, and why the consul (who nevertheless, like others, surpasses the praetor in dignity) is placed second and later, is this: the praetorship, insofar as it is treated here, was at that time a kind of foundation of all senatorial dignity, namely in providing the Circensian and scenic games, for which praetors were accustomed to make expenditures. Praetors who had been made members of the senatorial order were also compelled to pay certain taxes, contributions or duties, for instance the gleba and the follis of seven solidi. But these are abolished here, while the burdens of the games are not abolished. The gleba, moreover, is sometimes called gleba aurum (the gold of the soil), because it was a kind of tax which praetors paid to the senate in gold on account of their immovable goods, that is, their landed estates. The follis, however, is a sum of money, a small coin, a species of the larger solidus. The third title follows this one, On consuls and on not sprinkling, etc. Although this title is worded as if it concerned many matters, it treats of only two: the consulate and the patriciate. The rest are dealt with below, in the next title. Why mention of them is made in the title itself, or in its heading, is for this reason: patricians do not attain that dignity unless they have first been consuls, prefects or magistrates. And this is also the reason why, in this title and its heading, the consul is placed first and the patrician last, although the dignity of patrician is greater than the consular dignity. Why the consuls are treated immediately after the praetors, and before the praefects of the praetorium and of the city (who nevertheless hold the first place in the senate's assembly, as was said above in book 1), the reason is this: first, because we have just said of the praetors that they were accustomed to contribute money and expenses for the games and for the taxes payable to the senate (in which respect consuls are somewhat similar to praetors, for consuls too were compelled to scatter money and other largesses among the people, as is known from §. pen. Inst. On the divisions of things; the use of these largesses is here forbidden to consuls, and they are ordered to contribute that money to the repair of the public aqueducts); and second, because the consulate is the most ancient dignity, and therefore is placed first, here as in the Digest. There follows the fourth title, On the praefects of the praetorium or of the city, etc., in which three dignities are contained: the praefecture of the praetorium, the praefecture of the city, and the masters of the soldiers, each of which has its own title above in book 1. To this is joined the fifth title, On the officers in charge of the bedchamber. Rightly is it said "of the officers" (praepositi), for there are two imperial bedchambers, that of the Augustus and that of the Augusta; likewise there are several praefects of the praetorium, two masters of soldiers, three praetors, two consuls, one praefect of the city. But this discussion does not belong here. As for the reason for the order, it is this, with respect to the fifth title: just as the earlier ones, namely the consuls and the praefects, are illustrious (and these three dignities are of the first rank), so also these officers in charge are illustrious, as in the last law in the end and in this title; this is followed by the sixth title, On the quaestors and the masters of the offices, etc., in which the fourth title contains dignities which also have their own separate title above in book 1. All these too are illustrious, but lesser than the former, as was said in book 1. Thus the reason for the order is understood. One might wonder why the officers of the bedchamber are placed before the quaestors and the masters of the offices, but the order of dignities often depends on the will of the prince and not on reason. So far concerning the illustrious dignities; now concerning the lesser ones, which are called spectabiles. Those called clarissimi, moreover, are said of both the illustrious and the spectabiles. Among the spectabiles, therefore, the first place is held by the primicerii, title 7, On the primicerii, etc., both because their dignity was great (for they are the first secretaries of the prince, who are often called tribunes and notaries), and because these chief notaries were, as it were, assistants to the quaestor, that is, chancellors, of whom we spoke just before. To this is added the eighth title, so that the order of dignities may be preserved; indeed this title is rather inserted here only on the occasion of the last law of title 7, as is clear from the words of that law, in which the emperor sternly forbids the order of public grades to be disturbed; and so, on this occasion, he at once orders in general that the order of dignities be kept, in this eighth title. Otherwise this title, being general, could have been placed at the beginning of this book, as it is placed in the Theodosian Code, book 6. Among the spectabiles, in the second place, are placed the masters of the sacred offices, title 9, On the masters of the scrinia. The reason for the order is that, like the earlier ones, namely the secretaries, so these masters of the scrinia handled documents, such as letters, edicts, rescripts and the emperor's annotations. This is followed by the tenth title, On the consistorial counts, who are also spectabiles, by the second law of this title. To understand the reason for the order better, it must be noted that the dignity of count is of the first rank among the spectabiles, and it has many species, several of which are set out here in order in this tenth title. The reason why the consistorial counts are placed after the masters of the scrinia is that the masters had the greater dignity, which is understood from the fact that these counts stood while the former, unless I am mistaken, sat in the prince's consistory. And why among the counts of the first rank these consistorial counts are placed first, the reason seems to be that their dignity was greater, since they had access to the prince's consistory. Next to this is the eleventh title, On the counts and tribunes of the schools. There were formerly eleven schools, that is, bodies or companies of soldiers and certain servants of the prince. The reason for the order: as the earlier counts attend the consistory, so these attend the prince's banquets, which was no small dignity and privilege, or favour. The counts of the stables, and those to whom the care of the palace was entrusted, were given the same; for this reason three dignities are joined in this title. Next follows the twelfth title, On the counts of the military affairs, for civil offices are always placed after military ones. To this is added the thirteenth title, On the counts and archiatri of the sacred palace. The reason why the archiatri, who hold the rank of count, are placed after the counts of military affairs seems to be, first, that the counts of military affairs sometimes performed the role of the illustrious masters of soldiers, and second, that archiatri are not always given the rank of count of the first order, but sometimes of the second, see law 1 above, On professors and physicians. This is followed by the fourteenth title, On the counts who govern provinces. The reason for the order is that the provincial offices come after the civil ones. To this is joined the fifteenth title, On professors in the city of Constantinople. The reason for the order seems to be, why I say these are placed after the former, first because these attain the rank only slowly and late, that is, only after ten years of teaching, whereas the former attain it at once, or at least sooner, with no prescribed time; second, because the dignity or count's rank of the former is actual, while that of professors is only honorary by codicil; the former do something, either before the prince or in the prince's name, while these do nothing of the kind but merely profess their arts. An honorary dignity by codicil, moreover, is posterior to that which is actual, see law 5 of the Theodosian Code, On honorary codicils. So far has been said of the senatorial dignities, greater and lesser, that is, of the illustrious and the spectabiles, which are the two parts of the first member of this first chapter, which we have called the senatorial dignity. There remains a third part, in which the other dignities are contained, which we may call the least; these are rather administrators and assistants of the former. Of these least dignities, some were attendants of the prince himself, others served the greater dignities or magistracies and in a certain way were their servants; they are set out here in the order of their dignities. The first, therefore, is the sixteenth title, On the silentiaries, etc., who are the sentinels of the consistory and the bedchamber of the prince, and thus closest to him and most intimate in his retinue or palace; for this reason they are placed first here. Next to them is the seventeenth title, On the domestics and protectors, which come after the silentiaries, both because their dignity or service was more militant, and because these were present with the prince not only at home but also abroad, that is, in the field or in war. For the protectors, whether at home and in the palace (who are properly called domestics), or in war (who in general are here called protectors), guard the prince's side; commonly they are called stipatores, attendants. This is followed by the eighteenth title, On the officers in charge of the labarum, because these are a species of protectors. The standard of the Caesar, which is called the laborum, and sometimes the labarum, was carried, conveyed and guarded by some members of the Caesar's retinue, who were in charge of it. This is followed by the nineteenth title, On the nearest of the sacred scrinia. The reason for the order is that these are next in dignity to the former, which can be understood from the order which Tribonian observes here. For these dignities, so to speak, are subordinate, and are placed in the order of the dominant dignities: for example, the praefect of the praetorium is first among the dominant, and the officer in charge of the bedchamber is far below him. Now the masters of the sacred scrinia, like the earlier ones, such as the officers in charge of the labarum, pertain chiefly to the praefects of the praetorium; and these masters of the scrinia pertain to them, I mean to the praefects of the praetorium and the officers in charge of the bedchamber. But the nearest of the scrinia pertain chiefly to the quaestor of the palace, who is lower than the praefect and the officer in charge of the bedchamber. Below the quaestor is the master of the offices, and hence it is that the nearest of the scrinia, who follow most closely the quaestor, are the agents in rebus, who properly pertain to the master of the offices; these are the subject of the twentieth title, On the agents in rebus, who are also from this origin called magistriani. To these agents in rebus pertain also the twenty-first title, On the officers in charge of the agents in rebus, and the twenty-second title, On the chiefs of the agents in rebus. These two titles differ: that is, the officer in charge differs from the chief, for the officer in charge was their head, yet this head was subject to a higher head, namely the master of the offices. But the chiefship, or the principate, of the agents in rebus was only an honour or title, which is usually given to these agents when they have finished their service, as a kind of reward, just as veterans are called those who have completed their military service. Therefore the officership was greater, and the principate was an office and duty; hence the title On the officers in charge comes before the title On the chiefs, etc. To these agents in rebus pertains also the twenty-third title, On the couriers and the stations, for these too are among the number of agents in rebus, and are as it were a species of them; they were in charge only of the public post. These four titles on the agents in rebus are followed by the twenty-fourth title, On the palatine officers of the sacred largesses. The reason is that just as the counts of the sacred largesses and the counts of the private estate are lower in dignity than the quaestor and the master of the offices, as was said above in book 1, titles 30 and 4, laws, so also these palatine officers, namely of the sacred largesses, that is, those who serve these counts, are in a certain way lower than those who belong to the charge of the quaestor and the master. Rightly, moreover, are they here called palatines of the sacred largesses; for there are other palatines too, since the name of palatine is sometimes general and common to all dignities serving in the prince's palace. This title is followed by the twenty-fifth title, On the stratores. The reason for the order is that up to now what has been said concerns those offices which are civil and urban; now we come to those which are provincial, such as the office of the stratores, who belonged to the governors of provinces and had charge of the horses. To this is joined the twenty-sixth title, On the castrenses and ministeriales. The reason for the order is that all the earlier ones belong to and serve the illustrious and higher dignities, but these serve the lower, for example a certain officer called the castrensis of the sacred palace; and this castrensis was only a spectabilis. Hence those too are called castrenses, who, because they performed various ministries in the prince's palace, were called ministeriales, such as the cupbearers, bakers, cooks, dressers, pages and the pedagogical attendants, or boys of the pedagogium. Among these ministries were also the decani, that is, the undertakers, who in Latin are called vespillones, and sometimes in Greek are called cosmetae [κοσμήται]; to them pertains the twenty-seventh title, On the decani. Land surveyors also belonged to the ministerial staff, of whom there is the twenty-eighth title, On surveyors. As for the reason why the decani and surveyors are treated last, and the ministeriales in general, it is that the ministeriales were for the most part of lower rank, and the decani looked after funerals and the dead, and for that reason they are posterior. The surveyors come last because the office of surveyor pertains to fields, and rustic matters are posterior to urban ones. So far have been set out the titles on the individual dignities, the greatest, middle and least, I mean those pertaining to the senatorial dignity; the species of these, each in turn, have been expounded. After those special titles follow three titles common to all those dignities. Of these common titles, the first place is held by the twenty-ninth title, On the privileges of those who are in the palatine service and the military. The reason is that this title is plainly general and common to all, that is, to all the palatine offices. It is followed by the thirtieth title, On the privileges of the schools. The reason for the order is chiefly the resemblance, namely that both concern privileges: for as the earlier title, so this one treats of privileges; but the earlier is on the privileges of the palatines, that is, of those who hold offices of dignity, while this thirtieth title is on the privileges of the schools. The schools differ from the palatines, see law 2 above, title 28. The thirty-first title, On the castrense peculium of all the palatines, is also common. The reason for the order is that just as the twenty-ninth title is most general, namely concerning all palatines and all their privileges, so this thirty-first title is general too, concerning all palatines, but only one privilege, namely their castrense peculium; for the castrense peculium is properly the privilege of soldiers, but this privilege is given also to palatines, because they too are soldiers. For military service is twofold: armed, which is so properly, and urban or palatine, which is less properly. And this is the reason for the order, why this thirty-first title is last among the common ones: because it treats of one species of privilege; and also because it treats of a peculium. A peculium is an accessory of a kind, and therefore is usually placed in a later position. So far has been explained the first member of this first chapter, which member assigns the senatorial dignity to the greater, lesser and least dignities. We said that the second member of this first chapter concerns the equestrian dignity, to which belongs the thirty-second title, On the equestrian dignity, followed by the thirty-third title, On the dignity of perfectissimus, a title which, like others (for instance egregiatus, see law 1 of the Theodosian Code, On the sellers of ...), is posterior to the earlier dignities, the senatorial and the equestrian, in dignity, rank and origin (for this title seems to have been introduced by Constantine); and therefore in this first chapter it holds the last place. Next is the second chapter, on the military art, which is contained in sixteen titles. The first of these is the thirty-fourth title, Who may or may not serve in the army. The reason for the order is that it is necessary to speak of the infantry before the matter itself, as was also said elsewhere at title 22 above in book 6. Title 35 also pertains to persons, Let not merchants serve in the army, which title is special, that is, peculiar to merchants, and because it is prohibitive, it is rightly posterior to the former. It is followed by the thirty-sixth title, On military affairs. For after the treatment of persons, there follows the other, concerning the thing itself, and this title is wholly general. This is followed by the thirty-seventh title, On the castrense, military and praefectian peculium (for so the apparitores of the praefect of the praetorium and of the praefect of the city are called). The reason for the order is that the castrense peculium is gathered from the stipends and gifts, of which stipends was spoken in the earlier title, 36. This thirty-seventh title is followed by six titles, on those things which are customarily owed or given to soldiers besides their stipends, such as the military rations, clothing, lodging, salgamum and supplies. Of rations the first is treated, namely the thirty-eighth title, On the requisition of military rations. The reason is that the use of foodstuffs (for the rations here are bread, wine, vinegar, meat, bacon and other such species) is for the soldier most necessary and primary for life. To the rations pertains also the thirty-ninth title, On the exaction, collation and transfer of military rations; but the former is general, while this one is special, dealing only with exaction, and therefore posterior. The other is followed by clothing, the fortieth title, On military clothing, because its necessity is next. Then lodging, the forty-first title, On the quartering and the Epidemetica. Metata are lodgings which the metatores assign daily to soldiers. But some provincials, so that soldiers should not be received into their houses, often redeemed themselves with money, secretly giving money to the metatores; this money is here called epidemetica, as if you might say "hospitable", but that epidemetica is forbidden here in the last law. To lodging in some way also pertains the forty-second title, On salgamum, which the host need not supply, etc. Salgamum is the name for pickled herbs, such as cabbage, beet, elecampane, and so on; but under that name the soldiers exacted not herbs but other things from hosts, such as mattresses, oil, etc., which is forbidden here. And this title is prohibitive and therefore posterior. Finally, the forty-third title treats On supplies. The reason for the order is that the supply is as it were the end and discharge of military service. I say "as it were", because the true end is called discharge, but on leave the soldier is only dismissed for a time and receives permission to visit his family, look after his affairs, and so on. This title is followed by the forty-fourth title, On recruits. The reason for the order is that in the schools of soldiers recruits are always placed in a later position, as the last law of this title says. To it is joined the forty-fifth title, On the coasts and the guards of the coasts. The reason is that the guarding of the coasts was done by soldiers, but this title forbids a certain offence by which illicit wares are carried to the barbarians, concerning which offence see above book 4, titles 63 and 41. Therefore, since it is prohibitive, and treats of the soldiers who guard the coasts (who are inferior to the soldiers engaged in battle, concerning whom above), it is rightly placed after them. To this is joined the forty-sixth title, On the defence and concealment of them, which treats of soldiers. Yet the forty-seventh title, On veterans, also pertains to military matters. The reason is that the earlier titles concern those who serve, and this one concerns those who have served. To it is joined the forty-eighth title, On the sons of military officers, etc. The reason for the order is plain: the earlier titles concern soldiers and veterans, and this one concerns the sons of such men, now deceased, who obtain their fathers' estates and offices, or their military posts. units.la: mortuis & proinde est plane ultimus. Additur tamen tit. 49. de oblatione vetorum Cujus ordinis ratio intelligi non potest nisi ex C. Theod. lib. 7. qui liber totus est de re militari, & in fine duo sunt tit. unus de oblat. ne equorum, alter de oblatione votorum, sed Tribun. hunc ultimum retinuit, alterum reliquit. Hrc de secundo cujus libri. Reliquat tertium & ultimum cap quod dixi mus de apparitoribus & ministris magistratuum. Observanda autem est elegans Codicis Oeconomia. Nam ut dignitates quarum minime in jure scripta dicuntur militiae civilis) & militiae tam civiles, qui armatae ad principe potissimum pertinet, eiq; sunt adjutrices, atq; idcirco priori loco ponuntur: ita nunc posteriores agitur de iis, qui sunt administri & serviunt ipsis dignitatib. sive magistratibus. Continetur autem hoc cap. 15. tit. in quib. idem ordo tenetur apparitorum qui est ipsorum quibus apparent, magistratuum suorum. Quare cum inter dignitates & magistratus primus sit praefectus praetorio, ut supra dixi lib. 1. recte hic primum agitur de iis qui huic praefecto apparet de quib. agitur h. tit. 50. 51. 52. & 53. Nam tit. 50. de numerariis adiutoribus & c. est potissimum, & principaliter agit de, excelsae sedis hoc est, praefecti praetorio numerariis, consequenter tamen & de aliorum magistratuum numerariis. Cur autem de his numerariis inter praefectiones & apparitores praefecti, primum agitur ratio est quia isti aliis praeferuntur, propterea quod sunt scribae quorum honestior est ordo (inquit Cic. in Verr.) quam aliorum apparitorum. Numerarii enim rationes & chartas in officio magistratuum tractabant: tractarii item, quorum erant velut administri quidam & adjutores chartularii, scriniarii, exceptores. Est & altera ratio cur de his primo agatur quia sunt communes omnium magistratuum, sive quia hic tit. ad communes magistratus pertinet. Huic adjungitur tit. 51. de cursu publ. & angariis &c. Ratio ordinis est, quia ut numerarii, de quibus modo dictum ita & cursus publici ministri pertinent ad cur-am praefecti praetorio. Olim enim cursus publici potestas tantum a principe petebatur vel a praefecto praetorio, tanquam principe, & interdum a magistro officiorum: ab aliis magistratibus concedi non poterat. 9. h. tit. Ad cursum publicum angariae, & parangariae de quib. hic tit. 51 cocipitur. Na angariae frontem, sunt ministeria principalia ad publica Imperii necessitate & cursum publicum: parangariae sunt eadem ministeria, sed extra viam regiam & per locadesferta, sive non ordinaria. Ita Graeci distinguunt ad librum sextum, Καταλογὴ. Ad hunc cursum pertinet quoque titulus proximus puta 2. de transitoriis et statuis. Tractatoriae enim quae a veterib. Cicerone, Plinio secundo, &c. diplomata dicuntur, sunt epistolae sive rescripta principis aut praefecti praetorio quibus vectionis sive cursus publ. clabularis potestas alii datur. Stativa sunt diversoria sive mansiones, in quib. utetes cursu publico divertit per viam. Huc tit. sequitur 53. de apparitor. praefect. prae. &c. Priores tres ti. pertinet etiam ad hos praefectos, sed tamen & ad alios quosdam, & pinde sunt magis communes, sed hic tantum ad perfectionem pertinet. Quae sequitur tit. 54. de apparit. praefect. urb. Nam hic praefectus prior proximus est dignitate ut dicit est l.1.t.28. Atq; hi ,pprie Urbaniciani ut illi propriè praefectiani in jure dicūtur. Hūc sequitur tit.de app.magist.mil. Ratio ord.est, q a h:t ad militares apparitores priores ad civiles séper ptinēt. Ja civilia militarib. sūt priora: posterior sunt a. ,pvincialia. Et hinc etiam, quoniam tit. sequitur tit.56.de appar.proc.& leg.& tit.57.de appar.com. oriēt. q a hi magistratus sunt ,pvinciales Procōsul prior est comite oriētis, ut dictū est supra t.33.& seqq.l.1. Inter pvinciales apparitores ultimi sunt sub tit.58.de cohortal.b.princip.& etc. Ratio est, quia isti sunt apparitores magistratuum ,pvincialiū priorib.. (ut proconsule & comite oriētis) dignitate aut origine posteriorū, ut sunt praesides, cōsulares, correctores, &c. Quia sint cohortales videantur Lexicographi, juris maximè Brissonius & Cuj.ad hos ȝ lib.C. posteremos, & ad Novell. inter apparitores ult. locū tenet apparitores pfecti annonae tit.59.de appar.praef.ēt annonae. Ratio est q a & hic ipse magistrat. ul- timū locū inter magistratus obtineat, ut dictū supra. Quē sequitur tit.60.de div.eff & appar. q a & omniū priorū apparitorū cōmunis, & velut suppletorius est in ultimū locū rejectus. Est & altera ratio ordinis, q hic tit. ferē totus vitia ḡdā & delicta apparitorū ,phibeat. Priorib. igitur tit. singulae species apparitorū sunt expositae, quos tandē h tit. sequitur, tū qa cōis tū qa ferē phibitorius delictorū. Sic & huic ,pximus tit.61.de executor. & exactor. ferē est totus ,phibitorius ob vitia & delicta executorū & exactorū. Est & alia ratio: q a & hic quoq; tit. est cōis, nā ad exigendū & exsequendū mitti solēt omnis generis apparitores, & palatini. Huc sequitur tit.62.de lucris ad vocatorū, &c. qui ejusdē cū priorib' est argumēti. Continet n. delictū: sed unū dūtaxat puta cōcussionis. Quare cū sit specialis meritō illis duob est posterior. Huic adjungitur hoc loco, & velut interjicitur. (Nā in C. Theod. nō est, unde tamē reliqui omnes tit. sunt sumpti) tit.63.de primipilo. Ratio ordinis est tantū ,pptér similitudinē lucri. Nā ut tit.62 est de lucris advocatorū, & cōmodis interdū injustis, & apparitorib. ita & hic speciem quandā lucri, sive cōmodi militaris cōtinet & ,pinde ut specialis posterior est. Primipilus duo significat. Primū est ipse Centurio omnium in exercitu Rom. primus centurionū, q initio pti um' centurio, postea primipil' dici coepit, & praerat 60.co hortib, teste Liv. l.7 & Dionys. l.9. itēq; merita & cōmoda toti' legiōis cōsē quebat, teste Vegetio l.2.c.8.& 21 q cōmoda & lucra quoq; interdū, ut & h. & alibi primipili nomine appellātur. Quare & ipse centurio, & cōmoda ejus uno nomine dicūtur. Sed posterior significatio est reectior, & minus elegās. Officium autē dicitur primipilatus. l.1.h.tit. ut primipilaris, & primipilarius. q fuit primipilus. Ultimus tit. li.12. est tit.64.publicae vitae &c q ad idē illud argumētū de delictis & onerib & injustis in ,pvinciales exactionib pertinet. Ipēq; delicti cōtinet simile cōcussioni, sed graviore. quāq nō tātum in apparitores, sed interdū in ipsos judices f. rectores ,pvinciarū cadat. Quare cū hoc delictū sit gravi' & odiosus, meritō ultimū in locū fuit rejectum. Et hæc de ordine tit. Codicis.
units.tr: the dead, and so it is plainly the last. Yet title 49, "On the offering of vows" (de oblatione votorum), is added. The reason for this order can be understood only from the Theodosian Code, book 7, which is wholly concerned with military affairs. At its end there are two titles: one "On the offering of horses" (de oblatione equorum) and the other "On the offering of vows." Tribonian kept the latter and left out the former. So much on the second chapter of that book. The third and last chapter remains, which I said concerns the attendants (apparitores) and ministers of the magistrates. The arrangement of the Code is also worth noting. The dignities, which in the law are called civil military service, and the military service proper, which is armed and belongs chiefly to the prince and assists him, are therefore placed first. In the same way, the later titles now deal with those who serve the dignities or magistrates as their attendants. This chapter, title 15, contains the same order: the attendants follow the magistrates they attend. Since the praetorian prefect is the first of the dignities and magistrates, as I said above in book 1, it is right that this title first deals with those who attend this prefect, which is the subject of titles 50, 51, 52 and 53 here. Title 50, "On the numerary assistants," etc., is chiefly and principally concerned with the numerarii of the high seat, that is, of the praetorian prefect, and consequently also with the numerarii of the other magistrates. Why these numerarii are placed first, before the prefects' attendants, is that they rank above the others, because they are clerks, whose order is more honourable (as Cicero says in the Verrines) than that of the other attendants. The numerarii handled the accounts and records in the magistrates' offices. The tractarii likewise, whose assistants were certain subordinates, the chartularii, scriniarii and exceptores. There is also another reason why these are treated first: they serve all magistrates in common, or because this title belongs to the common magistrates. Title 51, "On the public post and angariae," etc., is added to this. The reason for the order is that, just as the numerarii of whom we have just spoken, so the ministers of the public post belong to the care of the praetorian prefect. For formerly the right to the public post was sought only from the prince, or from the praetorian prefect as the prince's representative, and sometimes from the master of offices; it could not be granted by other magistrates (9 h. tit.). To the public post belong the angariae and parangariae, which title 51 here deals with. The angariae are the principal services for the public needs of the empire and the public post; the parangariae are the same services, but off the royal road and through deserted places, or not regular. The Greeks distinguish them thus in the sixth book of the Katalogē. To this post belongs also the next title, namely title 2, "On transitory and stationary (things)." The tractatoriae, which the ancients, such as Cicero and Pliny the Elder, called diplomata, are letters or rescripts of the prince or praetorian prefect by which the power of using the public post is given to another. The stativa are lodgings or stations where those using the public post lodge on the road. The next title, 53, "On the attendants of the praetorian prefect," etc., follows. The first three titles pertain also to these prefects, but also to certain others, and so are more common; here they concern only the prefecture. The next is title 54, "On the attendants of the city prefect." For this prefect is next in rank after the praetorian prefect, as is said in book 1, title 28. These are properly called Urbaniciani, as the others are properly called Praefectiani in law. Next follows the title "On the attendants of the masters of the soldiery." The reason for the order is that the military attendants always come before the civil ones, the civil being prior to the military, while the provincial ones come last. For this reason, too, since title 56 ("On the attendants of proconsuls and legates") and title 57 ("On the attendants of the count of the East") follow, it is clear that these magistrates are provincial. The proconsul ranks before the count of the East, as was said above in title 33 and following, and book 1. Among the provincial attendants the last are those under title 58, "On the cohortales of the provincial governors," etc. The reason is that these are the attendants of the provincial magistrates who rank lower in dignity or origin than the proconsul and the count of the East, such as the presidents, consulars, correctors, etc. The lexicographers, and especially the legal writers Brissonius and Cujacius, have sought to explain why they are called cohortales, on this last book of the Code and on the Novels. Among the last of the attendants stands the attendants of the prefect of the grain supply, title 59, "On the attendants of the prefect of the grain supply." The reason is that this magistrate also holds the last place among the magistrates, as was said above. He is followed by title 60, "On the divisions of offices and attendants," since it is common to all the earlier attendants and is, as it were, a supplement, and is therefore pushed to the last place. There is also another reason for the order: this title almost entirely forbids certain faults and crimes of the attendants. Therefore the individual kinds of attendants have been set out in the earlier titles, and this title follows them, partly because it is general and partly because it is almost wholly a prohibition of crimes. Likewise the next title, 61, "On executors and exactors," is almost entirely a prohibition of the faults and crimes of executors and exactors. There is also another reason: this title too is general, for attendants of every kind and the palatine officials are usually sent to collect and carry out orders. Title 62, "On the profits of advocates," etc., follows, which is of the same subject as the earlier ones. For it contains a crime, but only one, namely extortion; therefore, since it is special, it is rightly placed after those two. Title 63, "On the primipilus," is added here and is, as it were, inserted. (In the Theodosian Code it is not found, though all the other titles were taken from it.) The reason for the order is only the similarity of gain. For as title 62 deals with the gains of advocates, and with benefits that are sometimes unjust, and with attendants, so this one also contains a certain kind of gain or military benefit, and therefore it is rightly placed after the special title. "Primipilus" has two meanings. The first is the centurion himself, the first of all the centurions in the Roman army. He was at first called primus centurio, but later began to be called primipilus, and he commanded sixty cohorts, according to Livy, book 7, and Dionysius, book 9. He also managed the pay and benefits of the whole legion, according to Vegetius, book 2, chapters 8 and 21. Sometimes the benefits and profits are also called by the name primipilus, as here and elsewhere; hence the centurion himself and his benefits are both called by one name. But the second meaning is more common and less elegant. The office is called primipilatus (book 1 h. tit.), and the holder primipilaris and primipilarius, that is, one who has been primipilus. The last title of book 12 is title 64, "On public life," etc., which likewise concerns the same subject of crimes, burdens and unjust exactions upon the provinces. It contains a crime like extortion, but more serious, though it falls not only on attendants but sometimes on the judges or governors of the provinces themselves. Since this crime is more grave and odious, it was rightly thrown to the last place. And so much on the order of the titles of the Code.

units.la: TERTIA PARS DE ORDINE Legum Codicis.
units.tr: THE THIRD PART: ON THE ORDER OF THE LAWS OF THE CODE.

units.la: RESTAT tertius & ultimus ordo, quem diximus legum sive capitum singulorum sub titulis Codicis quae res breviter confici poterit. Ordo namq; legū Codicis est accōmodatus tempori & successioni Imp atque Coll. adeo ut constitutio prior, sive prius edita, prior quoq; sit loco & ordine Quo ordine Justinianus, sive ejus nomine Tribun secutus videtur Codic. priores Gregorian. & Theodos. in quib. idem ordo temporis est adhibitus: ut videre est in C. Theod. & fragmentis Greg. Ratio a hujus ordinis ex tempore sumpti haec esse videtur, quod magni referat scire, quae constitutio sit prior, quae posterior tempore: Quid ita? quia posterior derogat priori. l. ul. de const. princ. quanquam in nostro C. nulla lex alteri derogat, aut eam abrogat propterea q; omnes hujus Cod constitutiones ita sunt accipiendae tanquam ab uno Imperatore puta Justiniano factae & editae, ut ipse ait in prefat. C. & l 2. C. de vet. jur. enucl. Ut a hic temporis ordo meliusintelligatur, duo sunt notanda. I. est de initio temporis & fine. Initium ergo ducitur ab Imp. Hadriano: cujus tamen una duntaxat in toto hoc Cod. extat constitutio, puta l. 1. C. de test. b. Ratio a, cur ab Hadriano ducatur initium, sive cur Imp. ante Hadrianum constitutiones nullae sint relatae in C. nostrum ratio, in quā pre- cipua haec est: quod Hadrianus Imp. primus fuerit juris civilis instaurator, cujus sc. mandato editum perpetuum compositum fuit a Juliano JC. d l. 2, §. sed qua a divina C. de vet. jur. enucl. l. pen. C. de cond. indeb. & Spartianus in Hadriano. Quae juris instauratio & editi compositio causam quoq; attulit JC. ut & ipsi in suis libris alium ordinem tenerent, puta ordinem edicti, alium, inquam, quam tenuerant JC. Hadriano priores qui priores, ordinem ferētenebant eum, quem Sabinus ipse instituerat. Nam & de Sabino scripsit Pōpon. in l. 2. inf. de orig. jur. eum primum fundasse jus civile. Est & altera ratio ab exemplo C. Gregor. in quoidem initium ab Hadriano repetitum fuisse videtur, sed eadem ex rōe, sive causa, quā expositum, ut arbitror. Nam ex trib illis codicibus, Greg. Hermogen & Theodos. & aliquot novellis posterioris, nostertic codex Justinian est conflatus. l. 1. in prof. C. Gregor. coeptus ut videtur ab Hadriano definit in Diocletiano. Hermogenianus a tantum Diocl. & Maximiniani Impp. constitutiones conturbat. Theodosian. denique a Constantino M. qui Diocl. successit coeptus definit in Theodosio juniore, ut ejus Cod auctore. Hunc Theodosium deniq; alii secuti aliquot Impp. usq; ad Justinianum multas quoq; constitutiones ediderūt, qui quia G. Theodos. ultimo essent posteriores, sive recentiores dictae sunt Novellae, quas tamen una cum suis constitutionibus Imper. Justinian huic C. suo inferendas mandavit, ut sc. ordine Impp. continuato leges sive constitutiones principium in Cod Justin. comprehensæ, cœptæ sint ab Hadriano, & desinant in Justiniano, hujus C. auctore. Et hæc de priore, ex quo initium & finis temporis intelligitur. II. hic notandum ad singulos Impp. pertinet & Coss. Nam si sub eodem titulo multæ sunt leges eæque non unius sed plurium Imperat. tum hic ordo servatur in legibus ut quemadmodum Imperatoris tempore alius alio est prior: ita & leges disponantur, ut Imperatoris tempore prioris constitutio prior sit constitutione Imperatoris tempore posterioris. Si vero unius Imperatoris multæ sub eodem titulo sint leges sive constitutiones, tum ordo earum ex annis imperii, hoc est, ratione consulum sumitur. Quamvis interdum, maximè in posterioribus libris sæpè consulum nomina desiderentur.
units.tr: There remains the third and last order, which we said concerns the individual laws or chapters under the titles of the Code. This can be dealt with briefly. The order of the laws in the Code is adapted to the time and succession of the emperors and consuls, so that an earlier enactment, or one published earlier, also comes earlier in place and order. Justinian, or Tribonian in his name, seems to have followed this order, as did the earlier Gregorian and Theodosian codes, in which the same chronological order was used, as can be seen in the Theodosian Code and the fragments of Gregory. The reason for taking this order from time seems to be that it matters greatly to know which constitution is earlier and which later in time. Why so? Because the later derogates from the earlier, l. ult. de const. princ. Yet in our Code no law derogates from another or abrogates it. For this reason all the constitutions of this Code are to be taken as if they had been made and published by one emperor, namely Justinian, as he himself says, in prefat. C. and l. 2 C. de vet. jur. enucl. So that this chronological order may be better understood, two things must be noted. First, the beginning and end of the period. The beginning is taken from the Emperor Hadrian, of whom only one constitution is found in this whole Code, namely l. 1 C. de test. b. The reason why the beginning is taken from Hadrian, or why no constitutions of the emperors before Hadrian are cited in our Code, is chiefly this: Hadrian was the first restorer of civil law, by whose command the Perpetual Edict was composed by Julian the jurist, d. l. 2, §. sed qua a divina C. de vet. jur. enucl., l. pen. C. de cond. indeb., and Spartianus in Hadrian. This restoration of the law and the composition of the Edict also gave the jurists cause to follow a different order in their books, namely the order of the Edict, different, I say, from the order which the jurists before Hadrian had kept, that is, the order which Sabinus himself had established. For Pomponius also wrote of Sabinus that he was the first to lay the foundations of civil law, in l. 2 inf. de orig. jur. There is also another reason, from the example of the Gregorian Code, in which the beginning seems to have been taken from Hadrian, but for the same reason, or cause, as explained above, in my opinion. For this present Code of Justinian was compiled from those three codes, Gregorian, Hermogenian and Theodosian, and some later novels. l. 1 in prof. C. The Gregorian Code, apparently begun with Hadrian, ends with Diocletian. Hermogenian deals only with the constitutions of Diocletian and Maximian. The Theodosian Code, begun by Constantine the Great, who succeeded Diocletian, ends with Theodosius the Younger, whose name it bears.
