Other emperors after this Theodosius also issued many constitutions down to Justinian, and because they were later, or more recent, than the Theodosian Code, they were called Novels. Justinian commanded that these be included in his Code together with his own constitutions, so that the laws or constitutions of the emperors, in a continuous imperial order, included in the Code of Justinian, begin with Hadrian and end with Justinian, the author of this Code. This is what I have to say about the first point, by which the beginning and end of the period are understood. Second, what must be noted here concerns each emperor and consul. For if under the same title there are many laws, and these are not of one emperor but of several, then the order of the laws follows the order of the emperors in time, so that the law of an earlier emperor is placed before that of a later emperor. If, however, there are many laws or constitutions under the same title from one emperor, then their order is taken from the years of his reign, that is, by reckoning the consulships. Yet sometimes, especially in the later books, the names of the consuls are often lacking.

units.la: Finis Oeconomiæ Codicis.
units.tr: The End of the Economy of the Code.

units.la: Prætoris officium est in Restitutionibus Actionibus. Bonorum possessionibus Missionibus in possessionem. Interdictis. Exceptionibus. Stipulationibus prætoriis. Hinc pendet ordo edicti perpetui.
units.tr: The office of the praetor concerns restitutions, actions, possessions of goods, missions into possession, interdicts, exceptions and praetorian stipulations. On this depends the order of the Perpetual Edict.

units.la: OECONOMIA PAN- DECTARVM ET EDICTI PERPETVI.
units.tr: THE ECONOMY OF THE PANDECTS AND THE PERPETUAL EDICT.

units.la: HACTENVS de Codice, eiusque ordine tripartito, librorum, titulorum, & legum sive constitutionum: Nunc de Pandectis videamus, quarum item tripartitus ordo est explicandus, librorum, titulorum, & legum sive responsorum prudentum.
units.tr: So far we have discussed the Code and its threefold order of books, titles and laws or constitutions. Now let us look at the Pandects, whose threefold order likewise must be explained: books, titles, and laws or responses of the jurists.

units.la: Sunt tamen & alia duo hic initio observanda, numerus librorum & numerus partium. Nam digesta, sunt 50. libri. Ratio vix reperiri potest, quod numerus librorum saepe ex arbitrio scriptoris, vel pro magnitudine & materiae & argumenti sumatur. Fortasse tamen Tribun. Julianum in hoc est secutus: qui Julianus ut auctor fuit sive (ut loquitur l. pen. Cod. de cond. indeb.) ordinator edicti perpetui, ita & primus edicti interpretationem & explicationem edidit, eamque complexus est digestorum libris ut puto 100. rotundo scil. numero. Dixi ut puto. Nam in indice librorum veterum prudentum praefixo nostris ff. Juliani tantum 90. libri digestorum commemorantur. Sed Cuiac. in observ. recte admonuit indicem illum saepe esse mutilum, multosque in eo libros desiderari: cujus rei exemplum & in his ff. Justiniani exstat. in l. 32. de LL. quae lex sumpta notatur ex Juliani digestorum libro 94. ut verisimile sit eum 100. scripsisse propter rotunditatem & perfectionem numeri.
units.tr: There are, however, two further matters to note here at the outset: the number of books and the number of parts. The Digest has 50 books. The reason for this number can hardly be found, since the number of books is often chosen at the writer's discretion, or according to the size and subject matter of the work. Perhaps, however, Tribonian followed Julian in this. Julian, who, as l. pen. Cod. de cond. indeb. puts it, was the compiler of the perpetual edict, was also the first to publish an interpretation and explanation of the edict, and he gathered it into what I think were 100 books, a round number. I say "I think", for in the index of the older jurists prefixed to our Digest only 90 books of Julian's Digest are mentioned. But Cujas, in observ., rightly warned that this index is often defective and that many books are missing from it. An example of this also exists in this Digest of Justinian, in l. 32. de LL., a law which is cited from book 94 of Julian's Digest. So it is likely that he wrote 100 books, for the sake of a round and complete number.

units.la: Quod si verum est, jam ratio fere intelligitur, cur Tribun. 50. libros ff. fecerit, sumpsit enim dimidium ut laudem brevitatis haberet, quam saepe praedicat in praefationib. ff. C. & Inst. & l. 1. & 2. C. de vet. iur. enucl. sic & alias solent Romani dimidium sumere eorum, quos imitantur, ut Cic. qui in lib. de LL. & de Rep. Platonem imitatur: Cum Plato scripsisset 12. de Rep. de LL. 10. Cic. 5. de LL. & 6. de rep. conscripsit. Sic & Virg. Homerum imitatur, cum Homerus 24. libris scripsit Illiada complexus. Virg. Aeneida in 12. contraxit: imo quod admirabilius Virg. totam Iliadem & Odysseam libros scil. 48. in 12. conclusit. Et hæc de numero librorum.
units.tr: If this is true, the reason why Tribonian made the Digest 50 books is more or less understood. For he took half, so as to have the praise of brevity, which he often proclaims in the prefaces of the Digest, the Code and the Institutes, and in l. 1. & 2. C. de vet. iur. enucl. Thus the Romans also commonly took half of the works they imitated. Cicero, who in his books de LL. and de Rep. imitates Plato: when Plato had written twelve books de Rep. and ten de LL., Cicero composed five de LL. and six de rep. So too Virgil imitated Homer, since Homer wrote the Iliad in 24 books; Virgil condensed it into the Aeneid in 12. Indeed, what is more remarkable, Virgil shut up the whole Iliad and Odyssey, that is 48 books, into 12. And so much on the number of books.

units.la: Nunc de numero partium. Voluit autem Justinianus Dig. gesta tribui in septem partes, quarum prima dicitur πρὸ πάντων, quasi dicat prima sive initia: quæ pars continetur primis quatuor libris. Altera pars continet septem libros, puta 5. 6. 7. 8. 9. 10. & 11. Eaque dicitur de judiciis. l. 2. §. igitur. & §. seq. C. devet. iur. enucl. Appellationis ratio, quo ad primam est, quia initia & quasi præparatoria judiciorum, in ea parte continentur: ut in jus vocatio, editio, pacta, transactiones, &c. Quod ad secundum attinet, non inde, ut quidam putant, dicitur de judiciis, quod in ea parte species iudiciorum, sive actionum habeantur (nam & in aliis partibus habentur) sed inde potius, quod in edicto perpetuo post πρὸ πάντων primus titulus videtur ita conceptus, de judiciis, à quo deinde titulo pars universa fuerit denominata. Solent enim veteres etiam ex primo verbo libri interdum libro nomen imponere, ut supra dictum, sic & pars tertia (quæ 8. libris, puta 12. & seq. 7. continetur) de rebus creditis appellatur. d. l. 2. §. in tertia, 4. à titulo edictide reb. creditis. Non enim ut quidem putant, in ea parte agitur de rebus, sed de rebus contrahendis sive creditis, hoc est de actionibus & judiciis, ex mutuo & aliis contractibus, qui res & consensu fiunt. Pars quarta continet item tres libros, nempe lib. 20. & 7. seq. sed ea vacat nomine; nisi quis appellet umbilicum sive medium, ut in d. l. 2 §. quartus. 5. Quinta pars 9. lib, complectitur puta lib. 28. & 8. seq. eaque dicitur de testamentis, ut ait d. l. 2. §. quintus. 6. Eădem scilicet ratione ita dicitur, qua priores illæ de judiciis & rebus. Sexta pars octo libris continetur, puta 37. & 7. seq. quæ rursus est ἀνάπαυμα, ut & septima, quæ est ultima, & 6. libris continetur, puta 45. & 5. seq.
units.tr: Now concerning the number of parts. Justinian wished the Digest to be divided into seven parts. The first is called πρὸ πάντων [pro panton], as if to say "the first things" or "beginnings"; this part is contained in the first four books. The second part contains seven books, namely 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10 and 11, and is called de judiciis (on judgments), l. 2. §. igitur. & §. seq. C. de vet. iur. enucl. The reason for the name of the first part is that it contains the beginnings and, as it were, the preparatory matters of judgments, such as summoning to court, production of documents, pacts, and settlements. As for the second, it is not called "on judgments" because, as some think, this part treats of kinds of judgments or actions (for these are also treated in other parts), but rather because in the perpetual edict, after πρὸ πάντων, the first title seems to have been headed de judiciis, and from this title the whole part was then named. For the ancients often gave a book a name from its first word, as mentioned above. So too the third part, which is contained in eight books, namely 12 to 19, is called de rebus creditis (on loans), d. l. 2. §. in tertia, 4. à titulo edicti de reb. creditis. For it is not, as some think, concerned with things, but with things lent or entrusted, that is with actions and judgments arising from loan and other contracts which are made by things and consent. The fourth part likewise contains three books, namely 20 to 22, but it has no name; unless one should call it the navel or middle, as in d. l. 2 §. quartus. 5. The fifth part comprises nine books, namely 28 to 36, and is called de testamentis (on wills), as d. l. 2. §. quintus. 6. says. It is named in the same way as the earlier ones de judiciis and de rebus. The sixth part is contained in eight books, namely 37 to 44, and this again is an ἀνάπαυμα [anapauma], a resting-place, as is the seventh, which is the last, and is contained in six books, namely 45 to 50.

units.la: Cur autem hoc pandectarum corpus in 7. partes sit distributum. rationem reddit ipse Imp. d. l. 2. §. omnia. 1. in VII. inquit, partes eas (scil. ff. libros) digessimus non perperam neque sine ratione, sed in numerorum naturam & artem respicientes, & consentaneam iis divisionem partium conficientes. Fuit enim hic numerus non tantum apud gentes profanas, sed etiam in libris nostris sacris mysticus & sanctus habitus, de quo videtur Macrob.l.b.1.commentar.in summum Scip.c.6. & pulcherrimè disserit Philo, in Lib.de opif.mundi.
units.tr: Why this body of the Pandects was divided into seven parts, the emperor himself gives the reason in d. l. 2. §. omnia. 1. He says that in the seventh part (namely the books of the Digest) "we have arranged it not carelessly or without reason, but with regard to the nature and art of numbers, making a division of parts consistent with them." For this number was held to be mystical and sacred not only among the profane nations but also in our holy books. On this see Macrobius, l. 1. commentar. in somnium Scipionis c. 6. and Philo discourses most beautifully on it, in lib. de opif. mundi.

units.la: Quod ad ordinem harum 7.partium inter se attinet,&ratio nem ordinis, ea ex librorum, & titulorum ordine explicando una intelligi debet.
units.tr: As to the order of these seven parts among themselves, and the reason for the order, this should be understood from the explanation of the order of the books and titles.

units.la: His duobus de numero librorum & de numero partium velut breviter præmunitis, & breviter jam expositis; proximum nunc est, ut de ipsa Oeconomia sive ordine librorum & titulorum explicemus, quia vero Tribunianus huius operis auctor, aut certè dux & princeps in eo componendo ordinem edicti perpetui, & interdum Codic. Justinianei & Institut. est secutus.l. 2. de statu hom.l. 1 §.cumque hæc, Cod.vet.jur.enucl. id quod & singulis in libris infra demonstrabitur: operæprecium erit ipsum edicti ordinem hic prius exponere. Nam de Codic. & Institut. ordine iam supra expositum est.
units.tr: Having thus briefly set out these two matters, the number of books and the number of parts, the next task is to explain the economy itself, that is the order of books and titles. Tribonian, the author and at least the leader and chief in compiling this work, followed the order of the perpetual edict, and at times that of the Justinianic Code and the Institutes, l. 2. de statu hom.; l. 1 §. cumque haec, Cod. vet. jur. enucl. This will be shown in detail under each book below. It will be worth while to set out first here the order of the edict itself. For the order of the Code and the Institutes has already been explained above.

units.la: Neque vero edicti ordinem Tribun. tantum in hoc opere ff. est secutus,sed omnes & J C.& Impp.illi quidem in libris totum ius continentibus, hi vero in iis, quos Codices appellant, ut videre licet in libris digestorum Juliani, Celsi, Marcelli, Scævolæ, in libris quæstionum,Papiniani,in Hermog.Epitome iuris, in Pauli sententiis, &c.item libris ad hoc edictum, ut Pomponii,Caii, Ulpiani,Pauli, &c. idem quoque videre licet in Codic.Hermogenis, Gregorii, & Theodosii. Tanta fuit huius libri sive edicti perpetui à Juliano compositi auctoritas, ut omnes fere de iure libri & commentarii ad hoc edictum fuerint accommodati,qui edicto isto sunt posteriores.
units.tr: Nor did Tribonian follow the order of the edict in this Digest alone; all the jurists and emperors did so as well, the former in books which contain the whole law, the latter in those which they call Codes. This can be seen in the books of the Digests of Julian, Celsus, Marcellus and Scaevola, in the books of Questions of Papinian, in the Epitome of Law of Hermogenianus, in the Sentences of Paul, and so on; likewise in the books ad edictum, such as those of Pomponius, Gaius, Ulpian, Paul, and so on. The same can also be seen in the Codes of Hermogenianus, Gregorius and Theodosius. So great was the authority of this book, or perpetual edict, compiled by Julian, that almost all the books and commentaries on law which came after this edict were adapted to it.

units.la: Nam ante hoc edictum,quod tempore Hadriani, ciusque mandato Iuliani opera est copositum. leg.2. §.sed quia divinares,18.C. de veter.jur. enucl.& leg.penultim.Cod.de condit.indebit. maxima fuit auctoritas Sabini Iurisconsulti librorum, adeo ut ipsius quoque ordinem sequerentur, & ipsum quoque commentariis interpretarentur, ut videre licet in libris ad Sabinum Pomponii, Ulpiani, Pauli,&c.
units.tr: For before this edict, which was compiled under Hadrian by the work of Julian at his command, leg. 2. §. sed quia divinares, 18. C. de vet. jur. enucl. and leg. penult. Cod. de condit. indebit., the greatest authority belonged to the books of the jurist Sabinus, to such an extent that they followed his order as well, and also interpreted it in commentaries, as can be seen in the books ad Sabinum of Pomponius, Ulpian, Paul, and so on.

units.la: Quin etiam hic ordo iuris Sabinianus, videtur antiquissimis quoque ICtis fuisse usitatus,Scævolæ,ServioSulpitio,Alphcno,Labeoni,&c.qui intelligi potest ex libris ff. Alpheni, ex libris Pomponii ad Q.Mutium,& ex posterioribus Labeonis. Quem ordinem iuris veteris illi ex ipsis fortasse legibus 12. tab. sumpserunt, quanquam de ordine libelli 12. tab. nihil certi affirmare possum. Putat Hotomannus in comment. ad frag. 12. tab. eius libri tripartitum fuisse ordinem, ut primo de iure sacro, secundo de iure publico. 3. de iure ciuili priuato ageretur. Nam & Ausonius:
units.tr: Indeed this Sabinian order of law seems also to have been in use among the most ancient jurists, Scaevola, Servius Sulpicius, Alfenus, Labeo, and others, as can be understood from the books of Alfenus in the Digest, from the books of Pomponius on Quintus Mucius, and from the later books of Labeo. Those jurists perhaps took this order of the old law from the Twelve Tables themselves, although I cannot assert anything certain about the order of the Twelve Tables. Hotman, in his commentary on the fragments of the Twelve Tables, thinks that this law had a threefold order, so that first it dealt with sacred law, second with public law, and third with private civil law. For Ausonius too says:

units.la: Iustriplex tabula, quod ter sanxere quaterna Sacrum, priuatum, & populi commune quod vsquam est.
units.tr: The tablet is threefold: four times three laws sanctioned what is sacred, what is private, and what is common to the people wherever it exists.

units.la: Et Cicero in suis quinque libris de L L. (quorum tantum 3. exstant) eundem ordinem tenuit. Nam primo proœmium, hoc est, de origine iuris: Ius, inquit, non ex opinione, ut quidam Philosophi, sed ex natura ipsa, ut Stoici, & veteres Academici exist. mabant, ortum est. Secundum sacrum. III. Publicum. IV. & V. Ius priuatum fuit comprehensum. Eandem tripartiti ordinis rationem & ordinem in suo Codice secutus est Imp. Iustin. vt alibi dictum. Verum de hoc ordine 12. Tab. quem expositi Hotomannus ijs fortasse rationibus quas attuli adductus, valde, ut dubitem, faciunt cum alia, tum quod apud Cic. in libris de legib. quaedam leges 12. Tab. de iure sacro proferantur, non exprimi, sed ex posterioribus tabulis
units.tr: Cicero too, in his five books on the Laws (of which only three survive), followed the same order. In the first book he gives the preface, that is, on the origin of law: Law, he says, arose not from opinion, as some philosophers held, but from nature itself, as the Stoics and the older Academics maintained. The second book deals with sacred law, the third with public law, and in the fourth and fifth private law is treated. The Emperor Justinian followed the same threefold division and order in his Code, as I have said elsewhere. But I doubt that this is the order of the Twelve Tables that Hotomannus sets out. I am moved to this doubt both by the reasons I have already given and by the fact that in Cicero's books on the Laws certain laws of the Twelve Tables on sacred law are quoted, which are not found in that order but are taken from the later tablets.

units.la: Vtvtsit, dubitari non debet, quin hic ordo Sabinianus sit pervetus, quem & ipse Iulianus in Edicto perpetuo componendo est secutus. Quare & hunc erit vtile breviter explicare, vt ordo edicti melius intelligatur. Et primum quidem in hac veteri iuris Oeconomia sive ordine, caput fuit de testamentis, & de variis legatorum generibus. Pars altera de contractibus, maxime tamen de emp-tione & societate. II. De dotibus. IV. De tutelis. V De privatis delictis, vt furto, damno, iniuria, &c. VI Pars varia cōtinuisse videtur, ut de damno infecto, de condictione, de solutione. VII. De stipulationibus, ubi & de Aedilitio Edicto. IIX. De interdictis, ubi & de vsucapionibus & seruitutibus praediorum. IX, Et ni fallor, ultima de pignoribus. Quem veteris iuris ordinem ex libris Vlpiani, Pauli, &c. ad Sabinum, ex Iavoleno, Labeone, Pomponio & Alpheno, observavimus.
units.tr: However that may be, there can be no doubt that this Sabinian order is very ancient, and that Julian himself followed it in composing the Perpetual Edict. It will therefore be useful to explain it briefly, so that the order of the Edict may be better understood. In this ancient plan of law, or order, the first head was on wills and the various kinds of legacies. The second part was on contracts, chiefly on sale and partnership. The third (II) was on dowries. The fourth (IV) was on guardianships. The fifth (V) dealt with private delicts, such as theft, damage, injury, and so on. The sixth (VI) part seems to have contained various matters, such as damage threatened, the action for a fixed sum (condictio), and payment. The seventh (VII) was on stipulations, where the Aedilician Edict also appears. The eighth (IIX) was on interdicts, where usucaptions and servitudes of land are also treated. The ninth (IX), and, unless I am mistaken, the last, was on pledges. We have worked out this ancient order from the books of Ulpian, Paul and others on Sabinus, and from Javolenus, Labeo, Pomponius and Alfenus.

units.la: Ratio autem huius ordinis part'm intelligitur ex iis, quae infr. dicentur ad edictum Iuliani qui in edicto perpetuo componendo, eum ordinem, vt modo dictum, fere est secutus, interdum tamen ab eo discessit, ut & à Juliano Tribun. in ff. sed omnia Julianus & uberius & subtilius digessit.: Tribunianus autem uberrimè & plenissimè.
units.tr: The reason for this order is understood from what will be said below on the edict of Julian, who, in composing the Perpetual Edict, followed that order, as just described, almost throughout, though at times he departed from it, as Tribonian also did in the Digest. But Julian arranged everything more fully and more subtly, and Tribonian most fully and most completely.

units.la: Prima autem laus huius ordinis veteribus debetur, licet minus accurati initio. Nam ut eleganter summus Philosophus res primum informari, & obscuris lineamentis adumbrari solet, posterius expoliri & variis coloribus, ut dicitur, exprimi ac describi, sive breviter, prius <bl>τύπῳ</bl>, posterius <bl>ἐκρίβεια</bl>, & exquisite agitur.
units.tr: The first praise for this order is due to the ancients, although at the beginning they were less exact. For, as the highest philosopher elegantly observes, things are usually first sketched out and outlined in rough lines, and afterwards refined and, as it were, portrayed and described in various colours. Put briefly, the first treatment is by type [τύπῳ], the later one is exact [ἀκρίβεια], and is handled with care.

units.la: Hocigitur veterum ordine iam cognito, paulò facilior est aditus ad ordinem edicti Iuliani cognoscendum: qui certè propter veteres libros amissos ad cognoscendum est difficilior. Quia tamen ad ff. & C. totum, qui nostrum eius cognitio est per quam utilis, & ad ordinem planè necessaria, videamus, an per veteres libros fragmenta, tanquam obscura quædam vestigia persequentes, ordinem ipsum edicti assequi possimus.
units.tr: Having thus come to know the ancient order, we have a somewhat easier approach to understanding the order of Julian's edict. That order is certainly harder to recognise because the ancient books have been lost. Yet, since the knowledge of it is very useful for our Digest and Code as a whole, and is quite necessary for understanding their order, let us see whether, by following the surviving fragments of the old books as obscure traces, we can grasp the order of the edict itself.

units.la: Multi adhuc in Paratitlis & aliis id genus Epitomis atq; commentariis parentum, nostraq; ætate sunt conati exponere ordinem ff. & Cod. sed ordine & primis velut vestigijs edicti non invenstigatis fieri non potuit, quin sæpè aberrarint. Nam utidem Philosophus ait, error initio licet parvus progressu tamen fit multiplex & maximus.
units.tr: Many writers in the Paratitla and similar epitomes and commentaries of our own age have tried to set out the order of the Digest and Code, but without investigating the order and first, as it were, footprints of the edict, they could not avoid often going astray. For, as the same philosopher says, an error, though small at the beginning, becomes manifold and very great as it proceeds.

units.la: Non puto hic esse opus iam explicare, vel de edicti origine, quæ debetur C. Cornelio Tribun. pl. vt est apud Dionem & apud Asconium in orationes Cic. vel deco, qui prius edicta composuit ante Julianum. Puta Servius Sulpitius, & eius discipulus Ofilius, qui primus id diligenter composuit, teste Pomp. l. 2. §. ex his, de orig. iur. vel denique de ipso edicto Juliani, cum id Imp. Hadriani mandato à Salvio Iuliano Iurisconsulto fit perfectum, quod & Spartianus in Hadriano confirmat, & supra iam indicavimus. Satis enim ea aliaque id genus iam nota, & ab aliis sunt explicata.
units.tr: I do not think it necessary here to explain anything further, either about the origin of the edict, which is attributed to Gaius Cornelius, tribune of the plebs, as found in Dio and in Asconius on Cicero's orations, or about Servius, who composed edicts before Julian, that is, Servius Sulpicius and his pupil Ofilius, who first drew it up with care, as Pomponius testifies (Digest 1.2.2.§ ex his, on the origin of law); or finally about Julian's own edict, which was completed by Salvius Julianus, the jurist, at the command of the Emperor Hadrian, as Spartianus confirms in his life of Hadrian, and as we have already indicated above. For these and similar matters are already well known and have been explained by others.

units.la: Nos igitur de ordine edicti, quem nemo adhuc indicavit, exponamus: & primum quidem summatim, dein vero singulatim & accuratius. Videtur ergo edictum P. Iuliani in 10. partes distribui posse: quarum I. dicatur <bl>πρὸ πεῶτα</bl>, & prima sive præparatoria judiciorum continet. II. Dicatur de iudiciis, quæ pars actiones in rem continet. III. De rebus, quæ actiones in personam: IV. Con. IV. Continet tractatus de dotibus, tutelis, & per consequentiam de furtis. V. Explicatur de bonorum possessione & testamentis. VI. De cautionibus quibusdam praetoriis, vicem actionum gerentibus. VII. De delictis quibusdam. IIX. De iudiciorum fine sive executione, ut de missione in possessionem & re iudicata. IX. De interdictis, quae olim ab actionibus & iudiciis longè differebant. X. Et ultima pars est velut accessoria, in qua de pignoribus, exceptionibus, & stipulationibus praetoriis, & aliis quibusdam de rebus fortasse non satis certis ageretur, Et haec breviter de summis capitibus edicti perpetui à Juliano compositi, quantum ex obscuris fragmentis & vestigiis veterum librorum consequi licuit.
units.tr: We shall therefore set out the order of the edict, which nobody has yet indicated, first in summary and then in detail, more exactly. The edict of P. Julian may thus be divided into ten parts. (I) The first may be called preliminaries [πρὸ πρώτα], and contains the preparatory matters of judgments. (II) The second deals with judgments, and contains actions in rem. (III) The third deals with things, and contains actions in personam. (IV) The fourth contains the treatise on dowries, guardianships, and, consequently, thefts. (V) It sets out possession of goods and wills. (VI) It deals with certain praetorian securities, which take the place of actions. (VII) It deals with certain delicts. (VIII) It deals with the end or execution of judgments, such as the grant of possession and res judicata. (IX) It deals with interdicts, which in former times differed widely from actions and judgments. (X) The last part is, as it were, an appendix, in which pledges, exceptions, praetorian stipulations, and certain other matters, perhaps not very certain, would be treated. This is a brief account of the main headings of the Perpetual Edict composed by Julian, as far as we could gather it from the obscure fragments and traces of the ancient books.

units.la: Nunc singulatim & titulos, atque edicta singula, quoad eius fieri potuit, explicemus. Qua in re non minor erit difficultas, quam in ordine illo summario, ut ita dicam: partim propter libros veteres amissos, partim, quod Tribunianus edicti perpetui ordinem saepè mutárit ac perturbárit: multa quoque Codicis adiecerit, quae non sunt in edicto, ut actionem rei uxor. ut edictum de alterutro, &c, de quibus infra. Quare condonandum erit, si tantum typo & rudi Minerva haec à nobis informentur ac digerantur.
units.tr: Now let us set out the individual titles and individual edicts one by one, as far as this can be done. In this matter the difficulty will be no less than in that summary order, partly because of the ancient books that have been lost, and partly because Tribonian often altered and disturbed the order of the Perpetual Edict, and also added much to the Code that is not in the edict, such as the action of the wife concerning her property, or the edict on the one or the other, and so on, which will be discussed below. Therefore it will be pardonable if these matters are sketched and arranged by us only in outline and with a rough hand.

units.la: DE
units.tr: Concerning

units.la: DE PRIMA EDICTI PERPE- TUI PARTE.
units.tr: On the First Part of the Perpetual Edict.

units.la: RGo edicti primus tit. videtur fuisse de Jurisdictione, sub quo, ut generali, aliquot fuerunt edicta, ad Jurisdictionem praetoris pertinentia ut edictum, si quis jus dicenti non obtemperaverit: deinde edictum in eum qui album praetoris corruperit, l. 7. de jurisd. & l. Item edictum, quod quisque juris in alium, &c. l. 1. quod quisq; juris. Videntur & alia edicta de jurisdictione fuisse, ut de die, à praetore, cautioni de damno infecto, definita l. 4. & 5. de damn. infect. ut & illa fortasse, si quis in jus vocatus, &c. & in jus vocati, ut eant. Ratio autem ordinis, tam de hoc titulo primo, quam de aliis non incommode exponetur ad ff. infra. quae & partim est expositia ad Cod. supra.
units.tr: Therefore the first title of the edict seems to have concerned jurisdiction. Under this general heading there were several edicts relating to the praetor's jurisdiction, such as the edict "if anyone has not obeyed one who pronounces law," then the edict against one who has corrupted the praetor's album, l. 7. de jurisd. & l. and the edict "whatever right anyone has against another," etc., l. 1. quod quisq; juris. There seem to have been other edicts on jurisdiction too, such as the one on the day fixed by the praetor for security against threatened damage, l. 4. & 5. de damn. infect. and perhaps also those "if anyone has been summoned to court," etc., and "those summoned to court, that they may go." The reason for the order, both of this first title and of the others, will not be inconveniently explained at the ff. infra. which is in part an exposition of the Code above.

units.la: Huic titulo de jurisdictione proximum fuit edictum de edendo, l. 1. & 4. ff. de ed. & ff. quod sequebatur edictum de pactis, hoc edictum de in jus voc.
units.tr: Next after this title on jurisdiction came the edict on production of documents, l. 1. & 4. ff. de ed. & ff. which was followed by the edict on agreements; this edict on summoning to court came after that.

units.la: Cur autem in ff. & C. de pactis agatur post titul. de in jus voc. & in edictoante; Ratio haec mihi esse videtur, quod olim ipsa editione actionis saepe deterriti & permoti statim decurrerent ad transactionem, & pactionem cum adversario, ut & in jus vocationem viro prudenti plerumque gravem, evitarent. Quia tamen etiam post vocationem licet transigere, adeo, ut in jus vocatus, si transigat, sit dimittendus l. 32. neque impuberes de in jus voc. & quia Justiniani aetate in jus vocatio & editio uno eodemque tempore fere simul fieri solebant propterea Tribunian. in Digest. in jus vocat. & editione anteponit pactis & transactionibus. Edicti igitur de pactis multa fit pilium mentio, l. 1. de pact. Verba ejus extant l. 7 § ait Praetor 7. d. tit.
units.tr: Why the Digest and Code treat of agreements after the title on summoning to court and on the edict on the action, I think the reason is this: in former times, men were often deterred and moved by the very issuing of the action, and at once hurried to a settlement and an agreement with their opponent, thereby avoiding summons to court, which was usually burdensome to a prudent man. Yet even after the summons it is still lawful to settle, so much so that a man summoned to court, if he settles, is to be dismissed, l. 32. and not the minors (neque impuberes, de in jus voc.). And because in the age of Justinian, summons to court and the issuing of the edict were usually made together, at one and the same time, for this reason Tribonian, in the Digest, puts "summons to court" and "the edict" before agreements and settlements. Of the edict on agreements, therefore, much mention is made by Pilius, l. 1. de pact. Its words are extant at l. 7 § ait Praetor 7. d. tit.

units.la: De in jus voc. plura fuerunt edicta, unum de personis, quae vocari aut non vocari possunt, l. 4. & sequentib. de in jus voc. Aliud de vocato in jus vi non eximendo, l. 1. & 4. Neque enim, &c. tertium de satisdatione judicio sistendi, quae in edicto, ni fallor, promissio sive cautio vadimonij dicta fuit l. 4. qui satisdare cog. Cujus edicti de sistendo pars est edictum, si ex noxali causa, &c. l. 1. si ex noxali causa. Ad hoc vadimonium titulus quoque ff. si quis caut. &c. pertinet. IV. Edictum est de judicio in factum contra eum, qui, impedit alium judicio sisti, leg. 1. de eo, perquem factum & c. Fortasse fuerunt & alia, ad hunc titulum, de in jus voc. dicta, sed ex fragmentis librorum elici commode non possunt. V. tamen satis aperte exstat. l. 2. quibus ex causa sis in possessionem eatur, quod hic positum fuit, ut indicat inscriptio, dicta leg. 2. quae est Ulpian. dict. libro 5. ad edictum, quo & priora abeo sunt explicata, quam vis à Tribuniano hoc sit rejectum ad edictum de missione in possessionem. Hunc titulum, edicti perpetui, de injuria voc. sequebatur titulus, de postu- lando, l. 1. de postul. quod subsequebatur edictum de his, qui notantur infam. l. prima, ff. dict. tit. Postea erat edictum de procuratoribus & Defensoribus, l. 8. §. Procuratorem, l. 33. §. aut Praetor, 3. l. 39. §. si quis, l. 43. §. 1. de Procuratoribus. Cui adjunctum fuit edictum, de negot. gest. Et huic edicto de his, qui pecuniam, ut negotium facerent vel non facerent accepisse dicantur, l. 2. & 3. & l. penultima, de calumn. Videntur haec edicta de postulando pertinuisse ad unum eundemque tit generalem de postulando, quia sunt ferè ejusdem argumenti; puta, de Advocatis, Procuratoribus & Negotiorum gestoribus.
units.tr: There were several edicts on summoning to court: one on the persons who may or may not be summoned, l. 4. & sequentib. de in jus voc. another on not removing by force a person who has been summoned, l. 1. & 4. Neque enim, &c. and a third on giving security for appearance in court, which in the edict, unless I am mistaken, was called a promise or a bail for appearance (vadimonium), l. 4. qui satisdare cog. Part of this edict on appearance is the edict "if it arises from a noxal cause," etc., l. 1. si ex noxali causa. The title si quis caut. of the Digest also belongs to this bail for appearance. Fourth, there is an edict on an action in factum against one who prevents another from appearing in court, leg. 1. de eo, per quem factum, etc. Perhaps there were other edicts belonging to this title on summoning to court, but they cannot conveniently be drawn out of the fragments of the books. Fifth, however, one is fairly clearly extant: l. 2. quibus ex causa (the wording "in possession is to be put" is found here, as the inscription indicates), which is the text of Ulpian in the fifth book on the edict cited above, where the earlier matters are also explained, although Tribonian has moved this to the edict on the sending into possession. After this title of the perpetual edict on summoning to court came the title on pleading (de postulando), l. 1. de postul. which was followed by the edict on those who are marked with infamy, l. prima, ff. dict. tit. Afterwards there was the edict on procurators and defenders, l. 8. §. Procuratorem, l. 33. §. aut Praetor, 3. l. 39. §. si quis, l. 43. §. 1. de Procuratoribus. To this was joined the edict on agency (de negotiis gestis), and to this edict on those who are said to have received money in order to do or not to do business, l. 2. & 3. & l. penultima, de calumn. These edicts on pleading seem to have belonged to one and the same general title on pleading, because they are almost of the same subject: namely, on advocates, procurators and agents of business.

units.la: Hunc autem tit. sequebatur item generalis tit. de in integrum restit. Nam & sub eo multa fuerunt edicta, quia & sex sunt restitutionum species, l. 1. & 2. de in int. gr. restit. Primum sub eo tit. Edictum est de metu, sive quod metus causa. II. Est de dolo malo, l. 1. §. verba autem, de dolo. III. De aetate, l. 1. §. praetor, de minor. IV. De status mutatione, l. 2. §. 1. de cap. dim. V. De absentia Reipub. causa, l. 1. ex quib. caus. major. VI. De justo errore, l. 2. & 3. quod falso tutore, &c. Nam & hoc tit. quod falso tutore &c. continetur species restitutionis in integrum, quem tamen tit. Tribun. rejicit ad tractatum de tutel. in ff. Ratio ibi exponetur. Ad hunc titulum, de in integrum restit. & tit. 7. ne qua alienatio mutandi judicii causa; &c. pertinere videtur; nam & ibi sit quaedam restitutio, l. 1. & 3. §. exhib. l. 4. & l. de alienat. jud. mut.
units.tr: This title was followed by another general title, on restitution in integrum. For under it too there were many edicts, since there are six kinds of restitution, l. 1. & 2. de in int. gr. restit. First, under this title, is the edict on fear, or what is done through fear. Second, the edict on wicked fraud, l. 1. §. verba autem, de dolo. Third, on age, l. 1. §. praetor, de minor. Fourth, on change of status, l. 2. §. 1. de cap. dim. Fifth, on absence for the sake of the commonwealth, l. 1. ex quib. caus. major. Sixth, on a just error, l. 2. & 3. quod falso tutore, etc. For this title, quod falso tutore, etc., also contains a kind of restitution in integrum, though Tribonian refers this title to the treatise on guardianship in the Digest. The reason will be explained there. To this title on restitution in integrum, and to title 7, ne qua alienatio mutandi judicii causa, etc., it seems also to belong; for there too there is a certain restitution, l. 1. & 3. §. exhib. l. 4. & l. de alienat. jud. mut.

units.la: Et huic titul. de restitut. in integr. Proximus videtur fuisse tit. de recept. ad quem titulum duo edicta pertinent de arbitris, l. 3. §. 1. & 2. de recept. alterum de nautis, cauponibus, &c. l. 1. naut. caup. stab. Atque hi sunt tituli, & Edicta ad primum caput, & περὶ pertinentia.
units.tr: And next after this title on restitution in integrum seems to have been the title on arbiters (de receptis). Two edicts belong to this title: one on arbiters, l. 3. §. 1. & 2. de recept. the other on shipmasters, innkeepers, etc., l. 1. naut. caup. stab. These are the titles and the edicts belonging to the first head, and to the περὶ [part].

units.la: II. Pars Edicti Perpetui.
units.tr: II. The Second Part of the Perpetual Edict.

units.la: PRoximo deinde loco videtur in edicto fuisse titul. de judiciis, tametsi reperire satis liquido & certo non potui, edicta sub hoc tit. comprehensa. Sed & hunc tit. fuisse in edicto argumenta probant. I. Paul. lib. 1. sent. tit. 10. & 4. seqq. qui edicti ordinem iis in libris est secutus. II. Ipse ordo ff. Lomne, §. & anima. verf. post eorum, & §. in secundo initio ff. l. 2. C. de jure vet. enucl. Ex quib. locis intelligitur jam olim fuisse primam juris partem dictam περὶ κρίσεως. III. Deinde judiciis: quae appellatio partis fortasse sumpta fuit ex ipso tit. primo edicti.
units.tr: Next in order, the edict seems to have contained a title de judiciis (on trials), although I could not find with any clarity the edicts comprised under this title. Yet the following arguments show that this title existed in the edict. I. Paulus, Sententiae lib. 1, tit. 10, and the following titles, who followed the order of the edict in those books. II. The very order of the Digest, in ff. Lomne, §. & anima, verse post eorum, and §. in secundo initio of ff. l. 2 C. de jure vet. enucl. From these passages it is understood that the first part of law was already long ago called περὶ κρίσεως [concerning judgment]. III. Then, de judiciis: which name of the part was perhaps taken from the first title of the edict itself.

units.la: Hunc tit. de judiciis videntur singulae actiones subsecutae & in edicto suisse propositae; & primo quidem actiones in rem universales; ut querela inofficiosi testamenti petitio hereditatis, si pars hereditatis petatur, possessoria hereditatis petitio, fideicommissaria hereditatis petitio, l. si pars hered. pet. l. 1. de possess. hered. pet. l. 1. de R. V. in quibus II. hic ordo edicti dilucide exponitur. Sed tamen de his actionibus nullae dictorum verba jut puto, ex hac, ut neque
units.tr: Under this title de judiciis the individual actions that followed were apparently set out in the edict; and first of all the actions in rem of universal scope, such as the complaint of an unduteous will (querela inofficiosi testamenti), the petition for an inheritance (petitio hereditatis) if a part of the inheritance is sought, the possessory petition for an inheritance, and the fideicommissary petition for an inheritance: l. si pars hered. pet., l. 1 de possess. hered. pet., l. 1 de R. V., in which passages this order of the edict is clearly set out. But I think there are no words of the edict about these actions, in this way, that neither...

units.la: {1} Quod. .. de rei vind. Cuius rei causa videtur esse hęc quod hæc actiones sint civiles, in edicto autem sua; hoc est, prætoria plenius, civilia nudè tantum proposuisse, & interdum deiis multa omisisse, exceptis tantum actionib. Dices. possessoriam hereditatis petitionem esse prætoriam, & tamen nullû de ea edictû reperiri. Sed id inde est quod illius eadem estratio, quæ petitionis civilis, quæ causa quoque est, car Jurisconsultiad edictum, de illa nil fere explicarint. l. 2. de poss. hered. pet.
units.tr: {1} Quod ... de rei vind. The reason for this seems to be that these actions are civil, whereas in the edict the praetor's own actions, that is, the praetorian ones, were set out more fully; the civil ones were merely stated briefly, and sometimes many of them were omitted, except for the actions. You may object that the possessory petition for an inheritance is praetorian, and yet no edict concerning it is found. But this comes about because its procedure is the same as that of the civil petition, which is also the reason why the jurists, in their commentaries on the edict, explained little or nothing about it: l. 2 de poss. hered. pet.

units.la: Possessiones de universitate propositæ fuerunt actiones rerum singularium. l. 1. de R. V. Ut est rei vindicatio. Publiciana actio de agro vectigali. Sed de publiciana tantum exstant verba edicti quia est prætoria, l. 1. de publician. in rem. Nam actio de agro vectigali civilis quoq; videtur quia jus hoc habet emphyteuticum, quod jus est quoddam in rem dominio non absimile, & proinde civile quiddam, sed à domino tamen distinctum & proinde propriam partiens actionem, leg. 63. de evictionis. leg. 5 in sin. arb. furtiva. l. leg. 15. de damno infecto.
units.tr: Of the actions in rem concerning things in general, the following were set out in the edict as actions concerning single things: l. 1 de R. V. Such as the vindication of a thing (rei vindicatio), the Publician action concerning land held on an emphyteutic lease. But of the Publician action only the words of the edict survive, because it is praetorian: l. 1 de publician. in rem. For the action concerning land held on an emphyteutic lease seems also to be civil, since the tenant has this emphyteutic right, which is a certain right not unlike ownership in a thing, and therefore something civil; but it is distinct from the owner's right, and therefore has its own separate action: leg. 63 de evictionis, leg. 5 in sin. arb. furtiva, l. leg. 15 de damno infecto.

units.la: Post in rem actiones de rebus corporalib. videtur in edicto propositæ fuisse actio confessoria & negatoria, de servitut. & usufructu leg. 15. §. de præteritis, de usufructu l. 2. siferv. vind. Sed & hæ sunt civiles ideoq; nulla exstant edicta & Jurisconsulti in libris ad edicta, valde breviter de his servitutibus explicarunt.
units.tr: After the actions in rem concerning corporeal things, the confessory and negatory actions, concerning servitudes and usufruct, seem to have been set out in the edict: leg. 15 §. de praeteritis, de usufructu l. 2 si serv. vind. But these too are civil, and therefore no edicts survive, and the jurists in their commentaries on the edict explained these servitudes very briefly.

units.la: Post has in Edicto fortasse propositæ fuerunt actiones de pauperie l. Aquilia, sinu regund. sum ercisc. communi divid. Sed de his quoq; nulla exstat edicta, q. ihæ sunt civiles, his ex legib. partim ex l. 12. tab. partim ex l. Aquilia nec sive introductæ An autè noxales actiones in edicto fuerint propositæ, ut in ff dubito. Ni videntur potius statim positæ fuisse post actionem l. Aquilia. ut videre est in l. 2. §. 6. & 7. de nox. act. quæ sunt ex Ulp. lib. 18. ad Edict. in quo et a de l. Aquil. explicavit. Mutavit igitur in Cod. ordine Edicti Tribunitius Ratio autè ordinis Edicti est, quia ut actio l. Aquiliæ est de damno, ita & hæ sunt de noxa hoc est, de damno. Quia autem hæ noxales actiones non sunt proprie & principales actiones, sed tantum accessoriæ & titulo tenus, ut & actiones de peculio, propterea hæ actiones, si accedunt civilib. dicuntur civiles si prætoriis dicuntur prætoriæ. §. 2 Inst. de noxal. act. Et hinc est quod de noxali actionibus Edictum exstat l. 21. quoties. §. prætor nil. de nox. act.
units.tr: After these, perhaps the actions concerning damage done by animals (de pauperie), the Aquilian law, boundary-marking (sinu regund.), partition of an inheritance (familiae erciscundae), and division of common property (communi dividundo) were set out in the edict. But of these too no edict survives, since these actions are civil, arising partly from the Twelve Tables and partly from the Aquilian law, and were not introduced by the praetor. I doubt whether the noxal actions were set out in the edict, as in the Digest. It seems rather that they were placed straight after the Aquilian action, as may be seen in l. 2 §. 6 & 7 de nox. act., which come from Ulpian, book 18 on the Edict, where he also explained the Aquilian law. The Tribunician editors therefore changed the order of the edict in the Code. The reason for the order of the edict is that just as the Aquilian action concerns damage, so these actions concern noxa, that is, damage. But because these noxal actions are not properly and principally actions, but only accessory and in name, like the action concerning the peculium, these actions, if they attach to civil ones, are called civil, and if to praetorian ones, praetorian: §. 2 Inst. de noxal. act. And hence it is that an edict on noxal actions exists: l. 21 quoties. §. praetor nil. de nox. act.

units.la: Post has actiones videntur quædam in Edicto fuisse de actionib. quæ propter inficiationem crescunt, & de beneficio ut vocant divisionis inter heredes sex Edicto prætoris. Id colligere licet ex Paulo l. 1. sent. rit. ulr. impr. §. ex Ulp. lib. 20. ad Edictum & 21. & ex Paulo ad Edictum l. b. 24. Sed edicti verba non exstant & in ff planè aliò loco illa tractantur: edictum in quam de divisione inter fidejussores sub ut, de fidejussoribus. Cur autè in Edicto de cognoscitur hoc loco, causam fuisse puto, quia hic agitur de causa communi dividundo cui propter similitudinem adjunctum fuit de beneficio divisionis vel etiam quod insiciainficiatione amitteretur beneficium divisionis l.10. §.1. ff. de fidejuss. qui mand. (puto autem hoc Edictum de divisione obligationis inter fidejussores fuisse novum; & esse a Juliano ex Constitutione Hadriani relatum in Edictum. Nam haec divisio solet alias plerunq; tribui Epistolae sive constitutioni Hadriani §. si plures Inst. de fidejuss.)
units.tr: After these actions, certain matters seem to have been set out in the edict: actions that grow on account of denial (propter inficiationem), and the benefit of division among heirs, as they call it, by the praetor's edict. This may be gathered from Paulus, Sent. lib. 1, tit. ult. impr. §. ; from Ulpian, book 20 and 21 on the Edict; and from Paulus on the Edict, book 24. But the words of the edict do not survive, and in the Digest these matters are treated quite elsewhere: the edict on division among sureties is under ut, de fidejussoribus. Why the edict is discussed here I think is because this passage deals with the action for division of common property, to which, on account of the similarity, was attached the benefit of division, or even because by denial the benefit of division would be lost: l. 10 §. 1 ff. de fidejuss. qui mand. (But I think this edict on the division of the obligation among sureties was new, and that Julian took it from a constitution of Hadrian and placed it in the edict. For this division is usually otherwise ascribed to a letter or constitution of Hadrian: §. si plures Inst. de fidejuss.)

units.la: Postea in Edicto propositum fuit edictum de interrogationibus, quod est planè praetorium, ejusque verba quaedam extant l.2. & 4. §. quod praetor de interrogat. in jure fac. Mirum autem videri possit Ulpianum lib.22. ad Edict explicasse non tantum Edictum de interrogationibus. Sed etiam Edictum de jurejurando, ut indicat L.3.5.7.9.11.13 de jurejur. quae leges huntex li.22. Ex quo etiam sunt leges 2 4.6.9.11.& 21. de interrogat. Sed responderi potest bifariam: vel quia olim interrogatio erat duplex, vel adhibito jurejurando, vel non illam vocabant rogare sacramento de quo videatur Festus in verbo sacramentum: ubi haec duo sacramento contendere & sacramento rogare explicantur: licet locus sit valde mendosus: vel dicendum has leges exli. 22. de jurejur. referendas esse ad lib.26. ut mendum sit in numero: quemadmodum in Paulo lib.17. ad Edictum ponuntur leges sub tit. de jurejur. quae pertinent potius ad lib.27. sic in eodem Paulo lib.18. ad Edictum, ponuntur 10. leges sub tit. de jurejur. quae pertinent potius ad lib.28.
units.tr: Afterwards in the edict was set out the edict on interrogations, which is plainly praetorian, and some of its words survive: l. 2 & 4 §. quod praetor de interrogat. in jure fac. It may seem strange that Ulpian, in book 22 on the Edict, explained not only the edict on interrogations but also the edict on the oath, as L. 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13 de jurejur. indicate; these laws are taken from book 22. From the same book come leges 2, 4, 6, 9, 11 & 21 de interrogat. But there are two possible answers: either because formerly there was a double interrogation, with or without an oath, and they called the latter "to interrogate by oath" (rogare sacramento), on which see Festus under the word sacramentum, where these two phrases, sacramento contendere and sacramento rogare, are explained, although the passage is very corrupt; or it must be said that these laws of book 22 on oaths should be referred to book 26, so that there is an error in the number. Just as in Paulus, book 17 on the Edict, laws are placed under the title on oaths which belong rather to book 27; so in the same Paulus, book 18 on the Edict, ten laws are placed under the title on oaths which belong rather to book 28.

units.la: Huia Edicto de interrogationibus adjuncta fuerunt Edicta primo, de his qui effuderunt: ejus verba extant in l.1. & 5. §. praetor ait d.tit. Secundo de servo corrupto, cujus verba item extant d.tit. Tertio, de aleatoribus. Cujus item verba extant in l.1. de aleatorib. Extant inquam, quia sunt hae actiones & Edicta plane praetoria, quibus adjunctum quoq; fuit Edictum sive actio, ime-forfal;mod.dix. quae actio ite est praetoria in factum l.1. & 5. §. hoc jure dicium. d. tit. Ratio ordinis autem, cur haec quatuor Edicta cojunctim & in finesuerint posita haec est, quia delicta continent. Tribunianus autem hunc ordinem mire mutavit in ff. ubi ratio exponitur.
units.tr: Joined to this edict on interrogations were the following edicts: first, on those who have poured out (de his qui effuderunt), whose words survive in l. 1 & 5 §. praetor ait d. tit.; second, on a corrupted slave, whose words likewise survive in d. tit.; third, on gamblers (de aleatoribus), whose words likewise survive in l. 1 de aleatorib. They survive, I say, because these actions and edicts are plainly praetorian, and to them was also joined an edict or action, ime-forfal; mod. dix., which is a praetorian action in factum: l. 1 & 5 §. hoc jure dicium. d. tit. The reason why these four edicts were placed together and at the end is that they concern delicts. Tribonian, however, strangely changed this order in the Digest, and the reason is explained there.

units.la: Post ea Edicta fuit proposita actio ad exhibendum: & tandem actio de religiosis & sumptibus funerum. Sed de illa non extat Edictum quia sequitur rei vindicationem, hoc est ejus naturam, cujus praeparandae causa est introducta l.1. ad exhib. De religiosis actio in factum est, & praetoria l.2. §. praetor aut, & alterum in l.12 §. praetor a t. de religios.
units.tr: After those edicts was set out the action for exhibition, and finally the action concerning religious places and the expenses of funerals. But for the former there is no edict, because it follows the action for recovery of property (rei vindicatio), that is, its nature, for the sake of preparing which it was introduced: Dig. 10.4, l. 1 (ad exhibendum). The action concerning religious places is an action on the case and praetorian: Dig. 11.7, l. 2 §. praetor aut, and the other at l. 12 §. praetor a t. de religios.

units.la: Quibus conjungitur Edictum de mortuo inferendo, positum in ff. sed non fuit junctum in Edicto perpetuo. Hoc enim Edictum de mortuo inferendo positum in Edicto perpetuo fuit eo loco, quo interdicta, propterea quod hoc de mortuo inferendo sit quoq; interdictum, ut ait l.1. de mortuo infer. Videatur inscriptio l.1. de mort. infer l.1. Ne quid in loco sacro &c.l.2 ne quid in loco publico.
units.tr: To these is joined the edict concerning carrying out the dead, set out in the Digest; but it was not joined to it in the Perpetual Edict. For this edict concerning carrying out the dead, set out in the Perpetual Edict, was placed in the same position in which the interdicts stood, because this edict concerning carrying out the dead is also an interdict, as the text says: Dig. 43.24, l. 1 (de mortuo inferendo). See the inscription: Dig. 11.7, l. 1 (de mortuo inferendo); l. 1 (ne quid in loco sacro etc.); l. 2 (ne quid in loco publico).

units.la: III. Pars Edicti Perpetui.
units.tr: III. Part of the Perpetual Edict.

units.la: POst ista judicia in rem aliaq; ejus adjuncta in Edicto perpetuo positus fuit tit.de reb.cred.sub quo titulo prætor inseruit multa ad varios contractus pertinentia, ut ait Ulp.l.1. §.1.ff.tit. Quæ autem fuerint ea inserta sub hoc tit.generali idem Ulp.indicat. Ait autem in d.l.1. prætorem sub hoc tit de commodato quoq; & de pignore edixisse. Nam de mutuo licet nihil dicat Ulp.tamen certum est propterea quod rerum creditarum appellatione mutuum proprie continentur, generaliter tamen & minus proprie etiam alius contractus: queadmodum creditoris & debitoris vocabula proprie in mutuo generaliter etiá in aliis contractibus dicuntur.l.creditores 19. de verb.sign. Sub hoc igitur tit.de reb.creditis. fuit Edictum de mutuo de commodato, de pignore, ut jâ dictum. Videtur & de indebito fuisse, quod i mutuo est similimum. Unde & per mutuum Cujacius putat appellatum, indebitum, de quo tamen alias dictum. Puto quoq; de constituto sub hoc tit.prætorem edixisse propterea quod mutuo sit simile in eo quod utrumq; tantum in rebus quæ pondere, numero & mensura constant locum habent jure veteri. Nam hodie constitutum in omnibus rebus locum habet l.2.C.de const.pec. Est & altera ratio constitutum sub hoc tit.fuisse positum in Edicto quia procedat commodatum & pignus: Nam tit.de constit.prior est titulo commod. & de pignorat. ast. Nunc si commodatum & pignus fuerint sub tit.de reb.cred.(ut testatur Ulp. in l.1.de reb.cred.)certè intelligitur etiam constitutum sub eo fuisse. Puto quoque de jurejurando prætorem sub eo tit.edixisse. tum quia jusiurandum ferè in mutuo adhibetur, tum quia ordo ff hoc indicat. & liberorum ad Edictum, in quib. de jurejurando statim agitur post mutuum. Ex his jam intelligitur quod Ulp.ait in d.l.1.de reb. cred. sub hoc tit de rebus creditis multa ad varios contractus pertinentia fuisse collocata, ut de mutuo, de jurejurando, de indebito, de constituto, de commodato de pignore. Etiam receptitia actio sub eodem tit.fuit comprehensa de qua infra.
units.tr: After these actions in rem and their accessories, the Perpetual Edict set out the title de rebus creditis, under which the praetor inserted many provisions relating to various contracts, as Ulpian says in l. 1, §1, ff. of the same title. Ulpian himself indicates which provisions were inserted under this general title. In the same law he says that the praetor also issued an edict under this title concerning commodatum and pledge. Ulpian says nothing about mutuum, but it is certain that it was included, because by the term res creditae (things lent) mutuum is properly meant, and the term also applies generally, though less properly, to other contracts; in the same way the words creditor and debtor properly belong to mutuum but are used generally of other contracts too (l. creditores 19, de verb. sign.). So under this title de rebus creditis there was an edict on mutuum, on commodatum and on pledge, as already said. It seems there was also one on what was not owed (indebitum), which is very like mutuum; Cujacius thinks that for this reason it was called indebitum by a kind of mutuum, though I have spoken of this elsewhere. I also think the praetor issued an edict on constitutum under this title, both because it resembles mutuum in that each applies only to things measured by weight, number or measure under the old law (for today constitutum applies to all things, l. 2, C. de const. pec.), and because commodatum and pledge came before the title de constitutis and de pignoratitia actione. Now if commodatum and pledge were under the title de rebus creditis (as Ulpian attests in l. 1, de reb. cred.), it is clearly to be understood that constitutum was under it as well. I also think the praetor issued an edict on oath (iusiurandum) under this title, both because an oath is commonly used in mutuum, and because the order of the Digest and of the Edict, in which the action on oath follows mutuum directly, indicates this. From these points it is now clear what Ulpian says in the same law, de reb. cred.: that under this title many provisions relating to various contracts were placed, such as those on mutuum, oath, what was not owed, constitutum, commodatum and pledge. The receptitia actio also was included under the same title, as will be discussed below.

units.la: Hinc quoq; quæstio illa inter recentiores Dd.(ut sunt Cujac.Hotom Cotius, Donellus, & Ravardus) agitata, explicari potest an hic tit.ff.de reb.cred. sit generalis, an vero specialis. Non enim est planè specialis quia pertinet non ad unam speciem contractus, sed ad multas. Non etiá est planè generalis, quia non pertinuit ad omnes, ut ad mandatum, depositum &c. sed tantum ad quosdam commodatum, mutuum &c. Quare generalis dici potest aliquatenus, non verò omninò, ut quidam putant, qui volunt hunc titulum esse generalem, & communem omnium contractuum, id quod refellitur ex l.1. ff. de rebus cred.
units.tr: From this also can be explained the question debated among the more recent jurists (such as Cujacius, Hotman, Cotius, Donellus and Ravardus): whether this title, de rebus creditis, is general or special. It is not wholly special, since it concerns not one kind of contract but many. Nor is it wholly general, since it did not extend to all contracts, such as mandate, deposit and the rest, but only to certain ones, such as commodatum and mutuum. It can therefore be called general in some respects but not absolutely, as some think, who wish this title to be general and common to all contracts; this view is refuted by l. 1, ff. de reb. cred.

units.la: Nunc videamus de Edictis, quo ordine sub hoc tit de rebus creditis fuerint posita. Et primum fuit Edictum de mutuo, sive de actione quæ condictio certi dicitur. Hujus autem Edicti de mutuo nullâ mentionem reperio, credo
units.tr: Now let us see in what order the edicts under this title de rebus creditis were set out. First came the edict on mutuum, or on the action which is called condictio certi. Yet I find no mention of this edict on mutuum; I believe it was

units.la: quod breve fuerit: propterea quod mutuum sit civile non vero praetorium. Dubitari tamen non debet quin aliquid, de mutuo fuerit edictum sub hoc titulo. Nam si sint de commodato, aliquod, ut ait Ulpian. l.b. certè & de mutuo fuisse necesse est hac ratione, quia verbum rerum creditarum proprie ad mutuum pertinet, ut supra dictum. Ordinis autem ratio, hoc est, cur in Edicto perpetuo judicia priora in rem & alia ejus adjuncta statim secuta fuerit hic titulus explicata est ad titulum C.t.& 2.lib.4.
units.tr: short, because mutuum is a civil, not a praetorian, institution. Still there should be no doubt that some edict on mutuum was issued under this title. For if there was one on commodatum, as Ulpian says in l.b., then there must certainly also have been one on mutuum, for the reason that the words res creditae properly belong to mutuum, as said above. The reason for the order, that is, why in the Perpetual Edict the actions in rem and their accessories were followed directly by this title, has been explained at the title C. 2, lib. 4.

units.la: Deinde sub eodem titulo fuit Edictum, de iurejur. cujus verba exstant l.34. §. ait praetor. D. iurejur. Ratio ordinis idem dictus est ad titulum C.de reb. cred.& iurejur.
units.tr: Next under the same title came the edict de iurejurando, whose words survive in l. 34, §. ait praetor, D. de iurejur. The reason for the order has been stated at the titles C. de reb. cred. and de iurejur.

units.la: Sub eodem titulo videtur etiam fuisse edictum de indebito, sive de condictione indebiti & aliis condictionibus quae tamen quia non ex jure praetorio, sed ex aequo & bono oriuntur, nulla fit mentio edicti de his condictionibus, l 66. hac condictio. de cond. indeb.
units.tr: Under the same title there also seems to have been an edict on what was not owed, that is, on the condictio indebiti and other condictiones. Since these do not arise from praetorian law but from equity and good faith, no mention is made of an edict on these condictiones (l. 66, hac condictio, de cond. indeb.).

units.la: Huic proximum fuit edictum de constituta pecunia, quod est planè praetorium, quia est pacto & fide pendet. §. in personarum Inst. de act. Ratio ordinis item propter similitudinem cum mutuo: utrumque enim ut supra dictum, iisdem in rebus locum habebat. Hujus autem edicti de constituto mentio & verba exstant. ml.1, l.16. 1 dato §. ait praetor. l.18 item illa. de constit. pec.
units.tr: Next to this was the edict on money promised by agreement (de constituta pecunia), which is purely praetorian, since it depends on a pact and on good faith (§. in personarum, Inst. de act.). The order is again explained by the resemblance to mutuum, for, as said above, both applied to the same kinds of things. The mention and words of this edict on constitutum survive in l. 1; l. 16, §1, dato, §. ait praetor; l. 18, item illa, de const. pec.

units.la: Quia autem vetus actio receptitia, huic constitutoriae fuit persimilis (nam recipere, constituere, & promittere fere idem valent) verisimile est hanc quoque receptitiam actionem sub eodem titulo de rebus creditis comprehensam fuisse.
units.tr: Since the old receptitia actio was very similar to this constitutoria (for recipere, constituere and promittere have nearly the same meaning), it is likely that this receptitia actio too was included under the same title de rebus creditis.

units.la: Huic proxima fuit actio commodati, de qua exstant verba edicti l.1. d. tit. Ratio ordinis propter similitudinem commodati cum mutuo, quod utrumque Graecè & Germanicè uno eodemque nomine appellatur: & plerumque commodatum in rebus mobilibus locum habet. l.1. §. inter commodatum. ff. commod. ut & mutuum.
units.tr: Next to this came the action of commodatum, whose edict words are given in l. 1, d. tit. The reason for the order is the resemblance of commodatum to mutuum: both are called by one and the same name in Greek and in German, and commodatum applies mostly to movable things, as does mutuum (l. 1, §. inter commodatum, ff. commod.).

units.la: Huic adjuncta fuit proxime in Edicto actio pignoratitia sub eodem titulo de reb. cred. ut ait l.1. de reb. cred. Ratio ordinis est item propter similitudinem quod scilicet hi contractus omnes, mutuum, indebitum, commodatum pignus, res fiant. Sed Edicti de pignore verba non exstant.
units.tr: Next to this, in the Edict, immediately followed the action of pledge under the same title de rebus creditis, as l. 1, de reb. cred. says. The reason for the order is again the resemblance: all these contracts, mutuum, what was not owed, commodatum and pledge, concern things. But the words of the edict on pledge do not survive.

units.la: Illud hic notandum, quod ib.2. tenent intertit de constituta pecunia, & de commodato interjecit tit. 2. de contract. b. (sic enim in libris de vulgatis inscribitur, sub quo agitur de stipulatione. Videtur autem sub eo tit. explicasse veterem actionem receptitiam de qua videtur l.2. C. de const. pec. Nam constitutoria & receptitia actio cum in aliis rebus differebant, tum in eo quod constitutum fieret verbis nudis, ut species pacti: receptitia actio fieret verbis solemnibus, ut species verborum obligationis. d.l. & idcirco Paulus ibi agit de stipulatione, dum scilicet propter verborum solemnitatem similis erat receptum.
units.tr: Here it should be noted that between the edicts on constitutum and on commodatum the Digest inserts title 2, de contract. b. (for so it is inscribed in the common editions), under which stipulation is treated. It seems that in that title Paulus explained the old receptitia actio, which is mentioned in l. 2, C. de const. pec. For the constitutoria and the receptitia actio differed in other respects, and in this, that constitutum was made by bare words, like a species of pact, whereas the receptitia was made by solemn words, like a species of verbal obligation. So Paulus there treats of stipulation, since the receptitia resembled it in its solemn form of words.

units.la: Has autem actiones Constitutoriam & receptitiam in Edicto proxime sequebatur actio exercitoria, de qua ipsum Edictum non exstat. Sed de eo fit mentio in l. 1. §. 1. in sin. de exerc. act. Verbatim en Edicti facile colligi possunt ex d. l. 1.
units.tr: The actions constitutoria and receptitia were directly followed in the Edict by the action exercitoria, of which the Edict itself does not survive. But mention of it is made in l. 1, §. 1, in fine, de exerc. act. The words of the Edict can be readily gathered from that law.

units.la: Huic proximum fuit edictum de institoria actione, cujus item verba non exstant, sed ejus fit mentio in l. 1. l. 17. §. de instit. act.
units.tr: Next to this was the edict on the institoria actio, whose words likewise do not survive, but mention of it is made in l. 1; l. 17, §. de instit. act.

units.la: Huic deinde adjunctum fuit Edictum de tributoria, cujus etiam verba non exstant, sed colligi possunt fere ex l. 1. d. tit. Ratio ordinis autem. Cur in Edicto perpetuo illas actiones de mutuo, indebito, constituto, commodato, pignore proxime secutae fuerint hae actiones, exercitoria, institoria, tributoria, haec mihi videtur, quia hae tres actiones ad merces & mercatum pertinent. l. 1. de exerc. act. l. 1. §. pen. de instit. act. l. 1. de trib. act. Merces autem sunt rerum mobilium, & plerumque vini, olei, frumenti, & similium rerum, quae sunt etiam in mutuo, propter quam similitudinem cum mutuo & prioribus contractibus recte hae actiones prioribus fuerunt adjunctae: & quidem postpositae, quia sunt praetoriae: cum illae sint civiles excepta constitutoria. Cetera autem praetoriis sunt digniora, & efficaciora, & antiquiora, ita & loco & ordine priora esse debent, ut saepe jam dictum.
units.tr: To this was then attached the edict on the tributoria, whose words also do not survive, but they can be roughly gathered from l. 1, d. tit. The reason for the order, why these actions, exercitoria, institoria and tributoria, followed directly after those on mutuum, what was not owed, constitutum, commodatum and pledge, seems to me to be that these three actions concern merchandise and trade (l. 1, de exerc. act.; l. 1, §. pen., de instit. act.; l. 1, de trib. act.). Merchandise consists of movable things, mostly wine, oil, grain and similar things, which are also the subject of mutuum; because of this resemblance to mutuum and the earlier contracts, these actions were rightly attached to the earlier ones, though placed after them, because they are praetorian, whereas the former are civil, with the exception of constitutoria. The other actions were more worthy, more effective and older than the praetorian ones, and so ought to come first in place and order, as has often been said already.

units.la: Proximum istis in Edicto, fuit Edictum de peculio, de in rem verso, de eo quod jussu. l. 1. de pecul. verba ejus exstant partim in d. l. 1. §. 1. partim in l. 2. quod cum eo, &c. partim in l. 1. quando de pecul. Ratio ordinis edicti exponitur ab ipso Ulp. in d. l. 1. de pecul.
units.tr: Next in the Edict after these came the Edict concerning the peculium, concerning what was turned to the owner's advantage (de in rem verso), and concerning what was done by command (de eo quod jussu). The words of this edict survive partly in l. 1 §1 de pecul., partly in l. 2 quod cum eo etc., and partly in l. 1 quando de pecul. The reason for the order of the edict is set out by Ulpian himself in the same l. 1 de pecul.

units.la: Dixi modo tres priores actiones exercitoriam &c. postpositas illis de mutuo, &c. quia sunt praetoriae: indicatur & altera ab Ulpiano in d. l. 1. d. pecul. haec: quia illae de mutuo, indebito, &c. sunt ex contractibus propriis hae tres exercitoria, &c. sunt ex contractibus alienis, hoc est dantur contra Dominos ex contractibus institorum, exercitorum & servorum. Propria autem sunt alienis priora & potiora.
units.tr: I have just said that the three earlier actions (the exercitoria and the others) are placed after those concerning loan, and so on, because they are praetorian. Ulpian, in the same l. 1 de pecul., points out another reason: those concerning loan, the indebitum and so on arise from the person's own contracts, whereas these three, the exercitoria and the rest, arise from the contracts of others; that is, they are given against owners on the contracts of their institores, exercitores and slaves. Actions arising from one's own contracts, however, come before and outrank those arising from the contracts of others.

units.la: Ex contractibus autem alienis nascuntur actiones aut in solidum, aut non in solidum sed in partem scilicet de peculio sive peculio tenus, aut quatenus in rem Domini sit versum In solidum sunt illae jam tres expositae inst. & tribut non in solidum sunt de peculio & de in rem verso. d. l. 1. Quae in solidum priore loco fuerunt positae reliquae posteriore. Ratio est quia universalia singularibus & tota partibus sunt priora. Et hinc est, quod ait Ulp. d. l. 1. de pecul. Ordinarium praetor arbitratus est prius eos contractus exponere eorum, qui alienae potestati subjecti sunt qui in solidum tribuunt actiones, sic deinde ad hunc pervenire, ubi de peculio datur actio.
units.tr: Actions arising from the contracts of others are either for the whole amount (in solidum), or not for the whole but only in part, namely de peculio (up to the value of the peculium), or as far as the thing has been turned to the owner's advantage (quatenus in rem domini versum sit). The three already explained in the Institutes are for the whole amount; the de peculio and de in rem verso actions are not for the whole. (l. 1 cited.) Those granting the whole amount were placed first, the rest afterwards. The reason is that universals come before singulars, and wholes before parts. Hence Ulpian says (l. 1 de pecul.): "The praetor thought it proper to set out first those contracts of persons subject to another's power which give actions for the whole amount; then to come to this, where an action de peculio is given."

units.la: Dicet aliquis, actionem quod jussit dari in solidum. f. 1. Instit. quod cum eo, &c. l. 1. f. quod jussu, & tamen eam non poni prius, nempe cum actionibus in solidum, exercitoria &c. sed ultimo loco post actiones non in solidum, ut de peculio & de in rem verso: & rectius videri in Instit. hanc actionem
units.tr: Someone may say that the action quod jussu is given for the whole amount (Inst. quod cum eo; l. 1 quod jussu), and yet it is not placed first, with the actions for the whole amount, exercitoria and the rest, but last, after the actions not for the whole, such as de peculio and de in rem verso; and that this action is seen more correctly in the Institutes...

units.la: {*} Hic vel inferius observa. nem quod jussu inter illos prætorias ex contractu alieno positam primo loco. Sed ratio Edicti hæc videtur esse, quod hæc actio quod jussu, etsi iis tribus, exercitoriæ, institoriæ & tributoriæ in eo est similis, quod datur in solidum, tamen in eo est dissimilis, quod datur ex contractu servi, sive in potestate nostra, sive non. Quare hæc actio, quod jussu similis est actioni de peculio, & de in rem verso, quia hæ restantum sunt de servorum & filiorumfam. contractibus.
units.tr: {*} Observe here or below: the edict placed the quod jussu action first among those praetorian actions arising from another's contract. But the reason for the edict seems to be this: although this action quod jussu is similar to those three (exercitoria, institoria and tributoria) in that it is given for the whole amount, it is dissimilar in that it arises from the contract of a slave, whether in our power or not. Therefore this action quod jussu is similar to the actions de peculio and de in rem verso, since these alone concern contracts of slaves and sons under power.

units.la: Cur ego, inquies hæc actio quod jussu inter has tres ponitur ultima? Ratio hæc est; quia maximè est specialis. Quid ita? quia tantum datur ex contractu qui factus est jussu qui contractus sunt rariores. At contractus, ex quibus de peculio actio oritur, ut actio de in rem verso, sunt longè communiores & frequentiores; quos scilicet servi & filiifa propria voluntate & liberè celebrant, non expectato jussu. Jam speciala & minus frequentia sunt posteriora communibus & frequentibus.
units.tr: Why, you will ask, is this action quod jussu placed last among these three? The reason is that it is most special. How so? Because it is given only on a contract made by command, and such contracts are rarer. But the contracts from which the action de peculio and the action de in rem verso arise are far more common and frequent; slaves and sons enter into them freely by their own will, without waiting for a command. Now special and less frequent things come after common and frequent ones.

units.la: Proximum in Edicto locum tenuit actio depositi: quæ duplex est, una civilis in simplum, altera prætoria in duplum, quia tumultus, ruinæ, incendii naufragi causa §. omnes. §. plane si depositi. Inst. de act. verba edicti extant in l. 1. §. depositi. Ratio ordinis est quia contractus depositi in prioribus contractibus mutui indebiti &c. est perseimilis in eo, quod hi quinq; soli re fiunt. Cur autem ex iis quinque, hic contractus depositi ultimum in Edicto locum tenuerit ratio hæc est: quia priores quatuor magis inter se sint similes ineo, quod illi fere in rebus qui numero pondere & mensura constant, locum habent. Deponuntur autem res alix potius, ut vestes, libri, servi, jumenta equi &c.
units.tr: Next in the Edict came the action of deposit, which is twofold: one civil, for the simple amount, the other praetorian, for double, because of tumult, collapse, fire or shipwreck (Inst. de act. §§ omnes, plane si depositi). The words of the edict survive in l. 1 §depositi. The reason for the order is that the contract of deposit is very like the earlier contracts of loan, indebitum and so on in this respect: that these five alone are made by delivery of the thing (re). Why, among these five, the contract of deposit holds the last place in the Edict, the reason is this: the first four are more alike in that they generally apply to things consisting in number, weight or measure. Things deposited, however, are rather other things, such as clothes, books, slaves, beasts of burden, horses and so on.

units.la: Erat olim & actio sive judicium fiduciæ similimum actioni depositi propter similitudinem. Non enim Cujacio assentiendum, putantiin notis ad Paul. lib. 2. sent. tit. 4 depositum nihil habere simile cum fiducia; quem non tantum nomen fiduciæ, sed etiam Paulus ipse refellit, qui de fiduciaagit eodem in loco, ubi de depósito lib. 2. sent. cap. 13. in quibus libris sententiarum Paulus edicti ordinem est secutus, ut supra dictum in initio Quod autem in ff. hujus judicii fiduciæ, (de quo tamen & Cic. interdum ut lib. 3. off. lib. 3. de nat. Deor.) neque mentio fit neque ullus est titulus, eaufa hæc est, quia contractus fiduciæ tempore Justiniani fuit sublatus. §. ult. Inst. de legi. agn. succes.
units.tr: Formerly there was also an action or judgment of fiducia, very like the action of deposit because of their similarity. For I cannot agree with Cujas, who in his notes to Paul (lib. 2 sent. tit. 4) thinks that deposit has nothing in common with fiducia; Paul himself refutes him, not only by the name of fiducia but also because he treats of fiducia in the same place where he treats of deposit (lib. 2 sent. cap. 13), in books of the Sentences in which Paul followed the order of the edict, as said above at the beginning. That the Digest says nothing of this judgment of fiducia (though Cicero too mentions it at times, as in lib. 3 off. and lib. 3 de nat. deor.), and has no title on it, the reason is that the contract of fiducia was abolished in Justinian's time (Inst. de leg. agn. succ. §ult.).

units.la: Hinc proximum locum tenuit actio mandati, ut videre est in libris Gaij. Ulp. Pauli ad Edict deinde actio pro socio: puta actio empti & venditi, deinde actio æstimatoria l. 1. de æstim. act. & tandem actio locati & conducti. Ratio ordinis, hoc est, cur postactiones ex contractibus qui re fiunt, ponantur hæ actiones, quæ sunt ex contractibus consensu; est hæc: quia hæc duo contractuum genera (re & consensu) sunt principalia, reliqua duo (verbis & literis sive ut olim nominibus) sunt accessoria, & ideo circò in ultimum locum merito rejecta.
units.tr: Hence the action of mandate held the next place, as may be seen in the books of Gaius, Ulpian and Paul on the Edict; then the action pro socio; then the action of purchase and sale (empti venditi), then the action aestimatoria (l. 1 de aestim. act.), and finally the action of hire (locati conducti). The reason for the order, that is, why after the actions arising from contracts made by delivery, these actions, which arise from contracts made by consent, are placed, is this: these two kinds of contract (by thing and by consent) are principal, while the remaining two (by words and by writing, or as formerly by names) are accessory, and so were rightly thrust into the last place.

units.la: Inter hos autem quiconsensu, cur actio mandati primum locum tenuerit in Edicto ratio haec esse videtur, quia mandatum depositi aliquatenus est simile, in eo, quod utrumque est gratuitum, & utrumque amicitia nixum, l. 1. §. mandatum ff. mand. §. praeterea, in verbo qui negligenter am co. Inst. quibus mod. re contrahitur 4. l. neque ff. de pos. quibus proximè adjungitur actio pro socio, propterea quod hic quoque contractus societatem amicitiam & jus quammodo fraternitatis in se habet, ut ait l. 6. §. ff. pro socio. Tertium inter hos consensu contractus locum tenuit emptio, & quartum locatio. quod emptio fit & celebrior & efficacior in eo, quod emptione si venditor est Dominus transferatur dominium §. vendita. l. ult. de rer. div. ff. locatione nunquam transferatur. l. 39. non solet ff. loc. Huic adjuncta fuit aestimatoria actio quia partim emptioni, partim locationi est similis, & utrique tamen dissimilis. l. 1. de aestim. act. Atque haec hactenus de actionibus in rem, atque actionibus in personam ex contractu.
