units.tr: Among those contracts made by consent, the reason why the action of mandate held the first place in the Edict seems to be this: mandate is somewhat like deposit, in that both are gratuitous and both rest on friendship (l. 1 §mandatum ff. mand.; Inst. quibus mod. re contrahitur, §praeterea, in verbo qui negligenter; l. neque ff. de pos.). Next to it is joined the action pro socio, because this contract too holds partnership, friendship and a certain bond of brotherhood within itself, as l. 6 §... ff. pro socio says. The third consensual contract in this group was purchase, and the fourth hire. Purchase is more common and more effective in this respect: by purchase, if the seller is owner, ownership is transferred (§vendita; l. ult. de rer. div. ff.), whereas by hire it is never transferred (l. 39 non solet ff. loc.). Joined to purchase was the aestimatory action, because it is partly like purchase and partly like hire, yet unlike both (l. 1 de aestim. act.). So much for the actions in rem and the actions in personam arising from contract.

units.la: IV. Pars Edicti Perpetui.
units.tr: IV. Part of the Perpetual Edict.

units.la: As proximè jam sequuntur actiones ex quasi contractu, & aliis causis, ut aequo & bono: actiones inquam in personam. Et primum quidem inter eas locum in Edicto tenuit actio tei uxoriae argumento sunt libri Jurisconsultorum ad Edictum. Ut Ulpia. lib. 33. & 34. Pauli lib. 35. 36. & 27 tot enim libris Edicti ad rem uxoriam, sive ad nuptias & dotes pertinentia illi explicarunt. Eundem quoque ordinem videre est apud Paul. l. 2. fenus. ut rep. de nupt. & 7. ut. seq. Ratio ordinis hoc est cur inter reliquas actiones in personam actio dotis (quae olim rei uxoriae dicta fuit. f. fuerat. Inst. de act.) primum in Edicto locum tenuerit, hoc esse videtur, tum quia dos fit matrimonii causa, l. 1. & 3. ac sur. dot. quod matrimonium est quaedam societas, & non longè a contractibus consensu, inter quos est societas (licet ab ea non parum differat) collocari debuit. tum quia videtur Julianus in Edicto, rationem habuisse ordinis naturae, qui ordo hic est, ut prius sit matrimonium, quam sunt liberi, quarum tutela deinde esse posset, mortuis parentibus. Ideoque prius de matrimonio & actione dotis, quam de actione tutelae agendum fuit: quem ordinem & Imp. l. 1. Inst. tenuit, ut prius de nuptiis, posterius de tutelis explicetur.
units.tr: Next in order come the actions arising from quasi-contract and from other causes, as aequo et bono: personal actions, I say. Among these, the action on the wife's property (actio rei uxoriae) held the first place in the Edict. The evidence is the books of the jurists on the Edict: Ulpian, books 33 and 34; Paul, books 35, 36 and 27. For they explained so many books of the Edict to the matter of the wife's property, that is, to marriages and dowries. The same order can be seen in Paul, l. 2, fenus ut rep. de nupt., and 7, ut seq. The reason why, among the other personal actions, the action for dowry (formerly called actio rei uxoriae, see Inst. de act.) held the first place in the Edict seems to be twofold. First, because the dowry exists for the sake of marriage (l. 1 and 3 ac sur. dot.), and marriage is a kind of partnership, so it ought to be placed not far from the consensual contracts, among which is partnership (although it differs from it not a little). Second, because Julian in the Edict seems to have followed the order of nature, which is that marriage comes before children, whose guardianship could then follow when the parents die. Therefore the matter of marriage and the action for dowry had to be treated before the action of guardianship. The Emperor (Inst. l. 1) also kept this order, so that marriages are explained first and guardianships afterwards.

units.la: Ad hunc locum Edicti perpetui de re uxor. Edictum quoq; de alterutro pertinet, quod tamen in ff. non exstat amplius, utpote sublatum cum re uxoria. l. 1. §. primum itaq. C. de rer. ux. act. ejus quoqj mentio fit in l. 7. C. Theod. lib. 4. de test. Sic enim inquit: mulier in edicto, quod de alterutro est, cum suam explanaverit optionem, ne poenitentia ad aliud posse transfire, &c. Quibus verbis & sententia ejus Edicti indicatur: quae haec est: mulierem, cui maritus aut hereditatem aut legatum aut fideicommissum reliquerit, debere conten-tam. tam esse alterutro, vel relicto vel dote, & hanc ipsam alterutrius optionem factaque semel optione amplius poenitere non poterit. Sed hodie non alterutro contenta esse cogitur, sed utrumque consequitur & relictum & dotem eadem actione ex stipulatu quae successit in locum actionis rei uxor. d. §. primum sitaj. & d. §. f. erat Iulii. de action. De hoc Edicto late Cujac. lib.3. obs.c.16.
units.tr: To this place of the Perpetual Edict concerning the wife's property belongs also the Edict concerning the alternative (de alterutro). It no longer survives in the Digest, having been abolished along with the action on the wife's property (l. 1 §. primum itaque C. de rer. ux. act.). Its mention is also made in l. 7 C. Theod. lib. 4 de test. For it says: "a woman, in the Edict which concerns the alternative, once she has explained her option, may not transfer her regret to another," and so on. These words also indicate the sense of that Edict, which is this: a woman to whom her husband has left either an inheritance, a legacy or a fideicommissum must be content with one of two things, either the bequest or the dowry, and once the option has been made she may no longer repent. But today she is not compelled to be content with one alternative; she obtains both the bequest and the dowry by the same action on stipulation, which succeeded in place of the action on the wife's property (d. §. primum itaque, and d. §. f. erat Iulii, de action.). On this Edict see Cujas at length, lib. 3 obs. c. 16.

units.la: Ad eundem locum de dotibus in Edicto perpetuo, fuit actio praejudicialis, sive praejudicium de partu agnoscendo, l.3. de agnosc. lib. Non fit quidem mentio edicti alicujus de hac actione, ut neque de multis aliis actionibus mandati, pro socio, de mutuo &c quia Edicta plerumque tantum commemorantur de actionibus praetoriis, raro de civilibus. Edicta autem sunt praetoria: haec autem actio de partu agnoscendo est civilis, utpote SCto quodam introducta, l.1. & toto tit. de agnosc. & al. lib. Plinius l.b.10. Epist. Postulantibus, &c.
units.tr: Also at this place, among the Edicts on dowries in the Perpetual Edict, there was the praejudicial action, or praejudicium, on acknowledging the offspring (de partu agnoscendo), l. 3 de agnosc. lib. Indeed no mention is made of any Edict on this action, nor of many other actions such as mandate, partnership, loan and so on, because Edicts for the most part mention only praetorian actions and rarely civil ones. This action on acknowledging the offspring is civil, being introduced by a certain senatusconsultum (l. 1 and the whole title de agnosc. and other laws). Pliny, letters book 10: "Postulantibus," and so on.

units.la: Huic actioni de partu agnoscendo proximum in Edicto locum tenuit edictum de partu custodiendo, ut dicitur in l.2. & 4. de inspic. vent. custodiendo, p. 1. 1. cujus Edicti verba exstant. d. tit. l. 1. §. 4. Ratio ordinis autem cur actio de partu agnoscendo prior fit Edicto de partu custodiendo, ut indicat d. tit. l. 1. §. 1. ex hoc rescripto haec esse videtur, quia actio rei uxoriae, de qua proxime dictum olim certis de causis cessabat: nempe propter retentiones varias, ex variis silicet causis, ut morum & impensarum, ut rerum amotarum ut liberorum, teste Ulp. l. b. reg. tit. 5 & l. 1. f. tacet. C. de rei uxor. act. Recte igitur de liberis agnoscendis (erat enim propter liberos retentio) statim adjungebatur rei uxor. Est & altera ratio, quia actio de partu sive liberis agnoscendis, agit tam de liberis jam natis, quam nascituris Edictum autem de partu custodiendo etsi est item de utrisque, maxime tamen est de nascituris. Tertia denique ratio est, quod actio de agnoscendo partu est civilis: cum reliquae de ventre sint praetoriae.
units.tr: Next after this action on acknowledging the offspring, the Edict on guarding the birth (de partu custodiendo) held a place in the Edict, as is said in l. 2 and 4 de inspic. vent. custodiendo; the words of this Edict survive (d. tit. l. 1 §. 4). The reason for the order, why the action on acknowledging the offspring comes before the Edict on guarding the birth, as d. tit. l. 1 §. 1 indicates, seems from this rescript to be this: the action on the wife's property, mentioned just before, formerly was held back for certain reasons, namely by various retentions arising from various causes, such as morals, expenses, removed goods and children, as Ulpian says (l. b. reg. tit. 5 and l. 1 f. tacet. C. de rei uxor. act.). It was rightly joined at once to the acknowledging of children, since there was a retention on account of the children. There is also another reason: the action on acknowledging the offspring or children applies both to children already born and to those yet to be born. The Edict on guarding the birth, although it likewise concerns both, is chiefly concerned with those yet to be born. The third reason, finally, is that the action on acknowledging the birth is civil, whereas the others concerning the womb are praetorian.

units.la: Sunt autem tria Edicta de ventre. I. Jam iam expositum est, de inspiciendo ventre custodiendoque partu quo edicto multa continentur, inter alia & istud, de ventre in possess. mittendo, de quo infra agetur. Nam in hoc Edicto de ventre inspiciendo tantum fit hujus missionis mentio, l.1. §. de inspiciendo. & f. quod autem ff. de inspic. vent.
units.tr: There are three Edicts concerning the womb. I. The one on inspecting the womb and guarding the birth has already been set out; many things are contained in it, among them the provision on sending into possession of the womb, to be treated below. For in this Edict on inspecting the womb only the mention of this sending is made (l. 1 §. de inspiciendo and f. quod autem ff. de inspic. vent.).

units.la: Alterum Edictum de ventre sive partu priori proximum est de actione in factum contra mulierem, quae possessionem, in quam ipsa ventris nomine missa fuit in alium dolo malo transtulit, cujus Edicti & actionis mentio & explicatio in tit. ff. si vent. nom.
units.tr: The second Edict concerning the womb or the birth, which comes next after the former, is on the action in factum against a woman who, having been sent into possession in the name of the womb, transferred that possession to another by fraud. The mention and explanation of this Edict and action are in the title ff. si vent. nom.

units.la: Tertium edictum item actionem in factum contra mulierem continet, quaeSciens prudens que se non esse praegnantem in possessionem tamen venit & ra per calumniam; de quo Edicto (quod illo altero fuit posterius, l. 1. f. mulier. vent. non. est tit. ff. si ad. vent. nom. &c.) Merito autem haec duo Edicta in hoc tractatu de dotibus sunt ultima, quia delictum mulieris dolum & calumniam continent. Hoc autem de calumnia est quasi poenale judicium, d. l. 1. §. hanc autem. si mulier. vent. nomi. cum illud de dolo sit rei persecutorium, d.l.1.§.ultim.sivent. nom. Et ideo illud superius, hoc posterius in Edicto fuit propositum: quia poenal a in ultimum locum rejici solent.
units.tr: The third Edict likewise contains an action in factum against a woman who, knowing and deliberately not being pregnant, nonetheless came into possession, and that by calumny. Concerning this Edict (which was later than the other, l. 1 f. mulier. vent. non est, title ff. si ad vent. nom., etc.): these two Edicts are rightly the last in this treatise on dowries, because they concern the woman's fraud and calumny. The action on calumny is a kind of penal judgment (d. l. 1 §. hanc autem, si mulier, vent. nomi.), whereas the action on fraud is persecutory of the thing (d. l. 1 §. ultim., si vent. nom.). Therefore the former was set out earlier in the Edict and this later, because penal matters are usually placed in the last position.

units.la: His Edictis ad dotes pertinentibus proximum in Edicto locum tenuerunt Edicta de tutelis, tum propter ordinem illum naturae, supra expositum: tum etiam propter similitudinem inter dotes & tutelas in eo, quod utraque causa & valde favorabilis est, & actionem parit in personam. Edicta igitur de tutelis ista reperio. I. De satisdatione tutorum, l.17.l.19.§ nemo. §1. de testl. tut.l.5. legitimus. §.1. de legit. tut. II. De administratione tutorum, nempe si plures sint tutores, quia non est utile pupillo, ut plures administrent, cui potissimum committenda sit administratio. d.l.19. §.1. verf. ideog. l.3. de administr. tut. III. Edictum est de suspectis tutoribus, cujus mentio fit initio l.1. de susp. tut. ubi clausula dicitur scilicet Edicti. Sic enim solent Edicta singula interdum dici vel clausulae vel partes, d.l.(nemo.l.1.§.2. cont.tab.l.1. & 7.§. ubicunque. de vent. in poss. mitt. l.1. unde cog. l.25. sed etsi. §.pen. nde de heted. pet.
units.tr: After these Edicts on dowries, the Edicts on guardianships held the next place in the Edict, both because of the natural order set out above and because of the likeness between dowries and guardianships: each cause is very favourable and gives rise to a personal action. I find these Edicts on guardianships: I. On the security given by guardians (de satisdatione tutorum), l. 17, l. 19 §. nemo, §. 1 de testl. tut., l. 5 legitimus §. 1 de legit. tut. II. On the administration by guardians, namely where there are several guardians, because it is not useful for the ward that several should administer, but rather that the administration be committed to one chiefly (d. l. 19 §. 1 verf. ideog.; l. 3 de administr. tut.). III. There is an Edict on suspect guardians, of which mention is made at the start of l. 1 de susp. tut., where the clause is named, that is, of the Edict. For individual Edicts are sometimes called clauses or parts in this way (d. l. nemo; l. 1 §. 2 cont. tab.; l. 1 and 7 §. ubicunque de vent. in poss. mitt.; l. 1 unde cog.; l. 25 sed etsi §. pen. nde de heted. pet.).

units.la: Ratio ordinis haec est: quia administratio non permittitur tutori, nisi ante satisdet, & propterea prius est Edictum de satisdatione edicto de administratione: quibus duobus posterius est de suspectis &c. tum quia est de crimine (at crimina in posteriorem locum rejiciuntur) tum quia hoc crimen suspecti oritur plerumque ex administratione mala, ideoque administratio prior est.
units.tr: The reason for this order is that administration is not permitted to a guardian unless he has first given security, and therefore the Edict on security comes before the Edict on administration. After these two comes the one on suspect guardians, both because it concerns a crime (and crimes are placed in a later position) and because suspicion of a crime for the most part arises from bad administration, so administration comes first.

units.la: Praeter haec tria Edicta de tutelis fuerunt & alia unum de actione tutela directa, alterum de actione tutelae contraria. III. De actione protutelae, IV. De actione subsidiaria. V. De actione rationibus distrahendis. VI. De utili actione curationis causa. Quae actiones tutelares etsi plerumque sunt civiles, tamen in Edicto quoque propositae fuerunt; ut indicat l.1, de contrar. tut. & utili. act. & l.1. deco, qui pro tut.
units.tr: Besides these three edicts on tutelages, there were also others: one on the direct action of tutelage, another on the contrary action of tutelage, (III) on the action of protutelage, (IV) on the subsidiary action, (V) on the action for distraction of accounts, and (VI) on the useful action for the sake of curatorship. Although these tutelary actions are for the most part civil, they were nevertheless also set out in the Edict, as l.1, de contrar. tut. & utili. act. & l.1. deco, qui pro tut. indicates.

units.la: Ratio ordinis cur hae actiones primum locum inter Edicta tutelaria obtineant, est, quia prius de ipsa tutela, hoc est, de causa harum actionum fuit agendum, & quia actio tutelae fere post finitam tutelam datur. Sunt autem septem jam expositae, suspecti tutelae &c. quibus adjungatur edicta utilis actio de qua in tit.ff. de contrar.tut. & ut l. act.
units.tr: The reason why these actions hold the first place among the tutelary edicts is that the tutelage itself, that is, the cause of these actions, had to be dealt with first, and because the action of tutelage is generally given after the tutelage has ended. There are, however, seven already explained, on the suspect of tutelage, and so on, to which is added the useful action, of which we speak in the title de contrar.tut. & ut l. act. of the Digest.

units.la: Haec autem Edicta de tutelis proxime sequebatur Edicta de furtis, ut videre est in Ulpian. lib.37. & 38. ad Ed. quibus ea de furtis Edicta explicavit, postquam Edicta de tutelis explicasset lib.35. & lib.36. Idem quoque videre est in Pauli sententiis, & in Paulo ad Ed. lib.39. & 40. Et hunc Edicti ordinem, ut scilicet tit. de tutelis sequeretur proxime de furtis Tribun. & in Cod. retinuit. Nam in fine l. b. 5. C. agitur de tutelis, & statim post initio l. b. 6. de furtis.
units.tr: These edicts on tutelages were immediately followed by the edicts on theft, as can be seen in Ulpian, lib.37. & 38. ad Ed., where he explained the edicts on theft after he had explained the edicts on tutelages in lib.35. & lib.36. The same order can be seen in the Sentences of Paulus and in Paulus on the Edict, lib.39. & 40. Tribonian and the Code also kept this order of the Edict, namely that the title on tutelages should be followed directly by the one on theft. For at the end of l. b. 5. C. the subject is tutelages, and straight after, at the beginning of l. b. 6., theft.

units.la: Ratio autem ordinis huius est propter similitudinem inter actionem unam tutelarum, quae dicitur rationibus distrahendis, & actionem furti: nam & illa de rationibus distrahendis est ex furto tutoris in rebus pupillaribus, sed habebat tamen nomen levius, & honestius, propter reverentiam & potestatem tutoris: quemadmodum & actio rerum amotarum est ex furto uxoris: & tamen honestiori nomine appellatur propter reverentiam matrimonii, & propter societatem vitae inter coniuges. l. 1. & 2. de actione rer. amot. Sed in ff. Trib. actionem de furtis alium in locum & quidem in posteriorem rejecit, certa de causa quam infra exponemus. Edicti autem de furtis mentio fit in l. Titia §. curam. in sin. de manumiss. testam. l. 195. pronuntiatum. §. servientum. de verbor. sign.
units.tr: The reason for this order is the similarity between one of the tutelary actions, called the action for distraction of accounts, and the action of theft. For that action too, the one on distraction of accounts, arises from a tutor's theft of property belonging to the ward; but it bore a milder and more honourable name, out of respect for the tutor's authority. Likewise the action for things removed arises from a wife's theft, yet it is called by a more honourable name because of the respect due to marriage and the companionship of life between spouses (l. 1. & 2. de actione rer. amot.). But in the Digest, Tribonian moved the action on theft to a different place, and indeed to a later one, for a reason which we shall explain below. Mention of the edict on theft is made in l. Titia §. curam. in sin. de manumiss. testam. and l. 195. pronuntiatum. §. servientum. de verbor. sign.

units.la: Ad hunc autem titulum de furtis multa Edicta sive clausulae pertinent. Nam I. sub hoc titulo fuit in Edicto proposita actio furti generalis, quae actio partim est civilis, nempe actio furti nec manifesti: partim est praetoria, nempe manifesti. §. sunt autem Institut. de nox. act. II. Actio specialis de tigno iuncto, ut indicat l. 1. de tigno iuncto. quae lex est ex lib. 37. Ulpian. ad Edict. in quo libro etiam prior generalis actio furti explicata fuit ab Ulp. ut indicat l. 50. & 52. de furtis. III. Actio contra manumissum testamento servum, qui anteaditam hereditatem aliquid ex rebus hereditariis surripuit; aut corrupit: Verba Edicti de hac actione, videntur esse ea, quae sunt initio l. 1. si qui test. lib. esse iusst. &c. IV. Actio furti speciale, adversus naut. caup. stab. quae est actio praetoria de qua titul ff. furti adversus naut. caup. stab. V. Si familia furtum fecisset de qua Edictum fuit cuius sit mentio in l. 1. & 3. si fam. furt. fec. dic. VI. Actio in publicanos, quorum familia furtum fecerit; cuius Edicti verba exstant in l. 12. quanta. de public. & vect. rembtad tractationem de furtis. VII. arborum furtim caesarum, quae actio est civilis ex duodecim tab. l. 1. arb. furt. caes.
units.tr: Many edicts or clauses belong to this title on theft. (I) Under this title, the general action for theft was set out in the Edict: this action is partly civil, namely the action for non-manifest theft, and partly praetorian, namely that for manifest theft (§ sunt autem, Institutes, de nox. act.). (II) A special action concerning a beam joined to a building, as l. 1. de tigno iuncto indicates, which law comes from Ulpian, lib. 37 ad Edictum, in which book Ulpian also explained the earlier general action for theft, as l. 50. & 52. de furtis indicates. (III) The action against a slave manumitted by will, who before entering upon the inheritance stole or spoiled something from the inheritance goods; the words of the Edict on this action seem to be those at the beginning of l. 1. si qui test. lib. esse iussus etc. (IV) The special action of theft against shipmasters, innkeepers and stablemen, which is the praetorian action treated under the title of the Digest furti adversus nautas, cauponas, stabularios. (V) The edict concerning theft committed by a household (si familia furtum fecisset), which is mentioned in l. 1. & 3. si fam. furt. fec. dic. (VI) The action against tax-farmers (publicani), whose household has committed theft; the words of this edict are found in l. 12. quanta. de public. & vect., and I shall return to the treatment of theft. (VII) The action for trees cut secretly, which is a civil action from the Twelve Tables, l. 1. arb. furt. caes.

units.la: Ratio ordinis inter haec Edicta sive clausulas & actiones de furtis primum est quia generalia speciali bus anteponuntur & ideirco actio de furtis generalis antepositi fuit 6. actionib. de furto speciali. jam expositis. Cur autem inter speciales primum locum teneat actio de tigno iuncto; ratio haec esse videtur quia ea actio est civilis, cum reliquae de furtis actiones speciales sint praetoriae exceptaactione arborum furtim caesarum. Cur ergo inquies, actio illa arborum furtim caesarum in ultimum locum est rejecta: cum tamen sit civilis, & civilia praetoriis sint priora & dignior. Ratio haec est: quia haec actio arborum furtim caesarum est de furto in agris, & de furto tantum unius rei, puta arboris: ideoque est maxime specialis de una tantum specie sive vere, cum priores sint de reb. urbanis, aut de pluribus. Ja notum est, quae urbana aut digniora rusticis, & plura sive generalia unifive specialib. maxime anteponantur. De reliquis 4. actionibus de furto praetoriis nempe, si is qui test. &c. adversus nauit. &c. sifa. fur. adversf. publ. quae ratio sit ordinis, exponetur infra ad ff.
units.tr: The reason for the order among these edicts or clauses on theft is first that general matters are placed before special ones; and therefore the general action for theft was placed before the six special actions on theft already set out. Why the action concerning a beam joined to a building holds the first place among the special actions seems to be this: that action is civil, whereas the other special actions on theft are praetorian, with the exception of the action for trees cut secretly. Why, then, you may ask, was that action for trees cut secretly put in the last place, when it is civil, and civil actions are prior to and more worthy than praetorian ones? The reason is this: the action for trees cut secretly concerns theft in the fields, and theft of only one thing, namely a tree; therefore it is most specific, being concerned with one species alone, whereas the earlier ones concern urban matters or several things. Thus it is well known that urban matters are placed before rural ones, and many or general matters before single or special ones. The reason for the order of the other four praetorian actions on theft, namely si is qui test. etc., adversus nautas etc., si familia furtum, and adversus publicanos, will be explained below in the Digest.

units.la: Fuit & Edictum, de oper. libert. cujus fit mentio in l. 2. & seq. oper. l. b. rt. quod proximum fuit & conjunctum Edictis de furtis, ut indicat l. 2. 13. & 15. de oper. libert. quae leges sunt ex Ulp. lib 38. quo explicarat actiones de furto speciales ut modo dictum. Ratio autem ordinis cur edictum hoc de oper. libert. proximum fuerit Edicto de furtis expositá est ad Cod. lib 6. Nam in C. Tribun diligentius ordinem Edicto secutus est, quam in ff.
units.tr: There was also an edict de operis libertorum, which is mentioned in l. 2. & seq. oper. l. b. rt., and which was next to and joined with the edicts on theft, as l. 2. 13. & 15. de oper. libert. indicates. These laws come from Ulpian, lib 38., in which he explained the special actions on theft, as has just been said. The reason why this edict de operis libertorum was placed next to the edict on theft has been set out at the Code, book 6. For in the Code Tribonian followed the order of the Edict more carefully than in the Digest.

units.la: V. Pars Edicti Perpetui.
units.tr: V. The Fifth Part of the Perpetual Edict.

units.la: PRoximum in Edicto locum habebant edicta de bonorum possessionibus ut videre est in ib.3.sent. Pauli, & in Ulpia. libris ad Edictum. Ulp. enim edicta de furtis & operis libertorum explicavit ib.36. & 38. Proximè deinde explicavit lib.39. & 10. sf. 97. edicta de bonorum possessione Edicto de furt. & oper libert. explicavit lib 39. & 40. puta de bonor possessione l.b.4. & 3. seqq. Ratio autem ordinis perobscuramihi videtur. Puto tamen hanc esse duplicem, tum quia hactenus actiones fere civiles sunt explicatae tam in rem quam in personam, ut non immerito jam de praetoriis remediis agatur, ut sunt bonorum possessiones missio in possessionem bonorum, cautiones praetoriae, interdicta & pignora &c quae admodum & supra dictum ad Cod. In his enim remediis praetoriis auctoritas & saepe decretum maximè requiritur, & pleraq; sunt omnia praetoria: tum quia hactenus dictum est de actionibus in personam ex contractu & quasi (ut est actio tutelae. f. tutores. Inst. de oblig. ex quasi contr.) viventium in bonis: ut proximum jam sitagere de bonis mortuorum.
units.tr: Next in the Edict came the edicts on possessions of goods (bonorum possessiones), as may be seen in Paul's Sentences, book 3, and in Ulpian's books on the Edict. For Ulpian explained the edicts on theft and on the services of freedmen in books 36 and 38. Next he explained the edicts on possession of goods in books 39 and 40, namely on possession of goods in books 4 and 3 et seq. But the reason for the order seems very obscure to me. I think, however, that it is twofold: first, because so far civil actions, both in rem and in personam, have been explained, so that it is now not inappropriately that praetorian remedies are treated, such as possessions of goods (bonorum possessiones), the missio in possessionem bonorum, praetorian stipulations (cautiones), interdicts and pledges, as was also said above on the Code. For in these praetorian remedies the authority and often a decree are chiefly required, and most of them are wholly praetorian. Second, because so far there has been discussion of personal actions arising from contract and quasi-contract (such as the action of guardianship, f. tutores, Inst. de oblig. ex quasi contr.) and of those living in possession of goods; so it is now next to treat of the goods of the dead.

units.la: Ergo inter Edicta de bon poss. primum locum tenuit Edictum, quibus detur aut denegetur bonor. poss. id indicat infra l. 1. 2. & 3. de bon. poss. & t. t. C qui admitti ad bon. p. s. Mentio ejus Edicti fit l. 3. Ed. Ulp. de bon. poss. verba non exstant. Ratio ordinis est, tum quia de personis primum agendum, l. 4. de testamentis, tum quia hoc Edictum est generale, quod subsequuntur speciales.
units.tr: Accordingly, among the edicts on possession of goods the first place was held by the Edict which determines whether possession of goods is granted or refused. This is indicated below in l. 1, 2 and 3 de bon. poss. and t.t. C qui admitti ad bon. poss. Mention of this edict is made in l. 3 Ed. Ulp. de bon. poss.; the words do not survive. The reason for the order is that persons must be dealt with first, l. 4 de testamentis, and because this edict is general, and the special ones follow it.

units.la: Eorum primum est Edictum de bon. poss. secund. Tab. cujus fit mentio in l. 1. f. hac autem & l. pen. & hoc sit consequens. d. tit. verba non exstant. Ratio ordinis est eadem, quae in civilibus petitionibus hereditatis. de quibus supra dictum inter quos primum locum tenet in querela inofficiosi testamenti. Ratio est quia scilicet nec hereditas civilis perITUR, neque bonorum possessio impeditur ab heredibus scriptis nisi prius constet de testamento rant sit mum maneat, hoc est, non exstinguatur per querelam, aut interitum recipiat per bon. poss. contra tabulas, quae est querela similima. Haec ergo bonorum possessio contra tab. quia datur liberis praeteritis, qui heredem scri-ptum ptum praeveniunt eumque hac bonorum possessione impetrata impediunt neadmittatur ipse ad suam hoc est bonorum possessionem secundum tabu. iccirco in Edicto primum locum tenuit bonorum possessio contr.tab.Quare & in jure dicitur primum Edictum l.12. de carb. Edict. & prima pars Edicti l.4.cod.de. sed hunc tamen ordinem Tribun. in C. migravit, & bonorum possessioni secund tab.postposuit bonorum possessionem cont tabul. Ratio differentiae ibi est exposita. Sed ordinem Edicti laudat Ulpian. eumque ait esse aequissimum: nempe ut prius habeatur ratio liberorum, quibus successio debetur natura quam scriptorum heredum forte extraneorum. l.2. de bon.poss.sec.tab.
units.tr: The first of these is the Edict on possession of goods according to the tablets (secundum tabulas), mentioned in l.1 f. hac autem & l. pen. & hoc sit consequens d. tit.; the words do not survive. The reason for the order is the same as for civil petitions of inheritance, among which, as said above, the first place is held by the complaint of an undutiful will (querela inofficiosi testamenti). The reason is that the civil inheritance is not lost, nor is possession of goods impeded for written heirs, unless it is first established that the will stands, that is, is not extinguished by the complaint or does not suffer loss through possession of goods against the tablets (contra tabulas), which is a very similar complaint. This possession of goods against the tablets is therefore given to children who were passed over, who anticipate the written heir and, having obtained this possession of goods, prevent him from being admitted to his own possession, that is, possession of goods according to the tablets. For this reason possession of goods against the tablets held the first place in the Edict. Hence also in law the first edict is so called, l.12 de carb. edict., and the first part of the edict, l.4 cod. de. But Tribonian in the Code moved this order and placed possession of goods according to the tablets after possession against the tablets. The reason for the difference is set out there. Ulpian, however, praises the order of the Edict and calls it most equitable: namely that the claims of children, to whom succession is due by nature, should be considered before those of written heirs, who may be strangers, l.2 de bon. poss. sec. tab.

units.la: Secundum locum inter Edicta de bon. poss. tenuit Edictum de legatis praestandis ut videre est in dictis libris JCtorum ad Edicta. Mentio ejus Edicti sive tituli exstat in l.1. & 6. Salvius de leg. praest. verba non exstant. Ratio ordinis est, quia haec clausula de legatis praestandis tantum habet locum in bon poss cont. tab. Nam ea petita a liberis praeteritis, rescinduntur tabulae testamenti: & proinde legata quoque & fideicommissa in iis praestanda exceptis tamen certis personis, quibus ea conservantur ex hoc Edicto, & sunt praestanda perinde ac si testamentum per hanc bon. poss. contr. tab. non esset rescissum, l.1. impr. de leg. praest.
units.tr: The second place among the edicts on possession of goods was held by the Edict on the payment of legacies, as may be seen in the said books of the jurists on the Edicts. Mention of this edict or title is found in l.1 & 6 Salvius de leg. praest.; the words do not survive. The reason for the order is that this clause on the payment of legacies applies only to possession against the tablets. For when that possession is sought by children who were passed over, the tablets of the will are rescinded, and accordingly the legacies and fideicommissa in them are also payable, except for certain persons, to whom they are preserved by this Edict. They are to be paid just as if the will had not been rescinded by this possession against the tablets, l.1 impr. de leg. praest.

units.la: Tertium locum tenuit edictum de collationibus, ut videre est in iisdem libris Juris consultorum & in ff. ubi idem est ordo. Ratio quoque ordinis hoc postulat quae est haec, ut emancipati, qui bona paterna appetunt per bonorum possessionem contra tab. etiam sua in medium conferant, inquit Ulpian. in l.1. de collat. Nam emancipatio praeteritis praetor permittit hanc bonorum possessionem sed non aliter dat, nisi recte caveant, se bona sua collatros fratribus in potestate retentis, l.1. §. jubet, d. tit. l.3. d. §. d.tit. Edicti autem hujus verba non exstant sed mentio ejus, in l.1. in princ. & §. jubet, d.ti. & in l.20. §. videamus, cont. tab. Pauca tamen verba, in l.2. §. de illis, & l.5. d. tit. Etsi autem in ff duo sunt tituli, nunc de collatione, alter de collatione dotis, puto tamen, non fuisse duo distincta edicta, sed particulam de dote adjectam fuisse titulo de collat. tum quia Edicti de collatione dotis nulla separatim fit mentio: tum quia in Cod unus titulus, sub quo tamen de dote quoque agitur.
units.tr: The third place was held by the edict on collations, as may be seen in the same books of the jurists and in the Digest, where the order is the same. The reason for the order also requires this: that emancipated children, who seek their father's goods by possession against the tablets, should also bring their own goods into the common stock, says Ulpian in l.1 de collat. For the praetor permits this possession of goods to the emancipated who were passed over, but grants it only if they properly give security that they have brought their goods into collation for the brothers who remained in potestas, l.1 §. jubet, d. tit. l.3 d. §. d. tit. The words of this edict do not survive, but it is mentioned in l.1 in princ. & §. jubet, d. tit., and in l.20 §. videamus, cont. tab. A few words survive, however, in l.2 §. de illis, and l.5 d. tit. Although in the Digest there are two titles, one on collation and the other on collation of dowry, I think there were not two distinct edicts, but the part about dowry was added to the title on collation. Both because no separate mention of an edict on collation of dowry is made, and because in the Code there is one title, under which, however, dowry is also treated.

units.la: Quartum edictum de conjungendis cum emancipato liberis, ut in iisdem libris videre est in ff. Ratio ordinis est, quia ut prius ad emancipatos, ita & illud pertinet: & quidem pertinere, quia novum. Est enim ab ipso Juliano auctore Edicti Perpetui inventum, quod & propterea edictum novum dicitur. l.3 in sin. de conjung. cum emancip. tib.l.1. §. si quid a patre, de vent. in poss. mit. &c. Verba non exstant quidem aperte: sed videntur fere esse ea quae sunt initio, l.1. de conjung. cum emancip. &c.
units.tr: The fourth edict is that on joining emancipated children with the others, as may be seen in the same books in the Digest. The reason for the order is that, as it pertains to emancipated children first, so this one also does; and indeed it pertains to them because it is new. For it was devised by Julian himself, the author of the Perpetual Edict, and for that reason it is called the new edict, l.3 in sin. de conjung. cum emancip. tit.; l.1 §. si quid a patre, de vent. in poss. mit. etc. The words do not clearly survive, but they seem to be almost those found at the beginning, l.1 de conjung. cum emancip. etc.

units.la: Quintum locum tenuit edictum de vent. in poss. mit. cujus mentio, in l.7
units.tr: The fifth place was held by the edict on sending into possession of the unborn child (de ventre in possessionem mittendo), mention of which is in l.7

units.la: S l.7. & ult. d. t. t. Verba quidem exstant, l.21. de l.g. l.13. sitta, infin. de manum. test. Ratio ordinis exponitur in d.l.1. de vent. in poss. mit. quia hactenus de bonorum possessione contra tab. data liberis viventibus sive natis, nunc de nondum natis.
units.tr: § 7 and last, d. tit. The words indeed survive, l.21 de leg.; l.13 §. sitta, infin. de manum. test. The reason for the order is explained in d. l.1 de vent. in poss. mit.: because hitherto possession of goods against the tablets has been dealt with as granted to children who are living or born, now it is dealt with for those not yet born.

units.la: Proximum est VI. edictum, quod dicitur Carbonianum a praetore Carbone cujus mentio in l.1. §. 1. & 3. ut. & l.1. de Carbon. edict. Verba non exstant. Ratio ordinis est, quia primum de liberis certis, tam natis quam non natis, deinde de liberis non certis, seu quibus movetur controversia status, ad quos proprie pertinet edictum Carbonianum, si sint impuberes. Nam his demum datur bonorum possessio contra tab. ex hoc edicto, etiamsi controversia ipsis fiat an sint inter liberos, l.1. de Carb. edict.
units.tr: The next is the sixth edict, called the Carbonian after the praetor Carbo, mention of which is in l.1 §.1 & 3 ut. & l.1 de Carbon. edict. The words do not survive. The reason for the order is that first it deals with certain children, both born and unborn, and then with uncertain children, or those whose status is disputed, to whom the Carbonian edict properly pertains, if they are under puberty. For only to these is possession of goods against the tablets given under this edict, even if a dispute arises for them whether they are among the children, l.1 de Carb. edict.

units.la: VII. Edictum est illud quo continetur bonorum possessio secundum tab. explicatur ab Ulp. lib.41. ad edict. Verba edicti non exstant: sed sententia explicatur toto tit. ff. sec. tab. Ratio ordinis ab Ulpiano ipso exponitur, & laudatur, l.2. d. tit. Voluit igitur praetor primum ad liberos bonorum possessionem contra tab. pertinere: mox, si inde non sit occupata, Judicium defuncti sequendum, quasi dicat prior est bonorum possessio contra tabul. de qua hactenus explicatum proxima est ei possessio secundum tabulas, qui est ordo, quisquis ut ait Ulp d l.2. Quid ita? Ratio supra dicta, ubi de bonorum possessione contra tab. de qua hactenus explicatum.
units.tr: The seventh edict is that which contains possession of goods according to the tablets. It is explained by Ulpian in book 41 on the Edict. The words of the edict do not survive, but its sense is explained in the whole title ff. sec. tab. The reason for the order is set out, and praised, by Ulpian himself, l.2 d. tit. The praetor therefore wished that possession of goods against the tablets should belong first to the children; then, if it is not taken up from there, the judgment of the deceased should be followed, as if to say: possession of goods against the tablets, explained so far, comes first, and next is possession according to the tablets, which is the order, as Ulpian says, d. l.2. Why so? The reason is the one given above, where possession of goods against the tablets was discussed.

units.la: Sequitur VIII. edictum de bonis libertorum, de quo actum est ab Ulp. lib.42. & 43. & 44. & partim 45. ad edict. a Paulo lib.42. & partim lib.43. Cujus edicti mentio est in l.1. de bon. libert. & toto tit. huj. ff. de succ. ff. libert. §.1. Verba non exstant, sententia est in d. §.1. & in d. l.1.
units.tr: Next comes the eighth edict, on the goods of freedmen, which Ulpian treated in books 42, 43, 44 and partly 45 on the Edict, and Paul in book 42 and partly in book 43. The edict is mentioned in l. 1 de bon. libert. and throughout the title of the Digest de successorio edicto, l. libert. §. 1. The words do not survive; the substance is in d. §. 1 and in d. l. 1.

units.la: Ad hunc autem locum de bonorum possessione patrono danda in bonis liberti pertinet actio Calusiana & Fabiana, quibus revocantur alienata a liberto in fraudem patroni, sive portionis legitimae patrono debitae a liberto quae actiones in edicto quoq; fuerunt propositae ut indicat l.1. & tit. ff. si quid in fraudem patroni. Paul. lib. sent. tit.3. Et hoc sit IX. edictum speciale ad hoc edictum sive titul. de bonorum possessione. Ratio ordinis est, quia prius de ingenuorum hereditatibus & bonorum possess. posterius de libertinorum, ut indigniorum agitur tam in edicto quam in Cod. & Inst. & in ff. Cur autem de bonorum possessione patrono danda, prius agatur & de actione Calusiana & Fabiana posterius ratio est perspicua, quia hae actiones fraudem & delictum liberti vindicant. Ad delictum autem pertinentia sunt, posteriora, ut saepe jam dictum.
units.tr: To this place belong also the Calusian and Fabian actions, which pertain to the grant of possession of the goods of a freedman to the patron; by these actions transfers made by the freedman in fraud of the patron are revoked, or the legitimate portion owed to the patron by the freedman. These actions were also set out in the edict, as l. 1 and the title of the Digest si quid in fraudem patroni indicate; Paul, Sent. tit. 3. And this is the ninth edict, a special one attached to this edict, or title, on the grant of possession. The reason for the order is that first the inheritances of freeborn persons and the possession of goods are treated, and afterwards those of freedmen, as the less worthy, both in the edict and in the Code and Institutes and the Digest. Why the grant of possession to the patron is treated first and the Calusian and Fabian actions afterwards is clear enough: these actions vindicate the fraud and wrong of the freedman. Matters pertaining to wrongdoing, however, come later, as has often been said.

units.la: X. Edictum est de bonorum possessione ex testam. mil priori de patrono proximum, & ab Ulpiano explicatum, utrumq; eodem lib.45. ad edict. ex quo libro multae sunt leges in tit. ff. de milit. test. sumptae scilicet ex hoc tractatu de bonorum possessione (ut ita dicam) militari, de qua fuit edictum. Ratio ordinis, cur scilicet prius de bonorum possessione paganorum, tam ingenuorum quàm libertinorum, posteriùs verò de bonorû possessionemilitari, in edicto fuerit actum & propositum hæc est: quia civilia militaribus præferuntur, ut sæpè demonstratum. In Cod. tamen Tribun. hanc interjecit inter ingenuos & libertinos: Credo dignitatem & propter similitudinem, quod scilicet militaris plerumque sit ingenuorum.
units.tr: Tenth is the edict on possession of goods under a military testament, next after the earlier one concerning the patron, and explained by Ulpian in the same book 45 on the Edict, from which many laws in the title de militari testamento of the Digest were taken, namely from this treatise on military possession of goods (so to speak), which was the subject of the edict. The reason for the order, namely why the possession of goods under civil wills, of freeborn and freedmen alike, was treated and set out in the edict first, and the military possession afterwards, is this: civil matters are preferred to military ones, as has often been shown. In the Code of Theodosius, however, he placed it between the freeborn and freedmen, I believe on account of dignity and also because of the resemblance, since the military testament is for the most part that of freeborn persons.

units.la: X I. Edictum est, si tab. test. nullæ exstabant de quo Ulp. explicavit lib. 46. Et sic inscriptio, l. 1. ff. d. tit. emendanda est, & non rectè vulgatum est 44. Hoc enim libro ut jam dictum explicavit Ulpian edictum si tab. test. & c. ut perspicuum est ex l. 2. unde legit. & l. 1. unde cogn.
units.tr: The eleventh edict is that if there were no written wills, on which Ulpian explained in book 46. And so the inscription of l. 1 of the Digest in that title should be corrected, and it is not rightly given as 44. For Ulpian explained in this book, as said already, the edict "if no written wills," etc., as is clear from l. 2 unde legitimi and l. 1 unde cognati.

units.la: Sub hoc enim edicto, si tab. & c. tanquam generali, decem species bonorum possessionis ab intestato prætor proposuit.
units.tr: For under this edict, "if no written wills," etc., as a general heading, the praetor set out ten kinds of possession of goods on intestacy.

units.la: I. De libertis, l. 1. ff. recte. d. tit. Recte inquit, prætor a libertis initium fecit.
units.tr: I. Concerning freedmen, l. 1 Digest, title cited. "Rightly," he says, "the praetor began with freedmen."

units.la: II. De agnatis, sive legitimis, l. 1. unde legit. & deinceps aliæ 8. ut indicat l. 1. unde cog. de quibus 8. in Institut. titul. de bonor. possession. §. sunt autem, & seqq.
units.tr: II. Concerning agnates, or legitimate heirs, l. 1 unde legitimi, and then eight others, as l. 1 unde cognati indicates; of these eight, in the Institutes, title de bonorum possessionibus, §. sunt autem, and following.

units.la: Ratio ordinis est quia ad causam testamenti, ut priorem, de qua hactenus, expostia sunt edicta proximè & rectè sequitur causa intestati, ad quam pertinent hæ decem species possessionum sive successionum, quas per ordinem prætor in edicto disposuerat, f. cum igitur, d. tit.
units.tr: The reason for the order is that, since the edicts concerning the cause of a testament, the earlier one, have been set out, the cause of intestacy closely and rightly follows; to it belong these ten kinds of possession or succession, which the praetor had arranged in order in the edict, f. cum igitur, d. tit.

units.la: Ordo inter eas exstat in d. tit. Nam ex his decem possessionibus ab intestato prima est unde liberi, quia successio illis primo & natura debetur.
units.tr: The order among them appears in the same title. For of these ten possessions on intestacy the first is unde liberi, because succession is owed to children first and by nature.

units.la: II. Species est unde legitimi Ratio ordinis est quia subsequitur prætor L X I I. Tab & Jus civile, l. sin. de testib. At jure civili hereditas secunda defertur legitimis seu agnatis initio Inst. tit. de legit. agnat. success.
units.tr: II. The second kind is unde legitimi. The reason for the order is that the praetor follows the Twelve Tables and the civil law, l. sin. de testibus. But by civil law the second inheritance is deferred to the legitimate heirs, or agnates, at the beginning of the Institutes, title de legitima agnatorum successione.

units.la: III Species erat quæ dabatur d cem personis, patri, matri, &c. d. f. sunt autem, verfic. tert. o d cem, & c. Ratio ordinis hæc est: quia scilicet ratio naturalis suadet ut hæ personæ, pater, mater, filius, &c. propter sanguinis proximitatem habeant aliquam prærogativam, & præferantur extraneo manumissori.
units.tr: III. The third kind was given to ten persons: father, mother, etc., d. f. sunt autem, verse tertio decem, etc. The reason for the order is this: natural reason suggests that these persons, father, mother, son, etc., by reason of the nearness of blood, should have some prerogative and be preferred to an outside manumittor.

units.la: I V Species est unde cognati. Ratio ordinis est, quod post ordinem liberorum, & post ordinem legitimorum sive agnatorum proximus sit ordo cognatorum quibus tamen cognatis præferuntur decem personæ, & constituunt tertiam speciem propter cam sam modo expositam. Hujus autem edicti verba non exstant: sed sententia & mentio continetur & explicatur ut ff. unde cognati, l. 1. § hoc autem d. tit.
units.tr: IV. The fourth kind is unde cognati. The reason for the order is that after the order of children, and after the order of legitimate heirs or agnates, the next order is that of cognates; yet the ten persons are preferred to these cognates, and they constitute the third kind, for the reason just set out. The words of this edict do not survive, but its substance and mention are contained and explained in the Digest, unde cognati, l. 1 §. hoc autem, d. tit.

units.la: V. Species est, quæ unius familia.
units.tr: V. The fifth kind is that which belongs to one family.

units.la: V I est, quæ datur patrono & liberis. Ratio ordinis est quia hæ duæ sunt libertinorum & proinde posteriores, cum expositæ quatuor sint ingenuorum & proinde priores.
units.tr: VI. The sixth is that given to the patron and children. The reason for the order is that these two are of freedmen and therefore later, since the four before them concern freeborn persons and are therefore earlier.

units.la: V I I Species eodem pertinet, quasi hodie sunt sublatæ, propterea, quod hæc in re non est amplius differentia inter ingenuos & libertinos. VIII. & ultimum est, unde vir & uxor. Ratio ordinis, cur haec sit ultima, quia inter eos nullum est vinculum, aut civile aut naturale, & proinde jure civili haec species successionis plane fuit ignota, ut & cognatorum, inter quos tamen est vinculum naturale.
units.tr: VII. The seventh kind belongs here, though today it has been abolished, because in this matter there is no longer any difference between freeborn and freedmen. The eighth and last is unde vir et uxor. The reason why this is last is that between them there is no bond, either civil or natural, and therefore by civil law this kind of succession was wholly unknown, as was that of cognates, among whom, however, there is a natural bond.

units.la: Et hic fuit ordo harum octo specierum ab intestato, & in edicto perpetuo, quas ad unum generalem titulum ab intestato, sive si tabul. testament. nulla ex iure ab &c. retuli, quas omnes explicavit Ulpianus duobus libris 46. & 47. ad edictum. Sed in Digest quatuor tantum adferuntur ut aded liberi, unde legitimi, unde cognati, unde vir & uxor, reliquis scilicet quatuor a Justiniano sublatis, ut est titul: Instit. de b. n. possess. & §. sed hodie, de bonis libert.
units.tr: This was the order of these eight kinds on intestacy in the perpetual edict, which I have referred to a single general title on intestacy, or "if no written wills from the law," etc.; Ulpian explained all of them in two books, 46 and 47, on the Edict. But the Digest cites only four: unde liberi, unde legitimi, unde cognati, unde vir et uxor, the other four having been abolished by Justinian, as in the title of the Institutes de bonorum possessionibus and §. sed hodie, de bonis libertorum.

units.la: XII. Edictum est de his, quibus non competit bonorum possessio, obdelictum aliquod, ut si quis dolo fecit, ne testamentum mutaretur. Cujus edicti sit mentio, in l. 1, quibus non competat bonorum possessio. Verba non exstant, sed sententia videtur ea fuisse, quam exposuit. Hoc autem loco positum fuisse illud edictum, indicant leges aliquot ex Ulpiano lib. 48. ad edictum, sumptae, ut si quis aliquem testari prohibuerit, l. 12 de bonorum possessione, 2. de poenis, quae omnes ad hoc edictum pertinere videntur; indicat & l. 2. si quia aliquem test. &c. sumpta ex Pauli lib. 40. ad ed. 8. Ratio ordinis autem est, quia ad delictum pertinentia ultima fere solent esse, ut saepe dictum.
units.tr: XII. The edict concerns those to whom possession of goods is not granted on account of some wrong, as if someone acted by fraud so that a testament should not be changed. Mention of this edict is made in l. 1, quibus non competat bonorum possessio. The words do not survive, but the substance seems to have been what he set out. That this edict was placed here is indicated by several laws taken from Ulpian, book 48 on the Edict, such as ut si quis aliquem testari prohibuerit, l. 12 de bonorum possessione, 2 de poenis, all of which seem to belong to this edict; l. 2 si quis aliquem test. etc., taken from Paul, book 40 on the Edict, also indicates it. The reason for the order is that matters pertaining to wrongdoing are usually the last, as often said.

units.la: XIII. Edictum est de bonorum possessione ex legibus, quod explicavit Ulpianus libro 49. ut prius XII: lib. 48 ut jam dictum. Ratio ordinis haec est: quia haec bonorum possessio ex legibus est extraordinaria, & ultimum quoddam auxilium, prioribus omnibus ordinariis deficientibus, ideoque merito ultimum locum tenet. Ita Imper. in §. antepen. Instit. de bon. poss.
units.tr: XIII. The edict concerns possession of goods under the laws, which Ulpian explained in book 49, as the twelfth in book 48, as already said. The reason for the order is this: this possession under the laws is extraordinary and a last resort, all the earlier ordinary ones having failed, and so it rightly holds the last place. So the Emperor says in §. antepen. Institutes de bonorum possessionibus.

units.la: XIV. Edictum dicitur successorium, quia successionis ordo in bonorum possessionibus eo praescribitur, & simul etiam tempus, intra quod petidebeat bonorum possessio. Haec enim duo tempus & ordo successionis uno hoc edicto successorio comprehensa fuerunt, ut indicat l. 1. de success. edict. quae est Ulp. ex lib. 49. ad edict. & l. 2. quis ordo in bonor. possess. &c. quae item est Ulpian. ex eodem libro. Sed Tribun. haec duo divulsit, & sejunxit. Nam 38. ff. tit. 19. est de success. edict. tit. 16. est, quis ordo in bonorum possess. &c. Ratio Trib. ibi exponetur.
units.tr: XIV. The edict is called the successory edict, because the order of succession in the possessions of goods is prescribed in it, and at the same time the time within which possession of goods must be sought. For these two, the time and the order of succession, were comprehended in this one successory edict, as l. 1 de successorio edicto indicates, which is Ulpian from book 49 on the Edict, and l. 2 quis ordo in bonorum possessionibus etc., which is likewise Ulpian from the same book. But Tribonian separated and divided these two. For 38 Digest, title 19, is de successorio edicto, and title 16 is quis ordo in bonorum possessionibus etc. Tribonian's reason will be explained there.

units.la: VI. Pars Edicti Perpetui.
units.tr: Part VI of the Perpetual Edict.

units.la: Dictis de bonorum possessi jam expositis sequebantur in edicto perpetuo edicta de testamentis, ut videre ex Ulpian. lib. 50. & 2. seqq. ad edictum, & Pauli lib. 45. & 3. seqq. quemadmodum & in C. prius de bonorum possessi posterius de hereditatibus, ex testamento & ab intestato agitur, ut supr. dictum in Cod. lib. 6. Ratio ordinis, cur prius de bonorum possessionibus, quam de testamentis agatur, cum tamen contra fiat in ff. & Instit. est hæc: quia in edicto de testamentis proprie non fuit actum: testamentum non pendet ex edicto sed ex 12. tab. uti quaeq; legassit. &c. initio tit. Instit. de Fidei. Falcid. Cur ergo dices, sunt aliqua edicta de testamentis? Respon. esse ea, quae pertinent ad possessionem legatorum, & alia quaedam ad officium praetoris pertinentia. Sed cur, inquies, ea ipsa non sunt praepositae edictis de bonorum possessi. Ratio haec est: quia agunt de iis quae locum habent nonnisi prius constet, quem esse heredem aut bonorum possessorem, aut saltem ad edictum aliquod pertinent.
units.tr: After the edicts on possession of goods, the perpetual edict went on to the edicts on wills, as can be seen from Ulpian, book 50 and the following books on the edict, and Paul, book 45 and the following. Likewise, in the Code the matter of possession of goods comes first and that of inheritances, whether under a will or on intestacy, comes after, as stated above in Code book 6. The reason for this order, that possession of goods is treated before wills, although the Digest and the Institutes do the reverse, is this: the edict did not properly deal with wills. A will does not depend on the edict but on the Twelve Tables, as each man shall have bequeathed, etc., at the beginning of the title of the Institutes on the Falcidian law. You will ask, then, whether there are any edicts on wills at all? I answer that there are, namely those that concern the possession of legacies, and certain others that belong to the praetor's office. But, you will ask, why were these not placed before the edicts on possession of goods? The reason is that they deal with matters that can only apply once it is settled who is the heir or possessor of goods, or at least they belong to some edict.

units.la: Fuisse autem aliqua edicta de testamentis tum ex aliis, de quibus mox, tum ex Cajo perspicuum est, qui duos libros scripsit ad edictum praetoris de testamentis, ut tres ad edictum praetoris de legatis.
units.tr: That there were some edicts on wills, both from the other edicts I shall mention shortly and from Gaius, is plain. He wrote two books on the praetor's edict concerning wills, just as he wrote three on the praetor's edict concerning legacies.

units.la: Edicta autem de testamentis 4. reperio, proposita in edicto perpetuo, quorum primum est de jure jurando, hoc est: de relictis testamento, sive hereditate sive legatis sub conditione jurisjurandi, quam conditionem Praetor hoc edicto remisit, & reprobavit. De hoc edicto est l. 8. de condit. instit. l. 29. §i admit. &c. de iis. mil. l. 26. hæc scriptura, decem it. & demonst. l. facta, §. fi sub cond. tione. §. ad Trebellian. l. 12. de manum. test. Ratio ordinis, hoc est, cur in edictis de testamentis hoc sit primum haec est: quia hoc edictum eo pertinet, ut quis possit esse heres, sive hereditatem aut legatum consequi. De eo enim prius constare oportet, quam hereditatem adire aut possidere possit.
units.tr: I find four edicts on wills set out in the perpetual edict. The first concerns the oath, that is, legacies or inheritances left in a will under the condition of an oath, a condition which the praetor by this edict removed and rejected. On this edict see Dig. 8, de condit. instit.; Dig. 29, §1 admit. etc. de iis mil.; Dig. 26, hæc scriptura, decem it. & demonst.; Dig. facta, §. fi sub condi­tione; §. ad Trebellian.; Dig. 12, de manum. test. The reason why this edict comes first among the edicts on wills is this: it aims at ensuring that a person can be an heir, or obtain an inheritance or legacy. For this must first be settled before he can enter upon or possess an inheritance.

units.la: II. Edictum est de tabulis testamenti aperiendis cujus velut mentio & sententia est, sub tit ff. si testam. quemadmodum aper. Verba non exstant. Ratio autem ordinis est, quia postquam constitit, aliquem esse heredem, proximum est, ut hereditatem adeat, & ea quae testamento sunt relicta & commissa, exsequatur: quod nisi apertis tabulis fieri non potest, & inspectis verbis testamentis; ut ait l. 3. d. t.
units.tr: II. There is an edict on opening the tablets of a will; its substance and purport is indicated under the title Dig. si testam. quemadmodum aper. The words of the edict do not survive. The reason for its order is that once it is established that someone is heir, the next step is that he should take up the inheritance and carry out what has been left and entrusted to him by the will. This cannot be done unless the tablets are opened and the words of the will inspected, as Dig. 3, in the same title, says.

units.la: III. Edictum est de eo herede scripto, in testamento, quod testamenti causa praetermissa, ab intestato hereditatem possidere coepit. Verba ejus pauca exstant: sed ipsum diligenter explicatur sub tit. ff. si quis testamenti causa, &c. & C. eod. Ratio ordinis est, tum, quia post apertas demum tabulas heres plerumq; primum acquirit possessionem rerum hereditariarum; tum, quia hoc edictum est de delicto, sive calliditate, & dolo malo heredis praeveniendo, & proinde posterius. Ex quo edicto est & actio in factum contra heredem, de qua dicitur titulus, & dicitur actio legatorum; l. 12. de libertatibus, §. primo, dict. tit. lo.
units.tr: III. There is an edict concerning the heir named in a will who, having been passed over for the purposes of the will, began to possess the inheritance on intestacy. Few of its words survive, but the edict itself is carefully explained under the title Dig. si quis testamenti causa, etc. and Code in the same title. The reason for its order is twofold: first, because usually the heir acquires possession of the estate's goods only after the tablets have been opened; second, because this edict deals with a wrong, or with cunning and wicked fraud on the part of the heir, and so it comes later. From this edict arises an action on the facts against the heir, which the title names, and it is called the action for legacies; Dig. 12, de libertatibus, §1, in the said title.

units.la: IV. Edictum est de testamento ejus; qui occisus erat non aperiendo. Verba non exstant; sed ejus sententia & mens explicatur, l. 2. quod ad causam, &c. de SC. Syllan. & passim dictis titulis; imo verba fere ipsa edicti videntur esse, in d. §. quod ad. Ratio ordinis est, quia & hoc de delicto agit, nimirum de occisi testamento; & est edictum prohibitorium. Prohibitoria autem solent in ultimum locum rejici, ut saepe jam dictum.
units.tr: IV. There is an edict on the will of a man who was killed, if it is not opened. Its words do not survive, but its sense and intention are explained in Dig. 2, quod ad causam, etc., de SC. Syllan. and in the titles passim; indeed the words of the edict itself seem to be those in the said §. quod ad. The reason for its order is that this too deals with a wrong, namely the will of one who was killed, and it is a prohibitory edict. Prohibitory edicts, however, are usually placed in the last position, as has often been said already.

units.la: Hunc autem ordinem edictorum de testamentis fuisse olim in edicto perpetuo, intelligi potest ex Ulpiano, libro 50. ad edictum, & Paul. lib. 45. & 46. ad edictum, & ex ordine Digest.
units.tr: That this order of the edicts on wills existed in the perpetual edict of old can be understood from Ulpian, book 50 on the edict, and Paul, books 45 and 46 on the edict, and from the order of the Digest.

units.la: Titulo de testamentis proximus fuit in edicto, titul. de legatis, ut ex lib. 31. & 32. Ulp. & Pauli. 47. & 48. ad edict. intelligitur. Cajus, ut modo dictum, tres libros scripsit ad edictum praetoris perpetui de leg. Non multa tamen edicta fuisse, id argumento est, quod Jurisconsulti in libris ad edicta pauca de legatis tractarint.
units.tr: The edict on legacies came next after the title on wills in the edict, as is understood from Ulpian and Paul, books 31 and 32, and 47 and 48 on the edict. Gaius, as has just been said, wrote three books on the praetor's perpetual edict on legacies. Yet there were not many edicts on this subject; the proof is that the jurists in their books on the edict treated few matters concerning legacies.

units.la: Unum ergo duntaxat reperio, quod est de mittendo legatario in possessionem legati servandi causa. Hujus edicti verba non exstant, sed sententia explicatur sub titul ff. ut in poss. legat. & c. ubi mentio quoque edicti saepe fit, ut l. 1. in sin. d. tit. Ratio ordinis, cur prius de testamentis quam de legatis agatur, haec est: quia legata ex testamento pendeant, eoque irrito, aut infirmato non debeantur, l. eam quam, C. de fideicomm. & l. 1. si fideicommissa causa, &c.
units.tr: I find, therefore, only one, which concerns sending the legatee into possession of the legacy for the purpose of safeguarding it. The words of this edict do not survive, but its substance is explained under the title Dig. ut in poss. legat. etc., where mention of the edict is also often made, as in Dig. 1, in the end of the said title. The reason why wills are treated before legacies is this: legacies depend on the will, and if it is void or invalidated they are not owed, Code, eam quam, de fideicomm. and Dig. 1, si fideicommissa causa, etc.

units.la: Videtur tamen & alterum de legatis edictum fuisse, quod ad usumfructum sive cautionem usufructuariam pertinuerit (credo quiusfusfructu legati nomine haec cautio fere praestari solet) & prius fuerit edicto jam expositum. Prius enim explicaturab Ulpiano, lib. 52. hoc explicatum videtur, lib. 51. ut & a Paulo illud lib. 48. hoc autem 47. lib. ad edict. Nihil tamen certi affirmare possum. Nam de cautione fructuaria edictum fuit, longe inferioriloco positum in edicto perpetuo ut infra dicetur. Saepe tamen diversis in locis de eadem re edicta proposita fuerunt in edicto perpetuo. Huic quoque argumento est, nempe ante edictum de legatario in possessionem mittendo fuisse edictum de cautione, argumento inquam est, & tit. ff. ut legatorum, & senatusconsultorum, &c. quae non est cautio fructuaria, sed est cautio legatorum & in edicto sint posita longe inferiori loco, ut & cautio fructuaria, nimirum inter cautiones. & sub tit. de cautionibus, de quo infra.
units.tr: Yet it seems there was another edict on legacies, which concerned usufruct or the usufructuary security (I believe that this security is usually given for a usufruct bequeathed as a legacy), and which came before the edict already set out. For Ulpian explained it in book 52, and it seems to have been set out in book 51, and likewise Paul treated it in book 48, while the other matter was in book 47 on the edict. I cannot, however, affirm anything certain on this. For there was an edict on the usufructuary security, placed in a much lower position in the perpetual edict, as will be said below. Yet the same matter was often set out in different places in the perpetual edict. This too is an argument that there was an edict on security before the edict on sending the legatee into possession. I mean the argument drawn from the title Dig. ut legatorum, et senatusconsultorum, etc., which concerns not usufructuary security but the security of legacies, and which, like the usufructuary security, stands in a much lower place in the edict, namely among the securities, under the title on securities, which will be discussed below.

units.la: VII. Pars Edicti Perpetui.
units.tr: VII. Part of the Perpetual Edict.

units.la: HUic autem edicto de legatis proximum fuit edictum de novi oper. nun. ut indicat l. 1. 3 5. d. tit. quae leges sunt ex Ulp. lib. 52. In quo edictum quoq; illud de legatario in possessionem mittendo, ut indicant inscriptiones, l. 35. & l. 37. ff. ut in poss. legat. &c. Ratio ordinis cur edictum de legatis sequatur edictum de novi operis nunciat haec est: quia ut priori de legatis mittitur in possessionem bonorum legatarius, si ei cautio non fuerit praestita, ita & illo edicto nunciator novi operis, si ei non caveatur, aut opus intermittatur, mittitur in possessionem. l. 6. § ficum §. sciendum. de novo oper. nunc. Verba edicti non exstant. Nam verba praetoris, sive edicti, quae exstant in l. 20. praetor ait d. tit. de novi oper. nunc. non ad hoc edictum, de quo nunc agitur, sed ad aliud de quo infra, subtit. de interdictis pertinent.
units.tr: Next after this edict on legacies came the edict on new work and its announcement (de novi oper. nun.), as l. 1, 3 and 5, d. tit. show; these laws are from Ulpian, book 52. In this edict was also the provision on sending the legatee into possession, as the titles show: l. 35 and l. 37 ff. ut in poss. legat. etc. The reason for this order, why the edict on legacies follows the edict on new work, is this: just as in the former the legatee is sent into possession of the goods if security has not been given to him, so in the latter the announcer of new work is sent into possession if security is not given to him, or if the work is not stopped. l. 6, § ficum, § sciendum, de novo oper. nunc. The words of the edict do not survive. For the words of the praetor, or of the edict, which survive in l. 20, "praetor ait", d. tit. de novi oper. nunc., do not belong to this edict now under discussion but to another, of which below, under the title on interdicts.

units.la: Ptoximum huic edicto fuit edictum de cautione damni infecti, argumento est l.7.9.11. quae sunt ex lib.III p.53. quo edictum hoc explicavit dedam. inf. ut prius de op. nov. nunc. l.1.52. Edicti hujus de damno infecto verba exstant l.7. praetor d. tit. de damn. inf. Ratio ordinis cur de damno infecto edictum proximum sit edicto de novi operis nunciatione est haec: quia ut illud est de damno facto, ita & istud de damno nondum facto. Cur ergo inquiers illud est prius? Ratio haec est: quia in illo jam coeptum est aliquid; in hoc nihil dum coeptum sed tantum est futurum. Utantem ex priore, ita & ex isto cavendum est, & nisi caveatur missio fit in possessionem. Exutraque cautione nascitur actio ex stipulatu.
units.tr: Next to this edict was the edict on security against damage not yet done (de cautione damni infecti), as l. 7, 9 and 11 show; these are from book 53 of Ulpian, in which he explained this edict, as he had explained the earlier one on new work, de op. nov. nunc. l. 1, 52. The words of this edict on damage not yet done survive in l. 7, "praetor", d. tit. de damn. inf. The reason for the order, why the edict on damage not yet done follows the edict on announcing new work, is this: just as the one concerns damage already done, so this one concerns damage not yet done. Why then, you will ask, does the former come first? The reason is this: in the former something has already been begun; in this one nothing has yet been begun, but something is only going to be. Just as security must be given in the former case, so it must in this one, and unless security is given, possession is sent to the applicant. From both securities an action arises from the stipulation.

units.la: Hinc autem actioni damni infecti similima est actio de aqua & aquae pluvia arc. Nam & ea datur ob damnum nondum factum, l.1.§.2.14. de aq. & aq.pluv.arc. Ideoque in edicto fuit proxime prioribus collocata, ut videretur ex lib.53. Ulpian. quo de damno infecto, & de aqua pluvia explicavit, & ex lib.49. Pauli, quo de aqua pluvia cum de damno infecto & de opere novo explicasset lib.48. scripsit. & Gajus librum ad edictum perpetuum de damno infecto & ad edictum de aqua pluvia, & de opere novo videatur. l.1. & 9. de op. nov. nunc. l.18. de damn. infect. l.13. de aq. & aq. & c. Edicti verba non exstant: credo, quia exiguum fuit propterea quod haec actio aquae pluvia sit civilis: cum duae priores sint praetoriae, haec est ex lege 12. tab. l.5. ne quid in loco publ. l.21. Labeo de fer. at. lib. Dices, cur igitur haec illis non fuerit praepositae? eum sit civilis, & civilia praetoriis praeponantur. Ratio haec est, quia illae sunt de damno urbano, haec de damno rustico sive in agris, test. Cic. in Top. l. 1.§.de ope. h. tit. Urbana autem rusticis praeponuntur, ut tit. de servitut. urbanor. titulo de rustic.
units.tr: Now, the action concerning water and rainwater (de aqua et aquae pluviae arcendae) is very similar to the action for damage not yet done. For this too is granted on account of damage not yet done, l. 1, § 2, 14, de aq. et aq. pluv. arc. Therefore in the edict it was placed immediately after the earlier ones, as is seen from Ulpian, book 53, in which he explained both the damage not yet done and the rainwater, and from Paul, book 49, who, after explaining the rainwater together with the damage not yet done and the new work, wrote in book 48. Gaius also wrote a book on the perpetual edict concerning damage not yet done, on the edict concerning rainwater and on new work, as can be seen in l. 1 and 9, de op. nov. nunc.; l. 18, de damn. infect.; l. 13, de aq. et aq. etc. The words of this edict do not survive. I believe this is because it was brief, since this action on rainwater is civil, whereas the two earlier ones are praetorian. This one arises from the Twelve Tables, l. 5, ne quid in loco publ.; l. 21, Labeo, de fer. at. lib. You may ask why it was not placed before those, since it is civil and civil actions are placed before praetorian ones. The reason is that those concern damage in the city, while this one concerns damage in the country or in the fields, as Cicero witnesses in the Topics, l. 1, § de ope. h. tit. Urban matters, however, take precedence over rural ones, as in the title de servitut. urbanor. and the title de rustic.

units.la: His proximum in edicto locum tenuit edictum de liberali causa ut vide-re est ex lib.54. Ulp. quo explicavit hanc actionem de liberali causa & ini-tio lib.55. cum lib.53. explicasset aq.plu utmodo dictum. Idem quoq; videre est ex lib. Pauli 50. & 51. quibus de liberali causa explicatur cum de aq. pluv. explicasset lib.49. scripsit autem & Cajus lib.2 ad edictum perpetuum tit. de lib. causa l. 2.4.9.11.12. & 15.d.tit.l.30.de bon.libert.l.1.de collus.dereg. Verba edicti hujus non exstant: sed eo propositae fuerunt duae actiones, una de liberali causa sive praejudicialis de libert. & servit. altera actio in factum adversus eum qui sciens pro servo venit. Illae est civilis. §. praejudiciales. de act. & explicatur passim tit. ff. de lib. caus. haec est praetoria & poenalis, de qua l.7. & aliquot ftqq. usq. ad l.24 d.tit.
units.tr: Next in the edict after these came the edict on the free status of a person (de liberali causa), as can be seen from Ulpian, book 54, in which he explained this action on the free status of a person, and at the beginning of book 55, when, after having explained the rainwater in book 53, as was said, he was beginning to explain this. The same can also be seen from Paul, books 50 and 51, in which the free status of a person is explained after he had explained the rainwater in book 49. Gaius also wrote in book 2 on the perpetual edict, title de lib. causa, l. 2, 4, 9, 11, 12 and 15, d. tit.; l. 30, de bon. libert.; l. 1, de collus. dereg. The words of this edict do not survive. But two actions were set out under it: one concerning the free status of a person, or preliminary, on freedom and slavery; the other an action on the case against one who knowingly presents himself as a slave. The former is civil, § praejudiciales, de act., and is explained throughout the title ff. de lib. caus. The latter is praetorian and penal, concerning which l. 7 and several following, up to l. 24, d. tit.

units.la: Ratio ordinis obscura est & difficilis ad explicandum ex qua tamen pendet & ordo C & ff. ubi idem est ordo. Duas igitur rationes reperio: una haec est: quia cum hactenus explicatum sit de actionibus tam in rem, quam in personam, tandem adjungitur actio, quae neque in rem neque in personam sit. Nam tametsi actiones praejudiciales in rem esse videntur, ut aitd. §. praeju-diciales. duciales, tamen proprie non sunt, quia iis non proprie de jure rei, ut dominio aut servitute prædii sed de jure personæ ut de libertate, & de servitute aut de ingenuitate agitur. Et hinc est, quod in dict. §. dicitur: videntur esse in rem. Quare cum hæc actio de liberali causa, à prioribus hactenus in edicto propositis tam in rem quam in personam habeat naturam distinctam: merito & ordine ab iis distingui debuit: quod & factum l. 1. de act. ubi prius de actionibus in rem. § omnium. deinde de actionibus in personam, f. sn personam & seqq. tandem de his præjudicialibus tanquam anomalis distincte explicatur §. præjudiciales.
units.tr: The reason for this order is obscure and difficult to explain, yet the order of the Codex and the Digest, where the order is the same, depends on it. I find two reasons. One is this: since up to this point actions both in rem and in personam have been explained, at last an action is added which is neither in rem nor in personam. For although the preliminary actions seem to be in rem, as in § praejudiciales, nevertheless they properly are not, because they do not properly concern a right to a thing, such as ownership or a servitude of an estate, but a right of a person, such as liberty, servitude or freeborn status. And hence it is said in the said § that they seem to be in rem. Therefore, since this action concerning the free status of a person has a nature distinct from the earlier actions set out in the edict, both in rem and in personam, it rightly ought to be distinguished from them in order, and this has been done: l. 1, de act., where first the actions in rem are treated, § omnium; then the actions in personam, § in personam and following; and finally these preliminary actions are explained separately, as anomalous, § praejudiciales.

units.la: Altera ratio est: quia hactenus de actionibus contra liberos sit actum, quibus non incommodè actio contra servos nunc tandem subjicitur: de liberis autem ut dignioribus prius agitur. Est & alia ratio cur hæc actio de liberali causa inter has actiones & edicta quibus bonorum possessio & missio in possessionem continentur, explicetur; ista: quia hæc quoq; actio de liberali causa aliquam possessionis rationem habet, propterea quod ex l. 12. tab. vindiciæ dentur secundum libertatem. l. 2. §. & cum placuit de origine hoc est, possessioni libertatis favetur, hoc est in actione sive judicio de liberali causa, quo quis alterum contendit esse servum suum, & is contra, liberum se esse contendit, in re dubia & pendente lite jubetur reus esse in possessione libertatis, non vero servitutis.
units.tr: The other reason is this: up to this point the actions against free persons have been treated, and now the action against slaves is at last added without inconvenience; but the free persons, as more worthy, are treated first. There is also another reason why this action concerning the free status of a person is explained among these actions and the edicts which contain bonorum possessio and the sending into possession: it is this, that this action on the free status of a person also has some character of possession, because, according to l. 12 of the Twelve Tables, claims are granted in favour of liberty. l. 2, § and since it has been decided, de origine. That is, the possession of liberty is favoured, in the action or lawsuit concerning the free status of a person, in which one party maintains that the other is his slave, and the other maintains that he is free; in a doubtful matter and while the case is pending, the defendant is ordered to be in possession of liberty, not of servitude.

units.la: Huic edicto de liberali causa proximum fuit edictum de publicanis, quod perspicuum est ex lib. 55. Ulpiani quo de publicanis explicavit, cum jam de liber. cauf. libr. 55. inchoaret explicare. l. 2. & 3. de public. (scripsit & Cajus librum ad edictum perpetuum urbani de publican. l. 5. de public. & vectigal. Ratio ordinis ut intelligatur, breviter admonendum adhuc esse propositas actiones tam in rem quam in personam, ex contractibus & quasi contractibus quibus nunc proxime adjunguntur actiones ex delictis. Ratio ordinis est in institut. expósita, cur posterius de delictis agatur. Inter actiones autem & interdicta de delictis cur primum locum in edicto perpetuo tenuerit actio furti: ratio item expósita est ad institut.
