Actiones autem furti sunt variæ & multiplices, quarum princeps & generalis actio furti jam supra expósita est, post titulum sive actionem tutelæ & de rebus distrahendis propter similitudinem furti, & rationibus distrahendis. ut ibidem dictum Expósita igitur jam ante actione furti generali, & quibusdam specialibus reliqua fuit item specialis actio de furtis publicanorum, quæ hic posita fuit in edicto. Verba edicti extant l. 1. de public.
units.tr: Next after this edict on the free status of a person came the edict on the publicans (de publicanis), which is clear from book 55 of Ulpian, in which he explained the edict on publicans, when he was already beginning to explain the matter of free status in book 55. l. 2 and 3, de public. (Gaius also wrote a book on the urban perpetual edict concerning publicans, l. 5, de public. et vectigal.) The reason for the order, that it may be understood, must briefly be noted: the actions both in rem and in personam, arising from contracts and quasi-contracts, have so far been set out, and now they are next joined by the actions arising from delicts. The reason for the order, why the matter of delicts is treated later, is given in the Institutes. Concerning why the action for theft held the first place among the actions and interdicts on delicts in the perpetual edict, the reason is likewise set out in the Institutes. The actions for theft, however, are various and manifold, of which the chief and general action for theft has already been set out above, after the title or action on guardianship and on the separation of goods, on account of the similarity to theft and the accounting, as was said in that place. Therefore, the general action for theft having been set out earlier, and some special actions too, there remained also a special action concerning the thefts of publicans, which was placed here in the edict. The words of the edict survive, l. 1, de public.

units.la: Cur autem hæc actio de public. cum sit specialis furti actio non fuerit una cum reliquis furti actionibus superius posita in edicto, sed in hunc locum rejecta ubi de reliquis delictis agitur, ratio hæc est: quod publicanorum delictum sæpe non sit simplex furtum, sed cum vi conjunctum, imò hoc edictum de publicanis proprie pertinet ad vim potius, quam ad furtum eorum l.1. in verb. vi ademerit. & mox: quippe in duplum dantur. cum vi bonorū raptorum, & de publ. & vett. Atque adeo hoc edictum omnem speciem delicti publicanorum continet & coërcet, vim, damnum, injuriam, furtum.
units.tr: Why this action concerning the publicans (de publicanis), although it is a special action for theft, was not placed in the edict together with the other theft actions above, but was set aside here, where the other delicts are treated, the reason is this: the delict of the publicans is often not simple theft but joined with violence; indeed this edict concerning the publicans properly pertains to violence rather than to theft ("if he has taken away by violence"; and soon after: "for they are given at double ... with violence, of goods seized by force", de publicanis et vectigalibus). And so this edict embraces and restrains every kind of delict of the publicans: violence, damage, injury, theft.

units.la: Est & aliud edictum de publicanis, sive potius eorum familia & servis, sed hoc de furto potissimum agit & de damno injuria non de vi: Ideoq; superius, ubi de furti speciebus fuit propositum: licet utrumque, hoc est, tam edictum de vi, aliisque delictis ipsius Publicani, quam de furto servorum ejus conjunctum sit à Tribun. sub uno titulo ff. de public. quod & alias ab eo factum, ut diversis in locis positas actiones Tribun posuerit eodem in loco ff ut videre est sub tit. de nov. op. nunc sub tit. de dam. infect. Cur igitur de publicanis edictum, & actio contra eos primum locum inter actiones de delictis teneat ratio est tum quia hoc edictum est generale; hoc est, continet omnia fere delicta furtum, damnum & vim: tum quia eorum munus est quasi publicum; & proinde primo loco ponendum.
units.tr: There is also another edict concerning the publicans, or rather concerning their household and slaves, but this deals chiefly with theft and with damage by injury, not with violence. Therefore above, where the kinds of theft were set out, both edicts, that is, the edict on violence and other delicts of the publican himself, and that on the theft of his slaves, were joined by the tribune under one title (ff. de publicanis); which he also did elsewhere, placing the actions in different places in the same place, as may be seen under the title de novi operis nuntiatione and now under the title de damno infecto. The reason why the edict and action against the publicans holds the first place among the actions concerning delicts is, first, because this edict is general, that is, it contains nearly all delicts: theft, damage and violence; and second, because their office is almost public, and therefore it must be placed first.

units.la: Huic proximum fuit edictum & actio vi bonorum raptorum & huic edictum de turba, sive de iis quae in turba hominum contracta & coacta damna sint data: Utrumque Ulpianus explicavit lib. 56. ad edictum de publicanis lib. 55. l.1 & 3. d publ. l.2. & 4. vi bon. rapt. & de turba. Sic & Paulus quoque lib 54. haec edicta de rapina & turba explicavit, edictum de publicanis prioribus libris eundem quoq; ordinem tenet Paulus in libr. sent. ubi lib.5. tit.3. est de his quae pet turb. & tit.4. de injur. de quibus & hic mox verba edicti de rapina sive de vi raptus exstant l. 2. vi bon. rapt. verba edicti de turba exstant in leg.4. eod.
units.tr: Next to this were the edict and action for violence and the taking of goods (vi bonorum raptorum), and next to this the edict concerning the crowd (de turba), that is, concerning damages done and caused in a crowd of men. Ulpian explained both in book 56 on the edict, and the edict concerning publicans in book 55 (laws 1 and 3 de publicanis; law 2 and 4 vi bonorum raptorum; and de turba). Paul likewise in book 54 explained these edicts on rapine and the crowd; Paul also keeps this same order in his Sentences, where book 5, title 3, concerns those things done in a crowd (de his quae per turbam), and title 4 concerns injury. Of these, the words of the edict on rapine, or on violence of seizure, stand in law 2 (vi bonorum raptorum); the words of the edict on the crowd stand in law 4 of the same title.

units.la: Est & tertium edictum ad rapinam & vim pertinens, de incendio, ruina, naufragio, &c. hic quoque positum in edicto ab Ulpiano explicato eod. l.56.l.1. & 2. de incend. ruin. naufrag. verba ejus exstant in dict. leg.1. Ratio ordinis cur inter delicta secundum locum teneat rapina & primum teneat furtum, de quo tamen supra dictum expositum est ad institutiones. Inter haec autem 3. edicta de vi aut rapina, ordinis ratio est perspicua, quia primum est generale, reliqua duo sunt specialia: inter quae illud de incendiis est posterius hac ratione quia illud de turba plerunque in urbe, hoc de incendio rui ri, etiam extra urbem committatur.
units.tr: There is also a third edict relating to rapine and violence, concerning fire, collapse, shipwreck, and so on. This too is placed in the edict and was explained by Ulpian in the same book 56 (laws 1 and 2 de incendio, ruina, naufragio); its words stand in the said law 1. The order by which rapine holds second place among the delicts, and theft first, which however was explained above in the Institutes. Among these three edicts on violence or rapine, the reason for the order is plain: the first is general, the other two are special; of these the one on fires comes later for this reason: the one on the crowd is committed mostly in the city, while that on fire, collapse, and so on, may be committed also outside the city.

units.la: His de rapina edictis proximum fuit edictum de injuriis, sub quo sunt unum edictum generale, & multa specialia, ut indicat l.15. item apud §. ait praetor. hoc tit. de injur. verba edicti generalis pauca tamen exstant / 7. praetor dict. tit. (specialia edicta de injuriis. I. tit. de verbis, seu conviciis, dict. leg.15. §.2. ait praetor. II. De factis infamandi causa, dict. leg.15. § 20. ait praetor. III. De injuria servo alieno facta, dict. leg.15. §.26. ait praetor. IV. De injuria filiofa. alieno facta leg.17. quod si. §. ait praetor. hoc tit. quae eo ordine explicantur ab Ulpiano lib.56. & 57. à Paulo. lib.52. 53.54. & 55. à Cajo libro 21. & 22 Ratio ordinis autem de primo est facilis, quia est generale edictum de injuriis In-
units.tr: Next after these edicts on rapine came the edict on injuries, under which there is one general edict and many special ones, as law 15, "item apud" and §. "ait praetor" in this title (de injuriis) indicates. The words of the general edict, however, are few and survive in the praetor's edict in law 7 (the special edicts on injuries are: I. on words or insults, in the said law 15 §2 "ait praetor"; II. on deeds done for the purpose of defamation, in law 15 §20 "ait praetor"; III. on injury done to another's slave, in law 15 §26 "ait praetor"; IV. on injury done to a son under power, law 17 "quod si" §"ait praetor" in this title). These are explained in that order by Ulpian in books 56 and 57, by Paul in books 52, 53, 54 and 55, and by Gaius in books 21 and 22. The reason for the order of the first is easy: it is the general edict on injuries, and the first special one concerns words or insults, since this species of injury is most frequent.

units.la: T ter speciali a primum de verbis, sive conviciis locum tenuit: quia hæc injuriæ species sit frequentissima. Alterum fuit de factis, quod vix fuit necessarium quia ex generali potuit agi de injuria facta: sed continentur hoc edicto specialia quædam facta, ut veluti lugubri uti, barbam demittere, carmen conscribere ad infamiam alicujus aut componere, & proinde est speciale, hoc est, non de omnibus sed de quibusdam tantum factis, cum prius sit de omnibus verbis. Tertium est de injuria servo facta quia ratio postulat, ut de injuria liberis facta prius agatur quam de facta servis. Sed cur prius est de injuria servo quam de injuria filiofam. facta agatur, cum tamen hic sit liber homo, ratio hæc est: quia hoc edictum de injuria filiofamil facta, quod est ultimum inter specialia est maxime speciale, nimirum de ea injuria, ex quaipsi filio datur actio. At de injuria ipsi filiofamil. facta, ex qua ipsi patri quoque datur actio prior a edicta, tam generale quam duo specialia intelliguntur. At edictum de injuria servo facta actionem parit ipsi domino. Ratio autem cur de injuriis inter delicta ultimo agatur expolita est ad Inst. Atque ita duo tantum delicta hoc in edicto fuere rapina & injuria, quia scilicet duo reliqua delicta furtum & damnum jam superius fuerint proposita, ubi de noxal. act. & leg. Aquil.
units.tr: The second was that concerning deeds, which was hardly necessary, since an action for injury done could be brought under the general edict; but certain special deeds are contained in this edict, such as wearing mourning, letting the beard grow long, composing a song to bring someone into infamy, and therefore it is special, that is, concerns only certain deeds and not all, whereas the earlier one concerns all words. The third is on injury done to a slave, because reason requires that injury done to free persons be treated before injury done to slaves. But why injury done to a slave is treated before injury done to a son under power, although the latter is a free man, the reason is this: this edict on injury done to a son under power, which is the last among the special ones, is most special, namely concerning that injury from which an action is given to the son himself. But the edict on injury done to the son under power itself, from which an action is also given to the father, is prior, and is understood as both general and two special ones. Yet the edict on injury done to a slave gives an action to the master himself. The reason why injuries are treated last among the delicts has been set out in the Institutes. And so only two delicts were in this edict, rapine and injury, because the other two delicts, theft and damage, had already been set out above, where we treated noxal actions and the lex Aquilia.

units.la: VIII. Pars Edicti Perpetui.
units.tr: VIII. The Part of the Perpetual Edict

units.la: Proximum in edicto locum tenuerunt edicta de missione in possessionem ad finem judiciorum pertinentia, quæ 10 fere reperio explicata ab Ulp. lib. 58. & 8. seqq. postquam de delictis explicaellet lib. 57. & duob. præced. à Paulo ib. 56. & 6. seqq. ad edictum, cum de delictis & injuriis explicasset lib. 55. & 3 prioribus. Ratio ordinis est perspicua, quia scilicet actionib. & edictis ad finem judiciorum pertinentibus ultimus locus jure debetur: quemadmodum primus datus ad initia judiciorum, ut de in jus voc. &c. pertinentibus.
units.tr: Next in the edict came the edicts concerning missio in possessionem, which belong to the end of the proceedings. I find about ten of these explained by Ulpian in book 58 and following, after he had dealt with delicts in book 57 and the two preceding books; Paul also treats them in book 56 and following on the edict, after he had dealt with delicts and injuries in book 55 and the three before it. The reason for this order is clear: edicts and actions that belong to the end of the proceedings rightly have the last place, just as the first place was given to those belonging to the beginning of the proceedings, such as those on summoning to court (in ius vocatio), and so on.

units.la: 2 Et primum quidem inter hæc edicta 10. ad finem judiciorum pertinentia locum tenuit edictum & actio judicialis in factum. l. 3. de re jud.
units.tr: 2. Among these ten edicts relating to the end of the proceedings, the first place was held by the edict and the judicial action in factum. D. 3, de re judicata.

units.la: 3 Huic proxima fuit clausula edicti de his qui condemnantur in id tantum quod facere possunt, non in solidum, cujus mentio fit int. 22. sed hoc ita, de re jud. & l. ult. Cod. de revoc. his quæ in fraud. cred (Cujac. lib. 1. 12. ob. c. 5. non viderat d. l. 22.) Nam & ea clausula huc pertinet ad sententiam & rem judicatam Ratio ordinis, cur hæc duo primum locum tenent: quia eorum primus est usus post sententiam ad exsequendum judicatum, & secundum videtur velut primi membrum. ideoque posterius.
units.tr: 3. Next to this came the clause of the edict concerning those who are condemned only to the extent of what they are able to pay, and not in full. It is mentioned in D. 22, but this should be read as "de re judicata", and in the last law of Cod. de revocandis his quae in fraudem creditorum (Cujacius, book 1 on the Twelve Tables, chapter 5, had not seen D. 22). For this clause also belongs to the sentence and the matter adjudged. The reason for the order, why these two hold the first place, is that the first of them is used after sentence to enforce the judgment, and the second seems to be a member of the first, and therefore comes after it.

units.la: 4 Jam si his primis edictis non pareat reus condemnatus, ad duriora remedia proceditur, hoc est, ad missionem in possessionem bonorum, ad bonorum venditionem. Itaque tertium hoc loco edictum fuit positum, quo creditor in possessionem bonorum debitoris iam condemnati ire jubetur, in quo tamen nominatim de debitore pupilli agitur, in cujus bona si non defendantur, creditores qui cum ipso pupillo contraxerint, ire jubentur. cujus edicti verba non extant, sed ejus mentio & sententia est in l. 3. 4. & 5. qu. b. ex causs. in possess.
units.tr: 4. Now if the condemned defendant does not obey these first edicts, recourse is had to harsher remedies, namely, missio in possessionem of the goods and the sale of the goods. Accordingly, the third edict in this place was that by which the creditor is ordered to go into possession of the goods of a debtor already condemned. In it, however, mention is made by name of the debtor's ward (pupillus), and if his goods are not defended, the creditors who contracted with the ward himself are ordered to go in. The words of this edict do not survive, but its mention and sense are found in D. 42.5.3, 4 and 5, quae bona, ex quibus causis in possessionem.

units.la: Fuit & edictum in edicto perpetuo de missione in possessionem non hic sed longè ante positum nempe ubi de principio judicii, sive de in jus vocando agitur, si scilicet reus in jus vocatus dederit fidejussorem sistendi, & postea non sistat neque defendatur: quod edictum supr. praetermissum, interjici debet nempe parte prima oeconomiae edicti perpetui ubi 4 edicta de in jus voc. sunt explicata cum sint 5. & hoc quintum esse videtur: quia scil. extremum remedium, & ideo ultimum inter edicta ab Ulpiano explicata lib. ad ed. Edum, in quo & hoc ultimum (inter ea edicta) de missione continetur, cujus verba extant l. 2. quib. ex causs. in poss. & c. quae est l. Ulp lib. 5. ad edictum. sed Trib. ut alias quoque solet edicta diversis locis edicti perpetui posita conjunxit sub eodem titulo, quia ejusdem sunt argumenti ad missionem scilicet pertinentia. Sed praetor quia edictum de missione generale posuit jam antea initio edicti ubi de in jus voc. actum, ut jam dictum, noluit in fine edicti idem edictum generale de missione inculcare, nisi cum aliquo additamento, aut potius speciali mentione de pupillo. Dixi verba edicti generalis de missione esse in l. 2. quib. ex causs. & c. quae exstat etiam apud Cic. in Quintiana, sed longe alia vel a Trib. mutata, vel ab ipsis praetoribus ut interdum ab ipsis factum esse indicat l. 1 Commod.
units.tr: There was also an edict in the perpetual edict on missio in possessionem, placed not here but far earlier, namely where the beginning of the proceedings, or the summoning to court, is treated: namely, if the defendant summoned to court has given a surety to appear, and afterwards does not appear nor defend himself. This edict, passed over above, must be inserted in the first part of the plan of the perpetual edict, where four edicts on summoning to court are explained, although there are five, and this is seen to be the fifth. For it is the final remedy, and therefore the last among the edicts explained by Ulpian in book 5 on the edict (ad Edictum), in which this last edict (among those) on missio is also contained, whose words survive in D. 42.4.2, quibus ex causis in possessionem, which is a law of Ulpian in book 5 on the edict. But Tribonian, as he often does elsewhere, joined edicts placed in different parts of the perpetual edict under one title, because they are of the same subject, namely concerning missio. But since the praetor had already placed the general edict on missio at the beginning of the edict, where summoning to court is treated, as has been said, he did not wish to repeat the same general edict at the end of the edict, except with some addition, or rather with a special mention of the ward. I have said that the words of the general edict on missio are in D. 42.4.2, quibus ex causis, which also survive in Cicero in Quintiana, but they were altered, either by Tribonian or by the praetors themselves, as the D. 1 Commod. indicates that was sometimes done by them.

units.la: Quartum edictum speciale de pupillo scil. fuit: sed in tertio creditor jubetur ire in possessionem bonorum pupilli: ita contra hoc jubetur decedere de possessione bonorum pupilli, & proinde est posterius. Ratio enim postulat, ut prius bona possideantur, posterius de possessis discedatur. Verba quarti exstant l. 5. 4. 1 praetor. qu. bus ex causs. in poss. earum. & c.
units.tr: The fourth edict was the special one on the ward: but in the third the creditor is ordered to go into possession of the ward's goods; here, on the contrary, he is ordered to withdraw from possession of the ward's goods, and so it comes later. For reason requires that the goods be taken into possession first, and afterwards that the creditors withdraw from what they have possessed. The words of the fourth survive in D. 42.5.4 and 1, quibus ex causis in possessionem earum, etc.

units.la: Quintum locum habebat edictum de bonis possidendis & vendendis. Videntur autem ad hoc argumentum de bonis possidendis & vendendis plures clausulae fuisse, una exstat l. 6. § 1. licet non tota: altera exstat. l. 7 § 1. qu. b. ex causs. in poss. item alia particula indicatur potius quam exponitur l. 1. § 1. in verb. sed contra sententiam de jure fisci. Ratio ordinis est, quia in missione in possessionem duo ponuntur a praetore decreta primum & secundum: primo jubetur ire in possessionem: secundo jubetur possidere & etiam vendere bona. plus est autem possidere quam esse in possessione.
units.tr: The fifth place was held by the edict on taking possession and selling the goods. There seem to have been several clauses on this subject of taking possession and selling the goods. One survives in D. 42.6.1, though not entire; another survives in D. 42.7.1, quibus ex causis in possessionem. Likewise another particle is indicated rather than set out, in D. 42.1.1, in the words "but against the opinion on the right of the treasury". The reason for the order is that in the missio in possessionem the praetor issued two decrees, the first and the second: first he orders them to go into possession; second, he orders them to possess and also to sell the goods. But to possess is more than to be in possession.

units.la: Hinc edicto de bonis possidendis & vendendis proximum edictum fuit edictum de jure delib. quod indicat l. 1. 3. & 7. de jur. delib. quae sunt ex Ulpia. lib. 60. quo libro edicta quaedam proxima de missione explicavit. Idem quoque indicat l. 2. de jur. delib. quae est Pauli ex lib. 55. quo idem explicavit edicta ad missionem pertinentia. Tribun. tamen hoc edictum de jure deliberandi longè alio in loco posuit inter tit de testamentis. Sed ordinis ratio hæc est: quia edicta de missione & venditione bonorum ad omnes creditores pertinent etiam hereditarios. His autem creditoribus hereditariis ne injuria fiat per diuturnam moram heredibus dubitantibus de adeunda hereditate, certum tempus præscriptiit ipsis prætor, intra quod hereditatem adire, & creditoribus satisfacere debeant aut eam repudiare, ut creditores postea in possessionem bonorum mittantur ipsisque venditione eorum satisfiat.
units.tr: Next after the edict on possessing and selling the goods came the edict on the right of deliberation, which is indicated by D. 28.8.1, 3 and 7, de iure deliberandi, which are from Ulpian's book 60, in which book he explained certain edicts next to those on missio. The same is also indicated by D. 28.8.2, de iure deliberandi, which is from Paul's book 55, in which he likewise explained the edicts pertaining to missio. Tribonian, however, placed this edict on the right of deliberation in a quite different place, among the titles on wills. But the reason for the order is this: the edicts on missio and on the sale of goods concern all creditors, including those of an inheritance. Lest injury be done to these inheritance creditors through a long delay by heirs who are hesitating about entering on the inheritance, the praetor prescribed a fixed time, within which the heirs ought either to enter the inheritance and satisfy the creditors, or to renounce it, so that the creditors may afterwards be sent into possession of the goods and be satisfied by their sale.

units.la: Hujus edicti sive tituli duæ clausulæ fuisse videntur, una generalis alteraspecialis de pupillis. Generalis verba exstant in l. 1. d. jur. delib. speciales clausulæ verba exstant l. 7. §. ait prætor. d. int. quæ ll. ut & l. 2. Ulp. sunt ex ejus libro 60 ad edictum quo libro, ut & prioribus & seqq. edicta de missionibus in possessionem bonorumque venditione explicavit.
units.tr: There seem to have been two clauses of this edict or title, one general and the other special, concerning wards. The words of the general clause survive in D. 28.8.1, de iure deliberandi; the words of the special clause survive in D. 38.15.7, "ait praetor", de interdictis. These laws, as also D. 2 of Ulpian, are from his book 60 on the edict, in which book, as in the earlier and later ones, he explained the edicts on missio in possessionem and on the sale of goods.

units.la: Cui edicto de jure deliberandi adjectum quoque fuit de jure abstinendi, quod suorum heredum est proprium. Extranei repudiare, sui abstinere dicuntur: extranei suo arbitratu & ipso jure hereditatem repudiare possunt: suis opus fuit auxilio prætoris: propterea quod ipso jure sunt heredes, sed prætor edicto fecit iis potestatem abstinendi. Ratio ordinis jam satis intelligitur, quia prius de jure deliberandi est de omnibus heredibus & generale: hoc est de suis & speciale: ideoque posterius. Utrumque autem est de heredibus ut hereditatem vel adeant vel repudient aut abstineant. Et illud quidem de jure delib. Ulp. libro 60, partim 61. ut l. 4. §. 8. d. tit. int. hoc lib 61. explicavit, ut leg. 20. 60. 66. & 71. quæ maximè eo facit de hered. acquir verba edicti de abstinendo non exstant, sed sententia est in lege 57 necessariis de acquir heredit. & d. l. 71. si ferum. §. ait prætor. ubi hæc adfertur, prætorem suis heredibus jus abstinendi non dedisse, si quid ex hereditate amoverint: Cujus exceptionis & clausulæ edicti verba exstant in d. §. prætor. sed Trib. hæc edicta de jure delib. & de jure abstin. non intermissionem in possessionem aut venditionem bonorum per creditores, ut in edicto perpetuo, sed in tractatu de testamentis posuit quæ re infra ad ff.
units.tr: To this edict on the right of deliberation was also added the edict on the right of abstention, which is peculiar to the heirs of the household (sui heredes). Strangers (extranei) are said to renounce, and the heirs of the household to abstain: strangers can renounce the inheritance at their own discretion and by the law itself; the sui heredes needed the help of the praetor, because they are heirs by law itself, but the praetor by edict gave them the power of abstaining. The reason for the order is already sufficiently clear: the right of deliberation comes first, as it concerns all heirs and is general; the right of abstention concerns the sui heredes and is special, and therefore comes later. Both, however, concern heirs, whether they enter upon the inheritance, renounce it or abstain from it. Ulpian explained the former, the right of deliberation, partly in book 60 and partly in book 61, as in D. 38.4.8 (under the title "int." (interdicts)); in this book 61 he explained it, as in D. 20, 60, 66 and 71, which especially bears on de acquirenda hereditate. The words of the edict on abstaining do not survive, but its sense is found in D. 57, "necessariis", de acquirenda hereditate, and in the said D. 71, "si ferum", §. "ait praetor", where it is stated that the praetor did not give the sui heredes the right to abstain if they had removed anything from the inheritance. The words of this exception and clause of the edict survive in the said §. "praetor". But Tribonian placed these edicts on the right of deliberation and on the right of abstention not in the sequence of missio in possessionem or of the sale of goods by creditors, as in the perpetual edict, but in the treatise on wills, as will be shown below in the Digest.

units.la: Huic autem edicto de jure abstinendi proximum fuit edictum de actione in factum quæ datur debitori cōtra creditorem in possessionem missum, ut creditor debitori jam parato soluere aut defendere possessionem restituat. Verba exstant l. 9. prætor ait, de reb. auct. jud. poss. quæ hæc est Ulpiani lib. 62. Nam liber 61. de jure delib. & abst. explicavit ut modo dictum.
units.tr: Next to this edict on the right of abstaining from an inheritance came the edict on the action in the factum that is given to a debtor against a creditor who has been put into possession, so that the creditor, once the debtor is ready to pay, restores either the payment or the possession. The words stand in l. 9, "the praetor says," de reb. auct. jud. poss. This is from Ulpian, book 62. For book 61 had explained the right of deliberating and abstaining, as I have just said.

units.la: Huic edicto proxima fuit clausula quædam de contractu, post fraudem, sive consilium fraudandi à debitore suscepțam, facto, cujus edicti verba exstant in lege 25. ait prætor. de reb. auct. jud. poss &c. de qua clausula valdè miror nullam ejus interpretationem vel adjungi statim, in dict. leg. 25 vel alibi exstare aut reperiri, contra morem Jurisconsultorum: quæ res suspicionem mihi adfert defectum & lacunam aliquam in ff. hic esse, quemadmodum &c al. as
units.tr: Next to this edict came a certain clause about a contract entered into after fraud, or after a plan to defraud made by the debtor, and the words of this edict stand in l. 25, "the praetor says," de reb. auct. jud. poss., etc. I am very surprised that no interpretation of this clause is attached straight away, or found anywhere, either in the said l. 25 or elsewhere, contrary to the custom of the jurists. This fact makes me suspect that there is a defect and some gap in the Digest here, as Cujas also detected and filled in other gaps in the Digest.

units.la: & alias lacunas ff.deprehendit & supplevit Cujac.ex lib Cæn λ.60.libr.3.obs. c.23. Nam sub eo tituloleg.7. vulgo est ult sed deest& leg.finis, & desunt legib.8.9 10.& 11. Ita ad finem tit.de interd.& releg.10.ll.desiderantur,quas idem restituit ex eodem libro 60 Cæn λ.ad l.121.de verbor.oblig.at.sic initium leg.1.de his qui not.inf. mihi mutilum videtur, aut certè italegendum: Prætorait: non ut vulgo, prætoris verba dicunt, quo modo nunquam Jurisconsulti loquuntur. Huic quoque rei argumento est, quod in ff aliis prætor Florentinos posthac l.25.ubi defectum esse videri, dixi novus ponitur titul. ita conceptus,de privilegiis creditorum. Et certè lex 26.& seqq. fere omnes, usquead proximum titulumde separat. sunt de privilegio maximè eo, quod τοῦτο ἐγγὺς dicitur hoc est privilegio creditorum. Ratio ordinis autem inter hoc edictum, & prius, est, quod prius est de danda actione, hoc est de deneganda.
units.tr: Cujas detected and supplied them from book 60 of his Caenas (Cæn λ.60.libr.3.obs. c.23.). For under that title the law 7 is commonly given as the last, but the final law is lacking, and laws 8, 9, 10 and 11 are missing. Likewise at the end of the title de interdictis et relegatis, ten laws are wanting, which he restored from the same book 60 of the Caenas, on l. 121 de verborum obligationibus. So the opening of l. 1 de his qui notantur infamia seems to me mutilated, or at least to be read: "The praetor says," not as commonly, "the words of the praetor say," which the jurists never use. Further evidence for this is that in the Digest, after the other praetorian edicts, a new title is placed, de privilegiis creditorum, following l. 25 of the Florentine text, where I said there seemed to be a defect. And certainly law 26 and the following, almost all down to the next title de separationibus, concern privilege, above all that which is called [τοῦτο ἐγγὺς], that is, the privilege of creditors. The order between this edict and the previous one is because the previous one concerns the granting of an action, that is, the refusing of one.

units.la: Quibus proxima fuit clausula edicti item de actione infactum, qua alienata in fraudem creditorum revocantur ejus verba extantin l.1.quæin fraud. cred.quæ lex ut & aliæ sub eodem titulo sunt sumptæ exlib.66. Ulpiani ad edictum,cum priores clausulæ de duabus actionibus sint ab Ulp.explicatæ partim 61 partim 63.& 64.
units.tr: Next to these came the clause of the edict, likewise on an action in the factum, by which alienations made to defraud creditors are revoked. Its words stand in l. 1 quae in fraudem creditorum, and this law, like the others under the same title, is taken from book 66 of Ulpian on the edict, since the earlier clauses on the two actions were explained by Ulpian partly in book 61 and partly in books 63 and 64.

units.la: An autem 64 aut 65 aliud aliquod edictum explicatum fuerit & propositum in edicto perpetuo ( ut edictum de privilegiis creditorum aut edictum separationibus ) nihil certi facile reperire potest. De privilegijs, non puto: propterea quod ea originem habent plerumque ex legibus & constitutionibus non ex edicto prætoris. leg.37.de reb.auct.jud.poss. (Reperi tamen mentionem edicti de priv.leg. leg.15.& mulieri, §.1.de curat. furiof.)
units.tr: But whether book 64 or 65 explained some other edict set out in the perpetual edict, such as the edict on the privileges of creditors or the edict on separations, one can hardly find anything certain. On privileges I do not think so, because these mostly derive their origin from laws and constitutions, not from an edict of the praetor (l. 37 de reb. auct. jud. poss.). Still, I have found a mention of an edict on privileges (l. 15, and mulieri §1 de curatoribus furiosi).

units.la: De separationibus sive de beneficio separationis (quod petisolet à prætore &concedi creditoribus certis de causis in vendendis bonis debitoris) justius dubitari poterit an edictum fuerit propterea quod hoc beneficium à prætore impetratur,& à JCtis hoc loco inter edicta de emptionibus & venditionibus bonorum explicatur.l.1.de separat.quæ est Ulp.lib.64. ad edictum, sed ut jam dixi,de separationibus nullius edicti,quod sciam fit mentio. Sed decreti tantumd.l.1. Differunt autem edicto aut decreto aliquid fieri: quemadmodū differt bonorū possessio edictalis à decretali.l.3.§.fi caus.de bon.poss.
units.tr: Concerning separations, or the benefit of separation (which was usually sought from the praetor and granted to certain creditors, for certain reasons, in the sale of a debtor's goods), it could be more reasonably doubted whether there was an edict. This benefit is obtained from the praetor, and jurists here explain it among the edicts on purchases and sales of goods, as in l. 1 de separationibus, which is Ulpian, book 64 on the edict. But, as I have already said, so far as I know, no edict on separations is mentioned, only a decree (decreti tantum, d. l. 1). Yet something done by edict differs from something done by decree, just as the edictal possession of goods differs from the decretal (l. 3 §fin. de bonorum possessione).

units.la: Videtur tamen aliud aliquod edictum hic fuisse,in edicto perpetuo, quod explicandum fuit ab Ulpian.lib.6t.& Paul.lib.6t. sed quod aut quale fuerit, non facile est explicatu.
units.tr: Nevertheless there seems to have been some other edict here in the perpetual edict, which had to be explained by Ulpian, book 6[1], and Paul, book 6[1], but what it was, or of what kind, is not easy to explain.

units.la: Ad proximum autem edictum de actione Pauliana,qua revocantur alienata in fraudem creditorum accommodavit Tribun edict fraudatorii,propter similitudinem argumenti: Conjunxit,inquam edictum & interdictum de fraude sub eodem titulo. Verba edicti suntin l.1.interdict.l.10.quæ in fraud. cred.sed in edicto perpetuo edictum fraudatorium alium locum habuit, lege remotiorem,ut infra dicetur.
units.tr: To the next edict, on the Pauline action by which alienations made to defraud creditors are revoked, the tribune attached the edict on fraudulent transfers, because of the similarity of the subject: I say he joined under one title the edict and the interdict on fraud. The words of the edict stand in l. 1 interdict, and l. 10 quae in fraudem creditorum. But in the perpetual edict the fraudulent edict had another place, more remote from the law, as will be said below.

units.la: Fuit olim quoddam edictum praetoris de praediatoribus, ad quod Cajus lib. scripsit, ut indicat inscriptio l. 54. res quae de jur. dot. & Cic. quoque praediatorum interdum ad Atticum facit mentionem, ut & Suetonius in Claudio meminit legis praediatoriae, & Valerius Maximus juris praediatorij. Dubitari potest, num hoc edictum de praediatoribus, cujus nulla in legibus juris est mentio amplius positum fuit ante edictum de actione Pauliana, quod praediatores a quibusdam putentur fuisse fidejussores, qui praediis & non tantum personis caverent, maximeReip sed nihil certi, ubi in edicto perpetuo hic titulus de praediatoribus fuerit collocatus. Atque haec de edictis ad finem judiciorum sive actionem, ut sententiam, missionem, &c. pertinentibus.
units.tr: There was once a certain edict of the praetor concerning praediatores, on which Gaius wrote a book, as the inscription of l. 54 res quae de jure dotium indicates. Cicero also sometimes makes mention of praediatores in his letters to Atticus, as Suetonius in Claudius remembers the praediatorian law and Valerius Maximus the praediatorian law. It may be doubted whether this edict on praediatores, of which no mention remains in the legal texts, was put in place before the edict on the Pauline action. Some think the praediatores were sureties who gave security by means of estates and not merely by persons, but nothing is certain about where this title on praediatores was placed in the perpetual edict. And these are the things to be said about the edicts that pertain to the end of trials, or to the action, such as the sentence, the missio in possessionem, and so on.

units.la: IX. Pars edicti perpetui.
units.tr: IX. Part of the Perpetual Edict.

units.la: RESTANT quatuor capita edicti perpetui, interdicta pignora, exceptiones, & stipulationes praetoriae. Et interdicta quidem proxima edictis ad finem judiciorum pertinentibus locum obtinebant, ut videre est in lib Ulp. 67. quo coepit edicta de interdictis explicare, eaqj persequitur lib. 68. & 4. seqq. cum lib. 66. ultimum edictum de actione Pauliana ad finem judiciorum pertinens explicasset. Ratio ordinis cur actionibus sive judiciis proximum locum teneant interdicta, est quia proprie quidem interdicta differunt ab actionibus, ideoque & distinctum ab iis locum habent, ut dictum supra ad tit. de act. & ad tit. de interdictis infra. magnam tamen cum actionibus similitudinem habent, adeo ut interdicta interdum actionis quoque verbo continentur, maxime hodie cum sublatis formulis interdictorum dantur actiones eorum loco. §. ult. inst. de interdictis. Hoc quoq; ad ordinis rationem pertinet.
units.tr: Four heads of the Perpetual Edict remain: interdicts, pledges, exceptions, and praetorian stipulations. The interdicts, being closest to the edicts that concern the close of trials, held the place next after them, as may be seen in book 67 of Ulpian, where he began to explain the edicts on interdicts, and which he pursues in book 68 and following, after he had explained in book 66 the last edict, on the Pauline action, which concerns the close of trials. The reason for this order, that interdicts hold the place nearest to actions or trials, is that interdicts, strictly speaking, differ from actions and therefore have a place distinct from them, as was said above under the title on actions, and will be said below under the title on interdicts. Yet they bear a great resemblance to actions, so much so that interdicts are sometimes included even under the word action, especially today, since the forms of interdicts have been abolished and actions are granted in their place, § last, Institutes, on interdicts. This also belongs to the reason for the order.

units.la: Hanc ordinis rationem postea edidit & Donell. in comment. ad tit. C. de interdictis. prius inquit compositores de actionibus & ijs juribus quae ad actionem pertinent: idque hactenus: deinde de interdictis tam in C. quam in ff. item in Inst quod interdicta sit potissimum de possessione, & pauca de proprietate l. 2. 6. quidam. de interdictis leg. 14. an & eadem. de except. res jud. Proxime aut expolita sunt edictade missione in possessionem, ideoque ijs recte proxime adjunguntur interdicta; quae vulgo judicia possessoria dicuntur.
units.tr: Donellus also set out this same reason for the order, in his commentary on the title On interdicts in the Code. He says that first the compilers dealt with actions and the rights that pertain to actions, and so far so good; then with interdicts, both in the Code and in the Digest, and likewise in the Institutes, because interdicts concern chiefly possession, and only a little ownership, l. 2 and 6, "quidam," On interdicts; l. 14, "an et eadem," On exceptions, res judicata. Next after these were set out the edicts on the granting of possession, and so the interdicts are rightly joined next to them; these are commonly called possessory judgments.

units.la: Cum autem plurima sint interdicta, diligenter ordo & ratio eorum intelligi debet. Et primum quidem observandum interdicta omnia competere vel hominum causa vel divini juris vel de religione: Et quae hominum causa competunt competere vel rei familiaris aut publicae utilitatis tuendae causa, aut officii tuendi causa aut juris sui l. 2. §. 1. de interdictis: Vel breviùs: Interdicta vel rerum esse, vel personarum.
units.tr: Since there are very many interdicts, their order and reason must be carefully understood. And first it must be noted that all interdicts are granted either for the sake of persons, or for the sake of divine law, or on account of religion; and those granted for the sake of persons are granted either to protect the public or private interest, or to protect a duty, or one's own right, l. 2 § 1, On interdicts. Or, more briefly: interdicts concern either things or persons.

units.la: Et primum quidem agi de interdictis rerum: postea de interdictis perfonarum hac ratione quia res proprie possidentur. personæ liberæ nō item. Interdicta possessionum causa potissimum sunt à prætore introducta, ut modo dictum. Vt autem actiones aliæ sunt generales sive universales, aliæ sunt speciales: & generales in edicto priorem locum, speciales posteriorem obtinent ut supra dictum initio ordinis edicti perpetui, ita & interdicta quædam sunt universalia, sive ad universitatem, ut bonorum possessionem pertinentia alia sunt specialia, sive ad singulares personas pertinentia: & illa sint priora, hæc posteriora.
units.tr: First we treat of interdicts concerning things, and afterwards of those concerning persons, for this reason: things are properly possessed, free persons are not. Interdicts were introduced by the praetor chiefly for the sake of possession, as has just been said. And just as some actions are general or universal and others special, and in the edict the general ones hold the first place and the special ones the later place, as was said above at the beginning of the order of the Perpetual Edict, so too some interdicts are universal, that is, relating to the whole estate, as those concerning possession of goods, while others are special, relating to particular persons; the former come first, the latter after.

units.la: Ergo primum in edicto locum renuit edictum quorum bonorum, ut indicat l.1. ff. quor. bon. quæ est Ulp. ex lib. 67. quocœpit explicare interdicta. Ratio ordinis jam expositá quia hoc interdictum & universale, sive ut ait Ulp. m d.l.1. ad universitatem bonorum, non adres singulas pertinet.
units.tr: Therefore the edict on the goods of persons (quorum bonorum) rightly holds the first place in the edict, as l. 1 ff., quorum bonorum shows, which is from Ulpian, from book 67, where he began to explain the interdicts. The reason for the order has already been set out: because this interdict is universal, or, as Ulpian says in the law just cited, it relates to the whole of the goods, not to single things.

units.la: II. Interdictum est, quod legatorum, ut indicat l.1. quæ lex sumpta ex eod lib. 67. Ratio ordinis; quia legata etsi rerum sunt singularium, tamen ad testamenta, quibus relinquuntur pertinent, quib testamentis universitas hereditas relinquitur f. nlt. quib. alien. hic & c. verba edicti quorum bonorum exstant l.1. quor. bon. verba edicti quod legatorum, non omnia exstant, sed quædam tantum. leg.1. §.7. quod ait. & §.12. quod ait, leg.2. §.1. quod legat.
units.tr: II. There is the interdict concerning legacies (quod legatorum), as l. 1, "quae lex" shows, taken from the same book 67. The reason for the order is this: although legacies concern single things, yet they pertain to the wills by which they are left, and by those wills an entire inheritance is left, last law, By which persons are alienated. The words of the edict on the goods (quorum bonorum) are extant in l. 1, quorum bonorum; the words of the edict quod legatorum are not all extant, but only some, l. 1 § 7 and § 12, "quod ait," l. 2 § 1, "quod legat."

units.la: Tertium interdictum est de tabulis exhibendis, quod proximè lib. 68. explicavit Ulp. l.1. & 3. de tab. exhib. Ratio ordinis est quia & hoc ad universitatem, sive testamenti tabulas pertinet Cur autem hoc interdictum de tabulis, & interdictum quod legatorum posteriora sint interdicto quorum bonorum. Ratio est, quia hæc duo pertinent ad hereditatem potissimum, illud, quorum bonorum ad bonorum possessionem. Ac bonorum possessio priorem in edicto locum habuit. Ratio expositá est supra. Et hæc sunt tria interdicta generalia.
units.tr: The third interdict is that concerning the production of tablets (de tabulis exhibendis), which Ulpian explained next, in book 68, l. 1 and 3, On the production of tablets. The reason for the order is that this too concerns the whole estate, or the tablets of a will. Why, however, this interdict on tablets, and the interdict quod legatorum, come after the interdict quorum bonorum, is as follows: these two concern chiefly the inheritance, while the first concerns possession of goods. And possession of goods held the earlier place in the edict. The reason has been set out above. These are the three general interdicts.

units.la: His proxima sunt specialia quæ partim sunt rerum, partim personarum, cum universalia tantum sint rerum. Res autem aliæ sunt divinæ; aut religiosæ, aliæ sunt humanæ l.1. §.1. de interdictis & divinæ ac religiosa ordine sunt, priora ratio est perspicua, propter dignitatem rei ut religiosæ.
units.tr: Next to these are the special interdicts, some concerning things and some persons, since only the universal ones concern things. Things are either divine or religious, or else human; and the divine and religious come in that order, the first reason being plain, namely the dignity of a thing as religious.

units.la: Primum igitur inter specialia interdicta locum obtinet interdictum, ne quid in loco sacro, quod Ulpianus eodem lib. 68. explicavit. Verba ejus exstant in l.1 ff. ne quid in loco sacro.
units.tr: First, then, among the special interdicts comes the interdict ne quid in loco sacro (that nothing be done in a sacred place), which Ulpian explained in the same book 68. Its words are extant in l. 1 ff., ne quid in loco sacro.

units.la: Huic proximo fuêre de religione i unum de mortuo inferendo, alterum de sepulchro ædificando quæ duo interdicta fuerunt in edicto posita hoc in loco, ut indicat inscriptio l.1. de mort. infer. quæ lex est Ulpiani ex libr. 68. ad edictum & in qua continentur & explicantur horum interdictorum verba. Ratio ordinis est: quia res sacræ primum, religiosæ secundum locum tenent §. nullius infra de re divisi. Quare & hoc interdictum de rebus sacris primum locum: interdicta de rebus religiosis, secundum locum obtinuerunt in edicto perpetuo, sed Tribun. hæc interdicta de religione adjunxit proximè ad tit. de relig. & sumpt. fun. Inter edicta 1. de religione prius est de mortuo inferendo, quia prius inferendus est mortuus, quam sepulchrum superimponatur & exstruatur.
units.tr: Next to this came two interdicts concerning religion: one on bringing in a dead body (de mortuo inferendo), the other on building a tomb (de sepulchro aedificando). These two interdicts stood in the edict in this place, as the heading shows, l. 1, On bringing in the dead, which is a law of Ulpian from book 68 on the edict, and in which the words of these interdicts are contained and explained. The reason for the order is that sacred things hold the first place and religious things the second, § nullius, Institutes, On the division of things. Therefore this interdict on sacred things holds the first place, and the interdicts on religious things the second place, in the Perpetual Edict; but Tribonian joined these interdicts on religion next to the title On religion and funeral expenses. Among the edicts on religion, that on bringing in the dead comes first, because the dead must be brought in before a tomb is laid over and built.

units.la: His proxima sunt interdicta humana, sive hominum causa proposita, & primum quidem publica, postea vero privata. Ratio ordinis per se nota est.
units.tr: Next to these are the human interdicts, that is, those proposed for the sake of men; first the public ones, and afterwards the private. The reason for this order is evident in itself.

units.la: Inter publica igitur primum locum tenet interdictum, ne quid in loco publico, &c. fiat quod de religione duobus fuit proximum edicto perpetuo omnia namque ea Ulp. lib. 68. explicavit verba edicti exstant in l. 2. ne quid in loco pub. Ratio ordinis cur hoc inter publica fit primum, hæc est: quia est generale de omni loco publico, & de omni eo; quidquid factum fuerit ex quo damnum aliquod detur publice vel privatim.
units.tr: Among the public interdicts, therefore, the first place is held by the interdict ne quid in loco publico, etc. (that nothing be done in a public place), which came next after those on religion in the Perpetual Edict; Ulpian explained all of them in book 68, and the words of the edict are extant in l. 2, ne quid in loco publico. The reason why this one comes first among the public interdicts is this: it is general, concerning every public place and everything done in it from which any damage is caused, publicly or privately.

units.la: Huic proximè fuerunt quinq; interdicta de via & itinere publico. I. Ne quid in via aut itinere publico fiat, quod ab Ulp statim post generale explicatum fuit, ut indicat l. 2. §. aut prætor. 12. ne quid in loco publ. verba exstant in d. aut prætor.
units.tr: Next to this came five interdicts concerning a public way and road. I. Ne quid in via aut itinere publico fiat (that nothing be done on a public way or road), which Ulpian explained immediately after the general one, as l. 2 § aut praetor, 12, ne quid in loco publico shows; the words are extant in the said § aut praetor.

units.la: II. De itinere, est de eo, quod in itinere publico factum fuit, restituendo, quod inferius sive posterius fuit, ut indicat Ulp. d. l. 22 § aut prætor. d. tit. ubi & verba exstant. Ratio ordinis inter hæc duo, est quia illud cavet damno nondum facto, hoc restituit jam factum opus in via publica aut aliud quid itineri impediendo.
units.tr: II. The interdict concerning a road (de itinere) is that concerning the restoration of what was done on a public road, which came below, or later, as Ulpian shows, the said l. 2 § aut praetor, On the same title, where the words are also extant. The reason for the order between these two is that the former guards against damage not yet done, while the latter restores a work already done on a public road, or some other obstruction to passage.

units.la: III. De itinere est, ne vis fiat, volenti itinere publico uti, sive brevius ut via publica utiliceat, quod quia ad vim & delictum pertinet, illis duobus est posterius, verba ejus exstant in d. l. 2. §. ult. ne quid in loco publico.
units.tr: III. The interdict concerning a road is that ne vis fiat, that no force be used against one who wishes to use a public road, or, more briefly, that a public road may be used freely; because it concerns force and wrong, it comes after those two, its words being extant in the said l. 2 § last, ne quid in loco publico.

units.la: Proximum huic fuit interdictum de loco publico. Ratio ordinis est quia ut prius fuit de utendo, ita hoc est de fruendo, itaque propter similitudinem argumenti dicens, hos poni debuisse ante interdicta de itinere (statim post generale de loco publico: quia & hoc est de loco publico, sed quia illud est maximè speciale (non enim omnibus datur, sed publicanis tantum, qui vectigalia, & loca quædam publica conducunt) & quia frui & uti sunt similia, recte in posteriorem locum fuit rejectum, & priori propter similitudinem conjunctum.
units.tr: The interdict concerning a public place came next after these. The reason for the order is that, as the interdict on using came first, so this one concerns enjoying; therefore, because of the similarity of subject, it ought to have been placed before the interdicts on the road, immediately after the general one on a public place, since this too concerns a public place. But because that one is highly special (for it is granted not to all, but only to the tax-farmers, who lease the taxes and certain public places), and because to enjoy and to use are similar, it was rightly moved to a later place, and joined to the earlier one because of the similarity.

units.la: Huic adjunctum fuit de via publica, sive itinere reficiendo, quod est quarum ad viam publicam pertinens. Nam propter similitudinem interjectum fuit de loco publico fruendo. Cur hoc fuit ultimum de itinere; ratio hæc est: quia priora pertinent ad iter quo utiliceat quoq; jam utamur: hoc pertinet ad iter, quo ut corrupto non liceat uti, & quod correctione opus habeat: priora sunt de recte factò itinere, hoc de reficiendo: refectio est posterior. Verba ejus exstant, in l. 1. de via publ.
units.tr: To this was attached the interdict concerning the public way, or the repair of the road, which pertains to the matters belonging to the public road. Because of their similarity, the interdict concerning the enjoyment of a public place was placed next to it. Why this was the last of the interdicts concerning roads, the reason is this: the earlier ones concern a road that is still usable and that we are now using; this one concerns a road which, if it has been damaged, cannot be used and needs correction. The earlier ones concern a road properly built, this one concerns its repair, and repair comes later. Its words are found in l. 1, de via publica.

units.la: His de itinere, proxima fuerunt interdicta de fluminibus publicis: Ratio ordinis est quia ut urbana rusticis, ita terrestria aquaticis praeferuntur. Sunt autem 6. I. Ne quid in flumine publico aut ripa fiat.
units.tr: After the interdicts concerning roads, the next were the interdicts concerning public rivers. The reason for this order is that, as urban matters are preferred to rural ones, so land matters are preferred to water matters. There are six. (1) That nothing be done in a public river or on its bank.

units.la: II. De eo quod in fluminē factum fuerit restituendo. Haec duo primum locum hic obtinēt, quia fuut generalia. Hoc autem cur posterius, illud prius? Ratio haec est: quia illud est de nondum facto sive ante factum hoc est de jam facto sive post factum succurrit & corrigit. Verba illius exstant, in l. 1. §. 15 deinde, 19, hoc tit. de fluminib.
units.tr: (2) Concerning the restoration of what has been done in a river. These two hold the first place here, because they are general. But why is this one later and that one earlier? The reason is this: the first concerns what is not yet done, or before the deed; the second concerns what is already done, or after the deed, and it gives help and corrects. Its words are found in l. 1, §§ 15, 19 (deinde), of this title, de fluminibus.

units.la: His adjunguntur quatuor speciália. Nam priora de quolibet facto aut impedimento, haec de specialibus factis agunt. Ex quibus primum est ne quid in flumine publico fiat quo aliter aqua fluat, atque priore aestate fluxit, quo prohibetur non omne factum, sed illud tantum quo fluxus in peditur, ut est derivatio fluminis, & mutatio cursus aquae. Verba ejus exstant, in l. 1. ne quid in flum. publ.
units.tr: To these are added four specific interdicts. For the earlier ones deal with any deed or obstruction whatever, while these deal with specific deeds. The first of these is: that nothing be done in a public river by which the water flows otherwise than it flowed the previous summer. It prohibits not every deed, but only that by which the flow is hindered, such as the diversion of a river or the alteration of the course of the water. Its words are found in l. 1, ne quid in flumine publico.

units.la: Cui adjunctum fuit interdictum de eo, quod in flumine factum, quo aliter aqua flueret restituendo, quod est posterius, quia illud est de nondum facto, hoc est de jam facto, verba ejus exstant, in d. l. 1. §. 11.
units.tr: To this was attached the interdict concerning what has been done in a river, for restoring the flow of water otherwise. It comes later, because the one concerns what is not yet done, and this what is already done. Its words are found in the said l. 1, § 11.

units.la: Huic proximum est, ut in flumine publico navigare liceat. Ratio ordinis est, quia hoc ad specialem usum, nimirum navigationem pertinet, & quia ad vim & delictum pertinet, ideoq; est posterius. Verba ejus exstant in leg. 1. hoc tit. nl. 14.
units.tr: Next to this is the interdict that it be lawful to navigate a public river. The reason for the order is that this concerns a special use, namely navigation, and because it concerns violence and wrong, it therefore comes later. Its words are found in l. 1 of this title, nn. 14.

units.la: Ultimum de fluminibus interdictum est de ripa munienda. Ratio ordinis 21 eadem est quae de via reficienda, supra jam exposita. Verba ejus exstant, in l. 1. hoc tit. nl. Et haec de interdictis ad publicam utilitatem pertinentibus.
units.tr: The last interdict concerning rivers is that concerning the fortifying of the bank. The reason for the order is the same as that for repairing the road, already explained above. Its words are found in l. 1 of this title. And these are the interdicts pertaining to public utility.

units.la: Fit mentio interdicti ut via publica uti liceat. l. 2. §. 1. vers. publ. de interd. 22 Sed hoc est idem quod expositum de via publica, & itinere publico reficiendo. Fit ibidem & mentio interdicti, ut flumine publico uti liceat, sed hoc quoque est idem, quod modo expositum de ripa muniēda. Fuit & edictum de retandis fluminibus, cujus mentionem facit Agell. lib. 1. cap. 17. Sed hoc aut primo aut secundo de fluminibus generalibus supra expositis, optime continetur.
units.tr: Mention is made of the interdict that it be lawful to use a public road (l. 2, § 1, vers. publicam, de interdictis). But this is the same as what was explained concerning the public road and the repair of the public road. In the same place there is also mention of the interdict that it be lawful to use a public river, but this too is the same as what was just explained concerning the fortifying of the bank. There was also an edict concerning the restraining of rivers, which Gellius mentions in book 1, chapter 17. But this is best covered under the first or second of the general interdicts concerning rivers explained above.

units.la: Post sacra igitur & publica restant privata, quae partim sunt rerum 23 partim personarum specialia ut & supra dictum. Eorum igitur, qui rei familiaris tuendae causa sunt proposita primum locum in edicto perpetuo temunt interdictum. Unde vi, ut videre licet apud Ulpianum, qui priora, sacra & publica explicavit libro 68. Hoc autem libro 69. una cum interdicto uti possidetis, leg. 1. & 3. de vi & vi armat. leg. 1. & 3. uti possid. Sed unde vi est duplex, unum quod quotidianum: quia fit sive armis, alterum de vi armata, quae fit coactis, armatisque hominibus utriusque edicti de vi verba adfert Cicero pro Cecin. Sed in Digest. tantum unius edicti verba adferuntur, l. 1. de vi & vi arm. Puto enim hodie tantum unum interdictum
units.tr: After the sacred and public matters, therefore, the private ones remain, which are partly special to things and partly to persons, as was said above. Among those proposed for the protection of family property, the interdict unde vi holds the first place in the Perpetual Edict, as may be seen from Ulpian, who explained the earlier, sacred and public matters in book 68, and here in book 69 together with the interdict uti possidetis (Digest 1 and 3, de vi et vi armata; 1 and 3, uti possidetis). But unde vi is twofold: one is daily (quotidiana), which is done without arms, and the other is de vi armata, which is done by men gathered and armed. Cicero, in Pro Caecina, gives the words of both edicts concerning violence. But in the Digest only the words of one edict are given (l. 1, de vi et vi armata). For I think that today there is only one interdict, under a common name: unde vi.

units.la: V esse, communi nomine: unde vi Paulus tamen l.2 §. hæc autem, verf. recuperante ait sub rubrica, unde vi, aliquo interdicto esse, quæ videtur de vi quotidiana, & vi armata intelligenda, ut & Cujacius interpretatur ad Paulum lib.5. sententiarum, tit. de interdictis.
units.tr: Paulus, however, in l. 2, § hæc autem, verb. recuperante, says under the rubric unde vi that there is a certain interdict, which seems to be understood as referring both to daily violence and to armed violence. Cujacius also interprets it so in his commentary on Paulus, Sentences, book 5, title de interdictis.

units.la: Huic edicto de vi duplici quotidiana & armata. proximum in edicto locum tenuit interdictum uti possidetis, quem ordinem Ulpianus exponit, in l.1. §. Siligitur, uti possidetis. Ubi post interdictum unde vi ait propositum, consequenter interdictum uti possidetis Ratio ordinis ibidem exposita est: quia illud unde vi restituit possessionem, at hoc uti possidetis, tuetur illam, ne amittatur. Sed hæc ratio contrarium ordinem potius postulare videtur. Nondum enim facta præferuntur factis, ut uti possidetis est ante, unde vi est post amissam possessionem. Quare hæc potius ordin s ratio esse videtur: tum quia interdictum unde vi partim continet publicam causam, propter vim tam privatam quàm publicam adhibitam, tum quia gravitas hujus delicti postulat ut ejus prima & potissima cura habeatur, & statim primoque tempore succurratur: ideoque primo loco ponit prætor ut ostenderet, maximè sibi esse curæ. Verba autem interdicti, uti possidetis, extant in leg. 1. ff. uti possideat.
units.tr: Next in the edict after this edict concerning double violence, daily and armed, the interdict uti possidetis held the place. Ulpian sets out this order in l. 1, § Igitur, uti possidetis, where, after the interdict unde vi, he says it was proposed, and consequently the interdict uti possidetis. The reason for the order is explained there: the unde vi restores possession, but uti possidetis protects it, lest it be lost. Yet this reason seems rather to demand the opposite order, for things not yet done are preferred to things already done, and uti possidetis comes before, while unde vi comes after possession has been lost. Therefore this seems rather to be the true reason for the order: first, because the interdict unde vi partly contains a public cause, on account of the violence used, both private and public; second, because the gravity of this wrong requires that its first and chief care be taken, and that help be given at once and at the earliest moment. Therefore the praetor placed it first, to show that it was his greatest concern. The words of the interdict uti possidetis are found in l. 1, ff. uti possideat.

units.la: Huic adjungitur interdictum de superficiebus. Ratio est, quia illud, uti possidetis, est de ædibus ipsis, quo nomine hic omnes res soli continentur, sive res immobiles & corporales cum superficies tantum sit pars ædium ut utile interdictum uti possidetis, cujus nomine competat, non verè directum, l.1. §. præponitur, de superficiebus. Verba ejus extant in ædes. ff. eod.
units.tr: To this is joined the interdict concerning superficies. The reason is that the former, uti possidetis, concerns the buildings themselves, under which name all things attached to the soil are here included, whether immovable and corporeal, since superficies is only a part of a building. The interdict uti possidetis, in whose name it is available, is not truly direct but useful; see l. 1, § praeponitur, de superficiebus. Its words are found in aedes, ff. eod.

units.la: Proximum est huic interdictum de itinere actuq; privato. Ratio ordinis est quod primum de rebus corporalibus deinde de incorporalibus agatur quemadmodum & supra de publicis interdictis primum de locis, deinde de itinere, & fluminib. publicis &c. Ita & hic de itinere & primum quidam de itinere deinde de aqua, ut & supra de publicis, primum de via, postea de fluminibus publicis. Ratio ibi exposita est.
units.tr: Next to this is the interdict concerning a private road and private driving. The reason for the order is that first corporeal things are treated and then incorporeal ones, just as above, among the public interdicts, first concerning places, then concerning roads and public rivers, and so on. So here too, first concerning the road and then concerning water, just as above among the public ones, first concerning the public road and afterwards concerning public rivers. The reason was explained there.

units.la: De itinere autem & actu privato duo sunt interdicta, unum de non impediendo usu itineris vel actus cujus verba extant l.1. de itin. act. priv. Alterum est de itinere reficiendo, cujus verba extant in l.3. §. ait prætor. d. tit. Ratio ordinis inter hæc duo est, tum quia refectio semper posterior est corrupto scilicet itinere usus est prior hoc est; statim ab initio itineris constituti, tum illud est generalis quia omnes eo uti possunt, qui hoc anno sunt usi, hic autem is demum potest uti, qui & usus est hoc anno, & jus sibi esse reficiendi necessario contendat l.3 §. 11.
units.tr: Concerning the road and private driving there are two interdicts. One, on not hindering the use of a road or of driving, whose words are found in l. 1, de itinere actuque privato. The other concerns repairing a road, whose words are found in l. 3, § ait praetor, of the same title. The reason for the order between these two is, first, that repair always comes later, namely when the road has been damaged, whereas use comes earlier, that is, from the moment the road was established. Second, the one is general, because all who have used the road this year may use it, whereas this one can be used only by a man who both has used it this year and necessarily contends that he has the right to repair it (l. 3, § 11).

units.la: Hic autem & interdictum de itinere privato commemoratur, in leg. 2. de interdictis. Hic verbis, quo itinere venditur usus, quominus emptor utatur vim fieri veto, quod his adjectum fuit, quia speciale tantum de emptore hodie non extat in Digest. eo in loco, quo interdicta de itinere explicantur: Credo, quod Tribunian. satis esse putavit generale interdictum de itinere, quo omnes uti possunt, qui hoc anno sunt usi, ut modo dictum.
units.tr: Here the interdict concerning a private road is also mentioned, in l. 2, de interdictis. Here are the words: "by which road the use is sold, so that the buyer may not use it, I forbid force to be used." These were added here because the special interdict concerning the buyer does not today appear in the Digest in the place where the interdicts concerning roads are explained. I believe Tribonian thought the general interdict concerning the road, which all may use who have used it this year, to be enough, as has just been said.

units.la: Nunc de aqua de qua tria sunt interdicta quam vis & alia tria eodem pertinent. I est de aqua quotidiana cujus verba exstant, l.i.ff.de aqua quotidiana. II. de aqua æstiva, cujus verba exstant in d.leg.i. §.29.deinde ait prætor. III est de aqua ex castello ducenda, ejus verba exstant item in d.l.g.i.f.38. ait prætor. Ratio ordinis, cur hoc de aqua ex castella ducenda sit ultimum, est hæc: quia duo priora sunt de aqua ex capite, hoc est, de castello d. §38. verfic. hoc interdictum. At ex capite, hoc est, ex eo, unde aqua nascitur, sive fonte, sive flumine, sive lacu ducere aquam, longe est præstantius, & magis perpetuum, quam ducere ex castello, hoc est, ex receptaculo aliquo publico, aut ex rivo aquæ publicæ: deinde quia hoc est rarum (non nisi a Principe permittitur, d.l.i. f.41.permittitur.) Illud est frequentius. Quod autem ad illa duo, de aqua ex capite attinet, cur de aqua quotidiana sit prius de aqua æstiva posterius, ratio est perspicua, quia illa sit præstantior, quam æstiva: eo quod quotidiana duci potest continuo & semper: æstiva tantum æstate, d.l.i. §.quod autem.& §.22.& 25.
units.tr: Now concerning water, there are three interdicts, although six others also pertain to it. The first concerns daily water, whose wording is found in l.i.ff.de aqua quotidiana. The second concerns summer water, whose wording is found in d.leg.i. §.29.deinde ait prætor. The third concerns water to be led from a castellum, whose wording is likewise found in d.l.g.i.f.38. ait prætor. The reason this interdict on water led from a castellum comes last is this: the two earlier ones concern water from the head, that is, from the castellum d. §38. verfic. hoc interdictum. But leading water from its head, that is, from the place where it rises, whether a spring, a river or a lake, is far more excellent and more lasting than leading it from a castellum, that is, from some public reservoir or from a channel of public water. Moreover, this latter is rare (it is granted only by the Prince, d.l.i. f.41.permittitur.), whereas the former is more frequent. As for the two earlier interdicts concerning water from the head, the reason why the one on daily water comes before the one on summer water is clear: the former is more excellent than the latter, because daily water can be led continually and always, whereas summer water only in summer d.l.i. §.quod autem.& §.22.& 25.

units.la: His de aqua adjunctum fuit interdictum de rivis: Ejus verba exstant in l.i.de rivis. Ratio ordinis quia hoc pertinet ad refectionem rivorum, per quos ducitur aqua: priora sunt de nsu aquæ.
units.tr: To these interdicts on water is added the interdict on channels. Its wording is found in l.i.de rivis. The reason for this order is that it concerns the repair of the channels through which the water is led; the earlier ones concern the use of the water.

units.la: Postea quatuor illis de aqua, adjungitur duo de fonte prius de usu fontis cujus verba exstant initio d.l.i.§.deinde ag r.6. Alterum de refectione. Usus & refectionis differentia rationem ordinis indicat.
units.tr: After those four interdicts on water, two interdicts on a spring are added: first, the one on the use of the spring, whose wording stands at the beginning of d.l.i.§.deinde ag r.6.; second, the one on its repair. The difference between use and repair indicates the reason for the order.

units.la: His duobus de fonte interdictis utendo & reficiendo adjunguntur duo de cloacis, prius de privatis, cujus verba in l.i.de cloac. alterum de publicis, cujus verba in d.l.i §.8.deinde aut. Ratio ordinis est propter sordes ut ultimum & postremum locum hæc obtineat: & priorem illud quidem de privatis, quia & interdicta priora proxima sunt privata: Nam de publicis cloacis tantum, adjungitur propter similitudinem.
units.tr: To these two interdicts on a spring, concerning use and repair, are added two concerning sewers: first, the one on private sewers, whose wording is in l.i.de cloac.; second, the one on public sewers, whose wording is in d.l.i §.8.deinde aut. The reason for the order is that, on account of their filth, this matter holds the last and final place. The first is the one on private sewers, because the earlier interdicts are also closest to private matters; the one on public sewers is added only on account of its similarity.

units.la: Proximum est interdictum, quod vi aut clam. Ratio ordinis est quod enim priora interdicta sint de justa possessione sive denturijs qui in jure suo justaque possessione impediuntur: Proximum nunc fuit, ut de injustis possessionibus agatur, quæ sunt tria, Violenta, Clandestina, & Precaria. Et duæ quidem priores conjunguntur, atque a precaria distinguuntur, propterea quod precaria etiam aliquo modo inter justas possessiones nominatur. licet non eam vim habeat hæc possessio, quam alia justa possessio. Verba hujus edicti, quod vi aut clam. exstant in d.l.i.quod vi aut clam. Potest & hæc ratio ordinis reddi quod cum priora interdicta a titulo, unde vi, ubi initium est interdictorum privatorum, sint omnia contra vim, & species aliquot factorum ij jam sunt expositæ; Jam tandem generale edictum subjungitur, quia
units.tr: The next is the interdict quod vi aut clam. The reason for the order is this: the earlier interdicts concern just possession, or the rights of those who are hindered in their own right and in lawful possession. It was next in order that unjust possessions be treated, which are three: violent, clandestine and precarious. The first two are joined together and are distinguished from the precarious, because precarious possession is also in some way counted among just possessions, although this possession does not have the force that other just possession has. The words of this edict, quod vi aut clam., are found in d.l.i.quod vi aut clam. This order can also be explained thus: since the earlier interdicts from the title unde vi, which is the beginning of the private interdicts, are all against force, and several species of such acts have now been set out, the general edict is at last added.

units.la: {30} Sic. {31} Sic. {32} Sic. {33} Sic. {34} Sic. difficile esset singula vi facta distinctis titulis explicare, ac specialibus interdictis coërcere. Atq; ita, quae prioribus interdictis sunt expressa ac comprehensa, non impediunt, quominus posteageneralis clausula subjungatur ad reliqua infinita, uno interdicto coërcenda. Est & haec ratio, quod priora pleraque sint ante factum, hoc est post factum, ut scilicet, quod vi aut clam factum aut aedificatum fuerit, restituatur.
units.tr: {30} Sic. {31} Sic. {32} Sic. {33} Sic. {34} Sic. It would be difficult to explain each act done by force under separate titles and to restrain them by special interdicts. Thus, those things that are expressed and included in the earlier interdicts do not prevent a general clause from being added afterwards to cover the remaining infinite cases, to be restrained by one interdict. This is also a reason: most of the earlier ones apply before the act, whereas this one applies after the act, namely, so that what has been done or built by force or secretly be restored.

units.la: Huic edicto conjungitur. Edictum de remissionibus, sub quo titulo plura interdicta fuere: Unum est in l.1. de remiss. alterum est in l. praetor, 20. de operib. nov. nunc. III. eadem l. 20. §. deinde ait. 9. Nam tota ea l. 20. ad titulum hunc de remissionibus pertinet, sumpta ex lib. 71. Ulpian. ut & l.1. de remiss. sed Tribunian eam leg. 20. posuit sub tit. d. oper. nov. nunc. Hac de causa, quia remissio operis pertineat quoque ad nunciationes novi operis. l.1. §.1. de remiss. Ratio autem ordinis, cur hi tituli sive interdicta de remissionibus interdicto quod vi aut clam, proximum locum in edicto perpetuo obtinuerint, haec est: quia interdictum, quod vi aut clam, pertinet ad opus & aedificationem, nempe cum aut inuitis nobis aut clam, etiam contra nuntiationem aut prohibitionem quis aedificaverit, opusque novum fecerit, quod iubetur restituere interdicto, quod vi aut clam. l.1. in pr. n. & l. 10. 0. 4. ff. quod vi aut clam. Ista igitur ratione titulus de remissionib. priori interdicto adiunctus fuit, quia & remissio ad novum opus pertinet vt iam dictum. Nihil est n. aliud remissio q; abolitio nuntiationis operis novi a praetore impetrata. Ratio autem, cur illud quod vi aut clam, sit prius, & haec de remissionibus sint posteriora haec est: quia illud succurrit laeso, hoc laedenti hoc est, aedificanti, ideoque praetor, ut curam gereret laesorum recte prius proposuit interdictum, quod vi aut clam. Est & haec ratio: quia aedificatio & nuntiatio priores sunt remissione nunciationis: ex illis nascitur edictum, quod vi aut clam ex hoc interdicto remissionum.
units.tr: To this edict is joined the edict on remissions, under which title there were several interdicts. One is in l.1. de remiss.; another is in l. praetor, 20. de operib. nov. nunc. A third is in the same l. 20. §. deinde ait. 9. For the whole of that l. 20. pertains to this title on remissions, being taken from book 71 of Ulpian, as also l.1. de remiss. But Tribunian placed that leg. 20. under the title d. oper. nov. nunc., for this reason: because the remission of a work also pertains to the notices of new work l.1. §.1. de remiss. The reason why these titles, or interdicts, on remissions have obtained the place next to the interdict quod vi aut clam in the perpetual edict is this: the interdict quod vi aut clam concerns building and construction, namely when someone, against our will or secretly, even against a notice or prohibition, has built and made a new work, which he is ordered to restore by the interdict quod vi aut clam l.1. in pr. n. & l. 10. 0. 4. ff. quod vi aut clam. For this reason, therefore, the title on remissions was attached to the earlier interdict, since a remission also pertains to a new work, as already said. For a remission is nothing other than the cancellation of a notice of new work obtained from the praetor. The reason why quod vi aut clam comes first, and these interdicts on remissions come later, is this: the former aids the injured party, the latter the one who injures, that is, the builder; therefore the praetor, in order to look properly after the injured, rightly put forward the interdict quod vi aut clam first. There is also this reason: building and the notice are prior to the remission of the notice; from them arises the edict quod vi aut clam, and from this interdict the remissions follow.

units.la: Hoc autem sequitur interdictum de precario, ratio ordinis jam est expositas, nempe quod duabus viciosis possessionibus expositis, jam reliquet tertia nempe precaria. Verba hujus interdicti extant, l.2. de precar. quod interdictum, ut & priora, quod vi aut clam de rebus soli & aedib. est: illa semper l. 1. & 2. quod vi aut clam. & c. hoc de precario plerunq; . Nam interdictum etiam in rebus mobilibus precarium constituit, & non tantum in aedibus, sed Scinfundis l.4. & 6. de precar.
units.tr: Next follows the interdict on precarium, whose order has already been explained, namely that, with the two faulty possessions set out, the third, precarious possession, now remains. The words of this interdict are found in l.2. de precar. This interdict, like the earlier one quod vi aut clam, concerns things of the soil and buildings; the laws l. 1. & 2. quod vi aut clam and so on always concern this, and the one on precarium usually does. For the interdict also establishes precarium in movable things, and not only in buildings, but also in plots of land l.4. & 6. de precar.

units.la: Huic adjungitur tria interdicta ad arbores pertinentia. Ratio ordinis haec esse videtur, quod priora omnia interdicta privata sint urbana, haec tria sint rustica, & proinde posteriora, atq; ab illis merito distincta. I. est de arboribus caedendis, cujus verba extant in l.1. ff. de arborib. caeden. II. Ejusdem argumenti, ejusque verba extant in d. leg. 1. §. deinde praetor 7. Et videtur Ulpian. unum facere interdictum, cujus duo sunt capita, quorum prius ad aedes, posterius ad agros proprie pertineat, d.l.1. §. ult. III. est de glande lenda. genda quod item ad agros pertinet, cujus verba exstant in l. unic. de glande leg. Et haec de interdictis rerum.
units.tr: To this are joined three interdicts relating to trees.
