The reason for this order seems to be that all the earlier interdicts are private and urban, while these three are rural, and therefore come later and are rightly distinguished from them. First, the interdict on felling trees, whose words are found in l.1. ff. de arborib. caeden. Second, one of the same subject, whose words are found in the same d. leg. 1. §. deinde praetor 7. Ulpian seems to make one interdict, of which there are two parts: the first properly pertains to buildings, the second to fields d.l.1. §. ult. Third is the interdict on gathering acorns, which likewise pertains to fields, whose words are found in l. unic. de glande leg. And these are the interdicts concerning things.

units.la: Nunc de interdictis personarum, in quibus primum est interdictum de libero homine exhibendo: cujus verba exstant in l. 1. ff. h.tit. Ratio ordinis expolita est supra, tum quia possessio, ad quam pertinent proprie interdicta sint rerum non personarum, ut & dominium: tum quia interdicta sint, vel rei familiaris tuendae, ut sunt illa: vel officii, ut est istud, vel juris seu confervandi causa, ut seqq. l. 2. §. 2. tit. de interdict. Cur autem inter personas hoc sit primum, est haec ratio, quia est de libero homine, cum reliqua sint deiis quae sunt in potestate aut filii aut servi.
units.tr: Now concerning the interdicts concerning persons, of which the first is the interdict on producing a free man, whose words are found in l. 1. ff. h.tit. The reason for the order has been set out above: partly because possession, to which the interdicts properly pertain, concerns things and not persons, as does ownership; partly because the interdicts are either for protecting one's household property, as those are, or of duty, as this one is, or for the sake of preserving right, as the following ones l. 2. §. 2. tit. de interdict. But why this one comes first among those concerning persons is for this reason: because it concerns a free man, whereas the rest concern those who are in the power of either a son or a slave.

units.la: Huic proximum est interdictum de liberis exhibendis, cujus verba exstant, in l. 1. hoc tit. quod est praeparatorium interdicti de liberis ducendis, ut ait l. 3. in princ. dict. tit. Nam exhibiti demum duci possunt, quemadmodum & actio ad exhibendum rei vindicationis est praeparatoria, d. l. 3. §. 1. Cujus de ducendis verba exstant initio, dicta l. 3.
units.tr: Next to this is the interdict concerning the exhibiting of free persons (de liberis exhibendis), whose words are found in l. 1 of this title. This is the preparatory interdict to the interdict concerning the leading away of free persons (de liberis ducendis), as l. 3 in principio of the said title says. For those who have been exhibited can only then be led away, just as the action for exhibition (ad exhibendum) in a real action for recovery of property is preparatory, d. l. 3 §. 1. The words of the interdict concerning leading away are found at the beginning of the said l. 3.

units.la: Fuit & interdictum de liberto exhibendo, l. 2. §. 1. in sin. ff. de interdict. quod quia patronus parenti est similis in edicto perpetuo, hic collocatum fuisse videtur. Sed in ff. nullum exstat. Credo quod Tribun. putarit sufficere interdictum generale de liberis hominibus exhibendis, maxime quod ex constit. Inst. de jure patronatus, libertini ingenuis fere sint adaequati, §. sed nostra 4. instit. de succeff. libert.
units.tr: There was also an interdict concerning the exhibiting of a freedman (de liberto exhibendo), l. 2 §. 1 at the end, ff. de interdictis. Since in the perpetual edict the patron is like a parent, it seems to have been placed here. But no text of it exists in the Digest. I believe the tribune thought that the general interdict concerning the exhibiting of free persons was sufficient, especially since by the Institutes on the right of patronage, freedmen are nearly equal to freeborn persons, §. sed nostra 4 of the Institutes on succession of freedmen.

units.la: Proximum in edicto locum tenuit interdictum utrubi. Ratio ordinis est, quia & hoc est de ducendo homine, sed servo, ideoque posterius. Pertinet tamen hoc interdictum non tantum ad servos, sed etiam ad reliquas res mobiles ex interpretatione scilicet prudentum. Nam verba interdicti, quae exstant in l. 1. ff. utrubi, sunt de homine, hoc est, servo. Estenim utrubi rerum mobilium, ut uti possidetis rerum immobilium sive soli, quamvis & ibi verba tantum sint de aedibus concepta. l. 1. ff. uti possid.
units.tr: In the edict the interdict utrubi held the next place. The reason for the order is that this too concerns the leading away of a person, but of a slave, and so it comes later. This interdict, however, pertains not only to slaves but also to other movable things, by the interpretation, that is, of the jurists. For the words of the interdict, which are found in l. 1 ff. utrubi, concern a man, that is, a slave. Indeed utrubi applies to movable things, as uti possidetis applies to immovable things or land, although there too the words are framed only with regard to buildings, l. 1 ff. uti possidetis.

units.la: Huic proximum videtur fuisse, interdictum, ne vis fiat ei, qui in possessionem missus, ut indicat inscriptio, l. 1. ne vis fiat ei, &c. quae indicat hoc interdictum explicatum ab Ulpiano, libro 72. ad edictum, quo libro prius quoque nempe utrubi explicavit, ut indicat inscriptio. l. 1. ff. utrubi. Ratio ordinis autem haec esse videtur, quod cum hoc interdictum ne vis fiat ei, &c. sit generale, d. l. 1. §. 1. ne vis fiat ei, &c. (pertinet enim ad omnes, qui a praetore in possessionem missi sunt) & hactenus omnes species missionum, & interdictorum, quibus etiam possessio restituitur aut adquiritur. l. 2. §. hoc autem. ff. de interd. §. sequent. Instit. eod. expositae sint, ordinis ratio postulat ut generali quodam Edicto & interdicto missos in possessionem tueatur praetor quod facit hoc interdicto, ne fiat vis ei, &c. Tribun. tamen hoc interdicto longe priori in loco posuit in ff. ut ibi latius. Verba hujus interdicti exstant, in ddi ne vis fiat.
units.tr: Next to this there seems to have been the interdict ne vis fiat ei, qui in possessionem missus (that no force be done to one who has been put in possession), as the title indicates, l. 1 ne vis fiat ei, etc., which indicates that this interdict was explained by Ulpian in book 72 on the edict; in that book he had also earlier explained utrubi, as the title indicates, l. 1 ff. utrubi. The reason for the order seems to be this: since this interdict ne vis fiat ei, etc., is general, d. l. 1 §. 1 ne vis fiat ei, etc. (for it applies to all who have been put in possession by the praetor), and since all the kinds of missions and interdicts by which possession is restored or acquired have been set out, l. 2 §. hoc autem ff. de interdictis, §. sequent. Institutes eodem, the order of things requires that the praetor protect those put in possession by a certain general edict and interdict, which is what the interdict ne fiat vis ei, etc. does. The tribune, however, placed this interdict in a much earlier position in the Digest, as explained there more fully. The words of this interdict are found under the heading ne vis fiat.

units.la: Huic autem proximum fuisse videtur interdictum de migrando, quod ab Ulp explicatum videtur lib.73. ut indicat inscriptio l.1. de mig. cujus verba extant in d.l.1.d.tit. Ratio ordinis est obscurior, propter Edictum illud generale, ne vis fiat &c. modo expositum & ut habent inscriptiones, interjectum inter haec duo interdicta utrubi & de migrando: quod nisi esset interjectum, facilis erat ratio inter utrubi & de migrando: quia ut utrubi, ita & de migrando de homine sive servo conceptum est. Sed pertinet ad alias quoque res & est magis speciale de migrando, quia pertinet tantum ad res mobiles importatas in habitationem sive domum conductam, hoc est, ad supellectilem, cum utrubi ad res fere pertinet. Quare nisi inscriptiones sint mendosae, ut saepe sunt, dicendum est priora interdicta, agere de possessione adquisitaque aut restituta, aut conservata, sive de iis, quibus praetor jussit possessionem restitui &c. hoc autem de migrando potius contrariam rationem & effectum continet: nempe ut conductori liceat suam supellectilem jam migranti, & soluta jam mercede exportare, ne impediat ipsum locator sive dominus aedium, cui est satisfactum: ideoque cum priora sint de possessione adipiscenda, hoc autem de migrando sit de possessione ex aedibus scil. migrando deducenda, sive de supellectili deportanda: hinc factum videtur, ut generale illud interdictum ne vis fiat ei &c. positum fuerit in Edicto inter haec duo interdicta utrubi & de migrando, quia scilicet hoc interdictum generale ad quendam possessionem pertinet.
units.tr: Next to this there seems to have been the interdict de migrando (concerning removal), which Ulpian seems to have explained in book 73, as the title indicates, l. 1 de migrando, whose words are found in the said l. 1 of the said title. The reason for the order is more obscure, because that general edict ne vis fiat etc., just set out and as the titles give it, was placed between the two interdicts utrubi and de migrando. Had it not been placed there, the reason for the order between utrubi and de migrando would be easy: for, as utrubi, so also de migrando is framed concerning a man or slave. But it pertains also to other things, and de migrando is more specific, since it pertains only to movable things brought into a dwelling or leased house, that is, to household furniture, whereas utrubi concerns things in general. Therefore, unless the titles are faulty, as they often are, it must be said that the earlier interdicts deal with acquiring possession, and with possession either acquired, restored or preserved, or with those by which the praetor ordered possession to be restored, etc. But this interdict de migrando has rather the opposite reason and effect: namely, that a tenant who is now moving out may, once the rent has already been paid, carry away his furniture, and that the landlord or owner of the house, to whom satisfaction has been made, may not hinder him. Therefore, since the earlier interdicts concern obtaining possession, while this one de migrando concerns removing possession from the house, that is, carrying away the household furniture, it seems to have come about that the general interdict ne vis fiat ei, etc. was placed in the edict between these two interdicts utrubi and de migrando, because that general interdict pertains to a certain possession.

units.la: Huic autem proximum fuisse videtur interdictum Salvianum. Id enim postulat ratio ordinis & in ff. quoque hic est ordo. Ratio est, quia ut prius de migrando ad inquilinos, sive ad urbanas habitationes ita Salvianum ad colonos supellectilem rusticam pertinet verba ejus non extant.
units.tr: Next to this there seems to have been the Salvian interdict. The order of things requires this, and the order in the Digest is the same here. The reason is that, just as the earlier interdict de migrando concerns tenants or urban dwellings, so the Salvian interdict concerns the household goods of farm tenants (coloni); its words are not extant.

units.la: Ultimum locum inter interdicta obtinet interdictum fraudatorium, cujus verba extant l.1. quam fraud. cred. quae lex, ut & l.2. d. tit. sumpta est ex L.73. Ulp quo libro postrema Edicta explicantur, ut Edictum de migrando quod indicat l.1. de migrand quae est ex eodem libro 73. Dicitur autem hoc interdictum fraudatorium, in l.96. pup. ll. ff. de solut. propterea quod eo restituantur alienata aut facta in fraudem creditorum. Interdum quoque praetor dat actionem in factum, ad eandem revocanda, de qua actione in factum in verbis ejusdem interdicti ind. l.10. & seqq. Ratio ordinis autem est hoc interdictum sit ultimum, haec esse videtur quod sit rebus quarum possessio non fuerit penes creditorem, ideoque non sit proprie de possessione: atque ita habeat aliquid singulare praeter alia interdicta, & proinde velut extraordinarium in ultimum locum rejectum. Et haec de interdictis.
units.tr: The last place among the interdicts is held by the fraudulent-transfer interdict (fraudatorium), whose words are found in l. 1 quam fraudationis causa creditorum, which law, like l. 2 of the same title, was taken from book 73 of Ulpian, in which the last edicts are explained, as the edict de migrando, which l. 1 de migrando indicates, comes from the same book 73. This interdict is called fraudatorium, in l. 96 pupillus ff. de solutionibus, because by it things alienated or done in fraud of creditors are restored. Sometimes also the praetor gives an action in the form of a fact (in factum) to revoke the same, concerning which action in factum the words of the same interdict speak, ind. l. 10 and following. The reason for the order, that this interdict stands last, seems to be that it concerns things whose possession was not in the hands of the creditor, and so it is not properly about possession; and thus it has something singular beyond the other interdicts, and accordingly, as if extraordinary, it was thrown to the last place. And so much for the interdicts.

units.la: X. Et ultima Pars Edicti Perpetui.
units.tr: X. And the Last Part of the Perpetual Edict.

units.la: INterdictis in Edicto proximum locum tenuit actio Serviana & actio quasi Serviana, hoc est, hypothecaria, quae est de pignoribus vel hypothecis. thæcis. Nam Serviana est tantum de tacito pignore, hoc est de rebus per inquilinum illatis in domum aut prædium urbanum conductum. Et hunc ordinem, ut prius de interdictis posteaque de pignoribus ageretur fuisse in Edicto perpetuo perspicuum esse ex inscriptionibus legum in ff. Nam ex lib. 73 Ulpian. quo ut modo dictum ultima interdicta explicavit plurimæ leges de pignoribus sunt sumptæ l. 6. §. 14. 21. dep. g. l. 3. 6. in qui. rauf. pig. Idem videre licet lib. 68. Pauli, quo libro fraudatorium interdictum & de pignoribus explicavit, ut indicat l. 7. 12. de pignor. 3. & l. 3. ff. quæ in fraud. cred. Ratio ordinis autem Edicti perpetui (quem & in C. lecutus est Tribun. non vero in ff. quo ad tractatum de pignoribus) est hæc: tum quia hæ duæ actiones, Serviana & quasi Serviana sint accessoriæ, (pignus enim est accessio ut fidejussor, quibus confirmantur priores contractus & obligationes. Quæ cum adhuc sit explicatum de principalibus & interdictis quæ vicem actionum gerunt, merito accessoria iis adjunguntur, sed ultimo loco. Accessio enim sequitur rem principalem: ) tum quia hæ duæ actiones cognationem & similitudinem cum proximis interdictis, nimirum fraudatorio & Salviano Nam his duabus actionibus partim agitur de rebus illatis in prædium, ut Serviana, partim consulitur creditoribus pignore scilicet, idq; utraque actione, quemadmodum Salvianum est de rebus illatis in prædium rusticum, & consulitur creditoribus tam Salviano quam fraudatorio. item Serviana, item Servi ani. ubi Salviani & Servlani judicii differentiæ similitudinesque explicari solent. Et hæc quoque altera potest esse ratio ordinis de interdicto fraudatorio cur scilicet illud post Salvianum in Edicto fuerit positum, quia simile est Salviano in eo quod utrumque pertinet ad securitatem creditorum. Est & tertia ratio ordinis de his duabus actionibus Serviana & quasi Serviana cur hæ in Edicto post interdicta hic fuerunt positæ, nempe quia pudam tantum possessionem avocant. l. sicut vendit. de Evict. Ideoque ut interdicta ad possessionem aliquatenus pertinent. Merito autem hæ duæ actiones in Edicto fuerunt, quia sunt prætoriæ. d. §. item S. Rutiana. verba tamen Edicti non exstant.
units.tr: After the interdicts, the Edict placed next the Serviana action and the quasi-Serviana action, that is, the hypothecary action, which concerns pledges or hypothecs. The Serviana applies only to the tacit pledge, that is, to goods brought by a tenant into a town house or rural estate that he has leased. That the interdicts were treated first and the pledges afterwards in the Perpetual Edict is clear from the inscriptions of the laws in the Digest. For many laws on pledges are taken from book 73 of Ulpian, in which he explained the last interdicts: l. 6 §. 14, 21 dep.; l. 3, 6 in qui. rauf. pig. The same can be seen in book 68 of Paul, in which he explained the fraudulent interdict and the pledges, as l. 7, 12 de pignor. 3 and l. 3 ff. quae in fraud. cred. indicate. The order of the Perpetual Edict (which Tribonian also followed in the Code, though not in the Digest, as regards the treatment of pledges) is as follows. First, because these two actions, Serviana and quasi-Serviana, are accessory, since a pledge is an accession, like a surety, by which earlier contracts and obligations are confirmed. Since the principal matters and the interdicts, which take the place of actions, have now been explained, these accessory actions are rightly added to them, but in the last place, for an accession follows the principal thing. Second, because these two actions have a kinship and resemblance with the neighbouring interdicts, namely the fraudulent interdict and the Salvian action. For these two actions deal partly with goods brought onto an estate, as the Serviana does, and partly provide for creditors by means of a pledge, and each of them does so: the Salvian concerns goods brought onto a rustic estate, and both the Salvian and the fraudulent action provide for creditors. Likewise, the Serviana and the quasi-Serviana; and the differences and resemblances of the Salvian and Serviana judgments are usually explained there. This may also be a second reason for the order, why the fraudulent interdict was placed after the Salvian in the Edict: it resembles the Salvian in that both pertain to the security of creditors. There is also a third reason for the order of these two actions, Serviana and quasi-Serviana, why they were placed here in the Edict after the interdicts: namely, because they only remove the possession of a thing pledged (l. sicut vendit. de Evict.), and so, like the interdicts, they pertain in some measure to possession. These two actions were rightly in the Edict because they are praetorian (d. §. item; S. Rutiana). The words of the Edict, however, do not survive.

units.la: Hactenus de actionibus in Edicto perpetuo propositis. His proximum locum tenuerunt exceptiones, ut videre licet ex Ulp. lib. 74. & 2. sequen. Pauli lib. 69. & 2 sequent. ad Edictum quibus explicantur exceptiones, post Edicta de pignoribus sive Serviana & quasi Serviana. Ratio ordinis est perspicua ut prius de actionibus sive de actore posterius de exceptionibus sive reo explicetur, quam rationem explicavimus supra ad Institut. & eundem ordinem tenuit Tribun. tam in ff quam in C. Merito autem exceptiones in Edicto propositas fuisse indicat l. 2. 6. 1. & l. 1. in prin. & verf. ideo autem, & o. Quare autem tractatio de exceptionibus proposita in Edicto ratio est quia omnes exceptiones sunt prætoriæ, ideoq; ad prætoris maximè pertinentes. Cic. lib. 1. de invent. & Cornif. lib. 2. ad Herenn. Cumautem multæ sunt tatsint exceptiones ut procuratoriæ. §. eque.de excepti: ut exceptiones in fáctum,l.21.generaliter.§.apud.f.adversus.de doli excepti.l. ult.ff.de recept. ut jurisjurandi, l.ultim.ff.d.tit. & passim sub tit. de jurejur. ut intercessionis, de quapassim sub titul.ff.ad Vellei: ut non numeratæ pecun.l.4 §.adversus,15.de doli except. Ut quod libertatis onerandæ causa petitur, l.7.exceptiones.§.1.ff. de excepti.ut litigiosi, de qua titul.de litigiosi Ut de serti vadimonii, sive promissionis judicio sistendi de qua titulus ff.si quis caut. Ut aliæ celebres, pacti rei judicatæ, rei venditæ & traditæ doli, metus, temporis, de quibus sunt tituli ff.& C. Cum igitur exceptiones tam sint multæ, dubitari potest, an omnes specialiter fuerint propositæ in Edicto, deinde quo ordine fuerint propositæ. Quantum ex fragmentis sive particulis librorum Ulpian. & Pauli ad Edictum colligere licet non omnes videntur, sed celebriores in Edicto fuisse propositæ, ut de serti vadimonii, rei judicatæ, doli mali, metus, litigiosi, & fortasse aliæ quædam. Et primo quidem exposita fuit exceptio deserti vadimonii, sive promissionis judicio sisti, ut l.2.& sequent.si quis caut. &c. indicant. Ratio ordinis est, quia hæc exceptio pertinet ad exordium judicii, ideoque & à Tribunian. posita fuit initio ff. ubi de in jus voc. Huic proxima fuisse videtur exceptio, rei judicatæ, quod indicat l.6.12. & 14.de exception. rei jud. quæ sunt ex libro Pauli 70. cum exceptio promissionis deserta judicio sisti, ab eo fuerit explicata lib.69. ut indicat l.3.5. & 7.ff.si quis caut. Ratio ordinis est, quia & hæc exceptio ad judicia pertinet: illa quidem deserta promissionis judicio sisti ad initium, hæc vero ad finem judicii.
units.tr: So far concerning the actions proposed in the Perpetual Edict. Next in place came the exceptions, as can be seen from Ulpian, book 74 and the following two, and from Paul, book 69 and the following two on the Edict, in which the exceptions are explained after the Edicts on pledges, that is, the Serviana and quasi-Serviana. The reason for the order is clear: first the actions, that is, the plaintiff, and afterwards the exceptions, that is, the defendant, are explained. We set out this reason above in the commentary on the Institutes, and Tribonian kept the same order both in the Digest and in the Code. It is rightly indicated by l. 2 §. 6, l. 1 in prin. and verb. ideo autem, & o. that the exceptions were proposed in the Edict. The reason why the treatment of exceptions was set out in the Edict is that all exceptions are praetorian and therefore belong chiefly to the praetor (Cic. lib. 1 de invent. and Cornif. lib. 2 ad Herenn.). Yet, since there are many exceptions, such as the procurator's exceptions (§. eque. de excepti.), the exceptions in factum (l. 21 generaliter §. apud f. adversus de doli excepti.; l. ult. ff. de recept.), the exception of an oath (l. ult. ff. d. tit., and passim under the title de jurejurando), the exception of intercession (de qua passim sub tit. ff. ad Vellei.), the exception of money not counted (l. 4 §. adversus; 15 de doli except.), the exception of what is sought for the sake of burdening liberty (l. 7 exceptiones §. 1 ff. de excepti.), the exception of litigious property (de qua titul. de litigiosi), the exception of the surety bond or promise to appear in court (de qua titulus ff. si quis caut.), and other famous ones, the exceptions of pact, of res judicata, of goods sold and delivered, of fraud, of fear, of time (for which there are titles in the Digest and Code), it may be asked whether all of them were specifically proposed in the Edict, and then in what order they were proposed. As far as can be gathered from the fragments or particles of the books of Ulpian and Paul on the Edict, not all of them seem to have been in the Edict, but the more famous ones were proposed there: such as the exception of the surety bond, of res judicata, of wilful fraud, of fear, of litigious property, and perhaps some others. The exception of the surety bond, or of the promise to appear in court, was set out first, as l. 2 and following, si quis caut., and so on, indicate. The reason for the order is that this exception pertains to the beginning of a trial; therefore Tribonian also placed it at the beginning of the Digest, under de in jus vocando. The exception of res judicata seems to have come next to it, as l. 6, 12 and 14 de exception. rei jud. indicate, which are taken from book 70 of Paul; and the exception of the surety bond was explained by Paul in book 69, as l. 3, 5 and 7 ff. si quis caut. indicate. The reason for the order is that this exception too pertains to trials: the former, the exception of the surety bond, to the beginning of a trial, and this one, of res judicata, to its end.

units.la: Cui fortasis proximè adjuncta fuit exceptio rei venditæ & traditæ de qua est tit. de excepti.rei vend. Nam l.1.h.tit. sumpta est ex libro 76. Ulpia cum librum 75. explicasset de exc.rei jud. Ratio ordinis videtur in nomine, quod ut prior est rei judicatæ, ita hæc est rei venditæ & ut prior ita & posterior est de re jam facta nempe de re judicata & jam vendita ac tradita.
units.tr: Perhaps the exception of goods sold and delivered was placed next to it, to which the title de exception. rei vend. belongs. For l. 1 of this title is taken from book 76 of Ulpian, after he had explained the exception of res judicata in book 75. The reason for the order seems to lie in the name: as the exception of res judicata comes first, so this one is of goods sold, and as the former is of a thing already adjudged, so the latter is of a thing already sold and delivered.

units.la: Post hos posita fuit in Edicto exceptio doli mali, & huic proxima quod metus causa, ut indicat l.2. §.1.est & f.pen.ff. de dol. & met. exc. ubi & verba, non tamen omnia eorum, exceptionum afferuntur: quæ duæ leges sunt item Ulp ex libro 76.ad Edictum. Ratio ordinis videtur esse, quia hæ exceptiones ex delicto vel quasi oriuntur, ex dolo & ex metu, ideoque in posteriorem locum rejectæ videntur. Cur autem doli exceptio sit prior cum tamen doli actio posterius, & actio quod metus causa prius fuerit proposita in Edicto ut supra dictum, non ita facile est reddere rationem. Sed tamen hæc mihi videtur ratio quod exceptio doli sit generalis adeo ut Jurisconsultus Cæsius, exceptionem metus causa non putarit separatim proponendam, sed eam sub exceptione doli fuerit complexus. Unde & antiquior videtur exceptio doli quam metus, l.4.metu. de exc.dol. Ideoque priorem locum obtinuit. Sunt & aliæ exceptiones, quæ item in Edicto fuisse videntur, ut onerandæ libertatis exceptio, ut litigiosi exceptio, quarum prior cōtinetur sub tit. quar.rer.actl.nō datur, ubi & exceptio iurisiurandi exponitur: altera litigiosi continetur sub titul.proximo de litigiof.& l.1.titul.quar.rer. &c. & l.1.de litig. Utraque est Ulpian.ex eodem libro 76.quo & priores ab ipso fuerunt explicatæ. Sed valdè dubito, an distinctæ fuerint propositæ in Edicto, videturtamen exceptio libertatis onerandæ fuisse propositæ, & quidem in ultimo ferè loco, eo quod ad libertatem & servitutem pertineat.
units.tr: After these the exception of fraud was placed in the Edict, and next to it the exception of fear (quod metus causa), as l. 2 §. 1 and the last paragraph, ff. de dol. & met. exc., indicates, where the words, though not all of them, of these exceptions are quoted. These two laws are likewise from Ulpian, book 76 on the Edict. The reason for the order seems to be that these exceptions arise from a delict, or something like one, from fraud and from fear, and so they seem to have been placed in a later position. Why the exception of fraud comes first, though the action of fraud is placed later, and the action quod metus causa was proposed earlier in the Edict, as said above, is not easy to explain. However, this seems to me the reason: the exception of fraud is so general that the jurist Caecilius did not think the exception of fear should be proposed separately, but included it under the exception of fraud. Hence the exception of fraud also seems older than that of fear (l. 4 metu de exc. dol.), and so it held the first place. There are also other exceptions which likewise seem to have been in the Edict, such as the exception of the burdening of liberty and the exception of litigious property. The former is contained under the title quar.rer.actl.non datur, where the exception of oath is also set out; the latter is contained under the next title de litigiosi and l. 1 titul. quar.rer. &c. and l. 1 de litig. Both are from Ulpian, from the same book 76 in which he had explained the earlier ones. But I very much doubt whether they were proposed as distinct exceptions in the Edict; it seems, however, that the exception of burdening liberty was proposed, and indeed almost in the last place, because it pertains to liberty and servitude.

units.la: De exceptione litigiosi extat etiam Cod. de litigiosis post tit. generalem de except. Ratio ordinis, cur hæc in ultimum locum rejecta sit, hæc esse videtur, quia est specialis, nimirum contra venditionem tantū, cum priores sint magis generales, & ad varia negocia opponantur. Fortasse huic exceptioni litigiosi statim adjuncta fuit exceptio rei venditæ propter similitudinem rei, quod utraq; scilicet, si de venditione. Nam utramq; Ulpian.lib.76.explicavit, ut indicat l.1.de litig.& l.1.de except.rei vend. quæ leges ambæ sunt ex d.lib.
units.tr: Concerning the exception of the litigious thing, the Code also has a title, De litigiosis, placed after the general title De exceptionibus. The reason this exception was put in the last place seems to be that it is special, applying only against sale, whereas the earlier ones are more general and are opposed to various transactions. Perhaps the exception of the litigious thing was joined at once to the exception of the thing sold, because of the similarity of the matter, since both concern sale. For Ulpian explained both in book 76, as l.1 de litig. and l.1 de except. rei vend. show, and both these laws come from that same book.

units.la: 2 Ulp.quod & probabilius esse videtur.
units.tr: So Ulpian, which also seems the more probable.

units.la: De exceptione pacti non videtur separatim in Edicto fuisse propositum hoc in loco, quia Edictum de pactis servandis, cujus verba extant in l.7.ju-r.gentium.§.ait pretor.ff.de pact. sufficere videatur.
units.tr: The exception of pact does not seem to have been set out separately in the Edict in this place, because the Edict on keeping pacts, whose words are extant in l.7 ius gentium §ait praetor ff. de pactis, seems to be sufficient.

units.la: De exceptione iurisiurandi quamvis sæpè agatur sub tit.eo, quo agitur de actione iurisiurandi ut l.28.in duob.§.exceptio.l.36.fiaflor.de jurei. Fortasse tamen & hic fuit separatim posita in Edicto. Nam Ulpian.d.lib.76.in l.1.in princ quar.rer actl & Paul.lib.71.in l.2.d.titul.de except.jurisjurand. explicant, in quibus libris alias quoque supra expositas, & in Edicto propositas exceptiones, ut dicli metus &c explicarunt.
units.tr: Although the exception of oath is often treated under the title where the action on oath is treated, as in l.28 in duobus §exceptio and l.36 fiaflor. de iureiurando, perhaps it too was set out separately in the Edict. For Ulpian in the said book 76, in l.1 in princ. quar. rer. actio, and Paul in book 71, in l.2 d. tit. de except. iurisiurandi, explain them. In those books they also explained other exceptions set out above and proposed in the Edict, such as the exception of fear.

units.la: Videtur & Edictum quoddam generale fuisse de exceptionibus, quo generaliter causas dandarum actionum prætor fuit complexus. Sed nihil est certi, quèadmodum & de exceptione temporis, de quæ est tit ff.de diverf.temp. p ef.r.& de exceptione quatenus quis facere possit, de qua in l.7.exceptiones. de except. Meritò dubitari potest, an ut & alia generali quoda Edicto fuerunt comprehensæ, an vero separatim & distincte, ut supra nonnullæ expositæ in Edicto. Et hæc de exceptionibus.
units.tr: There seems also to have been some general Edict on exceptions, in which the praetor embraced generally the grounds for granting actions. But nothing is certain, just as with the exception of time, which is in the title ff. de diversis temporibus praescriptionibus, and the exception of what a man is able to pay, of which in l.7 exceptiones de except. It may rightly be doubted whether these, like certain others, were included in some general Edict, or rather separately and distinctly, as some above were set out in the Edict. And so much for exceptions.

units.la: His proximum in Edicto locum tenuerunt stipulationes prætoriæ, quod intelligitur ex lib. Jurisconsultorum Nam Ulp.de exceptionibus explicavit lib.74.75.& 76. de stipulationib.prætoriis lib.77.& 4.sequent. Et Paul. de except.lib.69.& 2.sequent. de stipulationib.prætor.72.& 6.sequent.Idemq; videre est in Caio, & in aliis ad Edictum. Et hunc quoq; ordinem tenuit Paul. lib.5 sent. & Tribun.ipsein C.lib.8. ubi docet tit.de exceptionib. statim sequuntur 9.titulide st pulationib. Idem in ff est ord ubi tit. de except. sequuntur tit. de verbor.oblig.de ftipul.fero.& ff.pulat.pretor.&c.
units.tr: Next in the Edict after these came the praetorian stipulations, as is understood from the books of the jurists. For Ulpian explained the exceptions in books 74, 75 and 76, and the praetorian stipulations in book 77 and the following books. Paul treated exceptions in book 69 and the next two, and praetorian stipulations in book 72 and the following six. The same can be seen in Gaius and in the others who wrote on the Edict. Paul also kept this order in his Sentences, book 5, and Tribonian in the Code, book 8, where he teaches that the title De exceptionibus is immediately followed by title 9, De stipulationibus. The same order holds in the Digest, where the title De exceptionibus is followed by the titles De verborum obligationibus, De stipulatione servorum and De stipulationibus praetoriis, etc.

units.la: Ratio ordinis, cur scilicet in Edicto stipulationes ultimum ferè locum X tenuerint cum tamen vicem actionum repræsentent ideoque inter actiones poni debuisse videantur, l.37. actionis verb. oblig. & act. i. non solum ff. rem rat. h. t. Ratio igitur hæc est, quia stipulationes sunt accessiones aliarum omnium obligationum & actionum, quarum firmandarum causa sunt inductæ, ut ait Paulus, lib. 5. sent. tit. 7. §. 1. quemadmodum & fideiussores, initio titul. Inst. de fideiuss. qui item iure civili fiunt tantum stipulatione f. vltim. d. t. Nec obstat quod stipulationes prætoriæ in strictis actionum obtinent ut modo dictum. Nam in eo quidem obtinent vicem actionum, quod & actiones, ita & hæ stipulationes ex auctoritate prætoris, non vero ex auctoritate privatorum sive contrahentium (utaliæ stipulationes, nempe conventionales) pendent l. 9. in prætorijs de stipul. p. 41. Nam alioqui & præcipua in parte differunt ab actionibus. Stipulationes enim privatim fiunt, actiones apud judicem exercentur. Dices ex stipulatione nasci quoque actionem quæ dicitur ex stipulatu: imo duplicem actionem, nempe condictionem certi, si certa sit stipulatio, & actionem ex stipulatu si incerta sit stipulatio, initio titul. Inst. ae verbor. oblig. l. certi. 9. §. quoniam. de condict. cred. Respon. verum quidem esse duas illas actiones ex stipulatione oriri & de alterutra nempe condictione certi explicatum esse subd. titul. derib. cred. quia tamen ut iam dictum omnis stipulatio inducta est ad principales alias firmandas obligationes & actiones in personam, merito à principalibus actionibus stipulationesfuerunt distinctæ, & in ultimum locum reiectæ. Est & altera ratio, cur exceptiones priores sint stipulationibus quia exceptiones pertinent ad omnes actiones, tam in rem, quam in personam. Stipulationes tantum pactis & actionibus in personam adjiciuntur, sive potius obligationibus ex contractu, ad actiones in rem non pertinent, quia hæ non ex contractu, sed ex dominio similique iure in rem (ut servitute &c.) nascuntur. ff. de act. Atque ita exceptiones sunt magis generales latiusque patet quam stipulationes.
units.tr: The reason for the order, namely why stipulations stand in almost the last place in the Edict, although they take the place of actions and therefore seem to have had to be placed among the actions (l.37 de verb. oblig. and act. l.1 non solum ff. rem rat. h.t.), is this: stipulations are accessories to all other obligations and actions, for whose confirmation they were introduced, as Paul says (Sent. 5, tit. 7, §1), just as sureties are too (at the beginning of Inst. de fideiussoribus), and these also are made under civil law only by stipulation (l. ult. d. t.). Nor does it stand in the way that praetorian stipulations take the place of actions in strict law, as just said. For they take the place of actions in this respect: like actions, these stipulations depend on the authority of the praetor, not on the authority of private persons or contracting parties, unlike other stipulations, namely conventional ones (l.9 in praetoriis de stip. §41). In other respects, however, they differ from actions in a principal way: stipulations are made privately, whereas actions are pursued before a judge. You will say that from a stipulation there also arises an action which is called "from stipulation": indeed a double action, namely the condiction of a certain thing if the stipulation is certain, and the action from stipulation if the stipulation is uncertain (beginning of Inst. de verb. oblig.; l. certi 9 §quoniam de condict. cred.). I answer that those two actions do indeed arise from stipulation, and that one of them, namely the condiction of a certain thing, has been explained below under the title De rebus creditis. But because, as already said, every stipulation was introduced to confirm the other principal obligations and personal actions, stipulations were rightly distinguished from the principal actions and placed in the last place. There is also another reason why the earlier exceptions come before stipulations: exceptions pertain to all actions, both in rem and in personam. Stipulations are attached only to pacts and personal actions, or rather to obligations arising from contract. They do not pertain to actions in rem, because these arise not from contract but from ownership and a similar right in rem (such as servitude, etc.), ff. de act. And so exceptions are more general and extend more widely than stipulations.

units.la: Multæ autem fuerunt stipulationes prætoriæ, inter quas primum in Edicto locum videtur tenuisse stipulatio iudicatum solvi. Nam ut exceptiones l. b. 74. 75. & 76. explicavit Vlp. statim proximo lib. 77. & seq. explicavit hanc stipulationem iudicatum solvi, ut licet videre in l. 12. inter omnes qui satisfaciunt cog. & l. 6 iud. solvi item l. 3. & 5. d. tit. quæ sunt ex lib. 77. & 68. Ratio ordinis, cur hæc fuerit inter primos, aut prima potius hoc in loco est hæc: quia interponi solet initio iudiciorum, ut initio Inst. de satisdat.
units.tr: There were many praetorian stipulations, and among them the stipulation iudicatum solvi seems to have held the first place in the Edict. For just as Ulpian explained the exceptions in books 74, 75 and 76, he explained right after them, in book 77 and the following, this stipulation iudicatum solvi, as can be seen in l.12 inter omnes qui satisfaciunt cogi and l.6 iudicatum solvi, likewise l.3 and 5 d. tit., which come from books 77 and 68. The reason this was among the first, or rather the first at this point, is this: it is usually entered at the beginning of trials, as at the beginning of Inst. de satisdationibus.

units.la: Est & alia stipulatio iudicio sisti, quæ item initio litis interponitur: sed quia de ea priori in loco propositum fuit in edicto nimirum in tractatu & sub tit. de in ius voc. non opus fuit in fine edicti denuo eam iterare.
units.tr: There is also another stipulation, iudicio sisti (to appear in court), which is likewise entered at the beginning of the suit. But because it was set out earlier in the Edict, namely in the treatise and under the title De in ius vocando, there was no need to repeat it at the end of the Edict.

units.la: Secunda stipulatio videtur fuisse ea, quæ dicitur rem pupilli salvam fore propter similitudinem cum priore, iudicatum solvi. Similitudo est in eo, quod utraque prærequiritur a reo: Nam iudicatum solvi quolibet reo prærequiritur; rem pupilli salvam fore præstatur a tutore vel curatore, tanquam reo.
units.tr: The second stipulation seems to have been the one called that the ward's property will be kept safe, and it seems to have been second because of its similarity to the earlier one, iudicatum solvi. The similarity lies in this: each is required of the defendant beforehand. Iudicatum solvi is required of any defendant beforehand, and the promise that the ward's property will be safe is given by the tutor or curator as defendant.

units.la: In ff. tamen ordo est diversus & prima est, rem pupilli salvam fore, secunda iudicatum solvi, ubi id dicetur.
units.tr: In the Digest, however, the order is different: the first is that the ward's property will be safe, and the second is iudicatum solvi, where that is discussed.

units.la: 111. Videtur fuisse stipulatio legatorum, quam Vlp. eodem quo priorem rem pup &c. li.79 explicavit, ut videre est. l.2 & 4. ff. rem pup. salv. l.1.3. §14. ff. ut legat. nom. cav. & c. Ratio ordinis, cur haec stipulatio legatorum proxima sit stipulationi rem pupilli salvam fore est similitudo quaedam, nimirum quod ut illa rem pup. sal. & c. Tutor promittit rem pup. salvo. for. ita & hac legatorum, heres promittit rem legatam salvam. Dices, cur illa, rem pup. fuit prior in edicto, quia ad tutelam pertinet: At in edicto prius de tutelis propositum fuit posterius de legatis ut supra dictum. Ad legata autem pertinet haec quae dicitur cautio sive stipulatio legatorum, de qua in ff. agitur, in tractatu de leg. sub tit. ut legat. nom. cav.
units.tr: 111. The stipulation of legacies seems to have come next, which Ulpian explained in the same book 79 as the earlier stipulation on the ward's property, as is seen in l.2 and 4 ff. rem pupilli salvam fore and l.1, 3 §14 ff. ut legatorum nomine caveatur, etc. The reason for the order, why this stipulation of legacies is next to the stipulation that the ward's property will be safe, is a certain similarity: just as the tutor promises that the ward's property will be safe, so here the heir promises that the bequeathed thing will be safe. You may object: why was the stipulation on the ward's property earlier in the Edict? Because it pertains to guardianship. But in the Edict guardianships were treated before legacies, as said above. Yet this so-called caution or stipulation of legacies belongs to legacies, and in the Digest it is treated in the treatise on legacies under the title ut legatorum nomine caveatur.

units.la: Huic legatorum sive de legato stipulationi proxima fuisse videtur stipulatio ficus plus quam per leg. Falc. quam eodem libro 29. explicavit Vlp. cuius verba quaedam exstant l.1. §.7. ff. d. tit. Ratio ordinis, quia & haec ad legata pertinet, ideoque in ff. posita in tractatu legatorum.
units.tr: Next to this stipulation of legacies, or stipulation concerning a legacy, the stipulation that the fisc will not take more than the Falcidian law allows seems to have stood. Ulpian explained it in the same book 29, and some of its words are extant in l.1 §7 ff. d. tit. The reason for the order is that this too pertains to legacies, and so it is placed in the Digest in the treatise on legacies.

units.la: Est & cautio hereditatis restituendae. Huius cautionis mentio est, in l.1. Paulus notat. ff. de stip. praet. l 50. Imp. ad Treb. l.12. inter omnes qui fatisf. cog. De ea videatur & Dedebus cap.19. amot. ad l. aliquot. Cuiac. ad sent. Pauli l.b.f. & idem lib.79. obs c.37 quae cautio hereditatis restituendae fortasse tertium hic locum obtinuit, quia est de universitate: nempe hereditate, cui reliquae ut de legatis sint speciales: atque ita cautio sive stipulatio legatorum erit quarta.
units.tr: There is also the caution for restoring an inheritance. Mention of this caution occurs in l.1 Paulus notat. ff. de stip. praet., l.50 Imp. ad Treb., and l.12 inter omnes qui satisf. cog. On it see also Dedebus, ch. 19, Amot. on l. aliquot; Cuiac. on Paul's Sentences; and the same author, book 79, Observations, ch. 37. This caution for restoring an inheritance perhaps held the third place here, because it concerns the whole, namely the inheritance, to which the rest, such as legacies, are particular. And so the caution or stipulation of legacies will be the fourth.

units.la: Cui proximain edicto fortasse fuit stipulatio fructuaria. Nam ut stipulatio legatorum est generalis de omni legato, ita & haec stipulatio specialis de usufructu tantum legato de qua est totus titulus, ut ff. quemadmodum utatur. Nam Tribun. eam posuit non eo loco, quo de stipulatio n'bus praetoris sed longe ante, ubi de usufructu in edicto autem fuit hoc loco posita, ut videre est ex inscriptione l.1.2.3. & 7 quae Vlp. sunt, lib.79 ad ed. Illum, quo libro has stipulationes praetorias de legatis, & etiam illam rem pupillali & c. Huic autem fidei commissariae videtur proxima fuisse illa quae modo expositia est, ficus plus, & c quae & ipsa est de legatis sed quia ad praestationem legati pertinet, videtur duabus prioribus posterior, quamvis parum hic interfit.
units.tr: Perhaps the stipulation concerning fruits came next after this in the edict. For just as the stipulation on legacies is general, covering every legacy, so this stipulation is special, concerning only a legacy of usufruct, and the whole title as in ff. quemadmodum utatur. is devoted to it. Tribonian did not put it where he treated the praetorian stipulations but long before, where he treated usufruct. In the edict, however, it was placed in this position, as can be seen from the inscriptions of laws 1, 2, 3 and 7, which are by Ulpian, from his book 79 on the edict, the book in which he explained these praetorian stipulations concerning legacies, and also the one concerning the pupillary matter, etc. Closest to this fideicommissary stipulation seems to have been the one just set out, whether more, etc., which is also concerning legacies; but because it relates to the performance of the legacy, it seems to come after the two previous ones, although little turns on this here.

units.la: Est & stipulatio sive cautio de collatione, quae item pertinet ad successiones de qua nl.1 §. inber. l.20. filium. §. videamus de bon. poss. cont. ab. quae cautio etiam videtur fuisse praetoria, d. ff. inber. sed eius cautionis mentio facta fuit in edicto de collatione supra expositio. Videtur tamen & hoc loco inter stipulationes praetorias ea collocationis cautio sive stipulatio in edicto posita fuisse, ut indicat l.1. ff. de collat. bon. quae est Vlp. d. lib.79. & totaagit de stipulatione collationis. Idem quoque indicat l.1. §.9. inber. & §.11. juris. d. tit. ubi adducitur Pomp. lib.79. ad edictum de hac cautione, ut & Pomp in extremis libris ad edictum videatur de hac quoque cautione explicasse. Ratio ordinis ut prætoriis actionib: ideoq; fortasse in edicto perpetuo posita hoc in loco aut fortasse adhuc posteriori. Id enim indicat Imp. in d. l. 2 § quarius, C. de vt. jur. enucl. ubi ait illas actiones ædilitias una cum duplæ stipulationem in edicto perpetuo fuisse in loca devia, rejectas & multum distantia, scil. ut puto distantia ab actionibus empti & venditi. Verba autem edicti ædilitii exstant in l. 1. & 1. 3. ædiles aiunt. l. 42 quia vulgo. ff. de ædil. edicto. Fuerunt autem 3. actiones, aut 4 potius: Tres quidem ex edicto ædilitio, Nempe redhibitoria, æstimatoria, sive quanti minoris. l. si quid 10. de ædil. edict. quæ quanti minoris non tantum est ædilitia, sed etiam est altera eo nomine, sed civilis. l. 13. Julianus, de act. empti: & tertia actio in factum, ex tert a parte ædilitii edicti de qua l. b. n. 40. §. 1. & l. fqq. de ædil. edict. IV. Est actio duplæ ex hac cautione, sive stipulatione de evictione, de qua jam dictum. Hoc autem eodem libro 8o. alia stipulatio, sive cautio prætoria explicata fuit ab Ulpiano nimirum cautio novi operis, ut indicat. l. 21. stipulatio. de nov. op. nunc. quæ est ex hoc lib. 8o. Ulp. quæ interpretatio prætorias numeratur. l. 1 & 2 de st. p. pret. Cui fuit proxima cautio sive stipulatio dani infecti, quæ etiā inter stipulationes prætorias commemoratur, d. l. 1. & §. prætoria. Inst. de divis. stipul. quā Ulp. explicavit lib. 8. ut prioris novi operis, 8.1, ut indicat inscriptio. l. 24. 26. 28. & 30. quæ sunt ex eodem lib. 81. Idem quoq; indicat. l. 25. 27. & 31. quæ sunt Pauli ex lib. 78. ad edictum quævis à Tribun. hæ stipulationes novi operis & dani infecti sub tit. de novi op. nunc & sub tit. de dam. inf. fuerint relatæ, propter argumenti similitudinem. Ratio a. ordinis cur hæc dani infecti stipulatio inter prætorias ultimum locum obtineat, hæc mihi videtur, quia scil. ad hanc tu demum descendatur, cui aliis actionibus damnū farciri non potest, ita, ut quod ad damnū hæc actio & stipulatio, sit extremum subsidium. l. 32. § si ad bus in sin. & 2. ll. fqq. ff. de dam. inf. Plura edicta post has stipulationes prætorias in edicto prope sita non reperio, ut ea quod ex ultimis duob. lib. Ulp. nempe 82. & 83. ité Pauli duob. ultimis 29. & 30 ité Caii duobus ultimis, 31. & 32. (quod quis jure miretur) nullæ leges in ff. relatæ sint. Fortasse quod edicta quædam iis explicarentur inusitata & jam abolita, ut fortasse edictā de prædiatorib. quod ad fisci pertinere videtur. Et sane in sententiis Pauli lib. 5. post stipulationes statim ponitur tit. de jure fisc. Sed nihil certi. Et de edicto hos de prædiatoribus jā supra nonnulli dictum. Atque hæc de ordine, sive Oeconomia edicti perpetui, à Juliano cōpositi, jussu & mandato Hadriani Imperatoris ut supra d. l. pen. C. de condict. indeb. Prætoris officium in Restitutionibus Actionibus. Bonorum possessionibus Missionibus in possessionē. Interdictis: Exceptionibus, Stipulationibus prætoriis. Hinc pendet ordo edicti perpetui.
units.tr: There is also the stipulation or security concerning collation, which likewise pertains to successions; see l. 1 §. inber., l. 20, filium §. videamus de bon. poss. cont. tab., and this security also seems to have been praetorian (said ff. inber.). But mention of this security was made in the edict on collation, set out above. Yet here too it seems that this security or stipulation of collation was placed among the praetorian stipulations in the edict, as indicated by l. 1, ff. de collat. bon., which is by Ulpian in the said book 79, and which deals entirely with the stipulation of collation. The same is indicated by l. 1 §. 9 inber. and §. 11 juris, in the said title, where Pomponius, book 79 on the edict, is cited concerning this security; and Pomponius also seems, in the last books on the edict, to have explained this security as well. The reason for the order: as with the praetorian actions, this was perhaps placed in the perpetual edict at this point, or perhaps even later. For the Emperor indicates this in the said l. 2 §. quarto, C. de vet. jur. enucl., where he says that those aedilician actions, together with the double stipulation, stood in the perpetual edict in out-of-the-way places, set apart and far removed, namely, as I suppose, far from the actions of purchase and sale. The words of the aedilician edict survive in l. 1 and l. 3, "the aediles say," l. 42, quia vulgo, ff. de aedil. edicto. There were three actions, or rather four: three from the aedilician edict, namely the redhibitory action, the aestimatory action, or action for the lesser price (l. si quid 10, de aedil. edict.), which, as to the lesser price, is not only aedilician but also has another, civil form (l. 13, Julianus, de act. empti); and a third, the action in factum, from the third part of the aedilician edict, concerning which see l. b. n. 40 §. 1 and l. fqq., de aedil. edict. IV. There is the action for double from this security or stipulation concerning eviction, already mentioned. In this same book 80, another praetorian stipulation or security was explained by Ulpian, namely the security for new work, as indicated by l. 21, stipulatio, de nov. op. nunc., which is from this book 80 of Ulpian; this interpretation is counted among the praetorian ones (l. 1 and 2, de st. p. pret.). Next to it came the security or stipulation for damage not yet done (damni infecti), which is also mentioned among the praetorian stipulations (said l. 1, and §. praetoria, Inst. de divis. stipul.). Ulpian explained it in book 81, as the first of the security for new work, as the inscription indicates (l. 24, 26, 28 and 30), which are from the same book 81. The same is indicated by l. 25, 27 and 31, which are by Paulus, from book 78 on the edict; these stipulations for new work and for damage not yet done were reported by Tribonian under the title de novi operis nuntiatione and under the title de damno infecto, because of the similarity of their subject matter. My view of the reason for the order, why this stipulation for damage not yet done holds the last place among the praetorian ones, is that one comes to it only when the damage cannot be made good by other actions, so that this action and stipulation are the last resort concerning damage (l. 32 §. si ades in fin. and 2 ll. fqq., ff. de dam. inf.). I do not find more edicts placed near these praetorian stipulations in the edict, since no laws in the Digest are cited from the last two books of Ulpian, namely 82 and 83, nor from the last two of Paulus, 29 and 30, nor from the last two of Gaius, 31 and 32 (which one might wonder at). Perhaps some edicts were explained there which were unusual and already obsolete, such as perhaps the edict concerning the praediatores, which seems to pertain to the fisc. And indeed in the Sentences of Paulus, book 5, the title de jure fisci is placed immediately after the stipulations. But nothing is certain. And some have already said something above about the edict concerning the praediatores. So much concerning the order, or economy, of the perpetual edict, composed by Julian by command and mandate of the Emperor Hadrian, as above, in the said l. pen. C. de condict. indeb. The office of the praetor: in restitutions, actions, possessions of goods, missions into possession, interdicts, exceptions, praetorian stipulations. On this depends the order of the perpetual edict.

units.la: OECONOMIA LIBRO- RUM ET TITVLORVM DI- GESTORUM.
units.tr: The Arrangement of the Books and Titles of the Digest.

units.la: LIBER PRIMUS.
units.tr: BOOK ONE.

units.la: EXPLICATO, quantum ex fragmentis & reliquis veterum scriptorum juris in vestigare licuit ordine edicti perpetui reliquum nunc est, ut ad pandectarum oeconomiam & ordine accedamus. Et siquidem de 7. partium, in quas pandectæ sunt distributæ, ordine jam dictum proximum est, ut de librorum, qui sunt 50. collocatione dicamus. Sed ne longiores simus, cum librorum ordo, ex titulorum ordine recte intelligi possit, videamus statim de ipso, titulorum ordine: eoq; ordine explicato, de ipsarum legum & capitum inter se ordine sub titulis positorum explicabimus.
units.tr: Having explained, so far as I have been able to trace it from the fragments and remaining writings of the ancient jurists, the order of the Perpetual Edict, it now remains that we come to the arrangement of the Pandects. Since we have already dealt with the order of the seven parts into which the Pandects are divided, the next task is to speak of the arrangement of the books, which number fifty. But so that I do not become too long, since the order of the books can be rightly understood from the order of the titles, let us look first at the order of the titles itself. Once that order has been explained, we shall go on to explain the order of the laws and chapters placed under the titles.

units.la: Ergo primi tituli 4. pertinent ad principia juris eaq; est ratio, ut sint primi, quemadmodum & in initio sunt duo. Inter hos autem 4. titulos de principiis juris, hoc est, de definitionibus, divisionibus, & generalibus quibusdam regulis juris, cur primum locum teneat titulus de justitia et jure: ratio est tum quia generalis est, tum quia definitiones & divisiones justitiæ & juris continent. Justitia a. est principium juris, sive finis juris prudentiæ, Ideoque recte de ea statim initio agitur. Finis enim in scientiis practicis est verum & præcipuum earum principium. Huic tit. proximus adjungitur tit. 2. de orig. jur &c. tum quia & hic est generalis. Ut enim prior definitiones & divisiones justitiæ & juris, ita hic originem juris continet: tum quia cum juris scripti 6. sint partes, responsa Edicta plebiscita leges, Senatusconsulta, & constitutiones, sub hoc tit. de duabus partibus non nihil agitur, de edictis & responsis, & iis, ad quos hæ partes pertinent, nimirum de prætoribus & magistratib. jus dicentib. & de Jureconsultis, & de prudentibus jus reddentibus & interpretantibus: alioqui hæ duæ partes, edicta scil. & responsa prudentum in reliquo toto pandectarum corpore continentur. Tertius tit. de legibus, Senatusconsultis de longa consuetudine: quo aliæ duæ species juris leges & Senatusconsulta continentur, imo & plebiscita, quia legum appellatione comprehenduntur.
units.tr: First, then, the first four titles concern the principles of law, and the reason they come first is the same as that they stand at the beginning. Among these four titles on the principles of law, that is, on definitions, divisions and certain general rules of law, the reason why the title on justice and law holds the first place is twofold: it is general, and it contains the definitions and divisions of justice and law. Justice is indeed the principle of law, or the end of the science of jurisprudence, and so it is rightly treated first of all. For in the practical sciences the end is the true and chief principle of them. The title next to this, the second, On the origin of law, etc., is attached to it, because it too is general. Just as the earlier title contains the definitions and divisions of justice and law, so this one contains the origin of law. Moreover, since there are six parts of written law (responsa, edicts, plebiscites, laws, senatusconsults and constitutions), this title deals to some extent with two of these parts, namely edicts and responsa, and with those to whom these parts belong, that is, with praetors and magistrates who declare the law, and with jurists, and with the prudent men who give and interpret the law. Otherwise these two parts, namely edicts and the responsa of the jurists, are contained in the whole remaining body of the Pandects. The third title, On laws, senatusconsults and long custom, contains the two other kinds of law, laws and senatusconsults, and indeed plebiscites too, since they are comprehended under the name of laws.

units.la: §. constat. de jure naturali, &c. quo tit. & de consuetudine agitur, brevitatis causa ut principia juris, tam scripti quam non scripti initio hujus operis explicentur. Cur autem de constitutionibus principum, qui est tit. quartus ultimo agatur, ratio est quia hæc juris species est recentior. Ceteræ reliquæ sint antiquiores, ut leges plebiscita, Senatusconsulta, edicta & responsa, quæ omnes partes jam fuerunt ante principes sive Imperatores. Expositis principiis juris accedit Tribun ad jus ipsum quod jus quia vel ad personas pertinet, vel ad res vel ad actiones l. 1. de statu hom. Primo de jure personarum agitur tit. 5. §. 5. 6. & 7. Ratio supra ad instit. Ex his a tit. de jure personarum tit. 5. est de stahom. tum quia partim generalis est ad omne jus personarum pertinens partim quia prima personarum divisio in liberos & servos continetur. Cui adjungitur tit. 6. de his qui sui vel alieni juris sunt, quia sub eo continetur divisio personarum in eos qui sunt sui juris & in eos qui alieno juri sunt subjecti, ut supra dictum ad Instit. Huic proximus est tit. 7. de adopt. & emancipationib. ratio est, quia qui alieno juri sunt subjecti, aut sunt servi aut filiifam. de utrisq; dictum est tit. 6. sed filiifam. facit vel natura vel adoptio, l. 1. h. tit. 7 De natura, h. e. procreatione ex iustis nuptiis d. tit. 6. Nunc de adoptionibus qui modus est civilis & recentior, ideoq; posteriori loco hic positus, ut & in instit. ut autem filiusfam fit duobus modis potissimum natura & adoptione ita & definitum esse filiusfam certis modis, de quibus item h. tit. 7. Ratio ordinis ad instit. tit. 12 juri personarum proximum est jus rerum, ratio in instit. de quo jure unus est hic titulus 13. de div. fer. & qual. Reliquat pars tertia juris de actionibus sive judiciis, in quibus fere totum corpus ff. continetur, propterea quod pandectae sint accommodatae edicto perpetuo quod edictum ad judicia & actiones fuit dispositum, ut supra dictum. Judiciis autem quia praesunt praetores & magistratus statim initio hujus tertiae partis de magistratuum officiis explicatur, ut dictum libr. 1. Cod. Et primum quidem tit. 9. agitur de senatorio. Ratio ordinis est, quia ex ordine senatorio sunt plerique magistratus: cum etiam quia ipse Imperator est pars ordinis senatorii, qui tam quam caput senatui praesidet. Huic adjungitur tit. 10. de officio conf. & ei titul. 11. de off. praef. praetor. & huic titulus 2. de off. praef. urbi. cum tamen in Cod. prius de officio praefecti praetorio agitur. Sed ratio ordinis haec est, cur de consule primum agitur, quia scil hic magistratus est antiquissimus & summus. Namet si officium praefecti praetorio, & officium praefecti urbi, & quaestura etiam antiquiorem originem habent nimirum sub regib. ipsis ante Coss. inducta, tamen praefectura & quaestura de quib. hic agitur, longe differunt ab antiquis praefecturis, & quaestura Cura praesectura praetorio praeferatur praefecturae urbi dictum supra a 1 Cod. Ratio a. cur de officio praefecti praet. qui est tit. 11. statim post tit. de off. Coss. agitur est summa dignitas & potestas hujus praefecti, tempore Justiniani, quae eadem ratio est, cur ei statim adjungitur tit. 12. de off. praef. urb. & et huic adjungitur tit. 13. de off. quaest. ut explicatu in C. His adjunguntur duo praetores & praefecti vigiliae: praetores quidem prius, tit. 4. de of. pret. tu propter majorem eorum potestatem, tu propter antiquitate. Praetores n. diu ante Imperatores sunt creati. l. 2. §. cumq. Coss. de orig. jur. Praefectus a. vigilum ab Octaviano Augusto, l. 1. de off. praef. vig qui est titulus 1. Et haec de officio magistratuum urbanorum: nunc de provincialibus ut &c: in C. libo. in C.lib.1. Ex provincialib. a. I. de officio proconf. & leg.tit. 16. propter antiquiorem originem. Nam proconsul ante Imperatores, prælesab Imp.inductus est, ut explicat Dio lib. 53. Itaq; tit. de off. proconf. statim sequitur tit. de off.prafecti. Aug. ad.17. quia & hic proconsuli est similis.l.1.de off. praf.Aug. & huic posteatit. 18.de off. praf.cui recte adiungitur tit. 19.de off.procurat. Cæf. quia ut præses nomine Cæsaris præest Rëip. funde & legatus Cæsaris dicitur.l.1.de off.pra.)ita & hic procuratorem Cæsaris procurat in provinciis, ideoq; procurator Cæsaris dicitur. Sed præsidis nomen est generale, l 1. de off. pref. procuratoris est speciale: deinde illius maior est potestas, quàm huius ideoq; de hac posterius agitur, quem sequitur tit. 20. de off. iurid. Ratio est, quia priores sunt magis generales, nimirum universis prouinciis præfecti. Iuridicus autem est speciali ut puta uni civitati Alexandriæ præ- positus. Hunc sequitur tit. 21. de off. eius cui mand. est iur.fd. Ratio est quia priores habent propriam iurisdictionem, hic agitur de iis, qui non habent propriam sed mandatam, qui sæpè non magistratus sunt. Quibus adiungitur tit.ult. de officio assessorum. Nam & hi loco sunt magistratus, imò neque propriam neque mandatam habent iurisdictionem & magistratuum sunt consiliarii & comites. Et hæc de libro primo in quo hæc 4. Principia iuris, ius personarum, ius rerum, & officia magistratuum continentur.
units.tr: The paragraph "Constat" on natural law, etc., in which custom is also treated, is briefly explained at the beginning of this work, so that the principles of law, both written and unwritten, are set out at the outset. The reason why the fourth title, On the constitutions of the princes, is treated last is that this kind of law is more recent. The others are older: laws, plebiscites, senatusconsults, edicts and responsa, all of which existed before the princes or emperors. Having set out the principles of law, the Tribonian proceeds to law itself, which pertains either to persons, or to things, or to actions (l. 1, De statu hominum). First the law of persons is treated, in title 5, §§ 5, 6 and 7; the reason was given above, at the Institutes. Accordingly, after the title on the law of persons, title 5, De statu hominum, comes first, partly because it is general and pertains to all the law of persons, and partly because the first division of persons into free and slave is contained in it. To this is added title 6, On those who are under their own or another's power, because under it is contained the division of persons into those who are sui juris and those who are subject to another's power, as was said above at the Institutes. Next to it is title 7, On adoptions and emancipations. The reason is that those who are subject to another's power are either slaves or children in power. Both have been discussed in title 6, but children in power come into being either by nature or by adoption (l. 1, this title 7). By nature, that is, by procreation from lawful marriage, in the said title 6. Now adoptions, which are a civil and more recent mode, are placed in the later position here, as also in the Institutes. And just as a child in power arises chiefly in two ways, by nature and by adoption, so the state of being a child in power has been defined by certain modes, which are also treated in this title 7. The reason for this order is given in the Institutes, title 12. After the law of persons comes the law of things, the reason for which is in the Institutes, and of this law there is one title here, title 13, On divisions of things and their qualities. The remaining third part of law concerns actions or judicial proceedings, and in it nearly the whole body of the Digest is contained, because the Pandects were adapted to the Perpetual Edict, which was arranged with respect to judicial proceedings and actions, as said above. Since praetors and magistrates preside over judicial proceedings, the third part begins by explaining the duties of the magistrates, as was said in Book 1 of the Code. And first, indeed, title 9 treats of the senatorial office. The reason for this order is that most magistrates come from the senatorial order, and also because the emperor himself is a member of the senatorial order, presiding over the senate as its head. To this is joined title 10, On the office of the consul, and to that title 11, On the office of the praetorian prefect, and to this title 2, On the office of the prefect of the city. Yet in the Code the office of the praetorian prefect is treated first. But the reason for this order is this: why the consul is treated first, namely, that this magistracy is the most ancient and the highest. And although the office of the praetorian prefect, the office of the prefect of the city, and the quaestorship also have a more ancient origin, having been introduced under the kings themselves, before the consuls, nevertheless the prefecture and quaestorship with which this part is concerned differ greatly from the ancient prefectures and quaestorships. The prefecture of the praetorium is placed before the prefecture of the city, as was said above at 1 Code. The reason why the office of the praetorian prefect, which is title 11, is treated immediately after the title on the office of the consuls, is the high dignity and power of this prefect in the time of Justinian. For the same reason, title 12, On the office of the prefect of the city, is joined to it, and to this is joined title 13, On the office of the quaestor, as is explained in the Code. To these are added two praetors and the prefect of the watch: the praetors indeed, first, title 4, On the office of the praetor, both because of their greater power and because of their antiquity, for praetors were created long before the emperors (l. 2, § cumque Consules, On the origin of law). The prefect of the watch, however, was established by Octavian Augustus (l. 1, On the office of the prefect of the watch, which is title 1). And these are the things concerning the office of the urban magistrates. Now concerning the provincial magistrates, and so on, in the Code, Book 1. Among the provincial magistrates, the proconsul is treated in the Digest, title 16, On the office of the proconsul, on account of his more ancient origin. For the proconsul existed before the emperors, having been introduced by the praetors, as Dio explains in Book 53. Therefore title 16, On the office of the proconsul, is immediately followed by title 17, On the office of the prefect of Augustus, because this office too is similar to that of the proconsul (l. 1, On the office of the prefect of Augustus). After this comes title 18, On the office of the prefect, to which title 19, On the office of the procurator of Caesar, is rightly joined, because just as the president governs the commonwealth in the name of Caesar and is called Caesar's legate (l. 1, On the office of the praeses), so here the procurator of Caesar manages Caesar's affairs in the provinces, and is therefore called the procurator of Caesar. But "praeses" is a general name, while "procurator" is a special one; and further, the power of the former is greater than that of the latter, and therefore the latter is treated later. It is followed by title 20, On the office of the juridicus. The reason is that the earlier ones are more general, being prefects over all the provinces, whereas the juridicus is a special officer, set, for example, over a single city, Alexandria. He is followed by title 21, On the office of the one to whom jurisdiction has been entrusted. The reason is that the earlier officers have their own jurisdiction, whereas here the subject is those who do not have their own but a delegated jurisdiction, and who are often not magistrates at all. To these is added the last title, On the office of assessors, for these too hold a place as magistrates; indeed they have neither their own nor a delegated jurisdiction, but are counsellors and companions of the magistrates. And these are the things concerning the first book, in which these four principles of law, the law of persons, the law of things, and the offices of the magistrates are contained.

units.la: II. LIBER
units.tr: Book II

units.la: Vod ad librum secundum attinet in quo hæc quatuor. quoq; continentur I. tituli generales de iurisdictione. II. In ius vocatio. III. Editio. IV. Pacta & transactiones, quæ 15. titulis explicantur: quorum 1. est de iurisdictione. tum quia in edicto perpetuo hic ordo fuit, quem ff. imitantur.l. 2. de stat. hom. tum quia hic titulus est generalis naturam iurisdictionis & imperii generaliter explicans, quamvis sub eodictum quoq; contineatur contra corruptores albi prætoris Sed hoc quoq; est generale, contra omnium edictorum propositorum in albo corruptores Recte quoq; tit. magistratuum adiungitur tit. de iurisdict. quæ est illorum aut propria aut mandata 2. tit. quod quisq; iuris, &c. Nā & hic ut prior est generalis & ad officium pertinet cuiuslibet ius dicentis. Sic & 3. titulus, si quis in ius dit. non obtemp. est generalis: sed priorad ius dicentem hic ad eum, cui ius dicitur pertinet ut ius dicenti obtemperet ideoque Tribu.hunc titulum fecit posteriorem: quamvis in edicto prior fuerit. ut indicat l.1. si quis ius dic. &c. quæ est Vlp ex lib. 1. ad edictium, cum l.1. quod quisque iur. &c.l.7. de iurisdict. quæ est contra corruptores albi prætoris sint ex libro 3. eiusdem. His tribus generalibus titulis ad iurisdictionem pertinentibus subiicitur statim titulus 4. de in ius voc. cum tamen in edicto perpetuo prius fuerit edictum de edendo, ut dict. 5. in ordine edicti perpetui. Ratio ordinis differentiæ inter C. & ff. est quia in C. Iæpius, & accuratius ordinem edicti secutus est Trib. & ff. ut sæpè dictum. Deinde, quia tempore Justin. hæc duo (in jus vocatio & editio) simul fiebant, cum olim editio prius, vocatio posterius fieret. Et hinc est quod judicia exordium capere dicantur ab in jus vocatione. f. omnium Inst. de pœn. tem. litig. Sunt autem 9. tituli ad vocationem pertinentes, quorum primus est hic de in jus voc. tit. 4. quia est generalis. Huic proximus est tit. f. siquis in jus voc. &c. ubi edicta de jurisdictione fuerunt proposita ut indicat l. 1. tit. 5. & l. 1. tit. 6. quæ leges sunt ex 1. lib. usque ad edictum ideoq; ad jurisdictionem pertinentes, sed Tribun. ad in jus vocationem ista retulit, quia edicta hæc, etsi erant de jurisdictione, tamen etiam loquebantur de in jus vocando: ut si quis in jus vocarit ad jurisdictionem alienam. In jus autem vocatus aut ire debet aut causas habere, cur non veniat: ut si sit vocatus ad eum, cujus jurisdictioni non est subjectus, hoc est adjudicem non competentem, ut hodie vulgò loquimur. Et huc pertinet titulus f. aut si ipse statim non venit cogitur fidejussorem dare judicio sisti, quo pertinet titulus sextus. in jus vocati ut eant, aut satis vel cautum dent. Cui adjungitur titul. 7. ne quis eum qui in jus &c. qui est posterior, quia delictum continet vi impedientis vocatum. Huic adjungitur tit. 8. qui satis d. eog. Ratio ordinis est quia priores 4. tituli de in jus voc. ad eos pertinent, qui sunt vocati & non tum venerunt: hic autem & 4. seqq. sunt de iis qui jam venerunt, aut certè de iis qui sunt parati, nec recusant venire, sed impediuntur, aut aliqui dilationem petunt: itaq; cogantur promittere judicio sisti, & aut fidejussores dare, aut jurare, quo pertinet hic tit. 8. Eodem quoq; pertinet tit. 9. si ex nox. cauf. Nam ut tit. 8. ita & h est de cautione, sive promissione judicio sisti: sed hic est de servo, & proinde posterior. Servus tamen exhibetur potius, quia judicio sistitur: quia non est persona idonea sed Domin' ejus nomine conventus cautionem hanc judicio sisti præstat. l. 3. ne quis eum qui. &c. Huic est proximus titulus 10. de eo per quem fiat. &c Ratio est quia post promissionem judicio sisti, interdum fit ut per alium quis impediatur invitus: interdum ut iusta de causa excusetur. Ad alium pertinet hic tit 10. qui differt a titulo 7 supra. Nam ut iam dictum hic titulus est de eo quod fit post vocationem, sed ille 7. ut & 3. præced. sunt de ipsa vocatione, dum qui vocatur vi eximiturne in ius eat: hic tit. 10. de eo qui iam vocatus, & fortasse pergens in ius impeditur. Ad iustas autem causas excusationis, propter quas cautioni sive promissioni judicio sisti quis non obtemperat, pertinet titul. 11. si quis caution. &c. & tit. 12. de feriis, &c. Nam titulus 11. est generalis, h. e. plerasq; excusationis causas continet. tit 12. est specialis vnam tantum nempe feriás complectens. Hunc sequitur titulus 13. de Edicto. In edicto autem perpetuo alius fuit ordo. Nam cautiones istæ judicio sisti non omnes hic initio, sed quædam in fine ubi de cautionibus sive stipulationibus prætoriis positæ fuerunt, ut supra dictum. quemadmodum & hoc edictum, quo quis impeditur per alium obtemperare judicio sisti inferius posiEt haec ratio, quia priores duae restitutionum species metus & dolus simul generales omnib. tam maiorib. quam minoribus copetentes: haec est species, q minorib. tantu datur, ideoq; posterior. Cui proxima est species cap. diminutio, de qua tit. ff. de cap. min. Nam haec species est specialis h.e. tam ad cap. minutos sive ad emancipatos, deportatos, &c. pertinens. Meritoautem & iusta ratione prius de minoribus, quam de capite minutis agitur: quia illorum integer est status, ideoque melior. Huic proximus est tit. exquib. caus. maior. quo continetur f. species restitutionis in integrum, nempe absentia Reip causa, qui titulus item specialis est ad maiores pertinens. Prius autem de minoribus, posterius de maioribus agitur hic & in Cod. credo propterea quod etiamsi absentia haec est iustissima causa restitutionis l.1.b.tit. aetas tamen minor videtur iustior, quia aetati minori maxime favetur & succurritur: deinde minor aetas natura prior est. Est & species 6. just° error quaerine dicto hoc in loco fuit posita, sed a Tribun. reiecta est in tractatu de tutel. sub tit. quod falso tut. & c. l. 27 infra propterea quod ea species de tutore agit, eoque falso qui se pro tutore gessit. His restitutionum 6. speciebus adiungitur tit. 7. de alien. iud. mut. &c. Ratio dicta ad edictum. Huic proximus est tit. 8. de recept. & c Ratio dicti 9. Cui proximus est tit. 9. Naut. caup. stab. &c. Ratio est, q ut prior est de receptis arbitrorum, sive de arbitris ita & hic est de receptis nautarum &c. ita ut apter similitudinem tantum hic tit. priori sit adiectus cum tamen receptarum arbitrorum a receptis cauponum &c. multum differant. Nam recepta arbitrorum sunt negocia per arbitros, eorumq; sententia & arbitrio terminanda sed recepta nautarum, &c. sunt res ipsis commissae, & quasi depositae, ideoque recepta nautar. &c. sunt deposito similia: ideoque ut depositarius, ita & nautae, si gratis receperint depositi tenentur.
units.tr: As for the second book, which contains these four subjects: (I) the general titles on jurisdiction; (II) summons to court; (III) the edict; (IV) pacts and transactions. These are explained in fifteen titles, of which the first is on jurisdiction. It comes first because this was the order of the Perpetual Edict, which the Digest follows (l. 2. de stat. hom.), and because this title is a general one, explaining generally the nature of jurisdiction and of authority. It is placed under the heading concerning the corrupters of the praetor's white board, though this too is general, being directed against all who corrupt the edicts posted in the white board. Rightly, too, the title on magistrates is joined to the title on jurisdiction, since their jurisdiction is either their own or delegated (tit. quod quisq. iuris, &c.). For this title, like the first, is general and pertains to the office of anyone who pronounces law. Likewise the third title, si quis in ius dit. non obtemp., is general; but, since it concerns the one who pronounces law, it pertains here to the one to whom law is pronounced, that he should obey the one pronouncing it. Tribonian therefore made this title the later one, although in the edict it came first, as l. 1. si quis ius dic. &c. shows. That law is from Ulpian, book 1 on the edict, and with l. 1. quod quisque iur. &c. and l. 7. de iurisdict., which is against the corrupters of the praetor's white board, comes from book 3 of the same work. To these three general titles on jurisdiction there is at once added title 4, de in ius voc., although in the Perpetual Edict the edict de edendo came first, as the said title 5 indicates in the order of the Perpetual Edict. The reason for the difference in order between the Code and the Digest is that in the Code, Tribonian followed the order of the edict more often and more accurately, as is often said. Further, in Justinian's time these two things, summons to court and the edict, were done together, whereas formerly the edict came first and the summons after. Hence it is that trials are said to begin with the summons to court (Inst. de poen. temer. litig., f. omnium). There are nine titles concerning summons, of which the first is de in ius voc., title 4, because it is general. Next to it is the title si quis in ius voc. &c., where edicts on jurisdiction were posted, as l. 1. tit. 5 and l. 1. tit. 6 indicate. These laws come from book 1 up to the edict and so pertain to jurisdiction; but Tribonian referred them to summons, because these edicts, although they concerned jurisdiction, also spoke of summoning to court, as when someone summons another to a court of foreign jurisdiction. One summoned to court must either go or have reasons why he does not come, for example if he has been summoned before one to whose jurisdiction he is not subject, that is, before a judge who lacks competence, as we commonly say today. To this belongs the title f. aut si ipse statim non venit cogitur fidejussorem dare judicio sisti, to which the sixth title belongs, in jus vocati ut eant, aut satis vel cautum dent. To this is added title 7, ne quis eum qui in jus &c., which comes later, because it deals with the offence of using force to prevent a summoned person. To this is added title 8, qui satis d. eog.
