The reason for the order is that the first four titles on summons concern those who have been summoned and did not then come, whereas this title and the four following concern those who have already come, or at least those who are ready and do not refuse to come, but are hindered, or who ask for a delay; they are therefore compelled to promise to appear for judgment and to give sureties or swear an oath, which is the subject of this title 8. To this also belongs title 9, si ex nox. cauf. For, as with title 8, this too concerns the security or promise to appear for judgment; but this one concerns a slave, and so comes later. A slave, however, is produced rather than summoned, because he is not a competent person; his master, sued in his name, gives this security for appearance (l. 3. ne quis eum qui &c.). Next to this is title 10, de eo per quem fiat &c. The reason is that after the promise to appear, it sometimes happens that a person is hindered against his will by another, or is excused for a just cause. This title 10 concerns the latter and differs from title 7 above. For, as already said, this title concerns what happens after the summons, whereas title 7 and the third preceding title concern the summons itself, namely whether one who is summoned is freed by force from going to court. Title 10 concerns one who has already been summoned and is perhaps hindered while on his way to court. The just causes of excuse, on account of which someone does not obey the security or promise to appear for judgment, belong to title 11, si quis caution. &c., and title 12, de feriis, &c. For title 11 is general, that is, it contains most causes of excuse; title 12 is special, embracing only one, namely the holidays. This is followed by title 13, de Edicto. In the Perpetual Edict, however, the order was different. For those securities for appearance were not all placed here at the beginning, but some at the end, where the praetorian cautions or stipulations were set out, as said above; and so too this edict, by which someone is hindered by another from obeying the summons to appear, is placed further below. The reason is that the two earlier species of restitution, for fear and for fraud, are general and belong to both greater and lesser persons; this species is granted only to lesser persons, and is therefore later. Next to it is the species of capitis deminutio, concerning which the title is ff. de cap. min. For this species is special, that is, it pertains to those who have undergone capitis deminutio, or to the emancipated, the deported, and so on. And rightly and for good reason, the matter of minors is treated before that of those who have undergone capitis deminutio, because the status of the former is intact and therefore better. Next is the title ex quib. caus. maior., which contains the seventh species of restitution in integrum, namely absence on public business; this title is likewise special and pertains to greater persons. The minors are treated first and those of greater age afterwards here and, I think, in the Code, for this reason: although absence on public business is a most just cause of restitution (l. 1. b. tit.), minority nevertheless seems the more just, because the young are most favoured and helped, and because minority is prior by nature. There is also a sixth species, just error, which was placed in this position in the dictum, but Tribonian rejected it in the treatise on guardianship, under the title quod falso tut. &c., l. 27 infra, because that species concerns a guardian, and so one who falsely acted as guardian. To these six species of restitution is added title 7, de alien. iud. mut. &c. The reason has been given in the discussion of the edict. Next to it is title 8, de recept. &c., the reason of which has been given under the ninth. Next to it is title 9, Naut. caup. stab. &c. The reason is that, as the former is on the undertakings of arbiters, or on arbitrators, so this one is on the undertakings of shipmasters, and so on. It has been attached to the former title only for the sake of resemblance, although the undertakings of arbiters and those of innkeepers and the like differ greatly. For the undertakings of arbiters are matters to be settled through arbiters, by their opinion and decision; but the undertakings of shipmasters and the rest are things entrusted to them, and as it were deposited, and so the undertakings of shipmasters and the like are similar to deposit: and therefore, as a depositary, so too a shipmaster who has received goods without payment is liable.

units.la: DE II. PARTE DIGESTORUM,
units.tr: On the Second Part of the Digest,

units.la: V. LIBER.
units.tr: Book V.

units.la: ET hac de prima parte est quae dicitur de negotiis. Huic proxime adiungitur altera pars de iudiciis l. 2. f. secundum. C. de vet. iur. enucl. & f. & primi anniversi, post eorum prof. ff. quae pars secunda continetur 11. libris. Ratio ordinis dictum est supra paulo ante initiu edicti perpetui nempe ista: ut expositis iis, quae ante iudicia fieri solent, postea iam de ipsis iudiciis expletur, ut & in Cod. factum, & in edicto. Huius autem secundae partis libri primi cum sint 6. tantum tit. ad 1. cap. hic revocantur. 1. exponitur tit. generalis & communis omnium iudiciorum tit. 1. de sud. & ubi quis. Deinde adiunguntur 5. tituli speciales ad speciem illam actionis, quae generaliter petitio hereditatis dicitur pertinentes. Cur a. cu iudiciorum sive actionum species sive genera sint 2. in re & persona 3. 1. de act. prius agatur de actionib. in re, ut hac parte 2. posterius de actionib. in persona nimirum partes 3. & seqq. q idé ordo est
units.tr: This completes the first part, which is called the part on transactions. Next follows the second part, on trials, l. 2. f. secundum. C. de vet. iur. enucl. & f. & primi anniversi, post eorum prof. ff., which is contained in 11 books. The reason for this order was given above, shortly before the beginning of the perpetual edict: once the matters that usually precede trials have been set out, the trials themselves are then treated, as is done in the Code and in the Edict. Of the first book of this second part, which has only six titles, the first chapter is cited here. First, the general title common to all trials is explained, title 1, de sud. & ubi quis. Then come five special titles, relating to that kind of action which is generally called the petition of inheritance. Why the kinds of trials or actions are two, in rem and in personam, 1. de act., is explained as follows: the actions in rem are treated first, as in this second part (title 2), and afterwards the actions in personam, namely the titles 3 and following. The order is the same here.

units.la: VII. Liber.
units.tr: VII. Book

units.la: LIber 7 est de usufructu, ut lib. 6. de Rei vendic. five dominio vel quasi. Nam & ex usufructu actio in rem oritur, quæ confessoria & negatoria in rédicitur. Ex servitute quoq; prædij actio in rem oritur eodé nomine de qua posterius hic agitur, nempe lib. 8. Ratio, cur prius de usufructu quam de servitutibus prædiorum agatur, ut & in Cod. cum tamé in Inst. contrarius sit ordo, hæc est: quia usufructus dominio de quo lib. 6. fit similis. & longè similior quam servitus. l. 4. de usufructu. in eo scilicet quod ususfructus ut dominium contineat totam rei utilitatem, servitus non totam sed exiguâ duntaxat. l. 7. init. 0. de usufructu. ut & dictum ad C. Suntautem hujuslibri 7. de usufructu titul. 9. l. est de usufructu. quia generalis, & de natura atq; constitutione usufructus. Cui adjungitur tit. 2. de usufructu adcresi. quia est specialis. Nam tit. 1. exponuntur omnes modi, quibus constituitur usufructus, ut est pactum stipulatio, legatum. SCm & c quibus adjungitur hic unus nempe jus adcrescendi quo tamen modo augetur potius usus fructus jam constitutus, quam de novo constituitur. Hunc sequitur tit. 3 quando dies usufr. l. g. ced. Ratio ordinis est, quia aut prior tit. ita & hic ad legatum usumfr. pertinet Jus enim adcrescendi non in contradictibus sed in testamentis & legatis locum habet. I V. tit. est qu. b. mod. usufr. & usus amitt. Ratio est, quia priores sunt de modis constituendi, hic est de modis amittendi usufructus. Huic proximus est tit. V. de usufr. ear. rer. Ratio est quia hic est, de quo & improprio usufr. priores 4. sunt de vero. Propria minus proprijs sunt priora. ut: præstantiora & antiquiora. Huic est tit. 6. si usufr. pet. qui titul. est de actione: cófessoria & negatoria usufructs. Ratio ordinis est, quia actio est effectus, usufr. est causa. At causa prior est effectu, ita & infra sæpè. Huic adjungitur tit. 7. de op. serv. quia operæ servorum sunt usufructus hominis, hoc est servi. l. 4. d. tit. Proximus est tit. de usu & habit. Ratio est quia usus est fructui similimus, sed minus tamen juris continet quam usufructus ideoq; posterior tit. 9 & ultimus hujus libri est usufr. quemadmodum cav. sive de cautione & stipulatione fructuaria, quæ in Edicto non hic sed ultimo loco fuit posita, ut supra dictum, sed à Tribu. huc relata, quia ad usumfructum pertineat. Est autem hic tit. inter titulos de usufructu ultimus, tum propter exemplo Edicti, tum quia cautiones sunt accessoriæ, & proinde posteriores. Est igitur hic liber 7 de usufructu & aliis ei similibus, ut sunt operæ, usus, & habitatio.
units.tr: Book 7 deals with usufruct, as Book 6 dealt with the action for recovering property (de rei vindicatione), whether of ownership or of something similar to ownership. For the action in rem arising from usufruct is also called confessory and negatory. The action in rem arising from a servitude of an estate has the same name, and it is treated later here, namely in Book 8. The reason usufruct is treated before the servitudes of estates, although the order is reversed in the Code and the Institutes, is this: usufruct is similar to ownership, which was discussed in Book 6, and far more similar than servitude is (Dig. 7, de usufructu, l. 4). This is because usufruct, like ownership, takes in the whole use of a thing, whereas a servitude takes only a small part of it (l. 7 init., de usufructu, as also said in the commentary on C.). Title 1 of this Book 7, on usufruct, is general and concerns the nature and constitution of usufruct. To it is joined title 2, on the accrual of usufruct, which is more specific. Title 1 sets out all the ways in which usufruct is constituted, such as by agreement, by stipulation, and by legacy. To these is joined here the one mode, namely the right of accrual, by which usufruct already constituted is increased rather than newly constituted. This is followed by title 3, when usufruct begins (l. 9, de cedendo?). The reason for this order is that, as the previous title applies to legacies, so here also the right of accrual applies to legacies; for the right of accrual has its place not in contracts but in wills and legacies. Title 4 is on how usufruct and use are lost. The reason is that the earlier titles concern the ways of constituting usufruct, and this one concerns the ways of losing it. Next comes title 5, on the usufruct of consumable things, which is about improper usufruct, while the earlier titles treated true usufruct. Less proper things come after more proper ones, as things more excellent and more ancient come first. Next is title 6, on the action for claiming usufruct, which is the title on the confessory and negatory action for usufruct. The reason for this order is that the action is the effect, and usufruct is the cause; and the cause is prior to the effect, as is often the case further on. To this is joined title 7, on the services of slaves, because the services of slaves are the usufruct of a man, that is, of a slave (l. 4, d. tit.). Next is the title on use and habitation. The reason is that use is very similar to usufruct, but it contains less right than usufruct, and therefore it comes later. The ninth and last title of this book is on usufruct, and on the caution and stipulation concerning fruits (cautio fructuaria), which in the Edict was placed not here but in the last place, as said above, but which Tribonian brought here, because it pertains to usufruct. This title is the last among the titles on usufruct, both on account of the model of the Edict and because cautions are accessory, and therefore come later. Thus this seventh book is on usufruct and other similar things, such as services, use, and habitation.

units.la: VIII. Liber.
units.tr: VIII. Liber.

units.la: LIbri 8. argumentum est de servitutibus prædiorum continetq; 6. tit. Ratio ordinis lib. 7. supra dictum. Titul. 1. de servit. est generalis, quem duæ species servitutum sequuntur, nempe tit. 2. de serv. urb. pred. & tit. 3. de rust. prad. Ratio, quia urbana præferuntur Rusticis. Proximus est tit. 4.
units.tr: The subject of Book 8 is servitudes of estates (praedia), and it contains six titles. The reason for the order was stated above, under Book 7. Title 1, On Servitudes, is general, and it is followed by two kinds of servitude: title 2, On Urban Servitudes of Estates, and title 3, On Rural Servitudes of Estates. The reason is that urban matters take precedence over rural ones. The next is title 4.

units.la: Y. 3. communia pred.&c. ratio est, quia propria prius, communia posterius collocantur, ut jam saepe dictum, ut tit. Cod. communia utriusque jud. Hunc sequitur tit.s.sifero vind qui est de actione confessoria & negatoria: prius enim de taufa, hoc est de ipsa servitute: posterius de actione, ut de effectu explicatur. Quem sequitur tit.6.quemadmodum serv.amitt. Ratio est perspicua, quia priores tit. sunt de modis constituendae servitutis, hic est de modis amittendae.
units.tr: Title 4, On Common Estates, etc. The reason is that matters belonging to a particular person are placed first and common matters afterwards, as has often been said already, as in the title of the Code, On Matters Common to Both Judges. This is followed by title 5, If a Servitude Is Claimed, which concerns the action confessory and negatory: for the former deals with the claim, that is, with the servitude itself, and the latter with the action, which is explained as the effect. It is followed by title 6, In What Way Servitudes Are Lost. The reason is plain, since the earlier titles deal with the ways of establishing a servitude, and this one with the ways of losing it.

units.la: IX. LIBER.
units.tr: IX. BOOK.

units.la: Liber 9 Actiones de damno continet ut actio si quadr.&c. ut act. leg. Aquil. item, de effusis ac dejectis, & actiones noxales. Ratio ordinis, cur scilicet hae actiones prioribus in rem. ( cum tamen hae sint in persona adjungantur proximae, est, quia ut actio in rem domino datur: ita & istae plerraeque dantur domino & contra dominum l.1. s.alt.si quad.paup.fec.d.c.l.11 s.e M.la. s.legis.& l.43.ob id.ad leg.Aquil. Sunt autem hujus 9 libri 4 tit., quorum primo continetur si quadrup.&c. Ratio quia haec actio, utpote exl.12 tab.induct, l.1.hoc.s.reliquis actionib. hujus li.est antiquior, tit.2.ad l.Aqu l. est, hac ratione, quia ut prior, ita & ista actio est ex certa lege, quam sequitur actio de effusis & actio depositis sive dejectis. tit.3. de hu qui effuder. quae sunt non ex lege, sed ex Edicto, ideoque posteriores: imo in Edicto perpetuo non hoc loco latim post leg. Aquil. sed paulo inferius ubi de servo corrupto positae suerunt, ut supra dictum. Eo quod effusio corrumpit quoque vestimenta &c. l.1. s.hacautem verba.d. tit.3. A Tribun autem hae actiones de effusis & depositis prioremin locum sunt relatae, statim post actionem legis Aquiliae hac ratione, quia effusio & dejectio non tantum corrumpit, sed etiam laedit, & varie damnum adfert. Sed lex Aquilia multos modos damni, haec tantum effusione dejectionem & casum, hoc est certos quosdam modos speciales continet. Huc tit. sequitur tit.4. de nox. act. Nam & hic ad damnum pertinet ex servorum delicto datum alteri. Ideo autem inter actiones de damno posterimum loco tenent noxales, quia sunt tantum accessoriae, & velut adjectiones aliarum actionum, cum illae sint principales.
units.tr: Book 9 contains the actions for damage: the action "si quadrupes" etc., the action under the Lex Aquilia, likewise the actions concerning things poured out and thrown down, and the noxal actions. The reason for this order, why these actions are placed next after those in rem, although these are in personam, is that just as the action in rem is given to the owner, so these too are for the most part given to the owner and against the owner (l. 1 §. alt. si quadrupes pauperiem fecisse dicetur; l. 11 §. e Mela; §. legis; and l. 43 ob id, ad legem Aquiliam). There are four titles in this 9th book. The first treats of "si quadrupes" etc. The reason is that this action, being derived from the Twelve Tables (ex l. 12 tab. induct.; l. 1 hoc §. reliquis actionibus huius libri), is older than the other actions of this book; it is title 2, ad legem Aquiliam. The reason is this: just as the former is, so this action too rests on a certain law, and it is followed by the action concerning things poured out and the action concerning things deposited or thrown down (title 3, de his qui effuderint vel dejecerint), which do not rest on a law but on the Edict, and are therefore later. Indeed, in the Perpetual Edict they are not placed here immediately after the Lex Aquilia, but a little lower down, where they were set after the action concerning a corrupted slave, as said above, because pouring out also spoils clothes etc. (l. 1 §. hae autem verba, d. tit. 3). Among the Tribunes, however, these actions concerning things poured out and deposited were placed in the earlier position, immediately after the action of the Lex Aquilia, for this reason: pouring out and throwing down not only spoil but also injure, and bring damage in various ways. But the Lex Aquilia contains many modes of damage, while this action covers only pouring out and throwing down, that is, certain special modes. Next comes title 4, de noxalibus actionibus, for this too pertains to damage given to another by the wrongdoing of slaves. The noxal actions hold the last place among the actions for damage because they are merely accessory, and as it were additions to other actions, since those are principal.

units.la: X. LIBER.
units.tr: X. BOOK

units.la: Liber 10. est de actionibus duplicib. sive mixtis, ut in s.quadam actiones de act & de actione ad exhibendum illi persimili. Nam quatuor tantum tit hic liber continet. Ratio ordinis est, quia & hae actiones prioribus in rem sunt similes: sunt enim mixtae, hoc est partim in rem, partim in personam d. s. quadam. quarum prima hic ponitur actio finium regundorum tit.1.finium regundorum. quae tamen in C. est ultima. Ratio differentiae est quia in C ratio habitafuit rerum, de quibus est haec actio, quae sunt praediarustica, 1.2.de titulo. Rustica autem urbanis sunt posteriora. Est & altera ratio C. quia haec actio est specialis tantum ad agros pertinens, cum reliquae duae mixtæ, familiæ ercisцundæ & communi dividundo tàm ad urbana quàm ad rustica, imo etiam ad res mobiles pertineant. l. 4. famil. ercisc. Hic autem in ff. habita fuit ratio similitudinis cum actionib. in rem. Etenim hæc illis in eo persimilis, quæ fit pro vindicatione rei ut ait l. 1. hic & cohæret controversiæ proprietatis, ut ait l. 3. C. eod. Hac enim actione res petitur & vindicatur, ut actione in rem; cum reliquis non tàm vindicetur, quàm divisio petatur. 2. tit. est fam. ercisc. & 3. communi div. d. cui adjungitur tit. 4. ad exhib. quæ tamen actio & in Edicto perpetuo & in C. paulo inferius posita est quia scilicet cui fit in personam, sed tamen vindicantibus serviens, & propter eos introducta, l. 1. & 3. & 6. est autem hæc tit. recte ibi posita est, ferè in fine, sive potius in cosinio actionum in personam, sed hic priorem in locum relata est, hac de causa, quia sit quodammodo mixta ut priores. Nam tametsi proprie est in personam, d. §. est autem, maximè tamen propter vindicationem inducta est.
units.tr: Book 10 concerns mixed actions, or actions of double character, such as the actio finium regundorum and the actio ad exhibendum, which is very like it. For this book contains only four titles. The reason for the order is that these actions are similar to the earlier actions in rem: they are mixed, that is, partly in rem and partly in personam (d. §. quaedam). The first of them placed here is the action of fixing boundaries (tit. 1, finium regundorum), which in the Code, however, is last. The reason for the difference is that in the Code regard was had to the kind of things with which this action is concerned, namely rural estates (1.2 de titulo). Rural matters, however, come after urban ones. There is also a second reason in the Code: this action pertains only to fields, whereas the other two mixed actions, familiae erciscundae and communi dividundo, pertain both to urban and to rural property, and indeed even to movable goods (l. 4, famil. ercisc.). Here in the Digest, however, regard was had to the similarity with actions in rem. For this action is very like those in that it is brought for the vindication of a thing, as l. 1 hic says, and it is bound up with a dispute over ownership, as l. 3 C. eod. says. For by this action the thing is sought and claimed, as in an action in rem; whereas in the others it is not so much a claim to the thing as a demand for division. The second title is familiae erciscundae and the third communi dividundo (d.), to which is added tit. 4, ad exhibendum. This action, however, is placed in the perpetual Edict and in the Code somewhat further on, because, although it is brought in personam, it serves those who claim things and was introduced on their account (l. 1, 3 and 6). This title is rightly placed there, near the end, or rather in the company of the actions in personam; but here it has been brought forward to an earlier place, for this reason: that it is in a sense mixed, like the preceding ones. For although it is properly in personam (d. §. est autem), it was nevertheless chiefly introduced for the sake of vindication.

units.la: XI. LIBER.
units.tr: Book XI.

units.la: Libri II. sunt 8. tit. & 3. ferè partes. I. De interrogationibus tit. 1. & 2. II. Pars de quibusdam delictis. III. De religiosis. titul. 7. & ult. Ratio ordinis autem est, quia & hic liber II. affinitatem habet cum actionibus in rem, ut mox intelligetur. Nam 1. titul. est de interrogationibus in jure faciendis, &c. quia harum interrogationum usus est in actionibus in rem. & maximè interheredes, ubi de hereditate. Quæ ratio quoque est, cur hic titul sit primus, & vicinus actioni familiæ erciscundæ. Ad quem titul. 1. pertinet quoque tit. 2. de quib. reb. ad eund. judic. Nam & hic tit pertinet ad actionem familiæ erciscundæ, imò etiam ad reliquas duas mixtas actiones. l. 1. hoc tit. IV. est de servo corrupto. Ratio est, quia hæc actio datur dominio servi ab alio corrupti, quemadmodum & rei vindicat datur domino. l. 23. rem. de Rei vend. Ratio autem cur in posteriorem locum ut & sequent. sunt rejectæ, est, quia delicta continent. Ex quibus delicta continentibus hæc servi corrupti actio est prima: quia generalis est, hoc est, omnes servi corruptelas continés. Cui adjungitur titulus 4. de fugitivis, quo unna tantum species delicti & corrupti servi, nempe fuga continetur. Huic adjungitur titulus 5. de alcatoribus. tú quia & hoc est vicinum servi, tum quia ut priore titulo de fugitivis coërcentur receptatores fugitivorum, ita & hoc tit coercentur receptatores aleatorū, quod alioqui aleatoris vitium sive delictum est commune liberorum & servorum. Cui tit. proximus est tit. 6. si menf. falsi mod. Huic proximus tit. 7. de religios. Ratio est, quia & hæc actio datur domino, aut saltem jus aliquod in rē habenti ut nsumfructum ut servitutem, l. 8. offa f. in hac autem hoc tit. Ideoque est similis actionib in rem, quæ dantur habenti dominiū aut jus aliquod in rem, ut supra dictū. Cur a. in tractatu de actionib. in re hæc actio sit ultima, sive ultimū in locum rejecta, tam hic, quam in Cod. quam in ipso Edicto ratio hæc. ratio hęc est: tum quia actiones priores sunt de reb. humanis & privatis, hęc est de religiosis sive loco religioso, hoc est, sepulchro, & alterade sumptu in funus facto: quæ dicitur funeraria. Sunt enim hic plures actiones ad funus & sepulchra pertinentes, quæ merito sunt distinctæ à prioribus. & sunt posteriores quia sunt recentiores & prætoriæ, tum quia ad mortem pertinent, & ad finem hominis, tum deniq; quia hæ, ut jam dictum sint de rebus religiosis Et in Edictorum tantum de rebus humanis agatur, reĉtè prætoreas ut abEdicto suo alienas in ultimum locum rejecit, quemadmodum & in Cod. Theodos. de rebus sacris, ut de Episcopis. Ecclesiis &c. ultimo libro agitur. Huic adjungitur tit. 8. de mortuo infer. 9c. quo 2. interdicta continentur, quæ in Edicto perpetuo fuerunt posita, eo in loco ubi de interdictis, ut supra dictū, sed à Tribun. hic collocata, propter similitudinem cum priore titulo.
units.tr: Book II has 8 titles and roughly 3 parts. I. On interrogations, titles 1 and 2. II. A part on certain delicts. III. On religious places, title 7 and the last. The reason for the order is that this second book also has an affinity with the actions in rem, as will soon be seen. For the first title is on interrogations to be made in law, etc., because the use of these interrogations lies in actions in rem, and especially in the action between heirs concerning an inheritance. This is also the reason why this title stands first and is close to the action for dividing an inheritance (familiae erciscundae). The second title, tit. 2 on the matters that come before the same judge, also belongs to that title, since this title too relates to the action for dividing an inheritance, and indeed to the other two mixed actions. L. 1 of this title. IV is on the corrupted slave. The reason is that this action is given to the owner of a slave who has been corrupted by another, just as the action to recover a thing is given to its owner. L. 23, de rei vendicatione. The reason why this and the following titles are placed later is that they deal with delicts. Among the titles dealing with delicts, this action on the corrupted slave comes first, because it is general, that is, it covers all the corruptions of a slave. To it is joined title 4 on fugitives, which deals with only one species of delict and corruption of a slave, namely flight. To this is joined title 5 on gamblers, both because it is close to the slave and because, just as in the earlier title on fugitives those who harbour fugitives are punished, so in this title those who harbour gamblers are punished, since gambling is a vice or delict common to free persons and slaves alike. Next to this title comes title 6, if the document of a false measure. Next to that comes title 7, on religious places. The reason is that this action too is given to the owner, or at least to one who holds some right in the thing, such as a usufruct or a servitude (l. 8 offa f.); in this respect it is similar to the actions in rem, which are given to one who holds ownership or some right in the thing, as said above. Why this action, in the treatise on actions in rem, is the last, or placed in the last position, both here, in the Code, and in the Edict itself, the reason is this: first, because the earlier actions concern human and private affairs, whereas this one concerns religious matters or a religious place, that is, a tomb, and the expense incurred for a funeral, which is called funerary. For there are several actions here relating to funerals and tombs, which are rightly distinguished from the earlier ones; and they come later both because they are more recent and praetorian, and because they concern death and the end of a human being; and finally because, as has already been said, they concern religious things. And since the Edict deals only with human affairs, the praetor rightly placed these in the last position as foreign to his Edict, just as in the Theodosian Code, in the last book, the title on sacred things deals with bishops, churches, etc. To this is joined title 8, on the dead to be buried, which contains two interdicts that were placed in the perpetual Edict in the place where interdicts were treated, as said above, but which the Tribonian commission has placed here because of their similarity to the earlier title.

units.la: III. PARS PANDECTARUM.
units.tr: III. PART OF THE PANDECTS.

units.la: Liber XII.
units.tr: Book XII.

units.la: Liber 12. qui est initium tertiæ partis Digest continet 8 tit. Est autem dissensio inter recentiores, de 1 titulo, qui est de reb. cred. ut & de titulo secundæ partis, de judiciis, &c. sint ne hi duo tit. generales, an speciales. Nam pleriq; dicunt generales, veteres & recentes. Hotoman. in Commentar. in Paratit. ad hunc titulum, Cont. lib. 1. Disp. 4. Donell. latissimè in Comment. hic, & ante eos Alciat. hic, Anton. August. contra lib. 3. emend. cap. ult. Cujac. lib. 7. obs. cap. 32. putant esse speciales, hoc est non contineri, ut titulus de jud. totam secundam partem ff. & sub t. tul. de reb. cred. totam tertiam partem ff. ut illi putant, sed tantum ea, quæ legibus sub eo positis adferuntur. Rationes utrinque adferunt: Ut quod sint generales ad totam partem pertinentes, hæc præcipuè adfertur: quia pars secunda dicatur de judiciis pars tertia de rebus creditis l. 2. §. secundum. C. de jur. vet. enucl. & in præfat. ff. §. in secundo, sed facilius est responsio quod aliud sit de rebus, aliud de rebus creditis. Verum est tertiam partem dici de rebus sed titulus dicitur de rebus creditis. Alioqui si hæc verba de rebus creditis ad totam tertiam partem pertinerent, ponenda fuerunt paulò ante in hunc modum: Digestorum pars tertia de rebus creditis. & postea: Liber 12. & tandem: Ĉertum petatur. Idemq; initio partis secundæ fuerat faciedum. Ex quo intelligitur hæc verba de reb. creditis & de judiciis non ad ipsam partem sed ad tit. pertinere, ex quib. tamen verbis partes ipsæ appellationem sumserunt ut secunda de judiciis, tertia de rebus diceretur, quemadmodum supraad Cod. explicatum. Hoc autem lib 12. Condictiones continet: quarum prior est Condictio certi, de quâ sub hoc tit. de reb. cred. quia hæc condictio est generalis: hoc est datur vel competit ex omni causa sive obligatione & contractu certo. l. 9. certi hoc titulo. Est & altera ratio, cur hic titulus sit primus, quia sub hoc titulo, tanquam generali plures contractus à prætore propositi fuerunt in Edicto, ut supra dictum ad C. & Edictum perpetuum & ait l.1.bnjuatit. Cui adjungitur titul.2.de jurejur. quia primus est de mutuo potissimum, usus autem jurisjurandi maximè est in mutuo, quia plerunq; mutuum datur sine testibus aut instrumentis. Et hinc est quod Laberius Poëta apud Agell. 16.c.7.in sin. quid est, inquit, jurisjurandum templastrum aris alieni, hoc est, mutui ;ut Cujac. in Parat. hic. admonet. In C. tamen prius de jurejurando posterius de actione si certum petatur. Ratio ibi dicta & hæc fortassis est. quod Tribun. nihil interesse putaverit, uter priore loco ponatur, eò quod in Edicto & libris Jurisconsultorum eodem titulo de his fuerit actum. & quia in Cod alius titulus de suffragio, rectius adjungatur tit.si cert.pet. Huic autem tit. de jurejur. propter similitudinem adjungitur tit.3 de in lit.jur. quem sequitur tit.4 de cond.causa data,&c. Ratio ordinis ut intelligatur sciendum est 8. esse conditiones, quæ hic ordine explicantur. I est conditio certi de quatit 1.supra, quæ est generalis, ut ibi dictum quam nunc sequuntur 7. speciales, quorum hæc conditio causadata &c. priori proximum tenet locum. hac ratione, quia cum hæ conditiones vel sint ex causa vel sint fine causa proponuntur condictiones ex causa, ut primæ nempe condictioni certi similiores, quæ condictio certi ex omni causa est, ut ait '.9 supra de reb.cred. Est igitur secunda ex justa & honesta causa, sed non secuta. Cui adjungitur tit.5.de cond.ob turp.caus. quia honesta & justa causa est potior turpi & injusta. Hunc sequitur tit. 6 de cond.indeb. quia hæc est quidem ex causa sed falsa & putativa: cum priores sint ex vera. Verum autem falso rectè præponitur. In Codic. tamen contrarius est ordo, & post condictionem certi statim ponitur condictio indebiti quia ea valdè similis est condictioni certi, ut & in Instit quib.mod.re contrah.&c. initium est de condictione certi, §.proximus, de condictione indeb. Unde Cujac.lib.1.cap.34. hanc condictionem vocat ex promutuo illam ex mutuo & rectè sed priorem ex promutuo, non rectè. Titulus 7. & ultimus hujus libri duodecimi est de condictione sine causa. Ratio ordinis, quia priores tituli sunt de condictione ex causa quibus rectè nunc adjungitur condictio sine causa. Est & altera ratio, quia hæc condictio cum tribus proximis concurrit. Nam etsi 5. proximæ sunt ex causa, tamen quoad effectum sunt fine causa. Nam earum prima est ex causa, sed non secuta, hoc est, ad effectum perducta, & ita recidit ad non causam. II. Est ex causa turpi & injusta, quæ in jure pro nulla & non causa habetur .l.1.§.1.l.6.inf.de do.inter vir.& ux. III Est ex falsa causa & pinde valet ex nulla. Rectè igitur, ubi illæ datur, ibi & hæc datur dd.ll.& l.4.hic.
units.tr: Book 12, which begins the third part of the Digest, contains 8 titles. Recent writers disagree whether the first title, de rebus creditis, and the title that opens the second part, de judiciis, are general titles or special ones. Most call them general, both older and recent writers. Hotoman, in his Commentary on the Paratitla to this title, Contius book 1, Disp. 4, Donellus very fully in his commentary here, and before them Alciatus here, Antonius Augustinus against book 3 of the Emendations, last chapter, and Cujacius, book 7 of the Observations, chapter 32, hold that they are special. That is, the title de judiciis does not contain the whole second part of the Digest, nor the title de rebus creditis the whole third part, as the others think, but only those things that are brought under them by the laws placed beneath them. They give reasons on both sides. The main argument that they are general, extending to the whole part, is that the second part is said to be de judiciis and the third part de rebus creditis (l. 2, §. secundum, C. de jur. vet. enucl., and in the preface of the Digest, §. in secundo). But it is easier to answer that de rebus is one thing and de rebus creditis another. It is true that the third part is said to be de rebus, but the title is said to be de rebus creditis. Otherwise, if the words de rebus creditis applied to the whole third part, they should have been placed a little earlier in this form: "Digest part three, de rebus creditis", and then "Book 12", and finally "Certum petatur". The same would have had to be done at the beginning of the second part. From this it is understood that the words de rebus creditis and de judiciis pertain not to the part itself but to the title. Yet from these words the parts themselves took their names, so that the second was called de judiciis and the third de rebus, as explained above on the Code. This book 12 contains the condictiones. The first is the condictio certi, which is treated under this title, de rebus creditis, because this condictio is general: that is, it is given or lies from every cause, obligation and certain contract (l. 9, certi, this title). There is also another reason why this title comes first: under this title, as under a general one, several contracts were set out by the praetor in the Edict, as said above on the Code and the Perpetual Edict, and he says (l.1.bnjuatit.). To this is joined title 2.de jurejur., because the first is chiefly about loan, and the use of an oath is greatest in loan, since a loan is usually given without witnesses or documents. Hence the poet Laberius in Gellius (16.c.7.in sin.) says: "What is an oath but a plaster for debt?", that is, for a loan, as Cujacius reminds us in Parat. hic. In the Code, however, the order is de jurejurando first and de actione si certum petatur second. The reason given there is perhaps also this: the tribune thought it made no difference which came first, since in the Edict and the books of the jurists both were treated under one title; and because in the Code another title, de suffragio, is more fittingly joined to si certum petatur. To this title de jurejur. is joined, because of its similarity, title 3 de in lit.jur., which is followed by title 4 de cond. causa data, &c. To understand the order, it must be known that there are 8 condictiones, which are explained here in order. The first is the condictio certi of title 1 above, which is general, as said there. It is followed by seven special ones. Of these, the condictio causa data and the others hold the place nearest the first. The reason is this: since these condictiones either arise from a cause or arise without a cause, the condictiones from a cause are set out first, and the first of them, the condictio certi, is most like them, since it is a condictio from every cause, as is said in l. 9 above, de reb. cred. The second is therefore from a just and honest cause, but one that did not follow through. To it is joined title 5.de cond.ob turp.caus., because an honest and just cause is preferable to a shameful and unjust one. This is followed by title 6 de cond.indeb., because this is indeed from a cause, but a false and supposed one, whereas the earlier ones are from a true cause. A true cause, however, is rightly placed before a false one. In the Code the order is different: the condictio indebiti comes immediately after the condictio certi, because it is very similar to it. Thus also in the Institutes, quib. mod. re contrah. &c., the beginning is about the condictio certi, and §. proximus, de condictione indeb. Hence Cujacius, book 1, chapter 34, calls this condictio the one from a promutuum and the other from a mutuum, rightly, but says the earlier one is from a promutuum, not rightly. Title 7, the last of this twelfth book, is de condictione sine causa. The reason for the order is that the earlier titles concern condictiones from a cause, and to these the condictio without a cause is rightly joined. There is also another reason: this condictio occurs together with the three that come next. For although five of the following are from a cause, yet in their effect they are without a cause. The first of them is from a cause, but one that did not follow through, that is, was not carried into effect, and so falls back to no cause. The second is from a shameful and unjust cause, which in law is held to be no cause and nothing (l. 1, §. 1; l. 6, inf. de don. inter vir. et ux.). The third is from a false cause, and therefore is valid as from nothing. Rightly, therefore, where those are given, there this one is also given (dd. ll. and l. 4, hic.).

units.la: XIII. Liber.
units.tr: Book 13.

units.la: Liber 13. ad tres partes revocari potest I. Condictiones quædam singulares continentur. II. Duæ actiones prætoriæ, earque velut accellorie.
units.tr: Book 13 can be reduced to three parts: (1) it contains certain special condictions; (2) it contains two praetorian actions, which are in a sense accessory; (3) it contains two actions arising from an obligation that is created by a thing (re).

units.la: III. Actiones duæ ex obligatione, quæ re fit. Continet autem titulos 7. quorum primus est de condictione furtiva. Ratio, quia hæc condictio delictum continet sive ex delicto, hoc est furto oritur, ideoque in posteriorem locum rejicitur. Singularem autem eam voco, quia cum nemo rem suam condicat hæc sola condictio excipitur, qua scilicet à fure rem suam quis condicit f. itaque, verf. p. ancodio, de actt. Hunc sequitur titul. 1. de cond. ex leg. quæ quidem nihil habet proprie singulare, nisi quod datur in subsidium, hoc est cum aliæ nullæ competunt. hæc velut subsidiaria datur, ex legetamen ideoque merito in ultimum locum est rejecta. & hic in Cod. Ei tamen adjungitur alia tit 3. de condict. sine caus. Rationem hanc esse puto, quod & hæc habeat aliquid singulare, & plane distinctum à prioribus omnibus. Nam priores omnes etiam de pecunia numerata dantur, hæc solanon datur, l. 1. hæc. Alioquì hoc est, hoc solo excepto, hæc condictio ultima primæ valde similis est. His condictionibus adjunguntur duæ actiones prætoriæ: quia ut condictiones plerasque sunt ex naturali æquitate, ( ut condictio ex causa data & 4. seqq ) ita & hæ duæ actiones ex naturali potius, quam civili æquitate oriuntur, l. 1. n verb. fi d quia. njuftum, hoc tit. de eo quod certo loco. Earum prior est actio arbitraria de eo quod certo loco, tit. 4. Rationem ordinis reddunt Cujacius Hotoman. & alij quia actio hæc similis condictioni proxime triticiariæ in eo quod utraque sit arbitraria. Sed nulla ratio est, nulla quoq; lex, qua confirmari posset eam condictionem esse arbitrariam, sed verius videtur, esse fi ictam, ut sunt aliæ condictiones, maximè condictio certi, cui hæc est similis, ut modo dictum. Quare alia ratio ordinis hæc esse videtur, quod in utraque ad æstimationem sæpè decurrendum sit, l. 3. & 4. de condict. trit. l. 3. l. 8. censum, hoc tit. Quem sequitur tit. 5. de confiit. pecun. Ratio est, quia prior actio ad stipulationem pertinet hæc ad pactum, l. 1. titul. 4. & l. 1. tit. 5. Stipulatio autem pacto est efficacior. Adhuc dictum est de una actione obligationis, quæ re fit, nempe de condictione certi, quæ & ex mutuo datur, quamvis & indebitum interdum dicatur contractus re: cum tamen sit potius distractus vel quasi contractus §. item is, de obligat. ex quasi contr. §. 1. de oblig. quæ re contrab. Altera autem species contractus, qui re, est commodatum, ex quo actio commodati, de quanunc recte est tit. 6. commodatum vel contra, quia commodatum est mutuo simile, §. 2. l. ifit. de oblig. quæ re. Hunc sequitur titul. 7. de pignorat. act. quia pignus & depositum etiam est species contractus qui re. Restat quarta species, nempe depositum, de quo inferius lib. 16. tit. 3. In Institu. tamen depositum præponitur pignori, f. pen. & ult. quib. mod. re contrab. oblig. Ratio est, quod ut commodator utitur accipiens : ita & pignore interdum utitur accipiens creditor, sed hoc pignus dicitur proprie antichresis, l. si pecuniam, d. tit. Et hinc est quod in Edicto perpetuo sub titul. de reb. cred. de his quoque duobus pignore & commodato edixerit prætor, l. 1. §. 1. infin. supra de reb. cred.
units.tr: It contains seven titles. The first is de condictione furtiva. The reason is that this condiction involves a delict: it arises from a delict, namely theft, and so it is placed in a later position. I call it special because, although no one sues to recover his own property, this is the one condiction in which a person sues to recover his own property, namely from a thief (f. itaque, verb. p. ancodio, de actt.). This is followed by title 1, de condictione ex lege, which has nothing properly special about it, except that it is granted in subsidy, that is, when no other actions apply. It is given as a kind of subsidiary remedy, arising from law, and so it is rightly placed last. In the Code, however, another title is added, title 3, de condictione sine causa. I think the reason for this is that it too has something special, clearly distinct from all the earlier ones. For all the earlier ones are also granted for money counted out, but this one alone is not (l. 1. hæc.). Otherwise, apart from this one point, this last condiction is very similar to the first. These condictions are joined by two praetorian actions. Just as most condictions arise from natural equity (such as the condiction from a given cause, and the following ones), so these two actions arise from natural rather than civil equity (l. 1, verb. si quid iniustum, hoc tit., de eo quod certo loco). The first of these is the arbitrary action de eo quod certo loco, title 4. Cujacius, Hotomanus and others give the reason for this order, namely that this action is similar to the condiction of the nearest kind of triticaria, in that both are arbitrary. But there is no reason, nor any law, by which it could be confirmed that this condiction is arbitrary. It seems rather more truly to be a certain action, as other condictions are, especially the condiction of a certain thing, to which this is similar, as just said. So another reason for the order seems to be this: in both cases it is often necessary to resort to an estimation (l. 3. & 4. de condict. trit. l. 3. l. 8. censum, hoc tit.). This is followed by title 5, de constituta pecunia. The reason is that the former action pertains to stipulation, and this one to pact (l. 1. tit. 4. & l. 1. tit. 5.). But a stipulation is more effective than a pact. So far we have spoken of one action of obligation that arises from a thing, namely the condiction of a certain thing, which also arises from a loan, although an undue payment is sometimes also called a contract by the thing, though it is rather a distraction or quasi-contract (§. item is, de obligat. ex quasi contr.; §. 1. de oblig. quae re contrab.). The other species of contract that arises from a thing is loan for use (commodatum), from which comes the action of loan for use. This is rightly title 6, commodatum vel contra, because loan for use is similar to a loan for consumption (§. 2. l. ifit. de oblig. quae re.). This is followed by title 7, de pignoratitia actione, because pledge and deposit are also species of contract that arises from a thing. A fourth species remains, namely deposit, which is treated below in book 16, title 3. In the Institutes, however, deposit is placed before pledge (f. pen. & ult. quib. mod. re contrab. oblig.). The reason is that just as the borrower uses the thing lent, so sometimes the creditor who receives a pledge uses it. But this kind of pledge is properly called antichresis (l. si pecuniam, d. tit.). And hence it is that in the perpetual Edict, under the title de rebus creditis, the praetor issued an edict about these two as well, pledge and loan for use (l. 1. §. 1. infin. supra de reb. cred.).

units.la: Recte igitur hunc edicti ordinem Tribun. quemadmodum & Paul. l b. 2. sent. recp. 4. & 5. secutus est tam in Cod quam in ff. sed in Instit. depositum fuit praepositum pignori propter faciliorem causam de qua ibidem.
units.tr: Tribonian therefore rightly followed this order of the Edict, as Paul also did in his Sentences (lib. 2. sent. recp. 4. & 5.), both in the Code and in the Digest. But in the Institutes deposit was placed before pledge for an easier reason, which is explained there.

units.la: XIV. Liber.
units.tr: Book 14.

units.la: Liber 14. & 15. pertinent ad contractus non nostros proprie, sed ad eorum contractus, qui nostrae sunt potestatis, l. 1. inf. de pecul. Videbatur ratio ordinis postulare, ut cum sint quinque contractus, qui refiunt, & eorum quatuor jam expositis, nempe mutuo indebito, commodato & pignore, restet quintus, depositum, ut de eo ageretur, de quo tamen, neque lib. 14. neque 15 sed demum hb. 16. agitur interjectis sive ei praepositis his contractibus alienis. Ratio autem, cur alienas has actiones, hoc est, non ex nostris contractibus ortas, praetor interposuerit (nam & in Edicto idem est ordo, qui & in Cod & hic in ff. lib. 2. sent. tit. 6. & seq.) haec est: tum quia hae actiones exercitoria, institoria & tributoria, de iisdem fere rebus agunt, de quibus priores, nempe de pecunia de quantitate, aut certe de re mobili, ut commodatum & pignus (nam de mercibus fere ista agunt leg. 4. & 5. §. non tamen, & seqq. l. 3. l. 19 de instit. act. Mercium autem appellatio proprie quantitates, ut vinum, frumentum, &c. in quibus, & mutuum consistit pertinet, l. 1. § 1. de tribut. act. l. 66. & 207. de ver. sig.) tum quia, ut plerumque conditiones, sive causa &c. oriuntur ex aequo & bono sive causa & aequitate naturali non vero ex civili, l. 66. Haec conditio, de condit. indeb. Ita & ista actiones ex contractu aliorum oriuntur ex naturali quadam aequitate, l. 1. de exercit. act. l. 1. de tribut. act. ideoque & praetoriae sunt. Nam ut saepe dictum, praetor naturalem aequitatem intuetur. Sunt autem ex contractibus aliorum, istae actiones sex quarum 3. hoc libro 14. explicatur, quia sunt in solidum licet tertia, nempe tributoria non semper fit in solidum. At ordinarium & rationi consentaneum est, ut solidum sive totum parti praeponatur, ut petitio hereditatis totius petitioni partis, quae ratio ab ipso Ulpiano indicatur, in leg. 1. de pecul. Hujus igitur libri 14. titulus primus est, de exercit. act. Ratio videtur haec esse, quia hujus actionis aequissima sit causa, sive aequior quam fit institoriae. Cur sit aequior, expositum Ulpianus l. 1. b. major, inquit, necessitas est, cum magistro contrahendi, quam cum institore, quiperes patitur, ut de conditione institoris quis dispiciat, & sic contrahat: In navis magistro non item. Nam interdum locus aut tempus non patitur ulterius deliberandi consilium: quasi dicat in exercitoria saepe coguntur contrahere, nec habent tempus dispiciendi & deliberandi in institoria habent. Ergo in illa est aequius nobis succurri quam hic. Cui adjungitur tit 2. de l. Rhodia, de Jact. Ratio haec est quia haec lex pertinet ad mare, & nauticam rem, ut & actio exercitoria ad nauticos contractus.
units.tr: Books 14 and 15 deal with contracts that are not strictly our own, but with those contracts which fall under our power, l. 1. inf. de pecul. The order of the subject seemed to require that, of the five contracts which remain, four having already been explained (loan for consumption, the unowed loan, commodatum and pledge), the fifth, deposit, should be treated next. Yet deposit is not treated in lib. 14. or 15, but only in book 16, with these other people's contracts placed in between. The reason why the praetor set these alien actions, that is, actions arising not from our own contracts, before the others (the order in the Edict is the same as in the Code, and here in the Digest lib. 2. sent. tit. 6. & seq.) is this. First, because the actions exercitoria, institoria and tributoria deal with much the same things as the earlier ones, namely money, or at least movable goods, as commodatum and pledge do. (For these actions deal mostly with merchandise, leg. 4. & 5. §. non tamen, & seqq. l. 3. l. 19 de instit. act. The term "merchandise" properly refers to quantities such as wine, grain and the like, which also make up the subject of a loan, l. 1. § 1. de tribut. act. l. 66. & 207. de ver. sig.) Second, because, as condictions generally arise from what is fair and good, that is, from natural equity and not from civil law, l. 66. This is the condiction, de condit. indeb. So these actions too arise from another's contract out of a certain natural equity, l. 1. de exercit. act. l. 1. de tribut. act. and therefore they are praetorian. For, as has often been said, the praetor looks to natural equity. Of the actions arising from the contracts of others there are six, of which three are explained in this book 14, because they lie for the whole amount, although the third, the tributoria, does not always lie for the whole. But it is the normal and reasonable rule that the whole, or the total, be preferred to the part, as the petition for an inheritance as a whole is preferred to a petition for a part; Ulpian himself indicates this reason in leg. 1. de pecul. The first title of this book 14 is therefore de exercit. act. The reason seems to be that the case for this action is the most equitable, or more equitable than that for the institoria. Why it is more equitable Ulpian sets out l. 1. b. "There is," he says, "a greater necessity in dealing with the master of a ship than with a shop manager, since the latter allows one time to consider the terms of the manager's position and so to contract. This is not so with the master of a ship." For sometimes place or time does not allow further deliberation. He means that in the exercitoria men are often forced to contract, and do not have time to examine and deliberate, whereas in the institoria they do. Therefore it is fairer that we be helped in the former than in the latter. To this is joined title 2, de l. Rhodia, de Jact. The reason is that this law pertains to the sea and to maritime matters, just as the exercitoria action pertains to maritime contracts.

units.la: Hunc sequitur tit. 3. d. instit. act. Ratio ordinis est, quia ut exercitoria est ex contractu cum praeposito navis, hoc est magistro quem praepositus exercitor sive Dominus: ita & haec est ex praepositi tabernae contractu, hoc est, institoris, quem Dominus praeposuit. Et haec est ratio, quia utraque est in solidum semper. Proximus est titulus 4. de trib. act. tum quia & haec pertinet ad negotia, ad merces, ut institoria, tum quia haec etiam est in solidum, sed non semper. Pro rata enim portione plerunque datur, §. introduxit, & §. item quoque, quod cum eo, qui in al. &c. Hunc sequitur tit. 5. quod cum eo, &c. quititulus, etsi generalis est, & non tantum seqq. sed etiam priores actiones complectitur, ut in Instit. sub hoc titulo omnes actiones istae collocantur: priopriè tamen & rectius ad seqq tres tantum pertinet, quia priores, ut exercitoria, &c nascuntur ex contractu non tantum eorum, qui sunt in aliena potestate sed etiam eorum, qui sunt liberi, à nobis praepositi tabernae vel navi: sed seqq. ut de peculio, &c. tantum sunt ex negotio sive contractu eorum, qui sunt nostrae potestatis, ut liberorum ut servorum nostrorum, ut bona fide nobis servientium. Quae item ratio esse potest, cur illae sint priores quia sunt saepe cum liberis hominibus. cum istae seqq. sint cum servis & alienae potestatis hominibus. Etsi igitur hic titul. 5. ad 2 seqq. act. de quibus lib. seq. pertinet tamen sub eo speciali, quaedam actio ab illis tribus distincta continetur & illis tribus praeponitur, quae est actio ex contractu filiifamil. facto scilicet eo tempore, quo erat filiusfam sed in eum. cum jam non est amplius filius, sed est factus sui juris aut emancipatione, aut morte patris. Quam actionem reliquis praeposuit. Tribun quia habet similitudinem cum prioribus, quae sunt ex nostro contractu, ut sunt commodati ex mutuo, &c. Nam haec datur contra eum, qui contraxit ipse, sed quia contraxit filiusfamil. & datur contra ipsum jam patremfam. exantegesto, videtur non dari contra eundem: Nam ut servus post manumissionem videtur alius homo: & filius quoque post emancipationem alius videtur. l. 10. infra de opt. leg. l. 27. de adim. leg. Huic autem titulo recte adjungitur titul. de Senatusconsl. Macedon. ex quo mutuo non tenetur ipse, neque pater.
units.tr: This is followed by title 3, d. instit. act. The order is this: just as the exercitoria arises from a contract with the master of the ship (that is, the one whom the exercitor, or owner, placed in charge of it), so this one arises from the contract of the one placed in charge of the shop (that is, the manager whom the owner set over it). The reason for this is that both always lie for the whole amount. Next is title 4, de trib. act., both because it too concerns business and merchandise, like the institoria, and because it too lies for the whole amount, but not always. For usually it is given only pro rata, §. introduxit, and §. item quoque, quod cum eo, qui in al. etc. This is followed by title 5, quod cum eo, etc. This title, though general and covering not only the following actions but also the earlier ones (as in the Institutes all these actions are placed under this title), properly and more correctly pertains only to the following three. For the earlier ones, such as the exercitoria, arise from a contract not only with persons under another's power but also with free men whom we have placed in charge of a shop or ship. But the following ones, such as de peculio and the rest, arise only from the business or contract of those under our power, such as our children and slaves, and those who serve us in good faith. This may also be the reason why the earlier ones come first: they often involve free men, whereas these following ones involve slaves and persons under another's power. Although, therefore, this title 5 pertains to the two or three following actions, which the next book deals with, nevertheless under this special heading there is contained a certain action distinct from those three, and placed before them. This is the action arising from a contract of a son under power, made at the time when he was still a son under power, but brought against him when he is no longer a son, having become sui iuris either by emancipation or by his father's death. The author places this action before the rest. It is treated first because it resembles the earlier ones, which arise from our own contracts, such as commodatum and the loan for consumption. For this action is given against the one who himself made the contract; but because he made it while a son under power, and it is given against him now that he is already a paterfamilias, it seems not to be given against the same person. For just as a slave after manumission seems to be another man, so a son after emancipation also seems to be another. To this title is rightly joined the title on the Senatusconsultum Macedonianum, by which neither the borrower himself nor his father is bound by a loan.

units.la: XV. Liber.
units.tr: Book XV.

units.la: Libro 15. reliquae tres ex alieno contractu exponuntur. Ratio ordinis dictafupr 1 titulus est de peculio, quia haec actio est quodammodo principalis. Nam proxima actio de in rem verso, est accessionis de peculio, accessio sive adjectio, & quasi subsidiaria, quae tum demum datur, si non sit actio de peculio titulus 2. quando de pecul. actio, &c. est quasi pars tituli primi & ad eandem actionem de peculio pertinet. Nam actio de peculio est perpetua manente peculio, ut & aliae actiones in personam, mutuo Instit. de perp. & temp. &c. Exstinguitur autem peculio est annalis, ut hoc titulo 2. quem jam sequitur tit.3. de in rem verso, de quo jam dictum. Et hunc titul.4. quod iussu, quæ actio quod jussu inter hos sex exalieno contractu hic ultimo ponitur, &in Institu. quod cum eo, &c. primo: Ratio differentiæ sive Institut quidem hæc est: tum quia illæ exercitoria & institoria ita &hæc, quod jussu est in solidum, cum de peculio & de in rem verso non sint in solidum: tum quia hæc actio non videtur ex alieno, sed ex nostro contractu nasci: Nam quasi cótrahit cum eo, qui jubet, qui cum servo ejus cui jussum est, contrahit. Ratio autem ff est: tum quia hæc actio tátum est cum servo aut cum filiofam. Nam jussus est in eos, qui sunt in potestate nostra: mandatum in liberos, sive in- eos, qui non sunt nostræ potestatis.
units.tr: In Book 15 the remaining three actions arising from another's contract are expounded. The reason for the order has been stated above: the first title is on the peculium, because this action is in a way the principal one. For the next action, de in rem verso, is an accessory or addition to the action de peculio, and is in a way subsidiary, granted only when there is no action de peculio (title 2, Quando de peculio actio, etc.). It is as it were part of the first title and pertains to the same action de peculio. For the action de peculio lasts while the peculium remains, as do other personal actions (see Inst. de perpetuis et temporalibus actionibus). The action is extinguished when the peculium is gone; it is annual, as in this title 2, which is followed by title 3, de in rem verso, already discussed. And this is title 4, Quod iussu, the action which is placed last here among these six arising from another's contract; in the Institutes it is treated in Quod cum eo, etc., first. The reason for the difference, as the Institutes give it, is this: first, because the actions exercitoria and institoria, and likewise this one, quod iussu, lie for the whole amount (in solidum), whereas de peculio and de in rem verso do not; second, because this action seems to arise not from another's contract but from our own, for it is as if we contracted with the one who gives the order, since he contracts with the slave to whom the order was given. The reason given in the Digest is this: first, because this action exists only with a slave or with a son under power, for jussum applies to those in our power, whereas mandatum applies to free persons, that is, those not in our power.

units.la: Itaq; hæc actio, quod iussu, duabus proximis de peculio, & de in rem verso, est similis. Nam tres istæ actiones sunt ex negotio, quod cum eo, qui in aliena potestate gestum fuerit: at illæ: exercitoria & institoria, sunt non tantum ex contractu servorum. & filiorumf, sed etiam ex liberorum: tum quia hæc actio rarior est, quam duæ proximæ: Nam hæc non oritur, nisi jussus Domini aut patris præcesserit: quæ proximæ sine jussu, & quandocunque serviaut filiifam. contraxerint quod certè sæpius fit.
units.tr: Therefore this action, quod iussu, is similar to the two nearest, de peculio and de in rem verso. For these three actions arise from a transaction made with one who is under another's power. But the actions exercitoria and institoria arise not only from the contracts of slaves and sons but also from those of free persons. And this action differs in that it is rarer than the two nearest: it does not arise unless the order of the master or father has come first, whereas the two nearest arise without an order, whenever slaves or sons under power have contracted, which certainly happens more often.

units.la: XVI. Liber.
units.tr: Book XVI.

units.la: Liber 16. tres tantum titulos continet, quorum I. est ad Senatusconsul. Velleian. Ratio ordinis est propter similitudinem cum Senatusconsl. Macedon. Ea quoque causa est cur in Cod lib.4 tit.28 est ad Macedon & titu.29. ad Velleian. Similitudo in eo est quod in utroque Senatusconsulto rollitur sive impeditur actio ex pecunia mutuo data, nl.1. in verb. quifilio fam. mutuam pecuniam dedisset, ad Macedon. leg. 2. in verb. quod ad fidejussiones & mutuationes, pro quib. intercesserunt fœmine, pertinet &c. ad Velleian. Sed in ff nō statim post Maced agitur de Vellejano, quia ibi oes actiones ex contractibus alienis, ut filiorumfamil. ad quos pertinet Macedon. acfervorum, ordine ac deinceps propositæ sunt. Vellejanum autem non est de illis, qui sunt in aliena potestate, sive filijsfam. & servis, sed est de fœminis: ideoque recte post illas actiones demum de Senatusconsulto hoc separatim est actum, non tamen nimis longe à titulo ad Macedon. II. Tit est de compensat. Ratio ordinis est, quia ut Vellejano impeditur actio & exactio ejus, quod mulieri creditum est, & ejus, quod mulier intercessit pro alio, ita & compensatione tollitur actio, & tollitur exactio ejus pecuniæ, quæ nobis debetur. Etrecte hic tit. 2. de copensationibus, præponitur titulo depositi, quia compensatio in deposito locum non habet, sed plerunq; habet locum in contractibus proximè explicatis, ut in pecunia credita, sive mutuo data, quamvis etiam in omnibus contractib. & delictis, sive maleficijs si pecuniariæ agatur, locum habet compensatio, l. to.si ammo. §. quoties, hoc tit.l.pen.C.depos.
units.tr: Book 16 contains only three titles. The first is on the Senatusconsultum Velleianum. Its place follows from its similarity to the Senatusconsultum Macedonianum. This is also why, in the Code, book 4 title 28 is on the Macedonian and title 29 on the Velleian. The similarity lies in this: each senatusconsultum removes or impedes an action arising from money lent. Compare law 1, in the words "if a son under power had lent money" (Macedonian), with law 2, in the words "which pertains to suretyships and loans, for which women interceded" (Velleian). In the Digest, however, the Velleian is not treated immediately after the Macedonian. There, all actions arising from the contracts of others, such as those of sons under power, to whom the Macedonian applies, and of slaves, are set out in order and in succession. The Velleian, however, concerns not those who are under another's power, whether sons under power or slaves, but women. So it is rightly treated separately, after those actions, and yet not too far from the title on the Macedonian. II. The title on compensations. The reason for this order is that just as the Velleian impedes the action and recovery of what has been lent to a woman, and of what a woman has guaranteed for another, so compensation too removes an action and removes the recovery of money owed to us. And rightly this second title, on compensations, is placed before the title on deposit. Compensation has no place in deposit, but mostly applies in the contracts explained just before, such as money lent or loaned. Yet compensation also applies in all contracts and in delicts or wrongs, if a claim for money is brought: law 10, si animo, §. quoties, this title; last law, C. depos.

units.la: Tertius titulus est depositi vel cert. Ratio ordinis est quia hactenus omnes actiones ex contractibus, qui re fiunt, ut si certum petatur, ex mutuo condictio indebiti. actio commodati, & actio pignoris sunt propositæ, restabat una quæ est actio depositi quæ actio, cur hic & in Codic. sit ultima earum, quæ oriuntur ex contractibus, qui re fiunt ratio satis est prioribus intelligitur nimirum, quia illæ quatuor majorem similitudinem inter se habeant. Est & hæc ratio, quod actio depositi quædam est ex delicto in duplum. leg. 1. §. 1. hoc titul. §. plane, Inst. 1. de act. Delicta autem in posteriorem locum rejici solent.
units.tr: The third title is on deposit or on certain debt. The reason for the order is that until now all actions arising from contracts made by the thing (real contracts) have been set out: the action on a certain claim, the condictio indebiti arising from a loan, the action of commodatum, and the action of pledge. One remained, the action of deposit. Why this one comes last among the actions arising from real contracts, both here and in the Code, is sufficiently clear from what precedes: namely, those four have greater similarity to one another. There is also this reason, that the action of deposit is in a certain way an action arising from a delict, for double the value. Law 1, §. 1, this title; §. plane, Inst. 1, de act. Delicts, however, are customarily placed in the later position.

units.la: XVII. LIBER.
units.tr: XVII. BOOK

units.la: Liber 17. duos contractus, mandatum & societatem continet & actiones ex iis orientes. Ratio ordinis est, quia cum actiones in personam, oriantur ex quatuor contractibus, sive contractuum generibus, re, verbis & literis, & consensu: Verborum autem obligatio sit stipulatio, vel contractus accessorius, ad alios confirmandos inductus, ut supra dictum in fine edicti perpetui. Et literarum contractus antiquus non sit amplius in usu & novus non tam sit species nova contractus, quam nova species mutui (qui novus contractus literarum Juris consultis ex quorum scriptis ff. sunt compositæ, est ignotus, init. Inst. de lib. obl. g.) merito jam explicatis contractibus, qui re fiunt, sequitur, ut contractus qui consensu explicentur. Nam ut modo dictum, contractus literarum vetus non est amplius in usu & contractus verborum non est principalis, ut qui re & consensu, sed est accessorius, ideoque in fine rejectus, ut accessio sequitur principale. Contractus autem, qui consensu fiunt, sunt quatuor, quorum primus hic ponitur contractus & actio mandati b c tit. 1. hic Mandati vel contra. & secundus tit. 2. profoc. societas. Ratio ordinis est, quia ut depositum, de quo supra tit. proximo ita & mandatum est gratuitum, §. vlt. de mand. Cui, ut dictum, proximæ est societas, qui ut mandatum fere inter amicos & notos contrahi solet, ita & societas, & quædam quasi societas, l. 63. verum est. ff. profoc.
units.tr: Book 17 deals with two contracts, mandate and partnership, and the actions arising from them. The reason for this order is that, since actions in personam arise from four contracts, or kinds of contract: re, verbis, literis and consensu; and since the obligation by words is the stipulation, or an accessory contract introduced to confirm others, as was said at the end of the Perpetual Edict; and since the old contract by writing is no longer in use, and the new one is not so much a new kind of contract as a new kind of loan (this new contract by writing, which the jurists whose writings make up the Digest did not know, see the beginning of the Institutes on obligations); then, having now explained the contracts made re, it follows that we treat the contracts which are completed by consent. For, as just said, the old contract by writing is no longer in use, and the contract by words is not a principal one, as the contracts re and consensu are, but an accessory one, and therefore it has been put last, since an accessory follows its principal. There are four contracts which are made by consent, of which the first treated here is the contract and action of mandate (title 1 of this book, Mandati vel contra), and the second, in title 2, pro socio, partnership. The reason for this order is that, just as deposit, dealt with in the preceding title, is gratuitous, so mandate is also gratuitous (Institutes, last paragraph, on mandate). Partnership is closest to this, as stated; and just as mandate is usually contracted between friends and acquaintances, so is partnership, and a certain quasi-partnership (Digest, law 63, on partnership).

units.la: XVIII. LIBER.
units.tr: XVIII. BOOK.

units.la: Liber 18 continet septem titulos ad emptionem pertinentes. Ratio ordinis est, quia cum duo reflent contractus consensu, emptio & locatio, rectè prius de emptione agitur. Ratio dicta in Institut tum etiam, quia ut locietate, de qua proximè communicatur dominium rerum communium ita & in emptione, si venditor est dominus, transit dominium in emptorem, leg. 30. infra de act. empt. §. vendite. de rer. divis. At locatione non mutuatur dominium l. non solet 39. infra loc. Et hinc est quoq;, quod locatio dicitur proxima emptioni, l. 2. infra loc. Hujus autem libri titul. 1. est de contrah. empt. & c. quia hic titulus est generalis continens generalia præcepta & regulas de pretio, de origine, de consensu, de rebus, de pactis, &c. Cui adjungitur tit. 2. de in diem diem addixit. Ratio ordinis est, quia sub titulo generali, postquam etiam de pactis emptionis generaliter est actum adjunguntur hic duo pacta speciala reliquis notiora, & in emptionibus frequentiora, unum est addictionis in diem, de quo hic, alterum commissorum, de quo titul. 3. infr. de leg. commiss. Ratio, cur prius de in diem addictione, videtur haec esse, tum quia lex sive pactum commissorium, etiam diem in se continet atque ita velut species aut pars, eatenus videri potest ejus pacti addictionis. tum quia pactum addictionis ad constitutionem sive principium contractus & pretii convent one, lex commissoria ad perfectionem contractus, nempe solutionem pretii pertinet, l. 1 hic & l. 2. it. prox. de leg commiss. Cui adjungitur titul. 4 de hered. vel act. ven. Ratio ordinis est, quia ut titulo generaliagitur de pactis generaliter, quem sequuntur duo pacta specialia, ut jam dictum, ita eodem titulo agitur de rebus, quae venire possunt, aut non possunt ut ait ipse tit. quaeres, & c. Jam sequitur res quaedam, in qua speciale jus est, nempe hereditas & actio, quae interdum venduntur, & de hac speciali venditione hereditatis & actionis hic agitur tit. 4. Cui proximus est tit f. de refc. vend. Ratio ordinis, quia haec actus de constituenda, nunc de tollenda sive rescindenda venditione. Contractus n. distractu est prior. Hunc sequitur tit. 6. de peric. & commodo rei vend. Ratio ordinis dicta ad C. ultimus huius l. bri titul. est, de servis exportand. & c. tum quia hic titulus est de servis, tum quia pactum odiosum continet, ut prior tit. 6. agit de periculo, quod item est odiosum. At odiosa, ut & delicta in posteriore locum rejiciuntur, ut & servitia.
units.tr: Book 18 contains seven titles relating to purchase and sale. The reason for the order is that, since two contracts by consent remain, purchase and letting, it is rightly treated first of purchase. The reason is also stated in the Institutes, because, as in partnership, of which the next to be discussed is the communal ownership of goods, so in purchase, if the seller is the owner, ownership passes to the buyer (law 30, below, de actionibus empti, §. vendite, de rerum divisione). But in letting, ownership is not transferred (law 39, below, locati). And for this reason letting is also said to be next to purchase (law 2, below, locati). The first title of this book is de contrahenda emptione etc., because this title is general, containing general precepts and rules concerning price, origin, consent, things, agreements, and so on. To it is joined title 2, de in diem addictione. The reason for the order is that, after the general title has treated the agreements of purchase in general, two special agreements, better known than the rest and more frequent in purchases, are added here: one is the sale subject to a day (addictio in diem), dealt with here, and the other the commissory agreement, dealt with in title 3, below, de lege commissoria. The reason why the sale subject to a day is treated first seems to be this: both because the commissory law or agreement itself contains the day within it and so, as it were, is a species or part of it, and so may be seen in that respect to belong to the agreement of sale; and because the agreement of sale subject to a day concerns the establishment or beginning of the contract and the agreement on price, while the commissory law concerns the completion of the contract, namely the payment of the price (law 1 here and law 2, next, de lege commissoria). To it is joined title 4, de hereditate vel actione vendita. The reason for the order is that, just as in the general title agreements were treated in general, followed by two special agreements, as already said, so under the same title things are treated which can or cannot be sold, as the title itself says, quaeres, etc. Next follows a certain kind of thing in which there is a special law, namely inheritance and action, which are sometimes sold; and the special sale of inheritance and action is treated here, title 4. Next to it is title 5, de rescindenda venditione. The reason for the order is that this title treats of the rescinding or annulling of a sale, not of its establishment; for a contract of sale is prior to its undoing. This is followed by title 6, de periculo et commodo rei venditae. The reason for the order mentioned at the final law of this book's title is de servis exportandis, etc., both because this title is about slaves, and because it contains an odious agreement, as the earlier title 6 deals with risk, which is likewise odious. But odious matters, like crimes, are placed later, as are also slaveries.

units.la: XIX. LIBER.
units.tr: XIX. BOOK.

units.la: Liber 19 continet t titulos, & est de quibusdam actionibus, empti scilicet, locati & similibus. Illud hic observandum quod & alias dictum in Institut. genera Tyronum juris nulla explicari distincte, quae & in ff conjunctim explicantur: ut in Insti distincte de legatis & fidei commissis, distincte de contractibus & de actionibus ex iis contractibus agitur. At in ff sub eodem titulo explicatur & contractus, ut mutui & commodati ut depositi, ut locati, & actiones quoque ex iisdem contractibus natae, sed in contractu emptionis distincte Tribun. prius de contractu toto libr. 18. postea de actionibus in hoc lib 19. agendum putavit propter hujus contractus celebritatem, & prolixas disputationes. Et hinc est, quod lib. 19 titulus 1. est de action. empt. & vend. quem sequitur tit. 2. loc. cond. Ratio jam dicta supr. Huic proximus tit. 3. de aestimatoria, quia haec actio partim actioni empti, partim actioni locati & conducti est similis, l. 1. hoc tit. Quem sequitur tit. 4. de rer. permut. Nam & hic contractus est similis emptioni, leg. 1. hic, & 5. pretium. Institit. de empt. & vend. Cur autem aestimatoria praeponatur permutationi ratio haec est quia similior est emptioni, quae permutationi in eo, quod pretiu in quo subfstatia emptionis posita est, l. pacta, 72. supra de contrab. empt. sit in aestimatoria, non veroim permutatione Ultimus huius libri titul est, ut præscriptis verb. Ratio ordinis est, quia post expositas actiones ex contractibus ordinarias, vulgares & usitatas, merito jam exponuntur actiones extraordinariæ, quæ dicuntur præscriptis verbis & in factum, quibus agendum est cum deficiant usitatæ, l.1.2.&3 hoc titul. Est & actio ex permutatione extraordinaria, sive præscriptis verbis, de qua tamen prius actum fuit, & sepatatim, quia emptioni, ut dictum est similis. Quem statim sequitur titulus generalis, de act. præscript.verb.
units.tr: Book 19 contains five titles, and it deals with certain actions, namely of purchase, letting and similar matters. Here one should observe what was said elsewhere in the Institutes, that the kinds of contracts are not explained distinctly for beginners in law, and that they are explained together in the Digest. Thus in the Institutes legacies and trust-bequests are treated separately, and contracts and the actions arising from those contracts are treated separately. But in the Digest, under a single title, a contract is explained together with its actions: for example loan for consumption and loan for use, deposit, letting, and the actions also arising from these same contracts. However, in the case of the contract of sale, the Tribonian first thought it right to treat the contract as a whole in Book 18, and afterwards to treat the actions in this Book 19, on account of the frequency of this contract and its lengthy disputations. Hence it is that Book 19, title 1, is "on the actions of purchase and sale," which is followed by title 2, "on letting and hiring," for the reason already given above. Next to it is title 3, "on the estimatory action," because this action is partly similar to the action of purchase and partly to the action of letting and hiring, l. 1 of this title. This is followed by title 4, "on the exchange of things," for this contract too is similar to purchase, l. 1 here, and l. 5 pretium, Institutes on purchase and sale. Why the estimatory action is placed before exchange, the reason is this: because it is more similar to purchase, the point in which the substance of purchase lies being the price, l. pacta 72, supra on contracts of purchase; and the price is found in the estimatory action but not in exchange. The last title of this book is "on the praescriptive words." The reason for this order is that, after the ordinary, common and customary actions arising from contracts have been set out, the extraordinary actions, which are called praescriptis verbis and in factum, and which are to be brought when the usual ones fail, are now rightly explained, l. 1, 2 and 3 of this title. There is also an extraordinary action arising from exchange, namely praescriptis verbis, of which, however, it was treated earlier and separately, because it is similar to purchase, as has been said. This is immediately followed by the general title, "on the praescriptive actions."

units.la: DE IV. PARTE DIGESTORUM. XX. Liber.
units.tr: On the Fourth Part of the Digest. Book 20.

units.la: Liber 20. est de pignoribus & hypothecis. Ratio ordinis, ut intelligatur, meminisse oportet, ad hoc explicatum esse de actionib in rem & de actionibus in personam, tàm ordinariis, quàm extraordinariis ex contractu orientibus; Proximè nunc erat alias actiones in personam non ex contractu, sed ex aliis causis, ut ex quasi contractu ut ex æquitate, ut ex delictis adjungere quod in edicto & in Cod. & Instit factum. Sed in ff. interjecit tres libros singulares, 20.21 & 22. quib. quæ dam continentur partim ad priores actiones pertinétia partim omnium actionum communia. Et primum quidé locum tenent pignora, ex quibus nascitur actio Serviana & quasi Serviana.
