Ratio ordinis est, nl.2.§.2.verf.quartus.C.de vet.jur ennel. nempe, ut non longè pignora & hæ actiones distarent à pignoratitia actione, de qua supra parte tertia de rebus lib.13.t.1.7. Cur autem inter hæc interjecta, quæ sunt pignora & actiones ex illis item ædilitium edictum, & actiones ex eo evictiones, ut suræ & probationes Cur inquam, primum locum teneant pignora, hæc est ratio: tum quia actio pignoratitia ( de qua supra lib.13. cuiusmodi est falteni nomine hæc pignoratitia sive hypothecaria actio ) prius sit posita, quàm actio empti, ad quam pertinet ædilitium edictum, de quo infra lib.seq. tū quia in edicto perpetuo prius de pignoribus quàm de evictione actum fuerit ut supra dictum. De reliquis hic interjectis suo loco Ratio ordinis infra exponetur. Hujus igitur libri 20 titulus primus est de pignorib. Est enim generalis quo scilicet de contrahendo pignore, & de ipsa actione hypothecaria agitur. Pignus autem, interdum expresse, interdum tacitè contrahitur de expressio, ut præstantioria agitur tit.1. de tacito igitur titul. 2. in quib.causis pignus, &c. Quem sequitur tit.3. quæ e pign.dat.obl.non posf. Ratio ordinis est, quia ut titulo 1. de forma & modo expresso contrahendi, quem sequitur tacitus modus tit.2. ut modo dictum ita quoque; eodem tit.1. de rebus, quæ pignori obligantur. Hactenus actum est, hoc vero titul 3. de rebus, quæ pignori obligari non possunt, agitur: qui tit.1. est posterior, quia secundus ad formam & divisionem pignoris pertinet: qua pignus vel est tacitum, vel expressum. Hunc sequ. tit. 4. quipot. in pign. Ratio 2. ordinis est, quia ut prioribus titulis agitur de contrahendo pignore, ita hoc & duob. seqq. agitur de jam contracto: Et primum quidem isto tit. 4. agitur de pignore à pluribus contracto, sive plurib. obligato, quis eorum sit potior in pignore: quem sequitur tit. de distract. pignor. Ratio ordinis est, quia ut prior titul. ad jus & effectum, quod scilicet sit potior, pertinet, ita & hic tit. 7. ad jus pignoris, sive jus quod habet in pignore creditor, nempe jus distrahendi pignus, sive rem pignoratam, pertinet: qua distractione, quia pignus exstinguitur, merito hic titulus est posterior. Eumq; rectè statim sequitur tit. 6. quib. mod. pign. sol. Ratio ordinis est perspicua quia adhuc dictum est, de pignore contrahendo & contracto, quibus jam proximum est, ut explicetur, quemadmodum contractum finiatur & solvatur.
units.tr: Book 20 is de pignorib. on pledges and mortgages. To understand the order, one should remember that the preceding books explained actions in rem and actions in personam, both ordinary and extraordinary, arising from contract. Next came other actions in personam that arise not from contract but from other causes, such as quasi-contract, equity, and delicts. These were added in the Edict, the Code, and the Institutes. In the Digest, however, he inserted three separate books, 20, 21 and 22, which contain some matters that belong partly to the earlier actions and partly to all actions. Pledges come first, and from them arise the Serviana action and the quasi-Serviana. The reason for this order is nl.2.§.2.verf.quartus.C.de vet.jur ennel., namely, that pledges and these actions should not lie far from the pignoratitia action, discussed above in the third part, on things, lib.13.t.1.7. Why pledges hold the first place among the matters inserted between them, which are pledges and the actions arising from them, as also the aedilician edict and the actions on eviction, such as warranties and proofs, is explained thus. First, because the pignoratitia action (of which above, lib.13., and which is in fact this pignoratitia or hypothecary action) was set out before the action of purchase, to which the aedilician edict pertains, discussed below in lib.seq. Second, because in the perpetual edict pledges were treated before eviction, as said above. The other matters inserted here will be explained below in their proper place. The first title of this 20th book is de pignorib. It is the general title, dealing with the contracting of a pledge and with the hypothecary action itself. A pledge is contracted sometimes expressly and sometimes tacitly. The express kind is treated in title 1, and the tacit kind in title 2, in quib. causis pignus, &c. Title 3, quae e pign. dat. obl. non posf., follows. The reason for this order is that, as title 1 deals with the form and manner of contracting expressly, which is followed by the tacit manner in title 2, so also title 1 deals with the things that are pledged. So far the matter of contracting has been treated. Title 3 now deals with the things that cannot be pledged. This title is later than title 1 because the second title concerns the form and division of a pledge, which is either tacit or express. Next follows title 4, quipot. in pign. The reason for this order is that, as the earlier titles deal with contracting a pledge, this title and the two following ones deal with a pledge already contracted. Title 4 first treats of a pledge contracted with several persons, or bound to several creditors, and which of them has priority in the pledge. It is followed by the title de distract. pignor. The reason for this order is that, as the earlier title concerns the right and effect, namely which creditor is preferred, so this title, number 7, concerns the right in the pledge, that is, the right the creditor has in it, namely the right to sell the pledge or the pledged thing. Since a pledge is extinguished by such a sale, this title rightly comes later. It is rightly followed at once by title 6, quib. mod. pign. sol. The reason for this order is plain: so far it has been said about contracting and having contracted a pledge, and what is next in line is to explain how a contracted pledge is ended and discharged.

units.la: XXI. L- IBER
units.tr: XXI. Book 21

units.la: Liber 21 ad emptiones potissimum pertinet, quæ cum nō longè hinc sint positæ l. 8 & 1. maluit Tribun. hæc in loco emptionibus vicino interjicere contra ordinem edicti perpetui, in quo de evictionibus ferè extremæ agitur: hæc ratio redditur, in l. 2. §. quartus, verf. alio libro, C. de vet. iur. encl. quia, inquit hæc omnia titulis emptionum & venditionum sint consentanea. & actiones: hoc libro positæ. quasi pedisseque illarum ex empto & vendito per providentiam nostram sunt congregatæ, cum oportuerat, &c. Hujus autem lib. 21. hic interjecti tit. 1. est de edil. edict. quo duæ actiones aedilitiæ, redhibitoria, & quanti minoris continentur. Cui itaque adjungitur tit. 2. de evict. quia & priores duæ actiones & hæc ex stipulatione duplæ ad emptiones pertinet, sed illæ sunt principales: hæc ut omnis stipulatio accessoria ideoq; posterior tit. 3. de exc. rei vend. & trad. Ratio est, qui prius de actionibus, posterius de exceptionibus agi debeat. Ut autem evictio ita & hæc exceptio in edicto perpetuo, ferè extremo loco fuit posita: sed hic posita ob eadem causam, hoc est, ob emptiones paulo ante positas.
units.tr: Book 21 concerns chiefly purchases, which, since they are placed not far from here (in laws 8 and 1), the compiler preferred to insert here, next to the title on purchases, contrary to the order of the Perpetual Edict, in which eviction is treated almost at the very end. This reason is given in law 2, §. quartus, verse "alio libro", C. de veteri iure enucleando: because, he says, all these matters are consonant with the titles on purchases and sales, and the actions placed in this book have been gathered together by our providence as attendants of those actions arising from purchase and sale, as was proper, etc. Of this book 21, the title 1 inserted here is de aedilicio edicto, which contains the two aedilician actions, the redhibitory and the quanti minoris. To this is added title 2, de evictionibus, because both the former two actions and this one arising from the stipulation of double belong to purchases; but those two are the principal ones, and this one, like every stipulation, is accessory, and therefore comes later. Title 3, de exceptione rei venditae et traditae, follows. The reason is that actions should be treated first, and exceptions afterwards. Just as eviction was placed almost at the last position in the Perpetual Edict, so this (exception) is placed here for the same reason, that is, because of the purchases placed shortly before.

units.la: XXII. LIBER.
units.tr: BOOK XXII.

units.la: Liber 22 qui est tertius hic interjectus, varia continet: de usuris aliisque accessionibus & de probationibus. Ratio ordinis cur & hæc sint interjecta de usuris quidem fructibus aliisque accessionibus & de mora, hæc videtur esse quia eorum usus maximus est in actionibus hactenus explicatis in rem, in quibus de fructib. & causa in personam, in quibus de usuris & de mora & etiam de fructibus potissimum explicatur. De probationibus vero eorumque generibus, ut sunt testes & instrumenta, non video aliam rationem, quam quod per consequentiam hic de his agendum putarit Tribunianus, nempe, quia semel constituerat hæc interjecta uno in loco ponere, etiam de probationibus in fine adjiciendum putavit: nisi forte & hanc quoque rationem spectarit, quod probationum usus, etsi est communis omnium judiciorum & actionum, ut & usus, fructuum, vsurarum, & morae non tantum in contractibus, sed & in testamentis & legatis frequentior tamen usus probationum, testium & instrumentorum in prioribus actionibus in rem & in personam esse videatur. Nam in testamentis sunt quidem instrumenta sive tabulae testaméti, sunt etiam testes: sed in testamétis ea sunt singularia, ut quod sint septem testes, de quib. specialiter agitur suo loco infra qui testament facere pos. ut & tabulis testamenti, cod. tit. & tit testamenta quemadmodum aper. Sic & in nuptijs non adhibentur testes & tabulae, licet interdum propter dotem & pacta dotalia adhibeantur. Saepe tamen non adhibentur. Et de ijs quoq; si adhibeantur, specialiter agitur, tit. de dotib. & tit. de pactis dot. Sic & in tutelis, neq; testes adhibentur, neq; tabulae, excepto inventario. Ut a hic in ff. probationes interjectis conjunxit Tribun. ita & in C. eos conjunxit communib sive generalibus quae generaliter item interjicit, lib 4. C. tit. 19. & seqq. usque ad tit. 23. Nam in dicto perpetuo non videtur quidquid positum fuisse de probationibus quod probationes, neq; ex jure civili, neq; praetorio veniant, sed in facto constistant, & ad judicem pertinent, l. 3. infra de testib. Et binc quoq; est, quod in sententijs Pauli probationes ponantur ultimo fere loco, ubi de criminibus. Ratio autem, cur hic prius de usuris agatur, quam de probationib. est quia ut jadictum, usurae fructus & mora in prioribus actionibus in rem, & in personam maxime locum habent: & quia sunt contractuum accessiones de quibus est hic tit. de usur. & c. Quem sequitur tit. 2. de naut. foen. quia est specialis. Huic proximus est tit. 3. de probatio. Ratio ordinis dicta est sinp quia titulus est generalis. Sunt a probationu duae praecipuae species, instrumenta & testes, quare tit. 4. est de fide instr. tit. 5. est de testib. In C tamen prior est tit. de testib. tit. de fid. instr. quia hic in ff in l. ultim. de probat. agitur de Chirographo sive instrumento, ideoq; statim de instrumentis agitur. Sic in C. inl. ult. de prob. agitur de testib. ideoq; statim adjicitur tit. de testib. Nam & alias solet ob praecedentis tit. ultimam legem aut similitudinem statim in similem tit applicare. Praeterea id quoq; observandum parum referte de testibus, an de instrumentis prius agatur, cum utriusq; speciei eadem sit vis & potestas. Cum aute id accidit, ut nihil referat utrum sit prius aut posterius, solet Tribun. saepe quod in Cod. ponit prius. in ff ponere posterius, ut hoc ipso demonstret, nihil aut parum referte. utrum sit prius aut posterius, ut est dictum tit. de in jus voc. & tit. de edendo. Huic adjungitur tit. 6. de juris & facti ignor. quitamen in Cod. non libro 4. de probat. sed in libro 1. cum juris & juris speciebus conjungitur, quia sit de juris ignorantia. Ratio autem ff. tum quia hi tit prioribus actionibus in rem, item condictioni indebiti, SC. Macedo. Vellejan actionimandati, empti & venditi, & redhibitoris actionibus (quib. scilicet agitur de scientia & ignorantia) servit: tum quia ignoratia facti actionib. explicari, removeri & tolli solet, nam & ipsæ probationes infacto esse dicuntur, teste Paulo, lib.5.sent. de probat.
units.tr: The twenty-second book, which is the third inserted here, contains various matters: interest and other accessions, and proofs. The reason for the order, why these are inserted, is this: interest, fruits and other accessions, and delay are treated here, it seems, because they are most used in the actions explained so far, the actions in rem, in which fruits and the cause are dealt with, and the actions in personam, in which interest, delay and also fruits are chiefly explained. As for proofs and their kinds, such as witnesses and documents, I see no other reason than that Tribonian, having by then decided to place these inserted matters in one spot, thought that proofs too should be added at the end by way of sequence. Unless perhaps he also had this in view: although the use of proofs is common to all judgments and actions, as is the use of fruits, interest and delay, not only in contracts but also in wills and legacies, the more frequent use of proofs, witnesses and documents seems to lie in the earlier actions in rem and in personam. For in wills there are indeed documents, the tablets of the will, and there are also witnesses; but in wills these are peculiar, as that there must be seven witnesses, which is treated specially in its own place below, under who may make a will, as also under the tablets of a will in the same title and under how wills are opened. So too in marriages witnesses and tablets are not employed, although sometimes, on account of the dowry and dotal agreements, they are used; often, however, they are not. And even about these, if they are used, it is treated specially under the titles on dowries and on dotal agreements. Likewise in guardianships neither witnesses nor tablets are used, except the inventory. Just as Tribonian joined proofs here in the Digest, placed between these matters, so in the Code he joined them to the common or general matters, which he similarly inserts in book 4 of the Code, titles 19 and following, down to title 23. For in the said perpetual edict it does not seem that anything was laid down about proofs, because proofs belong neither to the civil law nor to the praetorian law, but consist in fact and pertain to the judge (l. 3, below, de testibus). And hence it is also that in the Sentences of Paul proofs are placed almost in the last place, where he treats of crimes. The reason, however, why interest is treated here before proofs is that, as has been said, interest, fruits and delay chiefly find their place in the earlier actions in rem and in personam; and because they are accessions of contracts, of which this title on interest etc. treats. This is followed by the title on nautical interest, because it is special. Next to it is title 3, on proofs. The reason for the order has been stated: the title is general. There are two principal kinds of proofs, documents and witnesses; therefore title 4 is on the credit of documents, and title 5 is on witnesses. In the Code, however, the title on witnesses comes first, then the title on the credit of documents, because in the Digest, in the last law, de probationibus, it treats of a chirograph or document, and therefore it treats of documents at once. Likewise in the Code, in the last law de probationibus, it treats of witnesses, and therefore the title on witnesses is added at once. For otherwise it is customary, on account of the last law of the preceding title or a similarity, to apply it at once to a similar title. Moreover, this too must be observed: it matters little whether one treats of witnesses or of documents first, since both kinds have the same force and power. Since it happens that it makes no difference whether a thing comes first or later, Tribonian often puts first in the Code what he puts later in the Digest, so that by this very fact he may show that it matters little or not at all whether it comes first or later, as is said in the title on summoning to court and the title on production. To this is joined title 6, on ignorance of law and of fact, which however in the Code is not in book 4, on proofs, but in book 1, where it is joined with the titles on law and on the kinds of law, because it concerns ignorance of law. The reason for its place in the Digest is twofold: first, because this title serves the earlier actions in rem, likewise the condictio of what is owed by mistake, the senatusconsultum Macedonianum, the senatusconsultum Velleianum, the actions of mandate, of purchase and sale, and the redhibitory actions (namely, those in which knowledge and ignorance are at issue); and second, because ignorance of fact is commonly explained, removed and taken away by actions; for proofs themselves are said to be in fact, as Paul testifies, book 5 of the Sentences, on proofs.

units.la: XXIII. LIBER
units.tr: XXIII. BOOK

units.la: SEquitur liber 23.24 & 25.quitres libri sunt de matrimonio, & de dotib. alijsque eò pertinentibus. Ratio ordinis est hæc: interiectis illis jam expositis, lib 20 & 2.seqq redit jam Tribu ad ordinem per interjecta interruptum, hoc est, post expositas antea actiones in personam ex contractu, adjungit Tribu actiones eas, quæ ex aliis causis ut ex æquo & bono, ex quasi contractibus ex delictis, ex quasi delictis oriuntur, ut est actio de dote, quæ nascitur ex æquo & bono l.eos.supr.de cap.min. Non enim est ex quasi contractu, ut dictum ad Cod.lib 5. Cum autem totus hic tractatus de matrimonio in quinq; ferè partes sit distributus, sponsalia, nuptias dotes, divortium & accessoria primù de sponsalib agitur hujus lib.23.tit.1. quia sponsalia sunt nuptiis priora l.1.hoc tit Quem sequitur tit.2.de ritu nuptiar. quia sponsalia nuptiæ sequuntur, ut jam dictum. Huic adjungitur tit.3.de iure dot. Ratio est, quia dos non est sine matrimonio, l.3.hoc tit. Cui adjungitur tit.4.de pact.dot. Ratio est, quia prior tit. de iure dot est generalis quo omnia ad naturam dotis pertinentia continentur, hic est specialis, quo quædam specialia in dotibus recepta pacta explicantur, quibus pactis interdum natura dotis aliquantulum mutari solet. Huic sequitur tit.5 de fundo dot. qui est titulus specialis, & ad dotem pertinet, non tamen ad omnem, sive ad omnes res dotales, sed tantum ad unam rem nempe fundum, ideoque hic titulus quia specialis, est posterior: & item, quia est prohibitorius, in quo scilicet explicantur prohibitio alienationis fundi dotalis.
units.tr: Book 23 follows, then books 24 and 25. These three books deal with marriage, dowries, and related matters. The order is as follows. Having explained the matters that intervene (books 20 and following), Tribonian returns to the sequence that those intervening books had interrupted. Having set out earlier the actions in personam arising from contract, he now adds the actions that arise from other causes: from equity and good conscience, from quasi-contracts, from delicts, and from quasi-delicts. The action on the dowry is one of these, since it arises from equity and good conscience (l. Eos, supra de capitis minutione). It does not arise from a quasi-contract, as was said on the Code, book 5. Since this whole treatment of marriage is divided into roughly five parts (betrothals, weddings, dowries, divorce, and accessories), the first is treated in this book 23, tit. 1, de sponsalibus, because betrothals come before weddings (l. 1, hoc tit.). It is followed by tit. 2, de ritu nuptiarum, because weddings follow betrothals, as already said. To this is added tit. 3, de iure dot., because a dowry does not exist without marriage (l. 3, hoc tit.). Next comes tit. 4, de pactis dotalibus. The reason is that the earlier title de iure dotium is general, containing everything pertaining to the nature of the dowry, whereas this one is special, explaining certain particular agreements accepted in dowries, by which the nature of the dowry is sometimes somewhat altered. This is followed by tit. 5, de fundo dotali, which is a special title pertaining to the dowry, though not to every dotal thing, but only to one thing, namely the dotal estate. Therefore this title, being special, comes later. It is also prohibitory, since it explains the prohibition on alienating a dotal estate.

units.la: XXIV. LIBER.
units.tr: XXIV. Book

units.la: Liber 24: De donatione inter virum & uxorem & de divortiis agit & actione dotis. Tres enim titulos continet: quorum primus est de donat.inter vir.& ux. Ratio ordinis est, quia hæ donationes constante matrimonio fiunt, sed dos plerumq; ante matrimonium, ideoq; prius de dotib. quàm de donationibus hic agitur. Recte autem hunc titulum sequitur tit.de fundo dot. Nam ut illo prohibetur alienatio, ita hoc prohibetur donatio ista: uterque scilicet est prohibitorius. Quem sequitur tit.2.de divort.& repud. Ratio est, quia hactenus de matrimonio contrahendo & contracto, ut proximum jam sit de eo dirimendo agere, quodfit dvortiis aliisque modis huius tit.1. Dirempto autem & soluto per divortium matrimonio, dos repeti solet raro enim eo constante repetitur. Recte igitur post titulum de divortio sequitur titulus 3.solut.matrim.&c. quo exponitur actio de dote, hoc est, quadós repetitur.
units.tr: Book 24 deals with gifts between husband and wife, with divorces, and with the action for dowry. It contains three titles, of which the first is "On gifts between husband and wife." The reason for the order is that these gifts are made while the marriage subsists, whereas the dowry is usually given before the marriage; therefore the dowries are treated before the gifts here. The title "On the dowry-land" rightly follows this one, for just as alienation is prohibited by that title, so this gift is prohibited: both, of course, are prohibitory. It is followed by the title "On divorce and repudiation" (2). The reason is that up to this point the subject has been contracting marriage and marriage already contracted, so that it is now next to treat of its dissolution, which happens by divorce and other means (title 1 of this book). Since the marriage has been dissolved and ended by divorce, the dowry is usually reclaimed, for it is rarely reclaimed while the marriage continues. Rightly, therefore, after the title on divorce follows the title (3) "On the dissolved marriage, etc.," in which the action for the dowry is set out, that is, by what means it is recovered.

units.la: XXV. Liber
units.tr: XXV. Book

units.la: Liber 25. accessoria quædam, ut dixi, continet tit. 7. quorum primus est de impensis in res dotales factis. Ratio ordinis est, quia dos & exactio dotis per impensas minuitur, hoc est, eominus petitur ex dote propter impensas quasdam in dotem constante matrimonio factas, ideoq; ad exactionem dotis hic quoq; titulus pertinet. Cui adjungitur titul. 2. de act. rer. amot. quia cum hic duæ sint actiones, unæ de dote, quæ datur uxori, altera rerum amotarum, quæ datur marito, de hac posterius agit, quia furtum & delictum uxoris cōtinet. Huic adjungitur titul. 3. de agnosc. & alend. lib. Ratio dicta supra ad Edictum, ut & titul. 4. de vent. insp. & d tit. 5. si ventris nom. & d. tit. 6. si mulier ventris nomine & ultimus titulus est de concubinis, quia hactenus actum est de justis uxoribus adjungitur nunc unus ti. de injustis uxoribus sive concubinis, quæ à justis tantum differunt dilectu, ut ait Paul in sent. tit. de cocub. hoc est animo proposito, sive quod illas maritus habeat pro matribus famil. has non item: ita & Cod. lib. 5. tit. 26. factum.
units.tr: Book 25 contains certain accessory matters, as I said, in title 7, the first of which is on expenses made on dotal property. The reason for this order is that the dowry, and the recovery of the dowry, is diminished by expenses: that is, less is claimed from the dowry on account of certain expenses made on the dowry during the marriage, and so this title too belongs to the recovery of the dowry. To it is joined title 2, on the action for things removed, because although there are two actions here, one concerning the dowry, which is given to the wife, and the other for things removed, which is given to the husband, the latter treats of this, because it covers the theft and offence of the wife. To this is joined title 3, on acknowledging and maintaining [children]. The reason was given above in the commentary on the Edict, and likewise title 4, on inspecting the womb, and title 5, if a woman is named as pregnant, and title 6, if a woman in the name of pregnancy. The last title is on concubines, because hitherto the discussion has been of lawful wives; now is added one title on unlawful wives, or concubines, who differ from lawful wives only in affection, as Paul says in the Sentences, title on concubines, that is, in the intention held, or because the husband regards the former as mothers of the household and not the latter. So also the Code, book 5, title 26, has been done.

units.la: XXVI. Liber
units.tr: XXVI. Book

units.la: His libris de matrimonio & de dote, adjunguntur libri de tutelis 26. 27. quibus quæ ad naturam tutelæ, & definitionem & divisionem & quæ ad officium tutoris sive administrationem & auctoritatem pertinent exponuntur. Nam 1. titulo de tutelis, definitio aliaque generalia continentur ideoq; hic titulus est 1. Cui proximus est tit. 2 de test. tut. Ratio dicta ad Instit. tit. 3 est de confirm. tut. Ratio, quia confirmatio in testamentario tutore locum habet l. 1. hoc titul. & §. ult. de tutel. tit. 4. cst de legit. tut. 5. de tutor. & curat. dat. & c. est de dativa tutela. Ratio ordinis dicta ad Instit. cui adiungitur tit. 6. qui pet. tut. vel cur. & c. id enim locum habet in dativis, ideoq; huic titulo, ut pars prioris. Huic est proximus tit. 7. de adminst. & peric. tut. Ratio ordinis, quia hactenus de ipsa tutela, & tutore constituendo: Nunc de constituto eiusq; officio: cujus duæ præcipuæ sunt partes, administratio & auctoritas: & prius de administratione, quia est generalis posterius de auctoritate, tit 8. de auctoritate & consensu tutorum & curatorum. quia auctoritas est quodammodo pars administrationis, & quia auctoritas non adhibetur in omnibus negociis. §. 1. Inst. de auct. tut. cum administratio sit magis generalis. In Cod tamen auctoritas non statim sequitur administrationem sed paulo post, nempe tit. 59. lib. 5. Ratio ibid. tit. 9. est, quando ex facto tutoris & c. qui titulus etiam ad officinam pertinet. nam eo agitur de actione, quæ ex officio & facto sive administratione tutoris oritur vel ipsi pupillo, vel contra pupillum vel minorem. Ratio ordinis quia actio tanquam effectus administrationis est posterior: tum etiam, quia hæc actio plerumque nascitur ex facto sive contractu & administratione tutoris per dolum & culpam, hoc est, factam non recte. Non est autem hæc actio tutelæ, ea enim datur contra tutorem, de qua infra lib. seq. tit. 3. sed hæc contra ipsum pupillum daturei,qui cum tutore contraxit Huic recte adjicitur titul. 10. de suspect. tut. quiaut titulus 9. est de actione ex facto tutoris, sæpè non recto ( ut si quid dolo aut culpa fecit in contrahendo cum alio ) ita & hic titulus est de actione sive accusatione suspecti, quæ item ex non recta,imo ex perniciosa pupilli administratione tutoris nascitur, de qua tamen posterius agitur, quia continet delicti & criminis speciem, & quia removet tutorem, cum illa ex facto tutoris,non removeat.
units.tr: To these books on marriage and dowry are added the books on guardianship, 26 and 27, which set out what belongs to the nature of guardianship, both its definition and division, and what pertains to the duty of the guardian, that is, his administration and authority. For title 1, de tutelis, contains the definition and other general matters, and so this is title 1. Next comes title 2, de test. tut. The reason for the order is given at Inst. title 3, de confirm. tut. The reason is that confirmation takes place for a testamentary guardian, l. 1. hoc titul. & §. ult. de tutel. Title 4, de legit. tut. 5. de tutor. & curat. dat. & c., concerns the dative guardianship. The reason for the order is given at Inst. To it is joined title 6, qui pet. tut. vel cur. & c., for this applies to dative guardians, and so it is attached to the previous title as a part of it. Next to this is title 7, de adminst. & peric. tut. The reason for the order is that until now the discussion has been about guardianship itself and the appointing of a guardian; now it turns to the one appointed and his office, whose two principal parts are administration and authority. And administration is treated first, because it is more general; authority afterwards, title 8, de auctoritate & consensu tutorum & curatorum, because authority is in a way part of administration, and because authority is not required in all transactions, §. 1. Inst. de auct. tut., since administration is the more general matter. In the Code, however, authority does not immediately follow administration but a little later, namely tit. 59. lib. 5. The reason for title 9 there is quando ex facto tutoris & c., which title also belongs to the office, for it deals with the action that arises from the office and deed, that is, the administration of the guardian, either for the pupil himself or against the pupil or the minor. The reason for the order is that an action, as the effect of administration, comes later; and also because this action usually arises from the deed or contract and administration of the guardian through fraud and fault, that is, something done improperly. This is not the action of guardianship, for that is given against the guardian and is discussed below, lib. seq. tit. 3. but this is given against the pupil himself who contracted with the guardian. Title 10, de suspect. tut., is rightly added to this. For as title 9 concerns the action arising from the guardian's deed, often an improper one (as when he has done something by fraud or fault in contracting with another), so this title concerns the action or accusation of suspicion, which likewise arises from the improper, indeed harmful, administration of the guardian. This is discussed later, however, because it contains the character of a delict and crime, and because it removes the guardian, whereas the action arising from the guardian's deed does not remove him.

units.la: XXVII. Liber.
units.tr: XXVII. Book

units.la: Liber 27. agit de actionibus pupillaribus initio tantum, quod non est de actionibus sed de cognitionibus excepto. Continet autem titulus 10. quorum primus est de excusat. Ratio ordinis est, quia proximus tit. de causis remotionis. hic tit. de causis excusationis Utriusque remotionis & excusationis est idem fere effectus, nempe ut quis non sit tutor. Sed remotionis ut non sit, qui jam fuit. excusationis, ut non sit, qui nondum fuit, aut certè nondum administravit: interdum tamen etiam ejus, qui jam est, §. tem qui Resp. de excusat. atque ita utraque finit tutelam. Cur autem prius de remotione hic & in Cod ratio est, quia remotio & accusatio suspecti, similitudinem habet cum titulo. quando ex facti tut. &c. In Inst. remotio posterior est, & excusatio prior. Ratio ibidem dicta titulus 2 est: ubi pup. educ. deb. Ratio ordinis hæc est: quia ut in excusationibus aditur prætor, qui de iis cognoscit: ita & de educatione, & alimentis pupillo præstandis aditur prætor, cujus est cognitio de alimentis pupillaribus & de loco, ubi educandus fit pupillus, l.1. &3. hic. Nunc sequuntur tituli actiones pupillares continentes.ut tit.3. de tut. & rat. distrahend. quæ contra tutorem dantur, & actio utilis negociorum gestorum, quæ contra curatorem. Ratio ordinis est perspicua, quia explicata jam ipsa tutela proximum est ut de actionibus agatur, quæ ex tutela & excuratione, tanquam ex causa, effecta oriuntur. Hunc sequuntur tit. 4. de contrar. tut. & ut act. Ratio est, quia prior titulus de principalibus & directis actionibus, quæ scilicet dominis, pupillo & adolescenti dantur contra tutorem & curatorem: hic est de contrariis tutelæ, quæ contra pupillum tutori, & utili negotiorum gestorum actione, quæ curatori contra adolescentem datur. Ratio ordinis enim postulat, ut directa & principalia contrariis anteponantur. Hanc sequitur tit. 5. de eo qui protutore, &c. quia superiores actiones dantur, ubi verus fuit tutor, aut curator, hæ dantur, cum falsus est tutor vel curator, nempe actio tutelæ in protutorem & negociorum gestor in procuratorem. Cui adjicitur titul 6. quod falso tutore, &c. quo continetur actio in factum, quæ ei, qui cum pupillo contraxit. auctore falso tutore, contra ipsum falsum-tutorem datur. Ratio ordinis est, qui ut prior titulus est de falso tutore, ita & iste. Sed priere titulo falsus tutor est, tàm qui scit se non esse tutorem, quàm qui putat se esse tutorem vel etiam qui bona fide gessit negocia. Sed in hoc titulo 6. semper mala fide & dolo fit auctor hic fallus tutor, ideoque hæc actio pro pœnali habetur. L.7. novissime, l.9. §.1. hic. & proinde hunc titulum recte titulus 5. sequitur, Cæterum in Edicto Perpetuo inter species restitutionis in integrum positum fuit hoc Edictum de falso tutore, ut dictum ad Edictum. Nam hæc actio est restitutoria. l.1. in f. l.5. & 7. titulus est de fideiuss. & nominat. &c. optima ratione: quia priores 4. tituli continent actiones contra ipsos tutores vel curatores, verosacfalsos; ut principa les personas: hic tit. & seq. continet actiones contra accessorias personas, ut fidejussores & nominatores, fidejussores, qui promiserunt pro tutoribus rem pupilli vel adolescentis salvam fore, tenentur actione ex stipulatu. Nominatores vero (qui nominarunt tutorem) & laudatores, quia fidejussorum loco sunt, utili actione teneentur ex stipulatu. Heredes autem tutorum & curatorum tenentur actionibus ut ipsi tutores, hoc est, directis illis nomine tutorum, & utilibus proprio nomine, ut ex proprio dolo vel ex propria administratione. l.1. & l. nlt. l.1.h.tit. Quem sequitur 8. de magistrat.conven. Nam ut tit.7. contra accessorias personas de subsidiariis, ita h.tit de subsidiaria, ut proprie videtur actione, contra magistratum principalem ut duumviros. l.1. hic titul 9. est de reb.eor.qui sub tit.&c. Ratio ordinis quia adhuc explicata sunt omnia, quæ ad tutelam & curationem adolescentum pertinent, tandem adjungitur hoc unum SCtm. de rebus pupillaribus & minorum non alienandis sine decreto: tum quia hoc SCtm. est recens, à Severo Imp. factum tum quia est prohibitorium: tum etiam quia actio fit subsidiaria in magistratum etiam est ex SCto. sed antiquiore, cui nunc recte alterum hoc prohibitorium adjungitur h tit.9. Quem sequitur tit 10. de curat.furiof. sed hic titul. in Cod.præcedit titulum. de reb.eor. sive de prædiis minorum. Ratio differentiæ, quod ad ff. quidem attinet est quia hactenus tantum de tutoribus & curatoribus minorum sive adolescentum est dictum, ad quos quoque hic titulus de rebus eorum, &c. pertinet: Ad titulus de cur.at.furiof. agit de aliis curatorib furiosi dementis, prodigi, muti, surdi &c ideoq; recte distinguitur ab illis qui agunt de curatoribus minoris. Quod ad C. attinet ratio est hæc: quia SCtm. & oratio Severi de prædiis minorum & pupillorum tandem fuit porrecta & ad curatores furiosi prodigi, &c. Tandem, inquam, hoc est, Constitutione Gordiani Imperatoris l.2. C. de curat.fur. sed in ff id fieri non debuit, quia ICtorum eorum tempore hoc SC de prædiis tantum ad tutores & curatores minorum pertinebat, non verò ad curatores furiosi &c. sic & tit. de magistr. conven. in Cod. ponitur ultimo loco etiam post tit. de prædiis minorum, qui tamen in ff. ante ponitur. Ratio diverhitatis est, quia in ff. habita est ratio actionis, ut scil. tituli de actionibus pupillarib. agentes conjungantur. In C. habita est ratio subsidii, h. e. ultimi adjutorii. Est enim hæc actio ultimum adjutorium, quo succurritur pupillis & minoribus, DE
units.tr: Book 27 deals with pupillary actions only at the start, since it concerns not actions but cognizances, with one exception. It contains ten titles, of which the first is de excusat. The reason for the order is that the next title is on the grounds of removal, and this title on the grounds of excuse. Removal and excuse have almost the same effect, namely that a person should not be guardian: removal, so that he is no longer guardian if he already was; excuse, so that he is not guardian if he has not yet been, or at least has not yet acted. Sometimes, however, excuse also ends the guardianship of one who already is guardian, §. tem qui Resp. de excusat., and so each ends the guardianship. Why removal is treated first here and in the Code is because removal and the accusation of suspicion have a likeness to the title quando ex facti tut. &c. In the Institutes, removal comes later and excuse earlier. The reason given there is that title 2 is ubi pup. educ. deb. The reason for the order is this: just as in excuses the praetor is approached, who takes cognizance of them, so too in regard to the upbringing and maintenance to be provided for the pupil the praetor is approached, whose cognizance covers pupillary maintenance and the place where the pupil is to be brought up, l. 1. & 3. hic. Next follow the titles containing pupillary actions, such as title 3, de tut. & rat. distrahend., which are given against the guardian, and the useful action of business transacted, which is given against the curator. The reason for the order is plain: since guardianship itself has now been explained, it is fitting that we should next treat of the actions arising from guardianship and curatorship as from their cause. These are followed by title 4, de contrar. tut. & ut act. The reason is that the earlier title concerns the principal and direct actions, which are given to the owners, to the pupil and to the young man against the guardian and curator; this one concerns the counter-actions of guardianship, which the guardian has against the pupil, and the useful action of business transacted, which is given to the curator against the young man. For the order requires that direct and principal actions be placed before counter-actions. This is followed by title 5, de eo qui pro tutore, &c., because the earlier actions are given where the guardian or curator was genuine, while these are given where the guardian or curator was false: namely the action of guardianship against the false guardian, and the action of business transacted against the agent. To it is added title 6, quod falso tutore, &c., which contains the action in fact that is given against the false guardian himself to the person who contracted with the pupil on the authority of the false guardian. The reason for the order is that, as the earlier title concerns the false guardian, so does this one. But in the earlier title the false guardian is one who knows that he is not guardian, as well as one who thinks he is guardian, or even one who has managed the business in good faith. In this title 6, however, the false guardian who authorises the act always acts with bad faith and fraud, and so this action is regarded as penal, l. 7. novissime, l. 9. §. 1. hic. and therefore title 5 rightly precedes this title. Moreover, in the Perpetual Edict this edict on the false guardian was placed among the species of restitution in integrum, as has been said on the Edict. For this action is restitutory, l. 1. in f. l. 5. & 7. Title 7, de fideiuss. & nominat. &c., follows for the very best reason: the four earlier titles contain actions against the guardians or curators themselves, whether genuine or false, as principal persons; this title and the next contain actions against accessory persons, such as sureties and nominators. Sureties, who promised for the guardians that the property of the pupil or young man would be safe, are bound by the action arising from stipulation. Nominators (who named the guardian) and commenders, since they stand in place of sureties, are bound by the useful action arising from stipulation. The heirs of guardians and curators are bound by the actions just as the guardians themselves were, that is, by the direct actions in the name of the guardians, and by the useful actions in their own name, as arising from their own fraud or their own administration, l. 1. & l. nlt. l. 1. h. tit. This is followed by title 8, de magistrat. conven. For as title 7 deals with subsidiary actions against accessory persons, so this title deals with the subsidiary action, which seems properly to be an action against the principal magistrates, such as the duumvirs, l. 1. hic. Title 9, de reb. eor. qui sub tit. &c., is the reason for the order: since all that pertains to the guardianship and curatorship of young men has now been explained, this one senatusconsultum is finally added, de rebus pupillaribus & minorum non alienandis sine decreto, partly because this senatusconsultum is recent, made by the Emperor Severus, partly because it is prohibitory, and partly because the action becomes subsidiary against the magistrate, and this also rests on a senatusconsultum, though an older one. To it is now rightly joined this other prohibitory provision, h. tit. 9. This is followed by title 10, de curat. furiof. But in the Code this title comes before the title de reb. eor., or de praediis minorum. The reason for the difference, so far as the Digest is concerned, is that until now only guardians and curators of minors or young men have been discussed, to whom this title de rebus eorum, &c. also pertains. The title de curat. furiosi deals with other curators of the insane, the prodigal, the mute, the deaf, etc., and so it is rightly distinguished from those who deal with curators of minors. As for the Code, the reason is this: the senatusconsultum and the oration of Severus concerning the lands of minors and pupils were at length extended also to the curators of the insane, the prodigal, etc. At length, I say, that is, by the constitution of the Emperor Gordian, l. 2. C. de curat. fur. But in the Digest this should not have been done, because at the time of the jurists this senatusconsultum concerning lands pertained only to guardians and curators of minors, and not to curators of the insane, etc. So also the title de magistr. conven. is placed last in the Code, even after the title de praediis minorum, although in the Digest it is placed before. The reason for the difference is that in the Digest the arrangement follows the nature of the action, so that the titles on pupillary actions are grouped together; in the Code the arrangement follows the nature of the remedy, that is, the last resort of aid. For this action is the last resort by which pupils and minors are helped.

units.la: XXVIII. Liber.
units.tr: Book XXVIII.

units.la: Equitur s. pars ff de testamentis & 9. libris continetur, nempe lib. 28. & 8 sequent Postea demum parte 6. agitur de bonorum possessione. Contrarius est ordo in Cod. ubi prius de bonorum possessionibus, posterius de hereditatibus agitur. Ratio C. est quia in C. Trib secutus est Edictum perpetuum, cujus ordinis ratio exposita est supra ad Edictum & in C. Ratio ff est, quia in ff Trib. ordinem actionum & judiciorum spectavit. Ut autem actio tutelæ est ex quasi contractu, ita & ex testamento actio. §. tutores. & § heres. de obl. quæ ex q. cont. Est & altera ratio, cur hereditates hic anteponantur bonorum possessionibus, quia hereditates sunt civiles, bonorum possessiones sunt prætoriæ. s.1. de bon.poss. Idem quoque dictum in Inst. ubi idem est ordo. Et his lib. 28. est de iis quæ ad formam testamenti, cujus est institutio & substitutio §. ante heredis. de leg.) pertinent, continetque; titu. §. quorum ultimus ad effectum potius pertinet, quam ad formam & initium testamenti 1. titulus est, qui test. fac. poss. quia ad formam testamenti quæ hoc libro exponitur, in primis animad vertere debemus de persona testatoris, an habuerit testamenti factionem. l.4. h. t. Quem sequitur tit. 2. de lib. & posth. &c. Ratio est, quia ad ordinanda testamenta, sive ad formam principale jus est de liberis heredib. instituendis, vel exheredandis. l.30. hic. His enim præteritis testamentum aut est injustum aut rumpitur. Et hinc est quod statim ei adjungitur tit. 3 de injusto, &c. Nempe 1. de justo hoc est, in quo forma & sollemnia juris sunt observata posterius de injusto rupto &c. agendum. tit 4. est de his quæ in test. del. &c. propter similitudinem cum priori. Nam ut testamentum infirmatur, quia sit injustum, ita etiam deletum consulto. l.1. hoc tit. s. est de hered. inst. Ratio ordinis est quia titulus 1. est de lib. hered. &c. hic est de extraneis. Duo autem tituli 3. & 4. propter dictam causam sunt interjecti. Ratio autem postulat ut prius de liberis & suis heredibus agatur, quàm de extraneis & alienis, quia illorum omissione seu præteritione, testamentum est injustum, horum non item. Hinc est tit ul. 6. de vulg. & pup. Ratio dicta est ad Instit titul. 7. est de cond. inst. Ratio est quia conditiones etisi testamentis adscribuntur, plerumque tamen post mortem testatoris existunt ideoque; post institutiones & substitutiones ponuntur. Est & hæc ratio quia substitutio, de quatit. proximus est quædam conditionalis institutio, ideoq; ei titulo statim rectè adjungitur hic titulus de cond. inst. Et rectè institutionum. Nàde legatorum & fideicommissorum. contractuum, libertatum, & omninò de omnibus conditionib. agitur infra in tit. de cond. & dem. titulus ultimus huius libri est de jure delib. Ratio est quia testamento jam facto, de quo hactenus dictum, mortuoque testatore, proximum est, ut hereditas adeatur: sed prius priùs tamen secum deliberat heres de adeundo & repudiando : itaque in C. hæc duo jus deliberandi, & aditio sub eodem titulo continentur, lib.6. tit.30. Sed ea his titulis separantur : & primum de jure deliberandi, quia ut dictum aditio præcedit deliberationem.
units.tr: The second part of the Digest, on wills, follows, and it is contained in nine books, namely Book 28 and the eight that come after it. Afterwards, in the sixth title, the subject of bonorum possessio is treated. The order is reversed in the Code, where bonorum possessiones are treated first and inheritances afterwards. The reason for the Code's order is that Tribonian followed the Perpetual Edict in the Code, and the reason for that order is explained above, under the Edict and in the Code. The reason for the Digest's order is that in the Digest Tribonian followed the order of actions and judgments. Just as the action of guardianship arises from a quasi-contract, so too the action arising from a will arises (see § tutores and § heres, de oblig. quae ex quasi contractu). There is also another reason why inheritances are placed before bonorum possessiones here: inheritances are civil, whereas bonorum possessiones are praetorian (s. 1, de bon. poss.). The same order is also followed in the Institutes. This Book 28 deals with those matters that pertain to the form of a will, whose essential parts are the institution and the substitution (§ ante heredis, de legatis), and it contains them. The last title (§ quorum) concerns the effect of a will rather than its form and beginning. The first title is qui testamenta facere possunt, because in examining the form of a will, which is set out in this book, we must first consider the person of the testator, whether he had the capacity to make a will (l. 4, h. t.). It is followed by title 2, de liberis et posthumis, and so on. The reason is that the principal law governing the drawing up of wills, that is, the form, concerns the instituting or disinheriting of children as heirs (l. 30, hic). For if these are passed over, the will is either invalid or is broken. Hence title 3, de iniusto, etc., immediately follows. Namely, under the title de iusto it is considered what is valid, where the forms and solemnities of the law have been observed, and afterwards the iniustum ruptum, etc., is to be discussed. Title 4 is de his quae in testamento delentur, etc., placed there because of its resemblance to the previous one. For just as a will is invalidated when it is unjust, so too a will deliberately cancelled. (l. 1, hoc tit., §. est de hered. inst.) The reason for the order is that title 1, de liberis et heredibus, etc., deals with the children, whereas this one deals with outsiders. Titles 3 and 4 have been inserted for the reason given. The reason requires that children and sui heredes be discussed before outsiders and strangers, because a will is unjust through the omission or passing over of the former, but not of the latter. Hence the title 6, de vulgari et pupillari. The reason for the position of the following title, de conditionibus institutionum (title 7), was given in the Institutes. The reason is that although conditions are attached to wills, they are for the most part fulfilled after the death of the testator, and therefore they are placed after the institutions and substitutions. There is also this reason: substitution, which is closest to it, is a sort of conditional institution, and so this title, de conditionibus institutionum, is rightly joined to it immediately, and rightly so in the Institutes. For conditions of legacies and fideicommissa, of contracts, of liberties, and in general of all conditions, are treated below in the title de conditionibus et demonstrationibus. The last title of this book is de iure deliberandi. The reason is that once the will has been made, as discussed so far, and the testator has died, the next thing is that the inheritance be entered upon; but the heir first deliberates with himself whether to enter or to renounce. Thus in the Code these two, the right of deliberation and acceptance, are contained under the same title (lib. 6, tit. 30). But in the Digest these are separated under different titles, and the right of deliberation is treated first, because, as has been said, acceptance comes before deliberation.

units.la: XXIX. Liber.
units.tr: XXIX. Book.

units.la: LIber 29. varia ad testamentum ejusque maximè effectum pertinentia continet. Quorum 1. tit est de testamento militis, quia hic titulus est inter deliberationem, de qua supra titulo proximo hac ni fallor de causa, quod initio libri conveniat: tum propter inscriptionem de testamento, ut intelligatur, adhucagi de testamentis, tum propter singularia in eo jura l. 2. h. tum quia etsi rectius alioquin ante titulum de jure deliberandi poni poterat nimis tamen prolixum facturum erat librum 28 Cur autem in Cod. inter tit. de testamentis, hic de testamento militis primus ponatur, ibi d. tit. 1. de adquir. vel omitt. hered. ratio jam dicta tit. 3. quomodo dum test. aper. Ratio est quia quamvis heredes ex asse scripti hered. tatem adquirere possint, nondum apertis, sed clausis etiam tabulis : ex parte tamen scriptis illorum non poterant hereditatem adire, nisi apertis tabulis, exceptis suis heredibus ideoque apertura tabularum ad aditionem pertinente recte hic titulus priorem sequitur. Quem sequitur tit. 4. si quis omissa causa test. Ratio ordinis quia tit. de adquir. vel omit. her. generaliter de omittenda hereditate dictum est hic specialiter. nimirum de uno casu omittendæ hereditatis, quo scilicet callidè quis & dolo malo hereditatem omittit ex testamento ad se delatam, & ab intestato eam possidere coepit, ex animo callido, ut non soluat legata, testamento sciliget omissione irrito facto. Ratio igitur ordinis, tum quia hic titulus specialis est tum quia dolum & delictum heredis continet. Cui rectè jam adjungitur titulus 5. de SC. Syllan. & Claudiano, &c. Nam & hoc delictum heredis continet. Sed hoc est recentius & gravius illud est antiquius & levius, ideoque priore loco exponitur. Sic & tit. 6. si quis aliquem testar. &c. delictum continet. Ratio ordinis est, quia hoc est recentissimum, nempe ab Adriano inductum, l.4. hoc tit. Quem sequitur tit. 7. de jure codicillorum. Ratio ordinis est, quia cum hactenus de ipso testamento sit actum & codicilli sint velut supplementum testamenti, ut loquitur Theoph. ad Inst. rectè post tractatum testamentorum de codicillis tanquam de accessione, parte & supplemento testamentorum agitur. Et hæc de testamentis. Ea enim quæ hactenus sunt exposita, ad ipsam testamentorum substantiam & effectum pertinent. Idem & Edicti (in quo tamen pauca de testamentis & legatis fuerunt,) ut supra dictum fuit ordo.
units.tr: Book 29 contains various matters relating to wills, and especially to their effect. Of these, the first title is "on the soldier's will." This title stands among the titles on deliberation (dealt with in the preceding title) for this reason, I think: it fits at the start of the book, partly because of the heading "on wills," so that it is understood that we are still dealing with wills, and partly because of the special rights it contains (l. 2. h.). Also, although it could otherwise rightly have been placed before the title on the right of deliberation, that would have made Book 28 too long. Why, in the Code, the title "on the soldier's will" is placed first among the titles on wills, while there the first title is "on acquiring or omitting an inheritance," has already been given under the third title, "how wills are opened." The reason is that, although heirs instituted for the whole can acquire the inheritance even before the tablets are opened, indeed while they are still sealed, heirs instituted only in part could not take up the inheritance unless the tablets were open, except for the heirs of the household (sui heredes). Therefore the opening of the tablets, which pertains to acceptance, rightly follows the earlier title here. The fourth title, "if anyone, with the cause of the will omitted," follows. The reason for this order is that the title "on acquiring or omitting an inheritance" spoke generally of omitting an inheritance, whereas this one speaks specifically, about one case of omitting an inheritance: namely, where someone cunningly and with evil intent omits an inheritance delivered to him by will, and begins to possess it on intestacy, with a crafty purpose, so that he does not pay the legacies, the will being made void by his omission. The reason for the order, then, is both that this title is special and that it contains the fraud and offence of the heir. Rightly, then, the fifth title follows: "on the Senatus-consultum Syllanianum and Claudianum, etc." For this too concerns an offence of the heir. But this one is more recent and more serious, while that one is older and lighter, and so the older one is set out in the earlier place. Likewise the sixth title, "if anyone has ... someone's will ...," concerns an offence. The reason for its order is that this is the most recent, namely introduced by Hadrian (l. 4. h.t.). It is followed by the seventh title, "on the right of codicils." The reason for this order is that, since the will itself has been treated so far, and codicils are, as Theophilus puts it in his commentary on the Institutes, as it were a supplement to the will, it is rightly treated after the discussion of wills, as an accession, part and supplement of wills. So much for wills; for what has been set out so far pertains to the very substance and effect of wills. The order of the Edict was the same, as was said above (though there were few matters on wills and legacies in it).

units.la: XXX. XXXI. XXXII. Liber.
units.tr: XXX. XXXI. XXXII. Book.

units.la: Odicillis adjunguntur legata & fideicommissa. Ratio est, quia & haec in testamentis relinquuntur: quamvis in Institut. prius de legatis & fideicommissis, posterius de codicillis agatur. Ratio differentiae est, quod in institut. habita est ratio modorum adquirendi dominii, qui sunt speciales aut universales, speciales: ut usucapio, donatio, legatum. universales: ut hereditas ex testamento, & ab intestato, bonorum possessio, &c. Et prius quidem modi speciales exponuntur, posterius universales, legata tamen non cum specialibus modis, sed cum universalibus ut ex hereditate, ex testamento explicantur. Ne tamen longe essent a specialibus remota, praeponuntur Codicillis. Sunt & aliae rationes ad Instit expositae quibus & haec accedat quod tractatus de legatis est valde prolixus, in ff. & C. ideoque titulus de Codicillis, ut testamenti pars rectius positus fuit legatis & fideicommissis nempe lib. 30. & 4. seqq. Quibus & alii duo libri, ad legata & fideicommissa pertinentes adjunguntur de lege Falcidia, & SC. Trebell. ut ait l. 2. §. Quinctius. C. de vet. jur. enucl. Et libri quidem 30. 31. & 32. qui singuli constant uno titulo ejusdem nominis, de legatis & fideicommissis, sunt generales, & omnium legatorum & fideicommissorum naturam, & praecepta generalia continentes. Ideoque inter hos libros de legatis & primum locum tenent. Quod autem ad hos 3. primos libros, hoc est, 30. 31. & 32. attinet, eorumque inter se ordinem sciendum est, hos tres libros ita ordine dispositos esse, quasi esset unus titulus, ita inscriptus de legatis & fideicommissis, tantum propter longitudinem sectus & distinctus in 3. integros libros. Ideo, in his tribus nullus est alius, quam qui est in uno titulo. At ordo in uno titulo jam est expositus, nempe quia hi titulus (hic 3. sunt libri) est generalis, ideoque primus in tractatu legatorum. Dices? An ergo in singulis legibus horum trium librorum nullus est ordo? Resp. est sane nempe idem est ordo legum in his libris, qui pro uno titulo habentur, qui est sub aliis titulis maxime longioribus. Nos autem agimus jam de ordine librorum & titulorum non de ordine legum sub tit. positarum, de quo infra.
units.tr: Codicils are joined to legacies and fideicommissa. The reason is that these too are left in wills, although in the Institutes the legacies and fideicommissa are treated first and codicils afterwards. The reason for the difference is that the Institutes considered the modes of acquiring ownership, which are either special or universal. Special modes are such as usucapion, donation, and legacy; universal modes are such as inheritance by will or on intestacy, bonorum possessio, and so on. The special modes are explained first and the universal ones afterwards, but legacies are explained not with the special modes but with the universal ones, as with inheritance by will. Yet so that they should not be far removed from the special modes, they are placed before codicils. There are also other reasons set out in the Institutes, to which this may be added: the treatise on legacies is very lengthy in the Digest and the Code, and so the title on codicils was rightly placed as a part of the will, after legacies and fideicommissa, namely in book 30 and the following. To these are added two further books concerning legacies and fideicommissa, on the Falcidian law and the Senatusconsultum Trebellianum, as the law 2, §. Quinctius, C. de veteris juris enucleatione says. The books 30, 31 and 32, each of which consists of one title of the same name, de legatis et fideicommissis, are general and contain the nature of all legacies and fideicommissa and their general precepts. Therefore among these books those on legacies hold the first place. As for these first three books, that is 30, 31 and 32, and their order among themselves, it must be known that these three books are arranged in order as if they were one title, inscribed de legatis et fideicommissis, and divided into three whole books only on account of their length. Therefore, in these three there is no other order than that which is in one title. But the order within one title has already been set out, namely that this title (these three books) is general and therefore first in the treatise on legacies. You will say: is there then no order at all among the individual laws of these three books? I reply: there certainly is; namely, the order of laws in these books, which are regarded as one title, is the same as that which obtains under other, much longer titles. But we are now dealing with the order of books and titles, not with the order of the laws placed under the titles, of which below.

units.la: XXXIII. Liber.
units.tr: XXXIII. Book.

units.la: Huncigitur titulum, id est hos 3. libros 30. 31. & 32. sequitur lib. 33. quo speciali legata continentur, ut annua, usufructus servitus. Ratio ordinis perspicua est, quia species sequitur genus. Hic autem liber 33 continet 10. titulos, in quibus tantum speciali legata exponuntur: quorum ordinem inter se exponere perdifficile est. Sunt autem haec specialia legata fere 20. quae partim hoc libro partim seq. tit. 1. 2. & 3. explicantur. Paul. lib. 3. sent. tit. 6. de leg. eodem tit. complexus est tam generalia quam specialia,
units.tr: This title, that is, the three books 30, 31 and 32, is followed by book 33, which contains the particular legacies, such as annual payments, usufruct and servitudes. The reason for this order is clear, since the species follows the genus. Book 33 contains ten titles, which deal only with particular legacies. It is very difficult to set out their order relative to one another. There are about twenty of these particular legacies, which are explained partly in this book and partly in the following titles 1, 2 and 3. Paulus, in Sentences book 3, title 6, de legatis, dealt under the same title with both general and particular legacies.

units.la: Inter hæc specialia, primum hic ordo videtur observandus, quod sa legata, quæ planè sunt specialia prius posuerit Tribun. de rebus scilicet singulis, & per se distinctis, ut est ususfructus reditus, servitus. Ea autem quæ sunt de rebus multa in se continentibus ut est peculium, supellex mundus muliebris, &c posterius posuerit, nempe ut.6. & seq. Quod & Cujac animadvertit in Parat. ut.6. Denique quod incorporalia prius, ut est reditus, ususfructus servitus: posterius corporalia ut fundus, triticũ, supellex vestis, &c. posuerit, quemadmodũ & intercdictis de via, flumine, itinere aqua. &c Ratio ordinis autem cur hujus libri 33. tit 1. de annuis leg. fit est hæc, quia hoc legatum legato usufructo est persimile l.8.h.t.& l.22.tit.seq. ususfructus autem legatum proximum locum titulo de legatis habet, propterea quod titulus de legatis generalis pertinet ad dominium Estenim legatum adquisitio dominii §.ult.per quas pers.l.8.legatum.supra de leg.2. Dominio autem similis est ususfructus l.4.& 5 de usufr. ut & supradictum ad titul.de usufr. Et hinc est, quod in Paulo d. tit. 6. statim generalia de legatis, sequitur ususfructus. Dices. cur sumfructum præcedit hic reditus sive annuum legatum? Ratio videtur esse quia legatum annuum sive in annos singulos tributũ plura legata continet l.ut.cum in annos.h.tit. Deinde est aliquid amplius in legato annuo, quàm in legato usufructus. Nam annuum legatum non tollitur capitis diminutione, ut usufructus d.tit.leg.8.hoc tit. in quo annum legatum dominio est similius quam usufructus. Nam & dominium non tolliturcapitisdiminutione tit 2 est de usu & usufr. leg. Ratio ordinis est propter similitudinem cum priore ut supra dictum, ubi hoc addendum fortasse, curde annuo legato primum agatur, quia hoc legatum initio anni sit præstandum cum usufructus non nisi post fructus perceptos habeat. d.tit.leg. in singulis. tertius titulus est de servit.leg. priùs enim de personalibus, posterius de realibus servitutibus agitur Ratio dicta supra ad tit.de usufr. Hunc sequitur titulus 4.de dote præleg. ratio videtur esse tum quia & dos videtur quiddam incorporale tum quia ut deactione servitutum prius, quàm de actione dotis, ita & prius de legato sit agendum Hunc sequitur titulus s. de opt. vel electi.l.g. tum quia optio sive electio est quiddam incorporale. ut & servitutes (est enim optio actus: ideoque magis differt à servitutibus quam dos, quia dosest res sive jus quoddam: optio est actus & proinde dotis legatum optionem præcedit) tum quia optionis legatum aliquo modo pertinet ad secundum genus specialium legatorum, quo genere continentur ea legata. de quibus quæri solet, quid verbo legati contineatur quamque latè pateat, quod de priore genere non quæritur. Satis enim constat quid nomine ususfructus, servitutis, dotis contineatur. At in legato optionis sæpè non satis constat, quid contineatur, quidàne sit eligendum proprie tamen & plerunque constat ideoque legatum optionis pertinet magis ad primum genus, titul 6.est, de irrito vino, &c. quod legatum est ex secundo genere
units.tr: Among these particular legacies, the first point to observe in this order seems to be that Tribonian placed first those legacies which are plainly particular, namely those concerning single and distinct things, such as usufruct, a yearly income, and a servitude. Later he placed those which concern things containing many items, such as a peculium, household goods, and a woman's ornaments, and so on, namely in title 6 and following. Cujacius also noted this in Paratitla, title 6. Finally, he placed incorporeal things first, such as income, usufruct and servitude, and later corporeal things, such as land, wheat, furniture, clothing, and so on, just as in the interdicts concerning a way, a river, a journey, water, and so on. The reason why book 33, title 1, de annuis legatis, comes first is this: an annual legacy is very similar to a legacy of usufruct (law 8, this title, and law 22, the following title). Usufruct holds the next place after the title on legacies, because the general title on legacies belongs to ownership. For the acquisition of ownership is a legacy (§ last, Per quas personas; law 8, Legatum, above de legatis 2). Usufruct is similar to ownership (laws 4 and 5, de usufructu), as is also stated above under the title de usufructu. Hence it is that in Paulus, said title 6, the general matters on legacies come first, followed by usufruct. You may ask why an income or annual legacy comes before usufruct. The reason seems to be that an annual legacy, that is one payable each year, contains several legacies (law Ut cum in annos, this title). Moreover, an annual legacy has something more than a legacy of usufruct. For an annual legacy is not extinguished by loss of status, as usufruct is (said title; law 8, this title), in which respect an annual legacy is more like ownership than usufruct is. For ownership too is not extinguished by loss of status (title 2, de usu et usufructu legato). The order is because of its similarity to the preceding title, as said above. Perhaps it should be added here that the annual legacy is treated first because this legacy must be paid at the beginning of the year, since usufruct only yields after the fruits have been taken (said title, law In singulis). The third title is de servitutibus legatis, for personal servitudes are treated first and real servitudes later. The reason is given above under the title de usufructu. The title 4, de dote praelegata, follows this. The reason seems to be both that a dowry also appears to be something incorporeal, and that just as the action concerning servitudes comes before the action concerning a dowry, so too the legacy concerning a dowry should be treated before the other. Title 5, de optione vel electione legata (law G), follows this, both because option or choice is something incorporeal, as servitudes are (for an option is an act, and so it differs from servitudes more than a dowry does, since a dowry is a thing or a right of a certain kind, whereas an option is an act; and therefore the legacy of a dowry precedes the legacy of an option), and because a legacy of option in some way belongs to the second kind of particular legacies, the kind which includes those legacies about which it is usually asked what is contained in the word "legacy" and how widely it extends. This is not asked about the first kind. For it is quite clear what is contained under the name of usufruct, servitude or dowry. But in a legacy of option it is often not clear what is included, or what is to be chosen. Yet it is generally clear in its proper sense, and so the legacy of option belongs more to the first kind. Title 6, de vino irrito and so on, is a legacy of the second kind.

units.la: ncre nere eorum scilicet: quibus de quaeritur, quid quantumve testatur hoc legato intellexerit aut complexus fuerit. Cur autem de tritico vino, &c. primum agatur, ratio videtur esse, tum quia haec pondere, numero & mensura constant (quae res aliis praeferuntur, ut videre est in contractuum ordine, ubi mutuum praefertur aliis quod in iis rebus consistit.) Tum quia in hoc legato tritici, &c. interdum quaestio est de electione vini, vetus an novum, bonum optimum aut deterius si relictum tum denique, quia hoc legatum videtur maximè urbanum. Cui adjungitur titulus septimus, de instrum. & instr. quod magis rusticum videtur, hoc est, magis ad fundus & rustica praedia pertinens, quamvis tamen de domo quoque ibi agatur, & de praediis urbanis & etiam de aliis rebus ut nave instructa, titulus octavus, est de peculio legato. Ratio ordinis videtur, tum quia in priore titulo, legato instructi fundi mancipia quoque continentur, quorum proprium est peculium, de quo item quaeri potest, an sub instructo contineatur l. 32. ff. ult. supra de instr. tum quia hic titulus ut prior maximè est de accessionibus, quae merito sunt posteriores. Haec autem accessio ut servilis & leviór, nempe peculium, priore accessione, nempe instrumento fundi & ipsis mancipiis posterior esse debet.
units.tr: Namely, the kind about which it is asked what, and how much, the testator intended or included in the legacy. As to why de tritico, vino and so on is treated first, the reason seems to be that these things consist of weight, number and measure. Such things are given precedence over others, as can be seen in the order of contracts, where loan precedes the others because it consists of such things. It also seems that in the legacy of wheat and so on there is sometimes a question about the choice of wine, whether old or new, good, best, or worse, if left. Finally, this legacy seems to be the most urban. To it is added title 7, de instructo vel instrumento, which seems more rural, that is, belonging more to farms and country estates, although a house is also discussed there, and town properties, and also other things such as a ship fitted out. Title 8 is de peculio legato. The reason for this order seems to be, first, that in the preceding title a legacy of a furnished farm also includes the slaves, to whom a peculium properly belongs, and it may likewise be asked whether these are included under "furnished" (law 32, D., last section, above de instructo vel instrumento). Second, this title, like the preceding one, deals mostly with accessories, which rightly come later. But this accessory, being servile and lesser, namely the peculium, ought to come after the earlier accessory, namely the equipment of the farm and the slaves themselves.

units.la: Est enim servus accessio fundi de quo tit. septimus & peculium est accessio servi, de quo hic tit 9. est lepenn.legato. Ratio videtur esse, quod penus legatum videtur convenire tam servis quam liberis. Pleraque omnia legata aut ut usufructus &c. liberis relinquuntur, sed legatum peculii etiam ipsi servo relinquitur una cum libertate. §. peculium dei g. legatum tamen peculii etiam liberis relinquitur, sive cum servo ut accessorium, sive separatum. Recte igitur titulo de pen. leg. tit. de pecul. leg. statim adjungitur, quia & hoc legatum tam servis quam liberis conveniat, ut supra dictum est & haec ratio quia ut peculium est servorum sive familiae, ita & penus est familiae l.3. hoc tit. Quem sequitur tit. 10. de supellect. leg. propter similitudinem, quia scilicet ad domum de qua dictum supra titulo septimo, necessaria est penus primo, & proximè supellex.
units.tr: For the slave is an accessory of the farm, which is the subject of title 7, and the peculium is an accessory of the slave, which is the subject of this title 9, de penu legata (legacy of provisions). The reason seems to be that a legacy of provisions seems to suit both slaves and free persons. Most legacies, such as usufruct, are left to free persons, but a legacy of peculium is also left to the slave himself together with his freedom (§ Peculium, Dei...). Yet a legacy of peculium is also left to free persons, whether with the slave as an accessory, or separately. Rightly, therefore, the title de penu legata is followed at once by the title de peculio legato, because this legacy also suits both slaves and free persons, as has been said above. And the reason is that just as the peculium belongs to slaves or the household, so the provisions belong to the household (law 3, this title). Title 10, de supellectile legata, follows it because of the similarity, namely that for the house mentioned above under title 7, provisions are necessary first, and household goods next.

units.la: XXXIV. LIBER.
units.tr: XXXIV. BOOK

units.la: Liber trigesimusquartus continet novem titulos, in quibus reliqua specialia legata deinde de ademptione & translatione legatorum agitur. titulus primus est de alim. vel cibar. leg. quod legatum quia & ad liberos & ad alumnos maximè pertinet, ideo ad finem specialium legatorum adjectum videtur: titulus secundus est de auro & arg. leg. Ratio videtur esse, quia hoc legatum sit paucorum ut & alimenta liberorum, ita & hoc ditiorum cum priora legata sint omnium. Et hoc de auro est posterius illo, de alimentis quia illud est accessorium & favorabilius de alimentis titulus tertius est de liberat. leg. quod est ultimum legatum ex iis, quae specialia vocavimus.Ratio ordinis tum quia & hoc valde speciale, tantum enim ad debitores pertinet: tum quia ut solutio & liberatio postremum locum obtinent, ut infra, de solut. ita & inter legata haec non male videtur legatum liberationis ultimo collocatum. Cui & recte statim adjungitur titulus quartus, de adim. vel transferen. leg. Nam & legato liberationis tollitur debitum, ita & hoc titulo de tollendis legatis agitur.
units.tr: The thirty-fourth book contains nine titles, in which the remaining special legacies are treated, and then the revocation and transfer of legacies. The first title is de alim. vel cibar. leg. (concerning legacies of food or provisions). Since this legacy pertains chiefly both to children and to foster-children, it seems to have been added at the end of the special legacies. The second title is de auro & arg. leg. (concerning legacies of gold and silver). The reason seems to be that this legacy, like the maintenance of children, belongs to few, whereas this one belongs to the wealthy, while the earlier legacies belong to all. And the title on gold follows the one on food because the latter is accessory and more favourable. The third title is de liberat. leg. (concerning the legacy of release), which is the last of those we have called special. The reason for this order is that this title is very special, since it pertains only to debtors; and because payment and release hold the last place, as below in de solut., so among legacies the legacy of release placed last seems not badly chosen. Directly after it is rightly joined the fourth title, de adim. vel transferen. leg. (concerning the revocation or transfer of legacies). For as a debt is removed by the legacy of release, so in this title the removal of legacies is treated.

units.la: Ordinis ratio haec est: quia hactenus a libro trigesimo usque ad hunc titulum de legatis constituendis sive relinquendis actum est, & de relictis. Proximum igitur est, ut de tollendis agitur hoc tit. & seqq. Itaque titulus quartus, de adim. est de modis, quibus per ipsum testatorem legata & fideicommissa tolluntur. Cui adjungitur titulus quintus, de reb. dub. Ratio ordinis est, quia adhuc dictum est de legatis utilibus, nunc de inutilibus, ut sunt ea, quae effectu carent & alicui auferuntur. Sed hic titulus est de quasi legatis dubiis, & mediis quodammodo inter utilia & inutilia, de quibus scilicet dubium est, sint utilia futura nec ne: ideoque hic titulus velut medius est inter iectus inter utilia & inutilia. Est autem hic titulus conceptus, non de legatis, sed de rebus dubiis, hoc est non specialiter sed generaliter non tantum de legatis, sed etiam de institutionibus heredum, & de ipsis contradictibus.
units.tr: The reason for this order is as follows. Up to this point, from the thirtieth book to this title, the making or leaving of legacies and bequests has been discussed. The next step is therefore to treat of their removal, which is done in hoc tit. & seqq.. Accordingly the fourth title, de adim., deals with the ways in which legacies and fideicommissa are revoked by the testator himself. It is followed by the fifth title, de reb. dub.. The reason for this order is that we have so far treated of effective legacies, and now treat of ineffective ones, such as those which lack effect or are taken away from someone. But this title deals with what are in a sense doubtful legacies, midway between effective and ineffective, about which it is uncertain whether they will take effect or not. For this reason the title stands, as it were, in the middle between effective and ineffective legacies. Moreover, this title is framed not as concerning legacies but as concerning doubtful matters. That is, it is general rather than specific: it deals not only with legacies but also with the institution of heirs and with the contradictions themselves.

units.la: Sic enim saepe solet Tribun. speciei occasione titulum concipere generalem, & sub eo non speciem tantum, loco & ordini convenientem, sed alia quoque similia complecti, ut & paulo infra sub titulo de cond. & dem. Ut autem hic primum utilia, deinde inutilia legata exponuntur, ita & in Cod. lib. 6. de stip. lib. 8. Idemque in institut. factum, ubi admonuimus, ubi & ratio dicta, sequitur hinc titulus 6. de his quae poena causa relinqu. quae legata olim quidem omnia erant inutilia, sed hodie non nisi uno casu §. poena. de legatis. Ut igitur titulus de rebus dubiis continet legata personis dubiis aut incertis relicta, aut etiam dubia ratione conscripta (quae etiam legata incertis personis relicta, olim quidem omnia erant inutilia, hodie non nisi certis casibus. §. legati. verf. sed nec, &c. de leg.) ita & haec legata poenae nomine illis similia recte statim illis adjuncta fuerunt. Quibus adjungitur tit 7. de reg. Caton. Nam & hoc titulo de legatis inutilibus agitur, sed incertis quoque an sint utilia.
units.tr: For the Tribonian compilers often frame a general title on the occasion of a particular kind, and under it embrace not only that kind, which fits the place and order, but also other similar matters, as also a little later under the title de cond. & dem.. And just as here the effective legacies are set out first and then the ineffective, so it is done in the Code, lib. 6. de stip. and lib. 8., and the same was done in the Institutes, where we have given notice, and where the reason has been stated. There follows here the sixth title, 6. de his quae poena causa relinqu., concerning legacies left by way of penalty. Formerly all these legacies were ineffective, but today only in one case, §. poena. de legatis.. Just as the title de rebus dubiis contains legacies left to doubtful or uncertain persons, or also those written on doubtful grounds (legacies left to uncertain persons were formerly all ineffective, but today only in certain cases, §. legati. verf. sed nec, &c. de leg.), so these legacies by way of penalty were rightly attached immediately to those similar ones. To these is added title 7, de reg. Caton.. For this title also treats of ineffective legacies, but of those whose effectiveness is also uncertain.

units.la: Nam haec ratio tantum pertinet ad ea legata quae inutilia sunt, si ipso test. facti tempore testator decesserit, quae legata scilicet ab initio sunt inutilia prorsus. Et haec est ordinis ratio.
