Nam priora duo incertis personis & poenae nomine, relicta hodie non sunt omnino inutilia, sed quaedam tantum) haec, de quibus reg Cat. sunt plane ab initio utilia. titulus 8. est de his, quae pro non scripta hab. Ratio ordinis haec est: quia & haec plane sunt inutilia, sed recte post regulam Catonianam. Nam quaedam pro non scriptis habentur propter crimen falsi (scilicet titulus nonus, de his quae ut indig. &c. agitur de delicto, sive de inutilibus propter delictum. Est autem hic titulus nonus, posterior illo de his quae pro non scriptis, quia illa non omnia propter delictum sunt inutilia, sed quaedam tantum ut ea, quae quis sibi adscripserit, quod est falsi species, quaedam ex aliis causis, & non ex delicto, ut quae ita sunt scripta in testamento, ut legi aut intelligi non possint, ut quae ei qui in rebus humanis non est, relicta sunt in testamento. Sed titulus nonus & ultimus huius libri 34 legata omnia sunt inutilia propter delicta eaque varia. Et haec de legatis, lib 30. & 4. seqq.
units.tr: For this reason applies only to those legacies which are ineffective, if the testator died at the time the will was made; that is, legacies which are wholly ineffective from the beginning. This is the reason for the order. For the first two, those left to uncertain persons and by way of penalty, are today not wholly ineffective, but only some of them; those under the Catonian rule are plainly effective from the beginning. The eighth title is de his, quae pro non scripta hab.. The reason for its order is that these are plainly ineffective, but rightly placed after the Catonian rule. For some are held as unwritten on account of the crime of forgery. The ninth title, de his quae ut indig. &c., deals with the wrong, or with what is ineffective on account of wrongdoing. This ninth title comes after the one on what is held as unwritten, because not all of those are ineffective on account of wrongdoing, but only some: such as those which someone has written in for himself, which is a species of forgery; others arise from other causes and not from wrongdoing, such as those written in a will in such a way that they cannot be read or understood, or those left in a will to someone who is not among the living. But the ninth and last title of this thirty-fourth book concerns legacies that are all ineffective on account of various wrongs. So much on legacies, book 30 and the following.

units.la: XXXV. LIBER.
units.tr: XXXV. Book

units.la: Quibus adjunguntur duo libri eodem, hoc est, ad legata & fideicommissa pertinentes, nempe liber trigesimus quintus, ad legata potissimum, & lib. 36 ad fideicommissa potissimum, ut & ait leg. secunda, §. Quintus C. de vet. iur. enucl. Nam liber trigesimus quintus de lege Falcidia, quae ad legata, & liber 36 de SConsult. Trebell. quod ad fideicommissa pertinet. Sunt igitur huius libri 3. tantum tituli, sed primus non tantum ad legata, verum etiam ad fideicommissa, imo ad omnes fere juris articulos pertinet ad manumissiones, tutelas, hereditates, institutiones, donationes, contractus, &c. in quibus locum habent conditiones & modi. Sed demonstrationes in legatis tantum & fideicommissis maxime sunt receptae. Quia autem regula juris est: falsis demonstrationibus non perimi, non inutilia reddi legata, ut neq; falsis causis. §. huic proxima, & seq. Inst. de leg. recte tractatur de inutilib. & tollendis legatis statim adjungitur hic tit. 1. de cond. & dem. Dixi hunc titulum ad alios quoq; tractatus pertinere, sed id factum occasione tantum: Nam proprie alioqui pertinet ad legata fideicommissa, libertates, aliaq; testamentis relicta exceptis heredum institutionibus, de quibus specialitulo jam ante dictum lib. 28. tit. 7. de cond. inst. tit. 2. ad leg. Falc. recte hic ponitur, tum quia aut proximi tituli fuerunt de legatis plane faciendis ita hic est de illis delibandis, sive de minuendis: tum quia hactenus dictum est, de legatis recte aut non recte relictis, sive de causa & primo ortu legatorum, quemadmodum relinquantur: proximum nunc est, ut de effectu recte relictorum agatur tam legatorum quam fideicommissorum. Ad effectum autem pertinet lex Falcidia, hoc est, ad solutionem legatorum. Nam heres legata praestiturus quadrantem Falcidianum detrahit, si velit potest enim & integra & illibata restituere. l. ult. C. b. tit. Huic adjungitur tit. 3. si cui plus quam per leg. Falc. &c. quo tit. continetur redictum praetoris, sive stipulatio praetoria, ideoque in edicto perpetuo fere extremo cum aliis stipulationibus posita, sed a Tribun. huc reducta quia ad leg Falcid. pertinet. Est autem titulus ad leg. Falcid. generalis, & hic titulus si cui plus, &c. est specialis, tantum agit de eo casu, quod heres dubitat, an lex Falcidia locum habere possit. Ideoque hic tutulus est posterior.
units.tr: To these are joined two books of the same kind, that is, relating to legacies and trust-bequests (fideicommissa): the thirty-fifth book, chiefly on legacies, and the thirty-sixth, chiefly on trust-bequests, as the author also says in leg. secunda, §. Quintus C. de vet. iur. enucl. For the thirty-fifth book deals with the Falcidian law, which concerns legacies, and the thirty-sixth with the Senatus consultum Trebellianum, which concerns trust-bequests. This book therefore has only three titles, but the first is not concerned only with legacies, but also with trust-bequests, indeed with almost all the articles of law: with manumissions, guardianships, inheritances, institutions, donations, contracts, and so on, in which conditions and modes have their place. Yet demonstrations are received chiefly in legacies and trust-bequests alone. Because it is a rule of law that legacies are not destroyed by false demonstrations, nor rendered void, nor by false causes, §. huic proxima, & seq. Inst. de leg. and rightly the treatment of what is void and of the removal of legacies is immediately followed by this first title, de cond. & dem. I have said that this title also pertains to other treatises, but that happened only by occasion; for properly it otherwise pertains to legacies, trust-bequests, liberties and other things left by testament, apart from the institutions of heirs, of which a special title has already been spoken of earlier, lib. 28. tit. 7. de cond. inst. The second title, ad leg. Falc., is rightly placed here, both because the preceding titles were about making legacies outright, and so this one is about diminishing them; and because up to now it has been said which legacies are rightly or not rightly left, that is, the cause and first origin of legacies and how they are bequeathed; the next step is to treat of the effect of those rightly left, both of legacies and of trust-bequests. Now the Falcidian law pertains to effect, that is, to the payment of legacies. For an heir who is about to pay legacies deducts the Falcidian quarter, if he wishes; for he can also restore them whole and unimpaired. l. ult. C. b. tit. To this is joined the third title, si cui plus quam per leg. Falc. &c., which title contains the edict of the praetor, or the praetorian stipulation, and therefore it is placed in the nearly final perpetual edict together with other stipulations, but the Tribonian compilers brought it here because it pertains to the Falcidian law. The title on the Falcidian law is general, and this title si cui plus, &c. is special; it treats only of the case in which the heir doubts whether the Falcidian law can apply. Therefore this title is the later one.

units.la: XXXVI. LIBER.
units.tr: XXXVI. BOOK.

units.la: Liber 36. quatuor titulos continet, quorum primus est ad S.C. Trebell. Ratio ordinis dicta est ad Institut. & ad Cod. Nam & hic titulus ad effectum SCti pertinet, sed fideicommissi universalis, de quo detrahit heres quadrantem non minus atque de legatis. tit 2. quando dies legat. vel fid. e comm. ut omnes reliqui, communis est, legatorum & fideicommissorum tantum excipitur prior titulus qui proprius est fideicommissorum & quidem universalium, interjectus ibi propter similitudinem cum leg. Falc. nempe in quadrantis detractione, ut jam dictum. Hic autem titulus secundus ad effectum quoq; pertinet nam de cessione hic agitur, cujus cessionis effectus est, ut legata quorum dies cesserit, ad heredem quoq; legatarii transeant. Sed neq; ad legatarium, neq; ad heredem ejus legata perveniunt, prius quam heres detraxerit quadrantem: ideoq; prius de lege Falcidia po\u0304terius de cessione hic agitur titulo secundo. Quem sequitur titulus tertius. ut leg. vel fid. causa cau quo continetur cautio praetoria, quae legatorum dicitur, ideoque hic posita, a Tribun cum in edicto fuerit extremo ubi de stipulat. ut indicaut inscriptiones legum. l. 13. 14. h. Ut autem supra lib 35 titulo 10 est stipulatio qua cavetur heredi ut ne amittat Falcidiam ita titul. hoc stipulatio est qua cavetur legatario, ut ipsi legatum sit salvum in diem forte aut sub conditione relictum, ne pendente conditione heres legatum perdat. Ratio ordinis est, quia & hic titulus ad effectum pertinet, ut suo tempore legatum praestari possit. Sed hic dices illud, quando dies, &c posterior est quia ille est magis generalis, pertinens scilicet ad omnia legata tam pura quam in diem, aut sub conditione: hic magis est specialis tantum ad legatum in diem, aut sub conditione relictum pertinens. Est & altera ratio, quia dies cedit saepe ante petitionem hujus cautionis, nempe in legatis puris, in quibus dies cedit statim a morte testatoris, cum haec cautio demum post mortem petatur, titulus quartus, ut in p. ff. legat. &c. Ratio ordinis est quia prius petitur cautio de conservandis legatis, quam si heres nolit praestare, tum legatarius petit, & impetret missionem in possessionem legati, quod est ultimum remedium, ut dictum ad Cod. lib 6. tit. 35. ut in p. ff. legat. &c. ubi sub uno eodemque titulo & missio & cautio sive satisdatio continentur. Et haec de quinta parte, ens libri & tit. quae pars de testamentis dicitur, ut supra dictum.
units.tr: Book 36 contains four titles, of which the first is on the Senatus consultum Trebellianum. The order is explained in the Institutes and in the Code. For this title too pertains to the effect of the senatus consultum, but to a universal fideicommissum, from which the heir deducts a quarter no less than from legacies. Title 2, "When the day of a legacy or fideicommissum falls due", is common to all the others. Only the former title, which belongs to fideicommissa, and indeed to universal ones, is excepted from legacies and fideicommissa; it is placed there on account of its similarity to the Lex Falcidia, namely in the deduction of a quarter, as has already been said. This second title is also concerned with effect, for here we treat of cession, and the effect of cession is that legacies whose day has fallen due pass also to the heir of the legatee. But legacies reach neither the legatee nor his heir before the heir has deducted the quarter. Therefore the Lex Falcidia is treated first, and cession afterwards, in the second title. It is followed by the third title, "On the cautio for a legacy or fideicommissum", which contains the praetorian cautio called that of legacies; it is placed here, having been moved from the Tribunes, whereas in the edict it stood at the end, where stipulations are treated, as the inscriptions of the laws indicate (laws 13 and 14 of this title). Just as above, in Book 35, title 10, there is the stipulation by which the heir is secured so that he does not lose the Falcidian quarter, so in this title the stipulation is one by which the legatee is secured that his legacy be safe, when it has been left for a day or under a condition, so that the heir does not lose the legacy while the condition is pending. The reason for the order is that this title also pertains to effect, so that the legacy can be paid at its proper time. But here you will say that the title "When the day falls due" comes later because it is more general, pertaining namely to all legacies, pure as well as those for a day or under a condition; this title is more specific, pertaining only to a legacy left for a day or under a condition. There is also another reason: the day often falls due before this cautio is demanded, namely in pure legacies, in which the day falls due immediately at the death of the testator, whereas this cautio is demanded only after death. Title 4, as in the Pandects "On legacies", etc. The reason for the order is that the cautio for preserving legacies is sought first; if the heir is unwilling to pay, then the legatee sues and obtains missio into possession of the legacy, which is the last remedy, as was said on Code Book 6, title 35; as in the Pandects "On legacies", etc., where both the missio and the cautio or satisdatio are contained under one and the same title. And this is said of the fifth part of the book and title, which part is called concerning testaments, as was said above.

units.la: De VI. Parte Digestorum.
units.tr: On the Sixth Part of the Digest.

units.la: XXXVII. LIBER.
units.tr: Book XXXVII.

units.la: Sexta parte initio est liber 37. qui est totus de bonorum possessionib. imo & liber 38 ex parte, nempe usq; ad titulum decimum sextum de eadem agit. Et hujus quidem libri trigesimi septimi, sunt quindecim tituli. Itaq; articulus, sive tractatus de bon. poss. hic in ff. trigesimus titulus explicatur de quibus est tantum unus in institut. & in C. sunt 13. lib. 6. Cur antem in Cod. prius de bonorum possessionibus agatur posterius de testamentis sive hereditatibus in ff prius de hereditatibus & posterius de bonorum possessionibus dictum est supra ad initium tituli, vers. iest. ff.lib. 28 Horum autem triginta tituulorum de bon. poff. inter se ordo primum generalis hic est: ut cum bonorum possessio sit duplex, ut & hereditas una ex testamento, altera ab intestato prius agitur de illa ex testamento, nempe hoc lib 37 & initio libri 38. tit. 1. & 2. & 3. Ratio ordinis est supra ad edictum. Deinde bonorum possessio ut & hereditas rursus est duplex, aut ingenuorum aut libertinorum, & de illa ingenuorum prius agitur, nempe hoc lib 37. usq; ad titulum decimumquartum, de iure patronat. & ab eo posteaa agitur de libertorum successione, usq; ad finem hujus libri, & libri seq. tit. 1. & 4. seqq. usq; ad sextum titulum si tab teft. nulla extitat. Ratio cur de ingenuis prius agatur, dictum in Institut. Cur ergo inquies in Cod fit contra ubi prius de libertis eorumq; successionibus agitur lib. f. sec. 6. tit. 3. 4. 5. 6. 7. & 8. Ratio haec est quia in Cod. initiolibri sexti, tit. 1. & 2. agitur de servis fugitivis & libertis ideoq; statim his duo tituli adjunguntur, & alii tituli de libertis ut omnia de libertis conjunctim, & continenter explicentur. At in ff. nulli hic sunt tituli ante bonorum possessione qui agant de libertis & servis. Cur autem sint in Cod ibi dictu? Rursus bonorum possessio potest tertio dividi in paginam & militarem: sed haec est subdivisio nempe bonorum possessionis testamentariae Et primum quidem de testamentaria paganorum usq; ad titulum decimumtertium postea de militum agitur d. titulo decimotertio. Ratio ordinis nota est quia urbana militaribus praeponuntur. Postremo paganum subdividitur quoq; bifariam, in contra tabulam & in secundum tabulam. Et prius quidem de illa usq; ad titulum undecimum, posterius de ista, dict. tit. 11. de bon. poss. cont. tabul. & 2. seq. Ratio dictaad ed: dictum tamen secundum tabulam est prior. Ratio ibidem. Ergo hujus libri 37. titulus primus est de bon. poss. qui est generalis definitionem & alia generalia continens titul. 2. si tab. test. exilab. qui jam est specialis. Nam ut dictum bonorum possessio vel est testamentaria, hoc est, si tab. testam. exilab. vel est ab intestato de qua lib 38 titulo sexto si tab. test. null. & c. tit. 2. est de bon. poss. fur osi. & c Ratio ordinis est, quia primum de personis, quibus datur bonorum possessio ex testamento, tit. 2. deinde adjungitur titulus tertius, de personis quibusdam, de quibus dubitari potest, an & quemadmodum iis detur, titulus quartus est de bon. poss. cont. tab. Ratio ordinis est, quia priores tituli sunt generales & primus quidem maxime generalis, hoc est communis tam bonorum possessioni ex testamento, quam ab intestato 2. vero & 3. minus generales, communes scil eorum tantum, quae ex testamento. At ex testamento possessionum sunt duae species, ut supra de contra tab. & secundu tabulas. Hinc jam est ratio ordinis quae postulat ut tit. generalib. adjungantur speciales. Cur autem prius haec species, nempe contra tab. ponatur quam secundum tabulas supradictum ad edict. Ad hanc autem speciem pertinent hic 7.tit.ut h tit. 4.de bon.poss.cont.rab. qui est in hac specie velut generalis.Cui adjungitur tit.5. de legatis praestandis,& huic tit.6.de collat.bon. Ratio ad edictum.Et huc tit.7.de aertis collat. Ratio est, quia prior de omni collatione ut generalis hic species collationis continet,nempe dote. Huc sequitur tit.8.de conjungend.cum emancip.lib. & hunc titulus ac vent. n poss. mitt. & hunc tit.10.de Carb.ed. Ratio supra ad edictum sequitur titul 11. de bon.poss.sec.tab. Ratio ad edictum cui proximus est tit. 12.si a parente quis manumiss. Ratio ordinis est quia adhuc expositum, de bonorum possessione ingenuorum ex testamento tam contra, quam secundum tabul. testamenti, proximum nunc erat adjungere, de bonorum possessione libert. ut & inedictis supradictum & factum. Sed hic in ff. interjiciuntur 2. tituli, nempe 12.si a parente,&c. & 13.de bon.poss.ex test.mil. Ratio haec est quia & hae possessiones sunt ingenuorum,nempe filiifam. quae datur parenti manumissori: & militis, quae datur scripto heredi in testamento militari. Cur autem prius de filiofam.quam de milite agatur. haec est ratio, quia urbana praeponuntur militaribus. At titulus de filiofam. pertinet ad testamentum urbanum sive paganum, ut titulus de milite ad militare. Et hic Tribun discessit ab ordine edicti. Nam hic de milite agitur ante libertum. Ratio edicti supra ad Ed.PP. Ratio ff. modo dicta quia scilicet testamenta ingenuorum tam pagana quam militaria testamentis libertorum, Tribun. putavit anteponenda. Titulus 14.est de jure patronatus. Ratio ordinis est quia post testamenta ingenuorum jam proximum est,ut de testamentis libertorum agatur, ut & in edicto supra dictum. Sed in edicto tantum de possessione bonorum contra tabulas libertorum, ut & in C. lib.6. tit 15.de bon.poss.libert.cont.rab. sed in ff. non tantum de bonor.possession.cont. tab.liberti, hoc est, de unojure, quod patronis competit:sed ejus occasione arrepta,omniaalia jura patrono competentia hic ponuntur, quae in Cod. nonnihil separantur. Et reliqua quidem patronijura in Cod.ponuntur. initio lib.6.tut.3.& 8.seqq. De possessione vero paulo post secundum ordinem edicti, nempe titulo decimotertio agitur. Quod igitur ad ff.attinet, titulus decimusquartus est de jure patronatus quia est generalis inter titulum septimum de libertis, sive de omni jure patronorum in personas & bona liberti.tit.15. cfl de obseq. parent.& patron.&c. Ratio ordinis est quia patronorum jura, licet multa tamen ad duas summas species revocari possunt: personarum & bonorum sive rerum. Itaque post titulum generalem, species illa de personis prius exponitur titulus decimusquintus, & titulus primus, lib.seqq. Personarum enim jura sunt obsequia, & operae, sed de obsequiis prius agitur, tum quia obsequia sunt honestiora jura, operae sunt viliores, & magis serviles. tum quia titulus 15. de obsequiis, est communior, titulus de operis est specialior, quia titulus de obsequiis pertinet tàm ad liberos quàm ad libertos, tàm ad parentes quàm ad patronos, titulus de operis tantum ad libertos.
units.tr: The sixth part begins with Book 37, which is entirely about bonorum possessiones, and in part Book 38, as far as title 16, deals with the same subject. Book 37 has fifteen titles. The treatise on possession of goods (de bonorum possessione) is explained here in the Digest under title 30, of which there is only one in the Institutes, and in the Code there are thirteen in book 6. Why in the Code possession of goods is treated first and wills or inheritances second, while in the Digest inheritances come first and possession of goods second, was said above at the beginning of the title, in the verse est, Digest book 28. Of these thirty titles on possession of goods, the first order among them is general: since possession of goods, like inheritance, is twofold, one from a will and the other on intestacy, the one from a will is treated first, namely in this book 37 and at the beginning of book 38, titles 1, 2 and 3. The reason for this order was given above under the edict. Next, possession of goods, like inheritance, is again twofold, either of freeborn persons or of freedmen, and the freeborn persons' possession is treated first, namely in this book 37 as far as title 14, on the right of patronage. After that the succession of freedmen is treated to the end of this book and the following book, titles 1 and 4 onward, as far as the sixth title, if no tablets of the will exist. The reason why the freeborn are treated first was given in the Institutes. So why, you will ask, does the Code do the opposite, where the freedmen and their successions are treated first, in book 6, titles 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 and 8? The reason is that at the beginning of book 6 of the Code, titles 1 and 2, runaway slaves and freedmen are treated, and therefore two titles are joined to these at once, and the other titles on freedmen follow, so that everything concerning freedmen is explained together and in sequence. But in the Digest there are no titles before the possession of goods that deal with freedmen and slaves. Why, then, are they placed where they are in the Code? Again, possession of goods can be divided thirdly into civilian (pagana) and military. But this is a subdivision, namely of the testamentary possession of goods. First, the civilian testamentary possession is treated as far as title 13, and afterwards the military, in title 13 itself. The reason for this order is well known: civil matters are placed before military ones. Finally, the civilian possession is also divided in two, into possession against the tablets and possession according to the tablets. The former is treated as far as title 11, the latter after it, said title 11, on possession of goods against the tablets, and the following two. The reason was given under the edict. Nevertheless, possession according to the tablets comes first. The reason is given in the same place. So the first title of this book 37 is on possession of goods, which is general, containing the definition and other general matters, and title 2, if the tablets of the will are produced, which is already specific. For, as has been said, possession of goods is either testamentary, that is, if the tablets of the will are produced, or on intestacy, of which book 38, title 6, if no tablets of the will exist, etc. Title 2 is on possession of goods of the thief's property, etc. The reason for the order is that first the persons to whom testamentary possession of goods is given are treated, title 2. Then title 3 is added, on certain persons about whom it may be doubted whether, and in what manner, it is to be granted to them. Title 4 is on possession of goods against the tablets. The reason for the order is that the earlier titles are general, and the first is the most general, that is, common both to possession of goods from a will and on intestacy. The second and third are less general, common only to what comes from a will. Now there are two kinds of possession from a will, as above under against the tablets and according to the tablets. Hence the reason for the order now requires that the general titles be followed by the specific ones. Why this kind, namely against the tablets, is placed before that according to the tablets, was said above under the edict. To this kind belong here seven titles, as follows: title 4, on possession of goods against the tablets, which is in this kind as it were the general title. To it is joined title 5, on legacies to be paid, and to this title 6, on collation of goods. The reason is given under the edict. And to this title 7, on collation of dowries. The reason is that the earlier title, on all collation, is the general title of this kind of collation, namely of dowry. To this follows title 8, on those joined with emancipated persons; and then the title on the sending into possession; and then title 10, on the edict of Carbo. The reason was given above under the edict. Title 11 follows, on possession of goods according to the tablets. The reason is given under the edict, and next to it is title 12, if someone was manumitted by a parent. The reason for this order is that, since the possession of goods of the freeborn from a will, both against and according to the tablets of the will, has now been set out, it was next to add the possession of goods of freedmen, as was said and done in the edict. But here in the Digest two titles are inserted, namely title 12, if by a parent, etc., and title 13, on possession of goods from a military will. The reason is that these possessions also belong to the freeborn: that of the son under power (filius familias), which is given to the parent who manumitted him, and that of the soldier, which is given to the heir written in a military will. Why the son under power is treated before the soldier is explained by the fact that civil matters are placed before military ones. The title on the son under power pertains to the civil or civilian will, just as the title on the soldier pertains to the military will. And here Tribonian departed from the order of the edict, for here the soldier is treated before the freedman. The reason for the edict was given above under the Praetor's edict. The reason for the Digest, just mentioned, is that Tribonian thought the wills of the freeborn, both civilian and military, should be placed before the wills of freedmen. Title 14 is on the right of patronage. The reason for the order is that, after the wills of the freeborn, the next thing is that the wills of freedmen should be treated, as was also said in the edict. But in the edict there is only possession of goods against the tablets of freedmen, as also in the Code, book 6, title 15, on possession of goods of freedmen against the tablets. In the Digest, however, not only on possession of goods against the tablets of a freedman is treated, that is, on the single right which belongs to patrons, but, on the occasion of that, all the other rights belonging to a patron are set out here, which in the Code are somewhat separated. The other rights of patrons are set out in the Code at the beginning of book 6, titles 3 and 8 onward. The possession itself is treated shortly afterwards, according to the order of the edict, namely in title 13. So, as far as the Digest is concerned, title 14 is on the right of patronage, because it is the general title among title 7, on freedmen, or on all the rights of patrons over the persons and goods of a freedman, title 15, on the duties of obedience to parents and patrons, etc. The reason for the order is that the rights of patrons, though many, can nevertheless be reduced to two main kinds: those over persons and those over goods or things. Therefore, after the general title, the kind concerning persons is set out first, title 15 and title 1 onward. For the rights over persons are obedience and services; but obedience is treated first, both because obedience is the more honourable right and services are the baser and more servile, and because the title 15, on obedience, is the more general, while the title on services is more specific, since the title on obedience pertains both to children and to freedmen, both to parents and to patrons, whereas the title on services pertains only to freedmen.

units.la: XXXVIII. LIBER.
units.tr: BOOK XXXVIII.

units.la: Liber trigesimus octavus videtur trimembris. Nam primo membro, hoc est, titulo primo & quatuor seqq. reliqua de libertis, 1. de bonorum possessione ab intestato, vide 6. & 9. seqq. 3. de hereditatibus ab intestato, tit. 6. & seq. agitur. Sunt autem hujus libri tit. 17. quorum primus est de op. lib. Ratio dicta supra de obseq. tit. 2 est de bon. libert. Ratio item ibi dicta, quia scil. priore specie de jure patroni in personam liberti expositâ, consequens sit ut de altera, hoc est, de bonis agatur. Et hoc tit. proprie jam agitur de bonorum possessione patrono competente in bona liberti, tit. 3. est de libertis universitatum. Ratio ordinis est, quia titul. 2. & priores sunt de omni liberto in genere: hic tit. est specialis de liberto alicujus corporis, ut municipii, collegii &c. tit. 4. est de assignatione libert. quia species est sive singularis potius. Nam eo agitur de assignatione quia scilicet à patre duorum aut plurium liberorum assignatur vni ex eis libertus, ut ille nunc sit liberti patronus. Videtur & haec esse ratio ordinis, quod haec assignatio sit jus novum, tempore Claudii primum inductum, l. 1. b. cum priora jura sint antiquiora. 5. est si quidem fraud. patr. quia est ultimus de libertis & jure patronorum. Ratio, quia de fraude & delicto agit. Et haec de bonorum possessione ex testamento. Nunc de iis quae ab intestato, de quibus est titulus sextus. sit ab. test. mil. Ratio ordinis dicta supra ad Cod. & edictum. Cui proximus est titulus septimus. unde legit & huic titulus octavus unde cogn. Ratio dicta ad edictum. Hunc sequitur titulus nonus, de successionibus edicti. Ratio ut intelligatur, meminisse oportet, quod supra dictum ad edictum, ubi indicavi, praetoris edictum bimembre fuisse. 1. de tempore, intra quod peti aut cognosci debeat bonorum possessio. 2. membrum de ordine successionis ut primo suis heredibus detur bonorum possessio, deinde legitimis quae duo membra in edicto coniuncta, hic in ff. sunt distincta. Nam de tempore hic agitur, tit. nono, de successorio edicto, de ordine agitur infra tit. 15. quis ordo, etc. Ratio ff. cur haec separavit Tribun. videtur haec esse, ut scil. pars ea de ordine sit proxima hereditati legitimae, fiveab intestato, propterea quod & hic ordo sit eorum qui ab intestato bonorum possessionem petunt, maxime cum & gradibus cognationum Tribun. in ff. tit. hoc loco ponendum putarit, statim scilicet post tit. vnde liberi, unde legitimi, unde cognati. Nam titulus 10. est de gradib. & affinib. &c. Ratio ordinis est, quia modo dictum est, de bonorum possessione quae datur liberis, agnatis, cognatis, &c. ideoque; mox rectè hic adjungitur tit. de gradibus. Quae disputatio, ad liberos, agnatos, & cognatos ptinet. Est & haec ratio, quia in successorio edicto ordo cognationis & gradus diligenter attendi debet, ut sciatur 1. de tempore (nam aliud tempus datur paretib. & liberis, aliud caeteris agnatis l. 1. §. sintra §. largum. Cc de succeff. edict.) Deindeut sciatur ordo, scil quo ordine cognatus cognato succedat in bonorum possessione ex edicto successorio. Et haec est ratio, cur hic tit. de successorio edicto quod ad tempus attinet, fuerit positus hoc loco, statim post titulum, unde cognati, & ante tit. de gradib. Cum in edicto perpetuo fuerit hoc edictum positum inferius, nempe post omnes species bonorum possessionis ab intestato: ut & in ff. pars huius edicti, quae est de ordine adhuc eumlocum retinet, nempe tit 15. quis ordo in bon. poff. titulus 11. est unde vir. & ux. Ratio supra dictaad Cod. Hunc sequitur tit 12. de re eran. & mil. succeff. Ratio ordinis est, quia ut supra libro 37. tit. 13. de bon. poff. ex teft. mil. post paganum testamentum, ita & hic post paganorum ab intestato bonorum possessione, agitur de veteranorum & militum ab intestato successione sive bonorum possessione. tit.13 est quibus non competit bon. vod. Ratio haec esse videtur, quia hactenus de ijs, quib competit, tam ex testamento, quam ab intestato, nunc de ijs quibus non competit, quod quia ex delicto fit recte quoq; hic tit. in fine ponitur, ut supra dictum ad edictum eoque magis hoc tit 13. convenit tit. 11. quia in utroque de delicto tit. 14. est ut ex ll. SCtis. ve. & c Ratio supra ad edictum. Hunc sequitur tit 15. quis ordo in bon. poff. serv. Ratio iam dicta supra tit. 9. Huic proximus est tit. 16. de suis & legit. &c. Ratio dicta iam supra ad tit. 1. libri 37. quia adhuc, hoc est a libri 28. tit. qui testamenta fac. poff. & seqq. usque ad hunc titulum explicatum est de hereditate ex testamento. Restat altera species hereditatis, quae legitima sive ab intestato dicitur, ad quam pertinet hic titulus 16. de suc. legit. rum seqq. Idem ordo est in Cod. & Instit. ubi est ratio dicta. Sed in Instit. prius de legitima hereditate, posterius de bonorum possessione agitur, quod contrafit in ff. & Cod. Ratio ff. & Cod. est, ut scil propius ad ordinem edicti accedatur in quo edicto de bonorum possessione fuerint praeposita edictis ad legata & fideicommissa pertinentibus, ut dictum supra ad edictum. Recte autem hic titulus 16. praecedit titulum 17. de SC. Tertull. quia legitima hereditas, vel est ex antiquis legibus, scil ex 12 tab. Nempe legitima suorum sive agnatorum, vel ex novis legibus matris, liberorum matri succedentium puta ex SCtis. l. 1. 2. & 3. supra de pet. hered. Veteres enim leges & successiones novis sunt praferendae. In edicto autem de successionib. ab intestato nulla edicta fuisse videntur, sed tantum de bonorum possessione ab intestato quia hereditates sunt civiles bonorum possessiones sunt praetoriae, & ad edictum praetoris pertinentes, ut alibi dictum.
units.tr: The thirty-eighth book appears to have three parts. The first part, that is, the first title and the four that follow, deals with the remaining matters concerning freedmen: on the possession of goods on intestacy, see titles 6 and 9 et seq.; and on inheritances on intestacy, titles 6 and following of book 3. This book contains seventeen titles, the first of which is on the services of freedmen. The reason is what was said above under on services, title 2, and it is on the goods of freedmen. The same reason is given there: once the first kind, the right of the patron over the person of the freedman, has been set out, it follows that the second kind, that is, the goods, should be treated. This title now deals properly with the possession of a freedman's goods that belongs to the patron. Title 3 is on the freedmen of corporations. The reason for this order is that the earlier titles 2 and following concern every freedman in general, while this title is specific to the freedman of some body, such as a municipality, a guild, and so on. Title 4 is on the assignment of freedmen, which is a species, or rather a singular case. For it deals with the case where a freedman is assigned by a father of two or more children to one of them, so that this child becomes the patron of the freedman. This seems also to be the reason for the order: this assignment is a new right, first introduced in the time of Claudius (l. 1, b.), whereas the earlier rights are older. Title 5 is if indeed in fraud of the patron, since it is the last title on freedmen and on the rights of patrons. The reason is that it deals with fraud and wrongdoing. This concludes the possession of goods under a will. Now we come to those that arise on intestacy, which are the subject of title 6, on the goods of a soldier's will. The reason for the order was given above under the Code and the edict. Next follows title 7, whence the legitimate heirs, and then title 8, whence the cognates; the reason was given under the edict. This is followed by title 9, on the successions under the edict. The reason for it is that one must remember what was said above under the edict, where I pointed out that the praetor's edict had two parts: (1) concerning the time within which possession of goods ought to be sought or granted, and (2) concerning the order of succession, so that possession of goods is given first to the sui heredes and then to the legitimate heirs. These two parts, joined together in the edict, are separated here in the Digest. For title 9, on the succession edict, deals with time, while the order is treated below in title 15, what order in the possession of goods. The reason the compilers of the Digest separated these parts seems to be this: the part concerning order lies close to legitimate inheritance, or inheritance on intestacy, because the order also concerns those who seek possession of goods on intestacy. Especially since the Tribonian compilers thought the degrees of kinship should be placed here in the Digest, namely immediately after the titles whence the children, whence the legitimate heirs, whence the cognates. For title 10 is on degrees and affinities, and so on. The reason for this order is that it has just been said that possession of goods is given to children, agnates, cognates, and so on; therefore the title on degrees is rightly added here, as the discussion concerns children, agnates and cognates. There is also this reason: in the succession edict the order of kinship and the degrees must be carefully observed, so that one knows (1) the time (for one time is granted to parents and children, another to the other agnates; l. 1, §. sintra §. largum, Cod. on the succession edict), and then (2) the order, namely in what order a cognate succeeds a cognate in possession of goods under the succession edict. This is the reason why this title on the succession edict, so far as it concerns time, was placed here, immediately after the title whence the cognates and before the title on degrees; in the perpetual edict this edict was placed lower, namely after all the kinds of possession of goods on intestacy. And the part of this edict in the Digest that concerns order still keeps the same place, namely title 15, what order in the possession of goods. Title 11 is whence husband and wife; the reason was given above under the Code. Next follows title 12, on the succession of veterans and soldiers. The reason for the order is that, as in book 37, title 13, on the possession of goods under a soldier's will, followed the pagan will, so here, after the possession of goods on intestacy of pagans, the succession or possession of goods on intestacy of veterans and soldiers is treated. Title 13 is to whom the possession of goods does not belong. The reason seems to be that, having dealt so far with those to whom possession belongs, both under a will and on intestacy, we now come to those to whom it does not belong. Since this arises from wrongdoing, this title is rightly placed at the end, as was said above under the edict; and this title 13 agrees all the more with title 11, because both concern wrongdoing. Title 14 is on the senatus-consulta, and so on; the reason is given above under the edict. This is followed by title 15, what order in the possession of goods of slaves; the reason was already given above under title 9. Next to it is title 16, on sui heredes and legitimate heirs, etc. The reason was already given above under title 1 of book 37: until now, that is, from book 28, title who may make a will, and the following titles up to this one, inheritance under a will has been explained. There remains the other kind of inheritance, called legitimate or on intestacy, to which this title 16 belongs, on legitimate successions, and those that follow. The order is the same in the Code and the Institutes, where the reason has been given. But in the Institutes the legitimate inheritance is treated first and the possession of goods afterwards, which is the reverse of the order in the Digest and the Code. The reason for the order in the Digest and the Code is that one comes closer to the order of the edict, in which possession of goods was placed before the edicts relating to legacies and trusts, as was said above under the edict. Title 16 rightly precedes title 17, on the Tertullian senatus-consultum, because a legitimate inheritance is either from the ancient laws, namely the Twelve Tables (the legitimate succession of sui or agnates), or from the newer laws of the mother, the succession of children to their mother, such as the senatus-consulta (l. 1, 2 and 3, above, on petition of inheritance). For older laws are to be preferred to newer ones. In the edict on successions on intestacy there seem to have been no edicts, but only concerning possession of goods on intestacy; because inheritances are civil, while possessions of goods are praetorian and belong to the praetor's edict, as has been said elsewhere.

units.la: XXXIX. LIBER.
units.tr: XXXIX. BOOK

units.la: LIBER 39 tria fere continet I. De stipulationibus praetorijs, operis novi, damni infecti. II. De publicanis. III. De donationib. ut & indicat. l. 2. f. 6. verf. post haec. C. de inr. vit. enucl. Continet autem tit 6. quorum 1. est de nov. op. nunc. Ratio ex edicto pendet. Nam & in eo post edicta de bonorum possessione testamentis, legatis positum fuit edictum de novi operis nunciatione. Cuius ratio ad Edictum fuit exposita.tit. 2.est de damno inf. tit.3.de aq.& aq.pluv.&c. Ratio ordinis dicta ad Edictū, tit 4.de publ. & vect. Ratio ité ex Edicto pédet quæ supra est exposita tit.5.est de donationib. Cuius ratio ut intelligatur sciendū Trib hic migrasse ordinem Edicti Nam tit.de public. prior fuisse videtur titulo de lib. ausa, ut supra ad edictum, ubi & ratio ordinis exposita est Cur autem & in ff alius fit ordo, hoc est, cur in ff prius de publicanis de liberali causa agatur hæc videtur esse ratio quia hoc libro 39. Tribun. diuersa voluerit compleći & conjúgere, ut postea commodius uno loco & longum & totum tractatum de liberalicausa sive manumissionibus & liberali causa non interruptum disponere melius posset. Itaque & hic de donationibus interjecit de quibus tamen in Edictonihil reperio, & longè inferius Jurisconsulti de iis tractant, ut Paul.lib.5.sent.tit.11. nempe post interdicta & stipulationes quem ordinem & Imp.in Cod tenet lib.8 Non autem sine causa cum tit. 4. de publ. adjungitur tit.5. de donat. Nam ut donationes sive dona sunt munera, ita & vectigalia sunt munera, sed vectigalia sunt munera,quæ præstantur Reip. & sunt necessaria donationes sunt munera privatorū plerumq;, & non necessaria, sed ex liberalitate profecta l.1.h. tit.de donat. Quem sequitur tit.6.de mort.cauf.donat. Ratio ordinis est, quia tit.5. est generalis.tit.6. est specialis. continens speciem donationis, quamvis & tit. 5 speciem donationis eam scilicet quæ est inter vivos continet. Sæpè enim fit,ut idem tit.partim sit generalis, partim specialis,ut d.tit. Instit. de tutel.
units.tr: Book 39 contains roughly three things: I. Praetorian stipulations: on new work (operis novi) and on damage not yet done (damni infecti). II. The publicans. III. Gifts, as also indicated in C. de inr. vit. enucl., l. 2, §6, "post haec". It contains six titles, of which the first is on the new work notice (de novi operis nunciatione). The rationale for this depends on the Edict: for in it, after the edicts on possession of goods under a testament and under a legacy, the edict on the notice of new work was also placed. Its rationale was explained in the commentary on the Edict at title 2 (de damno infecto), title 3 (de aqua et aqua pluvia, etc.). The rationale of the order is set out in the commentary on the Edict at title 4 (de publicanis et vectigalibus). The rationale also depends on the Edict, which was explained above at title 5, on gifts (de donationibus). To understand its rationale, it should be known that the Tribonian compilers here departed from the order of the Edict. For the title de publicanis was formerly placed before the title de liberali causa, as explained above in the commentary on the Edict, where the rationale of the order is also set out. Why, however, in the Digest the order is different, so that the case of liberal causes is treated first after the publicans, the reason seems to be this: in this 39th book the Tribonians wished to combine and join diverse matters, so that later they could more conveniently arrange the long and whole treatment of liberal causes, or manumissions, in one place without interruption. Thus they also inserted here the matter of gifts, of which, however, I find nothing in the Edict, and the jurists treat of them much further down, as Paul in lib. 5 Sent., tit. 11, namely after the interdicts and stipulations; which order the Emperor also follows in the Code, lib. 8. Nor is it without reason that title 5 on gifts (de donationibus) is joined to title 4 on the publicans. For as gifts are presents, so too taxes (vectigalia) are presents; but taxes are presents which are paid to the Commonwealth, while gifts are for the most part presents of private persons, and not necessary, but proceeding from liberality (l. 1, h. t., de donationibus). This is followed by title 6, on gifts made in view of death (de mortis causa donationibus). The rationale of the order is that title 5 is general, title 6 is special, containing one species of gift; although title 5 also contains a species of gift, namely that which is between the living (inter vivos). For it often happens that the same title is partly general and partly special, as in the said title of the Institutes, de tutelis.

units.la: XL. LIBER.
units.tr: BOOK XL.

units.la: TOTus est unius argumenti, nempe de libertate ac servitute, sive illis, quæ ad illa pertinent & cōtinet tit.16. Ratio ordinis partim ex Edicto pendet in quo post actione aqua pluv.arc.posita fuit actio & Edictum de liberali ut supra dictū ad Edictum, sed in ff. inter has duas actiones, & de liberali causa interjecti sunt duo tit. de public. & don. Ratio interpositionis jam dicta supra. Neq;sine causa donationem sequitur libertas, quia & libertas plerumq; ex donatione sive liberalitate contingit, unde summū beneficium dicitur.l.1.supra de bon.libert. & apud Terrull. Et ut donatio est aut inter vivos, aut mortis causa, ita & libertas datur aut inter vivos (ut vindicta) aut testamento. Est ergo libertatis donatio, velut species donationis, & quidem quæ servo fit,cū priores donationes liberis plerumq; hominib.fiant, ut meritò de donationibus prius agatur, posterius de libertate. Ea autem manumissionibus datur, ideoq; initio hujus lib.40 primum agitur de manumissionibus. Nā ibi agit de modis dandæ libertatis, in Edicto, tantum fuit Edictum deactionibus ob libertatem. Sed Tribun. hac occasione arrepta totam tractatione de libertate & servitute,hoc loco una explicanda putavit, ut & alias in ff ppter actione etiam de causis actionis (ut de contractu. de dote,) simul explicare solet quamvis in Instit. propter adolescentes distinguantur causæ absolutionibus, ut alias dictum. Causa igitur sive modus libertatis est manumissio. Itaq; 1. tit. hoc libro 4o. est de manumiss. titul. 2. ff de manumiss. vind. quia primus est generalis, hic secundus est specialis, continens speciem manumissionis, quæ dicitur vindicta. Quo pertinet tit. 3. de manumiss. quæ servis ad unive sitate, &c. Nam & hic tit ad tit. de manumissionib. vindicta pertinet. Est autem posterior, quia tit. 1. est de vindicta omnium, & est frequentior, sed hic tit. est de vindicta universitatis, & collegii tantùm, & infrequentior. Sic & supra lib. 58. tit. de libert. univers. Huc sequitur tit. 4. de manumiss. test. Ratio ordinis dictaad Cod. lib. 7. tit. 5. est de fideicommiss. libert. Ratio ibi ad Cod tit. 6. est de adempt. libert. Ratio est quia prius semper de dado, posterius de adimendo agitur. tit. 7. est de statu lib. Ratio videtur esse quia adhuc dictum est de libertate danda, & adimenda, nunc agitur de servi libertate quæ dicitur statulibertas, ideoque posterius de hac agitur. titulus 8 est qui jure manumiss. ad lib. & c ratio est quia adhuc dictum est de uno modo sive de causa libertatis, nempe manumissione, qui est modus frequentior & antiquior. Est & alius, nempe lex, ut scilicet lege, sive ipso jure & sine manumissione fiat liber, de quo hoc tit. Quem sequitur tit. 9. qui & aquib. manumiss. &c. Ratio est, quia prius & hactenus de iis, qui liberi fiunt, nunc de iis, qui non fiunt, ob delictum aut fraudem aliquam, ideoque de ipsis agitur posterius tit. 10. de jure aur. annul. Ratio ordinis, quia post libertatem jam datam manumissi, cum sint libertini, solet interdum beneficio principis ingenuitatis impetrare qui modus dicitur jus aurei annuli de quo hoc Cui recte adjungitur tit. 11. de natal. restit. Ratio ordinis, quia & hic tit est modus ingenuitatis restitutio natalium, ut ille jus annulorum: sed hic modus est ratior quia plenior Ni restitutione natalium patronus amittit jus suum in libertum, utpote plane ingenuu. Sed in jure aurei annuli non amittit jus suum patronus. ff. tit. pra de jur. aur. annul. Quare non tam facile concediturrestitutio, quam jus aurei annuli. l. ult. b. tit. 12. est de liber. caus. Ratio ordinis, quia hactenus dictu est, de causa sive libertate, quibus ea detur vel adimatur. Nunc de actione qua agatur de libertate. Huic adjungitur tit. 13. quib. ad libert. proclam. nol. c. Ratio ordinis est, quia prior tit. de lib. caus. est de iis, quib datur actio, de libertate, sive de iis, quib. proclamare licet ad libertatem hic tit. est de iis, quibus non licet. tit. 14. est ji libertas ingenuus esse dicatur. Ratio ordinis est quia & hic tit. est de actione, ut duo priores, sed duo priores, sunt de actione prejudiciali, qua quæritur, servus an liber quis sit. Est & tertia prejudicialis actio, sunt enim tres hujus generis actiones. ff. prejudiciales de act.) qua quæritur filius an nō quis sit alterius, de qua. est tit. 3. de agnosc. & alend. lib. supra lib. 25. Reliqua de hac sunt rejectæ: quia hoc libro de libertate & servitute agitur. Ideo dimis autem cur actio de libertate prius & actio de ingenuitate ponatur est, tū quia hoc libro maximè agitur de libertate, tum quia libertas prior est, quam esse libertinum. Nam ut quis sit libertinus, inetinus, necesse est, ut prius fuerit servus. multi Institut. de libert. titul. 5 est, Ne de statu def. &c. Ratio ordinis est, quia hic titul est de exceptione sive praescriptione temporis, hoc est quinquennii. Ordinis autem ratio postulat, ut prius de actionib, posterius de exceptionibus agatur, ut dictum supra libro 4. Instit. Cuiadjungitur tit. 16. de collus. deteg. Ratio ordinis est, tum quia & hic temporis quinquennii, ut & in priore tit. praescriptum est voleti detegere collusionem quae collusione quis pronunciatus fuit ingenuus colludere scilicet adversario, & id agente, ut vincatur tum quia hic tit. continet delictum ne pe collusionem, ideoq; merito est ultimus, tum denique quia agit de sententia pro ingenuitate, rescindenda & retractanda, ideoq; rectè postactionem de ingenuitate, de qua supra tit. 14 si liber ingenuus esse dic. ponitur.
units.tr: The whole book has one subject, namely liberty and servitude, and the matters that pertain to them, and it contains title 16. The order depends partly on the Edict, in which the action aqua pluviae arcendae was followed by the action and the Edict de liberali, as said above on the Edict; but in the Digest two titles, tit. de public. & don., were placed between these two actions and the de liberali causa. The reason for this interposition has been given above. Liberty rightly follows donation, since liberty too most often comes by gift or bounty, and for this reason it is called the greatest benefit. l.1.supra de bon.libert. & apud Terrull. And just as a donation is either inter vivos or mortis causa, so liberty is given either inter vivos (as by the rod) or by will. The donation of liberty is therefore, as it were, a species of donation, and indeed one made to a slave; since earlier donations are mostly made to free persons, it is rightly treated first concerning donations and afterwards concerning liberty. Liberty, however, is given by manumissions, and so at the beginning of this book 40 manumissions are treated first. For there he treats of the modes of giving liberty; in the Edict there was only the Edict on actions on account of liberty. But Tribonian, seizing this occasion, thought the whole treatment of liberty and servitude should be explained here in one place, just as elsewhere in the Digest he is accustomed to explain the causes of actions together with the actions themselves (as on contract, on dowry), although in the Institutes the causes of absolution are distinguished on account of minors, as said elsewhere. The cause or mode of liberty is therefore manumission. Thus the first title of this book 40 is de manumiss., and the second is titul. 2. ff de manumiss. vind., because the first is general and this second is special, containing the species of manumission called vindicta. To this belongs tit. 3. de manumiss. quae servis ad universitatem, &c., for this title too belongs to the title on manumissions by vindicta. It comes later, because title 1 concerns vindicta in general and is more frequent, whereas this title concerns vindicta of a corporation or college only and is less frequent. So also above, in book 58, tit. de libert. univers. To this follows tit. 4. de manumiss. test. The reason for the order given at Cod. lib. 7. tit. 5. is de fideicommiss. libert. The reason for the order there, at Cod. title 6, is de adempt. libert., because what is given always comes before what is taken away. Title 7 is de statu lib. The reason seems to be that, having spoken of giving and taking away liberty, we now treat of the liberty of a slave which is called statu-liberty, and so this is treated later. Title 8 is qui jure manumiss. ad lib. &c.; the reason is that so far we have spoken of one mode or cause of liberty, namely manumission, which is the more frequent and older mode. There is also another, namely by law, that is, a person becomes free by law or by operation of law without manumission, and this is the subject of this title. It is followed by title 9, qui & aquib. manumiss. &c. The reason is that so far we have treated of those who become free, and now of those who do not become free on account of some crime or fraud; and so these are treated afterwards. tit. 10. de jure aur. annul. The reason for the order is that, after liberty has been given, freedmen, since they are libertines, may sometimes obtain by the favour of the prince the status of freeborn; this mode is called the right of the golden ring, and to it is rightly joined tit. 11. de natal. restit. The reason for the order is that this title too is a mode of freeborn status, the restoration of birth, as the other is the right of rings; but this mode is more rational because it is fuller: by restoration of birth the patron loses his right over the freedman, since he is plainly made freeborn, whereas in the right of the golden ring the patron does not lose his right. ff. tit. pra de jur. aur. annul. Therefore restoration is not granted as easily as the right of the golden ring. l. ult. b. tit. 12. is de liber. caus. The reason for the order is that so far we have spoken of the cause or liberty, to whom it is given or taken away; now we speak of the action by which liberty is pursued. To this is joined tit. 13. quib. ad libert. proclam. nol. c. The reason for the order is that the earlier tit. de lib. caus. concerns those to whom an action for liberty is granted, whereas this title concerns those who are not permitted to claim liberty. Title 14 is ji libertas ingenuus esse dicatur. The reason for the order is that this title too concerns an action, like the two before it; but the two before it concern a preliminary action, by which it is asked whether someone is a slave or free. There is also a third preliminary action, for there are three actions of this kind (ff. prejudiciales de act.), by which it is asked whether a son is or is not the child of another; concerning this see tit. 3. de agnosc. & alend. lib. above in book 25. The remaining ones of this kind are set aside, because this book treats of liberty and servitude. The reason why the action on liberty is placed before the action on freeborn status is partly that this book chiefly treats of liberty, and partly that liberty comes before being a freedman; for in order to be a freedman one must first have been a slave. multi Institut. de libert. titul. 5 est, Ne de statu def. &c. The reason for the order is that this title concerns an exception or prescription of time, namely of five years. The order of the material requires that actions be treated first and exceptions afterwards, as said above in book 4 of the Institutes. To this is joined tit. 16. de collus. deteg. The reason for the order is, first, that this title too concerns a period of five years, as was prescribed in the earlier title for one who wishes to disclose a collusion by which someone was declared freeborn, namely by colluding with the adversary and pursuing the matter so that he is defeated; second, that this title concerns a crime, namely collusion, and so it is rightly last; and finally, that it treats of a judgment in favour of freeborn status which is to be rescinded and retracted, and so it is rightly placed after the action on freeborn status, which is treated above in tit. 14 si liber ingenuus esse dic. ponitur.

units.la: LIBER XLI.
units.tr: Book 41.

units.la: Liber 41. de possessione potissimum agit, ejusque natura & effectis. Ratio ordinis est petenda ex Edicto Perpetuo in quo post actiones & judicia, tandem de fine judiciorum agitur, ut de sententia & missione in possessionem, ut supra dictum ad Edictum. Ut igitur missio in possessionem melius intelligatur; prius de ipsa possessione explicandum putavit Tribun. quod idefactum est & in Cod. Praeterea hic tractatus de possessione non tantum servit ad proxime sequentem tractatum, de missione in possessionem, sed & ad alteram ei proximum, de interdictis, quae potissimum sunt de possessione; ideoq; in Instit. de possessione agitur initio tit. de interdictis & possideret. cod. Continet autem hic liber tit. 10 quorum primus est de adquir. rer. dom. n. qui tit. hic ponitur propterea, quod dominia ex possessione primum sunt capta in fra de adquir. poss. Cur autem cum possessio sit prior dominio ordine naturae, ut jam dictum, tamen hic dominium sit prius ordine sive priori loco ponatur, dignitas & praestantia est in causa Con. lib. 3 c. 3 aliam rationem adfert, hic scilicet quia dominium ordine juris & auctoritate est prius possessione, hoc est, non potest esse justa possessio, nisi prius adsit dominium seu titulus potius & causa justa. Nam cum in rebus nostris duo praecipua sint jura, dominium & possessio longe potius & praestantius est dominium, quam possessio; itaque tit. 2 est de adquir. vel amitt. poss. Quem sequitur tit. 3 de usurp. & usuc. Ratio ordinis est, quia usucapio est quasi effectus possessionis. Namusucapio est per possessionem adquisitio dominii, l. 3. b. Et inde nomen quoq; habet: Usus enim interdum est idem, quod possessio, licet proprie differat l. 115. quaestio est de verb. significat. Cum autem usucapionis multae sint species recte hic titulus 3. utpote generalis praeponitur, eumq; speciales sequuntur, ut titulus 4. pro empt. Nam titulus pro soluto, licet in aliis exemplaribus ante titulum pro emptore ponatur, nos tamen librum Florentinum sequimur, in quo nullus est titulus pro soluto, & leges ejus tituli ponuntur sub titulo generali, nempe sub tit. 3. de usucap. ut sunt leges istae 46 pro soluto & 3. sequent: quae sunt ultimae leges dL tit.generalis. Cur autem inter speciales hic tit.4 pro emptore primum locum teneat triplex reddi potest ratio. I Quia hæc species est propter contractum emptionis celeberrima. II. Deinde, quia ex contractu emptionis non transfertur dominium sed tantum ius habere licere, nisi venditor sit dominus. l. 1. supra de rer. permut. cum reliqui tituli transferant dominium III Quia ordo titulorum supra observatus & hic fuit observandus. Nam supra prius de emptione, quàm de hereditatis agitur. Hunc sequitur tit. 5. pro herede vel possessore. Ratio ordinis jam dicta est, quia prius de emptione, quam de hereditate vel bonorum possessione agitur. titul. 6. est pro donato. Ratio est, quia & supra prius de hereditatibus, posterius de donationibus agitur. Quem sequitur tit. 7. pro derelicto. Nam & hoc quasi species donationis continetur: qui enim rem pro derelicto habet eam velut donare alteri, sed incertæ personæ videtur. l. 36. quod servus de furto, serv. l. 5. quæ in fraud. cred. titul 8. est pro legato. Nam & legatum est species donationis, ut definito legati indicat. Cur autem prius pro derelicto, & posterius pro legato agatur, ratio est, quia pro derelicto fit inter vivos, legatum relinquitur testamento, sed donationes inter vivos, donationibus mortis causa præponuntur, ut dictum supra libro 39. tit. 5. & 6. Hunc sequitur titul. 9. pro dote. Nam & dos est donationis species. sed hæc species est valdè specialis, tantum conjugum propria, ideoque ultimum locum hic tenet: quamvis in Cod ultimum locum teneat titulus pro herede, propterea quod titul. pro herede, sit sæpè falsus, non verus titul., nempe cum quis opinione est heres, putat se heredem. Hic autem tit. ultimus sive 10. est profuso, quia hic titul. est tanquam accessorius, & supplementi loco, cum scilicet alij tituli deficiunt, tum iste succedit. Deinde hic tit. etiam prioribus titulis cohæret, ut si mihi res tradita sit tit. emptionis; usucapio eam & tit. emptionis & pro meo. Nam etiam ante usucapionem eam possideo pro meo, l. 1. & 2. hic.
units.tr: Book 41 deals chiefly with possession, its nature and its effects. The order of the titles is to be drawn from the Perpetual Edict, in which, after actions and trials, the end of trials is finally treated, namely judgment and putting into possession, as was said above on the Edict. So that the putting into possession may be better understood, Tribonian thought it right first to explain possession itself, which was also done in the Code. Moreover, this treatise on possession serves not only the immediately following treatise on putting into possession, but also the other closely related treatise, on interdicts, which are chiefly concerned with possession. Therefore in the Institutes possession is treated at the beginning of the title on interdicts and possession. This book contains ten titles, the first of which is on the acquisition of ownership of things, which is placed here because ownership was first obtained from possession (see below, on the acquisition of possession). Why, although possession is prior to ownership in the order of nature, as already said, ownership is nonetheless placed first here, by reason of its dignity and pre-eminence, Con. (book 3, chapter 3) gives another reason: namely, that ownership is prior to possession in the order of law and authority, that is, there cannot be lawful possession unless ownership, or rather a title and a just cause, is present beforehand. For since two chief rights exist in our affairs, ownership and possession, ownership is far more important and excellent than possession. Accordingly, title 2 is on the acquisition or loss of possession. It is followed by title 3, on usurpation and usucapion. The reason for this order is that usucapion is, as it were, an effect of possession, for usucapion is the acquisition of ownership through possession (law 3, b.), and it takes its name from this as well: for usus is sometimes the same as possession, although properly they differ (law 115, on the meaning of words). Since there are many kinds of usucapion, this title 3 is rightly placed first, as the general one, and the special titles follow it, such as title 4, on purchase. The title on payment (pro soluto), although in other copies it is placed before the title on purchase, we nevertheless follow the Florentine book, in which there is no title on payment, and its laws are placed under the general title, namely under title 3 on usucapion, as are the laws 46 (on payment) and the following 3, which are the last laws of the general title. Why, among the special titles, title 4 on purchase holds the first place may be given for three reasons. (1) Because this kind is the most common, on account of the contract of purchase. (2) Because ownership is not transferred by the contract of purchase, but only the right to hold arises, unless the seller is the owner (law 1, above, on exchange), whereas the other titles do transfer ownership. (3) Because the order of titles observed above was also to be observed here: for above, purchase is treated before inheritance. Title 5, on the heir or possessor, follows this. The reason for the order has already been stated: purchase is treated before inheritance or the possession of goods. Title 6 is on gifts. The reason is that above, inheritances are treated before gifts. It is followed by title 7, on abandoned property, for this too is contained as a kind of gift: for one who holds a thing as abandoned seems to give it, as it were, to another, but to an uncertain person (law 36, on the servant and theft; law 5, on fraud against creditors). Title 8 is on legacies, for a legacy too is a kind of gift, as the definition of legacy indicates. As to why abandonment is treated before legacy, the reason is that abandonment takes place between the living, whereas a legacy is left by will; and gifts between the living are placed before gifts in view of death, as said above in book 39, titles 5 and 6. It is followed by title 9, on dowry, for a dowry too is a kind of gift. But this kind is very special, belonging only to spouses, and therefore holds the last place here, although in the Code the title on the heir holds the last place, because the title on the heir is often false rather than true, namely when someone is heir in opinion and thinks himself heir. This title, the last or tenth, is added as a supplement, since it is, as it were, accessory, and when the other titles fail, this one succeeds. Moreover, this title also coheres with the preceding titles: for example, if a thing has been delivered to me under a title of purchase, I obtain it by usucapion both under the title of purchase and as my own, for even before usucapion I possess it as my own (laws 1 and 2, here).

units.la: XLII. LIBER.
units.tr: Book 42.

units.la: Liber 42 est de fine judiciorum, ut de sententia & exsecutione, & missione in possessionem. Ratio ordinis expositæ est supra ad Edictum. continet autem hic liber tit. 8. Sed id admonendum, quod ante hunc librum, nempe lib. 41. tit. ult. diximus pro suo cum tamen in indice præfixo ff. Flor. post tit. pro suo, ponatur etiam alius tit. nempe communia de accessionibus possessionis quod merito mirari quis possit. Et fortasse labes aliqua hic facta est, ut admonet Cujac. hic in Parat. Et sanè in Cod. post species possessionum (ut pro emptore, pro donato, &c.) tandem ponitur hic tit. communia de usucap. ut ita & hic quoque; fortasse eodem modo conceptius titul. fuerit positus. Sed nullum fuisse hic positum arbitrari licet: Nam illi tituli, qui ita sunt concepti (communia de &c. tantum in Cod. reperiuntur, ex quo illa verba in indicem Florent. videntur irrepsisse ita in Cod. est: titul., communia utrinsque judicii, & titul. communia de facde successef. & tit. communia de usucap. & etiam communia pred. Hujus igitur libri 41 primus tit. est de re judic. hoc est, de ejus sententia & effectu, ut est executio & actio judicati, quae ex sententia oritur tanquam excausa. Ratio ordinis expósita est supra ad Edictū, quia scilicet in extremis judiciorum haec sunt prima, sententia & executio tit. 2. est de conf. Ratio est, propter similitudinem confessi cum judicato. De judicato est tit. 1. de confesso est tit. 2. quia confessus pro judicato habetur & est species quasi judicati, l. 1. b. tit. 3. est de cess. sione bonorū. Ratio ordinis haec est, quia scilicet post sententiā & rem judicatā, si condemnatus non faciat judicatū, solet actor mitti in possessionē judicati sive rei, nisi reus ante bonis cedat. Hac enim cessione reus effugit sive prevertit missionē & postea demū bona creditoribus distrahenda dantur. Et hinc est quod hunc tit. de cessione sequitur tit. 4. quib. ex causa in possess. eat. Idēq; factū in C. l. b 7. tit. 71. & 72. sed in Cod post tit. de judicatis & confessis non statim sequitur tit. de cessione bonorum, sed cessioni praeponitur appellatio, omnesque tit. ad appellationem pertinentes, nempe tit. 61. & 9. sequen. dist. tit. 7 Cod cum tamen appellatio in ff. rejecta sit infra post tractatum de criminibus. Ratio differentiae dicetur infra ad tit. de appell. lib. 49. Huic autem tit. 4 proximus est tit 5. de reb. auct. jud. poss. Ratio est perspicua: quia missionem in possessionem bonorum, de qua tit. 4 sequitur ipsa possessio & postea distractio sive venditio. Hic enim est ordo, ut creditor in possessionem mittidesideret, deinde ut possidere desideret (aliud enim esse in possessione, aliud possidere, l. 3. f. ult. de adquir. poss.) & tandem desideret a praetore venditionem, & distractionem bonorum, ut & supra dictum ad Edictum titul. 6. est de separat. Sic enim in ff Flor. tituli distinguuntur, sed in aliis inter titul. 5. de reb. auct. jud. poss. & titulum de separationis, interponitur alius titul.: d. privileg. cred. ut & supra ad Edictum dictum, sed nos Flor. ff. sequuntur, ut emendatores. Ratio ergo huius tituli, de separat omb. haec est: quia titulus fuit de vendendis rebus debitoris, ad quam venditionem pertinet separatio, ut si debitor heredem relinquat filium, sive suum & necessarium, solet hic filius impetrare separationem bonorum, ut scilicet creditores vendant bona tantum propria debitoris defuncti, non vero ipsius filii, ut heredis: deinde separantur quoq; creditores hereditarii ab aliis hoc est, creditores defuncti, a creditoribus heredis in venditione bonorum, de qua utraque separatione bonorum, inquam, & creditorum agitur hoc tit. Quem sequitur tit. 7. de cession. bon. dando. Ratio est, quia & hic titulus ad venditionem pertinet, & admissionem. Nam creditoribus in possessionem missis curator eorum constituti solet a praetore qui bona custodiat, administret, & venditioni praesit a Cicero pro Quinctio dicitur magister de quo nt. t. Inst. de success. subl. titul. 8. quae in fraud. cred. Ratio ordinis est, quia & hic ad eandem causam creditorum pertinet sed est ultimus, quia de fraude & delicto agit ut dictum supra in fine libri 7. Cod. & supra ad Edictum.
units.tr: Book 42 deals with the end of judgments, namely with sentence and execution, and with the grant of possession. The reason for this order has been set out above, in the commentary on the Edict. This book contains eight titles. But this must be noted: before this book, that is at the end of book 41, we spoke of pro suo, yet in the index prefixed to the Florentine Digest, after the title pro suo, another title is also given, namely communia de accessionibus possessionis, which one may fairly wonder at. Perhaps some corruption has crept in here, as Cujas warns here in his Paratitla. Indeed, in the Code, after the species of possession (such as pro emptore, pro donato, etc.), the title communia de usucapionibus is finally placed, so that here too the title may have been placed in the same general form. But one may suppose that nothing was placed here at all. For those titles conceived in this way (communia de etc.) are found only in the Code, and from there those words seem to have crept into the Florentine index. In the Code the order is thus: the title communia utriusque judicii, and the title communia de successionibus, and the title communia de usucapionibus, and also communia praedictorum. The first title of this book 41 is de re judicata, that is, on the sentence and its effect, such as execution and the action on the judgment, which arises from the sentence as an accessory. The reason for the order has been explained above in the commentary on the Edict: namely, that among the final matters of judgments these come first, sentence and execution. Title 2 is de confessis. The reason is the resemblance of a confession to a judgment. On the judgment is title 1, on the confession is title 2, because the one who has confessed is treated as adjudged and is a kind of species of the adjudged (l. 1. b.). Title 3 is de cessione bonorum. The reason for this order is that, after sentence and a judgment that has become final, if the condemned man does not satisfy the judgment, the plaintiff is usually sent into possession of the judged property, unless the defendant first makes a cession of his goods. For by this cession the defendant escapes or forestalls the sending into possession, and afterwards the goods are at last given to the creditors to be distributed. And hence it is that this title on cession is followed by title 4, quibus ex causa in possessionem eatur. The same thing is done in the Code, in l. 7, titles 71 and 72. But in the Code, after the title de judicatis et confessis, the title de cessione bonorum does not immediately follow; rather, appeal is placed before cession, along with all the titles pertaining to appeal, namely titles 61 and 9 that follow, and title 7 of the Code. Yet in the Digest appeal has been placed after the treatise on crimes, below. The reason for this difference will be given below, at the title de appellationibus, book 49. Next to this title 4 is title 5, de rebus auctoritate judicis possidendis seu venditis. The reason is clear: after the sending into possession of goods, which is the subject of title 4, comes the possession itself and afterwards the distraction or sale. For the order is this: the creditor desires first to be sent into possession, then to possess (for being in possession is one thing, and possessing is another, l. 3, last paragraph, de adquirenda possessione), and finally desires from the praetor the sale and distraction of the goods, as was also said above in the commentary on the Edict, title 6, de separationibus. For in the Florentine Digest the titles are distinguished in this way; but in other editions an additional title is inserted between title 5, de rebus auctoritate judicis possidendis, and the title de separationibus, namely de privilegiis creditorum, as was also said above in the commentary on the Edict. But we follow the Florentine Digest, as the best editors do. The reason for this title, de separationibus omnium bonorum, is therefore this: because the title concerns the selling of the debtor's goods, and separation pertains to that sale. For example, if a debtor leaves an heir who is a son, whether his own and necessary heir, this son usually obtains separation of goods, so that the creditors sell only the goods belonging to the deceased debtor, and not those of the son himself as heir. Then the creditors of the inheritance are also separated from the others, that is, the creditors of the deceased from the creditors of the heir, in the sale of the goods. Of both these separations, of goods and of creditors, I say, this title treats. It is followed by title 7, de cessione bonorum dando. The reason is that this title too concerns the sale and the admission. For after the creditors have been sent into possession, the praetor usually appoints a curator for them, who guards and administers the goods and presides over the sale; Cicero in his speech for Quinctius calls him a "master", about whom see Inst. de successionibus sublatis. Title 8, quae in fraudem creditorum. The reason for the order is that this too pertains to the same matter of the creditors, but it is the last, because it treats of fraud and wrongdoing, as was said above at the end of book 7 of the Code and in the commentary on the Edict.

units.la: XLIII. LIBER.
units.tr: Book XLIII.

units.la: LIber 43 est tantum de interdictis. Ratio ordinis petenda est ex edicto per petitionem ubi idem est ordo, & in Cod. li. 8. & expolita supra ad edictum Continet hic liber titulos 33. quorum 1. est de interdictis, quem sequuntur 32. speciales, hoc est, species interdictorum continentes: Inter quos primum locum tenet Interdictum quorum bonorum, titul. 2. tit. 3. quod legatorum. Ratio ordinis de utroque titulo dicta ad edictum titulo 4. Ne vi fiat &c. in quo Trib. recessit ab ordine edicti perpetui, in quo post interdictum quod legatorum, statim erat interdictum, de tabulis exhibendis: Sed hic in ff. inter ea duo interdicta interiecit hoc interdictum, ne vi fiat, quod in edicto tamen fere fuit ultimum inter edicta de interdictis, ut tibi dictum. Ratio ordinis autem in ff. videtur esse, quia scilicet huius interdicti, et suus est generalis, l. t. f. 1. hic (Pertinet enim ad omnes in possessionem missos à praetore (habet tamen aliquid speciale in legatis, sive in missione in possessionem legatorum causa. Speciale hoc est, quod hoc interdictum sive actio in factum in aliis causis sive missionibus in possessionem est tantum annua, in legatis non item, d. l. t. hic. Quod speciale ius in legatis puto moville. Tribu. ut tit. 3. statim adjungeret hunc tit. 4. ne vi fiat, &c. quem sequitur tit 5. de tab. exhib. & hunc tit 6. Nequid in loco sacro, &c. Ratio supra ad edictum. A quo edicto rursus nonnihil discessit Tribun. Nam in edicto post interdictum de loco sacro, erat interdictum de loco religioso, quod hic in ff. omissum est, quia iam ante positum lib. 11. tit. vlt. Ita post titulum 6. statim est titulus 7. de locis & itin. pub. Quem recte sequitur titulus 8. Ne quid in loco publ. vel itinere fiat, quia speciali interdicta nunc publica sequuntur, inter quae, quia hoc interdictum, ne quid in loco publ fiat, primum in edicto, ut supra ad edictum dictum, ubi & ratio alta, merito hic titulus 8. inter speciales de publicis locis primus ponitur & sequitur tit 7. generalem. Et hoc tit 9 plura interdicta continentur, de quibus supra ad edictum tit. 8. de loco publ. fruendo. Ratio ad edictum, titulus 10. est de via publ. &, &c. Ratio ordinis est, quia cum modo dictum est in genere de loco publico fruendo, nunc in specie de via publica fruenda. Nam hic titulus id continet, ne qua impedimenta in viis publicis aut aedificia ponantur, quo minus ijs uti ac frui liceat. Hunc sequitur titulus 11. de via publica & itinere, &c. huic adjicitur titulus 12. de fluminibus, ne quid in flum. Ratio ordinis supra ad edictum, ubi & ratio sequentium titulorum, ut tit. 13. Ne quid in flum. publ. & 14. Ut in flum. publ. navig. hic, &c. titulus 15. de ripa munienda, &c intelligi potest. Hunc sequitur tit. 16. de vi & vi arm. ratio ibidem dicta, & hunc titul. 17. ne possideatur, & hunc titul. 18. de superficie. inde tit. 19. dolo mere actionis, &c. & tit. 20. de aqua quot. & æst. & tit. 21. de rivis, & tit. 22. de fonte, & tit. 23. de cloacis, & tit. 24. quod vi aut clam. & tit. 25. de remissionib. Ratio omnium horum tit. expositae ad edictum, ubi & dicta esse duo interdicta de remissionibus
units.tr: Book 43 deals only with interdicts. The order of the titles is to be sought from the Edict, by petition where the order is the same, and in Cod. lib. 8, and from the commentary above on the Edict. This book contains 33 titles. The first, title 1, is on interdicts in general, and it is followed by 32 special titles, that is, titles containing the species of interdicts. Among these, the first place is held by the Interdict Quorum bonorum, title 2, and then title 3, Quod legatorum. The reason for the order of both titles was given above under the Edict. Title 4, Ne vi fiat, etc., is where Tribonian departed from the order of the perpetual Edict. In the Edict, straight after the interdict Quod legatorum came the interdict De tabulis exhibendis. But here in the Digest he placed between those two interdicts this interdict Ne vi fiat, which in the Edict, however, was almost the last among the edicts on interdicts, as I told you. The reason for the order in the Digest seems to be this: the general rule of this interdict is l. 1 f. 1 hic. (For it applies to all who are put into possession by the praetor.)
