It does, however, have something special in the case of legacies, or in the putting into possession for the sake of legatees. This special point is that this interdict, or the action in factum, is only annual in other cases, or in the grants of possession, but not in legacies, as in the same law 1 hic. I think this special right in legacies should be moved. Tribonian then immediately added title 4 to title 3, namely Ne vi fiat, etc., which is followed by title 5, De tabulis exhibendis, and this title 6, Ne quid in loco sacro, etc. The reason is given above under the Edict. Tribonian again departed somewhat from that Edict. For in the Edict, after the interdict on a sacred place, there was an interdict on a religious place, which is omitted here in the Digest, because it had already been placed earlier, in book 11, last title. So after title 6 comes at once title 7, De locis et itineribus publicis, which is rightly followed by title 8, Ne quid in loco publico vel itinere fiat, since special interdicts concerning public places now follow. Among them, because this interdict, Ne quid in loco publico fiat, stood first in the Edict, as said above under the Edict, where the deeper reason is also given, title 8 is rightly placed first among the special titles on public places, and it is followed by the general title 7. Title 9 contains several interdicts, on which see above under the Edict, title 8, De loco publico fruendo. The reason for title 10, De via publica, etc., under the Edict is that, since it was just said in general about enjoying a public place, now it is said in particular about enjoying a public road. For this title contains that nothing is to be put in public roads, whether obstacles or buildings, to prevent their use and enjoyment. This is followed by title 11, De via publica et itinere, etc. To it is added title 12, De fluminibus, Ne quid in flumine. The reason for the order is above under the Edict, where also the reason for the following titles is given: title 13, Ne quid in flumine publico, and title 14, Ut in flumine publico navigare liceat, etc. Title 15, De ripa munienda, etc., may be understood from that. This is followed by title 16, De vi et vi armata, the reason being given there, and then title 17, Ne possideatur, and title 18, De superficiebus. Then title 19, De dolo malo, actio, etc.; title 20, De aqua quotidiana et aestiva; title 21, De rivis; title 22, De fonte; title 23, De cloacis; title 24, Quod vi aut clam; and title 25, De remissionibus. The reason for all these titles was set out under the Edict, where it was also said that there are two interdicts on remissions.

units.la: fionibus fronibus, quorum hic alterum in ff. alterum longe ante sub tit. de nov. oper. nunc. Tribun. posuit. Ratio ibidem dicta, tit. 26. est de prec. 27. de arb. cedd. 28. de glande leg. 29. de hom. lib. exhib. 30. de lib. exhib. 31. utrubi. Ratio supra ad edictum: quem sequitur tit. 32. de migrando. Sed hic quoq; discessum est ab edicto. Nam inter utrubi, & de migrando fuit interdictum, ne vis fiat eis in edicto. Ratio dicta ad edictum, quod tamen Tribun. posuit sub titulo quarto hujus libri. Ratio ibidem. Hunc sequitur tit. 33. de Salviano interd. Ratio supra ad edictum.
units.tr: Concerning remissions (or the repair of works), of which one is placed here in the Digest and the other long before, under the title De novi operis nuntiatione, Tribonian has placed them. The reason was given there. Title 26 is De precario; title 27, De arboribus caedendis; title 28, De glande legenda; title 29, De homine libero exhibendo; title 30, De liberis exhibendis; title 31, Utrubi. The reason is above under the Edict. This is followed by title 32, De migrando. But here too there is a departure from the Edict. For between Utrubi and De migrando there was, in the Edict, an interdict Ne vis fiat eis. The reason was given under the Edict, though Tribonian placed it under title 4 of this book, and the reason is given there. This is followed by title 33, De Salviano interdicto. The reason is above under the Edict.

units.la: XLIV. LIBER.
units.tr: Book XLIV.

units.la: Liber 44. duo continet, exceptiones & appendices sive supplementa, aut potius repetitionem generalem omnium tit. priorum (Cujac. Notell. 112.) Post interdicta igitur lib. 43. explicata, ponuntur hoc lib. 44. exceptiones. Sed in Cod. inter interdicta & exceptiones interponuntur pignora, exemplo edicti perpetui, a quo discessit hic Tribun.: quia pignora jam antea posuit. Cur autem ante posuerit, dictum est supra, libro 20. titulo primo. Itaque hujus libri, qui continet titulos septem, titulus 1. est de exceptionibus, quia est generalis de natura omnium exceptionum. Quem sequitur tit. 2. de rei jud. excep. quae est species exceptionis. Ratio cur sit prima hoc loco: quia hoc libro non omnes, sed paucae tantum sint positae exceptiones, quasdam vero alias jam supra Tribunian. posuit, ut tit. de exceptionib. rei venditae & trad. Inter has, hoc est, hoc libro positas, haec exceptio rei judicatae est praestantissima hoc est, ex optima causa proveniens, nimirum ex sententia sive re judicata, quae est causa publica. Ideoque haec exceptio merito hic prima ponitur. tit. 3. est de diversis temporalibus praescriptionibus, quo exceptiones temporis continentur. Ratio ordinis est quia & haec exceptiones quasi ex causa publica oriuntur: Tempora enim semper lege aliqua publica praescribuntur, ut quinquennium querelae, &c. tit. 4. de dolo malo & metu except., quae duae exceptiones, quia ex deliciis oriuntur, ex dolo scilicet & metu, merito sunt posteriores, tit. 5. quarum rerum actio non datur, titul 6. est de litigiosis. Ratio dicta ad edictum tit. 7. est de obligat. & act. Sic enim recte concipitur hic tit. in ff. Flor. ut & in Cod. libro quarto. Nam obligatio prior est actione. Ideoque non recte alii hunc titulum concipiunt de actionibus & obligationibus. Sic & dictus titulus 5. quarum rerum actio non datur interf. Hotoman. & Cujacius litigant. Nam Hotoman putat legendum, quarum rerum exceptio non datur. Cujac. actio, hoc est, scripturam omnium librorum tuetur, quia eodem tit, agitur de exceptionibus quibusdam, ubi scilicet non datur actio. Cur autem hic tit. de obligationibus & actionibus, sit ultimus & hoc loco positus a Tribun. ratio est, quia hactenus expositae omnes obligationes & actiones speciales (paucis exceptis, & propter certas causas inferius expositis (itaque hic nunc generalis ponitur titulus quo generales sive communes regulæ omnium obligationum & actionum continentur, quemadmodum & in fine ff ponuntur duo generales tit. quorum unus de verborum significatione, alter de regulis juris, quibus etiam regulæ generales ex omnibus prioribus tit. & libris collectæ, itaque explicationes verborum comprehensæ sunt. Itaque hic tit. est quasi ἀνακεφαλαίωσις, sive recapitulatio, & generalis regularum de oblig. & act. repetitio hic continetur. In Cod autem hic tit. de oblig. & act. positus est libro 4. Ratio ibi expósita.
units.tr: Book 44 contains two things: exceptions, and appendices or supplements. Or rather, it is a general recapitulation of all the earlier titles (Cujac. Notell. 112.). After the interdicts explained in Book 43, therefore, the exceptions are set out in this Book 44. In the Code, however, pledges are placed between the interdicts and the exceptions, following the perpetual Edict, from which Tribonian departs here, because he had already dealt with pledges earlier. Why he placed them earlier was said above, in Book 20, title 1. So this book, which contains seven titles, has as its title 1 "On exceptions", since it is the general title on the nature of all exceptions. It is followed by title 2, "On the exception of res judicata", which is a species of exception. The reason it stands first here is that in this book only a few exceptions are set out, not all of them; Tribonian had already set out some others earlier, such as the title on the exceptions of a thing sold and delivered. Among those set out in this book, the exception of res judicata is the most excellent, that is, it arises from the best cause, namely the judgment or res judicata, which is a public cause. For this reason this exception is rightly placed first here. Title 3 is "On various temporal prescriptions", which contains the exceptions of time. The reason for this order is that these exceptions too arise, as it were, from a public cause: periods of time are always prescribed by some public law, such as five years for a complaint, and so on. Title 4, "On the exceptions of fraud and fear", are rightly placed later, since these two exceptions arise from wrongful acts, namely fraud and fear. Title 5 is "For which things no action is given"; title 6 is "On matters in litigation", for which the reason was given under the Edict. Title 7 is "On obligations and actions". For this is how the title is rightly worded in the Florentine Digest, as also in Book 4 of the Code. For an obligation is prior to an action. Hence others wrongly word this title as "On actions and obligations". So too, title 5, "quarum rerum actio non datur", is disputed between Hotoman and Cujacius. Hotoman thinks one should read "quarum rerum exceptio non datur"; Cujacius defends the reading "actio", that is, the wording found in all the manuscripts, since in the same title certain exceptions are treated, namely cases where no action is given. As for why this title on obligations and actions is last, and placed here by Tribonian, the reason is that all the special obligations and actions explained so far (with a few exceptions, and for certain reasons explained further below) have been set out. Here, therefore, a general title is now placed, containing the general or common rules of all obligations and actions, just as at the end of the Digest two general titles are placed, one on the meaning of words and the other on the rules of law. Those general rules, gathered from all the earlier titles and books, and the explanations of words, are included in them. Thus this title is, as it were, a recapitulation [ἀνακεφαλαίωσις], and a general repetition of the rules concerning obligations and actions is contained here. In the Code, however, this title "On obligations and actions" is placed in Book 4, and the reason for that is set out there.

units.la: DE VII. ET ULTIMA PARTE PAND. XLV. LIBER.
units.tr: DE VII. ET ULTIMA PARTE PAND. XLV. LIBER.

units.la: Pars 7. sex libros continet, quorum primi sunt de stipulationibus aliisque ad pertinentibus, l. 2 §. septima, C. de vet. jur. enucl. Ratio, cur hic de stipulationib. agatur, petenda est ex edicto supra. Hic autem lib. 45 qui est primus partis 7. continet tres tit. quorum primus est de verb. oblig. quia est generalis, tit. 2. de duob. reis constit. tit. 3. de stipul. serv. Ratio exposita est supra ad Institut.
units.tr: The seventh part contains six books, of which the first are on stipulations and other matters pertaining to them, l. 2 §. septima, C. de vet. jur. enucl. The reason why stipulations are treated here is to be sought from the edict above. Here, however, book 45, which is the first of the seventh part, contains three titles: the first is de verb. oblig., because it is general; tit. 2. de duob. reis constit.; tit. 3. de stipul. serv. The reason has been explained above on the Institutes.

units.la: XLVI. LIBER.
units.tr: BOOK XLVI.

units.la: Liber 46. octo tit. continet, & agit de iis quoque, quæ ad stipulationem pertinent ut de fidejussoribus, de novationibus, aliisque modis tollendæ obligationis & de stipulationibus prætoriis. tit. 1. est de fidejussor. b. qa & hi per stipulationem constituuntur. Sed prioris libri tit. sunt de personis principalibus hic tit. de acceptilationibus ideoque posterior ut dictum ad Instit. tit. 2. de novationib. tit. 3. est de fidej. & liberat. Ratio supra ad Cod & edicto tit. 4. est de acceptilat. Ratio dicta ibidem & ad Instit. Hunc sequitur t. tut. 5. de strp. præt. Ratio ordinis est, quia in edicto statim post exceptiones fuerunt stipulationes prætoriæ. Cur ergo, inquies, tori tit. de verb. oblig. & de fidejuss. &c. hic sunt interpositi? Ratio hæc est quia Tribun. occasione unius speciei ut hic stipulationis prætoriæ voluit explicare de toto genere. hoc est de omnibus stipulationibus. Et hanc generalem tractationem recte præposuit hujus speciali de stipulationibus prætoriis. Sunt autem hi quatuor tit. de stipular. præt. unus generalis, ideoque primus, nempe de stipulatione prætoria, & tres speciales, nempe tit. 6. rem pup salv. forr. tit. 7. iudicatum solvi, & tit. 8. rem rat. hab. Ratio autem ordinis inter eos tit. sive species prætoriarum stipulationum expositae est supra ad edictū, ubi quoq; dictum, plures fuisse species. Sed Tribun. quasdam jam ante posuit discedens ab edicti ordine, propter certas causas, suo quasq; loco expositas, ut tit. qui satisd. cog. tit. de evict. & dupl. stip. tit. de novi operis nunc. tit. de damno infecto.
units.tr: Book 46 contains eight titles and deals also with matters that pertain to stipulation, such as sureties, novations, other ways of extinguishing an obligation, and praetorian stipulations. Title 1 is on sureties, because these too are constituted by stipulation. The titles of the previous book concern principal persons, whereas this one concerns acceptilations; for this reason the latter comes after, as was said on the Institutes. Title 2 is on novations. Title 3 is on sureties and release. The reason is given above on the Code and on the edict. Title 4 is on acceptilation. The reason is given there and on the Institutes. Title 5 follows, on praetorian stipulations. The reason for this order is that in the edict praetorian stipulations came immediately after the exceptions. Why then, you will ask, have the titles on verbal obligations and on sureties, etc. been placed here? The reason is that Tribonian, on the occasion of one species, namely praetorian stipulation, wished to explain the whole genus, that is, all stipulations; and he rightly placed this general treatment before the special one on praetorian stipulations. These four titles on praetorian stipulations consist of one general title, which is therefore first, namely on praetorian stipulation, and three special ones, namely title 6 that the ward's property shall be safe, title 7 on the payment of the judgment, and title 8 on ratification of the thing. The reason for the order among these titles, or species, of praetorian stipulations was explained above on the edict, where it was also said that there were several species. But Tribonian had already placed some of them earlier, departing from the order of the edict for certain reasons, each explained in its own place, such as those compelled to give security, on eviction and the double stipulation, on the notice of new work, and on threatened damage.

units.la: XLVII. LIBER.
units.tr: BOOK XLVII.

units.la: POft hæc duo terribiles lib., ut loquitur l.2. ff. Septimus autem, Cod. de iu-re vet. enucl. in ff sunt positi, de delictis, criminib & pœnis, nempe liber 47 & 48. In edicto de his nihil fuit positum præterquam de delictis, ut de furto & de injuriis &c. Sed in edicto de iis agabatur lege priori in loco, ut supra ad edictum. Sed Tribun. discessit ab ordine edicti tam in C quam in ff. hac in re, & conjunxit ea privata, quam publica delicta propter simi-litudinem rei sive argumenti. Cæterum in Cod. post stipulationes ante delicta & crimina ponuntur quidam tit. de aliis rebus, ut de donationibus, de patria potestate, de adoptionibus, &c. quæ in ff jam ante, certis de causis ibi expositis, sunt collocata.
units.tr: Of these two terrible books, as the law says in the second section, "Septimus autem" (Cod. de iure veteri enucleando), in the Digest they are placed concerning delicts, crimes and penalties, namely books 47 and 48. In the Edict nothing was laid down about these except delicts, such as theft and injuries, etc. But in the Edict these were treated in the earlier law, in its proper place, as above under the Edict. Yet the Tribonian departed from the order of the Edict, both in the Code and in the Digest in this matter, and joined private delicts with public ones on account of the likeness of the matter or subject. Moreover, in the Code, after stipulations and before delicts and crimes, certain titles are placed on other matters, such as donations, paternal power, adoptions, etc., which in the Digest had already been put in place earlier, for certain reasons expounded there.

units.la: In edicto quidem post stipulationes prætorias, an aliquid positum fuerit, nō facile sciri potest. Sed Jurisconsulti q de jure scripserunt post edictum à Juliano compositum in suis libris, solent ordine edicta sequi, & post stipulationes alia quædam tractant, nempe ea ipsa, quæ in C sunt posita ut de donationib. de adoptionibus de jure fisci, &c. de criminib. de appellationib. &c. ut videre est lib.5. Sententiarum Pauli, & in posteriis lib. ff Juliani, & lib. quæstionum & responsionum Pap. Hos igitur Tribun in iis quæ post edictum perpetuo erant reliqua, lecutus esse videtur, atq; etiā C. The Hic ergo liber 47. est de privatis delictis & extraordinariis criminib. Ratio ordinis h.e. cur prius de delictis, ut furto, &c. quæ de criminibus agatur, est tum quia actiones ex delictis sunt similes prioribus actionibus ex contractu &c. in eo, quod sunt privatæ & sunt actiones cū ex criminib sint publicæ & proprie dicantur accusationes: tum quia crimina ut ma is terribilia & gravia in posterum locum fuerint rejiciendi: tū quia in edicto de delictis quoq; fuerit actum non verò de criminib. qa pleraq; delicta ex edicto Prætoris. Crimina verò sunt ex legib. l.1. de publ. jud. ': Cod. cōtrarius est ordo ubi prius de criminib. posterius de delictis agitur. Ratio differentiæ est qa in Cod Tribun ordine edicti magis secutus est quàm in ff. multis in locis. Itaq; de privatis delictis jam ex parte ante tractatu de criminib. imo ante interdicta egit, ut de furto lib.6. Ut igitur Jurisconsulti ordine secuti post donationes de criminib. agunt ut modo dictum. ita & in Cod. post titulum de donat. in fine lib.8 (statim initio lib.9.) agitur de publicis judiciis, & postea de privatis tantum supplendi causa, ea quæ ante non fuerint posita. Deinde in Cod. habita est ratio dignitatis, ut publicæ de delictis judicia præferantur privatis. Hic igitur liber 47. continet tit.23 quorum primus est, de privatis delictis, quia est generalis. II. de furt. Ratio ad Institut. Cuiadiungitur tit.3. de tigno juncto, & 4. si in qui testamento liber, &c. & tit.4. Furtis adversus nautas caupones stabularios, &c tit.6. Si familia furtum fecisse dicatur, huie deniq; tit.7. arb. furt. cesar. qui 7. tit. species furti continent; quorum primus est de tigno juncto. Ratio ordinis de ea, ut & de
units.tr: In the edict, indeed, it cannot easily be known whether anything was placed after the praetorian stipulations. But the jurists who wrote on civil law after the edict was composed by Julian, in their books, are accustomed to follow the order of the edict, and after stipulations they treat certain other matters, namely those very things which are placed in the Code: on donations, on adoptions, on the right of the fisc, etc.; on crimes, on appeals, etc., as may be seen in book 5 of the Sentences of Paul, and in the later books of Julian's Digest, and in the book of Questions and Responses of Papinian. Tribonian therefore seems to have followed these in the matters that remained after the perpetual edict, and also in the Code. The 47th book here is therefore on private delicts and extraordinary crimes. The reason for the order, that is, why delicts such as theft are treated before the crimes, is twofold: first, because actions arising from delicts are similar to the earlier actions arising from contract, in that they are private, whereas actions arising from crimes are public and are properly called accusations; second, because crimes, as more terrible and grave, were to be placed in a later position. There is also a third reason: delicts were also dealt with in the edict, but not crimes, since most delicts come from the edict of the Praetor. Crimes, however, come from the laws, law 1, de publ. jud. In the Code the order is the reverse, where crimes are treated first and delicts afterwards. The reason for the difference is that in the Code Tribonian followed the order of the edict more closely than in the Digest, in many places. And so he treats private delicts, indeed in part even before the treatment of crimes, and even before the interdicts, as with theft in book 6. Therefore, just as the jurists, following the order, treat crimes after donations, as just said, so also in the Code, after the title on donations, at the end of book 8 (and at the very beginning of book 9), public judgments are treated, and afterwards private ones, only to supply those matters which were not placed earlier. Then in the Code regard was had to dignity, so that public judgments on delicts are preferred to private ones. This 47th book therefore contains twenty-three titles, of which the first is on private delicts, because it is general. Title 2, on theft: the reason is given in the Institutes of Cuiacius. To this is joined title 3, on the beam joined, and title 4, if the free man is in a will, etc., and title 4 again, on thefts against sailors, innkeepers, stablemen, etc.; title 6, if a household is said to have committed theft; and lastly title 7, on the arbiter of theft, Caesar, which contain seven titles on species of theft, of which the first is on the beam joined. The reason for the order concerning this, and also concerning

units.la: {y} ... sequentibus expositæ est supra ad edictum titul 8. est vi bon. rapt. Ratio supra dicta ad Instit. tit. 9. est de incend. ruin. naufr. Ratio ordinis supra a I edictum, tit. 10 de iniur. & fam. lib. Ratio supra ad Instit. Idemq; ordo est ad edictum, ut supra dictum ad edictum. Et hæc de privatis delictis, ex quib. actiones furti &c. oriuntur ordinariæ. Sed minus frequentantur, & invicem earum extraordinario iudicio criminaliter agitur, l. nlt. de publ. iud, l. ult. de furt. l. ult. de iniur. supra. Ea propter his proxime adjungitur generalis tit. de extraord crim. ut ait Cuiac. in Parat. ad hunc tit. Est & hæc ratio, cur tit. de delictis privatis statim sequatur tit. de crimin. extraord. quia hæc extraordinaria sunt similia privatis delictis & eorum nomine, non tantum extraordinariæ actiones, sed etiam privatæ dantur: ut nomine delictorum privatorum. Cur autem prius de delictis privatis, quam de criminib. agatur, hæc est ratio quia illa sunt delicta ordinaria, ut furtū, hæc sunt extraordinaria, ut sepulchri violati, concussio, abigeatus. De his autem extraordinarijs delictis sunt duodecim tituli, nempe tit. 11. de extraord. crim. qui est primus, quia generalis: tit. 12. & seqq sunt speciales, sive species delictorum extraordinariorum singulas continentes tit 12. de sepulchro violato qui est primus ex specialibus. Ratio ordinis cur de sepulchro violato inter species primò agitur, est quia de rebus religiosis, ut de sepulchro est quem sequitur titul. 13. de concess. Ratio ordinis est, quia hoc delictum est in quibusdam casib. publicum, l. 2. h. itaque propter gravitatē religiosis statim adjunctum fuit quasi publicum. tit. 14. est de abigeis, quod crimen abigeatus etiam gravius est ijs, quæ sequuntur ideoq; sæpè dur sime punitur, etiā capitali pœna, l. 1. §. 2. hic tit. 15. est de prævaric. Ratio est quia & hoc delictum est grave & interdum publicum: sed de extraordinario, nō de publico prævaricationis crimine hic agitur, tit. 16. est de receptator. bon. Ratio est, quia & hoc receptatorum genus est passivum, ut ait l. 1. h. quia receptator non ipse crimen committit, sed latrones, qui commiserunt, receptat & occultat. Sed priores tit. sunt de ipsis qui graviora delicta commiserunt, à quibus recte hic tit. distinguitur. & ponitur post illos priores. Hunc sequitur 17. de furtis balnearis. Ratio ordinis, quia hoc delictū est species furti, & proinde levius, crimen quam priora, quamvis hoc furtū balneorum, est gravius rei furto, ideoque dicitur delictum sive crimen extraordinarium, tit. 18. est de effractorib. & expilatorib. Ratio est, quia & hi sunt fures, sed atrociores communibus furibus, l. 1. §. 1. hic. Ratio autem cur prius de furibus balnearijs posterius de effractorib. agatur, hæc est: quia balnearij olim gravius puniri solebant, etiā capite, ut est in Problematib. Aristot. tit. 19 est expilat hered. qui recte adjungitur priori quo agitur de expilatoribus, qui effringunt domus & villas aut parietes perfodiunt, ut domos expilent: quib. similes sunt directarij & sacculari, Beuteldieb oder sackdieb. Sed hoc tit. 19. specialis expilatio. nēpe hereditatis expōitur, ideoq; priori tit. postponitur. Quem sequitur titulus 20. stellionatus, quod crimen dolo simile, inter haec extraordinaria est levius, ideoque posterius. Quem sequitur tit. de termino moto. Ratio ordinis, quia hoc crime tantum in agris locum habet, & non est ita grave, ideoque postremum est fere, nempe quia rustica postponuntur urbanis, ut supra dictum ad titulum de servit. et banorum praediorum, titulus 22. est de collegiis & corporibus. Ratio ordinis cur postremo agatur de collegijs, haec est: tum quia priores tituli ad singulos, hic ad plures pertinet, tum quia hoc crimen levius est reliquis; tum denique, quia sub hoc titulo, tanquam generali agitur non tantum de crimine, hoc est, de delictis, sed etiam de licitis collegijs, ideoque merito hic titulus a prioribus distinctus & postpositus fuit.
units.tr: {y} ... is set out in what follows; above, on the edict, title 8, is on violent robbery (de vi bonorum raptorum). The reason stated above, in the Institutes, title 9, is on arson, collapse and shipwreck (de incendio, ruina, naufragio). The order above, on the edict, title 10, is on injuries and defamatory libel (de iniuriis et famosis libellis). The reason above, in the Institutes, is the same order as on the edict, as said above on the edict. And these are the ordinary actions arising from private delicts, such as theft. But they are less frequently brought, and in their place the matter is prosecuted criminally in the extraordinary court (l. ult. de publ. iud.; l. ult. de furt.; l. ult. de iniur.; above). For this reason there follows directly the general title de extraordinariis criminibus, as Cujas says in his Paratitla on this title. There is also this reason why the title on private delicts directly follows the title on extraordinary crimes: these extraordinary offences are like private delicts, and in their name not only extraordinary actions but also private actions are granted, as in the name of private delicts. Why, however, private delicts are treated before crimes, the reason is this: the former are ordinary delicts, such as theft, while the latter are extraordinary, such as violation of a tomb, extortion, cattle-rustling. Now there are twelve titles on these extraordinary delicts: title 11, on extraordinary crimes, which is the first because it is general; and titles 12 and following are special, each containing a species of extraordinary delict. Title 12, on the violation of a tomb, is the first of the special titles. The reason for the order, why the violation of a tomb is treated first among the species, is that it concerns religious matters, as the tomb does; and it is followed by title 13, on concealment. The reason for this order is that this delict is in certain cases public (l. 2, h. itaque), and so on account of its gravity it was immediately joined as if it were public. Title 14 is on cattle-rustlers (de abigeis), since the crime of cattle-rustling is more grave than those that follow, and therefore is very often punished severely, even with capital punishment (l. 1, §2, h. t.). Title 15 is on collusion (de praevaricatione). The reason is that this delict too is grave and sometimes public; but here it is treated as an extraordinary, not as the public crime of collusion. Title 16 is on receivers of stolen goods (de receptatoribus bonorum). The reason is that this kind of receiving is also passive, as l. 1, h. t. says, since the receiver does not himself commit the crime, but harbours and conceals the robbers who committed it. But the earlier titles deal with those who committed more serious delicts, from whom this title is rightly distinguished, and it is placed after those earlier ones. It is followed by title 17, on bath thefts (de furtis balnearibus). The reason for the order is that this delict is a species of theft, and therefore a lighter crime than the earlier ones, although this bath theft is more grave than ordinary theft, and so it is called an extraordinary delict or crime. Title 18 is on housebreakers and plunderers (de effractoribus et expilatoribus). The reason is that these too are thieves, but more atrocious than common thieves (l. 1, §1, h. t.). The reason why bath thieves are treated before housebreakers is this: bath thieves were formerly punished more severely, even with death, as in the Problems of Aristotle. Title 19 is on the plundering of an inheritance (de expilatione hereditatis), which is rightly joined to the preceding title, which treats of plunderers who break into houses and villas or pierce walls in order to plunder houses; to these are similar the pickpockets and cutpurses (Beuteldieb oder Sackdieb). But this title 19 treats of a special plundering, namely of an inheritance, and therefore is placed after the preceding title. It is followed by title 20, on stellionate (de stellionatu), a crime similar to fraud, which among these extraordinary crimes is lighter, and therefore comes later. It is followed by the title de termino moto. The reason for the order is that this crime has place only in the fields and is not so grave, and therefore it is almost last, since rustic matters are placed after urban ones, as said above under the title de servitutibus praediorum urbanorum et rusticorum. Title 22 is on colleges and corporations (de collegiis et corporibus). The reason for the order, why the matter of colleges is treated last, is this: partly because the earlier titles concern single persons, while this one concerns several; partly because this crime is lighter than the rest; and finally because under this title, as a general one, is treated not only of crime, that is, of delicts, but also of lawful colleges, and so rightly this title was distinguished from the earlier ones and placed after them.

units.la: Restat titulus ultimus huius libri, nempe tit. 23. de popularibus actionibus. Ratio ordinis est elegans, quia popularia iudicia cum publicis magnam habent affinitatem, ut ipsum nomen indicat: ideoque recte hic titulus ponitur statim ante titulum de publicis iud. Est autem hic titulus generalis. Species autem harum actionum popularium, iam antea suis in locis aliquot sunt expositae, ut hoc libro tit. de sepulch. viol. & tit. 21. de term. mot. & supra lib. 2. tit. 1. l. 7. actio scilicet albi corrupti & lib. 9. tit. 3. Atque ita hoc libro tertio diversa genera actionum ex delictis no publicis cōtinētur, ordinaria, extraordinaria & popularia.
units.tr: There remains the last title of this book, namely title 23, on popular actions. The order is elegant, because popular judicial proceedings have a great affinity with public ones, as the very name indicates; and so this title is rightly placed immediately before the title on public judgments. This title, however, is general. The species of these popular actions have already been set out in several places earlier, as in this book in the title on violated sepulchres, and in title 21 on removed boundary markers, and above in book 2, title 1, law 7, namely the action on a corrupted album, and in book 9, title 3. And so in this third book diverse kinds of actions arising from non-public offences are contained: ordinary, extraordinary and popular.

units.la: XLIIX. LIBER.
units.tr: XLVIII. BOOK

units.la: Liber 48. est de publicis iudicijs, est quō trimembris. Nam I. agitur de eorum natura, & principio ac ritu rea in instituendi & exercendi. II. Ipsa ordine exponuntur. III. De effectu ut de poenis. Continet autem tit. viginti quatuor quorum primus est de publicis iudic. Ratio est, quia generalis. Nam quod ad rationem ordinis de libro attinet, ea supra expositā est ad Cod. & Institut. tit. 2. est de accusationib. & inscriptionib. Ratio est quia publicorum iudiciorum principium est accusatio & inscriptio; tit. 3. de custodia & exhib. reorum, quia rei & delati statim in custodiam dantur, titulus 4. est ad L. Iuliam maiest. quia hoc crimen est gravissimum, tit. 5. ad leg. Iul. de adult. Ratio est expositā ad Institut. titulus 6. ad legem Iuliam de vi publ. Ratio est, tum quia & hoc crimen est de lege Iulia, ut priora tum quia est capitale, ut & illa priora; quamvis in Institut. alius sit ordo, titulus 7. ad leg. Iul. de vi priv. propter similitudinem, qui prior est de vi publica, tit. 8. est ad legem Cornel. de sicar. Ratio quia & hoc crime est capitale, sive sanguinis, ut priora, excepta vi privata. Cui adjungitur titulus 10. de leg. Pomp. de Parricid. quia prior tit. genus continet, eadem hic speciem, nempe parricidium, hoc est, eadem parentum. titulus 10. est de leg. Cornel. de fals. cum quia hoc crimen interdum est capitale, nempe in servis & in liberis est deportatio l. prima in fine, hic. tit. 11. est de lege Iul. repetund. Ratio est, quia & huius criminis poena plerumque est deportatio, leg. 7. in fine, hic, titulus 12. est de leg. Iul. de annon. Ratio ordinis. quia hoc crimen est levius fulicet annonæ fraudatæ, & quia item est ex Iulia. Iam enim leviora exponuntur, titulus 13. ad Leg. Iul. pecul. Ratio, quia & hoc crimen est ex levioribus, hoc est, quæ non sunt sanguinis, ut & duo priora repetundarum. & annonæ fraudatæ.
units.tr: Book 48 concerns public trials and has three parts. First, it treats their nature, origin and the form of bringing and conducting an accusation. Second, it sets out the procedure in order. Third, it deals with the effects, namely the penalties. It contains twenty-four titles, the first of which is on public trials. The reason is that it is general. As for the order of the book, it was explained above in the commentary on the Code and the Institutes, title 2, on accusations and inscriptions. The reason is that the beginning of public trials is accusation and inscription. Title 3 is on the custody and production of the accused, because the accused and the denounced are at once placed in custody. Title 4 is on the Julian law of majesty, because this crime is the most serious. Title 5 is on the Julian law concerning adultery; the reason was explained in the Institutes. Title 6 is on the Julian law concerning public violence. The reason is that this crime too falls under the Julian law, as the earlier ones do, and that it is capital, as those earlier ones are. Although the order in the Institutes is different, title 7 is on the Julian law concerning private violence, placed after public violence because of their similarity. Title 8 is on the Cornelian law concerning assassins. The reason is that this crime too is capital, and concerns bloodshed, as the earlier ones do, except private violence. To this is joined title 9, on the Pompeian law concerning parricide, because the earlier title covers the genus and this one the species, namely parricide, that is, the killing of parents. Title 10 is on the Cornelian law concerning forgery, since this crime is sometimes capital, namely in the case of slaves, and for freemen it is deportation (law 1 at the end, here). Title 11 is on the Julian law concerning extortion. The reason is that the penalty for this crime too is usually deportation (law 7 at the end, here). Title 12 is on the Julian law concerning the food supply. The reason for the order is that this crime is lighter, namely the defrauding of the grain supply, and that it likewise comes from the Julian law. For lighter matters are set out first. Title 13 is on the Julian law concerning embezzlement. The reason is that this crime too is among the lighter ones, that is, those that do not involve bloodshed, as the two earlier ones, extortion and the defrauding of the grain supply, do not.

units.la: Cur autem inter hæc tria repetundarum primò & peculatus ultimò ponatur, in medio annonæ fraudatæ ratio videtur esse, quia repetundarum committitur à publicis personis hoc est magistratib, iudicibus, eorumq; Comitibus (Consiliarijs & Assessorib.) cum peculatus à privatis sæpè committatur. Deinde quia crimen repetundarum est sanguinis l. g. 7. repetundarum. Cum peculatus non sit, sed tantum deportatio l. 3. ad leg. Iul. pecul.
units.tr: Why extortion is placed first among these three, embezzlement last, and the defrauding of the grain supply in the middle, seems to be as follows. Extortion is committed by public persons, that is, magistrates, judges, and their companions (counsellors and assessors), whereas embezzlement is often committed by private persons. Further, extortion involves bloodshed (law 7, on extortion), whereas embezzlement does not, but only deportation (law 3, on the Julian law concerning embezzlement).

units.la: Cur autem ante peculatum ponatur crimen fraudatæ annonæ. ratio vide ture esse quia hoc crimen magis ad universam Rempubl. & populū pertinet, & etiam est singulorum civium, quam peculatus. quod tantum pertinet ad domum publicū ærarij ut crimen annonæ fraudatæ sit magis cōmune, ideoque priori loco positum. Sunt autem hæc crimina repetundarum, annonæ, peculatus, ut & sacrilegij & residuorū omnia furti species, sed furti publici tit. 14. est de leg. Iul. ambitus, quia & hoc est ex lege Iulia, sed levissimum, ideoque postremum.
units.tr: Why the crime of defrauding the grain supply is placed before embezzlement seems to be as follows. This crime concerns the whole commonwealth and the people more than embezzlement does, and it also concerns individual citizens, whereas embezzlement pertains only to the public treasury. Hence the crime of defrauding the grain supply is more general, and therefore placed first. All these crimes, extortion, the grain supply, and embezzlement, as well as sacrilege and the remaining kinds of theft, are forms of theft; but the public theft is title 14, on the Julian law concerning electoral bribery. This too comes from the Julian law, but it is the lightest, and therefore the last.

units.la: Cui adjungitur crime ultimum, tit. 15. de lege Fabia, de plagiariis. Ratio ordinis est, qa & hoc crimen est ex levioribus, & item species furti. Nam plagiū est liberi hominis furtum ut ita improprie loquamur. Nā furtū proprie est rerum & servorum nec vero liberorum hominum q. si surripiatur, vel supprimantur, plagium dicitur, & à furto proprie sic dicto distinguitur. l. penultima hic, & l. decima, Cod. de furtis tit 16. ad Senatusconsultum Turp. Ilav. Ratio ordinis est qa iudiciorum publicorum hic est ordo exercendorum. ut primo reus accusetur & deferatur, inde custodiatur, postea quæstio habeatur, & tandem sententia feratur, ac pœna imponatur, sed sæpè accusatori. Iam cœptum iudicium publicum deserere solet, sæpè etiam abolitione tolli, ut ad finem non perducatur.
units.tr: To this is joined the last crime, title 15, on the Fabian law concerning kidnappers. The reason for the order is that this crime too is among the lighter ones, and is likewise a kind of theft. For kidnapping is the theft of a free man, if we may speak improperly. For theft properly concerns things and slaves, not free men; if a free man is seized or concealed, it is called kidnapping, and it is distinguished from theft properly so called (law penultimate, here, and law 10, Code, on thefts). Title 16 is on the Senatus consultum Turpillianum. The reason for the order is that this is the order in which public trials are conducted: first the accused is accused and denounced, then he is held in custody, afterwards an inquiry is held, and finally sentence is pronounced and penalty imposed, though often on the accuser. Now a public trial that has begun is often abandoned, and often also annulled by abolition, so that it is not carried to its end.

units.la: Quare de desertione & abolitione hic iam agitur. priusquam reliqua ad finem pertinentia exponantur. In Cod. ordo hic fere idem est sed prius hic abolitio & postea requisitio. In Cod. contra prius de requirendis reis, posterius de abolitionib agitur, quia nihil referat, uter prior loco tit. ponatur; de a' abolitionibus, ut hic, an de requirendis reis, ut in Cod propterea, quod defertio & abolitio interdum fit ante requisitionem, interdum post.
units.tr: Therefore desertion and abolition are discussed here, before the remaining matters pertaining to the end of the trial are set out. In the Code the order here is nearly the same, but here abolition comes first and the requisition afterwards. In the Code, on the contrary, the demanding of the accused is treated first and abolitions afterwards. It makes no difference which comes first in the title, whether on abolitions, as here, or on the demanding of the accused, as in the Code, because desertion and abolition sometimes occur before the requisition and sometimes after.

units.la: Et hæc est ratio ad hunc titulum ad Senatusconsultum Turpil. & ad 17. de requirendis reis, 18 est, de quæstionib. quia nisi abolitio, & desertio intervenit, procedi tur ad quæstionem. Cui tit. 19. de pœnis adjungitur, quia post quæstionem ad sententiam & executionem sive pœnam delcēditur. Cui adjungitur titulus 20. de bon. d. vnnar. quia hic titulus speciem pœnæ continet, nempe publicationé bonorum, ideoque posterior est titulo de pœnis, ut generali, titulus 21 de bon. eorum, qui ante sentent. &. quia & hic titulus ad eandem speciem poenae pertinet. Sed agit de ijs casibus, quib interdum cessat hęc poena confiscationis, ut si reus moriatur ante sententiam titulus 22. de interdict. & relegat. quia & hoc titulo species quaedam poenarum continentur, nempe in terdictio, relegatio, & deportatio, quae tamen sunt leviores poenae, quam publicatio, ideoque posteriores, 23. de iure, pass. Optimo ordine prioriadjūctus, & fere ultimus a relegatiaut deportati interdum restituuntur a Principe, idē ordo fere in Cod. libri noni. Cuius ultim tit. est iste, de sententiis, passis, ut & ratio ibi exposita. Huic autem adjungitur hic tit. 24. de cadaver. b. punitorum, tum quia hoc in criminibus & judiciis est ultimum, tum quia ad mortem & cadavera pertinent, ut merito hic titulus ultimus locum teneat.
units.tr: This is the reason for this title, on the Senatus consultum Turpillianum, and for title 17, on the requisition of the accused. Title 18 is on the questions (examinations under torture), because unless abolition or desertion intervenes, the matter proceeds to questioning. To this is joined title 19, on penalties, because after the questioning the matter proceeds to sentence and execution or penalty. To this is joined title 20, on the goods of the condemned, because this title concerns a kind of penalty, namely the confiscation of goods, and it is therefore later than the title on penalties, as the general one. Title 21, on the goods of those who died before sentence, is also related, because this title too pertains to the same kind of penalty. But it deals with those cases in which this penalty of confiscation sometimes ceases, as when the accused dies before sentence. Title 22, on interdiction and relegation, is because this title too contains certain kinds of penalties, namely interdiction, relegation and deportation, which are nevertheless lighter penalties than confiscation, and so come later. Title 23, on the law of the condemned, is joined to the preceding in the best order, and is nearly last. The relegated or deported are sometimes restored by the Prince; the same order is nearly followed in the Code, book nine, whose last title is this one, on sentences passed, and the reason is set out there. To this is joined this title 24, on the bodies of the punished, both because this is the last thing in crimes and trials, and because it pertains to death and corpses, so that this title rightly holds the last place.

units.la: XLIX. LIBER.
units.tr: Book 49

units.la: Liber 49 item est trimembris. Nempe de appellationibus & de jure fisci, & de re militari. Ratio, quia appellationū usus est in omnib. judicijs, tam publicis, quam privatis ideoq; & libro quinto sententiarum Pauli ultimo loco agitur de appellationibus. Est enim appellatio ultimum adjutorium litigantium. Sed in Cod. alius est ordo ubi statim appellationes adjunguntur tit. de sententia longe ante judicia publica. Ratio Codicis est, quia appellationes plerumq; tantum in civilibus & privatis judicijs sunt receptae, raro in publicis. Continet autem hic liber 49 octodecim titulos quorū primus, de appellationibus, quia est generalis, quo ad appellationes, 2. a quibus appell. non lic. 3. quia a quo appelletur, quid duo tit ad personas judicum pertinent & tit. 2, quidem, ad judicem a quo, ut vulgo loquuntur, 3. ad judicem, ad quē scilicet appelletur, aut non appelletur. Ratio ordinis est quia semper de personis primū agitur, & judex a quo, prior est judice ad quem 4 quando appellandum sit 5. de appellat. recip. Ratio ordinis est, quia primo de persona judicis constare debet, deinde de tempore, quod est hodie decem diebus ex Novel. 11 five primum de ipsius appellantium officio deinde de officio judicum appellatorum sive ad quos appellatum est: Priores enim tituli sunt de officio appellantium, hic est de judicum officio, qui recipiunt appellationem vel non eodem quo que pertinet titulus 6. de libellis dimissorijs, &c. Nam & hic ad officium judicum pertinet: post appellationem enim interpositam quod est officium appellantium, & receptam, quod est officium judicum sive etiam ante receptam a judice ad quem, dantur Apostoli, hoc est litterae vel libelli dimissorij, quos judex a quo dat appellanti ad judicem ad quem, ideoque hic tit recte priori adjungitur. titul. 7. est, vel al innovari appellatione interposita. Ratio ordinis est, quia & hic titulus ad judicum officium pertinet, & plerumq; post receptā appellationem aut saltem introductam, sive recepta sit sive non, locum habet. Has innovationes vulgo vocant attentata octavus est, quae sententia sine appellatione rescind. Ratio ordinis videtur, quia hactenus dictum est de causis, in quibus locum habet appellatio, nunc de iis, in quibus locum non habet, quem statim sequitur tit.l.9. an per alium causa appellat. red li poss. Ratio ordinis haec est, quia adhuc dictum est de initio appellationu, hoc est, quomodo & quando, & apud quem sint interponendae & apud quē sint introducendae, ac rejiciendę: Breviter primum de appellatione institueda, proximum nunc est, ut de persequenda & exercenda agatur, ubi primum de personis quaeritur, an scilicet per Procuratorem exerceri possit appellatio, eoq; pertinet tit. nonus. Cui adjungitur tit.10.situtor vel curator magist. &c. Ratio ordinis, quia modo dictum est de causis appellationis reddendis per Procuratorem: nunc de speciali causa tutoris aut curatoris adjungitur. Suntenim variae appellationis causae, quaetamen ad duas praecipuas species revocantur, civiles & criminales, de quibus generibus agitur tit. 9. an per Procuratorem propon.poss. Hoc autem tit. 10. speciális causa civilis, nempe creatio tutoris aut curatoris Reip. continetur: ideoq; hic tit. est posterior, praesertim, quia hae personae Procurator, tutor, & curator comparari solent. tit. 11. est cu qui appellav. in provinc. &c. Ratio videtur, quia & hic tit. agit de defensione per alium. Nam tit. 9. est de ipsa causa appellationis per alium agenda. hic tit. non est de causa appellationis, sed de aliis causis appellatis, ipso scilicet causam appellationis suae agente, & persequente in alia quadam provincia ut interea domi non veniat in damnum aut periculum propter alias causas, ut est, apud eum, a quo appelletur, &c.
units.tr: Book 49 likewise has three parts: on appeals, on the rights of the fisc, and on military affairs. The reason is that the use of appeals extends to all judicial proceedings, public as well as private. For this reason, in the fifth book of the Sentences of Paul, appeals are treated last, since an appeal is the final aid of litigants. In the Code, however, the order is different: appeals are joined at once to the title on sentences, long before the public judgments. The reason for the Code's arrangement is that appeals were generally admitted only in civil and private judgments, and rarely in public ones. This book 49 contains eighteen titles. The first, on appeals, is general as regards appeals. The second, from which appeals are not permitted, and the third, from whom an appeal is made, both concern the persons of the judges, the second relating to the judge from whom (as they commonly put it), and the third to the judge to whom, that is, to whom an appeal is or is not made. The reason for this order is that persons are always treated first, and the judge from whom the appeal is made comes before the judge to whom it is made. The fourth, when appeal must be made, and the fifth, on receiving appeals, follow. The reason for this order is that first the identity of the judge must be settled, then the time, which by Novel 11 is now ten days; or, first the duty of the appellants themselves, then the duty of the judges to whom the appeal is made. The earlier titles concern the duty of the appellants; this one concerns the duty of the judges who receive the appeal or do not. The sixth title, on dismissory letters, belongs here too, since it also concerns the duty of judges. For after an appeal has been lodged (which is the duty of the appellant) and received (which is the duty of the judge), or even before it has been received by the judge to whom it is made, the apostoli are given, that is, the letters or dismissory libels which the judge from whom the appeal comes gives the appellant for the judge to whom it is made. So this title is rightly joined to the preceding one. The seventh title is or on innovations made after an appeal has been lodged. The reason for this order is that this title too concerns the duty of judges, and it applies mostly after an appeal has been received, or at least begun, whether or not it has been received. These innovations are commonly called attentata. The eighth is a sentence which is rescinded without appeal. The reason for this order seems to be that up to now we have discussed the cases in which appeal lies; now we discuss those in which it does not, which is followed immediately by the ninth title, whether a case of appeal can be pursued by another. The reason for this order is that so far we have discussed the beginning of appeals, that is, how, when, and before whom they are to be lodged and introduced, and rejected. Having briefly treated the instituting of an appeal, the next step is to discuss how it is to be pursued and carried on; first the question of persons arises, namely whether an appeal can be carried on through a procurator, and to this belongs the ninth title. To it is joined the tenth, tutor or curator of the magistrate, etc. The reason for this order is that we have just spoken of pleading appeals through a procurator; now the special case of a tutor or curator is added. There are various causes of appeal, which nevertheless are reduced to two principal kinds, civil and criminal; these kinds are treated in title nine, whether an appeal can be proposed through a procurator. But this tenth title deals with a special civil cause, namely the appointment of a tutor or curator for the commonwealth; therefore this title comes later, especially since these persons, procurator, tutor and curator, are usually compared with one another. The eleventh title is whoever has appealed in a province, etc. The reason seems to be that this title too treats of defence through another. For title nine concerns the appeal itself, which is to be conducted through another; this title does not concern the cause of appeal, but other causes that are pending, when the appellant himself conducts and pursues the cause of his appeal in some other province, so that meanwhile he does not come to harm or danger at home on account of other causes, as in before him from whom appeal is made, etc.

units.la: Ratio ordinis est, quia ut tit. 11. ita hic tit. est de diversis causis cum appellationis causa contendentibus sive comparatis. Nam tit. undecimus est de causa appellationis adhuc pendentis, an & quomodo eodem tempore in aliis causis domi defendatur appellans, & peregrinans: hic autem tit. duodecimus est item de aliis causis eodem tempore, quo agitur causa appellationis, aut etiam in quo jam finita est agendis, ideoq; tit. hic est posterior, tum quia rem continet magis dubiam. tum quia interdictum locum habeat post finitam appellationem, cum tit. 11 magis perspicua aequitate nitatur, ut semper adhuc pendente appellatione locum habeat tit.13.Si pendente appellatio. mors interven. qui est ultimus, in tractat. appellat. quia modum continet tollendae aut finiendae appellationis: mortem scilicet appellatoris sine herede defunc̄ ti. Hunc sequitur tit.14. de jure fisci. Ratio ordinis ex Cod petenda est. Nam ibi initio libri decimi agitur de jure fisci postomnes tit. de judiciis. tam civilibus quam criminalibus. Diximus autem in Cod cum jus omne sit aut publicum aut privatum; Publicum autem constet ex his tribus potissimum, sacris, sacerdotibus & magistratibus, §. 1. Institut. de justitia & jur. l. 1 §. hujus, verfic. Publici supra de just & jur.
units.tr: The reason for this order is that, as the eleventh title, so this title too is concerned with different causes which contend along with the cause of appeal, or which are brought alongside it. For the eleventh title concerns whether and how, while the cause of appeal is still pending, the appellant is defended at home in other causes while he is abroad; this twelfth title likewise concerns other causes that are pursued at the same time as the appeal, or even after the cause of appeal has ended. Therefore this title comes later, partly because it deals with a more doubtful matter, and partly because the remedy applies after the appeal has ended, whereas the eleventh rests on a more evident equity, so that it applies even while the appeal is still pending. The thirteenth title, if, while the appeal is pending, death intervenes, comes next and is the last in the treatise on appeals, since it contains the means of removing or ending an appeal, namely the death of the appellant without heir. This is followed by the fourteenth title, on the rights of the fisc. The reason for this order is to be sought in the Code. For there, at the beginning of the tenth book, the rights of the fisc are treated after all the titles on judicial proceedings, both civil and criminal. We have said in the Code that since all law is either public or private, public law consists chiefly of these three: sacred things, priests, and magistrates (Institutes, on justice and law, §1; Digest 1.1, §hujus, Publici; and above on justice and law).

units.la: De jure quidem publico, sive potius de tribus illis juris publici partib. in C. agi libro primo. Ex reliquis autem juris publici partibus sunt jus fisci jus militare, juraciv tatum aliaq; hujusmodi. Ut igitur in C. ita & in ff. publici juris partes distinctę sunt propositae: sed multo brevius sunt propositae, imo quaedam omissæ in ff. Nam initio Codic de tribus illis partibus sacris sacerdotibus, magistratibus agitur, in ff. tantum de una, nempe tantum de magistratibus, nihil de sacris & sacerdotibus. Ratio est quia corpus juris Justinianei xijs tantum collectum est, quæ tempore Justiniani erat in usu, ita enim componi corpus mandarat Justinianus, ut usitata tantum ponerentur, non ea quæ in desuetudinem abierant, leg. 1. §. sed & si, leg. secunda. §. sed cum porro eximus. C. de vet. iure enucl.
units.tr: Concerning public law, or rather those three parts of public law, we treated in the first book of the Code. The remaining parts of public law are the rights of the fisc, military law, the rights of taxation, and things of this kind. Thus, in the Code as in the Digest, the parts of public law are set out separately, but in the Digest they are set out much more briefly, and some are indeed omitted. For at the beginning of the Code the three parts, sacred things, priests and magistrates, are treated; in the Digest only one, namely magistrates, and nothing on sacred things and priests. The reason is that the body of Justinian's law was gathered only from those things which were in use in Justinian's time; for Justinian had ordered the corpus to be compiled so that only what was in use would be included, and not what had fallen into disuse (law 1, §sed et si; law 2, §sed cum porro; Code, on the ancient law, de veteri iure enucleando).

units.la: Justiniani autem ætate in Imperio vel orbe Romano sacra & sacerdotes tantum Christiani erant in usu, aboleta jam sacris & sacerdotib profanis & Ethnicis: Non debuerunt igitur veterum prudentum Ethnicorum scripta de suis sacerdotibus & sacris in hoc corpus, neq; in Digest neq; in Cod. referri. Christianorum autem sacra & sacerdotes in Cod. referri potuerunt, in ff. non potuerunt; quia ff. sunt compositæ ex prudentum Ethnicorum scriptis & quia constitutiones ac leges de religione Christiana sunt posteriores scriptis prudentum & in Cod. relatæ nimirum latæ ab Imperatoribus posterioribus & Christianis. Cur autem reliquæ partes juris publici, ut de jure fisci, tributi, re militari, &c. breviter in ff. copiose in Cod. exponuntur, ratio est, quia non tantum in sacris: ut modo dictum, sed etiam in his publicis rebus magna fuerit facta mutatio post tempora veterum prudentum, ex quibus ff. constant. Mutationis hujus auctor, tam in sacris, quam in publicis primus perhibetur Imperator Constantinus, eumque subsequentes alij, & ipse in primis Justinianus. Quare in Digest non multa potuere poni de his reliquis partibus, utpote jam non paucis eorum abrogatis, aut mutatis. Est & altera ratio, quia bis eadem poni voluit Imper. l. 1. C. de jur. vet. enucl.
units.tr: In Justinian's age, in the empire or the Roman world, only Christian sacred things and priests were in use, the profane and pagan sacred things and priests having now been abolished. Therefore the writings of the ancient pagan jurists concerning their own priests and sacred rites ought not to have been included in this corpus, neither in the Digest nor in the Code. Christian sacred things and priests could be referred to in the Code, but could not be in the Digest, because the Digest was composed from the writings of the pagan jurists, and because the constitutions and laws concerning the Christian religion are later than the writings of the jurists and are in the Code, namely enacted by later emperors who were Christians. As to why the remaining parts of public law, such as the rights of the fisc, of taxation, military affairs, and so on, are set out briefly in the Digest and at length in the Code, the reason is that a great change was made, not only in sacred things, as just said, but also in these public matters, after the time of the ancient jurists from whose writings the Digest is made up. The author of this change, both in sacred and in public matters, is said to have been the Emperor Constantine, and the subsequent emperors after him, and above all Justinian himself. Therefore not many of these remaining parts could be included in the Digest, since many of them had already been abrogated or changed. There is also a second reason: the emperor wished the same matters not to be set out twice (law 1, Code, on the ancient law, de veteri iure enucleando).

units.la: Cum igitur plene & diligenter de his reliquis partibus in Cod agatur tribus hujus libris posterioris, merito ea in Digest. sunt pauciora & breviora. Tres autem partes hujus juris publici, hic in fine ff. exponuntur, jus fisci, jus militare, jus municipale, ut dictum.
units.tr: Since, then, these remaining parts are treated fully and diligently in the three last books of the Code, it is right that they are fewer and briefer in the Digest. The three parts of this public law are set out here at the end of the Digest: the law of the fisc, military law, and municipal law, as has been said.

units.la: Et de jure fisci primum agitur, quia est Imperatoribus proprium. Et hæc est ratio ordinis, primum ad hunc titulum 14. de iure fisci, deinde ad totum hunc tractatum de jure militari, & titul. seqq. sed in Paulo, lib. 5 sent. tit. de jure fisci, non post crimina, ut hic & in Cod. sed ante crimina & appellationes exponitur.
units.tr: And the law of the fisc is treated first, because it is peculiar to the emperors. This is also the reason for the order: first comes this title 14, de iure fisci, then the whole of this treatise on military law and the following titles. But in Paulus, lib. 5 sent. tit. de jure fisci, it is set out not after the crimes, as here and in the Code, but before the crimes and appeals.

units.la: Ratio Pauli videtur esse, quia ex criminibus & condemnationibus fiscus maxime solet locupletari, propter bona damnatorum fisco applicanda. Sed Tribunianus Cod. Theodof. secutus, tam in Cod. quam in ff. maluit de jure fisci, ut de parte publici juris conjunctim agere; cum reliquis ejusdem juris partibus. Hunc autem titulum sequitur titulus de captiv. & postlimin. revers. Ratio ordinis videtur, quia & captivorum bona ad fiscum pertinent leg. 31. Divus. de iure fisci. Sed in Cod. hic titulus longe anteponitur, nempe ante publica jndicia,in fine libri.8.Ratio ibi dicta,titulus 1c. est de remiss. Rectè autem transitio sità titulo de captiv ad titulum de re mil. quia & ille ti. 15. ad rem militarem & bella referri potest: sed proponitur propter causam expositam.Cur autem jus fisci præferatur juri militari,jam supra dictû. Est & hæc ratio quia urbana præferuntur militaribus & jus fisci non tàm in militibus locum habet, quàm in paganis..17. est de castr. pecul. qui est specialis, ad rem tamen militarem quoque pertinens, sed 16. est generalis ideoque prior titul. 18. est de veteran. Ratio ordinis est perspicua,quia militia finita fiunt veterani: ideóque hic titulus est ultimus in hoc articulo de re militari.
units.tr: The reason for Paulus's order seems to be that the fisc is chiefly enriched by crimes and condemnations, because the goods of the condemned are to be applied to the fisc. But Tribonian, following the Theodosian Code, preferred in both the Code and the Digest to treat the law of the fisc together with the other parts of this public law. The title de captiv. & postlimin. revers. follows this title. The reason for this order seems to be that the goods of captives also belong to the fisc (leg. 31. Divus. de iure fisci). But in the Code this title is placed much earlier, namely before the public judgments, at the end of book 8. The reason given there, title 1c, is de remiss. The transition from the title on captives to the title on military affairs is rightly made, since that title 15 can also be referred to military affairs and wars; but it is put here on account of the stated cause. Why the law of the fisc is placed before military law has already been said above. There is also this reason: urban matters take precedence over military ones, and the law of the fisc applies not so much to soldiers as to civilians. .17. est de castr. pecul., which is special, though it also pertains to military affairs, but 16 is general, and therefore prior; titul. 18. est de veteran. The reason for the order is plain: when service is finished, men become veterans; therefore this title is the last in this section on military affairs.

units.la: L. & ULT. LIBER.
units.tr: Book 50, the last book

units.la: IBer 50. est bimembris partim de jure municipali, partim communem omnium priorum librorum & titulorum velut summam & supplementum rerum & verborum continens. Ratio ordinis de jure municipali, hoc est, cur ex his tribus partibus juris publici, nempe jure fisci, jure militari ac jure municipali cur inquam de hoc argumento ultimo loco agatur, hæc est quia municipia & civitates privatorum loco habentur. l. bona. 18. de verb. sig. Continet autem hic liber 17. titulos quorum primus est ad municipalem & de incol. quia hic titulus est generalis quem sequitur tit. 2. de decurionib. &c. Ratio ordinis est cur primo proximum locum obtineat, quia h. ti. inter speciales tit. de jure municipali est de senatu municipali, qui proprie curia dicitur, nt senatores isti dicuntur decuriones sive curiales. Ut igitur supra lib. 1. cum de magistratibus Populi Romani agitur locum primum obtinet ti 9. de senatoribus qui est de veto senatu Populi Romani: ita & hic primum post generalem titulum locum obtinet h. tit. de senatoribus sive curia municipiorum, sive civitatum tit. 3. est de albo scribendo, qui est velut particula prioris. Album enim hic est tabula in quam referuntur senatores. titul. 4. de mun. & honor. Ratio ordinis est quia ut primum locum tenet curia, ita proximum magistratus, & curationes, sive munera & honores municipales. Eodem pertinet tit. 5. de vacat. & excusat. mun. Ratio ordinis quia excusatio posterior est curatione, ut & supra de excusat. Huc quoque pertinet titulus 6 de iure immunitatis. Nam & hæc excusationis causa est, sed specialis nepe immunitas quæ speciali lege datur; ideoque hic titulus est potior, cum prior titulus sit generalis. Hunc sequitur titulus 7. de legationibus. Ratio est, quia & hic titulus est specialis: quia adhuc dictum est de muneribus & honoribus municipalibus: nunc separatim agitur de munere legationis municipalis. Non enim hic proprie agitur de legatis publicis populi Romani, sed tantum de legatis municipiorum, sive civitatum. Quem sequitur titul 8. de admin. istrat. rerum ad civit. pertin. Ratio ordinis est, quia & hic titulus est specialis, agens de officio administratoris, sive curatoris civitatis: sed hoc officium curatoris quia vilius est officio legationis recte ponitur posteriori titul. titulus 9. est de decret. ab ord. fac. Ratio ordinis, quia hactenus dictum est de ipso ordine, hoc est curia & honoribus atque muneribus municipalibus: recte nunc adjungitur de ordinis sive curiae decretis. Ut enim prius de judice, posterius de sententia agitur, ita & prius de senatu, posterius de curiae & senatus decretis agi debet. Huic sequitur titulus 10. de oper. public. Ratio ordinis, quia prius de personis, ut curialibus & magistratibus, eorumque decretis; posterius de rebus sive operibus civitatum publicis agi debuit. Personae enim rebus praeferuntur.
units.tr: The Liber 50 has two parts: partly on municipal law, and partly containing the general matter common to all the preceding books and titles, as a summary and supplement of the things and words treated there. The reason for the order, that is, why this subject of municipal law is treated last of the three parts of public law (namely the law of the fisc, military law and municipal law), is this: municipalities and cities are regarded as the equivalent of private persons. l. bona. 18. de verb. sig. This book contains seventeen titles, of which the first is On the municipal law and on residents, because this title is general and is followed by title 2, On the decurions, and so on. The reason it holds the first place among the special titles is that, under this heading, on the municipal senate (properly called the curia, whose members are called decurions or curials), is the first. Just as in book 1, when the magistrates of the Roman People are discussed, title 9, On senators, which concerns the senate of the Roman People, takes first place, so here too, after the general title, the present title, On senators, or on the curia of municipalities or cities, takes first place. Title 3, On enrolling on the list, which is a sort of appendix to the preceding, follows. For the album here is the tablet on which the senators are entered. Title 4, On public burdens and honours. The reason for this order is that as the curia holds the first place, so the magistracies, offices and municipal burdens and honours hold the next. To this belongs title 5, On vacation and excuse from public burdens. The reason for the order is that excuse follows the office, as also above in On excuse. To this too belongs title 6, On the right of immunity. For this too is a cause of excuse, but a special one, namely immunity, which is granted by a special law; and so this title is more important, since the preceding title is general. It is followed by title 7, On embassies. The reason is that this title is also special: since it has been said of public burdens and honours, now the burden of a municipal embassy is treated separately. For it is not properly the public embassies of the Roman People that are treated here, but only the embassies of municipalities or cities. This is followed by title 8, On the administration of the property belonging to cities. The reason for the order is that this title too is special, dealing with the office of the administrator or curator of a city; but since this office of curator is of less dignity than the office of embassy, it is rightly placed after it. Title 9, On decrees to be made by the order. The reason for the order is that, since what has been said so far concerns the order itself, that is, the curia and its honours and municipal burdens, it is now rightly added: on the decrees of the order or curia. For as the judge is treated first and the sentence afterwards, so the senate should be treated first and the decrees of the curia and senate afterwards. There follows title 10, On public works. The reason for the order is that the persons, such as the curials and magistrates, and their decrees, should be treated first, and the public things or works of the cities afterwards. For persons take precedence over things.

units.la: Huic adjungitur titulus 11. de annon. nis. Ratio ordinis est, quia utopera sive aedificia, ita & nundinae civitates ornare & celebrare solent, sed nundinae sunt rariores ac speciali jure impetrandae ab Imper ideoque inter haec duo, opera & nundinas, civitatum ornamenta meritò de nundinis agitur posterius. Eodem pertinet titulus 12. de pollicit. sed quia hic titulus est de operre futuro, aut pecuniae ad opus danda, per pollicitationem promissa merito utfutura de re & nondum perfecta posterior est, quam vis ad opera pertineat. Cui adjungitur titulus 13. de var. & extraord. cogn. Ratio videtur esse, quiaut titulo de pollicit. agitur de pecunia in opus civitatis liberaliter promissa, ita & hoc titulo agitur de pecunia sive honorario aut mercede quorundam ut profexcorum, medicorum, ludi literarii magistrorum, licet non sint professores, ut ait l. 1. §. Iudi. h. tit. itaq; tantum occasione tituli prioris de dono aut pecunia promissa civitati adjunctus hic fuit titulo de honorariis & mercedibus professorum. Nam alioqui hic titulus non pertinet ad jus municipale sed est communis tam urbis Romanae quam civitatum sive municipiorum. Et rursus eadem occasione adjungitur titul. 14. de proxenetis, quia proxenetica sunt honoraria, sive mercedulae quae dantur proxenetis, hoc est, interpretibus & parariis: sed hoc genus est vilius, ideoq; posterius. Hos autem 3. titulos de pecunia & honorariis recte sequitur titulus 15. de censib. Nam & hic titulus est de pecunia sed necessaria, nempe vectigalis & tributi, quod civitates Reip. sive Imperio praestant: quod onus, quia grave est necessarium & non voluntarium ut prioramunera, extremo hic loco ponitur. Proximi sunt 2. tituli tit. 16. de verb. sign. & titul. 17. de reg. iur. Rationem jam supra indicavimus ad titulum de oblig. & actio. Nam corpore toto ff jam perfecto, in singulos titulos ordine distributo, adjunguntur jam duo, unus verborum, alter rerum, communes & generales velut ἀναφαλαίωσις, ut quae in singulis tituli s supra posita, partim ad verborum interpretationem partim ad rerum & juris ipsius brevem comprehensionem, & velut conjectione pertinent, in extremo opere hic ponantur, tanquam collecta ex prioribus. Nam regulae ex jure jam prius constituto colliguntur, l. 1. de reg. jur. sic & verborum interpretatio sequitur ipsam legem, cujus verba sunt interpretanda. Atque ita Ulp. in l. 27. si servum. §. cum *. supra ad leg. Aquil. Non est novum inquit ut lex specialiter quibusdam enumeratis, generale subjiciat verbum, quo specialia comprehendantur: ut hic post speciales titulos, hi duo generales hic subjiciuntur & verborum quidem prior, iuris & rei posterior: quia prior est semper verborum interpretatio, utpote per quam ad sententiam & rerum cognitionem perveniatur. Haec de ff. libris & titulis. Reliquum est, ut de legum ordine dicamus.
units.tr: To this is joined title 11, On the grain supply. The reason for the order is that, just as cities are accustomed to adorn and celebrate their works or buildings, so also they hold markets; but markets are rarer and must be obtained by special right from the Emperor; therefore, between these two, works and markets, which are the ornaments of cities, it is rightly treated of markets afterwards. To this belongs title 12, On promises; but since this title concerns future work, or money promised by pledge to be given for work, and not yet completed, it is rightly placed after the matter of the future; although it pertains to works. To it is joined title 13, On various and extraordinary cognitions. The reason seems to be that, just as the title on promises treats of money freely promised for the work of a city, so this title treats of money, whether honorarium or fee, paid to certain persons, such as professors, physicians and schoolmasters, although they are not professors, as l. 1. §. Iudi. h. tit. says; and so it was joined to the preceding title, on a gift or money promised to a city, only on the occasion of it, as a title on honoraria and fees of professors. For otherwise this title does not belong to municipal law, but is common to the city of Rome as well as to the cities or municipalities. And again, on the same occasion, title 14, On brokers, is added, because the brokers' fees are honoraria, or small fees paid to brokers, that is, to interpreters and go-betweens; but this kind is of less dignity and therefore comes later. Rightly these three titles on money and honoraria are followed by title 15, On the census. For this title too concerns money, but necessary money, namely the tax and tribute which the cities pay to the Commonwealth or Empire; and because this burden, being grievous, necessary and not voluntary, unlike the earlier burdens, is placed in this last position. Nearest are the two titles, title 16, On the meaning of words, and title 17, On the rules of law. We have already indicated the reason for this at the title On obligations and actions. For when the whole of the Digest has been completed and distributed in order into individual titles, two more are added, one of words and the other of things, common and general, as a [ἀνακεφαλαίωσις] recapitulation; so that matters that were set out in the individual titles, partly pertaining to the interpretation of words, partly to the brief comprehension of things and of the law itself, and as it were to a collection, are placed here at the end of the work, as gathered from what precedes. For rules are gathered from law already established beforehand, l. 1. de reg. jur.; and so the interpretation of words follows the law itself, whose words are to be interpreted. And thus Ulpian in l. 27, si servum, §. cum *, above ad legem Aquiliam: "It is not new," he says, "that a law, after enumerating certain things specifically, subjoins a general word by which the specific things are comprehended." So here, after the special titles, these two general ones are subjoined: the first on words, the second on law and things; because the interpretation of words always comes first, since through it one arrives at the meaning and knowledge of things. So much on the books and titles of the Digest. It remains that we speak of the order of the laws.

units.la: Ordo legum in Pandectis.
units.tr: The order of the laws in the Pandects.

units.la: MULTI ex Interpretibus iuris, tum veteribus, tum recentioribus reprehendunt Tribun. quod is sine ordine iuris libros congesserit, & tum in titulorum & librorum, tum & maxime in legum ordine multa desiderant. Sed quem ordinem in digerendis libris & titulis servarit Tribun. hactenus demonstravimus. Nunc de singulis quoque legibus sub tit positis videamus. Est enim & hic certus, isque perpetuus ordo a Tribun. observatus, quamvis is vulgo non ita sit notus, neque esse potuit ante ff. Florentinam editionem, ante quam & libri & numerus librorum, ex quibus fragmenta, quae in ff. relata sunt, desumsit Tribunianus desiderabantur.
units.tr: MANY interpreters of the law, both older and more recent, criticise Tribonian because he arranged the books of law without order, and they find much to miss both in the order of the titles and books and, above all, in the order of the laws. But the order Tribonian observed in arranging the books and titles we have demonstrated so far. Now let us see how he ordered the individual laws placed under each title. For there is also a definite and consistent order observed by Tribonian here, although it is not commonly so well known, and indeed it could not have been known before the Florentine edition of the Digest, before which both the books and the number of books from which Tribonian drew the fragments cited in the Digest were lacking.

units.la: Fatendum autem in principio rei quidem ordinem pene nullum esse, nisi in prioribus aliquibus leg. titulorum. Hoc tamen operam dedit Tribunianus, ut si definitiones & divisiones reperit in libris Jurisconsultorum quibusvis, aut alia ad definitionem & divisiones pertinentia, illa statim in priores leg. titul. coniiceret, ut videre est statim. titu. de leg. l. 1. & 2. l. 1. de stat. homin. leg. 1. 2. & 3. de manumiss. leg. 1. & 2. de transact. leg. 1. & 2. de integr. restit. leg. 1. & 2. & 3. quod metus causa. leg. 1. de dolo leg. 1. de unfr. leg. 1. de tutel. leg. 1. qui test. fac. poss. leg. 1. de vulgar. & pupill. leg. de donat. leg. 1. de adquirend. rer. dom. leg. de obligat. & action. & pallim toto, quae plerraque leges sunt vel ex libris quaestionum, vel aureorum, vel disputationum vel pandectarum. & similibus non veto ad Sabinum, aut ad Edictum, quae alias priores esse solent. Alium rerum ordinem in ipsis legibus vix reperiri. Certum est enim multoties in titulis de una & eadem re particulatim tractari interiectis interdum aliquot legibus quae tamen prioribus non cohaerent.
units.tr: It must be admitted that at the beginning of a matter there is almost no order, except in some of the first laws of the titles. Nevertheless Tribonian took care that, if he found definitions and divisions in the books of any of the jurists, or other material pertaining to definitions and divisions, he would at once place them at the head of the titles' laws, as can be seen at once: title De legibus, laws 1 and 2; law 1 De statu hominum; laws 1, 2 and 3 De manumissis; laws 1 and 2 De transactionibus; laws 1 and 2 De integrae restitutione; laws 1, 2 and 3 Quod metus causa; law 1 De dolo; law 1 De fructibus; law 1 Qui testamenta facere possunt; law 1 De vulgari et pupillari; law De donationibus; law 1 De adquirendo rerum dominio; law De obligationibus et actionibus, and throughout almost everywhere, which laws are mostly taken from the books of Questions, of the Golden Books, of Disputations, of the Pandects and the like, not from the commentaries on Sabinus or on the Edict, which are usually found earlier. Another order of matters can scarcely be found in the laws themselves.
