For it is certain that in many titles a single matter is treated piecemeal, with some laws sometimes interposed which nonetheless do not cohere with the earlier ones.

units.la: Ergo alium quendam ordinem servatum esse a Tribun. necesse est, quod iam explicabimus. Sunt ergo duo quodammodo ordines in libris ff. qui alternatim & permixtim interdum quasi confunduntur. Nam post leges illas, quae definitiones ac divisiones, ut dixi, continent, ac priores plerumque esse solent, Tribunianus posuit leges ad Sabinum scriptas. Notum est enim Sabinum Masurium tanti a Jurisconsultis nostris factum esse, ut ad leges ipsius commentaria scripserint, ut Ulp. & Paulus, &c. Haec igitur leges plerasque que sunt priores, postillas proximè ponuntur leges ad Edictum, seu desumptæ ex legibus Jurisconsultorum ad Edictum. Interdum tamen hi duo ordines ita inter se permiscentur, ut aliquæ leges ad Edictum, aliquæ ad Sabinum mox rursus aliquæ ad Edictum, & rursus ad Sabinum collocentur, eo respectu, ut semper generaliores faciliores leges ab initio tituli collocarentur.
units.tr: Therefore it is necessary that Tribonian observed some other order, which we shall now explain. There are thus two orders, in a sense, in the books of the Digest, which alternate and are sometimes almost confused with each other. For after those laws which contain definitions and divisions, as I have said, and which are usually placed first, Tribonian put the laws written on Sabinus. For it is well known that Sabinus Masurius was so highly regarded by our jurists that they wrote commentaries on his laws, as Ulpian and Paul did, and so on. So these laws, which are mostly the earlier ones, are placed next, followed by the laws on the Edict, or taken from the jurists' laws on the Edict. Sometimes, however, these two orders are so intermixed that some laws on the Edict, then some on Sabinus, then again some on the Edict, and again on Sabinus, are placed in sequence, with the principle that the more general and easier laws were always placed at the beginning of a title.

units.la: Interdum quoq; initium fit statim ab Edicto prætoris, & legibus ad Edictum scriptis, maximè in iis juris capitibus, quæ ex prætoris jurisdictione vires capiunt, ut videre estin titul. de his qui not. infam. titul. quod metus causa & tit. de dolo & passim.
units.tr: Sometimes too the beginning is made at once from the praetor's Edict and from laws written on the Edict, especially in those chapters of law which draw their force from the praetor's jurisdiction, as can be seen in the title De his qui notantur infamia, the title Quod metus causa, the title De dolo, and elsewhere.

units.la: In his autem ipsis libris hic ordo est observatus ut leges sint collocatæ secundum ordinem librorum ad Edictum. Utfi sit aliqua lex Ulpia. ad Edictum desumpta ex libro 10 non erit post illam legem in eodem titulo alia desumpta ex priori aliquo veluti octavo, aut alio aliquo. Idem quoque ordo est observatus in libris ad Sabinum, ut videre est in titulis potissimum longioribus. (Nam breves tituli quia non continent multas leges, quamvis in earum compositione eandem rationem servaverit Tribun. tamen id non ita perspicuè apparet ut in longioribus) quales sunt de verb. obl. g. de adquir. h. r. d. in tribus libris de lega. de hered. instit. &c. & omnium pulcherrimè in libris de verb. sig. & de reg. juris. Nam in hoc postremo titulo 1. est extraordinaria, continet enim definitionem regulæ. Secunda statim cum multis seq usque ad leg. 41. omnes sunt ad Sabinum, & sequuntur deinde libri ad Edictum secundum ordinem ut diximus librorum ad Edictum scriptorum. Post has igitur leges sequuntur, deinde plerumque in fine titulorum, legum ex libris Digestorum, regularum, disputationum quæstionum, ex libris ad Plautium, ad Vitellium, ex libris Differentiarum, ad Quintum Mucium, adl. Juliam & Pap. variar. lectionum, Epistolarum &c in quibus rursus idem ordo librorum observatur, ut apparet ex d. tit. de verb. sign. & de reg. jur. & aliis longioribus.
units.tr: In these same books this order has been observed: the laws are arranged according to the order of the books on the Edict. So if there is a law of Ulpian on the Edict taken from book 10, there will not follow in the same title another law taken from an earlier book, say the eighth or some other. The same order has also been observed in the books on Sabinus, as can be seen especially in the longer titles. (For short titles, since they do not contain many laws, although Tribonian observed the same method in composing them, this is not so clearly apparent as in the longer ones.) Such are De verborum obligationibus, De adquirendo rerum dominio, De legatis, De heredibus instituendis, Institutes, etc., and most beautifully of all in the books De verborum significatione and De regulis iuris. For in this last title law 1 is extraordinary, since it contains a definition of the rule. The second law, and many following it up to law 41, are all on Sabinus, and then follow the books on the Edict in the order of the books written on the Edict, as we have said. After these laws follow, then, usually at the end of the titles, laws from the books of the Digests, of Rules, of Disputations, of Questions, from the books on Plautius, on Vitellius, from the books of Differences, on Quintus Mucius, on the Julian law and on Papinian, Miscellaneous Readings, Letters, etc., in which again the same order of books is observed, as appears from the said title De verborum significatione et de regulis iuris and other longer ones.

units.la: Hujus autem ordinis duæ sunt exceptiones, hoc est, duplici de causa ab eo Tribun interdum recedere solet. I. Jam supra indicata est, quod scilicet in principio tituli semper collocari soleant leges generalia quædam continentes ut definitiones, & divisiones, II. Si quæ sit sententia, quæ vel usu non sit recepta, & juri Justiniano minus accommodata & quomodocunque in eaaliquid à Tribun. fuerit desideratum, subjecit: & interdum interjecit Tribunus particulam ex alio Jurisconsulto, ubicunque illam invenit, quæ vel corrigat, vel limitet, vel producat & porrigat legem etiam ad alios casus vel etiam ei aliquid addat, vel interdum explicet &c. & tales passim videre est in libris ff. sunt enim tales leges interjectæ, plerumque breves & interdum sumptæ ex posterioribus libris, vel ad Edictum vel ad Sabinum. vel similibus eiusdem si jam ante ex prioribus aliæ fuerint prolatæ, contra ordinem aliàs observatum. Exemplum est in l. 10. ff. de dolo. quæ est Pauli cum prior & posterior sit Ulp. l. 10. de minor. l. 5. de alienat. iud. mut. caus. l. 34. de R. vind. l. 14. de usf. fr. l. 26. de procurat. & passim in jure. Et ex hac ordinis observatione interdum judicare possumus an aliqua lex sit alicujus Jurisconsulti necne. Interdum enim cum tali aliqua particula interjecta posterior lex sine interjectione novi nominis, cohæret, ut etiam ejus Jurisconsulti, cujus est illa particula, perperam existimetur: Cujus rei exempla adferri possent ex ff. Sed de ea re alias.
units.tr: There are two exceptions to this order; that is, for a twofold reason Tribonian sometimes departs from it. First, as has already been indicated above, laws containing certain general matters, such as definitions and divisions, are always wont to be placed at the beginning of a title. Second, if there was some opinion which had not been received in practice and was less suited to the law of Justinian, and in which Tribonian had found something lacking in any way, he added it; and sometimes he interposed a particle from another jurist, wherever he found it, which either corrects, limits, or extends the law even to other cases, or adds something to it, or sometimes explains it, and such are found everywhere in the books of the Digest. For such laws are interposed, usually short, and sometimes taken from later books, either on the Edict or on Sabinus, or similar works, if others from earlier books have already been brought forward, contrary to the order otherwise observed. An example is in law 10, De dolo, which is Paul's, though the prior and later law is Ulpian's; law 10 De minoribus; law 5 De alienatione iudicii mutandi causa; law 34 De rei vindicatione; law 14 De usufructu; law 26 De procuratoribus, and throughout the law. And from this observation of order we can sometimes judge whether a law belongs to a given jurist or not. For sometimes, when such a particle has been interposed, the later law coheres with it without any new name being inserted, so that it is mistakenly thought to belong to that jurist whose particle it is. Examples of this could be brought from the Digest, but of that matter elsewhere.

units.la: FINIS.
units.tr: END.
